Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Majjhimanikāye

The Middle Length Discourses

Majjhimapaṇṇāsa-aṭṭhakathā

Commentary on The Middle Fifty

1. Gahapativaggo

1. The Householder Chapter

1. Kandarakasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Kandaraka Sutta

1. Evaṃ [V 3.0001][P 3.0001][M 3.0001] me sutanti kandarakasuttaṃ. Tattha campāyanti evaṃnāmake nagare. Tassa hi nagarassa ārāmapokkharaṇīādīsu tesu tesu ṭhānesu campakarukkhāva ussannā ahesuṃ, tasmā campāti saṅkhamagamāsi. Gaggarāya pokkharaṇiyā tīreti tassa campānagarassa avidūre gaggarāya nāma rājamahesiyā khaṇitattā gaggarāti laddhavohārā pokkharaṇī atthi. Tassā tīre samantato nīlādipañcavaṇṇakusumapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ mahantaṃ campakavanaṃ. Tasmiṃ bhagavā kusumagandhasugandhe campakavane viharati. Taṃ sandhāya “gaggarāya pokkharaṇiyā tīre”ti vuttaṃ. Mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhinti adassitaparicchedena mahantena bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ. Pessoti tassa nāmaṃ. Hatthārohaputtoti hatthācariyassa putto. Kandarako [P 3.0002] ca paribbājakoti kandarakoti evaṃnāmo [V 3.0002] channaparibbājako. Abhivādetvāti chabbaṇṇānaṃ ghanabuddharasmīnaṃ antaraṃ pavisitvā pasannalākhārase nimujjamāno viya, siṅgīsuvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ dussavaraṃ pasāretvā sasīsaṃ pārupamāno viya, vaṇṇagandhasampannacampakapupphāni sirasā sampaṭicchanto viya, sinerupādaṃ upagacchanto puṇṇacando viya bhagavato cakkalakkhaṇapaṭimaṇḍite alattakavaṇṇaphullapadumasassirike pāde vanditvāti attho. Ekamantaṃ nisīdīti chanisajjadosavirahite ekasmiṃ okāse nisīdi.

1. Thus have I heard—this is the Kandaraka Sutta. Therein, 'at Campā' refers to a city of that name. For in that city, in various places such as parks and ponds, campaka trees were abundant; therefore, it came to be called Campā. 'On the bank of the Gaggarā pond' means that not far from the city of Campā, there is a pond called Gaggarā, so named because it was dug by a queen consort named Gaggarā. On its bank, all around, is a great campaka grove adorned with flowers of five colors, including blue. The Blessed One was dwelling in that campaka grove, fragrant with the scent of flowers. It is with reference to this that it was said, 'on the bank of the Gaggarā pond.' 'With a large company of monks' means with a great company of monks of an unspecified number. 'Pessa' is his name. 'Son of an elephant trainer' means the son of an elephant master. 'And the wanderer Kandaraka' means a wanderer named Kandaraka, who was a wanderer who wears clothes. 'Having paid homage' means: having venerated the Blessed One's feet—which were adorned with the wheel-markings and possessed the splendor of a blooming lotus the color of lac-dye—as if, having entered into the midst of the dense, six-colored Buddha-rays, one were sinking into clear lac-juice; as if, having spread out a superior cloth the color of pure gold, one were covering oneself including the head; as if receiving with one's head campaka flowers endowed with color and fragrance; like the full moon approaching the foot of Sineru. This is the meaning. 'He sat down at one side' means he sat in a suitable place, free from the six faults of sitting.

Tuṇhībhū [M 3.0002] taṃ tuṇhībhūtanti yato yato anuviloketi, tato tato tuṇhībhūtamevāti attho. Tattha hi ekabhikkhussāpi hatthakukkuccaṃ vā pādakukkuccaṃ vā natthi, sabbe bhagavato ceva gāravena attano ca sikkhitasikkhatāya aññamaññaṃ vigatasallāpā antamaso ukkāsitasaddampi akarontā sunikhātaindakhīlā viya nivātaṭṭhāne sannisinnaṃ mahāsamuddaudakaṃ viya kāyenapi niccalā manasāpi avikkhittā rattavalāhakā viya sinerukūṭaṃ bhagavantaṃ parivāretvā nisīdiṃsu. Paribbājakassa evaṃ sannisinnaṃ parisaṃ disvā mahantaṃ pītisomanassaṃ uppajji. Uppannaṃ pana antohadayasmiṃyeva sannidahituṃ asakkonto piyasamudāhāraṃ samuṭṭhāpesi. Tasmā acchariyaṃ bhotiādimāha.

The phrase 'silent, silent' means that from whatever direction one looked, they were simply silent. This is the meaning. For among them, not even a single monk had any restlessness of hand or restlessness of foot. All of them, both out of reverence for the Blessed One and because of their own trained discipline, were without conversation with one another. Not making even the sound of a cough, at the very least, they were motionless in body like deeply planted city-pillars or like the water of the great ocean settled in a windless place, and undistracted in mind. Like crimson clouds surrounding the peak of Sineru, they sat surrounding the Blessed One. Seeing the assembly so settled, great delight and gladness arose in the wanderer. Unable to contain the delight and gladness that had arisen within his heart, he gave rise to a pleasing utterance. Therefore, he spoke the words beginning with, 'It is marvelous, venerable sir...'

Tattha andhassa pabbatārohanaṃ viya niccaṃ na hotīti acchariyaṃ. Ayaṃ tāva saddanayo. Ayaṃ pana aṭṭhakathānayo[P 3.0003], accharāyogganti acchariyaṃ. Accharaṃ paharituṃ yuttanti attho. Abhūtapubbaṃ bhūtanti abbhutaṃ. Ubhayampetaṃ vimhayassevādhivacanaṃ. Taṃ panetaṃ garahaacchariyaṃ, pasaṃsāacchariyanti duvidhaṃ hoti. Tattha acchariyaṃ moggallāna abbhutaṃ moggallāna, yāva bāhāgahaṇāpi nāma so moghapuriso āgamessatīti (cūḷava. 383; a. ni. 8.20), idaṃ garahaacchariyaṃ nāma. “Acchariyaṃ nandamāte abbhutaṃ nandamāte, yatra hi nāma cittuppādampi parisodhessasīti (a. ni. 7.53) idaṃ pasaṃsāacchariyaṃ nāma. Idhāpi idameva adhippetaṃ” ayañhi taṃ pasaṃsanto evamāha.

Therein, 'marvelous' (acchariyaṃ) is so called because, like a blind person's climbing of a mountain, it is not something that always happens. This, first, is the textual method. This, however, is the commentarial method: it is 'marvelous' (acchariyaṃ) because it is 'worthy of a finger-snap' (accharāyoggaṃ). The meaning is that it is fit to snap one's fingers at. 'Amazing' (abbhutaṃ) is so called because what has not happened before, has happened. Both of these are terms for wonder. This, however, is of two kinds: astonishment by way of blame and astonishment by way of praise. Therein, 'Marvelous, Moggallāna! Amazing, Moggallāna! That worthless man will come even to the point of being seized by the arm!'—this is called astonishment by way of blame. 'Marvelous, Nandamātā! Amazing, Nandamātā! That you will even purify a thought-arising!'—this is called astonishment by way of praise. Here too, this very praise is intended. For this one, praising him, spoke thus.

Yāvañcidanti ettha idanti nipātamattaṃ. Yāvāti pamāṇaparicchedo, yāva sammā paṭipādito, yattakena pamāṇena sammā paṭipādito, na sakkā tassa vaṇṇe vattuṃ, atha kho acchariyamevetaṃ abbhutamevetanti vuttaṃ hoti. Etaparamaṃyevāti evaṃ sammā paṭipādito eso bhikkhusaṅgho [V 3.0003] tassāpi bhikkhusaṅghassa paramoti etaparamo, taṃ etaparamaṃ yathā ayaṃ paṭipādito, evaṃ paṭipāditaṃ katvā paṭipādesuṃ, na ito bhiyyoti attho. Dutiyanaye evaṃ paṭipādessanti, na ito bhiyyoti yojetabbaṃ. Tattha paṭipāditoti ābhisamācārikavattaṃ ādiṃ katvā sammā apaccanīkapaṭipattiyaṃ yojito. Atha kasmā ayaṃ paribbājako [M 3.0003] atītānāgate buddhe dasseti, kimassa tiyaddhajānanañāṇaṃ atthīti. Natthi, nayaggāhe pana ṭhatvā [P 3.0004] “yenākārena ayaṃ bhikkhusaṅgho sannisinno danto vinīto upasanto, atītabuddhāpi etaparamaṃyeva katvā paṭipajjāpesuṃ, anāgatabuddhāpi paṭipajjāpessanti, natthi ito uttari paṭipādanā”ti maññamāno anubuddhiyā evamāha.

Herein, in 'yāvañcidaṃ', 'idaṃ' is merely a particle. 'Yāvā' denotes a measure or limit. To the extent that it has been well guided in practice, to that measure it has been well guided in practice; it is not possible to speak of its virtues. Rather, it is to say: 'This is indeed marvelous, this is indeed amazing.' As for 'etaparamaṃ', it is to be understood in this way: This Sangha of monks, so well guided in practice, is the highest standard (paramo). Therefore, it is 'etaparamo' (having this as the highest standard). The meaning is: just as this Sangha has been guided in practice, so too did the past Buddhas guide theirs, making this the highest standard; there is nothing beyond this. In the second method, it should be connected thus: so too will the future Buddhas guide theirs; there is nothing beyond this. Therein, 'guided in practice' (paṭipādito) means yoked to right, non-antagonistic practice, beginning with the duties of proper conduct. Now, why does this wanderer refer to past and future Buddhas? Does he have the knowledge that knows the three periods of time? He does not. But, relying on inference, thinking, 'In whatever manner this Sangha of monks is assembled—tamed, disciplined, and peaceful—the past Buddhas too must have guided their disciples to practice, making this the highest standard, and the future Buddhas too will guide them to practice thus; there is no guidance higher than this,' he speaks thus through deductive reasoning.

2. Evametaṃ kandarakāti pāṭiekko anusandhi. Bhagavā kira taṃ sutvā “kandaraka tvaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ upasantoti vadasi, imassa pana bhikkhusaṅghassa upasantakāraṇaṃ tuyhaṃ apākaṭaṃ, na hi tvaṃ samatiṃsa pāramiyā pūretvā kusalamūlaṃ paripācetvā bodhipallaṅke sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ paṭivijjhi, mayā pana pāramiyo pūretvā ñātatthacariyaṃ lokatthacariyaṃ buddhatthacariyañca koṭiṃ pāpetvā bodhipallaṅke sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ paṭividdhaṃ, mayhaṃ etesaṃ upasantakāraṇaṃ pākaṭa”nti dassetuṃ imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi.

2. The connection 'So it is, Kandaraka,' is a distinct connection. The Blessed One, it is said, having heard that, began this discourse in order to show the following: 'Kandaraka, you say that the Sangha of monks is peaceful, but the reason for this Sangha of monks being peaceful is not manifest to you. For you have not fulfilled the thirty perfections, brought the roots of skillfulness to maturity, and penetrated omniscient knowledge at the seat of awakening. But I, having fulfilled the perfections, having brought the conduct for the welfare of relatives, the conduct for the welfare of the world, and the conduct for the attainment of Buddhahood to their culmination, have penetrated omniscient knowledge at the seat of awakening. To me, the reason for their being peaceful is manifest.'

Santi hi kandarakāti ayampi pāṭiekko anusandhi. Bhagavato kira etadahosi – “ayaṃ paribbājako imaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ upasantoti vadati, ayañca bhikkhusaṅgho kappetvā pakappetvā kuhakabhāvena iriyāpathaṃ saṇṭhapento cittena anupasanto na upasantākāraṃ dasseti. Ettha pana bhikkhusaṅghe paṭipadaṃ pūrayamānāpi paṭipadaṃ pūretvā matthakaṃ patvā ṭhitabhikkhūpi atthi, tattha paṭipadaṃ pūretvā matthakaṃ pattā attanā paṭividdhaguṇeheva upasantā, paṭipadaṃ pūrayamānā uparimaggassa vipassanāya upasantā, ito muttā pana avasesā catūhi satipaṭṭhānehi upasantā. Taṃ nesaṃ upasantakāraṇaṃ dassessāmī”ti “iminā ca iminā ca kāraṇena ayaṃ bhikkhusaṅgho upasanto”ti dassetuṃ “santi hi kandarakā”tiādimāha.

The phrase 'Santi hi Kandaraka'—this is also a distinct connective statement. It occurred to the Blessed One: 'This wanderer says that this community of monks is peaceful. And this community of monks is not one that shows a peaceful appearance while being unpeaceful in mind, arranging its deportment deceitfully by scheming and contriving. Rather, in this community of monks, there are those who are fulfilling the practice, and there are monks who have fulfilled the practice, reached the summit, and stand firm. Among them, those who have fulfilled the practice and reached the summit are peaceful through the qualities they have themselves realized. Those still fulfilling the practice are peaceful through insight for the sake of the higher path. Apart from these, the remaining ones are peaceful through the four foundations of mindfulness. I will show them the reason for their peacefulness.' To demonstrate that 'this community of monks is peaceful for this and that reason,' he said, 'For there are indeed, Kandaraka,' and so on.

Tattha arahanto khīṇāsavātiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ mūlapariyāyasuttavaṇṇanāyameva vuttaṃ. Sekhapaṭipadampi tattheva vitthāritaṃ. Santatasīlāti satatasīlā nirantarasīlā. Santatavuttinoti [P 3.0005] tasseva [V 3.0004] vevacanaṃ, santatajīvikā vātipi attho. Tasmiṃ santatasīle ṭhatvāva jīvikaṃ kappenti, na dussīlyaṃ maraṇaṃ pāpuṇantīti attho.

Here, regarding the phrases 'arahants whose taints are destroyed,' etc., what should be said has already been stated in the commentary on the Mūlapariyāya Sutta. The practice of the learner is also explained in detail there. 'Santatasīlā' means having constant virtue, uninterrupted virtue. 'Santatavuttino' is a synonym for that, or it can also mean 'having a constant livelihood.' The meaning is that they maintain their livelihood while established in that constant virtue; they do not engage in an immoral livelihood, but would rather meet death.

Nipakāti nepakkena samannāgatā paññavanto. Nipakavuttinoti paññāya vuttino, paññāya ṭhatvā jīvikaṃ kappenti. Yathā ekacco sāsane pabbajitvāpi [M 3.0004] jīvitakāraṇā chasu agocaresu carati, vesiyāgocaro hoti, vidhavathullakumārikapaṇḍakapānāgārabhikkhunigocaro hoti. Saṃsaṭṭho viharati rājūhi rājamahāmattehi titthiyehi titthiyasāvakehi ananulomikena gihisaṃsaggena (vibha. 514), vejjakammaṃ karoti, dūtakammaṃ karoti, pahiṇakammaṃ karoti, gaṇḍaṃ phāleti, arumakkhanaṃ deti, uddhaṃvirecanaṃ deti, adhovirecanaṃ deti, natthutelaṃ pacati, pivanatelaṃ pacati, veḷudānaṃ, pattadānaṃ, pupphadānaṃ, phaladānaṃ, sinānadānaṃ, dantakaṭṭhadānaṃ, mukhodakadānaṃ, cuṇṇamattikadānaṃ deti, cāṭukamyaṃ karoti, muggasūpiyaṃ, pāribhaṭuṃ, jaṅghapesaniyaṃ karotīti ekavīsatividhāya anesanāya jīvikaṃ kappento anipakavutti nāma hoti, na paññāya ṭhatvā jīvikaṃ kappeti, tato kālakiriyaṃ katvā samaṇayakkho nāma hutvā “tassa saṅghāṭipi ādittā hoti sampajjalitā”ti vuttanayena mahādukkhaṃ anubhoti. Evaṃvidhā ahutvā jīvitahetupi sikkhāpadaṃ anatikkamanto catupārisuddhisīle patiṭṭhāya yathābalaṃ buddhavacanaṃ uggaṇhitvā [P 3.0006] rathavinītapaṭipadaṃ, mahāgosiṅgapaṭipadaṃ, mahāsuññatapaṭipadaṃ, anaṅgaṇapaṭipadaṃ, dhammadāyādapaṭipadaṃ, nālakapaṭipadaṃ, tuvaṭṭakapaṭipadaṃ, candopamapaṭipadanti imāni ariyapaṭipadāni pūrento catupaccaya-santosa-bhāvanārāma-ariyavaṃsapaṭipattiyaṃ kāyasakkhino hutvā anīkā nikkhantahatthī viya yūthā vissaṭṭhasīho viya nipacchābandhamahānāvā viya ca gamanādīsu ekavihārino vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā ajjaajjeva arahattanti pavattaussāhā viharantīti attho.

‘Prudent’ (nipaka) means endowed with prudence and wisdom. ‘Living prudently’ (nipakavuttino) means living by wisdom, sustaining their livelihood while established in wisdom. For instance, some, even after having gone forth in the Dispensation, for the sake of livelihood, frequent the six improper resorts: the resort of prostitutes, the resort of widows, elderly maidens, eunuchs, taverns, and bhikkhunīs. He lives intermingled with kings, royal ministers, sectarians, and sectarian disciples, by inappropriate association with laypeople. He performs medical work, acts as a messenger, carries out errands; he lances boils, applies salve for sores, gives emetics, gives purgatives, prepares nose oil, prepares drinkable oil; he gives bamboo, gives leaves, gives flowers, gives fruits, gives bathing powder, gives tooth-sticks, gives mouth-water, gives powder and clay; he engages in flattery, engages in 'mung-bean-soup' talk (i.e., half-truths), performs attendant services, and runs errands. One who thus sustains his livelihood by these twenty-one kinds of improper seeking is called ‘one not living prudently’ (anipakavutti); he does not sustain his livelihood established in wisdom. Then, having died and become an ‘ascetic-demon,’ he experiences great suffering as stated: ‘Even his outer robe is ablaze, burning fiercely.’ Not being like that, one, without transgressing a training rule even for the sake of life, having established oneself in the fourfold purity of virtue, having learned the Buddha’s word according to one’s ability, fulfilling these noble practices—the Rathavinīta practice, the Mahāgosiṅga practice, the Mahāsuññata practice, the Anaṅgaṇa practice, the Dhammadāyāda practice, the Nālaka practice, the Tuvaṭṭaka practice, and the Candopama practice—and having become a body-witness to the practice of contentment with the four requisites, delight in meditation, and the noble lineage, like an elephant that has broken free from the army, like a lion released from its pride, and like a great elephant that has cast off its bonds, establishing insight while living alone in activities such as walking, one dwells with persistent effort [thinking]: ‘Today, this very day, I will attain arahantship!’ This is the meaning.

Suppatiṭṭhitacittāti catūsu satipaṭṭhānesu suṭṭhapitacittā hutvā. Sesā satipaṭṭhānakathā heṭṭhā vitthāritāva. Idha pana lokiyalokuttaramissakā satipaṭṭhānā kathitā, ettakena bhikkhusaṅghassa upasantakāraṇaṃ kathitaṃ hoti.

'Well-established mind' means having a mind well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness. The rest of the discussion on the foundations of mindfulness has already been explained in detail in the suttas below. Here, however, the foundations of mindfulness, mixed with the worldly and supramundane, are discussed. By this much, the reason for the peacefulness of the community of monks is explained.

3. Yāva supaññattāti yāva suṭṭhapitā sudesitā. Mayampi hi, bhanteti iminā esa attano [V 3.0005] kārakabhāvaṃ dasseti, bhikkhusaṅghañca ukkhipati. Ayañhettha adhippāyo, mayampi hi, bhante, gihi…pe… suppatiṭṭhitacittā viharāma, bhikkhusaṅghassa pana ayameva kasi ca bījañca yuganaṅgalañca phālapācanañca, tasmā bhikkhusaṅgho sabbakālaṃ satipaṭṭhānaparāyaṇo, mayaṃ [M 3.0005] pana kālena kālaṃ okāsaṃ labhitvā etaṃ manasikāraṃ karoma, mayampi kārakā, na sabbaso vissaṭṭhakammaṭṭhānāyevāti. Manussagahaneti [P 3.0007] manussānaṃ ajjhāsayagahanena gahanatā, ajjhāsayassāpi nesaṃ kilesagahanena gahanatā veditabbā. Kasaṭasāṭheyyesupi eseva nayo. Tattha aparisuddhaṭṭhena kasaṭatā, kerāṭiyaṭṭhena sāṭheyyatā veditabbā. Sattānaṃ hitāhitaṃ jānātīti evaṃ gahanakasaṭakerāṭiyānaṃ manussānaṃ hitāhitapaṭipadaṃ yāva suṭṭhu bhagavā jānāti. Yadidaṃ pasavoti ettha sabbāpi catuppadajāti pasavoti adhippetā. Pahomīti sakkomi. Yāvatakena antarenāti yattakena khaṇena. Campaṃ gatāgataṃ karissatīti assamaṇḍalato yāva campānagaradvārā gamanañca āgamanañca karissati. Sāṭheyyānīti saṭhattāni. Kūṭeyyānīti kūṭattāni. Vaṅkeyyānīti vaṅkattāni. Jimheyyānīti jimhattāni. Pātukarissatīti pakāsessati dassessati. Na hi sakkā tena tāni ettakena antarena dassetuṃ.

3. 'As well-instructed' means as well-established and well-taught. 'We too, venerable sir'—with this, he indicates his own role as an agent and also elevates the community of monks. The meaning here is this: 'We too, venerable sir, as householders… dwell with well-established minds. But for the community of monks, this alone is their plowing, seed, yoke and plow, and plowshare and goad. Therefore, the community of monks is always devoted to the foundations of mindfulness, while we, obtaining opportunity from time to time, engage in this attention. We too are agents, not entirely neglectful of our meditation subjects.' 'Human impenetrability' (manussagahana) means impenetrability due to the impenetrability of humans’ inclinations. It should also be understood that their inclinations too are impenetrable due to the impenetrability of defilements. The same applies to ‘coarseness and deceitfulness’ (kasaṭasāṭheyya). Here, ‘coarseness’ (kasaṭatā) should be understood by way of impurity, and ‘deceitfulness’ (sāṭheyyatā) by way of roguery. ‘He knows what is beneficial and harmful for beings’—thus, the Blessed One thoroughly knows the path of benefit and harm for humans who are impenetrable, coarse, and roguish. ‘Namely, beasts’ (pasavo)—here, all four-footed species are intended by ‘pasavo’. ‘I am able’ (pahomi)—I am capable. ‘Within the interval’ (yāvatakena antarena)—within that amount of time. ‘He will go back and forth to Campā’—he will travel from the horse stable to the gate of Campā city and return. ‘Deceitful acts’ (sāṭheyyāni)—states of being deceitful. ‘Fraudulent acts’ (kūṭeyyāni)—states of being fraudulent. ‘Crooked acts’ (vaṅkeyyāni)—states of being crooked. ‘Evasive acts’ (jimheyyāni)—states of being evasive. ‘He will reveal’—he will make known, he will show. For it is not possible for him to show those things within such a short interval.

Tattha yassa kismiñcideva ṭhāne ṭhātukāmassa sato yaṃ ṭhānaṃ manussānaṃ sappaṭibhayaṃ, purato gantvā vañcetvā ṭhassāmīti na hoti, tasmiṃ ṭhātukāmaṭṭhāneyeva nikhātatthambho viya cattāro pāde niccale katvā tiṭṭhati, ayaṃ saṭho nāma. Yassa pana kismiñcideva ṭhāne avacchinditvā khandhagataṃ pātetukāmassa sato yaṃ ṭhānaṃ manussānaṃ sappaṭibhayaṃ, purato gantvā vañcetvā pātessāmīti na hoti, tattheva avacchinditvā pāteti, ayaṃ kūṭo nāma. Yassa kismiñcideva ṭhāne maggā ukkamma nivattitvā paṭimaggaṃ ārohitukāmassa [P 3.0008] sato yaṃ ṭhānaṃ manussānaṃ sappaṭibhayaṃ, purato gantvā vañcetvā evaṃ karissāmīti na hoti, tattheva maggā ukkamma nivattitvā paṭimaggaṃ ārohati, ayaṃ vaṅko nāma. Yassa pana kālena vāmato kālena dakkhiṇato kālena ujumaggeneva gantukāmassa sato yaṃ ṭhānaṃ manussānaṃ sappaṭibhayaṃ, purato gantvā vañcetvā evaṃ karissāmīti na hoti, tattheva kālena vāmato kālena dakkhiṇato kālena ujumaggaṃ gacchati, tathā laṇḍaṃ vā passāvaṃ vā vissajjetukāmassa sato idaṃ ṭhānaṃ susammaṭṭhaṃ ākiṇṇamanussaṃ ramaṇīyaṃ, imasmiṃ ṭhāne evarūpaṃ kātuṃ na yuttaṃ, purato gantvā paṭicchannaṭhāne karissāmīti na hoti, tattheva karoti, ayaṃ jimho nāma. Iti imaṃ catubbidhampi [V 3.0006] kiriyaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Sabbāni tāni sāṭheyyāni [M 3.0006] kūṭeyyāni vaṅkeyyāni jimheyyāni pātukarissatīti evaṃ karontāpi te saṭhādayo tāni sāṭheyyādīni pātukaronti nāma.

Herein, for whichever animal, being desirous of standing in any particular place that is perilous for humans, the thought does not arise, 'Having gone ahead and maneuvered, I will stand,' but it stands right in that place where it desires to stand, making its four feet immovable like a driven-in post—this is called deceit (`saṭho`). Furthermore, for whichever animal, being desirous of throwing off its rider by bucking in any particular place that is perilous for humans, the thought does not arise, 'Having gone ahead and maneuvered, I will throw him off,' but it bucks and throws him off right there—this is called treachery (`kūṭo`). For whichever animal, being desirous of leaving the path, turning back, and taking the path it came on in any particular place that is perilous for humans, the thought does not arise, 'Having gone ahead and maneuvered, I will do so,' but it leaves the path right there, turns back, and takes the path it came on—this is called crookedness (`vaṅko`). Furthermore, for whichever animal, being desirous of going at times to the left, at times to the right, and at times straight along the path, in a place that is perilous for humans, the thought does not arise, 'Having gone ahead and maneuvered, I will do so,' but it goes right there, at times to the left, at times to the right, and at times straight. Likewise, for one desirous of discharging feces or urine, the thought does not arise, 'This place is well-swept, crowded with people, and pleasant; it is not proper to do such a thing in this place. Having gone ahead, I will do it in a concealed place,' but it does it right there—this is called deviousness (`jimho`). Thus, it was with reference to this fourfold action that this was said: 'He will make manifest all those acts of deceit, treachery, crookedness, and deviousness.' Even in acting thus, those deceitful ones and so forth are said to make manifest those acts of deceit and so forth.

Evaṃ pasūnaṃ uttānabhāvaṃ dassetvā idāni manussānaṃ gahanabhāvaṃ dassento amhākaṃ pana, bhantetiādimāha. Tattha dāsāti antojātakā vā dhanakkītā vā karamarānītā vā sayaṃ vā dāsabyaṃ upagatā. Pessāti pesanakārakā. Kammakarāti bhattavetanabhatā. Aññathāva kāyenāti aññenevākārena kāyena samudācaranti, aññenevākārena vācāya, aññena ca nesaṃ ākārena cittaṃ ṭhitaṃ hotīti dasseti. Tattha ye sammukhā sāmike disvā paccuggamanaṃ karonti, hatthato bhaṇḍakaṃ gaṇhanti, imaṃ [P 3.0009] vissajjetvā imaṃ gaṇhantā sesānipi āsana-paññāpana-tālavaṇṭabījana-pādadhovanādīni sabbāni kiccāni karonti, parammukhakāle pana telampi uttarantaṃ na olokenti, satagghanakepi sahassagghanakepi kamme parihāyante nivattitvā oloketumpi na icchanti, ime aññathā kāyena samudācaranti nāma. Ye pana sammukhā “amhākaṃ sāmi amhākaṃ ayyo”tiādīni vatvā pasaṃsanti, parammukhā avattabbaṃ nāma natthi, yaṃ icchanti, taṃ vadanti, ime aññathā vācāya samudācaranti nāma.

Having thus shown the obvious nature of animals, now, wishing to show the complex nature of humans, he said, 'But for us, venerable sir,' and so on. Therein, 'slaves' (`dāsā`) are those born in the household, bought with wealth, brought as captives from battle, or who have entered servitude of their own accord. 'Messengers' (`pessā`) are those who perform errands. 'Workers' (`kammakarā`) are those who serve for food and wages. 'Otherwise with the body' (`aññathāva kāyena`) shows that they conduct themselves with the body in one way, with speech in another way, and their mind is established in yet another way. Therein, there are those who, upon seeing their masters in their presence, go out to meet them, take the goods from their hands—letting go of what is in their own hand to take what is in the master's—and perform all other duties such as preparing seats, fanning with palm-leaf fans, and washing the feet. But in the master's absence, they do not even look at oil overflowing. Even when work worth a hundred or a thousand is being ruined, they do not wish to turn back and look. These are said to 'conduct themselves otherwise with the body.' Furthermore, there are those who in the master's presence praise him, saying, 'Our master, our lord,' and so on, but in his absence there is nothing unspeakable they will not say; whatever they wish, they say it. These are said to 'conduct themselves otherwise with speech.'

4. Cattārome pessapuggalāti ayampi pāṭiekko anusandhi. Ayañhi pesso “yāvañcidaṃ, bhante, bhagavā evaṃ manussagahaṇe evaṃ manussakasaṭe evaṃ manussasāṭheyye vattamāne sattānaṃ hitāhitaṃ jānātī”ti āha. Purime ca tayo puggalā ahitapaṭipadaṃ paṭipannā, upari catuttho hitapaṭipadaṃ, evamahaṃ sattānaṃ hitāhitaṃ jānāmīti dassetuṃ imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi. Heṭṭhā kandarakassa kathāya saddhiṃ yojetumpi vaṭṭati. Tena vuttaṃ “yāvañcidaṃ bhotā gotamena sammā bhikkhusaṅgho paṭipādito”ti. Athassa bhagavā “purime tayo puggale pahāya upari catutthapuggalassa hitapaṭipattiyaṃyeva paṭipādemī”ti dassentopi imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi. Santoti idaṃ saṃvijjamānāti padasseva vevacanaṃ. “Santā honti samitā vūpasantā”ti (vibha. 542) ettha hi niruddhā santāti vuttā. “Santā ete vihārā ariyassa vinaye vuccantī”ti ettha (ma. ni. 1.82) nibbutā. “Santo have sabbhi pavedayantī”ti ettha (jā. 2.21.413) paṇḍitā. Idha pana vijjamānā upalabbhamānāti attho.

4. Regarding 'There are these four individuals, Pessa...': this too is a separate connection. For this Pessa said: 'It is wonderful, venerable sir, how the Blessed One, while such human complexity, such human corruption, and such human deceit are occurring, knows what is beneficial and unbeneficial for beings.' The first three individuals have entered upon an unbeneficial practice, while the fourth, who is superior, has entered upon a beneficial practice. To show, 'Thus I know what is beneficial and unbeneficial for beings,' the Blessed One began this discourse. It is also fitting to connect this with the preceding discourse of Kandaraka. Therefore it was said: 'To this extent has the community of monks been well-guided by the venerable Gotama.' Then the Blessed One, to show, 'Having abandoned the first three individuals, I guide the fourth individual only in the beneficial practice,' also began this discourse. The word `santo` is a synonym for the word `saṃvijjamānā` (existing). For in the passage, 'They are `santā`, calmed, fully calmed,' `santā` is said to mean 'ceased' (`niruddhā`). In, 'These are `santā` abidings, they are called, in the discipline of the Noble One,' it means 'extinguished' (`nibbutā`). In, 'The `santo` indeed make it known among the good,' it means 'the wise' (`paṇḍitā`). Here, however, the intended meaning is 'existing' (`vijjamānā`) and 'found' (`upalabbhamānā`).

Attantapādīsu [V 3.0007][M 3.0007] attānaṃ tapati dukkhāpetīti attantapo. Attano [P 3.0010] paritāpanānuyogaṃ attaparitāpanānuyogaṃ. Paraṃ tapati dukkhāpetīti parantapo. Paresaṃ paritāpanānuyogaṃ paraparitāpanānuyogaṃ. Diṭṭheva dhammeti imasmiṃyeva attabhāve. Nicchātoti chātaṃ vuccati taṇhā, sā assa natthīti nicchāto. Sabbakilesānaṃ nibbutattā nibbuto. Anto tāpanakilesānaṃ abhāvā sītalo jātoti sītibhūto. Jhānamaggaphalanibbānasukhāni paṭisaṃvedetīti sukhapaṭisaṃvedī. Brahmabhūtena attanāti seṭṭhabhūtena attanā. Cittaṃ ārādhetīti cittaṃ sampādeti, paripūreti gaṇhāti pasādetīti attho.

Regarding `attantapa` and other such terms, it should be understood thus: 'He torments (`tapati`), causes suffering to (`dukkhāpeti`) himself (`attānaṃ`)'; therefore, he is a self-tormentor (`attantapo`). The devotion to the torment of oneself is `attaparitāpanānuyoga`. 'He torments, causes suffering to another (`paraṃ`)'; therefore, he is an other-tormentor (`parantapo`). The devotion to the torment of others is `paraparitāpanānuyoga`. `Diṭṭheva dhamme` means 'in this very existence.' `Nicchāto`: Craving (`taṇhā`) is called 'thirst' (`chāta`); because he is without it, he is `nicchāto` (thirstless). `Nibbuto`: He is `nibbuto` (extinguished) because of the extinguishing of all defilements. `Sītibhūto`: 'He has become cool (`sītalo jāto`) because of the absence of defilements that burn (`tāpana`) within'; therefore, he is `sītibhūto` (one who has become cool). `Sukhapaṭisaṃvedī`: 'He experiences (`paṭisaṃvedeti`) the bliss (`sukha`) of jhāna, path, fruition, and Nibbāna'; therefore, he is `sukhapaṭisaṃvedī` (an experiencer of bliss). `Brahmabhūtena attanā` means 'with a self (`attanā`) that has become supreme (`seṭṭhabhūtena`).' `Cittaṃ ārādheti` means he accomplishes (`sampādeti`) the mind, fulfills (`paripūreti`) it, grasps (`gaṇhāti`) it, and clarifies (`pasādeti`) it.

5. Dukkhapaṭikkūlanti dukkhassa paṭikūlaṃ, paccanīkasaṇṭhitaṃ dukkhaṃ apatthayamānanti attho.

5. `Dukkhapaṭikkūlanti` means being averse to suffering; the meaning is not desiring suffering, which is established as contrary.

6. Paṇḍitoti idha catūhi kāraṇehi paṇḍitoti na vattabbo, satipaṭṭhānesu pana kammaṃ karotīti paṇḍitoti vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Mahāpaññoti idampi mahante atthe pariggaṇhātītiādinā mahāpaññalakkhaṇena na vattabbaṃ, satipaṭṭhānapariggāhikāya pana paññāya samannāgatattā mahāpaññoti vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Mahatā atthena saṃyutto agamissāti mahatā atthena saṃyutto hutvā gato bhaveyya, sotāpattiphalaṃ pāpuṇeyyāti attho. Kiṃ pana yesaṃ maggaphalānaṃ upanissayo atthi, buddhānaṃ sammukhībhāve ṭhitepi tesaṃ antarāyo hotīti. Āma hoti, na pana buddhe paṭicca, atha kho kiriyaparihāniyā vā pāpamittatāya vā hoti. Tattha kiriyaparihāniyā hoti nāma – sace hi dhammasenāpati dhanañjānissa [P 3.0011] brāhmaṇassa āsayaṃ ñatvā dhammaṃ adesayissā, so brāhmaṇo sotāpanno abhavissā, evaṃ tāva kiriyaparihāniyā hoti. Pāpamittatāya hoti nāma – sace hi ajātasattu devadattassa vacanaṃ gahetvā pitughātakammaṃ nākarissā, sāmaññaphalasuttakathitadivaseva sotāpanno abhavissā, tassa vacanaṃ gahetvā pitughātakammassa katattā pana na hoti, evaṃ pāpamittatāya hoti. Imassāpi upāsakassa kiriyaparihāni jātā, apariniṭṭhitāya desanāya uṭṭhahitvā pakkanto. Apica, bhikkhave, ettāvatāpi pesso hatthārohaputto mahatā atthena saṃyuttoti katarena mahantena atthena? Dvīhi [V 3.0008] ānisaṃsehi. So kira upāsako saṅghe ca pasādaṃ paṭilabhi, satipaṭṭhānapariggahaṇatthāya cassa abhinavo nayo udapādi. Tena vuttaṃ “mahatā atthena saṃyutto”ti. Kandarako pana saṅghe pasādameva [M 3.0008] paṭilabhi. Etassa bhagavā kāloti etassa dhammakkhānassa, catunnaṃ vā puggalānaṃ vibhajanassa kālo.

6. Here, one should not be called 'wise' on account of four reasons, such as skill in the elements; rather, it is fitting to call one 'wise' who engages in the practice with regard to the foundations of mindfulness. Similarly, one should not be called 'greatly wise' on account of the characteristic of great wisdom, such as 'encompassing great benefits'; rather, it is fitting to call one 'greatly wise' on account of being endowed with wisdom that grasps the foundations of mindfulness. 'He will go connected with a great purpose' means that, having been connected with a great purpose—that is, the fruit of stream-entry—he would have gone; he would have attained the fruit of stream-entry. But is it that for those who have the supporting condition for the paths and fruits, an obstacle arises even when they are in the presence of the Buddhas? Yes, it does. However, it is not on account of the Buddhas; rather, it arises due to a decline in conduct or due to association with bad friends. Therein, 'it arises due to a decline in conduct' is as follows: if the General of the Dhamma, having known the inclination of the brahmin Dhanañjāni, had taught the Dhamma, that brahmin would have become a stream-enterer. Thus it arises due to a decline in conduct. 'It arises due to association with bad friends' is as follows: if King Ajātasattu, not having accepted the word of Devadatta, had not committed the act of patricide, he would have become a stream-enterer on the very day the Discourse on the Fruits of Recluseship was taught. But because he accepted his word and committed the act of patricide, he did not become one. Thus it arises due to association with bad friends. For this lay follower, too, a decline in conduct occurred; he rose and departed before the teaching was concluded. Furthermore, monks, even to this extent Pessa the elephant trainer's son is 'connected with a great purpose.' By what great purpose? By two benefits. Indeed, that lay follower gained faith in the Sangha, and a new method for grasping the foundations of mindfulness arose for him. Therefore, it was said, 'connected with a great purpose.' Kandaraka, however, only gained faith in the Sangha. 'Now is the time, Blessed One' means: it is the time for this exposition of the Dhamma, or the time for the analysis of the four individuals.

8. Orabbhikādīsu urabbhā vuccanti eḷakā, urabbhe hanatīti orabbhiko. Sūkarikādīsupi eseva nayo. Luddoti dāruṇo kakkhaḷo. Macchaghātakoti macchabandhakevaṭṭo. Bandhanāgārikoti bandhanāgāragopako. Kururakammantāti dāruṇakammantā.

8. In 'sheep-butchers' and the like, sheep are called 'urabbhā'; one who kills sheep is a 'sheep-butcher' (orabbhiko). This same method should be understood for 'pig-butchers' and the like. 'Ruthless' (luddo) means cruel (dāruṇo), harsh (kakkhaḷo). 'Fish-killer' (macchaghātako) means a fisherman who traps fish. 'Jailer' (bandhanāgāriko) means a prison guard. 'Those of cruel deeds' (kurūrakammantā) means those who perform cruel actions.

9. Muddhāvasittoti [P 3.0012] khattiyābhisekena muddhani abhisitto. Puratthimena nagarassāti nagarato puratthimadisāya. Santhāgāranti yaññasālaṃ. Kharājinaṃ nivāsetvāti sakhuraṃ ajinacammaṃ nivāsetvā. Sappitelenāti sappinā ca telena ca. Ṭhapetvā hi sappiṃ avaseso yo koci sneho telanti vuccati. Kaṇḍūvamānoti nakhānaṃ chinnattā kaṇḍūvitabbakāle tena kaṇḍūvamāno. Anantarahitāyāti asanthatāya. Sarūpavacchāyāti sadisavacchāya. Sace gāvī setā hoti, vacchopi setakova. Sace gāvī kabarā vā rattā vā, vacchopi tādiso vāti evaṃ sarūpavacchāya. So evamāhāti so rājā evaṃ vadeti. Vacchatarāti taruṇavacchakabhāvaṃ atikkantā balavavacchā. Vacchatarīsupi eseva nayo. Barihisatthāyāti parikkhepakaraṇatthāya ceva yaññabhūmiyaṃ attharaṇatthāya ca. Sesaṃ heṭṭhā tattha tattha vitthāritattā uttānamevāti.

9. 'Anointed on the head' (muddhāvasitto) means one who has been anointed on the head with the royal consecration of khattiyas. 'To the east of the city' (puratthimena nagarassa) means in the eastern direction from the city. 'Assembly hall' (santhāgāraṃ) means a sacrificial hall. 'Having put on a rough hide' (kharājinaṃ nivāsetvā) means having worn a black antelope hide with its hooves. 'With ghee and oil' (sappitelena) means with ghee and with oil. Indeed, setting aside ghee, whatever remaining oleaginous substance there is, is called 'oil'. 'Scratching' (kaṇḍūvamāno) means, because his nails were cut, he was scratching with a deer horn when it was time to scratch. 'On the bare ground' (anantarahitāya) means on uncovered ground. 'With a calf of like form' (sarūpavacchāya) means with a calf of similar form. If a cow is white, the calf is also white. If a cow is mottled or red, the calf is also of a similar appearance. Thus, 'with a calf of like form'. 'He spoke thus' (so evamāha) means that king spoke thus. 'Young bulls' (vacchatarā) means strong calves that have passed the state of being young calves. This same method should be understood in the case of 'young heifers' (vacchatarīsu) as well. 'For the sacred grass' (barhisatthāya) means for the purpose of making an enclosure and for spreading on the sacrificial ground. The remainder is clear, as it has been explained in detail in various places below.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya

Kandarakasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Kandaraka Sutta is concluded.

2. Aṭṭhakanāgarasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Aṭṭhakanāgara Sutta

17. Evaṃ [V 3.0009] me sutanti aṭṭhakanāgarasuttaṃ. Tattha beluvagāmaketi vesāliyā dakkhiṇapasse avidūre beluvagāmako nāma atthi, taṃ gocaragāmaṃ katvāti attho. Dasamoti [P 3.0013] so hi jātigottavasena ceva [M 3.0009] sārappattakulagaṇanāya ca dasame ṭhāne gaṇīyati, tenassa dasamotveva nāmaṃ jātaṃ. Aṭṭhakanāgaroti aṭṭhakanagaravāsī. Kukkuṭārāmoti kukkuṭaseṭṭhinā kārito ārāmo.

17. Thus have I heard—the Aṭṭhakanāgara Sutta. Therein, “in Beluvagāmaka” means: not far from the southern side of Vesālī, there is a small village named Beluvagāmaka; the meaning is that it was made a village for alms-gathering. “Dasama” means: he is counted in the tenth place both by way of birth and lineage and by the count of families that have attained great wealth; therefore, the name “Dasama” arose for him. “Aṭṭhakanāgara” means a resident of the city of Aṭṭhaka. “Kukkuṭārāma” means the monastery caused to be built by the merchant Kukkuṭa.

18. Tena bhagavatā…pe… akkhātoti ettha ayaṃ saṅkhepattho, yo so bhagavā samatiṃsa pāramiyo pūretvā sabbakilese bhañjitvā anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambuddho, tena bhagavatā, tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ āsayānusayaṃ jānatā, hatthatale ṭhapitaāmalakaṃ viya sabbaṃ ñeyyadhammaṃ passatā. Apica pubbenivāsādīhi jānatā, dibbena cakkhunā passatā, tīhi vijjāhi chahi vā pana abhiññāhi jānatā, sabbattha appaṭihatena samantacakkhunā passatā, sabbadhammajānanasamatthāya paññāya jānatā, sabbasattānaṃ cakkhuvisayātītāni tirokuṭṭādigatānipi rūpāni ativisuddhena maṃsacakkhunā passatā, attahitasādhikāya samādhipadaṭṭhānāya paṭivedhapaññāya jānatā, parahitasādhikāya karuṇāpadaṭṭhānāya desanāpaññāya passatā, arīnaṃ hatattā paccayādīnañca arahattā arahatā, sammā sāmañca saccānaṃ buddhattā sammāsambuddhena. Antarāyikadhamme vā jānatā, niyyānikadhamme passatā, kilesārīnaṃ hatattā arahatā, sāmaṃ sabbadhammānaṃ buddhattā sammāsambuddhenāti evaṃ catuvesārajjavasena catūhi kāraṇehi thomitena. Atthi nu kho eko dhammo akkhātoti.

18. Regarding the passage “By that Blessed One… and so on… declared”: Herein, this is the summary meaning. That Blessed One who, having fulfilled the thirty perfections, having destroyed all defilements, has fully awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment; by that Blessed One, who knows the dispositions and latent tendencies of those various beings, who sees all knowable things like a myrobalan fruit placed on the palm of the hand; and who knows by means of former existences and so on, who sees with the divine eye, who knows with the three true knowledges or with the six supernormal knowledges, who sees with the all-seeing eye that is unobstructed in every way, who knows with the wisdom capable of knowing all dhammas, who sees with the extremely purified fleshly eye even forms that are beyond the range of vision of all beings, such as those that have gone behind walls, who knows with the wisdom of penetration which accomplishes his own welfare and has concentration as its proximate cause, who sees with the wisdom of teaching which accomplishes the welfare of others and has compassion as its proximate cause; who is an Arahant because of having destroyed the enemies and because of being worthy of requisites and so on, and a Perfectly Enlightened One because of having rightly and by himself awakened to the truths; or, who knows the obstructive dhammas, who sees the dhammas that lead out of saṃsāra; who is an Arahant because of having destroyed the enemies, the defilements, and a Perfectly Enlightened One because of having by himself awakened to all dhammas—thus praised by means of the four kinds of fearlessness for four reasons—is there, indeed, one Dhamma declared?

19. Abhisaṅkhatanti kataṃ uppāditaṃ. Abhisañcetayitanti cetayitaṃ pakappitaṃ. So tattha ṭhitoti so tasmiṃ samathavipassanādhamme ṭhito. Dhammarāgena dhammanandiyāti padadvayehi samathavipassanāsu chandarāgo vutto. Samathavipassanāsu [P 3.0014] hi sabbena sabbaṃ chandarāgaṃ pariyādiyituṃ sakkonto arahā hoti, asakkonto anāgāmī hoti. So samathavipassanāsu chandarāgassa [V 3.0010] appahīnattā catutthajjhānacetanāya suddhāvāse nibbattati, ayaṃ ācariyānaṃ samānakathā.

19. “Formed” (abhisaṅkhata) means made, produced. “Intended” (abhisañcetayita) means willed, devised. “He is established therein” (so tattha ṭhito) means he is established in that Dhamma of serenity and insight. By the two terms “through passion for the Dhamma, through delight in the Dhamma” (dhammarāgena dhammanandiyā), strong passion for serenity and insight is spoken of. For one who is able to completely exhaust all strong passion for serenity and insight is an Arahant; one who is not able to is a Non-returner. He, because of not having abandoned strong passion for serenity and insight, is reborn in the Pure Abodes through the volition of the fourth jhāna. This is the common account of the teachers.

Vitaṇḍavādī panāha “teneva dhammarāgenāti vacanato akusalena suddhāvāse nibbattatī”ti so “suttaṃ āharā”ti vattabbo, addhā aññaṃ apassanto idameva āharissati, tato vattabbo “kiṃ panidaṃ suttaṃ neyyatthaṃ nītattha”nti, addhā nītatthanti vakkhati. Tato vattabbo – evaṃ sante anāgāmiphalatthikena [M 3.0010] samathavipassanāsu chandarāgo kattabbo bhavissati, chandarāge uppādite anāgāmiphalaṃ paṭividdhaṃ bhavissati “mā suttaṃ me laddha”nti yaṃ vā taṃ vā dīpehi. Pañhaṃ kathentena hi ācariyassa santike uggahetvā attharasaṃ paṭivijjhitvā kathetuṃ vaṭṭati, akusalena hi sagge, kusalena vā apāye paṭisandhi nāma natthi. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

But a sophist says, “Because of the phrase ‘by that very passion for the Dhamma,’ one is reborn in the Pure Abodes through an unwholesome state.” He should be told, “Bring the sutta.” Surely, not seeing another, he will bring this very one. Then he should be asked, “But is this sutta of interpretable meaning or of definitive meaning?” Surely, he will say, “It is of definitive meaning.” Then he should be told: “If so, then by one who desires the fruit of a Non-returner, strong passion for serenity and insight will have to be produced. When strong passion is produced, the fruit of a Non-returner will be realized.” Thinking, “I have found a sutta!”, he points to just anything. For one who would speak on a question should learn it in the presence of a teacher, penetrate its meaning and essence, and then speak. For there is no such thing as rebirth in heaven through the unwholesome, or rebirth in the lower realms through the wholesome. This has been stated by the Blessed One:

“Na, bhikkhave, lobhajena kammena dosajena kammena mohajena kammena devā paññāyanti, manussā paññāyanti, yā vā panaññāpi kāci sugatiyo, atha kho, bhikkhave, lobhajena kammena dosajena kammena mohajena kammena nirayo paññāyati, tiracchānayoni paññāyati, pettivisayo paññāyati, yā vā panaññāpi kāci duggatiyo”ti –

“Monks, it is not through kamma born of greed, kamma born of hatred, or kamma born of delusion that gods appear, that humans appear, or that any other good destinations appear. But rather, monks, it is through kamma born of greed, kamma born of hatred, and kamma born of delusion that hell appears, that the animal womb appears, that the sphere of ghosts appears, or that any other bad destinations appear.”

Evaṃ paññāpetabbo. Sace sañjānāti sañjānātu, no ce sañjānāti, “gaccha pātova vihāraṃ pavisitvā yāguṃ pivāhī”ti uyyojetabbo.

Thus he should be made to understand. If he understands, let him understand. If he does not understand, he should be dismissed, saying, “Go, enter the monastery early and drink your gruel.”

Yathā ca pana imasmiṃ sutte, evaṃ mahāmālukyovādepi mahāsatipaṭṭhānepi kāyagatāsatisuttepi samathavipassanā kathitā. Tattha imasmiṃ sutte samathavasena gacchatopi vipassanāvasena gacchatopi samathadhurameva dhuraṃ, mahāmālukyovāde vipassanāva dhuraṃ, mahāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ pana vipassanuttaraṃ [P 3.0015] nāma kathitaṃ, kāyagatāsatisuttaṃ samathuttaranti.

And just as in this sutta, so too in the Mahāmālukyovāda, in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna, and in the Kāyagatāsati Sutta, serenity and insight are taught. Therein, in this sutta, for one who proceeds by way of serenity and for one who proceeds by way of insight, the yoke of serenity itself is the main yoke. In the Mahāmālukyovāda, insight itself is the main yoke. But the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna is said to be that which has insight as supreme, while the Kāyagatāsati Sutta is that which has serenity as supreme.

Ayaṃ kho gahapati…pe… ekadhammo akkhātoti ekadhammaṃ pucchitena ayampi ekadhammoti evaṃ pucchāvasena kathitattā ekādasapi dhammā ekadhammo nāma jāto. Mahāsakuludāyisuttasmiñhi [V 3.0011] ekūnavīsati pabbāni paṭipadāvasena ekadhammo nāma jātāni, idha ekādasapucchāvasena ekadhammoti āgatāni. Amatuppattiyatthena vā sabbānipi ekadhammoti vattuṃ vaṭṭati.

“This, householder… and so on… one Dhamma has been declared.” Because, when one had asked about “one Dhamma,” it was declared in response to the question, “This too is one Dhamma,” all eleven dhammas thus came to be called “one Dhamma.” Indeed, in the Mahāsakuludāyi Sutta, nineteen sections came to be called “one Dhamma” by way of the path of practice; here they have come as “one Dhamma” by way of eleven questions. Or, in the sense of being a cause for the arising of the Deathless, it is proper to call all of them “one Dhamma.”

21. Nidhimukhaṃ gavesantoti nidhiṃ pariyesanto. Sakidevāti ekapayogena. Kathaṃ pana ekapayogeneva ekādasannaṃ nidhīnaṃ adhigamo hotīti. Idhekacco araññe nidhiṃ gavesamāno carati, tamenaṃ aññataro atthacarako disvā “kiṃ bho carasī”ti pucchati. So “jīvitavuttiṃ pariyesāmī”ti [M 3.0011] āha. Itaro “tena hi samma āgaccha, etaṃ pāsāṇaṃ pavattehī”ti āha. So taṃ pavattetvā uparūpari ṭhapitā vā kucchiyā kucchiṃ āhacca ṭhitā vā ekādasa kumbhiyo passeyya, evaṃ ekapayogena ekādasannaṃ nidhīnaṃ adhigamo hoti.

21. “Seeking a treasure-mouth” means searching for treasure. “Just once” means with a single application. But how is it that with just one application, one attains eleven treasures? Here, a certain person wanders in the forest seeking treasure. A certain benefactor sees him and asks, “What are you doing, friend?” He replies, “I am seeking a means of livelihood.” The other says, “Well then, come here, roll this stone.” Having rolled it, he would see eleven pots placed one on top of another or placed belly to belly, abutting each other. Thus, with a single application, one attains eleven treasures.

Ācariyadhanaṃ pariyesissantīti aññatitthiyā hi yassa santike sippaṃ uggaṇhanti, tassa sippuggahaṇato pure vā pacchā vā antarantare vā gehato nīharitvā dhanaṃ denti. Yesaṃ gehe natthi, te ñātisabhāgato pariyesanti, tathā alabhamānā bhikkhampi caritvā dentiyeva. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ.

“Seeking the teacher's fee”: Followers of other sects, from whomever they learn a craft, give a fee taken from their homes before, after, or during the training. Those without wealth at home seek it from kinsmen and associates, and if still unable to obtain it, they even go on an alms-round to give it. This was said in reference to that.

Kimaṅgaṃ panāhanti bāhirakā tāva aniyyānikepi sāsane sippamattadāyakassa dhanaṃ pariyesanti; ahaṃ pana evaṃvidhe niyyānikasāsane ekādasavidhaṃ amatuppattipaṭipadaṃ desentassa ācariyassa pūjaṃ kiṃ na karissāmi, karissāmiyevāti vadati. Paccekadussayugena [P 3.0016] acchādesīti ekamekassa bhikkhuno ekekaṃ dussayugamadāsīti attho. Samudācāravacanaṃ panettha evarūpaṃ hoti, tasmā acchādesīti vuttaṃ. Pañcasatavihāranti pañcasatagghanikaṃ paṇṇasālaṃ kāresīti attho. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

“What then of me?” Outsiders seek wealth even in a non-liberating teaching for one who merely imparts a craft; as for me, in such a liberating teaching, why should I not make an offering to the teacher who teaches the elevenfold practice for the attainment of the Deathless? I will certainly do so, he says. “He clothed them with an individual pair of cloths” means he gave a pair of cloths to each and every monk. Here, such a term is a conventional expression; therefore, it is said “he clothed them.” “A monastery of five hundred” means he had a leaf-hut built worth five hundred. The rest is clear everywhere.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Middle Length Discourses.

Aṭṭhakanāgarasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Aṭṭhakanāgara Sutta is concluded.

3. Sekhasuttavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Sekha Sutta

22. Evaṃ [V 3.0012] me sutanti sekhasuttaṃ. Tattha navaṃ santhāgāranti adhunā kāritaṃ santhāgāraṃ, ekā mahāsālāti attho. Uyyogakālādīsu hi rājāno tattha ṭhatvā “ettakā purato gacchantu, ettakā pacchā, ettakā ubhohi passehi, ettakā hatthīsu abhiruhantu, ettakā assesu, ettakā rathesu tiṭṭhantū”ti evaṃ santhaṃ karonti, mariyādaṃ bandhanti, tasmā taṃ ṭhānaṃ santhāgāranti vuccati. Uyyogaṭṭhānato ca āgantvā yāva gehesu allagomayaparibhaṇḍādīni karonti, tāva dve tīṇi divasāni te rājāno tattha santhambhantītipi santhāgāraṃ. Tesaṃ rājūnaṃ saha atthānusāsanaṃ agārantipi santhāgāraṃ gaṇarājāno hi te[M 3.0012], tasmā uppannakiccaṃ ekassa vasena na chijjati, sabbesaṃ chando laddhuṃ vaṭṭati, tasmā sabbe tattha sannipatitvā anusāsanti. Tena vuttaṃ “saha atthānusāsanaṃ agārantipi santhāgāra”nti. Yasmā panete tattha sannipatitvā “imasmiṃ kāle kasituṃ vaṭṭati, imasmiṃ kāle vapitu”nti evamādinā nayena gharāvāsakiccāni sammantayanti, tasmā chiddāvachiddaṃ [P 3.0017] gharāvāsaṃ tattha santharantītipi santhāgāraṃ. Acirakāritaṃ hotīti kaṭṭhakamma-silākamma-cittakammādivasena susajjitaṃ devavimānaṃ viya adhunā niṭṭhāpitaṃ. Samaṇena vāti ettha yasmā gharavatthupariggahakāleyeva devatā attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gaṇhanti, tasmā “devena vā”ti avatvā “samaṇena vā brāhmaṇena vā kenaci vā manussabhūtenā”ti vuttaṃ.

22. “Thus have I heard”—this is the Sekha Sutta. Therein, “a new assembly hall” means a recently constructed assembly hall; the meaning is a great hall. For during times of mobilization and so on, the kings stand there and make arrangements, saying, “Let this many go in front, this many behind, this many on both flanks; let this many mount elephants, this many horses, this many stand in chariots,” and they establish the boundaries. Therefore, that place is called an assembly hall (santhāgāra). And, having returned from the place of mobilization, for the two or three days until they have prepared their houses with fresh cow-dung plaster and so on, those kings rest and relax there; for this reason also it is an assembly hall. It is also an assembly hall because it is a house for the joint deliberation of affairs for those kings. For they are kings of a republic; therefore, a matter that has arisen is not decided by one alone—it is proper to obtain the consent of all. Therefore, they all assemble there and deliberate. For that reason it was said, “it is also an assembly hall because it is a house for the joint deliberation of affairs.” Furthermore, since they assemble there and consult on the affairs of household life, in such a way as, “At this time it is suitable to plow, at this time it is suitable to sow,” and so on, they thereby put in order the disjointed affairs of household life; for this reason also it is an assembly hall. “It was recently constructed” means it was just now completed, well-adorned by means of woodwork, stonework, painting, and so on, like a celestial mansion. Regarding “by an ascetic...”: here, since deities take their dwelling place at the very time the house-site is acquired, it was not said “by a deity,” but rather “by an ascetic or a brahmin or by some human being.”

Yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsūti santhāgāraṃ niṭṭhitanti sutvā “gacchāma, naṃ passissāmā”ti gantvā dvārakoṭṭhakato paṭṭhāya sabbaṃ oloketvā “idaṃ santhāgāraṃ devavimānasadisaṃ ativiya manoramaṃ sassirikaṃ kena paṭhamaṃ paribhuttaṃ amhākaṃ dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāya assā”ti cintetvā “amhākaṃ ñātiseṭṭhassa paṭhamaṃ diyyamānepi satthunova anucchavikaṃ, dakkhiṇeyyavasena diyyamānepi satthunova anucchavikaṃ, tasmā paṭhamaṃ satthāraṃ paribhuñjāpessāma, bhikkhusaṅghassa āgamanaṃ karissāma, bhikkhusaṅghe āgate tepiṭakaṃ buddhavacanaṃ āgatameva bhavissati, satthāraṃ tiyāmarattiṃ amhākaṃ dhammakathaṃ kathāpessāma, iti tīhi ratanehi paribhuttaṃ mayaṃ pacchā paribhuñjissāma[V 3.0013], evaṃ no dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāya bhavissatī”ti sanniṭṭhānaṃ katvā upasaṅkamiṃsu.

Regarding “They approached where the Blessed One was”: Having heard that the assembly hall was completed, they thought, “Let us go, we will see it.” Having gone, they inspected everything starting from the gatehouse. Reflecting, “This assembly hall is exceedingly delightful and splendid. Who should use it first for our long-lasting welfare and happiness?” They concluded, “Even if offered first to our chief kinsman, it is only fitting for the Teacher. If given by way of a worthy recipient, it is only fitting for the Teacher. Therefore, we will first have the Teacher use it. We will arrange for the community of monks to come. When the community of monks arrives, the Tipiṭaka, the Buddha's word, will also have arrived. We will have the Teacher speak the Dhamma to us for the three watches of the night. Thus, after it has been used by the Three Jewels, we will use it afterward. In this way, it will be for our long-lasting welfare and happiness.” Having made this decision, they approached.

Yena santhāgāraṃ tenupasaṅkamiṃsūti taṃ divasaṃ kira santhāgāraṃ kiñcāpi rājakulānaṃ dassanatthāya devavimānaṃ viya susajjitaṃ hoti supaṭijaggitaṃ, buddhārahaṃ pana katvā appaññattaṃ. Buddhā hi nāma araññajjhāsayā araññārāmā antogāme vaseyyuṃ vā no vā, tasmā bhagavato manaṃ [P 3.0018] jānitvāva paññāpessāmāti cintetvā te bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamiṃsu. Idāni pana manaṃ labhitvā paññāpetukāmā yena santhāgāraṃ tenupasaṅkamiṃsu.

“They approached the place where the assembly hall was”: On that day, it is said, although the assembly hall was beautifully adorned and well-prepared like a celestial mansion for the royal families to see, it was made worthy of a Buddha, but the seating had not yet been prepared. For Buddhas, indeed, are inclined to the forest and delight in the forest; they may or may not reside within a village. Therefore, thinking, “We will prepare the seating only after knowing the Blessed One’s mind,” they approached the Blessed One. But now, having received his consent and wishing to prepare the seating, they approached the place where the assembly hall was.

Sabbasanthariṃ santhāgāraṃ santharitvāti yathā sabbameva santhataṃ hoti, evaṃ taṃ santharāpetvā. Sabbapaṭhamaṃ tāva “gomayaṃ nāma sabbamaṅgalesu vaṭṭatī”ti [M 3.0013] sudhāparikammakatampi bhūmiṃ allagomayena opuñchāpetvā parisukkhabhāvaṃ ñatvā yathā akkantaṭṭhāne padaṃ na paññāyati, evaṃ catujjātiyagandhehi limpāpetvā upari nānāvaṇṇe kaṭasārake santharitvā tesaṃ upari mahāpiṭṭhikakojavake ādiṃ katvā hatthattharaka-assattharaka-sīhattharaka-byagghattharaka-candattharaka-sūriyattharaka-cittattharakādīhi nānāvaṇṇehi attharaṇehi santharitabbakayuttaṃ sabbokāsaṃ santharāpesuṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “sabbasanthariṃ santhāgāraṃ santharitvā”ti.

“Having spread the assembly hall with a complete covering”—this means having had it spread so that it was entirely covered. First of all, thinking, “Cow dung is suitable for all auspicious occasions,” they had the ground, even though prepared with plaster, wiped with fresh, moist cow dung. Knowing it was completely dry, they had it smeared with the four kinds of fragrances in such a way that a footprint would not be visible where stepped upon. On top of this, having spread variegated coarse mats, and upon these, beginning with large carpets such as those spread on an elephant's back, they had the entire space suitable for being covered spread with various colored coverings such as elephant-figure rugs, horse-figure rugs, lion-figure rugs, tiger-figure rugs, moon-figure rugs, sun-figure rugs, and rugs with floral and creeper designs. Therefore it is said, “having spread the assembly hall with a complete covering.”

Āsanāni paññāpetvāti majjhaṭṭhāne tāva maṅgalatthambhaṃ nissāya mahārahaṃ buddhāsanaṃ paññāpetvā tattha yaṃ yaṃ mudukañca manoramañca paccattharaṇaṃ, taṃ taṃ paccattharitvā bhagavato lohitakaṃ manuññadassanaṃ upadhānaṃ upadahitvā upari suvaṇṇarajatatārakavicittaṃ vitānaṃ bandhitvā gandhadāmapupphadāmapattadāmādīhi paccattharaṇehi alaṅkaritvā samantā dvādasahatthaṭṭhāne pupphajālaṃ karitvā tiṃsahatthamattaṃ ṭhānaṃ paṭasāṇiyā parikkhipāpetvā [P 3.0019] pacchimabhittiṃ nissāya bhikkhusaṅghassa pallaṅkapīṭha-apassayapīṭha-muṇḍapīṭhāni paññāpetvā upari setapaccattharaṇehi paccattharāpetvā pācīnabhittiṃ nissāya attano attano mahāpiṭṭhikakojavake paññāpetvā haṃsalomādipūritāni upadhānāni ṭhapāpesuṃ “evaṃ akilamamānā sabbarattiṃ dhammaṃ suṇissāmā”ti. Idaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “āsanāni paññāpetvā”ti.

“Having prepared the seats”—this means that first, in the central place, near the auspicious pillar, they had the Buddha's seat, worthy of great ones, prepared. On top of that, they spread whatever covering was soft and pleasing, and for the Blessed One they placed nearby a delightful-looking pillow, red on both sides. Above the seat, they fastened a canopy adorned with gold and silver stars and decorated it with garlands of perfume, flowers, and leaves. All around, in a space of twelve cubits, they made a flower-net and had a space of about thirty cubits enclosed with a cloth screen. Near the western wall, for the Sangha of monks, they had seats prepared—such as couches, seats with backrests, and seats without backrests—and had white coverings spread over them. Near the eastern wall, for themselves, they had large carpets prepared and had pillows filled with swan's down and the like placed, thinking, “Thus, without fatigue, we will listen to the Dhamma all night.” This is what is meant by “having prepared the seats.”

Udakamaṇikanti [V 3.0014] mahākucchikaṃ udakacāṭiṃ. Upaṭṭhapetvāti evaṃ bhagavā ca bhikkhusaṅgho ca yathāruciyā hatthe vā dhovissanti pāde vā, mukhaṃ vā vikkhālessantīti tesu tesu ṭhānesu maṇivaṇṇassa udakassa pūrāpetvā vāsatthāya nānāpupphāni ceva udakavāsacuṇṇāni ca pakkhipitvā kadalipaṇṇehi pidahitvā patiṭṭhāpesuṃ. Idaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “upaṭṭhapetvā”ti.

“Water vessel” means a large-bellied water jar. “Having set them up” means: thinking, “Thus the Blessed One and the Sangha of monks may wash their hands or feet, or rinse their mouths, according to their wish,” they had vessels in various places filled with water the color of a jewel. For the purpose of scenting, they put in various flowers and fragrant powders for water, covered them with banana leaves, and set them in place. This is said with reference to “having set them up.”

Telappadīpaṃ āropetvāti rajatasuvaṇṇādimayadaṇḍāsu dīpikāsu yonakarūpakirātarūpakādīnaṃ hatthe ṭhapitasuvaṇṇarajatādimayakapallakādīsu ca telappadīpaṃ jalayitvāti attho. Yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsūti ettha pana te sakyarājāno na kevalaṃ santhāgārameva, atha kho yojanāvaṭṭe kapilavatthusmiṃ nagaravīthiyopi sammajjāpetvā dhaje [M 3.0014] ussāpetvā gehadvāresu puṇṇaghaṭe ca kadaliyo ca ṭhapāpetvā sakalanagaraṃ dīpamālādīhi vippakiṇṇatārakaṃ viya katvā “khīrapāyake dārake khīraṃ pāyetha, dahare kumāre lahuṃ lahuṃ bhojetvā sayāpetha, uccāsaddaṃ mā karittha, ajja ekarattiṃ satthā antogāme vasissati, buddhā nāma appasaddakāmā hontī”ti bheriṃ carāpetvā sayaṃ daṇḍadīpikā ādāya yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu.

“Having lit oil lamps”—this means they lit oil lamps on lamp stands made of silver, gold, and the like, and in lamp-bowls made of gold, silver, and the like, placed in the hands of figures of Yonakas, Kirātas, and so on. Regarding “they approached where the Blessed One was”: those Sakyan kings did not only prepare the assembly hall. Rather, within a circumference of one yojana in Kapilavatthu, they also had the city streets swept, had banners raised, and had full water pots and banana trees placed at the house doors. Having made the entire city like a sky with scattered stars with rows of lamps and so forth, they had a drum beaten to announce: “Let the milk-drinking children be fed milk. Feed the young boys quickly and put them to sleep. Do not make a loud noise. Today, for this one night, the Teacher will dwell within the town. Buddhas, it is said, desire quiet.” Then, taking staff-lamps themselves, they approached the place where the Blessed One was.

Atha [P 3.0020] kho bhagavā nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya saddhiṃ bhikkhusaṅghena yena navaṃ santhāgāraṃ tenupasaṅkamīti. “Yassa dāni, bhante, bhagavā kālaṃ maññatī”ti evaṃ kira kāle ārocite bhagavā lākhārasena tintarattakoviḷārapupphavaṇṇaṃ rattadupaṭṭaṃ kattariyā padumaṃ kantanto viya saṃvidhāya timaṇḍalaṃ paṭicchādento nivāsetvā suvaṇṇapāmaṅgena padumakalāpaṃ parikkhipanto viya vijjullatāsassirikaṃ kāyabandhanaṃ bandhitvā rattakambalena gajakumbhaṃ pariyonaddhanto viya ratanasatubbedhe suvaṇṇagghike pavāḷajālaṃ khipamāno viya suvaṇṇacetiye rattakambalakañcukaṃ paṭimuñcanto viya gacchantaṃ puṇṇacandaṃ rattavaṇṇavalāhakena paṭicchādayamāno viya kañcanapabbatamatthake supakkalākhārasaṃ parisiñcanto viya cittakūṭapabbatamatthakaṃ vijjullatāya parikkhipanto viya ca sacakkavāḷasineruyugandharaṃ mahāpathaviṃ cāletvā gahitaṃ nigrodhapallavasamānavaṇṇaṃ rattavarapaṃsukūlaṃ pārupitvā gandhakuṭidvārato nikkhami kañcanaguhato sīho viya udayapabbatakūṭato puṇṇacando viya ca. Nikkhamitvā pana gandhakuṭipamukhe aṭṭhāsi.

Then the Blessed One, having dressed and taken his bowl and robe, together with the Sangha of monks, approached the new assembly hall. When the time was announced, “Venerable sir, the Blessed One now knows the time,” the Blessed One dressed, covering the three circles. He arranged his red double-layered lower robe—the color of a koviḷāra flower, moist and red with lac-dye—as if cutting a lotus with scissors. He tied his waistband, resplendent like a flash of lightning, as if encircling a cluster of lotuses with a golden cord. Then, as if covering an elephant's frontal globes with a red blanket; as if casting a net of coral over a great golden reliquary one hundred cubits high; as if putting a red blanket-cloak on a golden cetiya; as if covering the full moon in motion with a red cloud; as if pouring well-cooked lac-dye over the peak of a golden mountain; and as if encircling the peak of Cittakūṭa mountain with a flash of lightning, He donned his excellent red rag-robe, the color of a banyan sprout, which had been taken after shaking the great earth along with the Cakkavāḷa, Sineru, and Yugandhara mountains. He emerged from the door of the Gandhakuti like a king of lions from a golden cave, and like the full moon from the peak of the eastern mountain. Then, having emerged, He stood at the front of the Gandhakuti.

Athassa [V 3.0015] kāyato meghamukhehi vijjukalāpā viya rasmiyo nikkhamitvā suvaṇṇarasadhārāparisekamañjaripattapupphaphalaviṭape viya ārāmarukkhe kariṃsu. Tāvadeva ca attano attano pattacīvaramādāya mahābhikkhusaṅgho bhagavantaṃ parivāresi. Te pana parivāretvā ṭhitā bhikkhū evarūpā ahesuṃ appicchā santuṭṭhā pavivittā asaṃsaṭṭhā āraddhavīriyā [P 3.0021] vattāro vacanakkhamā codakā pāpagarahī sīlasampannā samādhisampannā paññāvimuttivimuttiñāṇadassanasampannāti. Tehi parivārito bhagavā rattakambalaparikkhitto viya suvaṇṇakkhandho rattapadumasaṇḍamajjhagatā viya suvaṇṇanāvā pavāḷavedikāparikkhitto viya suvaṇṇapāsādo virocittha. Sāriputtamoggallānādayo mahātherāpi naṃ meghavaṇṇaṃ paṃsukūlaṃ [M 3.0015] pārupitvā maṇivammavammikā viya mahānāgā parivārayiṃsu vantarāgā bhinnakilesā vijaṭitajaṭā chinnabandhanā kule vā gaṇe vā alaggā.

Then, from His body, rays emerged like bundles of lightning from the mouths of clouds, making the trees of the grove appear as if they were shoots, leaves, flowers, fruits, and branches sprinkled with streams of golden liquid. At that very moment, the great community of monks, taking their own bowls and robes, surrounded the Blessed One. Those monks who stood surrounding Him were of such a nature: of few wishes, easily contented, dwelling in seclusion, not mingling with others, of aroused energy, able to speak rightly, able to endure being spoken to, able to admonish oneself, censuring of evil, endowed with virtue, endowed with concentration, and endowed with wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. Surrounded by them, the Blessed One shone like a mass of gold wrapped in a red blanket, like a golden boat amidst a grove of red lotuses, and like a golden palace surrounded by a coral railing. The great elders, such as Sāriputta and Moggallāna—who had vomited out passion, whose defilements were destroyed, whose tangle was unraveled, whose bonds were severed, and who were unattached to a family of supporters or to a group—also surrounded Him, having donned dust-heap robes the color of a rain-cloud, like great elephants covered in jeweled armor.

Iti bhagavā sayaṃ vītarāgo vītarāgehi, vītadoso vītadosehi, vītamoho vītamohehi, nittaṇho nittaṇhehi, nikkileso nikkilesehi, sayaṃ buddho bahussutabuddhehi parivārito, pattaparivāritaṃ viya kesaraṃ, kesaraparivāritā viya kaṇṇikā, aṭṭhanāgasahassaparivārito viya chaddanto nāgarājā, navutihaṃsasahassaparivārito viya dhataraṭṭho haṃsarājā, senaṅgaparivārito viya cakkavatti, marugaṇaparivārito viya sakko devarājā, brahmagaṇaparivārito viya hāritamahābrahmā, tārāgaṇaparivārito viya puṇṇacando, asamena buddhavesena aparimāṇena buddhavilāsena kapilavatthugamanamaggaṃ paṭipajji.

Thus the Blessed One, Himself free from passion, was surrounded by those free from passion; Himself free from hatred, was surrounded by those free from hatred; Himself free from delusion, was surrounded by those free from delusion; Himself free from craving, was surrounded by those free from craving; Himself free from defilements, was surrounded by those free from defilements; Himself fully enlightened, was surrounded by those of great learning who were enlightened. Like a stamen surrounded by petals, like a pericarp surrounded by stamens, like Chaddanta, the king of elephants, surrounded by eight thousand elephants, like Dhataraṭṭha, the king of geese, surrounded by ninety thousand geese, like a wheel-turning monarch surrounded by the four divisions of his army, like Sakka, the king of gods, surrounded by the host of gods, like the great Brahmā Hārita surrounded by the host of Brahmās, and like the full moon surrounded by the host of stars—with an incomparable Buddha-appearance and limitless Buddha-grace, He set out on the road to Kapilavatthu.

Athassa puratthimakāyato suvaṇṇavaṇṇā rasmī uṭṭhahitvā asītihatthaṭṭhānaṃ aggahesi. Pacchimakāyato dakkhiṇahatthato, vāmahatthato suvaṇṇavaṇṇā rasmī uṭṭhahitvā asītihatthaṭṭhānaṃ aggahesi. Upari kesantato paṭṭhāya sabbakesāvattehi moragīvavaṇṇā rasmī uṭṭhahitvā gaganatale asītihatthaṭṭhānaṃ aggahesi. Heṭṭhā pādatalehi pavāḷavaṇṇā rasmī uṭṭhahitvā ghanapathaviyaṃ asītihatthaṭṭhānaṃ aggahesi. Evaṃ samantā asītihatthamattaṃ ṭhānaṃ chabbaṇṇā buddharasmiyo vijjotamānā [P 3.0022] vipphandamānā kañcanadaṇḍadīpikāhi niccharitvā ākāsaṃ pakkhandajālā viya cātuddīpikamahāmeghato nikkhantavijjullatā viya vidhāviṃsu. Sabbadisābhāgā suvaṇṇacampakapupphehi vikiriyamānā viya, suvaṇṇaghaṭā nikkhantasuvaṇṇarasadhārāhi [V 3.0016] siñcamānā viya, pasāritasuvaṇṇapaṭaparikkhittā viya, verambhavātasamuṭṭhitakiṃsukakaṇikārapupphacuṇṇasamokiṇṇā viya vippakiriṃsu.

Then from the front of His body, a golden-colored ray arose and took up a space of eighty cubits. From the back of His body, from His right hand, and from His left hand, a golden-colored ray arose and took up a space of eighty cubits. Above, starting from the tips of the hair, from all the hair-whorls, a peacock-neck-colored ray arose and took up a space of eighty cubits in the sky. Below, from the soles of His feet, a coral-colored ray arose and took up a space of eighty cubits in the solid earth. Thus, all around, in a space of about eighty cubits, the six-colored Buddha-rays, shining and pulsating, darted about like a mass of flames leaping into the sky after shooting out from golden torches, and like a creeper of lightning emerging from a great cloud that covers the four continents. All the regions of the directions appeared as if being scattered with golden campaka flowers, as if being sprinkled with streams of golden liquid emerging from golden pots, as if covered with outstretched golden cloths, and as if strewn with the powder of kiṃsuka and kaṇikāra flowers raised up by the Verambha wind.

Bhagavatopi asītianubyañjanabyāmappabhādvattiṃsavaralakkhaṇasamujjalaṃ sarīraṃ samuggatatārakaṃ viya gaganatalaṃ, vikasitamiva padumavanaṃ, sabbapāliphullo viya yojanasatiko pāricchattako, paṭipāṭiyā ṭhapitānaṃ dvattiṃsūcandānaṃ dvattiṃsasūriyānaṃ dvattiṃsacakkavattīnaṃ dvattiṃsadevarājānaṃ dvattiṃsamahābrahmānaṃ [M 3.0016] siriyā siriṃ abhibhavamānaṃ viya virocittha, yathā taṃ dasahi pāramīhi dasahi upapāramīhi dasahi paramatthapāramīhi supūritāhi samatiṃsapāramitāhi alaṅkataṃ. Kappasatasahasādhikāni cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni dinnadānaṃ rakkhitasīlaṃ katakalyāṇakammaṃ ekasmiṃ attabhāve osaritvā vipākaṃ dātuṃ ṭhānaṃ alabhamānaṃ sambādhapattaṃ viya ahosi. Nāvāsahassabhaṇḍaṃ ekanāvaṃ āropanakālo viya, sakaṭasahassabhaṇḍaṃ ekasakaṭaṃ āropanakālo viya, pañcavīsatiyā nadīnaṃ oghassa sambhijja mukhadvāre ekato rāsībhūtakālo viya ca ahosi.

The Blessed One’s body, resplendent with the eighty minor characteristics, the fathom-wide radiance, and the thirty-two excellent major characteristics, shone forth like the expanse of the sky with its stars well-risen, like a blossomed lotus grove, and like the Pāricchattaka tree, a hundred yojanas in size, in full bloom from root to tip. It shone as if overwhelming with His own splendor the splendor of thirty-two moons, thirty-two suns, thirty-two wheel-turning monarchs, thirty-two kings of gods, and thirty-two great Brahmās arranged in sequence, adorned as it was by the thirty perfections, which were well-fulfilled through the ten perfections, the ten supplementary perfections, and the ten ultimate perfections. The giving that was given, the virtue that was protected, and the wholesome kamma that was done for four incalculable aeons and over one hundred thousand kappas, being unable to find the opportunity to descend and give its result in a single existence, was as if it had reached a state of constriction. It was like the time of loading the cargo of a thousand boats onto a single boat, like the time of loading the cargo of a thousand carts onto a single cart, and like the time when the currents of twenty-five rivers, having merged, become a single mass at the mouth of the ocean.

Imāya buddhasiriyā obhāsamānassāpi ca bhagavato purato anekāni daṇḍadīpikasahassāni ukkhipiṃsu. Tathā pacchato. Vāmapasse dakkhiṇapasse. Jātikusumacampakavanamallikarattuppalanīluppalamakulasinduvārapupphāni [P 3.0023] ceva nīlapītādivaṇṇasugandhagandhacuṇṇāni ca cātuddīpikameghavissaṭṭhodakavuṭṭhiyo viya vippakiriṃsu. Pañcaṅgikatūriyanigghosā ceva buddhadhammasaṅghaguṇappaṭisaṃyuttā thutighosā ca sabbadisā pūrayiṃsu. Devamanussanāgasupaṇṇagandhabbayakkhādīnaṃ akkhīni amatapānaṃ viya labhiṃsu. Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne ṭhatvā padasahassena gamanavaṇṇaṃ vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Tatridaṃ mukhamattaṃ –

And even as the Blessed One was shining with this Buddha-splendor, many thousands of torches were raised before Him, and likewise behind Him, on His left side, and on His right side. Jāti flowers, campaka flowers, wild jasmine, red lotuses, blue lotuses, buds, and sinduvāra flowers, as well as fragrant powders of good scent and of blue, yellow, and other colors, were scattered like showers of water released from a great cloud covering the four continents. The sounds of the five kinds of musical instruments and sounds of praise connected with the virtues of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Sangha filled all directions. The eyes of gods, humans, nāgas, supaṇṇas, gandhabbas, yakkhas, and others received as if a drink of the deathless. Furthermore, standing in this place, it is fitting to speak of the excellence of His gait with a thousand verses. Therein, this is but the introduction:

“Evaṃ sabbaṅgasampanno, kampayanto vasundharaṃ;

Aheṭhayanto pāṇāni, yāti lokavināyako.

Thus, endowed with all noble qualities, making the earth tremble, yet not harming living beings, the Leader of the World proceeds.

Dakkhiṇaṃ paṭhamaṃ pādaṃ, uddharanto narāsabho;

Gacchanto sirisampanno, sobhate dvipaduttamo.

Lifting His right foot first, the Bull among Men, endowed with splendor, the Foremost of Bipeds shines as He walks.

Gacchato [V 3.0017] buddhaseṭṭhassa, heṭṭhā pādatalaṃ mudu;

Samaṃ samphusate bhūmiṃ, rajasā nupalippati.

As the Supreme Buddha walks, the soft sole of His foot underneath evenly touches the ground; it is not smeared by dust.

Ninnaṭṭhānaṃ unnamati, gacchante lokanāyake;

Unnatañca samaṃ hoti, pathavī ca acetanā.

When the Leader of the World walks, the low places rise up; and the high places become level, although the earth is without consciousness.

Pāsāṇā sakkharā ceva, kathalā khāṇukaṇṭakā;

Sabbe maggā vivajjanti, gacchante lokanāyake.

When the Leader of the World proceeds, all stones, gravel, potsherds, stumps, and thorns avoid the path.

Nātidūre [M 3.0017] uddharati, naccāsanne ca nikkhipaṃ;

Aghaṭṭayanto niyyāti, ubho jāṇū ca gopphake.

He does not lift His foot too far, nor set it down too near; without knocking His knees or ankles, He proceeds.

Nātisīghaṃ [P 3.0024] pakkamati, sampannacaraṇo muni;

Na cātisaṇikaṃ yāti, gacchamāno samāhito.

He does not step too quickly, the sage of perfect conduct; nor does He go too slowly, proceeding with composure.

Uddhaṃ adho ca tiriyaṃ, disañca vidisaṃ tathā;

Na pekkhamāno so yāti, yugamattamhi pekkhati.

Upwards, downwards, and across, and likewise in the cardinal and intermediate directions; He does not go looking around, He gazes only on the extent of a yoke.

Nāgavikkantacāro so, gamane sobhate jino;

Cāruṃ gacchati lokaggo, hāsayanto sadevake.

He whose gait is like that of a lordly elephant, in His walking, the Conqueror shines forth; the Foremost of the World walks gracefully, delighting the world with its devas.

Uḷurājāva sobhanto, catucārīva kesarī;

Tosayanto bahū satte, puraṃ seṭṭhaṃ upāgamī”ti.

Shining like the king of stars, and like a lion walking freely, delighting many beings, He approached the excellent city.”

Vaṇṇakālo nāma kiresa, evaṃvidhesu kālesu buddhassa sarīravaṇṇe vā guṇavaṇṇe vā dhammakathikassa thāmoyeva pamāṇaṃ cuṇṇiyapadehi vā gāthābandhena vā yattakaṃ sakkoti, tattakaṃ vattabbaṃ. Dukkathitanti na vattabbaṃ. Appamāṇavaṇṇā hi buddhā, tesaṃ buddhāpi anavasesato vaṇṇaṃ [V 3.0018] vattuṃ asamatthā, pageva itarā pajāti. Iminā sirivilāsena alaṅkatappaṭiyattaṃ sakyarājapuraṃ pavisitvā bhagavā pasannacittena janena gandhadhūmavāsacuṇṇādīhi pūjayamāno santhāgāraṃ pāvisi. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho bhagavā nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya saddhiṃ bhikkhusaṅghena yena evaṃ santhāgāraṃ tenupasaṅkamī”ti.

It is said that this is called the time for proclaiming virtues. On such occasions, whether praising the Buddha’s bodily form or his qualities, the strength of the Dhamma speaker is the only measure; as much as one is able to speak, whether in prose or in verse, so much should be spoken. It should not be said, “It is poorly spoken.” For the Buddhas are of immeasurable virtue; even Buddhas are unable to describe their virtues completely, let alone other beings. Having entered the royal city of the Sakyans, which was adorned and prepared with this majestic splendor, the Blessed One, being honored by people with devoted minds with perfumes, incense, fragrant powders, and the like, entered the assembly hall. Therefore it is said: “Then the Blessed One, having dressed, taking his bowl and outer robe, together with the community of monks, approached the new assembly hall.”

Bhagavantaṃyeva purakkhatvāti bhagavantaṃ purato katvā. Tattha bhagavā bhikkhūnañceva upāsakānañca majjhe nisinno gandhodakena nhāpetvā dukūlacumbaṭakena vodakaṃ katvā jātihiṅgulakena majjitvā rattakambalapaliveṭhite [P 3.0025] pīṭhe ṭhapitarattasuvaṇṇaghanapaṭimā viya ativirocittha. Ayaṃ panettha porāṇānaṃ vaṇṇabhaṇanamaggo –

“Having placed the Blessed One at the forefront” means having placed the Blessed One in front. There, the Blessed One, seated in the midst of the monks and lay devotees, having been bathed with fragrant water, dried with a fine white cloth, polished with pure vermilion, on a seat wrapped with a red blanket, shone forth exceedingly like a solid statue of red gold. This, moreover, is the way of proclaiming the virtues by the ancients:

“Gantvāna maṇḍalamāḷaṃ, nāgavikkantacaraṇo;

Obhāsayanto lokaggo, nisīdi varamāsane.

“Having gone to the assembly hall, he whose gait is like that of a lordly elephant, illuminating, the Foremost of the World, sat on the excellent seat.”

Tasmiṃ [M 3.0018] nisinno naradammasārathi,

Devātidevo satapuññalakkhaṇo;

Buddhāsane majjhagato virocati,

Suvaṇṇanekkhaṃ viya paṇḍukambale.

Seated there, the Charioteer of men to be tamed, the God surpassing gods, endowed with the marks of a hundred merits, shines forth in the midst of the assembly on the Buddha-seat, like a golden ornament on the Paṇḍukambala stone.

Nekkhaṃ jambonadasseva, nikkhittaṃ paṇḍukambale;

Virocati vītamalo, maṇiverocano yathā.

Like an ornament of Jambu-river gold placed upon the Paṇḍukambala stone, so shines the Stainless One, like a radiant, flawless jewel.

Mahāsālova samphullo, nerurājāvalaṅkato;

Suvaṇṇayūpasaṅkāso, padumo kokanado yathā.

Like a great Sāla tree in full bloom, adorned like the king of mountains; like a golden sacrificial post, like a red paduma lotus.

Jalanto dīparukkhova, pabbatagge yathā sikhī;

Devānaṃ pāricchattova, sabbaphullo virocathā”ti.

“Like a shining lamp-tree, like a fire on a mountain peak, and like the fully blossomed Pāricchattaka tree of the devas, he shone forth.”

Kāpilavatthave [V 3.0019] sakye bahudeva rattiṃ dhammiyā kathāyāti ettha dhammī kathā nāma santhāgāraanumodanappaṭisaṃyuttā pakiṇṇakakathā veditabbā. Tadā hi bhagavā ākāsagaṅgaṃ otārento viya pathavojaṃ ākaḍḍhanto viya mahājambuṃ khandhe gahetvā cālento viya yojanikaṃ madhubhaṇḍaṃ cakkayantena pīḷetvā madhupānaṃ pāyamāno viya kāpilavatthavānaṃ sakyānaṃ hitasukhāvahaṃ [P 3.0026] pakiṇṇakakathaṃ kathesi. “Āvāsadānaṃ nāmetaṃ mahārāja mahantaṃ, tumhākaṃ āvāso mayā paribhutto bhikkhusaṅghena paribhutto mayā ca bhikkhusaṅghena ca paribhutto pana dhammaratanena paribhutto yevāti tīhi ratanehi paribhutto nāma hoti. Āvāsadānasmiñhi dinne sabbadānaṃ dinnameva hoti. Bhūmaṭṭhakapaṇṇasālāya vā sākhāmaṇḍapassa vāpi ānisaṃso nāma paricchindituṃ na sakkā”ti nānānayavicittaṃ bahuṃ dhammakathaṃ kathetvā –
