Here, in the phrase “for much of the night, a Dhamma talk to the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu,” the Dhamma talk should be understood as a miscellaneous discourse connected with the rejoicing in the assembly hall. For at that time, the Blessed One, as if bringing down the celestial Ganges, as if drawing up the earth’s essence, as if taking the great Jambu tree by its branches and shaking it, as if pressing a yojana-sized pot of honey with a machine and causing them to drink the honey-drink, gave a miscellaneous discourse bringing welfare and happiness to the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu. “Great kings, this gift of a dwelling is of great fruit. Your dwelling has been used by me and used by the Sangha of monks. When it is used, it is indeed used by the Jewel of the Dhamma. Thus, it is called ‘used by the Three Jewels.’ For when the gift of a dwelling is given, all gifts are indeed given. The benefit of a leaf-hut on the ground or even a pavilion of branches cannot be measured.” Having delivered a diverse and splendid Dhamma talk in many ways—

“Sītaṃ uṇhaṃ paṭihanti, tato vāḷamigāni ca;

Sarīsape ca makase, sisire cāpi vuṭṭhiyo.

“A dwelling wards off cold and heat, and furthermore, beasts of prey; and reptiles and mosquitoes, and also rains in the cold season.

Tato vātātapo ghoro, sañjāto paṭihaññati;

Leṇatthañca sukhatthañca, jhāyituñca vipassituṃ.

Furthermore, fierce wind and sun’s heat, when they arise, are dispelled. It is for the purpose of shelter and for comfort, for meditating and for insight.

Vihāradānaṃ saṅghassa, aggaṃ buddhena vaṇṇitaṃ;

Tasmā hi paṇḍito poso, sampassaṃ atthamattano.

The gift of a dwelling to the Sangha is praised by the Buddha as supreme; therefore indeed, a wise person, seeing his own welfare,

Vihāre [M 3.0019] kāraye ramme, vāsayettha bahussute;

Tesaṃ annañca pānañca, vatthasenāsanāni ca.

Should have delightful dwellings built, and have the learned reside there. To them, he should give food and drink, and clothing, beds, and seats.

Dadeyya ujubhūtesu, vippasannena cetasā;

Te tassa dhammaṃ desenti, sabbadukkhāpanūdanaṃ;

Yaṃ so dhammaṃ idhaññāya, parinibbāti anāsavo”ti. (cūḷava. 295) –

He should give to the upright with a serene mind. They teach him the Dhamma that dispels all suffering. Having understood that Dhamma here, he, being without taints, attains Parinibbāna.”

Evaṃ ayampi āvāse ānisaṃso, ayampi ānisaṃsoti bahudevarattiṃ atirekataraṃ diyaḍḍhayāmaṃ āvāsānisaṃsakathaṃ [V 3.0020] kathesi. Tattha imā gāthāva saṅgahaṃ āruḷhā, pakiṇṇakadhammadesanā pana saṅgahaṃ na ārohati. Sandassesītiādīni [P 3.0027] vuttatthāneva.

Thus, saying, “This too is a benefit of a dwelling, this too is a benefit,” for much of the night, for more than one and a half watches, he spoke on the benefits of a dwelling. Therein, only these verses were included in the canonical collection, but the miscellaneous Dhamma teaching was not included in the collection. The meaning of `Sandassesi` and so forth is as has been stated.

Āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ āmantesīti dhammakathaṃ kathāpetukāmo jānāpesi. Atha kasmā sāriputtamahāmoggallānamahākassapādīsu asītimahātheresu vijjamānesu bhagavā ānandattherassa bhāramakāsīti. Parisajjhāsayavasena. Āyasmā hi ānando bahussutānaṃ aggo, pahosi parimaṇḍalehi padabyañjanehi madhuradhammakathaṃ kathetunti sākiyamaṇḍale pākaṭo paññāto. Tassa sakyarājūhi vihāraṃ gantvāpi dhammakathā sutapubbā, orodhā pana nesaṃ na yathāruciyā vihāraṃ gantuṃ labhanti, tesaṃ etadahosi – “aho vata bhagavā appaṃyeva dhammakathaṃ kathetvā amhākaṃ ñātiseṭṭhassa ānandassa bhāraṃ kareyyā”ti. Tesaṃ ajjhāsayavasena bhagavā tasseva bhāramakāsi.

“He addressed the Venerable Ānanda” means: wishing to have a Dhamma talk delivered, he made it known. Now, why, when the eighty great elders such as Sāriputta, Mahāmoggallāna, and Mahākassapa were present, did the Blessed One place the burden on the Venerable Ānanda? It was due to the inclination of the assembly. For the Venerable Ānanda was foremost among those of great learning; he was able to deliver a sweet Dhamma talk with well-rounded words and phrases, and thus he was well-known and recognized in the Sakyan circle. The Sakyan kings had previously gone to the monastery and heard his Dhamma talk. Their women of the royal household, however, could not get to go to the monastery as they pleased. This thought occurred to them: “Oh, if only the Blessed One, having given a brief Dhamma talk, would place the burden on our noble kinsman, Ānanda!” Because of their inclination, the Blessed One placed the burden on him alone.

Sekho pāṭipadoti paṭipannako sekhasamaṇo. So tuyhaṃ paṭibhātu upaṭṭhātu, tassa paṭipadaṃ desehīti paṭipadāya puggalaṃ niyametvā dasseti. Kasmā pana bhagavā imaṃ paṭipadaṃ niyamesi? Bahūhi kāraṇehi. Ime tāva sakyā maṅgalasālāya maṅgalaṃ paccāsīsanti vaḍḍhiṃ icchanti, ayañca sekhapaṭipadā mayhaṃ sāsane maṅgalapaṭipadā vaḍḍhamānakapaṭipadātipi imaṃ paṭipadaṃ niyamesi. Tassañca parisati sekhāva bahū nisinnā, te attanā paṭividdhaṭṭhāne kathīyamāne akilamantāva sallakkhessantītipi imaṃ paṭipadaṃ niyamesi. Āyasmā ca ānando sekhapaṭisambhidāpattova, so attanā paṭividdhe paccakkhaṭṭhāne kathento akilamanto viññāpetuṃ sakkhissatītipi imaṃ paṭipadaṃ niyamesi. Sekhapaṭipadāya ca tissopi sikkhā osaṭā[M 3.0020], tattha adhisīlasikkhāya [P 3.0028] kathitāya sakalaṃ vinayapiṭakaṃ kathitameva hoti, adhicittasikkhāya kathitāya sakalaṃ suttantapiṭakaṃ kathitaṃ hoti, adhipaññāsikkhāya kathitāya sakalaṃ abhidhammapiṭakaṃ kathitaṃ hoti, ānando ca bahussuto tipiṭakadharo, so pahoti tīhi piṭakehi tisso sikkhā kathetuṃ, evaṃ kathite sakyānaṃ maṅgalameva vaḍḍhiyeva bhavissatītipi imaṃ paṭipadaṃ niyamesi.

“The trainee’s practice”: this means the trainee-monk who is engaged in the practice. “May he be clear to you; teach his practice”—thus, having specified the person by the practice, he shows it. But why did the Blessed One specify this practice? For many reasons. Firstly, these Sakyans in the hall of blessings hope for blessings and desire growth, and this practice of the trainee in my Dispensation is a practice of blessing, a practice conducive to growth—for this reason too, he specified this practice. And in that assembly, many trainees were seated; when what they have personally penetrated is being taught, they will be able to understand it without becoming weary—for this reason too, he specified this practice. Moreover, the Venerable Ānanda has attained the analytical knowledge of a trainee; he, teaching about a matter he has personally penetrated and directly experienced, will be able to make it known without becoming weary—for this reason too, he specified this practice. And in the trainee’s practice, the three trainings are also included: when the training in higher virtue is taught, the entire Vinaya Piṭaka is indeed taught; when the training in higher mind is taught, the entire Suttanta Piṭaka is taught; when the training in higher wisdom is taught, the entire Abhidhamma Piṭaka is taught. And Ānanda is of great learning, a bearer of the Three Piṭakas; he is capable of teaching the three trainings by means of the Three Piṭakas. When it is taught thus, for the Sakyans there will be only blessing and only growth—for this reason too, he specified this practice.

Piṭṭhi me āgilāyatīti kasmā āgilāyati? Bhagavato hi chabbassāni padhānaṃ padahantassa [V 3.0021] mahantaṃ kāyadukkhaṃ ahosi, athassa aparabhāge mahallakakāle piṭṭhivāto uppajji. Akāraṇaṃ vā etaṃ. Pahoti hi bhagavā uppannaṃ vedanaṃ vikkhambhetvā ekampi dvepi sattāhe ekapallaṅkena nisīdituṃ. Santhāgārasālaṃ pana catūhi iriyāpathehi paribhuñjitukāmo ahosi, tattha pādadhovanaṭṭhānato yāva dhammāsanā agamāsi, ettake ṭhāne gamanaṃ nipphannaṃ. Dhammāsanaṃ patto thokaṃ ṭhatvā nisīdi, ettake ṭhānaṃ. Diyaḍḍhayāmaṃ dhammāsane nisīdi, ettake ṭhāne nisajjā nipphannā. Idāni dakkhiṇena passena thokaṃ nipanne sayanaṃ nipphajjissatīti evaṃ catūhi iriyāpathehi paribhuñjitukāmo ahosi. Upādinnakasarīrañca nāma “no āgilāyatī”ti na vattabbaṃ, tasmā ciraṃ nisajjāya sañjātaṃ appakampi āgilāyanaṃ gahetvā evamāha.

“My back is aching”—why was it aching? For the Blessed One, who strove for six years, great bodily pain arose; then, in a later part of his life, in his old age, a wind in the back arose. Or, this was without cause. For the Blessed One is capable of suppressing an arisen feeling and sitting in one cross-legged posture for one day, two days, or even a week. But he wished to make use of the assembly hall in the four postures. There, he went from the place for washing feet up to the Dhamma seat; in that space, the posture of walking was accomplished. Having reached the Dhamma seat, he stood for a short while and then sat down; in that space, the posture of standing was accomplished. He sat on the Dhamma seat for one and a half watches; in that space, the posture of sitting was accomplished. “Now, by lying down for a short while on my right side, the posture of lying down will be accomplished”—thus he wished to make use of it in the four postures. And of a body that is the result of past appropriation, it cannot be said, “it does not ache”; therefore, taking even the slight ache that arose from prolonged sitting, he spoke thus.

Saṅghāṭiṃ paññāpetvāti santhāgārassa kira ekapasse te rājāno paṭṭasāṇiṃ parikkhipāpetvā kappiyamañcakaṃ paññapetvā kappiyapaccattharaṇena attharitvā upari suvaṇṇa-tāraka-gandhamālā-dāmapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ vitānaṃ bandhitvā gandhatelappadīpaṃ āropayiṃsu “appeva nāma satthā dhammāsanato [P 3.0029] vuṭṭhāya thokaṃ vissamanto idha nipajjeyya, evaṃ no imaṃ santhāgāraṃ bhagavatā catūhi iriyāpathehi paribhuttaṃ dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāya bhavissatī”ti. Satthāpi tadeva sandhāya tattha saṅghāṭiṃ paññapetvā nipajji. Uṭṭhānasaññaṃ manasi karitvāti ettakaṃ kālaṃ atikkamitvā vuṭṭhahissāmīti vuṭṭhānasaññaṃ citte ṭhapetvā.

“Having had the outer robe spread out”: It is said that on one side of the assembly hall, those kings, having had a cloth screen set up around it, had a suitable couch prepared, spreading it with a suitable covering, and having tied a canopy above, adorned with golden stars, fragrant garlands, and floral wreaths, they lit a lamp with fragrant oil, thinking: “Perhaps the Teacher, rising from the Dhamma seat and resting for a short while, might lie down here. Thus, this assembly hall of ours, having been used by the Blessed One in the four postures, will be for our welfare and happiness for a long time.” The Teacher, too, with that very intention, had his outer robe spread out there and lay down. “Having kept the perception of rising in mind” means: having placed in his mind the perception of rising, thinking, “I will rise after this much time has passed.”

23. Mahānāmaṃ sakkaṃ āmantesīti so kira tasmiṃ kāle tassaṃ parisati jeṭṭhako pāmokkho, tasmiṃ saṅgahite sesaparisā saṅgahitāva [M 3.0021] hotīti thero tameva āmantesi. Sīlasampannoti sīlena sampanno, sampannasīlo paripuṇṇasīloti attho. Saddhammehīti sundaradhammehi, sataṃ vā sappurisānaṃ dhammehi.

23. “He addressed Mahānāma the Sakyan”: It is said that at that time, in that assembly, he was the eldest and the foremost. When he was included, the rest of the assembly was also included; thus, the elder addressed him alone. “Endowed with virtue” means: endowed with virtue, possessing accomplished virtue, possessing perfected virtue—this is the meaning. ‘By good dhammas’ means: by beautiful dhammas, or by the dhammas of good people, of true persons.

24. Kathañca mahānāmāti iminā ettakena ṭhānena sekhapaṭipadāya mātikaṃ ṭhapetvā paṭipāṭiyā vitthāretukāmo evamāha. Tattha sīlasampannotiādīni “sampannasīlā, bhikkhave, viharathā”ti ākaṅkheyyasuttādīsu vuttanayeneva veditabbāni.

24. “And how, Mahānāma?”: Having established the matrix for the trainee’s practice with this much of a statement, and wishing to elaborate in sequence, he spoke thus. Therein, “endowed with virtue” and so on should be understood in the very way it was taught in the Ākaṅkheyya Sutta and others, as in: “Monks, dwell endowed with virtue.”

25. Kāyaduccaritenātiādīsu [V 3.0022] upayogatthe karaṇavacanaṃ, hiriyitabbāni kāyaduccaritādīni hiriyati jigucchatīti attho. Ottappaniddese hetvatthe karaṇavacanaṃ, kāyaduccaritādīhi ottappassa hetubhūtehi ottappati bhāyatīti attho. Āraddhavīriyoti paggahitavīriyo anosakkitamānaso. Pahānāyāti pahānatthāya. Upasampadāyāti [P 3.0030] paṭilābhatthāya. Thāmavāti vīriyathāmena samannāgato. Daḷhaparakkamoti thiraparakkamo. Anikkhittadhuro kusalesu dhammesūti kusalesu dhammesu anoropitadhuro anosakkitavīriyo. Paramenāti uttamena. Satinepakkenāti satiyā ca nipakabhāvena ca. Kasmā pana satibhājaniye paññā āgatāti? Satiyā balavabhāvadīpanatthaṃ. Paññāvippayuttā hi sati dubbalā hoti, sampayuttā balavatīti.

25. In 'by bodily misconduct,' etc., the instrumental case is used in the sense of the object; the meaning is: one is ashamed of and disgusted with bodily misconduct, etc., which are things one ought to be ashamed of. In the explanation of moral dread, the instrumental case is used in the sense of cause; the meaning is: on account of bodily misconduct, etc., which are the causes of moral dread, one is alarmed and fears. 'With energy aroused' means with aroused energy, with an unretreating mind. 'For abandoning' means for the purpose of abandoning. 'For attainment' means for the purpose of acquiring. 'Strong' means endowed with the strength of energy. 'With firm effort' means with steadfast exertion. 'Not having laid down the yoke in wholesome qualities' means not laying down the burden in wholesome qualities, with unretreating energy. 'Supreme' means the utmost. 'With mindfulness and discernment' means with both mindfulness and the state of being discerning. Why, then, is wisdom included in the analysis of mindfulness? To show the strength of mindfulness. For mindfulness disconnected from wisdom is weak, but when connected, it is strong.

Cirakatampīti attanā vā parena vā kāyena cirakataṃ cetiyaṅgaṇavattādi asīti mahāvattapaṭipattipūraṇaṃ. Cirabhāsitampīti attanā vā parena vā vācāya cirabhāsitaṃ sakkaccaṃ uddisana-uddisāpana-dhammosāraṇa-dhammadesanā-upanisinnakathā-anumodaniyādivasena pavattitaṃ vacīkammaṃ. Saritā anussaritāti tasmiṃ kāyena cirakate “kāyo nāma kāyaviññatti, cirabhāsite vācā nāma vacīviññatti. Tadubhayampi rūpaṃ, taṃsamuṭṭhāpikā cittacetasikā arūpaṃ. Iti ime rūpārūpadhammā evaṃ uppajjitvā evaṃ niruddhā”ti sarati ceva anussarati ca, satisambojjhaṅgaṃ samuṭṭhāpetīti attho. Bojjhaṅgasamuṭṭhāpikā hi sati idha adhippetā. Tāya satiyā esa sakimpi saraṇena saritā, punappunaṃ saraṇena anussaritāti veditabbā.

‘Long performed’—whether by oneself or by others, bodily actions long performed, such as the fulfillment of the eighty great observances beginning with the observance of the stupa grounds. ‘Long spoken’—whether by oneself or by others, verbal actions long spoken, such as respectful recitation, instruction, chanting the Dhamma, giving Dhamma talks, conversation while seated near, or giving blessings. ‘Remembered and recollected’—regarding those long-performed bodily actions, one reflects: “The body is bodily intimation, and long-spoken speech is verbal intimation. Both are materiality, and the mind and mental factors that produce them are immateriality. Thus, these material and immaterial phenomena, having arisen in this way, have ceased in this way”—one remembers and recollects, arousing the enlightenment factor of mindfulness. This is the meaning. For mindfulness that arouses the enlightenment factors is intended here. By that mindfulness, this person is to be understood as ‘one who has remembered’ for remembering even once, and as ‘one who has recollected’ for remembering again and again.

Udayatthagāminiyāti [M 3.0022] pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ udayavayagāminiyā udayañca vayañca paṭivijjhituṃ samatthāya. Ariyāyāti vikkhambhanavasena ca samucchedavasena ca kilesehi ārakā ṭhitāya parisuddhāya. Paññāya samannāgatoti vipassanāpaññāya ceva maggapaññāya ca samaṅgībhūto. Nibbedhikāyāti [P 3.0031] sāyeva nibbijjhanato nibbedhikāti vuccati, tāya samannāgatoti attho. Tattha maggapaññāya samucchedavasena anibbiddhapubbaṃ apadālitapubbaṃ lobhakkhandhaṃ dosakkhandhaṃ mohakkhandhaṃ nibbijjhati padāletīti nibbedhikā. Vipassanāpaññāya tadaṅgavasena nibbedhikāya maggapaññāya paṭilābhasaṃvattanato cāti vipassanā “nibbedhikā”ti vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Sammā dukkhakkhayagāminiyāti idhāpi maggapaññā “sammā hetunā nayena vaṭṭadukkhaṃ khepayamānā gacchatīti [V 3.0023] sammā dukkhakkhayagāminī nāma. Vipassanā tadaṅgavasena vaṭṭadukkhañca kilesadukkhañca khepayamānā gacchatīti dukkhakkhayagāminī. Dukkhakkhayagāminiyā vā maggapaññāya paṭilābhasaṃvattanato esā dukkhakkhayagāminī”ti veditabbā.

‘Leading to arising and passing away’ means with wisdom capable of penetrating the arising and passing away of the five aggregates. ‘Noble’ means standing far from the defilements by way of suppression and eradication, and thus purified. ‘Endowed with wisdom’ means endowed with both insight wisdom and path wisdom. ‘Penetrative’: it is called ‘penetrative’ because it penetrates; being endowed with it is the meaning. Herein, path wisdom is called ‘penetrative’ because, by way of eradication, it pierces and shatters the masses of greed, hatred, and delusion, which had not been pierced or shattered before. And because insight wisdom, by way of momentary abandonment, leads to the attainment of penetrative path wisdom, it is fitting to call insight ‘penetrative.’ ‘Rightly leading to the destruction of suffering’: here too, path wisdom is called ‘rightly leading to the destruction of suffering’ because it proceeds rightly, by the proper method, destroying the suffering of the round. Insight is called ‘leading to the destruction of suffering’ because, by way of momentary abandonment, it proceeds destroying both the suffering of the round and the suffering of defilements. Alternatively, this insight should be understood as ‘leading to the destruction of suffering’ because it leads to the attainment of path wisdom, which leads to the destruction of suffering.

26. Abhicetasikānanti abhicittaṃ seṭṭhacittaṃ sitānaṃ nissitānaṃ. Diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārānanti appitappitakkhaṇe sukhapaṭilābhahetūnaṃ. Nikāmalābhīti icchiticchitakkhaṇe samāpajjitā. Akicchalābhīti nidukkhalābhī. Akasiralābhīti vipulalābhī. Paguṇabhāvena eko icchiticchitakkhaṇe samāpajjituṃ sakkoti, samādhipāripanthikadhamme pana akilamanto vikkhambhetuṃ na sakkoti, so attano anicchāya khippameva vuṭṭhāti, yathāparicchedavasena samāpattiṃ ṭhapetuṃ na sakkoti ayaṃ kicchalābhī kasiralābhī nāma. Eko icchiticchitakkhaṇe ca samāpajjituṃ sakkoti, samādhipāripanthikadhamme ca akilamanto vikkhambheti, so yathāparicchedavaseneva vuṭṭhātuṃ sakkoti, ayaṃ akicchalābhī akasiralābhī nāma.

26. ‘Of the higher mental states’ means of those states dependent on the higher mind, the supreme mind. ‘Of pleasant abidings in this very life’ refers to those states that are causes for attaining happiness at every moment of absorption. ‘One who attains at will’ means one who is able to enter absorption at the moment of wishing. ‘One who attains without difficulty’ means one who attains without trouble. ‘One who attains without hardship’ means one who attains abundantly. One person, through proficiency, is able to enter absorption at the moment of wishing, but is unable to suppress the hindrances to concentration effortlessly. That person quickly emerges against their will and is unable to sustain the absorption for the determined period; this one is called ‘one who attains with difficulty’ and ‘one who attains with hardship’. Another is able to enter absorption at the moment of wishing, and suppresses the hindrances to concentration effortlessly. That person is able to emerge according to the determined period; this one is called ‘one who attains without difficulty’ and ‘one who attains without hardship’.

27. Ayaṃ [P 3.0032] vuccati mahānāma ariyasāvako sekho pāṭipadoti mahānāma ariyasāvako sekho pāṭipado vipassanāgabbhāya vaḍḍhamānakapaṭipadāya samannāgatoti vuccatīti dasseti. Apuccaṇḍatāyāti apūtiaṇḍatāya. Bhabbo abhinibbhidāyāti vipassanādiñāṇappabhedāya bhabbo. Sambodhāyāti ariyamaggāya. Anuttarassa yogakkhemassāti arahattaṃ [M 3.0023] anuttaro yogakkhemo nāma, tadabhigamāya bhabboti dasseti. Yā panāyamettha atthadīpanatthaṃ upamā āhaṭā, sā cetokhilasutte vuttanayeneva veditabbā. Kevalañhi tattha “tassā kukkuṭiyā aṇḍesu tividhakiriyakaraṇaṃ viya hi imassa bhikkhuno ussoḷhipannarasehi aṅgehi samannāgatabhāvo”ti yaṃ evaṃ opammasaṃsandanaṃ āgataṃ, taṃ idha evaṃ sīlasampanno hotītiādivacanato “tassā kukkuṭiyā aṇḍesu tividhakiriyakaraṇaṃ viya imassa bhikkhuno sīlasampannatādīhi pannarasehi dhammehi samaṅgibhāvo”ti. Evaṃ yojetvā veditabbaṃ. Sesaṃ sabbattha vuttasadisameva.

27. ‘This, Mahānāma, is called the noble disciple who is a trainee on the path’: this shows that the noble disciple who is a trainee on the path is said to be endowed with the practice that develops the embryo of insight. ‘Like an unrotten egg’ means like an unputrid egg. ‘Capable of breaking through’ means capable of breaking through to the various kinds of knowledge beginning with insight. ‘For awakening’ means for the noble path. ‘For the unsurpassed security from bondage’: Arahantship is called the unsurpassed security from bondage; this shows he is capable of attaining it. The simile brought here to explain the meaning should be understood in the same way as explained in the Cetokhila Sutta. The only difference is that there, the comparison is given thus: ‘Just as that hen’s threefold action on her eggs, so is this bhikkhu’s possession of the fifteen factors of striving.’ Here, based on the words ‘he is endowed with virtue,’ etc., that comparison is to be understood as: ‘Just as that hen’s threefold action on her eggs, so is this bhikkhu’s possession of the fifteen qualities beginning with virtue.’ It should be connected and understood in this way. The rest is the same everywhere.

28. Imaṃyeva anuttaraṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhinti imaṃ paṭhamādijjhānehi asadisaṃ uttamaṃ catutthajjhānikaṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ. Paṭhamābhinibbhidāti paṭhamo ñāṇabhedo. Dutiyādīsupi eseva [V 3.0024] nayo. Kukkuṭacchāpako pana ekavāraṃ mātukucchito ekavāraṃ aṇḍakosatoti dve vāre jāyati. Ariyasāvako tīhi vijjāhi tāyo vāre jāyati. Pubbenivāsacchādakaṃ [P 3.0033] tamaṃ vinodetvā pubbenivāsañāṇena paṭhamaṃ jāyati, sattānaṃ cutipaṭisandhicchādakaṃ tamaṃ vinodetvā dibbacakkhuñāṇena dutiyaṃ jāyati, catusaccapaṭicchādakaṃ tamaṃ vinodetvā āsavakkhayañāṇena tatiyaṃ jāyati.

28. “This very unsurpassed purity of mindfulness due to equanimity”—this refers to the supreme purity of mindfulness due to equanimity, associated with the fourth jhāna, which is dissimilar to the first and other jhānas. “First breakthrough” means the first breaking forth of knowledge. The same method should be understood for the second and subsequent breakthroughs. A chick, for instance, is born twice: once from its mother's belly and once from the eggshell. The noble disciple is born three times through the three kinds of knowledge. Having dispelled the darkness that conceals past lives, one is born for the first time through the knowledge of past lives. Having dispelled the darkness that conceals the passing away and rebirth of beings, one is born for the second time through the knowledge of the divine eye. Having dispelled the darkness that conceals the Four Truths, one is born for the third time through the knowledge of the destruction of the cankers.

29. Idampissa hoti caraṇasminti idampi sīlaṃ assa bhikkhuno caraṇaṃ nāma hotīti attho. Caraṇaṃ nāma bahu anekavidhaṃ, sīlādayo pannarasadhammā, tattha idampi ekaṃ caraṇanti attho. Padattho pana carati tena agatapubbaṃ disaṃ gacchatīti caraṇaṃ. Esa nayo sabbattha.

29. “This too is his conduct”—this means that this morality is also called the conduct of that bhikkhu. Conduct is manifold and of various kinds; there are the fifteen qualities beginning with morality. In this context, the meaning is that this morality is also one kind of conduct. The meaning of the word is as follows: by means of it one travels, one goes to a direction never gone before; therefore, it is called conduct. This is the method in all instances.

Idampissa hoti vijjāyāti idaṃ pubbenivāsañāṇaṃ tassa vijjā nāma hotīti attho. Vijjā nāma bahu anekavidhā, vipassanañāṇādīni aṭṭha ñāṇāni, tattha idampi ñāṇaṃ ekā vijjātipi attho. Padattho pana vinivijjhitvā etāya jānātīti vijjā. Esa nayo sabbattha. Vijjāsampanno itipīti tīhi vijjāhi vijjāsampanno itipi. Caraṇasampanno itipīti pañcadasahi dhammehi caraṇasampanno itipi. Tadubhayena pana vijjācaraṇasampanno itipīti.

“This too is his knowledge”—this means that this knowledge of past lives is called his knowledge. Knowledge is manifold and of various kinds; the eight knowledges beginning with insight knowledge are called knowledge. In this context, this knowledge is also one kind of knowledge. The meaning of the word is as follows: one knows by penetrating with it; therefore, it is called knowledge. This is the method in all instances. “Endowed with knowledge” means one is called endowed with knowledge on account of the three kinds of knowledge. “Endowed with conduct” means one is called endowed with conduct on account of the fifteen qualities. And by both of these, one is called “endowed with knowledge and conduct.”

30. Sanaṅkumārenāti [M 3.0024] porāṇakakumārena, cirakālato paṭṭhāya kumāroti paññātena. So kira manussapathe pañcacūḷakakumārakakāle jhānaṃ nibbattetvā aparihīnajjhāno brahmaloke nibbatti, tassa so attabhāvo piyo ahosi manāpo, tasmā tādiseneva attabhāvena carati, tena naṃ sanaṅkumāroti sañjānanti. Janetasminti [P 3.0034] janitasmiṃ, pajāyāti attho. Ye gottapaṭisārinoti ye janetasmiṃ gottaṃ paṭisaranti “ahaṃ gotamo, ahaṃ kassapo”ti, tesu loke gottapaṭisārīsu khattiyo seṭṭho. Anumatā bhagavatāti mama pañhabyākaraṇena saddhiṃ saṃsanditvā desitāti ambaṭṭhasutte buddhena bhagavatā “ahampi, ambaṭṭha, evaṃ vadāmi –

30. “By Sanaṅkumāra” means by the ancient youth, a Brahmā known as ‘Kumāra’ since a long time ago. It is said that in his human existence, at the time when he was a youth with five top-knots, he developed jhāna and, with his jhāna undiminished, was reborn in the Brahma world. That form of existence was dear and pleasing to him. Therefore, even though he has become a Brahmā, he continues to exist in that same form. For that reason, they recognize him as Sanaṅkumāra. “Among this folk” means among the people, among beings. “Those who resort to lineage” means those who, among this folk, repeatedly call to mind their lineage, saying, “I am of the Gotama clan,” “I am of the Kassapa clan.” Among those in the world who resort to lineage, the Khattiya is the best. “Approved by the Blessed One” means that it was taught by the Blessed One, the Buddha, in the Ambaṭṭha Sutta, in agreement with my explanation of the question, stating, “I too, Ambaṭṭha, say thus—

‘Khattiyo [V 3.0025] seṭṭho janetasmiṃ, ye gottapaṭisārino;

Vijjācaraṇasampanno, so seṭṭho devamānuse’ti”. (dī. ni. 1.277) –

“The Khattiya is best among this folk, among those who resort to lineage; but one accomplished in knowledge and conduct is best among gods and humans.”

Evaṃ bhāsantena anuññātā anumoditā. Sādhu sādhu ānandāti, bhagavā kira ādito paṭṭhāya niddaṃ anokkamantova imaṃ suttaṃ sutvā ānandena sekhapaṭipadāya kūṭaṃ gahitanti ñatvā uṭṭhāya pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā nisinno sādhukāraṃ adāsi. Ettāvatā ca pana idaṃ suttaṃ jinabhāsitaṃ nāma jātaṃ. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

Thus speaking, it was assented to and approved. ‘Good, good, Ananda!’ The Blessed One, indeed, having heard this discourse from the very beginning without falling asleep, and knowing that Ananda had grasped the pinnacle of the trainee’s practice, rose, sat cross-legged, and gave his approval. And by this much, this discourse came to be known as ‘The Conqueror’s Word.’ The rest is clear everywhere.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Sekhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Sekha Sutta is completed.

4. Potaliyasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Potaliya Sutta

31. Evaṃ [V 3.0026] me sutanti potaliyasuttaṃ. Tattha aṅguttarāpesūti aṅgāyeva so janapado, mahiyā panassa uttarena yā āpo, tāsaṃ avidūrattā uttarāpotipi vuccati. Kataramahiyā uttarena yā āpoti, mahāmahiyā. Tatthāyaṃ āvibhāvakathā – ayaṃ kira jambudīpo [P 3.0035] dasasahassayojanaparimāṇo. Tattha ca catusahassayojanappamāṇo padeso udakena ajjhotthaṭo samuddoti saṅkhaṃ gato[M 3.0025]. Tisahassayojanappamāṇe manussā vasanti. Tisahassayojanappamāṇe himavā patiṭṭhito ubbedhena pañcayojanasatiko caturāsītikūṭasahassapaṭimaṇḍito samantato sandamānapañcasatanadīvicitto, yattha āyāmavitthārena ceva gambhīratāya ca paṇṇāsapaṇṇāsayojanā diyaḍḍhayojanasataparimaṇḍalā anotattadaho kaṇṇamuṇḍadaho rathakāradaho chaddantadaho kuṇāladaho mandākinīdaho sīhapapātadahoti satta mahāsarā patiṭṭhitā. Tesu anotattadaho sudassanakūṭaṃ citrakūṭaṃ kāḷakūṭaṃ gandhamādanakūṭaṃ kelāsakūṭanti imehi pañcahi pabbatehi parikkhitto.

31. ‘Thus have I heard’ – this is the Potaliya Sutta. Therein, ‘in Aṅguttarāpa’ means that region is Aṅga itself. Moreover, the waters to its north, of the Mahī river, are also called ‘Uttarāpa’ (Northern Waters) due to their proximity. Which Mahī? The Great Mahī. Here is a clarifying account: This Jambudīpa is said to be ten thousand yojanas in extent. Within it, a region of four thousand yojanas is covered by water and is known as the ocean. Humans dwell in an area of three thousand yojanas. The Himavanta, extending for three thousand yojanas and standing five hundred yojanas high, is adorned with eighty-four thousand peaks and beautified with five hundred rivers flowing all around, where the seven great lakes are established—Lake Anotatta, Lake Kaṇṇamuṇḍa, Lake Rathakāra, Lake Chaddanta, Lake Kuṇāla, Lake Mandākinī, and Lake Sīhapapāta—each fifty yojanas in length and breadth, and fifty yojanas in depth, and one hundred and fifty yojanas in circumference. Among them, Lake Anotatta is encircled by these five mountains: Sudassana Peak, Citra Peak, Kāḷa Peak, Gandhamādana Peak, and Kelāsa Peak.

Tattha sudassanakūṭaṃ sovaṇṇamayaṃ dviyojanasatubbedhaṃ antovaṅkaṃ kākamukhasaṇṭhānaṃ tameva saraṃ paṭicchādetvā ṭhitaṃ. Citrakūṭaṃ sabbaratanamayaṃ. Kāḷakūṭaṃ añjanamayaṃ. Gandhamādanakūṭaṃ sānumayaṃ abbhantare muggavaṇṇaṃ, mūlagandho sāragandho pheggugandho tacagandho papaṭikagandho rasagandho pattagandho pupphagandho phalagandho gandhagandhoti imehi dasahi gandhehi ussannaṃ nānappakāraosadhasañchannaṃ, kāḷapakkhauposathadivase ādittamiva aṅgāraṃ jalantaṃ tiṭṭhati. Kelāsakūṭaṃ rajatamayaṃ. Sabbāni sudassanena samānubbedhasaṇṭhānāni, tameva saraṃ paṭicchādetvā ṭhitāni. Tāni sabbāni [P 3.0036] devānubhāvena nāgānubhāvena ca vassanti, nadiyo ca tesu sandanti. Taṃ sabbampi udakaṃ anotattameva pavisati. Candimasūriyā dakkhiṇena vā uttarena vā gacchantā pabbatantarena tattha obhāsaṃ karonti, ujuṃ gacchantā na karonti, tenevassa anotattanti saṅkhā udapādi.

There, Sudassana Peak, made of gold, two hundred yojanas in height, bent inward, shaped like a crow’s beak, stood covering that very lake. Citra Peak was made of all kinds of jewels. Kāḷa Peak was made of collyrium stone. Gandhamādana Peak consists of mountain slopes, within which is the color of a green bean, and it is abundant with these ten kinds of fragrance: root-fragrance, heartwood-fragrance, sapwood-fragrance, bark-fragrance, outer-layer-fragrance, resin-fragrance, leaf-fragrance, flower-fragrance, fruit-fragrance, and the fragrance of all fragrances. Covered with various kinds of medicinal plants, on the Uposatha day of the dark fortnight, it stands blazing like a glowing ember. Kelāsa Peak was made of silver. All these peaks, equal in height and shape to Sudassana, stood covering that very lake. All these peaks give rain by the power of the devas and the power of the nāgas, and rivers flow from them. All that water enters Lake Anotatta. The moon and sun, proceeding either to the south or to the north, illuminate that place by passing between the mountains, but when proceeding straight, they do not. Hence arose the designation ‘Anotatta’.

Tattha [V 3.0027] manoharasilātalāni nimmacchakacchapāni phalikasadisanimmaludakāni nhānatitthāni supaṭiyattāni honti, yesu buddhapaccekabuddhakhīṇāsavā ca iddhimanto ca isayo nhāyanti, devayakkhādayo uyyānakīḷakaṃ kīḷanti.

There are delightful stone terraces, free from fish and turtles, with waters clear as crystal, and well-prepared bathing places, where Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and arahants, as well as powerful sages, bathe, while devas, yakkhas, and others engage in garden sports.

Tassa catūsu passesu sīhamukhaṃ hatthimukhaṃ assamukhaṃ usabhamukhanti cattāri mukhāni honti, yehi catasso nadiyo sandanti. Sīhamukhena nikkhantanadītīre sīhā bahutarā honti. Hatthimukhādīhi hatthiassausabhā. Puratthimadisato nikkhantanadī anotattaṃ tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā itarā tisso nadiyo anupagamma [M 3.0026] pācīnahimavanteneva amanussapathaṃ gantvā mahāsamuddaṃ pavisati. Pacchimadisato ca uttaradisato ca nikkhantanadiyopi tatheva padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pacchimahimavanteneva uttarahimavanteneva ca amanussapathaṃ gantvā mahāsamuddaṃ pavisanti. Dakkhiṇadisato nikkhantanadī pana taṃ tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā dakkhiṇena ujukaṃ pāsāṇapiṭṭheneva saṭṭhiyojanāni gantvā pabbataṃ paharitvā vuṭṭhāya parikkhepena tigāvutappamāṇā udakadhārā ca hutvā ākāsena saṭṭhiyojanāni gantvā tiyaggaḷe nāma pāsāṇe patitā, pāsāṇo udakadhārāvegena bhinno. Tattha paññāsayojanappamāṇā tiyaggaḷā nāma pokkharaṇī jātā, pokkharaṇiyā kūlaṃ bhinditvā pāsāṇaṃ pavisitvā saṭṭhiyojanāni gatā. Tato ghanapathaviṃ bhinditvā umaṅgena saṭṭhiyojanāni gantvā viñjhuṃ nāma tiracchānapabbataṃ [P 3.0037] paharitvā hatthatale pañcaṅgulisadisā pañcadhārā hutvā pavattanti. Sā tikkhattuṃ anotattaṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā gataṭṭhāne āvaṭṭagaṅgāti vuccati. Ujukaṃ pāsāṇapiṭṭhena saṭṭhiyojanāni gataṭṭhāne kaṇhagaṅgāti, ākāsena saṭṭhiyojanāni gataṭṭhāne ākāsagaṅgāti, tiyaggaḷapāsāṇe paññāsayojanokāse ṭhitā tiyaggaḷapokkharaṇīti, kūlaṃ bhinditvā pāsāṇaṃ pavisitvā saṭṭhiyojanāni gataṭṭhāne bahalagaṅgāti, umaṅgena saṭṭhiyojanāni gataṭṭhāne umaṅgagaṅgāti vuccati. Viñjhuṃ nāma tiracchānapabbataṃ paharitvā pañcadhārā hutvā pavattaṭṭhāne pana gaṅgā yamunā aciravatī sarabhū mahīti pañcadhā saṅkhaṃ gatā. Evametā pañca mahānadiyo himavantato pabhavanti. Tāsu yā ayaṃ pañcamī mahī nāma, sā idha mahāmahīti adhippetā. Tassā uttarena yā āpo, tāsaṃ avidūrattā so janapado aṅguttarāpoti veditabbo. Tasmiṃ aṅguttarāpesu janapade.

On its four sides, there are four mouths: a lion’s mouth, an elephant’s mouth, a horse’s mouth, and a bull’s mouth, from which four rivers flow. On the banks of the river issuing from the lion’s mouth, lions are very abundant. From the elephant’s mouth and the others, elephants, horses, and bulls are abundant. The river issuing from the eastern side circles Lake Anotatta three times clockwise and, without approaching the other three rivers, travels along the eastern Himavanta through a path not for humans and enters the great ocean. The rivers issuing from the western and northern sides likewise circle it clockwise and travel along the western and northern Himavanta through a path not for humans before entering the great ocean. The river issuing from the southern side, however, circles it three times clockwise, then moves straight south along a rock surface for sixty yojanas. Striking a mountain, it rises up and becomes a water current three gāvutas in circumference. It then travels sixty yojanas through the sky and falls onto a rock named Tiyaggaḷa, which is shattered by the force of the water current. There, a pond named Tiyaggaḷa, fifty yojanas in size, is formed. Breaking the bank of the pond, the water enters the rock and travels sixty yojanas. Then, piercing through the solid earth, it moves sixty yojanas through a tunnel, strikes a transverse mountain named Viñjhu, and flows onward as five streams resembling the five fingers on the palm of a hand. That river, at the place where it flowed after circling Lake Anotatta three times, is called Āvaṭṭagaṅgā. The stretch where it flows straight along the rock surface for sixty yojanas is called Kaṇhagaṅgā. The part where it travels sixty yojanas through the sky is named Ākāsagaṅgā. The part situated in the fifty-yojana space at the Tiyaggaḷa rock is called Tiyaggaḷapokkharaṇī. The section where it breaks the bank, enters the rock, and flows sixty yojanas is known as Bahalagaṅgā. The stretch where it travels sixty yojanas through the tunnel is called Umaṅgagaṅgā. Moreover, at the place where it flows after striking the Viñjhu mountain and becoming five streams, these are reckoned as the five rivers: Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Aciravatī, Sarabhū, and Mahī. Thus, these five great rivers originate from the Himavanta. Among them, this fifth one, named Mahī, is what is meant here by Mahāmahī. Because the waters to its north are not far, that region should be known as Aṅguttarāpa. In that region of Aṅguttarāpa...

Āpaṇaṃ [V 3.0028] nāmāti tasmiṃ kira nigame vīsati āpaṇamukhasahassāni vibhattāni ahesuṃ. Iti so āpaṇānaṃ ussannattā āpaṇantveva saṅkhaṃ gato. Tassa ca nigamassa avidūre nadītīre ghanacchāyo ramaṇīyo bhūmibhāgo mahāvanasaṇḍo, tasmiṃ bhagavā viharati. Tenevettha vasanaṭṭhānaṃ na niyāmitanti veditabbaṃ. Yenaññataro vanasaṇḍo tenupasaṅkamīti [M 3.0027] bhikkhusaṅghaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ pesetvā ekakova upasaṅkami potaliyaṃ gahapatiṃ sandhāya. Potaliyopi kho gahapatīti potaliyoti evaṃnāmako gahapati. Sampannanivāsanapāvuraṇoti paripuṇṇanivāsanapāvuraṇo[P 3.0038], ekaṃ dīghadasaṃ sāṭakaṃ nivattho ekaṃ pārutoti attho. Chattupāhanāhīti chattaṃ gahetvā upāhanā āruyhāti attho. Āsanānīti pallaṅkapīṭhapalālapīṭhakādīni. Antamaso sākhābhaṅgampi hi āsananteva vuccati. Gahapativādenāti gahapatīti iminā vacanena. Samudācaratīti voharati.

‘Āpaṇa’ by name: It is said that in that settlement, twenty thousand market entrances were distributed. Thus, owing to the abundance of markets, it came to be known simply as Āpaṇa. And not far from that settlement, on the riverbank, there is a great forest grove, a delightful portion of land with dense shade; in it, the Blessed One dwells. Therefore, it should be known that a dwelling place was not specified here. As for ‘He approached a certain forest grove’: Having sent the community of monks to their dwelling place, he approached all alone, with Potaliya the householder in mind. As for ‘Potaliya the householder’: ‘Potaliya’ refers to the householder with this name. As for ‘completely dressed and cloaked’: This means fully clad in lower and upper garments. The meaning is: having worn one long-fringed garment and having draped another. As for ‘with umbrella and footwear’: The meaning is: having taken an umbrella and having put on footwear. As for ‘seats’: This refers to couches, stools, straw mats, and the like. Indeed, at the very least, even a broken-off branch is called a seat. As for ‘with the address “householder”’: This means with this word, ‘householder.’ As for ‘he addresses’: This means he speaks to.

Bhagavantaṃ etadavocāti tatiyaṃ gahapatīti vacanaṃ adhivāsetuṃ asakkonto bhagavantametaṃ “tayidaṃ, bho, gotamā”tiādivacanaṃ avoca. Tattha nacchannanti na anucchavikaṃ. Nappatirūpanti na sāruppaṃ. Ākārātiādīni sabbāneva kāraṇavevacanāni. Dīghadasavatthadhāraṇa-kesamassunakhaṭhapanādīni hi sabbāneva gihibyañjanāni tassa gihibhāvaṃ pākaṭaṃ karontīti ākārā, gihisaṇṭhānena saṇṭhitattā liṅgā, gihibhāvassa sañjānananimittatāya nimittāti vuttā. Yathā taṃ gahapatissāti yathā gahapatissa ākāraliṅganimittā bhaveyyuṃ, tatheva tuyhaṃ. Tena tāhaṃ evaṃ samudācarāmīti dasseti. Atha so yena kāraṇena gahapativādaṃ nādhivāseti, taṃ pakāsento “tathā hi pana me”tiādimāha.

As for ‘He said this to the Blessed One’: Being unable to endure the address ‘householder’ for the third time, he spoke this speech to the Blessed One: ‘This indeed, venerable Gotama…’ and so on. Therein, ‘unsuitable’ means not appropriate. ‘Unbefitting’ means not proper. The words beginning with ‘appearances’ are all synonyms for ‘reason.’ Indeed, all the characteristics of a householder—such as wearing long-fringed garments, keeping hair, beard, and nails—make his lay status manifest. Therefore, they are called ‘appearances’; because they are established in the manner of a householder, they are ‘marks’; because they are a cause for knowing the lay state, they are called ‘signs.’ As for ‘Just as for that householder’: This shows the meaning: ‘Just as the appearances, marks, and signs would be for a householder, so they are for you. Therefore, I address you thus.’ Then, explaining the reason why he cannot endure the address ‘householder,’ he says, ‘But indeed, for me…’ and so on.

Niyyātanti niyyātitaṃ. Anovādī anupavādīti “tātā, kasatha, vapatha, vaṇippathaṃ payojethā”tiādinā hi nayena ovadanto ovādī nāma hoti. “Tumhe na kasatha, na vapatha, na vaṇippathaṃ payojetha, kathaṃ jīvissatha, puttadāraṃ vā bharissathā”tiādinā nayena pana upavadanto upavādī nāma hoti. Ahaṃ pana ubhayampi taṃ na karomi. Tenāhaṃ tattha anovādī anupavādīti dasseti. Ghāsacchādanaparamo [P 3.0039] viharāmīti ghāsamattañceva acchādanamattañca paramaṃ katvā viharāmi, tato paraṃ natthi, na ca patthemīti dīpeti.

As for ‘It has been relinquished’: This means it has been given up. As for ‘Not admonishing, not reproaching’: Indeed, one who instructs in this way, ‘Dears, plow, sow, engage in commerce,’ is called an admonisher. But one who reproaches in this way, ‘You do not plow, you do not sow, you do not engage in commerce—how will you live, or how will you support your wife and children?’ is called a reproacher. But I do not do either of these two. This shows the meaning: ‘Therefore, in that matter, I am one who does not admonish and does not reproach.’ As for ‘I dwell with food and clothing as the highest’: This indicates the meaning: ‘I dwell having made mere food and mere clothing the utmost limit; beyond that there is nothing, nor do I long for it.’

32. Giddhilobho [V 3.0029] pahātabboti gedhabhūto lobho pahātabbo. Anindārosanti anindābhūtaṃ aghaṭṭanaṃ. Nindārosoti nindāghaṭṭanā. Vohārasamucchedāyāti ettha vohāroti byavahāravohāropi paṇṇattipi vacanampi cetanāpi. Tattha –

32. As for ‘Ravenous greed should be abandoned’: Greed that has become ravenous should be abandoned. As for ‘non-censure and non-abuse’: This means non-impingement that is blameless. As for ‘censure and abuse’: This means blame and impingement. As for ‘for the cutting off of conventional expression’: Herein, ‘conventional expression’ can be conventional expression as transaction, as designation, as speech, and as intention. Therein—

“Yo [M 3.0028] hi koci manussesu, vohāraṃ upajīvati;

Evaṃ vāseṭṭha jānāhi, vāṇijo so na brāhmaṇo”ti. (ma. ni. 2.457) –

‘Whoever among humans lives by commerce, know this, Vāseṭṭha, he is a merchant, not a brahmin.’

Ayaṃ byavahāravohāro nāma. “Saṅkhā samaññā paññatti vohāro”ti (dha. sa. 1313-1315) ayaṃ paṇṇattivohāro nāma. “Tathā tathā voharati aparāmasa”nti (ma. ni. 3.332) ayaṃ vacanavohāro nāma. “Aṭṭha ariyavohārā aṭṭha anariyavoharā”ti (a. ni. 8.67) ayaṃ cetanāvohāro nāma, ayamidhādhippeto. Yasmā vā pabbajitakālato paṭṭhāya gihīti cetanā natthi, samaṇoti cetanā hoti. Gihīti vacanaṃ natthi, samaṇoti vacanaṃ hoti. Gihīti paṇṇatti natthi, samaṇoti paṇṇatti hoti. Gihīti byavahāro natthi, samaṇoti vā pabbajitoti vā byavahāro hoti. Tasmā sabbepete labbhanti.

This is called ‘conventional expression as transaction.’ ‘Term, name, designation, conventional expression’—this is called ‘conventional expression as designation.’ ‘They speak in such and such a way without grasping’—this is called ‘conventional expression as speech.’ ‘Eight noble conventional expressions and eight ignoble conventional expressions’—this is called ‘conventional expression as intention,’ and this is what is intended here. Or, because from the time of going forth, the intention ‘I am a householder’ does not exist; only the intention ‘I am an ascetic’ exists. The speech ‘householder’ does not exist; only the speech ‘ascetic’ exists. The designation ‘householder’ does not exist; only the designation ‘ascetic’ exists. The transaction of a ‘householder’ does not exist; but the expression ‘ascetic’ or ‘one gone forth’ exists. Therefore, all these are obtained.

33. Yesaṃ kho ahaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ hetu pāṇātipātīti ettha pāṇātipātova saṃyojanaṃ. Pāṇātipātasseva hi hetu pāṇātipātapaccayā pāṇātipātī nāma hoti. Pāṇātipātānaṃ pana bahutāya “yesaṃ kho aha”nti vuttaṃ. Tesāhaṃ [P 3.0040] saṃyojanānanti tesaṃ ahaṃ pāṇātipātabandhanānaṃ. Pahānāya samucchedāya paṭipannoti iminā apāṇātipātasaṅkhātena kāyikasīlasaṃvarena pahānatthāya samucchedanatthāya paṭipanno. Attāpi maṃ upavadeyyāti kunthakipillikampi nāma jīvitā avoropanakasāsane pabbajitvā pāṇātipātamattatopi oramituṃ na sakkomi, kiṃ mayhaṃ pabbajjāyāti evaṃ attāpi maṃ upavadeyya. Anuviccāpi maṃ viññū garaheyyunti evarūpe nāma sāsane pabbajitvā pāṇātipātamattatopi oramituṃ na sakkoti, kiṃ etassa pabbajjāyāti evaṃ anuvicca tulayitvā pariyogāhetvā aññepi viññū paṇḍitā garaheyyuṃ. Etadeva kho pana saṃyojanametaṃ nīvaraṇanti dasasu saṃyojanesu pañcasu ca nīvaraṇesu apariyāpannampi “aṭṭha nīvaraṇā”ti desanāvasenetaṃ vuttaṃ. Vaṭṭabandhanaṭṭhena hi hitapaṭicchādanaṭṭhena [V 3.0030] ca saṃyojanantipi nīvaraṇantipi vuttaṃ. Āsavāti pāṇātipātakāraṇā eko avijjāsavo uppajjati. Vighātapariḷāhāti vighātā ca pariḷāhā ca. Tattha [M 3.0029] vighātaggahaṇena kilesadukkhañca vipākadukkhañca gahitaṃ, pariḷāhaggahaṇenapi kilesapariḷāho ca vipākapariḷāho ca gahito. Iminā upāyena sabbattha attho veditabbo.

33. Herein, in the passage ‘For which fetters’ cause I would be a killer of living beings,’ the volition to kill a living being is itself the fetter. Indeed, it is because of the cause, which is the volition to kill, and on account of the act of killing, that one is called a ‘killer of living beings.’ Furthermore, because of the multiplicity of beings, it is stated in the plural as ‘For which…’ ‘Of those fetters, I…’ means ‘of those bonds which are the killing of living beings.’ ‘Practicing for abandoning, for eradicating’ means: one practices for the purpose of abandoning, for the purpose of complete cutting off, by means of the bodily restraint of virtue known as non-killing of living beings. ‘Even my own self would reproach me’ means: ‘Having gone forth in a Dispensation where one should not deprive even a termite or an ant of its life faculty, I am unable to abstain even from the mere act of killing a living being. What is the benefit of my going forth?’ Thus, my own self would reproach me. ‘Having investigated, the wise would censure me’ means: ‘Having gone forth in such a Dispensation, he is unable to abstain even from the mere act of killing a living being. What is the benefit of his going forth?’ Thus, having investigated, weighed, and penetrated the matter, other wise and learned ones would censure him. ‘This itself is a fetter, this is a hindrance’ means: although not included among the ten fetters and the five hindrances, this was stated by the power of the teaching as ‘there are eight hindrances.’ For, in the sense of binding to the round of existence and in the sense of concealing what is beneficial, it is called both a ‘fetter’ and a ‘hindrance.’ As for ‘taints’: because of the killing of living beings as a cause, the one taint of ignorance arises. As for ‘distresses and fevers’: there are distresses and fevers. Therein, by the taking of the word ‘distress,’ both the suffering of defilements and the suffering of result are taken. And by the taking of the word ‘fever,’ both the fever of defilements and the fever of result are taken. By this method, the meaning should be understood in all cases.

34-40. Ayaṃ pana viseso – tesāhaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ pahānāyāti imasmiṃ pade iminā dinnādānasaṅkhātena kāyikasīlasaṃvarena, saccavācāsaṅkhātena vācasikasīlasaṃvarena, apisuṇāvācāsaṅkhātena vācasikasīlasaṃvarena, agiddhilobhasaṅkhātena mānasikasīlasaṃvarena, anindārosasaṅkhātena kāyikavācasikasīlasaṃvarena[P 3.0041], akodhupāyāsasaṅkhātena mānasikasīlasaṃvarena, anatimānasaṅkhātena mānasikasīlasaṃvarena pahānatthāya samucchedanatthāya paṭipannoti evaṃ sabbavāresu yojanā kātabbā.

Furthermore, this is the distinction: in this phrase, ‘for the abandoning of those fetters,’ the connection should be made thus in all cases: ‘one practices for the purpose of abandoning, for the purpose of complete cutting off’ by means of this bodily restraint of virtue known as abstention from taking what is not given; by means of this verbal restraint of virtue known as truthful speech; by means of this verbal restraint of virtue known as non-slanderous speech; by means of this mental restraint of virtue known as non-ravenous greed; by means of this bodily and verbal restraint of virtue known as non-censure and non-abuse; by means of this mental restraint of virtue known as non-anger and non-vexation; by means of this mental restraint of virtue known as non-conceit.

Attāpi maṃ upavadeyya anuviccāpi maṃ viññū garaheyyunti imesu pana padesu tiṇasalākampi nāma upādāya adinnaṃ aggahaṇasāsane pabbajitvā adinnādānamattatopi viramituṃ na sakkomi, kiṃ mayhaṃ pabbajjāyāti evaṃ attāpi maṃ upavadeyya. Evarūpe nāma sāsane pabbajitvā adinnādānamattatopi oramituṃ na sakkoti, kiṃ imassa pabbajjāyāti evaṃ anuviccāpi maṃ viññū garaheyyuṃ? Hasāpekkhatāyapi nāma davakamyatāya vā musāvādaṃ akaraṇasāsane pabbajitvā. Sabbākārena pisuṇaṃ akaraṇasāsane nāma pabbajitvā. Appamattakampi giddhilobhaṃ akaraṇasāsane nāma pabbajitvāpi. Kakacena aṅgesu okkantiyamānesupi nāma paresaṃ nindārosaṃ akaraṇasāsane pabbajitvā. Chinnakhāṇukaṇṭakādīsupi nāma kodhupāyāsaṃ akaraṇasāsane pabbajitvā. Adhimānamattampi nāma mānaṃ akaraṇasāsane pabbajitvā atimānamattampi pajahituṃ na sakkomi, kiṃ mayhaṃ pabbajjāyāti evaṃ attāpi maṃ upavadeyya. Evarūpe nāma sāsane pabbajitvā atimānamattampi pajahituṃ na sakkoti, kiṃ imassa pabbajjāyāti evaṃ anuviccāpi maṃ viññū garaheyyunti evaṃ sabbavāresu yojanā kātabbā.

Furthermore, in these phrases, ‘Even my own self would reproach me’ and ‘Having investigated, the wise would censure me,’ the connection should be made thus in all cases: ‘Having gone forth in a Dispensation where one should not take what is not given, beginning with even a blade of grass or a sliver of bamboo, I am unable to refrain from the mere act of taking what is not given. What is the benefit of my going forth?’ Thus, my own self would reproach me. ‘Having gone forth in such a Dispensation, he is unable to refrain from the mere act of taking what is not given. What is the benefit of his going forth?’ Thus, having investigated, the wise would censure me. ‘Having gone forth in a Dispensation where one should not speak falsehood, even for the sake of a joke or out of a desire for sport, I am unable to refrain from the mere act of speaking falsehood…’ ‘Having gone forth in a Dispensation where one should not engage in slander in any way, I am unable to refrain from the mere act of slander…’ ‘Having gone forth in a Dispensation where one should not have even the slightest ravenous greed, I am unable to abandon it…’ ‘Having gone forth in a Dispensation where one should not engage in censure and abuse of others, even while one’s limbs are being cut with a saw, I am unable to abandon even the mere act of censure and abuse…’ ‘Having gone forth in a Dispensation where one should not have anger and vexation, even towards things like cut stumps and thorns, I am unable to refrain from the mere act of anger and vexation…’ ‘Having gone forth in a Dispensation where one should not have even the slightest conceit, I am unable to abandon even the mere act of conceit. What is the benefit of my going forth?’ Thus, my own self would reproach me. ‘Having gone forth in such a Dispensation, he is unable to abandon even the mere act of conceit. What is the benefit of his going forth?’ Thus, having investigated, the wise would censure me.

Āsavāti imasmiṃ pana pade adinnādānakāraṇā kāmāsavo [P 3.0042] diṭṭhāsavo avijjāsavoti tayo [V 3.0031] āsavā uppajjanti, tathā musāvādakāraṇā pisuṇāvācākāraṇā ca, giddhilobhakāraṇā diṭṭhāsavo avijjāsavo [M 3.0030] ca, nindārosakāraṇā avijjāsavova, tathā kodhupāyāsakāraṇā, atimānakāraṇā bhavāsavo avijjāsavo cāti dveva āsavā uppajjantīti evaṃ āsavuppatti veditabbā.

Furthermore, in this word ‘taints’: due to the cause of taking what is not given, three taints arise: the taint of sensual pleasure, the taint of views, and the taint of ignorance. Likewise, due to the cause of false speech and the cause of slanderous speech, three taints arise: the taint of sensual pleasure, the taint of views, and the taint of ignorance. Due to the cause of ravenous greed, two taints arise: the taint of views and the taint of ignorance. Due to the cause of censure and abuse, only the one taint of ignorance arises. Likewise, due to the cause of anger and vexation, only the one taint of ignorance arises. Due to the cause of conceit, two taints arise: the taint of becoming and the taint of ignorance. Thus, the arising of the taints should be understood.

Imesu pana aṭṭhasupi vāresu asammohatthaṃ puna ayaṃ saṅkhepavinicchayo – purimesu tāva catūsu viramituṃ na sakkomīti vattabbaṃ, pacchimesu pajahituṃ na sakkomīti. Pāṇātipātanindārosakodhupāyāsesu ca eko avijjāsavova hoti, adinnādānamusāvādapisuṇāvācāsu kāmāsavo diṭṭhāsavo avijjāsavo, giddhilobhe diṭṭhāsavo avijjāsavo, atimāne bhavāsavo avijjāsavo, apāṇātipātaṃ dinnādānaṃ kāyikaṃ sīlaṃ, amusā apisuṇaṃ vācasikasīlaṃ, ṭhapetvā anindārosaṃ sesāni tīṇi mānasikasīlāni. Yasmā pana kāyenapi ghaṭṭeti roseti vācāyapi, tasmā anindāroso dve ṭhānāni yāti, kāyikasīlampi hoti vācasikasīlampi. Ettāvatā kiṃ kathitaṃ? Pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlaṃ. Pātimokkhasaṃvarasīle ṭhitassa ca bhikkhuno paṭisaṅkhāpahānavasena gihivohārasamucchedo kathitoti veditabbo.

Furthermore, regarding these eight cases, for the sake of non-confusion, this again is a brief determination: In the first four cases, it should be said, 'I am unable to refrain.' In the latter four cases, it should be said, 'I am unable to abandon.' In the cases of killing living beings, censure and abuse, and anger and vexation, there is only the one taint of ignorance. In the cases of taking what is not given, false speech, and slanderous speech, there are the three taints: the taint of sensual pleasure, the taint of views, and the taint of ignorance. In the case of covetous greed, there are two taints: the taint of views and the taint of ignorance. In the case of conceit, there are two taints: the taint of becoming and the taint of ignorance. Abstention from killing living beings and from taking what is not given are bodily virtue. Abstention from falsehood and from slander are verbal virtue. Setting aside non-censure and non-abuse, the remaining three are mental virtues. Furthermore, because one strikes and abuses with the body and also with speech, non-censure and non-abuse pertains to two bases: it is both bodily virtue and verbal virtue. By this much, what has been taught? The virtue of Pātimokkha restraint. And it should be understood that for a monk established in the virtue of Pātimokkha restraint, the cutting off of lay dealings is taught by way of abandonment through reflective knowledge.

Kāmādīnavakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Dangers of Sensual Pleasures

42. Vitthāradesanāyaṃ tamenaṃ dakkhoti padassa upasumbheyyāti iminā saddhiṃ sambandho veditabbo. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti, tamenaṃ kukkuraṃ upasumbheyya, tassa samīpe khipeyyāti attho. Aṭṭhikaṅkalanti uraṭṭhiṃ vā piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃ vā sīsaṭṭhiṃ vā. Tañhi nimmaṃsattā kaṅkalanti vuccati. Sunikkantaṃ [P 3.0043] nikkantanti yathā sunikkantaṃ hoti, evaṃ nikkantaṃ nillikhitaṃ, yadettha allīnamaṃsaṃ atthi, taṃ sabbaṃ nillikhitvā aṭṭhimattameva katanti attho. Tenevāha “nimmaṃsa”nti. Lohitaṃ pana makkhitvā tiṭṭhati, tena vuttaṃ “lohitamakkhita”nti.

42. In the detailed discourse, the connection of the phrase 'tamenaṃ dakkho' with this phrase 'upasumbheyya' should be understood. This is what is meant: one should toss it to that dog; that is, one should throw it near him. This is the meaning. 'Aṭṭhikaṅkala' means a breastbone, a spine, or a skull bone. Indeed, because it is fleshless, it is called 'kaṅkala'. 'Sunikkantaṃ nikkantaṃ' means: just as something is well-scraped, so this is scraped clean; the meaning is that whatever adhering flesh there is, having scraped all of it off, it is made into just a bone. For that very reason, He said 'fleshless'. However, it remains smeared with blood; for that reason, it was said 'blood-smeared'.

Bahudukkhā bahupāyāsāti diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikehi dukkhehi bahudukkhā, upāyāsasaṃkilesehi bahupāyāsā. Yāyaṃ upekkhā nānattā nānattasitāti yā ayaṃ pañcakāmaguṇārammaṇavasena nānāsabhāvā, tāneva [M 3.0031] ca ārammaṇāni nissitattā “nānattasitā”ti [V 3.0032] vuccati pañcakāmaguṇūpekkhā, taṃ abhinivajjetvā. Ekattā ekattasitāti catutthajjhānupekkhā, sā hi divasampi ekasmiṃ ārammaṇe uppajjanato ekasabhāvā, tadeva ekaṃ ārammaṇaṃ nissitattā ekattasitā nāma. Yattha sabbaso lokāmisūpādānā aparisesā nirujjhantīti yattha catutthajjhānupekkhāyaṃ yaṃ upekkhaṃ āgamma yaṃ paṭicca sabbena sabbaṃ aparisesā lokāmisasaṅkhātā pañcakāmaguṇāmisā nirujjhanti. Pañcakāmaguṇāmisāti ca kāmaguṇārammaṇachandarāgā, gahaṇaṭṭhena teyeva ca upādānātipi vuttā. Tamevūpekkhaṃ bhāvetīti taṃ lokāmisūpādānānaṃ paṭipakkhabhūtaṃ catutthajjhānupekkhameva vaḍḍheti.

'Bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā' means: they are of much suffering because of sufferings in the present life and in the next; they are of much distress because of the defilements that are distress. 'Yāyaṃ upekkhā nānattā nānattasitā' means: this equanimity which, by way of having the five strands of sensual pleasure as its object, is of diverse natures, and because it is based on those very objects, is called 'nānattasitā' (based on diversity)—this is the equanimity concerning the five strands of sensual pleasure; one should avoid that. 'Ekattā ekattasitā' refers to the equanimity of the fourth jhāna. For that equanimity, because it arises on a single object even for a whole day, is of a single nature; and because it is based on that very single object, it is named 'ekattasitā' (based on singularity). 'Yattha sabbaso lokāmisūpādānā aparisesā nirujjhantīti' means: wherein, in the equanimity of the fourth jhāna, relying on which equanimity, the worldly allurements and clingings cease completely and without remainder. 'Pañcakāmaguṇāmisā' means the passionate desires for the objects of the five strands of sensual pleasure; and because of the meaning of grasping, those very same passionate desires are also called 'upādāna' (clinging). 'Tamevūpekkhaṃ bhāvetīti' means: one develops that very equanimity of the fourth jhāna, which is the opponent of worldly allurements and clinging.

43. Uḍḍīyeyyāti [P 3.0044] uppatitvā gaccheyya. Anupatitvāti anubandhitvā. Vitaccheyyunti mukhatuṇḍakena ḍaṃsantā taccheyyuṃ. Vissajjeyyunti maṃsapesiṃ nakhehi kaḍḍhitvā pāteyyuṃ.

43. 'Uḍḍīyeyya' means: having flown up, one should go. 'Anupatitvā' means: having followed after. 'Vitaccheyyuṃ' means: biting with their beaks, they would peck. 'Vissajjeyyuṃ' means: having pulled a piece of flesh with their claws, they would drop it.

47. Yānaṃ vā poriseyyanti purisānucchavikaṃ yānaṃ. Pavaramaṇikuṇḍalanti nānappakāraṃ uttamamaṇiñca kuṇḍalañca. Sāni harantīti attano bhaṇḍakāni gaṇhanti.

47. 'Yānaṃ vā poriseyyaṃ' means a vehicle befitting a man. 'Pavaramaṇikuṇḍalaṃ' refers to various kinds of excellent gems and earrings. 'Sāni haranti' means they take their own goods.

48. Sampannaphalanti madhuraphalaṃ. Upapannaphalanti phalūpapannaṃ bahuphalaṃ.

48. 'Sampannaphalaṃ' means having sweet fruit. 'Upapannaphalaṃ' means endowed with fruit, bearing much fruit.

49. Anuttaranti uttamaṃ pabhassaraṃ nirupakkilesaṃ.

49. 'Anuttaraṃ' means supreme, radiant, and without defilement.

50. Ārakā ahaṃ, bhanteti pathavito nabhaṃ viya samuddassa orimatīrato paratīraṃ viya ca suvidūravidūre ahaṃ. Anājānīyeti gihivohārasamucchedanassa kāraṇaṃ ajānanake. Ājānīyabhojananti kāraṇaṃ jānantehi bhuñjitabbaṃ bhojanaṃ. Anājānīyabhojananti kāraṇaṃ ajānantehi bhuñjitabbaṃ bhojanaṃ. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

50. 'Ārakā ahaṃ, bhante' means: I am very, very far away, just as the sky is from the earth, and as the far shore of the ocean is from the near shore. 'Anājānīya' refers to those who do not know the reason for the cutting off of the designation 'householder'. 'Ājānīyabhojanaṃ' means the food to be eaten by those who know the reason. 'Anājānīyabhojanaṃ' means the food to be eaten by those who do not know the reason. The rest is clear in all respects.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya

Potaliyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Potaliya Sutta is concluded.

5. Jīvakasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Jīvaka Sutta

51. Evaṃ [V 3.0033][P 3.0045][M 3.0032] me sutanti jīvakasuttaṃ. Tattha jīvakassa komārabhaccassa ambavaneti ettha jīvatīti jīvako. Kumārena bhatoti komārabhacco. Yathāha “kiṃ etaṃ bhaṇe kākehi samparikiṇṇanti? Dārako devāti. Jīvati bhaṇeti? Jīvati devāti. Tena hi bhaṇe taṃ dārakaṃ amhākaṃ antepuraṃ netvā dhātīnaṃ detha posetunti. Tassa jīvatīti jīvakoti nāmaṃ akaṃsu, kumārena posāpitoti komārabhaccoti nāmaṃ akaṃsū”ti (mahāva. 328). Ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthārena pana jīvakavatthu khandhake āgatameva. Vinicchayakathāpissa samantapāsādikāya vinayaṭṭhakathāya vuttā.

51. The sutta beginning with 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ' is the Jīvaka Sutta. Therein, in the phrase 'in the mango grove of Jīvaka Komārabhacca,' 'Jīvaka' is so called because 'jīvati' (he is alive). 'Komārabhacca' is so called because he was 'kumārena bhato' (nourished by a prince). As it was said: 'Sirs, what is this surrounded by crows?' 'It is a child, lord.' 'Sirs, is he alive?' 'He is alive, lord.' 'Then, sirs, take that child into our inner palace and give him to the nurses to be raised.' Because it was said, 'He is alive,' they gave him the name Jīvaka. Because he was caused to be raised by the prince, they gave him the name Komārabhacca. This is the summary here. The detailed story of Jīvaka, however, has come in the Khandhaka. And the decisive discussion of this has been stated in the Samantapāsādikā, the Vinaya commentary.

Ayaṃ pana jīvako ekasmiṃ samaye bhagavato dosābhisannaṃ kāyaṃ virecetvā sīveyyakaṃ dussayugaṃ datvā vatthānumodanapariyosāne sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāya cintesi – “mayā divasassa dvattikkhattuṃ buddhupaṭṭhānaṃ gantabbaṃ, idañca veḷuvanaṃ atidūre, mayhaṃ uyyānaṃ ambavanaṃ āsannataraṃ, yaṃnūnāhamettha bhagavato vihāraṃ kāreyya”nti. So [P 3.0046] tasmiṃ ambavane rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānaleṇakuṭimaṇḍapādīni sampādetvā bhagavato anucchavikaṃ gandhakuṭiṃ kāretvā ambavanaṃ aṭṭhārasahatthubbedhena tambapaṭṭavaṇṇena pākārena parikkhipāpetvā buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ cīvarabhattena santappetvā dakkhiṇodakaṃ pātetvā vihāraṃ niyyātesi. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “jīvakassa komārabhaccassa ambavane”ti.

Now, this Jīvaka, on one occasion, having administered a purgative to the Blessed One’s body, which was afflicted with a disorder, and having given a pair of Sīveyyaka cloths, became established in the fruit of stream-entry at the conclusion of the rejoicing over the robes. He thought: 'I should attend upon the Buddha two or three times a day, but this Veḷuvana is very far away. My own park, the mango grove, is much closer. It would be good if I were to have a monastery built for the Blessed One here.' So, in that mango grove, having prepared places for the night, places for the day, caves, huts, pavilions, and so on, and having had a suitable perfumed chamber built for the Blessed One, he had the mango grove enclosed with a wall eighteen cubits high, the color of a copper plate. Then, having satisfied the Sangha of bhikkhus with the Buddha at its head with an offering of food and robes, he poured the water of dedication and handed over the monastery. It was with reference to this that it was said: 'in the mango grove of Jīvaka Komārabhacca.'

Ārabhantīti ghātenti. Uddissakatanti uddisitvā kataṃ. Paṭiccakammanti attānaṃ paṭicca kataṃ. Atha vā paṭiccakammanti nimittakammassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ, taṃ paṭicca kammamettha atthīti maṃsaṃ “paṭiccakamma”nti vuttaṃ hoti yo evarūpaṃ maṃsaṃ paribhuñjati, sopi tassa kammassa dāyādo hoti, vadhakassa viya tassāpi pāṇaghātakammaṃ hotīti tesaṃ laddhi. Dhammassa cānudhammaṃ byākarontīti bhagavatā vuttakāraṇassa anukāraṇaṃ kathenti. Ettha ca kāraṇaṃ nāma tikoṭiparisuddhamacchamaṃsaparibhogo, anukāraṇaṃ nāma mahājanassa tathā byākaraṇaṃ. Yasmā pana [V 3.0034] bhagavā uddissakataṃ na paribhuñjati, tasmā neva taṃ kāraṇaṃ hoti, na titthiyānaṃ tathā byākaraṇaṃ [M 3.0033] anukāraṇaṃ. Sahadhammiko vādānuvādoti parehi vuttakāraṇena sakāraṇo hutvā tumhākaṃ vādo vā anuvādo vā viññūhi garahitabbakāraṇaṃ koci appamattakopi kiṃ na āgacchati[P 3.0047]. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “kiṃ sabbākārenapi tumhākaṃ vāde gārayhaṃ kāraṇaṃ natthī”ti. Abbhācikkhantīti abhibhavitvā ācikkhanti.

‘They undertake’ (ārabhanti) means they kill. ‘Prepared for a purpose’ (uddissakataṃ) means made having intended it for someone. ‘Done on account of’ (paṭiccakammaṃ) means made on account of oneself. Alternatively, ‘paṭiccakammaṃ’ is a designation for the causal action, that is, the kamma of destroying life; because the kamma exists on account of that, the meat is called ‘done on account of.’ Whoever consumes such meat becomes an heir to that kamma. Just as for the slayer there is the kamma of killing a living being, so too for that person there is the kamma of killing a living being—this is their doctrine. ‘And they declare a teaching in conformity with the Dhamma’ means they state a conforming reason for the reason stated by the Blessed One. Here, ‘reason’ means the consumption of fish and meat that is pure in three aspects. ‘Conforming reason’ means the declaration of the great populace in that way. But since the Blessed One does not consume what is prepared for a purpose, that is neither a reason, nor is the declaration of the sectarians in that way a conforming reason. ‘A discussion and subsequent discussion in accordance with the Dhamma’ means: When a reason is stated by others, does your statement or subsequent statement, being thus based on a reason, not incur some reason, however small, for censure by the wise? This is what is meant: ‘Is there no censurable reason at all in your statement?’ ‘They slander’ (abbhācikkhanti) means they overwhelm with accusations.

52. Ṭhānehīti kāraṇehi. Diṭṭhādīsu diṭṭhaṃ nāma bhikkhūnaṃ atthāya migamacche vadhitvā gayhamānaṃ diṭṭhaṃ. Sutaṃ nāma bhikkhūnaṃ atthāya migamacche vadhitvā gahitanti sutaṃ. Parisaṅkitaṃ nāma diṭṭhaparisaṅkitaṃ sutaparisaṅkitaṃ tadubhayavimuttaparisaṅkitanti tividhaṃ hoti.

52. ‘On grounds’ (ṭhānehi) means by reasons (kāraṇehi). Among these, beginning with ‘seen,’ ‘seen’ refers to meat from game or fish that one has seen being taken after it was killed for the sake of bhikkhus. ‘Heard’ refers to meat that one has heard of thus: ‘It was taken after killing game or fish for the sake of bhikkhus.’ ‘Suspected’ is threefold: suspicion based on what is seen, suspicion based on what is heard, and suspicion free from both of these.

Tatrāyaṃ sabbasaṅgāhakavinicchayo – idha bhikkhū passanti manusse jālavāgurādihatthe gāmato vā nikkhamante araññe vā vicarante. Dutiyadivase ca nesaṃ taṃ gāmaṃ piṇḍāya paviṭṭhānaṃ samacchamaṃsaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ abhiharanti. Te tena diṭṭhena parisaṅkanti “bhikkhūnaṃ nu kho atthāya kata”nti, idaṃ diṭṭhaparisaṅkitaṃ nāma, etaṃ gahetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Yaṃ evaṃ aparisaṅkitaṃ, taṃ vaṭṭati. Sace pana te manussā “kasmā, bhante, na gaṇhathā”ti pucchitvā tamatthaṃ sutvā “nayidaṃ, bhante, bhikkhūnaṃ atthāya kataṃ, amhehi attano atthāya vā rājayuttādīnaṃ atthāya vā kata”nti vadanti, kappati.

Herein is the all-encompassing decisive explanation: In this teaching, bhikkhus see people with nets, traps, and the like in hand, either leaving a village or wandering in the forest. And on the next day, when they have entered that village for alms, people bring forward almsfood with fish and meat. On account of what was seen, they suspect, 'Could it have been prepared for the sake of the bhikkhus?' This is called 'suspicion based on what is seen,' and it is not allowable to accept it. Whatever is not suspected in this way is allowable. But if those people, on being asked, 'Venerable sirs, why do you not accept it?' and having heard the reason, say, 'Venerable sirs, this was not prepared for the sake of the bhikkhus; it was prepared by us for our own sake or for the sake of royal officials and so on,' then it is permissible.

Na heva kho bhikkhū passanti, apica suṇanti “manussā kira jālavāgurādihatthā gāmato vā nikkhamanti araññe vā vicarantī”ti. Dutiyadivase ca nesaṃ taṃ gāmaṃ piṇḍāya paviṭṭhānaṃ samacchamaṃsaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ abhiharanti. Te tena sutena parisaṅkanti “bhikkhūnaṃ nu kho atthāya kata”nti, idaṃ sutaparisaṅkitaṃ nāma, etaṃ gahetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Yaṃ evaṃ aparisaṅkitaṃ, taṃ vaṭṭati. Sace pana te manussā “kasmā, bhante, na gaṇhathā”ti pucchitvā tamatthaṃ sutvā “nayidaṃ, bhante, bhikkhūnaṃ atthāya kataṃ, amhehi [P 3.0048] attano atthāya vā rājayuttādīnaṃ atthāya vā kata”nti vadanti, kappati.

Bhikkhus do not actually see, but they hear: 'It is said that people with nets, traps, and the like in hand leave the village or wander in the forest.' And on the next day, when they have entered that village for alms, people bring forward almsfood with fish and meat. On account of what was heard, they suspect, 'Could it have been prepared for the sake of the bhikkhus?' This is called 'suspicion based on what is heard,' and it is not allowable to accept it. Whatever is not suspected in this way is allowable. But if those people, on being asked, 'Venerable sirs, why do you not accept it?' and having heard the reason, say, 'Venerable sirs, this was not prepared for the sake of the bhikkhus; it was prepared by us for our own sake or for the sake of royal officials and so on,' then it is permissible.

Na heva kho pana passanti na suṇanti, apica tesaṃ gāmaṃ piṇḍāya paviṭṭhānaṃ pattaṃ gahetvā [V 3.0035] samacchamaṃsaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ abhisaṅkharitvā abhiharanti. Te parisaṅkanti “bhikkhūnaṃ nu kho atthāya kata”nti, idaṃ tadubhayavimuttaparisaṅkitaṃ nāma. Etampi gahetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Yaṃ evaṃ aparisaṅkitaṃ, taṃ vaṭṭati[M 3.0034]. Sace pana te manussā “kasmā, bhante, na gaṇhathā”ti pucchitvā tamatthaṃ sutvā “nayidaṃ, bhante, bhikkhūnaṃ atthāya kataṃ, amhehi attano atthāya vā rājayuttādīnaṃ atthāya vā kataṃ, pavattamaṃsaṃ vā kataṃ, kappiyameva labhitvā bhikkhūnaṃ atthāya sampādita”nti vadanti, kappati.

Furthermore, they do not see, nor do they hear. But indeed, when they have entered the village for alms, people take their bowls and, having prepared almsfood with fish and meat, bring it to them. They suspect, 'Could it have been prepared for the sake of the bhikkhus?' This is called suspicion that is free from both seeing and hearing. Even this is not allowable to accept. Whatever is not suspected in this way is allowable. However, if those people, on being asked, 'Why, venerable sirs, do you not accept it?' and having heard the reason, say, 'Venerable sirs, this was not prepared for the sake of the bhikkhus. It was prepared by us for our own sake, or for the sake of royal officials and so on. Or it was readily available meat that was prepared. Or, having obtained what is allowable, it was arranged for the sake of the bhikkhus,' then it is allowable.

Matānaṃ petakiccatthāya maṅgalādīnaṃ vā atthāya katepi eseva nayo. Yaṃ yañhi bhikkhūnaṃyeva atthāya akataṃ, yattha ca nibbematikā honti, taṃ sabbaṃ kappati. Sace pana ekasmiṃ vihāre bhikkhū uddissa kataṃ hoti, te ca attano atthāya katabhāvaṃ na jānanti, aññe jānanti. Ye jānanti, tesaṃ na vaṭṭati, itaresaṃ vaṭṭati. Aññe na jānanti, teyeva jānanti, tesaṃyeva na vaṭṭati, aññesaṃ vaṭṭati. Tepi “amhākaṃ atthāya kataṃ”ti jānanti aññepi “etesaṃ atthāya kata”nti jānanti, sabbesampi taṃ na vaṭṭati. Sabbe na jānanti, sabbesaṃ vaṭṭati. Pañcasu hi sahadhammikesu yassa kassaci vā atthāya uddissa kataṃ sabbesaṃ na kappati.

This same principle should be understood even when it is prepared for the sake of rites for the deceased, or for the sake of auspicious occasions and so on. Indeed, whatever meat is not prepared for the sake of the monks, and regarding which they are free from doubt, all of that is allowable. However, if in a certain monastery it is prepared intended for the monks, and they do not know the fact that it was prepared for their sake, but others know, it is not allowable for those who know, but it is allowable for the others. If others do not know, and only they themselves know, it is not allowable only for them, but it is allowable for the others. If they too know, 'It was prepared for our sake,' and others also know, 'It was prepared for their sake,' it is not allowable for any of them. If none of them know, it is allowable for all of them. For, among five companions in the Dhamma, if it is prepared intended for the sake of any one of them, it is not allowable for all of them.

Sace pana koci ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ uddissa pāṇaṃ vadhitvā tassa pattaṃ pūretvā deti, so ce attano atthāya katabhāvaṃ jānaṃyeva gahetvā aññassa bhikkhuno deti, so tassa saddhāya paribhuñjati. Kassāpattīti? Dvinnampi anāpatti. Yañhi uddissa [P 3.0049] kataṃ, tassa abhuttatāya anāpatti, itarassa ajānanatāya. Kappiyamaṃsassa hi paṭiggahaṇe āpatti natthi. Uddissakatañca ajānitvā bhuttassa pacchā ñatvā āpattidesanākiccaṃ nāma natthi. Akappiyamaṃsaṃ pana ajānitvā bhuttena pacchā ñatvāpi āpatti desetabbā. Uddissakatañhi ñatvā bhuñjatova āpatti, akappiyamaṃsaṃ ajānitvā bhuttassāpi āpattiyeva. Tasmā āpattibhīrukena rūpaṃ sallakkhentenāpi pucchitvāva maṃsaṃ paṭiggahetabbaṃ, paribhogakāle pucchitvā paribhuñjissāmīti vā gahetvā pucchitvāva paribhuñjitabbaṃ. Kasmā? Duviññeyyattā. Acchamaṃsañhi sūkaramaṃsasadisaṃ hoti, dīpimaṃsādīni ca migamaṃsasadisāni, tasmā pucchitvā gahaṇameva vaṭṭatīti vadanti.

However, if someone, having killed a living being intended for a certain monk, fills his bowl and gives it, and if that monk, knowing full well the fact that it was prepared for his sake, takes it and gives it to another monk, and that one consumes it with faith in him, whose is the offense? For both, there is no offense. For the one for whom it was intended, because of not having eaten it, there is no offense; for the other, because of not knowing. Indeed, there is no offense in the acceptance of allowable meat. For one who has eaten what was intended for him without knowing, there is no duty of confessing an offense upon knowing later. However, for one who has eaten unallowable meat without knowing, the offense must be confessed even upon knowing later. Indeed, an offense occurs only for one who eats what was intended for him while knowing it; for one who has eaten unallowable meat even without knowing, there is indeed an offense. Therefore, a monk who is fearful of offenses should accept meat only after asking, even while observing its appearance. Or, having taken it with the thought, 'I will consume it after asking at the time of consumption,' it should be consumed only after asking. Why? Because of the difficulty in distinguishing. For bear meat is similar to pork, and leopard meat and so on are similar to deer meat. Therefore, the teachers say that only accepting it after asking is allowable.

Adiṭṭhanti [V 3.0036] bhikkhūnaṃ atthāya vadhitvā gayhamānaṃ adiṭṭhaṃ. Asutanti bhikkhūnaṃ atthāya vadhitvā gahitanti asutaṃ. Aparisaṅkitanti diṭṭhaparisaṅkitādivasena aparisaṅkitaṃ. Paribhoganti vadāmīti imehi tīhi kāraṇehi parisuddhaṃ tikoṭiparisuddhaṃ nāma hoti, tassa paribhogo araññe jātasūpeyyasākaparibhogasadiso hoti, tathārūpaṃ paribhuñjantassa mettāvihārissa [M 3.0035] bhikkhuno doso vā vajjaṃ vā natthi, tasmā taṃ paribhuñjitabbanti vadāmīti attho.

'Not seen' means: not having seen it being killed and taken for the sake of monks. 'Not heard' means: not having heard that it was killed and taken for the sake of monks. 'Not suspected' means: not suspected by way of suspicion from seeing and so on. Regarding the allowance for consumption, the meaning is this: what is pure by these three reasons is called 'pure in three aspects.' Its consumption is like the consumption of naturally grown vegetables suitable for curry in the forest. For a monk who dwells in loving-kindness consuming such a thing, there is no fault or blame. Therefore, I say, 'It should be consumed.'

53. Idāni tādisassa paribhoge mettāvihārinopi anavajjataṃ dassetuṃ idha, jīvaka, bhikkhūtiādimāha. Tattha kiñcāpi aniyametvā bhikkhūti vuttaṃ, atha kho attānameva sandhāya etaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Bhagavatā hi mahāvacchagottasutte, caṅkīsutte, imasmiṃ sutteti tīsu ṭhānesu attānaṃyeva sandhāya desanā katā. Paṇītena [P 3.0050] piṇḍapātenāti heṭṭhā anaṅgaṇasutte yo koci mahaggho piṇḍapāto paṇītapiṇḍapātoti adhippeto, idha pana maṃsūpasecanova adhippeto. Agathitoti taṇhāya agathito. Amucchitoti taṇhāmucchanāya amucchito. Anajjhopannoti na adhiopanno, sabbaṃ ālumpitvā ekappahāreneva gilitukāmo kāko viya na hotīti attho. Ādīnavadassāvīti ekarattivāsena udarapaṭalaṃ pavisitvā navahi vaṇamukhehi nikkhamissatītiādinā nayena ādīnavaṃ passanto. Nissaraṇapañño paribhuñjatīti idamatthamāhāraparibhogoti paññāya paricchinditvā paribhuñjati. Attabyābādhāya vā cetetīti attadukkhāya vā citeti. Sutametanti sutaṃ mayā etaṃ pubbe, etaṃ mayhaṃ savanamattamevāti dasseti. Sace kho te, jīvaka, idaṃ sandhāya bhāsitanti, jīvaka, mahābrahmunā vikkhambhanappahānena byāpādādayo pahīnā, tena so mettāvihārī mayhaṃ samucchedappahānena, sace te idaṃ sandhāya bhāsitaṃ, evaṃ sante tava idaṃ vacanaṃ anujānāmīti attho. So sampaṭicchi.

53. Now, to show the blamelessness in the consumption of such food even for one who dwells in loving-kindness, he said, 'Here, Jīvaka, a monk...' and so on. Therein, although 'a monk' is said without specifying, it should be known that this was said referring only to himself. For the Blessed One, in the Mahāvacchagotta Sutta, the Caṅkī Sutta, and in this sutta—in these three places—the teaching was given referring only to himself. Regarding 'with excellent almsfood': whereas below, in the Anaṅgaṇa Sutta, any highly valued almsfood is intended by 'excellent almsfood,' here, only almsfood with meat as a condiment is intended. 'Not greedy' (agathito) means not greedy with craving. 'Not infatuated' (amucchito) means not infatuated with the delusion of craving. 'Not overwhelmed' (anajjhopanno) means not overcome by it; the meaning is not being like a crow that, making a lump of all the food, desires to swallow it in a single gulp. 'Seeing the danger' (ādīnavadassāvī) means seeing the danger in this way: 'Having stayed for one night and entered the lining of the stomach, it will exit through the nine wound-openings,' and so on. 'Consumes with wisdom of escape' (nissaraṇapañño paribhuñjati) means one consumes having determined with wisdom that this is the purpose of consuming food. 'Or intends for self-affliction' (attabyābādhāya vā ceteti) means or intends for one's own suffering. 'This has been heard by me' (sutametaṃ) indicates: 'This has been heard by me before; for me, this is a mere matter of hearing.' As for 'If, Jīvaka, this was spoken by you with reference to this': the meaning is, 'Jīvaka, by the great Brahmā, ill will and so on are abandoned by suppression-abandonment, and by that he is one who dwells in loving-kindness. For me, they are abandoned by eradication-abandonment. If this was spoken by you with reference to this, this being so, I permit this statement of yours.' He accepted.

54. Athassa bhagavā sesabrahmavihāravasenāpi uttari desanaṃ vaḍḍhento “idha, jīvaka, bhikkhū”tiādimāha. Taṃ uttānatthameva.
