54. Then the Blessed One, further extending the discourse by way of the remaining divine abodes, said: 'Here, Jīvaka, a monk...' and so on. That has a plain meaning.

55. Yo [P 3.0051] kho jīvakāti ayaṃ pāṭiekko anusandhi. Imasmiñhi ṭhāne bhagavā dvāraṃ thaketi, sattānuddayaṃ dasseti. Sace hi kassaci evamassa “ekaṃ rasapiṇḍapātaṃ datvā kappasatasahassaṃ [V 3.0037] saggasampattiṃ paṭilabhanti, yaṃkiñci katvā paraṃ māretvāpi rasapiṇḍapātova dātabbo”ti, taṃ paṭisedhento “yo kho, jīvaka, tathāgataṃ vā”tiādimāha.

55. The phrase 'Yo kho, Jīvaka...' is a particular connection. For at this point the Blessed One blocks a door and shows compassion for beings. For if someone were to think, “By giving a single choice meal one obtains heavenly bliss for a hundred thousand aeons; therefore, having done anything whatsoever, even having killed another, a choice meal ought to be given,” then, forbidding this, he said: “Whoever, Jīvaka, for the Tathāgata or…” and so on.

Tattha [M 3.0036] iminā paṭhamena ṭhānenāti iminā āṇattimatteneva tāva paṭhamena kāraṇena. Galappavedhakenāti yottena gale bandhitvā kaḍḍhito galena pavedhentena. Ārabhiyamānoti māriyamāno. Akappiyena āsādetīti acchamaṃsaṃ sūkaramaṃsanti, dīpimaṃsaṃ vā migamaṃsanti khādāpetvā – “tvaṃ kiṃ samaṇo nāma, akappiyamaṃsaṃ te khādita”nti ghaṭṭeti. Ye pana dubbhikkhādīsu vā byādhiniggahaṇatthaṃ vā “acchamaṃsaṃ nāma sūkaramaṃsasadisaṃ, dīpimaṃsaṃ migamaṃsasadisa”nti jānantā “sūkaramaṃsaṃ idaṃ, migamaṃsaṃ ida”nti vatvā hitajjhāsayena khādāpenti, na te sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Tesañhi bahupuññameva hoti. Esāhaṃ, bhante, bhagavantaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi dhammañca bhikkhusaṅghañcāti ayaṃ āgataphalo viññātasāsano diṭṭhasacco ariyasāvako. Imaṃ pana dhammadesanaṃ ogāhanto pasādaṃ uppādetvā dhammakathāya thutiṃ karonto evamāha. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

Here, 'by this first ground' means: in the first place, by this first reason, which is a mere command. 'By the neck-wrapper' means: dragged by the neck, having been bound and wrapped with a rope. 'Being harmed' means being killed. 'He makes one partake of the unfitting' means: having made one eat bear's meat, saying it is pork, or leopard's meat, saying it is deer's meat, he then harasses them, saying: 'What kind of monk are you? You have eaten unfitting meat.' But as for those who, during times of famine and so on, or for the purpose of treating an illness, knowing that 'bear's meat is like pork, and leopard's meat is like deer's meat,' say, 'This is pork, this is deer's meat,' and make one eat it with a beneficial intention—it was not said in reference to them. Indeed, for them there is much merit. The phrase 'Venerable sir, I go for refuge to the Blessed One, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus' is spoken by one who is a noble disciple, who has attained the fruit, understood the teaching, and seen the truth. But, having penetrated this Dhamma discourse and aroused faith, he speaks thus, offering praise for the Dhamma talk. The rest is clear in every case.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Middle Length Discourses.

Jīvakasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Jīvaka Sutta is finished.

6. Upālisuttavaṇṇanā

6. Explanation of the Upāli Sutta

56. Evaṃ [V 3.0038][P 3.0052] me sutanti upālisuttaṃ. Tattha nāḷandāyanti nālandāti evaṃnāmake nagare taṃ nagaraṃ gocaragāmaṃ katvā. Pāvārikambavaneti dussapāvārikaseṭṭhino ambavane. Taṃ kira tassa uyyānaṃ ahosi, so bhagavato dhammadesanaṃ sutvā bhagavati pasanno tasmiṃ uyyāne kuṭileṇamaṇḍapādipaṭimaṇḍitaṃ bhagavato vihāraṃ katvā niyyādesi, so vihāro jīvakambavanaṃ viya pāvārikambavananteva saṅkhaṃ gato. Tasmiṃ pāvārikambavane viharatīti attho. Dīghatapassīti dīghattā evaṃladdhanāmo. Piṇḍapātapaṭikkantoti piṇḍapātato paṭikkanto. Sāsane viya kiṃ pana bāhirāyatane piṇḍapātoti vohāro atthīti, natthi.

56. Thus have I heard—this is the Upāli Sutta. There, 'in Nāḷandā' means in a city named Nāḷandā, having made that city a village for alms-going. 'In Pāvārika’s mango grove' means in the mango grove of the merchant Pāvārika. It seems that was his park; having heard the Blessed One’s teaching and gained faith in the Blessed One, he had a monastery built for the Blessed One in that park, adorned with huts, caves, pavilions, and so on, and dedicated it. That monastery, like Jīvaka’s mango grove, came to be known as Pāvārika’s mango grove. 'He dwells in Pāvārika’s mango grove'—this is the meaning. 'Dīghatapassī' was the name he received on account of his tallness. 'Returned from alms-round' means returned from the alms-round. But is there also the usage 'alms-round' in outside doctrines, as in the Teaching? There is not.

Paññapetīti dasseti ṭhapeti. Daṇḍāni paññapetīti idaṃ nigaṇṭhasamayena pucchanto āha. Kāyadaṇḍaṃ vacīdaṇḍaṃ manodaṇḍanti ettha purimadaṇḍadvayaṃ te acittakaṃ payyapenti. Yathā kira vāte vāyante sākhā calati, udakaṃ [M 3.0037] calati, na ca tattha cittaṃ atthi, evaṃ kāyadaṇḍopi acittakova hoti. Yathā ca vāte vāyante tālapaṇṇādīni saddaṃ karonti, udakāni saddaṃ karonti[P 3.0053], na ca tattha cittaṃ atthi, evaṃ vacīdaṇḍopi acittakova hotīti imaṃ daṇḍadvayaṃ acittakaṃ paññapenti. Cittaṃ pana manodaṇḍanti paññapenti. Athassa bhagavā vacanaṃ patiṭṭhapetukāmo “kiṃ pana tapassī”tiādimāha.

'He lays down' means he shows, he establishes. He said this—'Does he lay down rods?'—asking in accordance with the Nigaṇṭha doctrine. Here, regarding 'bodily rod, verbal rod, and mental rod,' they lay down the first two rods as being without mind. Just as when the wind blows, a branch moves and water moves, yet there is no mind there, so too the bodily rod is without mind. And just as when the wind blows, palm leaves and so on make a sound and waters make a sound, yet there is no mind there, so too the verbal rod is without mind. Thus they lay down these two rods as being without mind. The mind, however, they lay down as the mental rod. Then the Blessed One, wishing to have his statement established, said the words beginning: 'But what, ascetic…'

Tattha kathāvatthusminti ettha kathāyeva kathāvatthu. Kathāyaṃ patiṭṭhapesīti attho. Kasmā pana bhagavā evamakāsi? Passati hi bhagavā “ayaṃ imaṃ kathaṃ ādāya gantvā attano satthu mahānigaṇṭhassa ārocessati, tāsañca parisati, upāli gahapati nisinno, so imaṃ kathaṃ sutvā mama vādaṃ āropetuṃ āgamissati, tassāhaṃ dhammaṃ desessāmi, so tikkhattuṃ saraṇaṃ gamissati, athassa cattāri saccāni pakāsessāmi, so saccapakāsanāvasāne sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahissati, paresaṃ saṅgahatthameva hi mayā pāramiyo pūritā”ti. Imamatthaṃ passanto evamakāsi.

Here, in the phrase 'on the topic of discussion' (kathāvatthusmiṃ), the talk itself is the topic of discussion (kathāvatthu). The meaning is that he established it in the talk. But why did the Blessed One do so? For the Blessed One sees: 'This person will take this talk, go, and report it to his teacher, the great Nigaṇṭha. And in that assembly, the householder Upāli is seated. Having heard this talk, he will come to me to raise an objection against my teaching. I will teach him the Dhamma. He will go for refuge three times, and then I will reveal the Four Truths to him. At the conclusion of the revealing of the truths, he will be established in the fruit of stream-entry. Indeed, it was for the very purpose of helping others that the perfections were fulfilled by me.' Seeing this purpose, he acted thus.

57. Kammāni [V 3.0039] paññapesīti idaṃ nigaṇṭho buddhasamayena pucchanto āha. Kāyakammaṃ vacīkammaṃ manokammanti ettha kāyadvāre ādānagahaṇamuñcanacopanapattā aṭṭhakāmāvacarakusalacetanā dvādasākusalacetanāti vīsaticetanā kāyakammaṃ nāma. Kāyadvāre ādānādīni apatvā vacīdvāre vacanabhedaṃ pāpayamānā uppannā tāyeva vīsaticetanā vacīkammaṃ nāma. Ubhayadvāre copanaṃ appatvā manodvāre uppannā ekūnatiṃsakusalākusalacetanā manokammaṃ nāma. Apica saṅkhepato tividhaṃ kāyaduccaritaṃ kāyakammaṃ nāma, catubbidhaṃ vacīduccaritaṃ vacīkammaṃ nāma, tividhaṃ manoduccaritaṃ manokammaṃ nāma. Imasmiñca sutte kammaṃ dhuraṃ, anantarasutte [P 3.0054] “cattārimāni puṇṇa kammāni mayā sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā paveditānī”ti (ma. ni. 2.81) evamāgatepi cetanā dhuraṃ. Yattha katthaci pavattā cetanā “kaṇhaṃ kaṇhavipāka”ntiādibhedaṃ labhati. Niddesavāre cassa “sabyābajjhaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkharotī”tiādinā nayena sā vuttāva. Kāyadvāre pavattā pana idha kāyakammanti adhippetaṃ, vacīdvāre [M 3.0038] pavattā vacīkammaṃ, manodvāre pavattā manokammaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ – “imasmiṃ sutte kammaṃ dhuraṃ, anantarasutte cetanā”ti. Kammampi hi bhagavā kammanti paññapeti yathā imasmiṃyeva sutte. Cetanampi, yathāha – “cetanāhaṃ, bhikkhave, kammaṃ vadāmi, cetayitvā kammaṃ karotī”ti (a. ni. 6.63). Kasmā pana cetanā kammanti vuttā? Cetanāmūlakattā kammassa.

57. 'He declares actions'—this was said by the Nigaṇṭha, questioning according to the Buddha's doctrine. Regarding bodily action, verbal action, and mental action: herein, the twenty volitions—eight wholesome sense-sphere volitions and twelve unwholesome volitions—that arise through the body-door, involving taking, holding, releasing, and striking, are called bodily action. The same twenty volitions, not reaching taking, etc., through the body-door but arising through the speech-door and causing an utterance, are called verbal action. The twenty-nine mundane wholesome and unwholesome volitions that arise through the mind-door, not reaching striking through either of the two doors, are called mental action. Furthermore, in brief, the threefold bodily misconduct is called bodily action, the fourfold verbal misconduct is called verbal action, and the threefold mental misconduct is called mental action. And in this discourse, action is primary, but in the immediately following discourse, where it is stated, 'These four actions, Puṇṇa, have been declared by me after realizing them myself through direct knowledge,' even there, volition is primary. Volition, occurring anywhere, receives classifications such as 'dark with dark result.' In the section on detailed explanation, that volition is spoken of by the method beginning with, 'He forms a harmful bodily formation,' and so on. Here, however, volition arising through the body-door is intended as bodily action, that arising through the speech-door as verbal action, and that arising through the mind-door as mental action. Therefore it was said: 'In this discourse, action is primary; in the immediately following discourse, volition is.' For the Blessed One also declares action as action, as in this very discourse. And also volition, as he said: 'Volition, O monks, I say is action; having willed, one performs an action.' But why is volition called action? Because action has volition as its root.

Ettha ca akusalaṃ patvā kāyakammaṃ vacīkammaṃ mahantanti vadanto na kilamati, kusalaṃ patvā manokammaṃ. Tathā hi mātughātādīni cattāri kammāni kāyeneva upakkamitvā kāyeneva karoti, niraye kappaṭṭhikasaṅghabhedakammaṃ vacīdvārena karoti. Evaṃ akusalaṃ patvā kāyakammaṃ vacīkammaṃ mahantanti vadanto na kilamati nāma. Ekā pana jhānacetanā caturāsītikappasahassāni saggasampattiṃ āvahati, ekā maggacetanā sabbākusalaṃ samugghātetvā arahattaṃ gaṇhāpeti. Evaṃ kusalaṃ patvā manokammaṃ mahantanti vadanto na kilamati nāma. Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne bhagavā akusalaṃ patvā manokammaṃ mahāsāvajjaṃ vadamāno niyatamicchādiṭṭhiṃ sandhāya vadati. Tenevāha – “nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, aññaṃ ekadhammampi samanupassāmi, yaṃ evaṃ mahāsāvajjaṃ, yathayidaṃ, bhikkhave, micchādiṭṭhi. Micchādiṭṭhiparamāni, bhikkhave, mahāsāvajjānī”ti (a. ni. 1.310).

And here, with respect to the unwholesome, one does not tire of saying that bodily action and verbal action are great. For indeed, the four deeds such as matricide are undertaken with the body and done with the body; the act of creating a schism in the Saṅgha, which makes one remain in hell for an eon, is done through the verbal door. Thus, with respect to the unwholesome, one does not tire of saying that bodily action and verbal action are great. However, a single jhāna-volition brings heavenly bliss for eighty-four thousand eons, and a single path-volition, having eradicated all that is unwholesome, causes one to attain Arahantship. Thus, with respect to the wholesome, one does not tire of saying that mental action is great. In this instance, however, the Blessed One, when speaking of mental action with respect to the unwholesome as being greatly blameworthy, speaks with reference to fixed wrong view. Therefore He said: 'Monks, I do not see even one other thing that is so greatly blameworthy as this wrong view. Monks, faults have wrong view as their utmost.'

Idāni [V 3.0040] nigaṇṭhopi tathāgatena gatamaggaṃ [P 3.0055] paṭipajjanto kiñci atthanipphattiṃ apassantopi “kiṃ panāvuso, gotamā”tiādimāha.

Now, the Nigaṇṭha, though attempting to follow the path taken by the Tathāgata and not seeing any accomplishment of purpose, said, 'But what, friend Gotama?' and so on.

58. Bālakiniyāti upālissa kira bālakaloṇakāragāmo nāma atthi, tato āyaṃ gahetvā manussā āgatā, so “etha bhaṇe, amhākaṃ satthāraṃ mahānigaṇṭhaṃ passissāmā”ti tāya parisāya parivuto tattha agamāsi. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “bālakiniyā parisāyā”ti, bālakagāmavāsiniyāti attho. Upālipamukhāyāti upālijeṭṭhakāya. Apica bālakiniyāti bālavatiyā bālussannāyātipi attho. Upālipamukhāyāti upāligahapatiyeva tattha thokaṃ sappañño, so tassā pamukho jeṭṭhako. Tenāpi vuttaṃ “upālipamukhāyā”ti. Handāti vacasāyatthe nipāto. Chavoti lāmako. Oḷārikassāti mahantassa[M 3.0039]. Upanidhāyāti upanikkhipitvā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti, kāyadaṇḍassa santike nikkhipitvā “ayaṃ nu kho mahanto, ayaṃ mahanto”ti evaṃ olokiyamāno chavo manodaṇḍo kiṃ sobhati, kuto sobhissati, na sobhati, upanikkhepamattampi nappahotīti dīpeti. Sādhu sādhu, bhante, tapassīti dīghatapassissa sādhukāraṃ dento, bhanteti nāṭaputtamālapati.

58. Regarding Bālakiniyā: It is said that Upāli had a village named Bālakaloṇakāra. People returned from there after collecting the revenue. He then said, 'Come, sirs, let us see our teacher, the great Nigaṇṭha,' and surrounded by that assembly, he went there. With reference to this, it was said 'by the assembly of Bālakiniyā,' the meaning of which is 'of the residents of the village Bālaka.' 'With Upāli as its chief' means 'with Upāli as its elder.' Furthermore, 'Bālakiniyā' can also be understood to mean 'of an assembly with fools, abounding in fools.' 'With Upāli as its chief' means that only the householder Upāli was somewhat wise in that assembly; he was their chief, their elder. For that reason also it was said 'with Upāli as its chief.' 'Handa' is a particle used in connection with speech. 'Chavo' means base. 'Oḷārikassa' means of the great one. 'Upanidhāya' means having placed beside. This is what is meant: having placed it beside the bodily rod and while it is being examined thus, 'Is this one great, or is this one great?', the base mental rod—how could it shine? From where would it shine? It does not shine. This shows that even the mere act of placing it beside is not sufficient. 'Excellent, excellent, venerable ascetic'—while giving approval to Dīghatapassī, he addresses Nāṭaputta as 'bhante'.

60. Na [P 3.0056] kho metaṃ, bhante, ruccatīti, bhante, etaṃ mayhaṃ na ruccati. Māyāvīti māyākāro. Āvaṭṭanimāyanti āvaṭṭetvā gahaṇamāyaṃ. Āvaṭṭetīti āvaṭṭetvā parikkhipitvā gaṇhāti. Gaccha tvaṃ gahapatīti kasmā mahānigaṇṭho gahapatiṃ yāvatatiyaṃ pahiṇatiyeva? Dīghatapassī pana paṭibāhateva? Mahānigaṇṭhena hi bhagavatā saddhiṃ ekaṃ nagaraṃ upanissāya viharantenapi na bhagavā diṭṭhapubbo. Yo hi satthuvādapaṭiñño hoti, so taṃ paṭiññaṃ appahāya buddhadassane abhabbo. Tasmā esa buddhadassanassa aladdhapubbattā dasabalassa dassanasampattiñca niyyānikakathābhāvañca ajānanto yāvatatiyaṃ pahiṇateva. Dīghatapassī pana kālena kālaṃ bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā tiṭṭhatipi nisīdatipi pañhampi pucchati, so tathāgatassa dassanasampattimpi niyyānikakathābhāvampi jānāti. Athassa etadahosi – “ayaṃ gahapati paṇḍito, samaṇassa gotamassa santike gantvā dassanepi pasīdeyya, niyyānikakathaṃ sutvāpi pasīdeyya. Tato na puna amhākaṃ santikaṃ āgaccheyyā”ti. Tasmā yāvatatiyaṃ paṭibāhateva.

60. 'This does not please me, venerable sir,' means, 'Venerable sir, this is not pleasing to me.' 'Deceptive' means one who practices deception. 'The art of winning over' means the art of winning over by turning one from a previous practice. 'He wins over' means having encircled, he captures. Why does the great Nigaṇṭha send the householder up to the third time? But why does Dīghatapassī repeatedly forbid it? Truly, although the great Nigaṇṭha dwelt depending on the same city as the Blessed One, he had never seen the Blessed One before. Truly, whoever claims to be a teacher, without abandoning that claim, is unfit to see a Buddha. Therefore, because he had never before attained the sight of a Buddha, not knowing the perfection of seeing the Ten-Powered One and the nature of the liberating discourse, he sends him up to the third time. But Dīghatapassī, having approached the Blessed One from time to time, stands, sits, and asks questions; he knows the perfection of seeing the Tathāgata and the nature of the liberating discourse. Then this thought occurred to him: 'This householder is wise. Having gone to the presence of the ascetic Gotama, he might gain faith even by merely seeing him, or he might gain faith by hearing the liberating discourse. Then he would not return to our presence.' Therefore, he forbids him up to the third time.

Abhivādetvāti [V 3.0041] vanditvā. Tathāgatañhi disvā pasannāpi appasannāpi yebhuyyena vandantiyeva, appakā na vandanti. Kasmā? Atiucce hi kule jāto agāraṃ ajjhāvasantopi vanditabboyevāti. Ayaṃ pana gahapati pasannattāva vandi, dassaneyeva kira pasanno. Āgamā nu khvidhāti āgamā nu kho idha.

'Having paid homage' means having bowed. Truly, upon seeing the Tathāgata, both those who are pleased and those who are not pleased, for the most part, do indeed pay homage; few do not pay homage. Why? Because he was born into a very high family, even while living as a householder, he is indeed worthy of homage. But this householder paid homage precisely because he was pleased; it seems he was pleased at the mere sight. The phrase 'Āgamā nu khvidha' should be parsed as 'Āgamā nu kho idha,' meaning, 'Has Dīghatapassī come here?'

61. Sādhu sādhu, bhante, tapassīti dīghatapassissa sādhukāraṃ dento, bhanteti, bhagavantaṃ ālapati. Sacce patiṭṭhāyāti thusarāsimhi ākoṭitakhāṇuko viya acalanto vacīsacce patiṭṭhahitvā. Siyā [P 3.0057] noti bhaveyya amhākaṃ.

61. Regarding 'Excellent, excellent, venerable ascetic': This means that while giving approval to Dīghatapassī, he addresses the Blessed One with the word 'venerable sir' (`bhante`). 'Established in truth' means, like a stake hammered into a heap of chaff, unmoving, having established oneself in verbal truth. 'Let there be for us' means, 'Let there be a conversation between us.'

62. Idhāti [M 3.0040] imasmiṃ loke. Assāti bhaveyya. Sītodakapaṭikkhittoti nigaṇṭhā sattasaññāya sītodakaṃ paṭikkhipanti. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Manosattā nāma devāti manamhi sattā laggā lagitā. Manopaṭibaddhoti yasmā manamhi paṭibaddho hutvā kālaṅkaroti, tasmā manosattesu devesu upapajjatīti dasseti. Tassa hi pittajararogo bhavissati. Tenassa uṇhodakaṃ pivituṃ vā hatthapādādidhovanatthāya vā gattaparisiñcanatthāya vā upanetuṃ na vaṭṭati, rogo balavataro hoti. Sītodakaṃ vaṭṭati, rogaṃ vūpasameti. Ayaṃ pana uṇhodakameva paṭisevati, taṃ alabhamāno odanakañjikaṃ paṭisevati. Cittena pana sītodakaṃ pātukāmo ca paribhuñjitukāmo ca hoti. Tenassa manodaṇḍo tattheva bhijjati. So kāyadaṇḍaṃ vacīdaṇḍaṃ rakkhāmīti sītodakaṃ pātukāmo vā paribhuñjitukāmo vā sītodakameva dethāti vattuṃ na visahati. Tassa evaṃ rakkhitāpi kāyadaṇḍavacīdaṇḍā cutiṃ vā paṭisandhiṃ vā ākaḍḍhituṃ na sakkonti. Manodaṇḍo pana bhinnopi cutimpi paṭisandhimpi ākaḍḍhatiyeva. Iti naṃ bhagavā dubbalakāyadaṇḍavacīdaṇḍā chavā lāmakā, manodaṇḍova balavā mahantoti vadāpesi.

62. 'Here' means in this world. 'There might be' means there could be. 'One by whom cold water is rejected': the Nigaṇṭhas reject cold water due to the perception of living beings within it. This was said with reference to that. 'Gods called mind-attached' are those attached to, clinging to, stuck in the mind. 'Bound to the mind': this shows that because one dies while bound to the mind, one is reborn among the mind-attached gods. Truly, such a person will have a disease caused by bile. For him, it is not proper to be brought hot water to drink, or for washing his hands and feet, or for pouring on his body, as the disease becomes stronger. Cold water is suitable; it soothes the disease. But this person uses only hot water, and when unable to get it, uses rice gruel. In his mind, however, he desires to drink and to use cold water. Because of that, his mental rod breaks right there. Thinking, 'I will guard the bodily rod and the verbal rod,' though desiring to drink or use cold water, he does not dare to say, 'Give me cold water.' For him, the bodily and verbal rods, even when guarded in this way, are not able to draw one to death or rebirth. The mental rod, however, even when broken, certainly does draw one to death and rebirth. Thus, the Blessed One made him say: 'The bodily and verbal rods are weak and inferior; the mental rod is strong and great.'

Tassapi upāsakassa etadahosi. “Mucchāvasena asaññibhūtānañhi sattāhampi assāsapassāsā nappavattanti, cittasantatipavattimatteneva pana te matāti na vuccanti. Yadā nesaṃ cittaṃ nappavattati, tadā ‘matā ete nīharitvā te jhāpethā’ti vattabbataṃ āpajjanti. Kāyadaṇḍo nirīho abyāpāro, tathā [P 3.0058] vacīdaṇḍo. Citteneva pana tesaṃ cutipi paṭisandhipi hoti[V 3.0042]. Itipi manodaṇḍova mahanto. Bhijjitvāpi cutipaṭisandhiākaḍḍhanato eseva mahanto. Amhākaṃ pana mahānigaṇṭhassa kathā aniyyānikā”ti sallakkhesi. Bhagavato pana vicittāni pañhapaṭibhānāni sotukāmo na tāva anujānāti.

This thought also occurred to that lay follower: 'Truly, for those who have become unconscious due to fainting, for as long as seven days their in-breaths and out-breaths do not occur; however, merely by the persistence of the mental continuum, they are not said to be dead. When their mind ceases to function, then they become liable to be spoken of thus: "These are dead; take them out and cremate them." The bodily rod is without effort and without activity; likewise the verbal rod. But it is by the mind alone that their death and rebirth occur. In this way also, the mental rod is indeed great. Even having been broken, because it draws one to death and rebirth, it is indeed great. But the talk of our great Nigaṇṭha is not liberating.' Thus he reflected. However, desiring to hear the Blessed One’s varied and skillful replies to questions, he did not yet consent.

Na kho te sandhiyatīti na kho te ghaṭiyati. Purimena vā pacchimanti “kāyadaṇḍo mahanto”ti iminā purimena vacanena idāni “manodaṇḍo mahanto”ti idaṃ vacanaṃ. Pacchimena vā purimanti tena vā pacchimena aduṃ purimavacanaṃ na ghaṭiyati.

'It does not connect for you' means it does not fit for you. 'The latter with the former' means: with this former statement, 'the bodily rod is great,' this statement just now spoken, 'the mental rod is great,' does not connect. 'Or the former with the latter' means: with that latter statement, this former statement does not connect.

63. Idānissa [M 3.0041] bhagavā aññānipi kāraṇāni āharanto “taṃ kiṃ maññasī”tiādimāha. Tattha cātuyāmasaṃvarasaṃvutoti na pāṇamatipāteti, na pāṇamatipātayati, na pāṇamatipātayato samanuñño hoti. Na adinnaṃ ādiyati, na adinnaṃ ādiyāpeti, na adinnaṃ ādiyato samanuñño hoti. Na musā bhaṇati, na musā bhaṇāpeti, na musā bhaṇato samanuñño hoti. Na bhāvitamāsīsati, na bhāvitamāsīsāpeti, na bhāvitamāsīsato samanuñño hotīti iminā catukoṭṭhāsena saṃvarena saṃvuto. Ettha ca bhāvitanti pañcakāmaguṇā.

63. Now the Blessed One, bringing forth other reasons, said, 'What do you think?' and so on. Therein, 'restrained by the fourfold restraint' means: he does not kill a living being, he does not cause another to kill, and he does not approve of one who kills. He does not take what is not given, he does not cause another to take what is not given, and he does not approve of one who takes what is not given. He does not speak falsely, he does not cause another to speak falsely, and he does not approve of one who speaks falsely. He does not long for sensual pleasures, he does not cause another to long for them, and he does not approve of one who longs for them. Thus, he is restrained by this restraint with four parts. And here, 'bhāvitaṃ' means the five strands of sensual pleasure.

Sabbavārivāritoti vāritasabbaudako, paṭikkhittasabbasītodakoti attho. So hi sītodake sattasaññī hoti, tasmā na taṃ valañjeti. Atha vā sabbavārivāritoti sabbena pāpavāraṇena vāritapāpo. Sabbavāriyuttoti sabbena pāpavāraṇena [P 3.0059] yutto. Sabbavāridhutoti sabbena pāpavāraṇena dhutapāpo. Sabbavāriphuṭoti sabbena pāpavāraṇena phuṭo. Khuddake pāṇe saṅghātaṃ āpādetīti khuddake pāṇe vadhaṃ āpādeti. So kira ekindriyaṃ pāṇaṃ duvindriyaṃ pāṇanti paññapeti. Sukkhadaṇḍaka-purāṇapaṇṇasakkhara-kathalānipi pāṇoteva paññapeti. Tattha khuddakaṃ udakabindu khuddako pāṇo, mahantaṃ mahantoti saññī hoti. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Kismiṃ paññapetīti kattha katarasmiṃ koṭṭhāse paññapeti. Manodaṇḍasminti manodaṇḍakoṭṭhāse, bhanteti. Ayaṃ pana upāsako bhaṇantova sayampi sallakkhesi – “amhākaṃ mahānigaṇṭho ‘asañcetanikaṃ kammaṃ appasāvajjaṃ, sañcetanikaṃ mahāsāvajja’nti paññapetvā cetanaṃ manodaṇḍoti paññapeti, aniyyānikā etassa kathā, bhagavatova niyyānikā”ti.

'Restrained from all water' means one for whom all water is forbidden, one for whom all cold water is rejected—this is the meaning. For he perceives beings in cold water; therefore, he does not use it. Alternatively, 'restrained from all water' means one whose evil is restrained by all restraining of evil. 'Endowed with all restraint' means endowed with all restraining of evil. 'With all restraint shaken off' means one whose evil is shaken off by all restraining of evil. 'Pervaded by all restraint' means pervaded by all restraining of evil. 'He brings about the destruction of small creatures' means he causes the killing of small creatures. It is said that he declares, 'A being has one faculty,' 'A being has two faculties.' He even declares dried sticks, old leaves, gravel, and potsherds as beings. Therein, he perceives a small drop of water as a small being, and a large one as a large being. This was said in reference to that. 'In what does he declare it?' means in what place, in which section does he declare it? 'In the mental rod,' that is, 'in the section of the mental rod, venerable sir.' But this lay follower, even while speaking, himself reflected: 'Our great Nigaṇṭha, having declared, "Unintentional action has little fault, intentional action has great fault," then declares intention as the mental rod. His teaching is not liberating; only the Blessed One’s teaching is liberating.'

64. Iddhāti [V 3.0043] samiddhā. Phītāti atisamiddhā sabbapāliphullā viya. Ākiṇṇamanussāti janasamākulā. Pāṇāti hatthiassādayo tiracchānagatā ceva itthipurisadārakādayo manussajātikā ca. Ekaṃ maṃsakhalanti ekaṃ maṃsarāsiṃ. Puñjanti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Iddhimāti ānubhāvasampanno. Cetovasippattoti citte vasībhāvappatto. Bhasmaṃ [P 3.0060] karissāmīti chārikaṃ karissāmi. Kiñhi sobhati ekā chavā nāḷandāti idampi bhaṇanto so gahapati – “kāyapayogena paññāsampi manussā ekaṃ nāḷandaṃ ekaṃ maṃsakhalaṃ kātuṃ na sakkonti, iddhimā pana eko [M 3.0042] ekeneva manopadosena bhasmaṃ kātuṃ samattho. Amhākaṃ mahānigaṇṭhassa kathā aniyyānikā, bhagavatova kathā niyyānikā”ti sallakkhesi.

64. 'Prosperous' means flourishing. 'Thriving' means exceedingly flourishing, like being fully blossomed. 'Teeming with people' means crowded with people. 'Beings' refers to animals such as elephants and horses, and also humans such as women, men, and children. 'A single heap of flesh' means a single mass of flesh. 'A pile' is a synonym for that very word. 'Possessing psychic power' means endowed with power. 'Having attained mastery over the mind' means having reached a state of mastery over the mind. 'I will make it into ash' means I will make it into cinders. The householder, while also saying, 'How indeed does Nāḷandā shine as a single corpse?', reflected: 'Even fifty people, with physical effort, are not able to make this Nāḷandā into a single heap of flesh, but one person with psychic power is able to reduce it to ash with just a single thought of malice. Our great Nigaṇṭha’s teaching is not liberating; only the Blessed One’s teaching is liberating.'

65. Araññaṃ araññabhūtanti agāmakaṃ araññameva hutvā araññaṃ jātaṃ. Isīnaṃ manopadosenāti isīnaṃ atthāya katena manopadosena taṃ manopadosaṃ asahamānāhi devatāhi tāni raṭṭhāni vināsitāni. Lokikā pana isayo manaṃ padosetvā vināsayiṃsūti maññanti. Tasmā imasmiṃ lokavāde ṭhatvāva idaṃ vādāropanaṃ katanti veditabbaṃ.

65. 'A wilderness become a wilderness' means, having become a village-less forest, it became a complete wilderness. 'By the mental corruption of the sages' means: those countries were destroyed by deities who could not endure that mental corruption of the sages. But worldly people think that the sages, having corrupted their minds, destroyed them. Therefore, it should be known that this assertion was made while standing within this worldly view.

Tattha daṇḍakīraññādīnaṃ evaṃ araññabhūtabhāvo jānitabbo – sarabhaṅgabodhisattassa tāva parisāya ativepullataṃ gatāya kisavaccho nāma tāpaso mahāsattassa antevāsī vivekavāsaṃ patthayamāno gaṇaṃ pahāya godhāvarītīrato kaliṅgaraṭṭhe daṇḍakīrañño kumbhapuraṃ nāma nagaraṃ upanissāya rājuyyāne vivekamanubrūhayamāno viharati. Tassa senāpati upaṭṭhāko hoti.

Therein, how the lands of King Daṇḍakī and others became a wilderness should be known thus: Firstly, when the assembly of the Bodhisatta Sarabhaṅga had become exceedingly vast, an ascetic named Kisavaccha, a disciple of the Great Being, desiring a secluded dwelling, left the group. Coming from the bank of the Godhāvarī river, he dwelt in the Kaliṅga country, cultivating seclusion in the royal park and depending on the city named Kumbhapura of King Daṇḍakī. A general was his attendant.

Tadā ca ekā gaṇikā rathaṃ abhiruhitvā pañcamātugāmasataparivārā nagaraṃ upasobhayamānā vicarati. Mahājano tameva olokayamāno parivāretvā vicarati, nagaravīthiyo nappahonti. Rājā vātapānaṃ vivaritvā ṭhito taṃ disvā kā esāti pucchi. Tumhākaṃ nagarasobhinī [P 3.0061] devāti. So ussūyamāno “kiṃ etāya sobhati, nagaraṃ sayaṃ sobhissatī”ti taṃ ṭhānantaraṃ acchindāpesi.

And at that time, a certain courtesan, having mounted a chariot with a retinue of five hundred women, went about beautifying the city. The great crowd, looking only at her, surrounded her as they went about, and the city streets were not sufficient. The king, standing having opened a window, saw her and asked, 'Who is this?' 'She is your city's adornment, Your Majesty.' He, being envious, said, 'How is the city adorned by her? The city will be adorned on its own,' and had her special position revoked.

Sā tato paṭṭhāya kenaci saddhiṃ santhavaṃ katvā ṭhānantaraṃ pariyesamānā ekadivasaṃ rājuyyānaṃ pavisitvā caṅkamanakoṭiyaṃ ālambanaphalakaṃ nissāya pāsāṇaphalake nisinnaṃ tāpasaṃ disvā cintesi [V 3.0044] – “kiliṭṭho vatāyaṃ tāpaso anañjitamaṇḍito, dāṭhikāhi paruḷhāhi mukhaṃ pihitaṃ, massunā uraṃ pihitaṃ, ubho kacchā paruḷhā”ti. Athassā domanassaṃ uppajji – “ahaṃ ekena kiccena vicarāmi, ayañca me kāḷakaṇṇī diṭṭho, udakaṃ āharatha, akkhīni dhovissāmī”ti udakadantakaṭṭhaṃ āharāpetvā dantakaṭṭhaṃ khāditvā tāpasassa sarīre piṇḍaṃ piṇḍaṃ kheḷaṃ pātetvā dantakaṭṭhaṃ jaṭāmatthake khipitvā mukhaṃ vikkhāletvā udakaṃ tāpasassa matthakasmiṃyeva siñcitvā [M 3.0043] – “yehi me akkhīhi kāḷakaṇṇī diṭṭho, tāni dhotāni kalipavāhito”ti nikkhantā.

She, from then on, seeking a special position after establishing a connection with someone, one day entered the royal park. Seeing the ascetic seated on a stone slab, leaning against a support board at the end of the walking path, she thought: 'Alas, this ascetic is filthy and unadorned! His mouth is covered by an overgrown beard, his chest is covered by his beard, and both his armpits are overgrown with hair.' Then displeasure arose in her: 'I am wandering about on some business, and I have seen this unlucky person. Bring water, I will wash my eyes.' Having had water and a tooth-stick brought, and having chewed the tooth-stick, she made lumps of spittle fall on the ascetic's body, threw the tooth-stick on top of his matted hair, rinsed her mouth, and poured the water right on the ascetic's head, saying, 'The eyes with which I saw the unlucky person have been washed; the stain has been washed away,' and departed.

Taṃdivasañca rājā satiṃ paṭilabhitvā – “bho kuhiṃ nagarasobhinī”ti pucchi. Imasmiṃyeva nagare devāti. Pakatiṭṭhānantaraṃ tassā dethāti ṭhānantaraṃ dāpesi. Sā pubbe sukatakammaṃ nissāya laddhaṃ ṭhānantaraṃ tāpasassa sarīre kheḷapātanena laddhanti saññamakāsi.

And on that very day, the king, having regained his senses, asked, 'Sirs, where is the city's adornment?' 'She is in this very city, Your Majesty.' When this was said, he said, 'Give her her normal special position,' and had the special position given. She formed the perception that the special position, which she had obtained by relying on her past good deeds, had been regained by spitting on the ascetic's body.

Tato katipāhassaccayena rājā purohitassa ṭhānantaraṃ gaṇhi. So nagarasobhiniyā santikaṃ gantvā “bhagini kinti katvā ṭhānantaraṃ paṭilabhī”ti pucchi. “Kiṃ brāhmaṇa aññaṃ kātabbaṃ atthi, rājuyyāne [P 3.0062] anañjitakāḷakaṇṇī kūṭajaṭilo eko atthi, tassa sarīre kheḷaṃ pātehi, evaṃ ṭhānantaraṃ labhissasī”ti āha. So “evaṃ karissāmi bhaginī”ti tattha gantvā tāya kathitasadisameva sabbaṃ katvā nikkhami. Rājāpi taṃdivasameva satiṃ paṭilabhitvā – “kuhiṃ, bho, brāhmaṇo”ti pucchi. Imasmiṃyeva nagare devāti. “Amhehi anupadhāretvā kataṃ, tadevassa ṭhānantaraṃ dethā”ti dāpesi. Sopi puññabalena labhitvā “tāpasassa sarīre kheḷapātanena laddhaṃ me”ti saññamakāsi.

Then, after a few days had passed, the king took the purohita's special position. He went to the city's adornment and asked, “Sister, how did you regain your special position?” She replied, “Brahmin, what else is there to be done? In the king's park, there is a certain deceitful, matted-hair ascetic, a wretch without eye-makeup. Spit spittle on his body; thus you will regain the special position.” He said, “Very well, sister, I shall do so,” and having gone there, he did everything just as she had said and then departed. On that very day, the king also regained his senses and asked, “Sirs, where is the Brahmin?” They replied, “Your Majesty, he is in this very city.” The king said, “It was done by us without due consideration. Give that very special position back to him,” and had it given. He too, having obtained it through the power of his merit, formed the perception: “It was obtained by me through spitting spittle on the ascetic's body.”

Tato katipāhassaccayena rañño paccanto kupito. Rājā paccantaṃ vūpasamessāmīti caturaṅginiyā senāya nikkhami. Purohito gantvā rañño purato ṭhatvā “jayatu mahārājā”ti vatvā – “tumhe, mahārāja, jayatthāya gacchathā”ti pucchi. Āma brāhmaṇāti. Evaṃ sante rājuyyāne anañjitakāḷakaṇṇī eko kūṭajaṭilo vasati, tassa sarīre kheḷaṃ pātethāti. Rājā tassa vacanaṃ gahetvā yathā gaṇikāya ca tena ca kataṃ, tatheva sabbaṃ katvā orodhepi āṇāpesi – “etassa kūṭajaṭilassa sarīre kheḷaṃ pātethā”ti. Tato orodhāpi orodhapālakāpi tatheva akaṃsu. Atha rājā uyyānadvāre rakkhaṃ ṭhapāpetvā “raññā saddhiṃ nikkhamantā [V 3.0045] sabbe tāpasassa sarīre kheḷaṃ apātetvā nikkhamituṃ na labhantī”ti āṇāpesi. Atha sabbo balakāyo ca seniyo ca teneva niyāmena tāpasassa upari kheḷañca dantakaṭṭhāni ca mukhavikkhālita udakañca pāpayiṃsu, kheḷo ca dantakaṭṭhāni ca sakalasarīraṃ avatthariṃsu.

Then, after a few days had passed, the king's border region was in revolt. The king, thinking, “I will pacify the border region,” went forth with his four-limbed army. The purohita went and stood before the king, and after saying, “May the great king be victorious!” he asked, “Great king, are you going forth for the sake of victory?” “Yes, Brahmin,” the king replied. “If that is so, in the king's park lives a certain deceitful, matted-hair ascetic, a wretch without eye-makeup. Spit spittle upon his body and then go forth.” The king, accepting his words, did everything just as had been done by the courtesan and by him, and also commanded the women of the harem, “Spit spittle upon the body of this deceitful, matted-hair ascetic.” Then the harem women and the harem attendants also did just so. Then the king, having had guards posted at the park gate, commanded, “All those departing with the king are not allowed to depart without having spit spittle on the ascetic's body.” Then the entire body of troops and the army, by that same rule, caused spittle, tooth-sticks, and water for rinsing the mouth to fall upon the ascetic. The spittle and the tooth-sticks covered his entire body.

Senāpati [M 3.0044] sabbapacchā suṇitvā “mayhaṃ kira satthāraṃ bhavantaṃ puññakkhettaṃ saggasopānaṃ evaṃ ghaṭṭayiṃsū”ti usumajātahadayo mukhena assasanto [P 3.0063] vegena rājuyyānaṃ āgantvā tathā byasanapattaṃ isiṃ disvā kacchaṃ bandhitvā dvīhi hatthehi dantakaṭṭhāni apaviyūhitvā ukkhipitvā nisīdāpetvā udakaṃ āharāpetvā nhāpetvā sabbaosadhehi ceva catujjātigandhehi ca sarīraṃ ubbaṭṭetvā sukhumasāṭakena puñchitvā purato añjaliṃ katvā ṭhito evamāha “ayuttaṃ, bhante, manussehi kataṃ, etesaṃ kiṃ bhavissatī”ti. Devatā senāpati tidhā bhinnā, ekaccā “rājānameva nāsessāmā”ti vadanti, ekaccā “saddhiṃ parisāya rājāna”nti, ekaccā “rañño vijitaṃ sabbaṃ nāsessāmā”ti. Idaṃ vatvā pana tāpaso appamattakampi kopaṃ akatvā lokassa santiupāyameva ācikkhanto āha “aparādho nāma hoti, accayaṃ pana desetuṃ jānantassa pākatikameva hotī”ti.

The general, hearing of this after everyone else, with his heart agitated and exhaling through his mouth, thought, "They have thus assailed my venerable teacher, a field of merit, a stairway to the celestial realm!" He came quickly to the king's park, and seeing the sage who had met with such disaster, he tucked up his lower garment, swept aside the tooth-sticks with both hands, lifted him up, and had him seated. He had water brought, bathed him, anointed his body with all kinds of medicinal herbs and the four kinds of perfumes, and wiped him with a fine cloth. Standing before him with his hands joined in reverence, he said, "Venerable sir, an improper deed has been done by these men. What will be the consequence for them?" "General, the devas are divided into three factions. Some say, 'We will destroy the king alone'; some say, 'The king together with his retinue'; and some say, 'We will destroy the king's entire domain.'" Having said this, the ascetic, without showing even the slightest anger and declaring only the means for the world's peace, said, "An offense, so-called, does occur. But for one who knows how to confess a transgression, things become normal again."

Senāpati nayaṃ labhitvā rañño santikaṃ gantvā rājānaṃ vanditvā āha – “tumhehi, mahārāja, nirāparādhe mahiddhike tāpase aparajjhantehi bhāriyaṃ kammaṃ kataṃ, devatā kira tidhā bhinnā evaṃ vadantī”ti sabbaṃ ārocetvā – “khamāpite kira, mahārāja, pākatikaṃ hoti, raṭṭhaṃ mā nāsetha, tāpasaṃ khamāpethā”ti āha. Rājā attani dosaṃ kataṃ disvāpi evaṃ vadati “na taṃ khamāpessāmī”ti. Senāpati yāvatatiyaṃ yācitvā anicchantamāha – “ahaṃ, mahārāja, tāpasassa balaṃ jānāmi, na so abhūtavādī, nāpi kupito, sattānuddayena pana evamāha khamāpetha naṃ mahārājā”ti. Na khamāpemīti. Tena hi senāpatiṭṭhānaṃ aññassa detha, ahaṃ tumhākaṃ āṇāpavattiṭṭhāne na vasissāmīti. Tvaṃ yenakāmaṃ gaccha, ahaṃ mayhaṃ senāpatiṃ labhissāmīti. Tato senāpati tāpasassa santikaṃ āgantvā vanditvā [P 3.0064] “kathaṃ paṭipajjāmi, bhante”ti āha. Senāpati ye te vacanaṃ suṇanti, sabbe saparikkhāre sadhane sadvipadacatuppade gahetvā sattadivasabbhantare bahi rajjasīmaṃ gaccha, devatā ativiya kupitā dhuvaṃ raṭṭhampi araṭṭhaṃ karissantīti. Senāpati tathā akāsi.

The general, having learned the way, went to the king, paid homage, and said: "Great king, a grave deed has been done by you in offending a blameless and powerful ascetic. It is said the devas are divided into three factions and are speaking thus." Having reported everything, he added: "Great king, it is said that if forgiveness is asked, things will become normal again. Do not destroy the kingdom; ask forgiveness of the ascetic." Even though the king saw the fault he had committed, he said, "I will not ask forgiveness of him." The general, having begged up to the third time, said to the unwilling king: "Great king, I know the power of that ascetic. He is not one who speaks falsehood, nor is he angry; rather, out of compassion for beings he spoke thus. Ask his forgiveness, great king." "I will not ask his forgiveness." "In that case, give the position of general to another. I will not dwell in the place where your authority extends." "You may go wherever you wish. I will find a general for myself." Then the general went to the ascetic, paid homage, and asked, "Venerable sir, how should I act?" The ascetic replied, "General, as for those who listen to your words, take all of them, together with their belongings, wealth, bipeds, and quadrupeds, and within seven days, go beyond the kingdom's border. The devas are extremely angry and will surely make the kingdom a non-kingdom." The general acted accordingly.

Rājā [V 3.0046] gatamattoyeva amittamathanaṃ katvā janapadaṃ vūpasametvā āgamma jayakhandhāvāraṭṭhāne nisīditvā nagaraṃ paṭijaggāpetvā antonagaraṃ pāvisi. Devatā [M 3.0045] paṭhamaṃyeva udakavuṭṭhiṃ pātayiṃsu. Mahājano attamano ahosi “kūṭajaṭilaṃ aparaddhakālato paṭṭhāya amhākaṃ rañño vaḍḍhiyeva, amitte nimmathesi, āgatadivaseyeva devo vuṭṭho”ti. Devatā puna sumanapupphavuṭṭhiṃ pātayiṃsu, mahājano attamanataro ahosi. Devatā puna māsakavuṭṭhiṃ pātayiṃsu. Tato kahāpaṇavuṭṭhiṃ, tato kahāpaṇatthaṃ na nikkhameyyunti maññamānā hatthūpagapādūpagādikatabhaṇḍavuṭṭhiṃ pātesuṃ. Mahājano sattabhūmikapāsāde ṭhitopi otaritvā ābharaṇāni piḷandhanto attamano ahosi. “Arahati vata kūṭajaṭilake kheḷapātanaṃ, tassa upari kheḷapātitakālato paṭṭhāya amhākaṃ rañño vaḍḍhi jātā, amittamathanaṃ kataṃ, āgatadivaseyeva devo vassi, tato sumanavuṭṭhi māsakavuṭṭhi kahāpaṇavuṭṭhi katabhaṇḍavuṭṭhīti catasso vuṭṭhiyo jātā”ti attamanavācaṃ nicchāretvā rañño katapāpe samanuñño jāto.

The king, just upon his return, having crushed his enemies and pacified the kingdom, sat down at the victory camp, had the city prepared, and entered the inner city. The deities first caused a rain of water to fall. The great populace was delighted, saying, 'Ever since the time the deceitful ascetic was wronged, our king has only prospered; he has crushed his enemies, and on the very day of his return, the sky has rained!' The deities again caused a rain of jasmine flowers to fall, and the great populace became even more delighted. The deities again caused a rain of māsaka coins to fall. After that, they caused a rain of kahāpaṇa coins to fall. Then, thinking, 'Lest they should have to go out for the kahāpaṇas,' they caused a rain of goods such as ornaments for the hands and feet to fall. The great populace, even those standing in seven-storied palaces, came down and, while putting on the ornaments, became delighted. 'Indeed, the deceitful ascetic deserved to have spit fall on him! From the time spit was made to fall upon him, our king's prosperity has arisen, the crushing of enemies has been done, and on the very day of his return, the sky rained. After that, a rain of jasmine flowers, a rain of māsaka coins, a rain of kahāpaṇa coins, and a rain of ornaments—thus four rains have occurred!' Uttering these words of delight, they became approving of the evil deed done by the king.

Tasmiṃ samaye devatā ekatodhāraubhatodhārādīni nānappakārāni āvudhāni mahājanassa upari phalake [P 3.0065] maṃsaṃ koṭṭayamānā viya pātayiṃsu. Tadanantaraṃ vītaccike vītadhūme kiṃsukapupphavaṇṇe aṅgāre, tadanantaraṃ kūṭāgārappamāṇe pāsāṇe, tadanantaraṃ antomuṭṭhiyaṃ asaṇṭhahanikaṃ sukhumavālikaṃ vassāpayamānā asītihatthubbedhaṃ thalaṃ akaṃsu. Rañño vijitaṭṭhāne kisavacchatāpaso senāpati mātuposakarāmoti tayova manussabhūtā arogā ahesuṃ. Sesānaṃ tasmiṃ kamme asamaṅgībhūtānaṃ tiracchānānaṃ pānīyaṭṭhāne pānīyaṃ nāhosi, tiṇaṭṭhāne tiṇaṃ. Te yena pānīyaṃ yena tiṇanti gacchantā appatteyeva sattame divase bahirajjasīmaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Tenāha sarabhaṅgabodhisatto –

At that time, the deities caused various kinds of weapons, such as single-edged and double-edged ones, to fall upon the great populace, as if mincing meat on a board. Immediately after that, they rained down flameless, smokeless embers the color of kiṃsuka flowers; immediately after that, stones the size of gabled houses; and immediately after that, causing a rain of fine sand that could not be held in a closed fist to fall, they made a mound eighty cubits high. In the king's territory, only three who were human beings—Kisavaccha the ascetic, the general, and Rāma who supported his mother—were unharmed. For the remaining animals that were not party to that deed, there was no water in the watering places and no grass in the grassy places. They, thinking, 'Where might there be water? Where might there be grass?' went along, and before they could arrive, on the seventh day they reached the border outside the kingdom. Therefore, the Bodhisatta Sarabhaṅga said:

“Kisañhi vacchaṃ avakiriya daṇḍakī,

Ucchinnamūlo sajano saraṭṭho;

Kukkuḷanāme nirayamhi paccati,

Tassa phuliṅgāni patanti kāye”ti. (jā. 2.17.70);

"Having scattered spittle on Kisavaccha, Daṇḍakī,

Uprooted, with his people and his kingdom,

Is tormented in the hell named Kukkuḷa;

Embers fall upon his body."

Evaṃ tāva daṇḍakīraññassa araññabhūtabhāvo veditabbo.

Thus, in the first place, how the Daṇḍaka kingdom became a wilderness is to be understood.

Kaliṅgaraṭṭhe [V 3.0047][M 3.0046] pana nāḷikiraraññe rajjaṃ kārayamāne himavati pañcasatatāpasā anitthigandhā ajinajaṭavākacīradharā vanamūlaphalabhakkhā hutvā ciraṃ vītināmetvā loṇambilasevanatthaṃ manussapathaṃ otaritvā anupubbena kaliṅgaraṭṭhe nāḷikirarañño nagaraṃ sampattā. Te jaṭājinavākacīrāni [P 3.0066] saṇṭhapetvā pabbajitānurūpaṃ upasamasiriṃ dassayamānā nagaraṃ bhikkhāya pavisiṃsu. Manussā anuppanne buddhuppāde tāpasapabbajite disvā pasannā nisajjaṭṭhānaṃ saṃvidhāya hatthato bhikkhābhājanaṃ gahetvā nisīdāpetvā bhikkhaṃ sampādetvā adaṃsu. Tāpasā katabhattakiccā anumodanaṃ akaṃsu. Manussā sutvā pasannacittā “kuhiṃ bhadantā gacchantī”ti pucchiṃsu. Yathāphāsukaṭṭhānaṃ, āvusoti. Bhante, alaṃ aññattha gamanena, rājuyyāne vasatha, mayaṃ bhuttapātarāsā āgantvā dhammakathaṃ sossāmāti. Tāpasā adhivāsetvā uyyānaṃ agamaṃsu. Nāgarā bhuttapātarāsā suddhavatthanivatthā “dhammakathaṃ sossāmā”ti saṅghā gaṇā gaṇībhūtā uyyānābhimukhā agamaṃsu. Rājā uparipāsāde ṭhito te tathā gacchamāne disvā upaṭṭhākaṃ pucchi “kiṃ ete bhaṇe nāgarā suddhavatthā suddhuttarāsaṅgā hutvā uyyānābhimukhā gacchanti, kimettha samajjaṃ vā nāṭakaṃ vā atthī”ti? Natthi deva, ete tāpasānaṃ santike dhammaṃ sotukāmā gacchantīti. Tena hi bhaṇe ahampi gacchissāmi, mayā saddhiṃ gacchantūti. So gantvā tesaṃ ārocesi – “rājāpi gantukāmo, rājānaṃ parivāretvāva gacchathā”ti. Nāgarā pakatiyāpi attamanā taṃ sutvā – “amhākaṃ rājā assaddho appasanno dussīlo, tāpasā dhammikā, te āgamma rājāpi dhammiko bhavissatī”ti attamanatarā ahesuṃ.

Now, in the Kaliṅga country, while King Nāḷikira was ruling, five hundred ascetics in the Himalayas, being averse to the scent of women, wearing antelope hides, matted hair, and bark-cloth garments, and subsisting on forest roots and fruits, after spending a long time there, descended to the path of humans to partake of salt and sour tastes. They gradually arrived at the city of King Nāḷikira in the Kaliṅga country. Arranging their matted hair, hides, and bark-cloth garments, and displaying the serene dignity befitting renunciants, they entered the city for alms. The people, seeing ascetics who had gone forth at a time when no Buddha had arisen, were filled with confidence. They prepared a place for sitting, took the alms-bowls from their hands, had them sit down, prepared alms-food, and gave it. The ascetics, having finished their meal, gave the anumodanā. The people, having heard it, with confident minds, asked, 'Venerable sirs, where are you going?' 'To a comfortable place, friends.' 'Venerable sirs, enough of going elsewhere. Dwell in the royal park. We, after our morning meal, will come and listen to a Dhamma talk.' The ascetics consented and went to the park. The citizens, having eaten their morning meal, dressed in clean clothes, thinking, 'We will listen to a Dhamma talk,' formed into groups and companies and went towards the park. The king, standing on the upper floor of his palace, saw them going thus and asked his attendant, 'My good man, why do these citizens, dressed in clean clothes with clean upper robes, go towards the park? Is there some festival or play there?' 'There is not, Your Majesty. They are going to listen to the Dhamma in the presence of the ascetics.' 'In that case, my good man, I too will go. Let them go with me.' That man went and announced to them, 'The king also wishes to go. Go only after surrounding the king.' The citizens, who were already delighted by nature, upon hearing that, became even more delighted, thinking, 'Our king is faithless, without confidence, and of bad virtue. On account of these righteous ascetics, the king too will become righteous.'

Rājā nikkhamitvā tehi parivārito uyyānaṃ gantvā tāpasehi saddhiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ katvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Tāpasā rājānaṃ disvā parikathāya kusalassekassa tāpasassa “rañño dhammaṃ kathehī”ti saññamadaṃsu, so tāpaso [P 3.0067] parisaṃ oloketvā pañcasu veresu ādīnavaṃ pañcasu ca sīlesu ānisaṃsaṃ kathento –

The king departed and, surrounded by them, went to the park. Having exchanged friendly greetings with the ascetics, he sat down to one side. The ascetics, seeing the king, gave a sign to one ascetic who was skilled in conversation, saying, 'Preach the Dhamma to the king.' That ascetic, looking over the assembly, while explaining the danger in the five enmities and the benefit in the five precepts, said:

“Pāṇo [M 3.0047] na hantabbo, adinnaṃ nādātabbaṃ, kāmesumicchācāro na caritabbo, musā na bhāsitabbā, majjaṃ na pātabbaṃ, pāṇātipāto nāma nirayasaṃvattaniko hoti tiracchānayonisaṃvattaniko pettivisayasaṃvattaniko, tathā adinnādānādīni. Pāṇātipāto niraye paccitvā manussalokaṃ āgatassa vipākāvasesena appāyukasaṃvattaniko hoti, adinnādānaṃ [V 3.0048] appabhogasaṃvattanikaṃ, micchācāro bahusapattasaṃvattaniko, musāvādo abhūtabbhakkhānasaṃvattaniko, majjapānaṃ ummattakabhāvasaṃvattanika”nti –

“A living being should not be killed; what is not given should not be taken; wrong conduct in regard to sensual pleasures should not be practiced; false speech should not be spoken; intoxicants should not be drunk. The taking of life is conducive to rebirth in hell, conducive to the animal realm, and conducive to the realm of ghosts; likewise are taking what is not given and the others. The taking of life, having ripened in hell, for one who has come to the human world, is, by the power of its remaining result, conducive to a short life. Taking what is not given is conducive to few possessions. Wrong conduct in regard to sensual pleasures is conducive to having many enemies. False speech is conducive to being falsely accused. The drinking of intoxicants is conducive to a state of madness.”

Pañcasu veresu imaṃ ādīnavaṃ kathesi.

He spoke of this danger in the five enmities.

Rājā pakatiyāpi assaddho appasanno dussīlo, dussīlassa ca sīlakathā nāma dukkathā, kaṇṇe sūlappavesanaṃ viya hoti. Tasmā so cintesi – “ahaṃ ‘ete paggaṇhissāmī’ti āgato, ime pana mayhaṃ āgatakālato paṭṭhāya maṃyeva ghaṭṭentā vijjhantā parisamajjhe kathenti, karissāmi nesaṃ kāttabba”nti. So dhammakathāpariyosāne “ācariyā sve mayhaṃ gehe bhikkhaṃ gaṇhathā”ti nimantetvā agamāsi. So dutiyadivase mahante mahante koḷumbe āharāpetvā gūthassa pūrāpetvā kadalipattehi nesaṃ mukhāni bandhāpetvā tattha tattha ṭhapāpesi, puna bahalamadhukatelanāgabalapicchillādīnaṃ kūṭe pūretvā nisseṇimatthake ṭhapāpesi, tattheva ca mahāmalle baddhakacche hatthehi muggare gāhāpetvā ṭhapetvā āha “kūṭatāpasā ativiya maṃ viheṭhayiṃsu, tesaṃ pāsādato otaraṇakāle [P 3.0068] kūṭehi picchillaṃ sopānamatthake vissajjetvā sīse muggarehi pothetvā gale gahetvā sopāne khipathā”ti. Sopānapādamūle pana caṇḍe kukkure bandhāpesi.

The king, by nature, was without faith, lacking in confidence, and immoral. For one who is immoral, talk of virtue is unpleasant; it is like a stake piercing the ear. Therefore, he thought: ‘I came here thinking, “I will honor these men,” but from the moment of my arrival, they have been criticizing and assailing me in the midst of the assembly. I will do to them what ought to be done.’ At the end of the Dhamma talk, he invited them, saying, ‘Venerable sirs, tomorrow, please accept alms at my residence,’ and then departed. The next day, he had very large pots brought, had them filled with excrement, and had their mouths tied with banana leaves, placing them here and there. Furthermore, he had pots filled with thick madhuka oil, nāgabala oil, and other sticky substances and placed them at the top of the staircase. There, he also stationed great wrestlers with their lower garments tucked up, had them take clubs in their hands, and said: ‘These deceitful ascetics have greatly vexed me. When they are descending from the palace, release the sticky substance from the pots onto the top of the staircase, strike their heads with the clubs, seize them by the neck, and throw them down the stairs.’ At the foot of the staircase, he had fierce dogs tied up.

Tāpasāpi “sve rājagehe bhuñjissāmā”ti aññamaññaṃ ovadiṃsu – “mārisā rājagehaṃ nāma sāsaṅkaṃ sappaṭibhayaṃ, pabbajitehi nāma chadvārārammaṇe saññatehi bhavitabbaṃ, diṭṭhadiṭṭhe ārammaṇe nimittaṃ na gahetabbaṃ, cakkhudvāre saṃvaro paccupaṭṭhapetabbo”ti.

The ascetics also, thinking, ‘Tomorrow we will eat at the king’s residence,’ advised one another: ‘Sirs, a royal residence is a place of apprehension and is fraught with danger. Those who have gone forth must be restrained in regard to the objects of the six sense-doors. One should not grasp at the sign of any object seen. Restraint at the eye-door should be established.’

Punadivase [M 3.0048] bhikkhācāravelaṃ sallakkhetvā vākacīraṃ nivāsetvā ajinacammaṃ ekaṃsagataṃ katvā jaṭākalāpaṃ saṇṭhapetvā bhikkhābhājanaṃ gahetvā paṭipāṭiyā rājanivesanaṃ abhiruḷhā. Rājā āruḷhabhāvaṃ ñatvā gūthakoḷumbamukhato kadalipattaṃ nīharāpesi. Duggandho tāpasānaṃ nāsapuṭaṃ paharitvā matthaluṅgapātanākārapatto ahosi. Mahātāpaso rājānaṃ olokesi. Rājā – “ettha bhonto yāvadatthaṃ bhuñjantu ceva harantu ca, tumhākametaṃ anucchavikaṃ, hiyyo ahaṃ tumhe paggaṇhissāmīti āgato, tumhe pana maṃyeva ghaṭṭento vijjhantā parisamajjhe kathayittha[V 3.0049], tumhākamidaṃ anucchavikaṃ, bhuñjathā”ti mahātāpasassa uluṅkena gūthaṃ upanāmesi. Mahātāpaso dhī dhīti vadanto paṭinivatti. “Ettakeneva gacchissatha tumhe”ti sopāne kūṭehi picchillaṃ vissajjāpetvā mallānaṃ saññamadāsi. Mallā muggarehi sīsāni pothetvā gīvāya gahetvā sopāne khipiṃsu, ekopi sopāne patiṭṭhātuṃ nāsakkhi[P 3.0069], pavaṭṭamānā sopānapādamūlaṃyeva pāpuṇiṃsu. Sampatte sampatte caṇḍakukkurā paṭapaṭāti luñcamānā khādiṃsu. Yopi nesaṃ uṭṭhahitvā palāyati, sopi āvāṭe patati, tatrāpi naṃ kukkurā anubandhitvā khādantiyeva. Iti nesaṃ kukkurā aṭṭhisaṅkhalikameva avasesayiṃsu. Evaṃ so rājā tapasampanne pañcasate tāpase ekadivaseneva jīvitā voropesi.

The next day, noting the time for the alms-round, they dressed in bark-cloth garments, placed an antelope hide over one shoulder, arranged their topknots of matted hair, took their alms-bowls, and in due order ascended to the royal residence. The king, knowing they had ascended, had the banana leaf removed from the mouth of the pot of excrement. The foul smell struck the ascetics’ nostrils and became so intense it was as if their brains would fall out. The chief ascetic looked at the king. The king said: ‘Sirs, eat and take from this as much as you wish. This is suitable for you. Yesterday I came thinking, “I will honor you,” but you, criticizing and assailing me, spoke thus in the midst of the assembly. This is suitable for you. Eat!’ And with a ladle, he offered the excrement to the chief ascetic. The chief ascetic, exclaiming, ‘Fie! Fie!’ turned back. ‘Will you leave with only this?’ said the king, and having had a sticky substance released from the pots on the staircase, he gave the signal to the wrestlers. The wrestlers struck their heads with clubs, seized them by the neck, and threw them down the stairs. Not even one was able to stand on the stairs; rolling, they reached the very foot of the staircase. As each one arrived, the fierce dogs, making tearing sounds, ripped them apart and devoured them. And if any among them got up and fled, he would fall into a pit, and there too the dogs would pursue and devour him. Thus, the dogs left only their skeletons. In this way, that king, in a single day, deprived five hundred ascetics, accomplished in ascetic practice, of their lives.

Athassa raṭṭhe devatā purimanayeneva puna navavuṭṭhiyo pātesuṃ. Tassa rajjaṃ saṭṭhiyojanubbedhena vālikathalena avacchādiyittha. Tenāha sarabhaṅgo bodhisatto –

Then, in his kingdom, the devas, in the same way as before, again caused the nine kinds of rain to fall. His kingdom was covered by a bed of sand sixty yojanas deep. Therefore, the Bodhisatta Sarabhaṅga said:

“Yo saññate pabbajite avañcayi,

Dhammaṃ bhaṇante samaṇe adūsake;

Taṃ nāḷikeraṃ sunakhā parattha,

Saṅgamma khādanti viphandamāna”nti. (jā. 2.17.71);

“He who deceived the restrained ascetics, the blameless recluses who spoke the Dhamma—that Nāḷikira, the dogs in the next world, coming together, devour him as he writhes.”

Evaṃ kāliṅgāraññassa araññabhūtabhāvo veditabbo.

Thus, how the Kāliṅga country became a forest is to be understood.

Atīte pana bārāṇasinagare diṭṭhamaṅgalikā nāma cattālīsakoṭivibhavassa seṭṭhino ekā dhītā ahosi dassanīyā pāsādikā. Sā rūpabhogakulasampattisampannatāya bahūnaṃ patthanīyā ahosi. Yo [M 3.0049] panassā vāreyyatthāya pahiṇāti, taṃ taṃ disvānassa jātiyaṃ vā hatthapādādīsu vā yattha katthaci dosaṃ āropetvā “ko esa dujjāto dussaṇṭhito”tiādīni vatvā – “nīharatha na”nti nīharāpetvā “evarūpampi nāma addasaṃ, udakaṃ āharatha, akkhīni dhovissāmī”ti akkhīni dhovati. Tassā diṭṭhaṃ diṭṭhaṃ vippakāraṃ pāpetvā nīharāpetīti [P 3.0070] diṭṭhamaṅgalikā tveva saṅkhā udapādi, mūlanāmaṃ antaradhāyi.

In the past, in the city of Bārāṇasī, a treasurer possessing forty crores of wealth had a sole daughter named Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā, who was lovely to see and pleasing. Due to her endowment with beauty, wealth, and noble birth, she was desired by many. Now, whoever sent a suitor to her for marriage, upon seeing him, she would impute some fault to his birth, or his hands and feet, or somewhere else, and saying such things as, ‘Who is this ill-born, misshapen man?’ she would have him driven out, saying, ‘Drive him out!’ After having him driven out, she would say, ‘To think I saw such a person! Bring water, I will wash my eyes!’ and she would wash her eyes. Because she had everyone she saw driven out after finding fault with them, the designation ‘Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā’ arose for her, and her original name disappeared.

Sā [V 3.0050] ekadivasaṃ gaṅgāya udakakīḷaṃ kīḷissāmīti titthaṃ sajjāpetvā pahūtaṃ khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ sakaṭesu pūrāpetvā bahūni gandhamālādīni ādāya paṭicchannayānaṃ āruyha ñātigaṇaparivutā gehamhā nikkhami. Tena ca samayena mahāpuriso caṇḍālayoniyaṃ nibbatto bahinagare cammagehe vasati, mātaṅgotvevassa nāmaṃ ahosi. So soḷasavassuddesiko hutvā kenacideva karaṇīyena antonagaraṃ pavisitukāmo ekaṃ nīlapilotikaṃ nivāsetvā ekaṃ hatthe bandhitvā ekena hatthena pacchiṃ, ekena ghaṇḍaṃ gahetvā “ussaratha ayyā, caṇḍāloha”nti jānāpanatthaṃ taṃ vādento nīcacittaṃ paccupaṭṭhapetvā diṭṭhadiṭṭhe manusse namassamāno nagaraṃ pavisitvā mahāpathaṃ paṭipajji.

One day, she, thinking, 'I will play a water-sport in the Ganges river,' had the bathing place well prepared. Having had carts filled with much hard and soft food, and having taken many perfumes, garlands, and so forth, she mounted a covered vehicle and, surrounded by her retinue of relatives, went forth from her house. And at that time, the Great Being, having been born in the womb of a caṇḍāla, was living outside the city in a house roofed with leather; his name was indeed Mātaṅga. He, being sixteen years of age and wishing to enter the city for some business, wore one worn-out blue cloth, tied another on his arm, and took a basket in one hand and a gong in the other. For the purpose of making it known, 'Make way, sirs, I am a caṇḍāla!' he struck that gong, and having established a humble mind and paying homage to every person he saw, he entered the city and proceeded along the main road.

Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā ghaṇḍasaddaṃ sutvā sāṇiantarena olokentī dūratova taṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā “kimeta”nti pucchi. Mātaṅgo ayyeti. “Kiṃ vata, bho, akusalaṃ akaramha, kassāyaṃ nissando, vināso nu kho me paccupaṭṭhito, maṅgalakiccena nāma gacchamānā caṇḍālaṃ addasa”nti sarīraṃ kampetvā jigucchamānā kheḷaṃ pātetvā dhātiyo āha – “vegena udakaṃ āharatha, caṇḍālo diṭṭho, akkhīni ceva nāma [P 3.0071] gahitamukhañca dhovissāmī”ti dhovitvā rathaṃ nivattāpetvā sabbapaṭiyādānaṃ gehaṃ pesetvā pāsādaṃ abhiruhi. Surāsoṇḍādayo ceva tassā upaṭṭhākamanussā ca “kuhiṃ, bho diṭṭhamaṅgalikā, imāyapi velāya nāgacchatī”ti pucchantā taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā – “mahantaṃ vata, bho, surāmaṃsagandhamālādisakkāraṃ caṇḍālaṃ nissāya anubhavituṃ na labhimha, gaṇhatha caṇḍāla”nti gataṭṭhānaṃ gavesitvā nirāparādhaṃ mātaṅgapaṇḍitaṃ tajjitvā – “are mātaṅga taṃ nissāya idañcidañca sakkāraṃ anubhavituṃ na labhimhā”ti kesesu [M 3.0050] gahetvā bhūmiyaṃ pātetvā jāṇukapparapāsāṇādīhi koṭṭetvā matoti saññāya pāde gahetvā kaḍḍhantā saṅkārakūṭe chaḍḍesuṃ.

Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā, hearing the sound of the gong and looking from within a curtain, saw him coming from afar and asked, 'What is this?' They replied, 'Noble lady, it is Mātaṅga.' 'Alas, sirs, what unwholesome deed have I done? Of what kamma is this the result? Has misfortune now presented itself to me? While going forth on an auspicious occasion, I have seen a caṇḍāla!' Making her body tremble and being filled with disgust, she spat and said to her nurses, 'Quickly, bring water! I have seen a caṇḍāla. I will wash my eyes and the mouth that uttered his name.' Having washed, she had the chariot turned back, had all the provisions sent home, and ascended to her palace. The drunkards and her other male attendants, asking, 'Sirs, where is Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā? She has not come even at this hour,' heard the news of what had happened and said, 'Indeed, sirs, on account of a caṇḍāla, we did not get to enjoy the great honor of liquor, meat, perfumes, and garlands! Seize the caṇḍāla!' Having searched for the place where he had gone, they found the innocent and wise Mātaṅga and threatened him, saying, 'Hey, Mātaṅga! On account of you, we did not get to enjoy this and that honor!' Seizing him by the hair, they threw him to the ground, beat him with knees, elbows, stones, and so forth, and with the perception that he was dead, they seized him by the feet, dragged him, and threw him onto a rubbish heap.

Mahāpuriso saññaṃ paṭilabhitvā hatthapāde parāmasitvā – “idaṃ dukkhaṃ kaṃ nissāya uppanna”nti cintento – “na aññaṃ kañci, diṭṭhamaṅgalikaṃ nissāya uppanna”nti ñatvā “sacāhaṃ puriso, pādesu naṃ nipātessāmī”ti cintetvā vedhamāno diṭṭhamaṅgalikāya kuladvāraṃ gantvā – “diṭṭhamaṅgalikaṃ labhanto vuṭṭhahissāmi, alabhantassa ettheva maraṇa”nti gehaṅgaṇe nipajji. Tena ca samayena jambudīpe ayaṃ dhammatā hoti – yassa caṇḍālo kujjhitvā gabbhadvāre [V 3.0051] nipanno marati, ye ca tasmiṃ gabbhe vasanti, sabbe caṇḍālā honti. Gehamajjhamhi mate sabbe gehavāsino, dvāramhi mate ubhato anantaragehavāsikā, aṅgaṇamhi mate ito satta ito sattāti cuddasagehavāsino sabbe caṇḍālā hontīti. Bodhisatto pana aṅgaṇe nipajji.

The Great Being, having regained consciousness and felt his hands and feet, reflected, 'On account of whom has this suffering arisen?' Knowing, 'It has not arisen on account of anyone else, but on account of Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā,' he thought, 'If I am a man, I will make her fall at my feet.' Trembling, he went to the door of Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā's family home and, having resolved, 'If I obtain Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā, I will rise; for me who does not obtain her, death is right here,' he lay down in the courtyard of the house. And at that time, this was the custom in Jambudīpa: if a caṇḍāla, having become angry, lies down at the door of an inner chamber and dies, all who dwell in that inner chamber become caṇḍālas. If he dies in the middle of the house, all the house-dwellers become caṇḍālas. If he dies at the main door, the dwellers of the immediately adjacent houses on both sides become caṇḍālas. If he dies in the courtyard, the dwellers of the fourteen houses—seven on this side and seven on that side—all become caṇḍālas. The Bodhisatta, however, lay down in the courtyard.

Seṭṭhissa ārocesuṃ – “mātaṅgo te sāmi gehaṅgaṇe patito”ti [P 3.0072] gacchatha bhaṇe, kiṃ kāraṇāti vatvā ekamāsakaṃ datvā uṭṭhāpethāti. Te gantvā “imaṃ kira māsakaṃ gahetvā uṭṭhahā”ti vadiṃsu. So – “nāhaṃ māsakatthāya nipanno, diṭṭhamaṅgalikāya svāhaṃ nipanno”ti āha. Diṭṭhamaṅgalikāya ko dosoti? Kiṃ tassā dosaṃ na passatha, niraparādho ahaṃ tassā manussehi byasanaṃ pāpito, taṃ labhantova vuṭṭhahissāmi, alabhanto na vuṭṭhahissāmīti.

They informed the great merchant, 'Master, Mātaṅga is lying in your courtyard.' The merchant said, 'Go, sirs, ask for what reason he is lying there, and giving him one māsaka, make him get up.' They went and said, 'Take this māsaka, they say, and get up.' He replied, 'I am not lying down for the sake of a māsaka; I am lying down for the sake of Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā.' When they asked, 'What fault is there in Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā?' he said, 'Why do you not see her fault? I, who am innocent, was brought to misfortune by her people. Only upon obtaining her will I rise; not obtaining her, I will not rise.'

Te gantvā seṭṭhissa ārocesuṃ. Seṭṭhi dhītu dosaṃ ñatvā “gacchatha, ekaṃ kahāpaṇaṃ dethā”ti peseti. So “na icchāmi kahāpaṇaṃ, tameva icchāmī”ti āha. Taṃ sutvā seṭṭhi ca seṭṭhibhariyā ca – “ekāyeva no piyadhītā, paveṇiyā ghaṭako añño dārakopi natthī”ti saṃvegappattā – “gacchatha tātā, koci amhākaṃ asahanako etaṃ jīvitāpi voropeyya, etasmiñhi mate sabbe mayaṃ naṭṭhā homa, ārakkhamassa gaṇhathā”ti parivāretvā ārakkhaṃ saṃvidhāya yāguṃ pesayiṃsu, bhattaṃ dhanaṃ pesayiṃsu, evaṃ so sabbaṃ paṭikkhipi. Evaṃ eko divaso gato; dve, tayo, cattāro, pañca divasā gatā.

They went and informed the great merchant. The merchant, knowing his daughter's fault, sent them, saying, 'Go, give him one kahāpaṇa.' But he said, 'I do not want a kahāpaṇa, I want only her.' Hearing this, the great merchant and his wife became distressed and said, 'We have only one beloved daughter, and there is no other child to continue the lineage.' They said, 'Go, dears. Some intolerant person among our people might deprive this man of his life. For if he dies, all of us will be ruined. Set a guard for him.' Having surrounded him and arranged for a guard, they sent gruel, they sent cooked rice, they sent wealth. But he rejected everything. Thus one day passed; two, three, four, and five days passed.

Tato [M 3.0051] sattasattagehavāsikā uṭṭhāya – “na sakkoma mayaṃ tumhe nissāya caṇḍālā bhavituṃ, amhe mā nāsetha, tumhākaṃ dārikaṃ datvā etaṃ uṭṭhāpethā”ti āhaṃsu. Te satampi sahassampi satasahassampi pahiṇiṃsu, so paṭikkhipateva. Evaṃ cha divasā gatā. Sattame divase ubhato cuddasagehavāsikā sannipatitvā – “na mayaṃ caṇḍālā bhavituṃ sakkoma, tumhākaṃ akāmakānampi mayaṃ etassa dārikaṃ dassāmā”ti āhaṃsu.

After that, the dwellers of the fourteen houses rose up and said, 'We cannot become caṇḍālas on account of you. Do not ruin us! Give your daughter and make this man get up.' The parents sent a hundred, a thousand, and even a hundred thousand, but he just kept rejecting it. Thus six days passed. On the seventh day, the dwellers of the fourteen houses from both sides gathered together and said, 'We cannot become caṇḍālas. Even though you are unwilling, we ourselves will give your daughter to this man.'

Mātāpitaro sokasallasamappitā visaññī hutvā sayane nipatiṃsu. Ubhato cuddasagehavāsino pāsādaṃ āruyha supupphitakiṃsukasākhaṃ [P 3.0073] ucchindantā viya tassā sabbābharaṇāni omuñcitvā nakhehi sīmantaṃ katvā kese bandhitvā nīlasāṭakaṃ nivāsāpetvā hatthe [V 3.0052] nīlapilotikakhaṇḍaṃ veṭhetvā kaṇṇesu tipupaṭṭake piḷandhāpetvā tālapaṇṇapacchiṃ datvā pāsādato otārāpetvā dvīsu bāhāsu gahetvā – “tava sāmikaṃ gahetvā yāhī”ti mahāpurisassa adaṃsu.

Her mother and father, pierced by the arrow of sorrow, became unconscious and lay down on their bed. The fourteen householders from both sides ascended the palace, and as if breaking a branch of a well-blossomed Kiṃsuka tree, they stripped her of all her ornaments, parted her hair with their nails, tied up her hair, made her wear a blue cloth, wrapped a piece of worn-out blue cloth around her hand, made her wear tin plates in her ears, gave her a palm-leaf basket, had her descend from the palace, and taking her by both arms, they gave her to the Great Man, saying, 'Take your husband and go.'

Nīluppalampi atibhāroti anukkhittapubbā sukhumāladārikā “uṭṭhāhi sāmi, gacchāmā”ti āha. Bodhisatto nipannakova āha “nāhaṃ uṭṭhahāmī”ti. Atha kinti vadāmīti. “Uṭṭhehi ayya mātaṅgā”ti evaṃ maṃ vadāhīti. Sā tathā avoca. Na tuyhaṃ manussā uṭṭhānasamatthaṃ maṃ akaṃsu, bāhāya maṃ gahetvā uṭṭhāpehīti. Sā tathā akāsi. Bodhisatto uṭṭhahanto viya parivaṭṭetvā bhūmiyaṃ patitvā – “nāsitaṃ, bho, diṭṭhamaṅgalikāya paṭhamaṃ manussehi koṭṭāpetvā, idāni sayaṃ koṭṭetī”ti viravittha. Sā kiṃ karomi ayyāti? Dvīhi hatthehi gahetvā uṭṭhāpehīti. Sā tathā uṭṭhāpetvā nisīdāpetvā gacchāma sāmīti. Gacchā nāma araññe honti, mayaṃ manussā, atikoṭṭitomhi tuyhaṃ manussehi, na sakkomi padasā gantuṃ, piṭṭhiyā maṃ nehīti. Sā onamitvā piṭṭhiṃ adāsi. Bodhisatto abhiruhi. Kuhiṃ nemi sāmīti? Bahinagaraṃ nehīti. Sā pācīnadvāraṃ gantvā – “idha te sāmi vasanaṭṭhāna”nti pucchi. Kataraṭṭhānaṃ etanti? Pācīnadvāraṃ sāmīti. Pācīnadvāre caṇḍālaputtā vasituṃ na labhantīti [P 3.0074] attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ anācikkhitvāva sabbadvārāni āhiṇḍāpesi. Kasmā? Bhavaggapattamassā [M 3.0052] mānaṃ pātessāmīti. Mahājano ukkuṭṭhimakāsi – “ṭhapetvā tumhādisaṃ añño etissā mānaṃ bhedako natthī”ti.

The delicate girl, who had never before lifted a burden, thinking even a blue lotus was too heavy, said, 'Arise, master, let us go.' The Bodhisatta, still lying down, said, 'I will not get up.' Then she asked, 'What then shall I say?' He replied, 'Address me thus: "Arise, noble Mātaṅga."' She spoke accordingly. He said, 'Your people have rendered me unable to get up; take me by the arm and help me up.' She did so. The Bodhisatta, as if getting up, rolled over and fell on the ground, crying out, 'Sirs, I am ruined by Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā! First, she had me beaten by her people, and now she beats me herself!' She asked, 'What shall I do, noble sir?' 'Take me with both hands and help me up.' Having helped him up and seated him thus, she said, 'Let us go, master.' He replied, 'Trees are in the forest; we are human beings. I have been severely beaten by your people; I cannot go on foot. Carry me on your back.' She bent down and offered her back. The Bodhisatta mounted. 'Where shall I take you, master?' 'Take me outside the city.' She went to the eastern gate and asked, 'Is your dwelling place here, master?' 'What place is this?' 'The eastern gate, master.' Saying, 'Sons of caṇḍālas are not allowed to live at the eastern gate,' without revealing his own dwelling place, he made her wander to all the gates. Why? He thought, 'I will cause her pride, which has reached the highest level of existence, to fall.' The great crowd raised a shout: 'Except for one such as you, there is no other who can break her pride!'

Sā pacchimadvāraṃ patvā “idha te sāmi vasanaṭṭhāna”nti pucchi. Kataraṭṭhānaṃ etanti? Pacchimadvāraṃ sāmīti. Iminā dvārena nikkhamitvā cammagehaṃ olokentī gacchāti. Sā tattha gantvā āha “idaṃ cammagehaṃ tumhākaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ sāmī”ti? Āmāti piṭṭhito otaritvā cammagehaṃ pāvisi.

Having reached the western gate, she asked, 'Is your dwelling place here, master?' 'What place is this?' 'The western gate, master.' He said, 'Go out through this gate, and while going, look at the leather house.' She went there and asked, 'Is this leather house your dwelling place, master?' 'Yes,' he said. Getting down from her back, he entered the leather house.

Tattha sattaṭṭhadivase vasanto sabbaññutagavesanadhīro ettakesu divasesu na ca jātisambhedamakāsi. “Mahākulassa dhītā sace maṃ nissāya mahantaṃ yasaṃ na pāpuṇāti, na camhāhaṃ catuvīsatiyā buddhānaṃ antevāsiko. Etissā pādadhovanaudakena sakalajambudīpe rājūnaṃ [V 3.0053] abhisekakiccaṃ karissāmī”ti cintetvā puna cintesi – “agāramajjhevasanto na sakkhissāmi, pabbajitvā pana sakkhissāmī”ti. Cintetvā taṃ āmantesi – “diṭṭhamaṅgalike mayaṃ pubbe ekacarā kammaṃ katvāpi akatvāpi sakkā jīvituṃ, idāni pana dārabharaṇaṃ paṭipannamha, kammaṃ akatvā na sakkā jīvituṃ, tvaṃ yāvāhaṃ āgacchāmi, tāva mā ukkaṇṭhitthā”ti araññaṃ pavisitvā susānādīsu nantakāni saṅkaḍḍhitvā nivāsanapārupanaṃ katvā samaṇapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā ekacaro laddhakāyaviveko kasiṇaparikammaṃ katvā aṭṭha samāpattiyo pañca abhiññāyo ca nibbattetvā “idāni sakkā diṭṭhamaṅgalikāya avassayena mayā bhavitu”nti bārāṇasiabhimukho gantvā cīvaraṃ pārupitvā bhikkhaṃ caramāno diṭṭhamaṅgalikāya [P 3.0075] gehābhimukho agamāsi.

Dwelling there for seven or eight days, the wise one searching for omniscience did not, during those days, commit the mixing of castes. He thought, 'If the daughter of a great family does not attain great fame on account of me, then I am not a disciple of the twenty-four Buddhas. With the water from washing her feet, I will perform the consecration ceremony for the kings in all of Jambudīpa.' He thought again, 'Living in the midst of a household, I will not be able, but having gone forth, I will be able.' Having thought thus, he addressed her, 'Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā, previously we were solitary wanderers and were able to live whether we worked or not. But now we have undertaken the support of a wife; it is not possible to live without working. Until I return, do not be distressed.' Having entered the forest, gathered rags from charnel grounds and other such places, made them into a lower and upper robe, and gone forth into the ascetic life, as a solitary wanderer, having obtained bodily seclusion, having done the preliminary kasiṇa practice, he produced the eight attainments and the five supernormal knowledges. He then thought, 'Now it is possible for me to be a refuge for Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā.' He went towards Bārāṇasī, put on his robe, and while wandering for alms, he went towards Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā's house.

Sā taṃ dvāre ṭhitaṃ disvā asañjānantī – “aticchatha, bhante, caṇḍālānaṃ vasanaṭṭhānameta”nti āha. Bodhisatto tattheva aṭṭhāsi. Sā punappunaṃ olokentī sañjānitvā hatthehi uraṃ paharitvā viravamānā pādamūle patitvā āha – “yadi te sāmi edisaṃ cittaṃ atthi, kasmā maṃ mahatā yasā parihāpetvā anāthaṃ akāsī”ti. Nānappakāraṃ paridevaṃ paridevitvā akkhīni puñchamānā uṭṭhāya bhikkhābhājanaṃ gahetvā antogehe nisīdāpetvā bhikkhaṃ adāsi. Mahāpuriso bhattakiccaṃ katvā āha – “diṭṭhamaṅgalike mā soci mā paridevi, ahaṃ tuyhaṃ pādadhovanaudakena sakalajambudīpe rājūnaṃ abhisekakiccaṃ kāretuṃ samattho, tvaṃ pana [M 3.0053] ekaṃ mama vacanaṃ karohi, nagaraṃ pavisitvā ‘na mayhaṃ sāmiko caṇḍālo, mahābrahmā mayhaṃ sāmiko’ti ugghosayamānā sakalanagaraṃ carāhī”ti.

Seeing him standing at the door, and not recognizing him, she said, 'Pass by, venerable sir, this is the dwelling place of caṇḍālas.' The Bodhisatta stood right there. Looking again and again, she recognized him and, striking her chest with her hands and wailing, she fell at his feet and said, 'Master, if you had such an intention, why did you cause me to fall from great fame and make me helpless?' Having lamented in various ways, wiping her eyes, she got up, took his alms bowl, had him sit inside the house, and gave him alms-food. The Great Man, having finished his meal, said, 'Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā, do not sorrow, do not lament. I am able to have the consecration ceremony for the kings in all of Jambudīpa performed with the water from washing your feet. But you must do one thing I say: enter the city and, proclaiming, "My husband is not a caṇḍāla, my husband is Mahābrahmā," wander through the entire city.'

Evaṃ vutte diṭṭhamaṅgalikā – “pakatiyāpi ahaṃ sāmi mukhadoseneva byasanaṃ pattā, na sakkhissāmevaṃ vattu”nti āha. Bodhisatto – “kiṃ pana tayā mayhaṃ agāre vasantassa alikavacanaṃ sutapubbaṃ, ahaṃ tadāpi alikaṃ na bhaṇāmi, idāni pabbajito kiṃ vakkhāmi, saccavādī puriso nāmāha”nti vatvā – “ajja pakkhassa aṭṭhamī, tvaṃ ‘ito sattāhassaccayena uposathadivase mayhaṃ sāmiko mahābrahmā candamaṇḍalaṃ bhinditvā mama santikaṃ āgamissatī’ti sakalanagare ugghosehī”ti vatvā pakkāmi.

When this was said, Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā replied, 'Master, even by nature, it is only because of the fault of my speech that I have met with ruin. I will not be able to speak thus.' The Bodhisatta said, 'But have you ever heard a false word from me while I was living in the house? Even then I did not speak falsely; now that I have gone forth, why would I speak it? I am a man who speaks the truth.' Having said this, he instructed, 'Today is the eighth day of the fortnight. You must proclaim throughout the entire city: "After the passing of seven days from today, on the Uposatha day, my husband, the Great Brahmā, will come to my presence after shattering the disc of the moon."' Having said this, he departed.

Sā [V 3.0054] saddahitvā haṭṭhatuṭṭhā sūrā hutvā sāyaṃpātaṃ nagaraṃ pavisitvā tathā ugghosesi. Manussā pāṇinā pāṇiṃ paharantā – “passatha, amhākaṃ diṭṭhamaṅgalikā caṇḍālaputtaṃ mahābrahmānaṃ karotī”ti hasantā keḷiṃ karonti. Sā punadivasepi tatheva sāyaṃpātaṃ pavisitvā – “idāni chāhaccayena, pañcāha-catūha-tīha-dvīha-ekāhaccayena mayhaṃ sāmiko mahābrahmā candamaṇḍalaṃ bhinditvā mama santikaṃ āgamissatī”ti ugghosesi.

She, having faith, was delighted and overjoyed. Becoming courageous, she entered the city in the evening and the morning and proclaimed it in that manner. The people, clapping their hands, laughed and made sport, saying, 'Look, our Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā is making the son of a caṇḍāla into the Great Brahmā!' On the next day as well, she entered the city in the evening and the morning in that same way and proclaimed, 'Now, after the passing of six days, then five, four, three, two, and one day, my husband, the Great Brahmā, will come to my presence after shattering the disc of the moon!'

Brāhmaṇā [P 3.0076] cintayiṃsu – “ayaṃ diṭṭhamaṅgalikā atisūrā hutvā katheti, kadāci evaṃ siyā, etha mayaṃ diṭṭhamaṅgalikāya vasanaṭṭhānaṃ paṭijaggāmā”ti cammagehassa bāhirabhāgaṃ samantā tacchāpetvā vālikaṃ okiriṃsu. Sāpi uposathadivase pātova nagaraṃ pavisitvā “ajja mayhaṃ sāmiko āgamissatī”ti ugghosesi. Brāhmaṇā cintayiṃsu – “ayaṃ bho na dūraṃ apadissati, ajja kira mahābrahmā āgamissati, vasanaṭṭhānaṃ saṃvidahāmā”ti cammagehaṃ samajjāpetvā haritūpalittaṃ ahatavatthehi parikkhipitvā mahārahaṃ pallaṅkaṃ attharitvā upari celavitānaṃ bandhitvā gandhamāladāmāni osārayiṃsu. Tesaṃ paṭijaggantānaṃyeva sūriyo atthaṃ gato.

The brahmins thought: 'This Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā speaks having become very courageous; perhaps it may be so. Come, let us prepare Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā’s dwelling place.'
