Having thought this, they had the ground outside the house roofed with leather leveled all around and scattered sand upon it. She too, on the Uposatha day, entered the city very early in the morning and proclaimed: 'Today my husband will come!' The brahmins thought: 'Sirs, she does not speak of a distant time. It seems the Great Brahmā will come today. Let us arrange the dwelling place.' Having thought this, they had the house roofed with leather swept, smeared it with fresh cow-dung, draped it with new cloths, spread out a couch of great value, fastened a cloth canopy above, and hung up garlands of perfume and flowers. Even while they were preparing, the sun went to its setting.

Mahāpuriso cande uggatamatte abhiññāpādakajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya kāmāvacaracittena parikammaṃ katvā iddhicittena dvādasayojanikaṃ brahmattabhāvaṃ māpetvā vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā candavimānassa anto pavisitvā [M 3.0054] vanantato abbhussakkamānaṃ candaṃ bhinditvā candavimānaṃ ohāya purato hutvā “mahājano maṃ passatū”ti adhiṭṭhāsi. Mahājano disvā – “saccaṃ, bho, diṭṭhamaṅgalikāya vacanaṃ, āgacchantaṃ mahābrahmānaṃ pūjessāmā”ti gandhamālaṃ ādāya diṭṭhamaṅgalikāya gharaṃ parivāretvā aṭṭhāsi. Mahāpuriso matthakamatthakena sattavāre bārāṇasiṃ anuparigantvā mahājanena diṭṭhabhāvaṃ ñatvā dvādasayojanikaṃ attabhāvaṃ vijahitvā manussappamāṇameva māpetvā mahājanassa passantasseva cammagehaṃ pāvisi. Mahājano disvā – “otiṇṇo no mahābrahmā, sāṇiṃ āharathā”ti nivesanaṃ mahāsāṇiyā parikkhipitvā parivāretvā [P 3.0077] ṭhito.

The Great Being, just as the moon rose, entered the jhāna that is the basis for supernormal knowledge. Having emerged from it, he performed the preliminary work with a sense-sphere mind and then, with a mind of psychic power, he created a Brahma-form spanning twelve yojanas. He ascended into the sky, entered the lunar mansion, and as he rose up from the moon-disc, he shattered it. Leaving the lunar mansion, he stood in front and resolved: 'Let the great multitude see me.' Seeing him, the great multitude said: 'Sirs, the word of Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā is true! We will pay homage to the Great Brahmā who is coming.' Taking perfumes and garlands, they surrounded Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā’s house and stood there. The Great Being circled Bārāṇasī seven times high above, and knowing that he had been seen by the great multitude, he abandoned his twelve-yojana form, created one of human proportions, and entered the house roofed with leather even as the great multitude was watching. Seeing this, the great multitude said: 'Our Great Brahmā has descended! Bring a curtain!' They enclosed the dwelling with a great curtain and stood surrounding it.

Mahāpurisopi sirisayanamajjhe nisīdi. Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā samīpe aṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ pucchi [V 3.0055] “utusamayo te diṭṭhamaṅgalike”ti. Āma ayyāti. Mayā dinnaṃ puttaṃ gaṇhāhīti aṅguṭṭhakena nābhimaṇḍalaṃ phusi. Tassā parāmasaneneva gabbho patiṭṭhāsi. Mahāpuriso – “ettāvatā te diṭṭhamaṅgalike pādadhovanaudakaṃ sakalajambudīpe rājūnaṃ abhisekodakaṃ bhavissati, tvaṃ tiṭṭhā”ti vatvā brahmattabhāvaṃ māpetvā passantasseva mahājanassa nikkhamitvā vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā caṇḍamaṇḍalameva paviṭṭho. Sā tato paṭṭhāya brahmapajāpatī nāma jātā. Pādadhovanaudakaṃ labhanto nāma natthi.

The Great Being also sat in the middle of the glorious couch. Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā stood nearby. Then he asked her, 'Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā, is it your season?' 'Yes, lord.' 'Receive the son given by me,' he said, and touched the circle of her navel with his thumb. By that mere touch, conception was established. The Great Being said, 'Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā, by this much alone, your foot-washing water will become the consecration water for the kings in all of Jambudīpa. You remain here.' Having said this, he created a Brahma-form and, even as the great multitude was watching, he departed, ascended into the sky, and entered the very disc of the moon. From that time on, she came to be known as Brahmāpajāpatī, the consort of Brahmā. There was no one who could obtain the foot-washing water.

Brāhmaṇā – “brahmapajāpatiṃ antonagare vasāpessāmā”ti suvaṇṇasivikāya āropetvā yāva sattamakoṭiyā aparisuddhajātikassa sivikaṃ gahetuṃ na adaṃsu. Soḷasa jātimantabrāhmaṇā gaṇhiṃsu. Sesā gandhapupphādīhi pūjetvā nagaraṃ pavisitvā – “na sakkā, bho, ucchiṭṭhagehe brahmapajāpatiyā vasituṃ, vatthuṃ gahetvā gehaṃ karissāma, yāva pana taṃ karīyati, tāva maṇḍapeva vasatū”ti maṇḍape vasāpesuṃ. Tato paṭṭhāya cakkhupathe ṭhatvā vanditukāmā kahāpaṇaṃ datvā vandituṃ labhanti, savanūpacāre vanditukāmā sataṃ datvā labhanti, āsanne pakatikathaṃ savanaṭṭhāne vanditukāmā pañcasatāni datvā labhanti, pādapiṭṭhiyaṃ sīsaṃ ṭhapetvā vanditukāmā sahassaṃ datvā labhanti, pādadhovanaudakaṃ patthayamānā dasasahassāni datvā labhanti. Bahinagarato antonagare yāva maṇḍapā āgacchantiyā laddhadhanaṃyeva koṭisatamattaṃ ahosi.

The brahmins said, 'We will have Brahmāpajāpatī reside within the city.' Placing her on a golden palanquin, they did not allow anyone of impure birth up to the seventh generation to even hold the palanquin. Sixteen brahmins of pure birth carried it. The rest, having paid homage with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, brought her into the city and said, 'Sirs, it is not proper for Brahmāpajāpatī to dwell in a previously occupied house. We will acquire a plot of land and build a new house. Until that is built, let her reside in a pavilion.' Thus, they had her stay in a pavilion. From that time on, those wishing to pay homage while standing within sight could do so by giving a kahāpaṇa. Those wishing to pay homage from within hearing range could do so by giving a hundred. Those wishing to pay homage from a place nearby where her ordinary conversation could be heard could do so by giving five hundred. Those wishing to pay homage by placing their heads on the top of her feet could do so by giving a thousand. Those desiring her foot-washing water could obtain it by giving ten thousand. Just in coming from outside the city to the pavilion within, the wealth she received amounted to one hundred crores.

Sakalajambudīpo [M 3.0055] saṅkhubhi, tato sabbarājāno “brahmapajāpatiyā pādadhovanena [P 3.0078] abhisekaṃ karissāmā”ti satasahassaṃ pesetvā labhiṃsu. Maṇḍape vasantiyā eva gabbhavuṭṭhānaṃ ahosi. Mahāpurisaṃ paṭicca laddhakumāro pāsādiko ahosi lakkhaṇasampanno. Mahābrahmuno putto jātoti sakala jambudīpo ekakolāhalo ahosi. Kumārassa khīramaṇimūlaṃ hotūti tato tato āgatadhanaṃ koṭisahassaṃ ahosi. Ettāvatā nivesanampi niṭṭhitaṃ. Kumārassa nāmakaraṇaṃ karissāmāti nivesanaṃ sajjetvā kumāraṃ gandhodakena nhāpetvā alaṅkaritvā maṇḍape jātattā maṇḍabyotveva nāmaṃ akaṃsu.

The entire Jambudīpa was agitated. Then all the kings, thinking, 'We shall perform the consecration with Brahmāpajāpatī's foot-washing water,' sent one hundred thousand and obtained it. While she was dwelling in the pavilion, the birth occurred. The prince, obtained on account of the Great Being, was pleasing and endowed with auspicious marks. The whole of Jambudīpa became a single uproar, proclaiming, 'The son of the great Brahmā has been born!' Saying, 'Let this be the price for the prince's milk-gem,' the wealth that came from here and there amounted to a thousand crores. With that much, the residence was also completed. Thinking, 'We shall perform the naming ceremony for the prince,' they prepared the residence, bathed the prince with fragrant water, adorned him, and because he was born in a pavilion (maṇḍapa), they gave him the name Maṇḍabya.

Kumāro sukhena saṃvaḍḍhamāno sippuggahaṇavayapattoti sakalajambudīpe sippajānanakā tassa santike āgantvā sippaṃ sikkhāpenti. Kumāro medhāvī paññavā sutaṃ sutaṃ mutaṃ āvuṇanto viya [V 3.0056] gaṇhāti, gahitagahitaṃ suvaṇṇaghaṭe pakkhittatelaṃ viya tiṭṭhati. Yāvatā vācuggatā pariyatti atthi, tena anuggahitā nāma nāhosi. Brāhmaṇā taṃ parivāretvā caranti, sopi brāhmaṇabhatto ahosi. Gehe asītibrāhmaṇasahassāni niccabhattaṃ bhuñjanti. Gehampissa sattadvārakoṭṭhakaṃ mahantaṃ ahosi. Gehe maṅgaladivase jambudīpavāsīhi pesitadhanaṃ koṭisahassamattaṃ ahosi.

The prince, growing up happily, reached the age for learning skills. Then, those from all over Jambudīpa who knew how to teach skills came to his presence and taught him skills. The prince was intelligent and wise; whatever he heard, he grasped it as if stringing pearls. Whatever he grasped remained like lion's oil poured into a golden pot. There was no worldly scripture transmitted orally that had not been learned by him. Brahmins, surrounding him, went about with him, and he too became one who constantly fed the brahmins. In his house, eighty thousand brahmins ate a constant meal. His house was also large, with seven gate-chambers. On the day of the house-warming ceremony, the wealth sent by the inhabitants of Jambudīpa amounted to a thousand crores.

Bodhisatto āvajjesi – “pamatto nu kho kumāro appamatto”ti. Athassa taṃ pavattiṃ ñatvā – “brāhmaṇabhatto jāto, yattha dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ hoti, taṃ na jānāti, gacchāmi naṃ damemī”ti cīvaraṃ pārupitvā bhikkhābhājanaṃ gahetvā – “dvārakoṭṭhakā atisambādhā, na sakkā koṭṭhakena pavisitu”nti ākāsenāgantvā asītibrāhmaṇasahassānaṃ bhuñjanaṭṭhāne ākāsaṅgaṇe otari. Maṇḍabyakumāropi [P 3.0079] suvaṇṇakaṭacchuṃ gāhāpetvā – “idha sūpaṃ detha idha odana”nti parivisāpento bodhisattaṃ disvā daṇḍakena ghaṭṭitaāsiviso viya kupitvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

The Bodhisatta reflected: 'Is the prince heedless or heedful?' Then, knowing his state of being, he thought: 'He has become one who feeds brahmins; he does not know the recipient in whom a gift given is of great fruit. I shall go and discipline him.' Having put on his robe and taken his alms bowl, he thought: 'The gate-chambers are very congested; it is not possible to enter through a gate-chamber.' So he came through the sky and descended in the open space at the eating place of the eighty thousand brahmins. Prince Maṇḍabya also, having caused a golden ladle to be taken and saying, 'Give curry here, give rice here,' was causing them to serve. When he saw the Bodhisatta, he became angry like a venomous snake struck with a stick and spoke this verse:

“Kuto [M 3.0056] nu āgacchasi dummavāsī,

Otallako paṃsupisācakova;

Saṅkāracoḷaṃ paṭimuñca kaṇṭhe,

Ko re tuvaṃ hosi adakkhiṇeyyo”ti. (jā. 1.15.1);

'From where do you come, you of foul appearance, you of base desires, like a dust-goblin? Wearing a rag from a rubbish heap on your neck, who, pray tell, are you, unworthy of a gift?'

Atha naṃ mahāsatto akujjhitvāva ovadanto āha –

Then the Great Being, without becoming angry, advising him, said:

“Annaṃ tavedaṃ pakataṃ yasassi,

Taṃ khajjare bhuñjare piyyare ca;

Jānāsi maṃ tvaṃ paradattūpajīviṃ,

Uttiṭṭha piṇḍaṃ labhataṃ sapāko”ti. (jā. 1.15.2);

O glorious one, this food of yours is prepared. It is being chewed, eaten, and drunk. For what reason are you angry with me alone? Do you know me, one who lives sustained by what is given by others? Let an outcaste obtain the offered alms-food.

So nayidaṃ tumhādisānaṃ paṭiyattanti dassento āha –

He, wishing to show, 'This is not prepared for the likes of you,' said:

“Annaṃ [V 3.0057] mamedaṃ pakataṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ,

Atthatthitaṃ saddahato mamedaṃ;

Apehi etto kimidhaṭṭhitosi,

Na mādisā tuyhaṃ dadanti jammā”ti. (jā. 1.15.3);

This food was prepared by me for the brahmins. This food was prepared by me, who has faith in the benefit of the hereafter. Go away from here! Why do you stand here? O wretch, persons like me do not give to you.

Atha bodhisatto “dānaṃ nāma saguṇassapi nigguṇassapi yassa kassaci dātabbaṃ, yathā hi ninnepi thalepi patiṭṭhāpitaṃ bījaṃ pathavīrasaṃ āporasañca āgamma sampajjati, evaṃ [P 3.0080] nipphalaṃ nāma natthi, sukhette vapitabījaṃ viya guṇavante mahapphalaṃ hotī”ti dassetuṃ imaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the Bodhisatta, in order to show that 'a gift should be given to anyone whatsoever, whether virtuous or without virtue; for just as a seed planted in a low place or a high place thrives, relying on the essence of the earth and the essence of water, so too there is no such thing as a fruitless gift; like a seed sown in a good field, in a virtuous person it is of great fruit,' spoke this verse:

“Thale ca ninne ca vapanti bījaṃ,

Anūpakhette phalamāsamānā;

Etāya saddhāya dadāhi dānaṃ,

Appeva ārādhaye dakkhiṇeyye”ti. (jā. 1.15.4);

Those desiring fruit sow seed on high ground and in low ground, in a fertile field. So too, with this faith, you should give a gift; one might just please a worthy recipient.

Atha kumāro kodhābhibhūto – “kenimassa muṇḍakassa paveso dinno”ti dvārarakkhādayo tajjetvā –

Then the prince, overcome by anger, having threatened the gatekeepers and others, asked: 'By whom was entry given to this shaveling?'

“Khettāni [M 3.0057] mayhaṃ viditāni loke,

Yesāhaṃ bījāni patiṭṭhapemi;

Ye brāhmaṇā jātimantūpapannā,

Tānīdha khettāni supesalānī”ti. (jā. 1.15.5) –

The fields in the world where I establish seeds are known to me. Those brahmins who are endowed with birth and mantras, and are very virtuous—those are the fields here.

Gāthaṃ vatvā “imaṃ jammaṃ veṇupadarena pothetvā gīvāyaṃ gahetvā sattapi dvārakoṭṭhake atikkamitvā bahi nīharathā”ti āha. Atha naṃ mahāpuriso āha –

Having spoken the verse, he said: 'Strike this wretch with a sliver of bamboo, seize him by the neck, pass beyond the seven gate-chambers, and throw him out!' Then the Great Being said to him:

“Giriṃ nakhena khaṇasi, ayo dantebhi khādasi;

Jātavedaṃ padahasi, yo isiṃ paribhāsasī”ti. (jā. 1.15.9);

You dig a mountain with your fingernail; you chew iron with your teeth; you assail the fire, you who revile a sage.

Evañca [V 3.0058] pana vatvā – “sace myāyaṃ hatthe vā pāde vā gaṇhāpetvā dukkhaṃ uppādeyya, bahuṃ apuññaṃ pasaveyyā”ti sattānuddayatāya vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā antaravīthiyaṃ otari. Bhagavā sabbaññutaṃ patto tamatthaṃ pakāsento imaṃ gāthamāha –

And having spoken thus, thinking, 'If this man, having caused my hand or foot to be seized, should cause me suffering, he would produce much demerit,' out of compassion for that being, he rose up into the sky and descended in the main street. The Blessed One, having attained omniscience, making that meaning clear, spoke this verse:

“Idaṃ vatvāna mātaṅgo, isi saccaparakkamo;

Antalikkhasmiṃ pakkāmi, brāhmaṇānaṃ udikkhata”nti. (jā. 1.15.10);

Having said this, Mātaṅga, the sage of true endeavor, departed into the sky while the brahmins looked on.

Tāvadeva nagararakkhikadevatānaṃ jeṭṭhakadevarājā maṇḍabyassa gīvaṃ parivattesi. Tassa mukhaṃ parivattetitvā [P 3.0081] pacchāmukhaṃ jātaṃ, akkhīni parivattāni, mukhena kheḷaṃ vamati, sarīraṃ thaddhaṃ sūle āropitaṃ viya ahosi. Asītisahassā paricārakayakkhā asītibrāhmaṇasahassāni tatheva akaṃsu. Vegena gantvā brahmapajāpatiyā ārocayiṃsu. Sā taramānarūpā āgantvā taṃ vippakāraṃ disvā gāthamāha –

At that very moment, the chief divine king among the city-protecting deities twisted Maṇḍabya's neck. His face, having been twisted, turned backward; his eyes were twisted, he vomited saliva from his mouth, and his body became stiff as if impaled on a stake. Eighty thousand attendant yakkhas did the very same to the eighty thousand brahmins. They went quickly and reported to Brahmapajāpati's wife. She came in haste and, seeing that distorted state, spoke this verse:

“Āvedhitaṃ piṭṭhito uttamaṅgaṃ,

Bāhuṃ pasāreti akammaneyyaṃ;

Setāni akkhīni yathā matassa,

Ko me imaṃ puttamakāsi eva”nti. (jā. 1.15.11);

His head is twisted from behind; he stretches out his arms, unfit for work. His eyes are white, like those of a dead man. Who has done this to my son?

Athassā [M 3.0058] ārocesuṃ –

Then they informed her:

“Idhāgamā samaṇo dummavāsī,

Otallako paṃsupisācakova,

Saṅkāracoḷaṃ paṭimuñca kaṇṭhe,

So te imaṃ puttamakāsi eva”nti. (jā. 1.15.12);

Hither came a slovenly, base ascetic, like a dust-goblin, having draped a rag from a refuse heap about his neck. It was he who did this to your son.

Sā sutvāva aññāsi – “mayhaṃ yasadāyako ayyo anukampāya puttassa pamattabhāvaṃ ñatvā āgato bhavissatī”ti. Tato upaṭṭhāke pucchi –

Upon hearing this, she understood: 'My noble lord, the giver of glory, must have come out of compassion, knowing my son’s state of heedlessness.' Then she asked the attendants:

“Katamaṃ [V 3.0059] disaṃ agamā bhūripañño,

Akkhātha me māṇavā etamatthaṃ;

Gantvāna taṃ paṭikaremu accayaṃ,

Appeva naṃ putta labhemu jīvita”nti. (jā. 1.15.13);

To which direction did the one of vast wisdom go? Tell me this matter, young men. Having gone to him, let us make amends for the transgression; perhaps we may yet obtain life for this son.

Te āhaṃsu –

They said:

“Vehāyasaṃ agamā bhūripañño,

Pathaddhuno pannaraseva cando;

Apicāpi [P 3.0082] so purimadisaṃ agacchi,

Saccappaṭiñño isi sādhurūpo”ti. (jā. 1.15.14);

The one of vast wisdom went through the sky, like the moon, a traveler on the fifteenth day. Moreover, that sage of truthful profession and virtuous nature went to the eastern direction.

Mahāpurisopi antaravīthiyaṃ otiṇṇaṭṭhānato paṭṭhāya – “mayhaṃ padavaḷañjaṃ hatthiassādīnaṃ vasena mā antaradhāyittha, diṭṭhamaṅgalikāyeva naṃ passatu, mā aññe”ti adhiṭṭhahitvā piṇḍāya caritvā yāpanamattaṃ missakodanaṃ gahetvā paṭikkamanasālāyaṃ nisinno bhuñjitvā thokaṃ bhuttāvasesaṃ bhikkhābhājaneyeva ṭhapesi. Diṭṭhamaṅgalikāpi pāsādā oruyha antaravīthiṃ paṭipajjamānā padavaḷañjaṃ disvā – “idaṃ mayhaṃ yasadāyakassa ayyassa pada”nti padānusārenāgantvā vanditvā āha – “tumhākaṃ, bhante, dāsena katāparādhaṃ mayhaṃ khamatha, na hi tumhe kodhavasikā nāma, detha me puttassa jīvita”nti.

The Great Being, starting from the place where he had descended into the main street, resolved: 'Let my footprint not be effaced by the trampling of elephants, horses, and the like. Let only Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā see it, and no other.' Having made this resolution, he went for alms, received just enough mixed rice for sustenance, and sat in the refectory. Having eaten, he placed the small amount of leftover food in the alms-bowl itself. Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā, too, descended from the palace, and while proceeding along the main street, she saw the footprint. Thinking, 'This is the footprint of my noble lord, the giver of glory,' she came following the tracks, paid homage, and said: 'Venerable sir, please forgive me for the offense committed by your slave. For you are not ones who are under the sway of anger. Please grant the life of my son.'

Evañca pana vatvā –

And having said this as well:

“Āvedhitaṃ [M 3.0059] piṭṭhito uttamaṅgaṃ,

Bāhuṃ pasāreti akammaneyyaṃ;

Setāni akkhīni yathā matassa,

Ko me imaṃ puttamakāsi eva”nti. (jā. 1.15.15) –

His head is twisted from behind; he stretches out his arms, unfit for work. His eyes are white, like those of a dead man. Who has done this to my son?

Gāthaṃ [V 3.0060] abhāsi. Mahāpuriso āha – “na mayaṃ evarūpaṃ karoma, pabbajitaṃ pana hiṃsante disvā pabbajitesu sagāravāhi bhūtayakkhadevatāhi kataṃ bhavissatī”ti.

She spoke the verse. The Great Being said: 'We do not do such a thing. However, upon seeing a renunciate being harmed, it must have been done by spirits, yakkhas, and devas who have reverence for renunciates.'

Kevalaṃ, bhante, tumhākaṃ manopadoso mā hotu, devatāhi kataṃ hotu, sukhamāpayā[P 3.0083], bhante, devatā, apicāhaṃ, bhante, kathaṃ paṭipajjāmīti. Tena hi osadhaṃ te kathessāmi, mama bhikkhābhājane bhuttāvasesaṃ bhattamatthi, tattha thokaṃ udakaṃ āsiñcitvā thokaṃ gahetvā tava puttassa mukhe pakkhipa, avasesaṃ udakacāṭiyaṃ āloḷetvā asītiyā brāhmaṇasahassānaṃ mukhe pakkhipāti. Sā evaṃ karissāmīti bhattaṃ gahetvā mahāpurisaṃ vanditvā gantvā tathā akāsi.

“Venerable sir, just let there be no defilement of mind on your part. Let it have been done by the devas. The devas, venerable sir, desire happiness. But still, venerable sir, how should I proceed?” “In that case, I shall tell you a remedy. In my alms-bowl there is leftover rice from my meal. Pour a little water on it, take a small amount, and place it in your son’s mouth. Stir the remainder into a large water jar and place it in the mouths of the eighty thousand brahmins.” She, saying, “I shall do so,” took the rice, paid homage to the Great Being, departed, and did as instructed.

Mukhe pakkhittamatte jeṭṭhakadevarājā – “sāmimhi sayaṃ bhesajjaṃ karonte amhehi na sakkā kiñci kātu”nti kumāraṃ vissajjesi. Sopi khipitvā kiñci dukkhaṃ appattapubbo viya pakativaṇṇo ahosi. Atha naṃ mātā avoca – “passa tāta tava kulupakānaṃ hirottapparahitānaṃ vippakāraṃ, samaṇā pana na evarūpā honti, samaṇe tāta bhojeyyāsī”ti. Tato sesakaṃ udakacāṭiyaṃ āluḷāpetvā brāhmaṇānaṃ mukhe pakkhipāpesi. Yakkhā tāvadeva vissajjetvā palāyiṃsu. Brāhmaṇā khipitvā khipitvā uṭṭhahitvā kiṃ amhākaṃ mukhe pakkhittanti pucchiṃsu. Mātaṅgaisissa ucchiṭṭhabhattanti. Te “caṇḍālassa ucchiṭṭhakaṃ khādāpitamhā, abrāhmaṇā dānimhā jātā, idāni no brāhmaṇā ‘asuddhabrāhmaṇā ime’ti sambhogaṃ na dassantī”ti tato palāyitvā majjharaṭṭhaṃ gantvā majjharājassa nagare aggāsanikā brāhmaṇā nāma mayanti rājagehe bhuñjanti.

The moment it was placed in his mouth, the chief of the deva kings, thinking, “When the master himself prepares the medicine, we are unable to do anything,” released the young man. He, after convulsing, became of normal complexion, as if he had never experienced any suffering. Then his mother said to him: “See, my dear, the perversity of those who frequent our family, who are devoid of shame and moral dread. Renunciates, however, are not of such a nature. My dear, you should feed true renunciates.” Then, having had the remainder stirred in a large water jar, she had it placed in the mouths of the brahmins. The yakkhas released them at that very moment and fled. The brahmins, convulsing again and again, stood up and asked, “What was placed in our mouths?” When it was said, “The leftover rice of the sage Mātaṅga,” they lamented, “We have been made to eat the leftovers of an outcaste! Now we have become non-brahmins. From now on, pure brahmins will not grant us communion, saying, ‘These are impure brahmins.’” Fleeing from there, they went to the middle country, and in the city of the king of the middle country, they ate in the king’s palace, claiming, “We are brahmins who sit in the highest seats.”

Tasmiṃ samaye bodhisatto pāpaniggahaṃ karonto mānajātike nimmadayanto vicarati. Atheko “jātimantatāpaso nāma mayā sadiso [M 3.0060] natthī”ti aññesu saññampi na karoti. Bodhisatto taṃ gaṅgātīre vasamānaṃ disvā “mānaniggahamassa karissāmī”ti tattha agamāsi[P 3.0084]. Taṃ jātimantatāpaso pucchi – “kiṃ jacco bhava”nti? Caṇḍālo ahaṃ ācariyāti. Apehi caṇḍāla apehi caṇḍāla, heṭṭhāgaṅgāya vasa, mā uparigaṅgāya udakaṃ ucchiṭṭhamakāsīti.

At that time, the Bodhisatta was wandering about, suppressing the wicked and subduing the arrogant. There was a certain ascetic proud of his birth who, thinking, “There is no one equal to me,” did not so much as acknowledge others. The Bodhisatta, seeing him dwelling on the bank of the Ganges, thought, “I shall crush his pride,” and went there. That ascetic proud of his birth asked him, “Of what caste are you?” “I am an outcaste, teacher.” “Go away, outcaste! Go away! Dwell downstream on the Ganges; do not make the water upstream into a remnant!”

Bodhisatto [V 3.0061] – “sādhu ācariya, tumhehi vuttaṭṭhāne vasissāmī”ti heṭṭhāgaṅgāya vasanto “gaṅgāya udakaṃ paṭisotaṃ sandatū”ti adhiṭṭhāsi. Jātimantatāpaso pātova gaṅgaṃ oruyha udakaṃ ācamati, jaṭā dhovati. Bodhisatto dantakaṭṭhaṃ khādanto piṇḍaṃ piṇḍaṃ kheḷaṃ udake pāteti. Dantakaṭṭhakucchiṭṭhakampi tattheva pavāheti. Yathā ce taṃ aññattha alaggitvā tāpasasseva jaṭāsu laggati, tathā adhiṭṭhāsi. Kheḷampi dantakaṭṭhampi tāpasassa jaṭāsuyeva patiṭṭhāti.

The Bodhisatta said, “Very well, teacher, I shall dwell in the place you have indicated.” Dwelling downstream on the Ganges, he resolved, “Let the water of the Ganges flow upstream!” Early in the morning, the ascetic proud of his birth descended into the Ganges, rinsed his mouth, and washed his matted hair. The Bodhisatta, while chewing a tooth-stick, let lumps of saliva fall into the water. He also cast the chewed remnant of the tooth-stick into that very water. And he resolved in such a way that it, not sticking elsewhere, would stick only in that very ascetic’s matted hair. Both the saliva and the tooth-stick lodged only in the ascetic’s matted hair.

Tāpaso caṇḍālassidaṃ kammaṃ bhavissatīti vippaṭisārī hutvā gantvā pucchi – “idaṃ, bho caṇḍāla, gaṅgāya udakaṃ tayā paṭisotagāmikata”nti? Āma ācariya. Tena hi tvaṃ heṭṭhāgaṅgāya mā vasa, uparigaṅgāya vasāti. Sādhu ācariya, tumhehi vuttaṭṭhāne vasissāmīti tattha vasanto iddhiṃ paṭippassambhesi, udakaṃ yathāgatikameva jātaṃ. Puna tāpaso tadeva byasanaṃ pāpuṇi. So puna gantvā bodhisattaṃ pucchi, – “bho caṇḍāla, tvamidaṃ gaṅgāya udakaṃ kālena paṭisotagāmiṃ kālena anusotagāmiṃ karosī”ti? Āma ācariya. Caṇḍāla, “tvaṃ sukhavihārīnaṃ pabbajitānaṃ sukhena vasituṃ na desi, sattame te divase sattadhā muddhā phalatū”ti. Sādhu acariya, ahaṃ pana sūriyassa uggantuṃ na dassāmīti.

The ascetic proud of his birth, becoming remorseful and thinking, “This must be the work of the outcaste,” went and asked, “O outcaste, was this water of the Ganges made to flow upstream by you?” “Yes, teacher.” “In that case, do not live downstream on the Ganges; live upstream on the Ganges,” he said. “Very well, teacher, I will live in the place you have spoken of,” he replied. While living there, he suppressed his psychic power, and the water returned to its natural flow. Again, the ascetic proud of his birth met with that same misfortune. He went again and asked the Bodhisatta, “O outcaste, do you at times make this water of the Ganges flow upstream and at times downstream?” “Yes, teacher,” he replied. The ascetic cursed him, saying, “Outcaste, you do not allow renunciants who dwell in happiness to live peacefully. On the seventh day, may your head split into seven pieces!” “Very well, teacher,” said the Bodhisatta, “but I will not allow the sun to rise.”

Atha mahāsatto cintesi – “etassa abhisāpo etasseva upari patissati, rakkhāmi na”nti sattānuddayatāya punadivase iddhiyā sūriyassa uggantuṃ na adāsi. Iddhimato iddhivisayo [P 3.0085] nāma acinteyyo, tato paṭṭhāya aruṇuggaṃ na paññāyati, rattindivaparicchedo natthi, kasivaṇijjādīni kammāni payojento nāma natthi.

Then the Great Being thought, “This curse will fall upon the ascetic himself; I shall protect him.” Out of compassion for beings, on the following day, he did not allow the sun to rise by his psychic power. The domain of psychic power of one who possesses it is indeed inconceivable. From that time onwards, the light of dawn did not appear, and there was no division between night and day. There was no one who engaged in work such as farming, trade, and so on.

Manussā – “yakkhāvaṭṭo nu kho ayaṃ bhūtadevaṭṭonāgasupaṇṇāvaṭṭo”ti upaddavappattā “kiṃ nu kho kātabba”nti cintetvā “rājakulaṃ nāma mahāpaññaṃ, lokassa hitaṃ cintetuṃ sakkoti, tattha gacchāmā”ti rājakulaṃ gantvā [M 3.0061] tamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. Rājā sutvā bhītopi abhītākāraṃ katvā – “mā tātā bhāyatha, imaṃ kāraṇaṃ gaṅgātīravāsī jātimantatāpaso jānissati, taṃ pucchitvā nikkaṅkhā bhavissāmā”ti katipayeheva atthacarakehi manussehi saddhiṃ tāpasaṃ upasaṅkamitvā katapaṭisanthāro tamatthaṃ pucchi. Tāpaso āha – “āma mahārāja, eko [V 3.0062] caṇḍālo atthi, so imaṃ gaṅgāya udakaṃ kālena anusotagāmiṃ kālena patisotagāmiṃ karoti, mayā tadatthaṃ kiñci kathitaṃ atthi, taṃ pucchatha, so jānissatī”ti.

The people, having met with great danger, thought, “Is this derangement of the times caused by yakkhas? Or is it caused by spirits, devas, nāgas, or supaṇṇas?” Pondering, “What is to be done?” they consulted, saying, “The royal family is indeed of great wisdom; it is able to consider the welfare of the world. Let us go there.” Going to the royal residence, they reported the matter. The king, having heard, though afraid, assumed a fearless demeanor and said, “Dears, do not be afraid. The ascetic proud of his birth who dwells on the bank of the Ganges will know the reason for this. Having asked him, we shall be without doubt.” Together with only a few men who act for the welfare of others, he approached the ascetic, and after exchanging friendly greetings, asked about the matter. The ascetic said, “Yes, great king. There is a certain outcaste. He makes this water of the Ganges flow downstream at times and upstream at times. Something was said by me for that reason. Ask him; he will know.”

Rājā mātaṅgaisissa santikaṃ gantvā – “tumhe, bhante, aruṇassa uggantuṃ na dethā”ti pucchi. Āma, mahārājāti. Kiṃ kāraṇā bhanteti? Jātimantatāpasakāraṇā, mahārāja, jātimantatāpasena āgantvā maṃ vanditvā khamāpitakāle dassāmi mahārājāti. Rājā gantvā “etha ācariya, tāpasaṃ khamāpethā”ti āha. Nāhaṃ, mahārāja, caṇḍālaṃ vandāmīti. Mā ācariya, evaṃ karotha, janapadassa mukhaṃ passathāti. So puna paṭikkhipiyeva. Rājā bodhisattaṃ upasaṅkamitvā [P 3.0086] “ācariyo khamāpetuṃ na icchitī”ti āha. Akhamāpite ahaṃ sūriyaṃ na muñcāmīti. Rājā “ayaṃ khamāpetuṃ na icchati, ayaṃ akhamāpite sūriyaṃ na muñcati, kiṃ amhākaṃ tena tāpasena, lokaṃ olokessāmā”ti “gacchatha, bho, tāpasasantikaṃ, taṃ hatthesu ca pādesu ca gahetvā mātaṅgaisissa pādamūle netvā nipajjāpetvā khamāpetha etassa janapadānuddayataṃ paṭiccā”ti āha. Te rājapurisā gantvā taṃ tathā katvā ānetvā mātaṅgaisissa pādamūle nipajjāpetvā khamāpesuṃ.

The king went to the presence of the ascetic Mātaṅga and asked, 'Venerable sir, do you not allow the dawn to rise?' 'Yes, great king,' he replied. 'For what reason, venerable sir?' When this was asked, he said, 'Great king, it is on account of the ascetic proud of his birth. When the ascetic proud of his birth comes, pays homage to me, and asks for forgiveness, I will allow it, great king.' The king went and said, 'Come, teacher, ask forgiveness of the ascetic.' 'Great king, I will not pay homage to an outcaste,' he replied. 'Teacher, do not act thus. Look upon the troubled face of the country,' said the king. But he refused again. The king approached the Bodhisatta and said, 'The teacher does not wish to ask for forgiveness.' The Bodhisatta replied, 'If forgiveness is not asked, I will not release the sun.' The king thought, 'This one does not wish to ask for forgiveness, and that one will not release the sun if forgiveness is not asked. What use is that ascetic to us? We shall look to the welfare of the world.' Then he commanded, 'Go, sirs, to the ascetic. Seize him by the hands and feet, bring him to the feet of the ascetic Mātaṅga, make him lie down, and make him ask for forgiveness on account of his compassion for the people of the country.' Those royal men went, did as they were told, brought him, made him lie down at the feet of the ascetic Mātaṅga, and made him ask for forgiveness.

Ahaṃ nāma khamitabbaṃ khamāmi, apica kho pana etassa kathā etasseva upari patissati. Mayā sūriye vissajjite sūriyarasmi etassa matthake patissati, athassa sattadhā muddhā phalissati. Tañca kho panesa byasanaṃ mā pāpuṇātu, etha tumhe etaṃ galappamāṇe udake otāretvā mahantaṃ mattikāpiṇḍamassa sīse ṭhapetha. Athāhaṃ sūriyaṃ vissajjissāmi. Sūriyarasmi mattikāpiṇḍe patitvā taṃ sattadhā bhindissati. Athesa mattikāpiṇḍaṃ chaḍḍetvā nimujjitvā aññena titthena uttaratu, iti naṃ vadatha, evamassa sotthi bhavissatīti. Te manussā “evaṃ karissāmā”ti tathā kāresuṃ. Tassāpi tatheva sotthi jātā. So tato paṭṭhāya – “jāti [M 3.0062] nāma akāraṇaṃ, pabbajitānaṃ abbhantare guṇova kāraṇa”nti jātigottamānaṃ pahāya nimmado ahosi.

I, for my part, forgive one who should be forgiven. But without fail, the words of this ascetic will fall upon him alone. When the sun is released by me, the light of the sun will fall upon his head, and then his head will split into seven pieces. But indeed, may he not meet with that destruction. Come, you must place him in deep water up to his neck and put a large lump of clay on his head. Then I will release the sun. The sun's light, falling on the lump of clay, will shatter it into seven pieces. Then let him discard the lump of clay, dive down, and emerge from another ford. Tell him this; thus he will be safe.' Those men, having agreed, saying, 'We will do so,' acted accordingly. For that ascetic, too, safety arose in just that way. From that time onwards, thinking, 'Birth is not the reason; among renunciants, virtue alone is the reason,' he abandoned pride based on birth and lineage and became free from arrogance.

Iti jātimantatāpase damite mahājano bodhisattassa thāmaṃ aññāsi, mahākolāhalaṃ jātaṃ. Rājā attano nagaraṃ gamanatthāya bodhisattaṃ yāci. Mahāsatto [P 3.0087] paṭiññaṃ datvā tāni ca [V 3.0063] asītibrāhmaṇasahassāni damessāmi, paṭiññañca mocessāmīti majjharājassa nagaraṃ agamāsi. Brāhmaṇā bodhisattaṃ disvāva – bho, “ayaṃ so, bho mahācoro, āgato, idāneva sabbe ete mayhaṃ ucchiṭṭhakaṃ khāditvā abrāhmaṇā jātāti amhe pākaṭe karissati, evaṃ no idhāpi āvāso na bhavissati, paṭikacceva māressāmā”ti rājānaṃ puna upasaṅkamitvā āhaṃsu – “tumhe, mahārāja, etaṃ caṇḍālapabbajitaṃ mā sādhurūpoti maññittha, esa garukamantaṃ jānāti, pathaviṃ gahetvā ākāsaṃ karoti, ākāsaṃ pathaviṃ, dūraṃ gahetvā santikaṃ karoti, santikaṃ dūraṃ, gaṅgaṃ nivattetvā uddhagāminiṃ karoti, icchanto pathaviṃ ukkhipitvā pātetuṃ maññe sakkoti. Parassa vā cittaṃ nāma sabbakālaṃ na sakkā gahetuṃ, ayaṃ idha patiṭṭhaṃ labhanto tumhākaṃ rajjampi nāseyya, jīvitantarāyampi vaṃsupacchedampi kareyya, amhākaṃ vacanaṃ karotha, mahārāja, ajjeva imaṃ māretuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti.

Thus, when the ascetic proud of his birth was subdued, the great multitude recognized the Bodhisatta’s power, and a great uproar arose. The king requested the Bodhisatta to come to his city. The Great Being, giving his promise and thinking, 'I will also subdue those eighty thousand brahmins and be released from my promise,' went to the city of the Middle King. The brahmins, as soon as they saw the Bodhisatta, said: 'Sirs, this great thief has come! Now he will make it known that all of us have become non-brahmins by eating his leftovers. Thus, we will have no place to live here either. Let us kill him beforehand!' Having approached the king again, they said: 'Great king, do not think this outcaste ascetic is a virtuous person. He knows a powerful spell: he can turn earth into sky and sky into earth; make the distant near and the near distant; reverse the Ganges and make it flow upstream. If he wishes, we think he is able to lift up the earth and let it fall. Indeed, another's mind cannot be grasped at all times. If he gains a foothold here, he could destroy your kingdom, endanger your life, and cut off your lineage. Heed our words, great king—it is fitting to kill him this very day!'

Rājāno nāma parapattiyā honti, iti so bahūnaṃ kathāvasena niṭṭhaṃ gato. Bodhisatto pana nagare piṇḍāya caritvā udakaphāsukaṭṭhāne missakodanaṃ bhuñjitvā rājuyyānaṃ gantvā nirāparādhatāya nirāsaṅko maṅgalasilāpaṭṭe nisīdi. Atīte cattālīsa, anāgate cattālīsāti asītikappe anussarituṃ samatthañāṇassa [P 3.0088] anāvajjanatāya muhuttamattake kāle sati nappahoti, rājā aññaṃ ajānāpetvā sayameva gantvā nirāvajjanatāya pamādena nisinnaṃ mahāpurisaṃ asinā paharitvā dve bhāge akāsi. Imassa rañño vijite aṭṭhamaṃ lohakūṭavassaṃ, navamaṃ kalalavassaṃ vassi. Iti imassāpi raṭṭhe nava vuṭṭhiyo patitā. So ca rājā sapariso mahāniraye nibbatto. Tenāha saṃkiccapaṇḍito –

Kings, by nature, are swayed by the desires of others; thus, influenced by the words of many, that king came to a decision. The Bodhisatta, however, having wandered for alms in the city, ate his meal of mixed rice at a place with convenient water, and went to the royal park. Being without fault, he sat fearlessly on the auspicious stone slab. For him, whose knowledge was capable of recollecting eighty aeons—forty in the past and forty in the future—due to a lack of reflection, mindfulness did not arise in that brief moment. The king, without informing anyone else, went there himself and, due to that lack of reflection, struck the great being, who was sitting heedlessly, with his sword and cut him into two pieces. In this king's domain, the eighth rain was a rain of iron clubs, and the ninth was a rain of mud. Thus, in his kingdom too, nine rains fell. And that king, together with his retinue, was reborn in the great hell. Therefore, the wise Saṃkicca said:

“Upahacca [M 3.0063] manaṃ majjho, mātaṅgasmiṃ yasassine;

Sapārisajjo ucchinno, majjhāraññaṃ tadā ahūti”. (jā. 2.19.96) –

'The Majjha king, having conceived ill will towards the glorious Mātaṅga, was cut off along with his retinue; then it became the Majjha forest.'

Evaṃ majjhāraññassa araññabhūtabhāvo veditabbo. Mātaṅgassa pana isino vasena tadeva mātaṅgāraññanti vuttaṃ.

Thus, how the Majjha kingdom became a forest should be understood. Furthermore, on account of the sage Mātaṅga, that very place is called the Mātaṅga Forest.

66. Pañhapaṭibhānānīti [V 3.0064] pañhabyākaraṇāni. Paccanīkaṃ katabbanti paccanīkaṃ kātabbaṃ. Amaññissanti vilomabhāgaṃ gaṇhanto viya ahosinti attho.

66. `Pañhapaṭibhānāni` means the explanations of questions. `Paccanīkaṃ kātabbaṃ` means something to be done in opposition. `Avamaññissaṃ` means: 'I became as if taking up a contrary view.'

67. Anuviccakāranti anuvicāretvā cintetvā tulayitvā kātabbaṃ karohīti vuttaṃ hoti. Sādhu hotīti sundaro hoti. Tumhādisasmiñhi maṃ disvā maṃ saraṇaṃ gacchante nigaṇṭhaṃ disvā nigaṇṭhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchante – “kiṃ ayaṃ upāli diṭṭhadiṭṭhameva saraṇaṃ gacchatī”ti? Garahā uppajjissati, tasmā anuviccakāro tumhādisānaṃ sādhūti dasseti. Paṭākaṃ parihareyyunti te kira evarūpaṃ sāvakaṃ labhitvā [P 3.0089] – “asuko nāma rājā vā rājamahāmatto vā seṭṭhi vā amhākaṃ saraṇaṃ gato sāvako jāto”ti paṭākaṃ ukkhipitvā nagare ghosentā āhiṇḍanti. Kasmā? Evaṃ no mahantabhāvo āvi bhavissatīti ca, sace tassa “kimahaṃ etesaṃ saraṇaṃ gato”ti vippaṭisāro uppajjeyya, tampi so “etesaṃ me saraṇagatabhāvaṃ bahū jānanti, dukkhaṃ idāni paṭinivattitu”nti vinodetvā na paṭikkamissatīti ca. “Tenāha paṭākaṃ parihareyyu”nti.

67. `Anuviccakāraṃ` means: 'Do what should be done after investigating, thinking, and weighing.' `Sādhu hoti` means it is good. For if someone like you, upon seeing me, goes to me for refuge, and then upon seeing a Nigaṇṭha, goes to a Nigaṇṭha for refuge, blame will arise, such as: 'Why does this Upāli go for refuge to whomever he sees?' Therefore, it shows that for distinguished people like you, acting with investigation is good. `Paṭākaṃ parihareyyuṃ` means: it is said that upon gaining such a disciple, they would raise a banner and wander about the city proclaiming, 'Such-and-such a king, royal minister, or merchant has gone to us for refuge and become our disciple!' Why? Both because they think, 'In this way our greatness will become manifest,' and because if regret should arise in that disciple, thinking, 'Why did I go to them for refuge?', he would dispel it by reasoning, 'Many people know that I have gone to them for refuge; it is difficult to turn back now,' and thus he would not retreat. Therefore, he said, 'They would carry a banner.'

68. Opānabhūtanti paṭiyattaudapāno viya ṭhitaṃ. Kulanti tava nivesanaṃ. Dātabbaṃ maññeyyāsīti pubbe dasapi vīsatipi saṭṭhipi jane āgate disvā natthīti avatvā deti. Idāni maṃ saraṇaṃ gatakāraṇamattenava mā imesaṃ deyyadhammaṃ, upacchindittha, sampattānañhi dātabbamevāti ovadati. Sutametaṃ, bhanteti kuto sutaṃ? Nigaṇṭhānaṃ santikā, te kira kulagharesu evaṃ pakāsenti – “mayaṃ ‘yassa kassaci sampattassa dātabba’nti vadāma, samaṇo pana gotamo ‘mayhameva dānaṃ dātabbaṃ…pe… na aññesaṃ sāvakānaṃ dinnaṃ mahapphala’nti vadatī”ti. Taṃ sandhāya ayaṃ gahapati “sutameta”nti āha.

68. `Opānabhūtaṃ` means standing ready like a prepared well. `Kulaṃ` means your dwelling. `Dātabbaṃ maññeyyāsi` means that previously, upon seeing ten, twenty, or even sixty people arrive, you would give without saying, 'There is nothing.' He advises: 'Now, merely for the reason that you have gone to me for refuge, do not cut off the alms-food for these people. For it should indeed be given to those who have arrived.' `Sutametaṃ, bhante` means: 'This has been heard, venerable sir.' From where was it heard? From the Nigaṇṭhas. It is said that they declare thus in the homes of their lay supporters: 'We say, "A gift should be given to anyone who arrives." But the ascetic Gotama says, "A gift should be given only to me... a gift given to the disciples of others is not of great fruit."' Referring to this, the householder said, 'This has been heard.'

69. Anupubbiṃ [M 3.0064] kathanti dānānantaraṃ sīlaṃ, sīlānantaraṃ saggaṃ, saggānantaraṃ magganti evaṃ anupaṭipāṭikathaṃ. Tattha [P 3.0090] dānakathanti idaṃ dānaṃ nāma sukhānaṃ nidānaṃ, sampattīnaṃ mūlaṃ, bhogānaṃ patiṭṭhā, visamagatassa tāṇaṃ leṇaṃ gatiparāyaṇaṃ, idhalokaparalokesu dānasadiso avassayo patiṭṭhā ārammaṇaṃ tāṇaṃ leṇaṃ gati parāyaṇaṃ natthi. Idañhi avassayaṭṭhena ratanamayasīhāsanasadisaṃ, patiṭṭhānaṭṭhena mahāpathavisadisaṃ, ālambanaṭṭhena ālambanarajjusadisaṃ. Idañhi [V 3.0065] dukkhanittharaṇaṭṭhena nāvā, samassāsanaṭṭhena saṅgāmasūro, bhayaparittāṇaṭṭhena susaṅkhatanagaraṃ, maccheramalādīhi anupalittaṭṭhena padumaṃ, tesaṃ nidahanaṭṭhena aggi, durāsadaṭṭhena āsīviso. Asantāsanaṭṭhena sīho, balavantaṭṭhena hatthī, abhimaṅgalasammataṭṭhena setavasabho, khemantabhūmisampāpanaṭṭhena valāhako assarājā. Dānaṃ nāmebhaṃ mayhaṃ gatamaggo, mayheveso vaṃso, mayā dasa pāramiyo pūrentena velāmamahāyañño, mahāgovindamahāyañño mahāsudassanamahāyañño, vessantaramahāyaññoti anekamahāyaññā pavattitā, sasabhūtena jalite aggikkhandhe attānaṃ niyyādentena sampattayācakānaṃ cittaṃ gahitaṃ. Dānañhi loke sakkasampattiṃ deti, mārasampattiṃ deti, brahmasampattiṃ deti, cakkavattisampattiṃ deti, sāvakapāramīñāṇaṃ, paccekabodhiñāṇaṃ, abhisambodhiñāṇaṃ detīti evamādiṃ dānaguṇapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ kathaṃ.

69. The gradual discourse means a sequential discourse, thus: after the talk on generosity, the talk on virtue; after the talk on virtue, the talk on heaven; after the talk on heaven, the talk on the path. Herein, the talk on generosity is as follows: This which is called generosity is the cause of happiness, the root of accomplishments, the foundation of wealth, a protection, a shelter, a destination, and a final resort for one who has met with misfortune. In this world and the next, there is no refuge, foundation, support, protection, shelter, destination, or final resort like generosity. Indeed, in the sense of being a refuge, it is like a jeweled lion-throne; in the sense of being a foundation, it is like the great earth; in the sense of being a support, it is like a rope to hold on to. Indeed, in the sense of crossing over suffering, it is like a boat; in the sense of giving comfort, it is like a hero in battle; in the sense of protecting from fear, it is like a well-fortified city; in the sense of being unstained by the impurities of stinginess and so on, it is like a lotus; in the sense of burning them away, it is like fire; in the sense of being difficult to approach, it is like a venomous serpent. In the sense of being a cause for fearlessness, it is like a lion; in the sense of being powerful, it is like an elephant; in the sense of being considered a supreme blessing, it is like a white bull; in the sense of enabling one to reach the land of safety, it is like Valāhaka, the king of horses. This which is called generosity is my traveled path; this is my very lineage. While fulfilling the ten perfections, I initiated many great offerings: the great offering of Velāma, the great offering of Mahāgovinda, the great offering of Mahāsudassana, and the great offering of Vessantara. As a hare, by offering myself into a blazing mass of fire, I captured the hearts of the mendicants who had come to me. Indeed, in the world, generosity gives the accomplishment of Sakka, it gives the accomplishment of Māra, it gives the accomplishment of Brahmā, it gives the accomplishment of a wheel-turning monarch; it gives the knowledge of a disciple's perfection, the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha, and the knowledge of supreme enlightenment. Such is the discourse connected with the qualities of generosity.

Yasmā pana dānaṃ dadanto sīlaṃ samādātuṃ sakkoti, tasmā tadanataraṃ sīlakathaṃ kathesi. Sīlakathanti sīlaṃ nāmetaṃ avassayo patiṭṭhā ārammaṇaṃ tāṇaṃ leṇaṃ [P 3.0091] gati parāyaṇaṃ, sīlaṃ nāmetaṃ mama vaṃso, ahaṃ saṅkhapālanāgarājakāle, bhūridattanāgarājakāle, campeyyanāgarājakāle, sīlavanāgarājakāle, mātuposakahatthirājakāle, chaddantahatthirājakāleti anantesu attabhāvesu sīlaṃ paripūresiṃ. Idhalokaparalokasampattīnañhi sīlasadiso avassayo, sīlasadisā patiṭṭhā, ārammaṇaṃ tāṇaṃ leṇaṃ gati parāyaṇaṃ natthi, sīlālaṅkārasadiso alaṅkāro natthi, sīlapupphasadisaṃ pupphaṃ natthi, sīlagandhasadiso gandho natthi. Sīlālaṅkārena hi alaṅkataṃ sīlakusumapiḷandhanaṃ sīlagandhānulittaṃ [M 3.0065] sadevakopi loko olokento tittiṃ na gacchatīti evamādiṃ sīlaguṇapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ kathaṃ.

Furthermore, because one who gives generosity is able to undertake virtue, he therefore spoke the talk on virtue immediately after that. The talk on virtue is as follows: This which is called virtue is a refuge, a foundation, a support, a protection, a shelter, a destination, and a final resort. This which is called virtue is my lineage. When I was the nāga-king Saṅkhapāla, the nāga-king Bhūridatta, the nāga-king Campeyya, the nāga-king Sīlava, the elephant-king Mātuposaka, and the elephant-king Chaddanta—thus in countless existences, I fulfilled virtue. Indeed, for the accomplishments of this world and the next, there is no refuge, foundation, support, protection, shelter, destination, or final resort like virtue. There is no ornament like the ornament of virtue, no flower like the flower of virtue, no fragrance like the fragrance of virtue. Indeed, the world with its devas, while gazing upon one adorned with the ornament of virtue, wearing the flower of virtue, and anointed with the fragrance of virtue, does not reach satisfaction. Such is the discourse connected with the qualities of virtue.

Idaṃ pana sīlaṃ nissāya ayaṃ saggo labbhatīti dassetuṃ sīlānantaraṃ saggakathaṃ kathesi. Saggakathanti ayaṃ saggo nāma iṭṭho kanto manāpo, niccamettha kīḷā, niccaṃ sampattiyo labbhanti, cātumahārājikā devā navutivassasatasahassāni dibbasukhaṃ dibbasampattiṃ anubhavanti, tāvatiṃsā tisso ca vassakoṭiyo saṭṭhi ca vassasatasahassānīti evamādiṃ saggaguṇapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ kathaṃ. Saggasampattiṃ kathayantānañhi buddhānaṃ mukhaṃ nappahoti. Vuttampi cetaṃ “anekapariyāyena kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, saggakathaṃ katheyya”ntiādi (ma. ni. 3.255).

Furthermore, to show that 'by relying on this virtue, this heaven is obtained,' he spoke the talk on heaven immediately after the talk on virtue. The talk on heaven is as follows: This which is called heaven is desirable, lovely, and pleasing. Here, sport is constant, and accomplishments are constantly obtained. The devas of the Four Great Kings experience divine happiness and divine accomplishment for nine million years. The Tāvatiṃsa devas experience them for thirty-six million years. Such is the discourse connected with the qualities of heaven. Indeed, the mouths of the Buddhas do not suffice for speaking of the accomplishment of heaven. And this was also said: 'Monks, I could give a talk on heaven in many ways,' and so on.

Evaṃ [V 3.0066] saggakathāya palobhetvā puna hatthiṃ alaṅkaritvā tassa soṇḍaṃ chindanto viya – “ayampi saggo anicco addhuvo, na ettha chandarāgo kātabbo”ti dassanatthaṃ – “appassādā kāmā vuttā mayā bahudukkhā [P 3.0092] bahupāyāsā, ādīnavo ettha bhiyyo”tiādinā (pāci. 417; ma. ni. 1.235) nayena kāmānaṃ ādīnavaṃ okāraṃ saṃkilesaṃ kathesi. Tattha ādīnavoti doso. Okāroti avakāro lāmakabhāvo. Saṃkilesoti tehi sattānaṃ saṃsāre saṃkilissanaṃ. Yathāha “kilissanti vata, bho, sattā”ti (ma. ni. 2.351).

Having thus enticed them with a talk on heaven, then, like one who, having adorned an elephant, cuts off its trunk—in order to show that ‘this heaven, too, is impermanent, not lasting; desire and lust should not be cultivated for it’—he spoke, by way of the passage beginning ‘Sensual pleasures have been declared by me to be of little gratification, of much suffering, of much tribulation; the danger in them is greater,’ of the danger, baseness, and defilement of sensual pleasures. Therein, ‘danger’ means fault. ‘Baseness’ means a low or worthless state. ‘Defilement’ means the defiling of beings in saṃsāra through them. As it is said: ‘Alas, sirs, beings are defiled.’

Evaṃ kāmādīnavena tajjitvā nekkhamme ānisaṃsaṃ pakāsesi. Kallacittanti arogacittaṃ. Sāmukkaṃsikāti sāmaṃ ukkaṃsikā attanāyeva gahetvā uddharitvā gahitā, sayambhūñāṇena diṭṭhā, asādhāraṇā aññesanti attho. Kā panesāti, ariyasaccadesanā? Tenevāha – “dukkhaṃ samudayaṃ nirodhaṃ magga”nti.

Having thus threatened them with the danger of sensual pleasures, he revealed the benefit of renunciation. ‘A receptive mind’ means a mind free from disease. ‘Sāmukkaṃsikā’ means that which is personally exalted: a Dhamma teaching taken up and raised up by himself, seen with self-arisen knowledge, and unshared with others—this is the meaning. What, then, is this teaching? It is the teaching of the Noble Truths. Therefore, he said: ‘Suffering, the origin, the cessation, the path.’

Virajaṃ vītamalanti rāgarajādīnaṃ abhāvā virajaṃ, rāgamalādīnaṃ vigatattā vītamalaṃ. Dhammacakkhunti upari brahmāyusutte tiṇṇaṃ maggānaṃ, cūḷarāhulovāde āsavakkhayassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Idha pana sotāpattimaggo adhippeto. Tassa uppattiākāradassanatthaṃ “yaṃkiñci samudayadhammaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ nirodhadhamma”nti āha. Tañhi nirodhaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā kiccavasena evaṃ sabbasaṅkhataṃ paṭivijjhantaṃ uppajjati.

‘Dust-free and stainless’ means dust-free due to the absence of the dust of lust and so on, and stainless due to the departure of the stain of lust and so on. The ‘eye of the Dhamma’ is a name for the three lower paths in the Brahmāyu Sutta, and for the destruction of the taints in the Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta. Here, however, the path of stream-entry is intended. To show the manner of its arising, he said: ‘Whatever is subject to arising is all subject to cessation.’ For it arises by way of its function, penetrating all conditioned things, having made cessation its object.

Diṭṭho [M 3.0066] ariyasaccadhammo etenāti diṭṭhadhammo. Esa nayo sesapadesupi. Tiṇṇā [P 3.0093] vicikicchā anenāti tiṇṇavicikiccho. Vigatā kathaṃkathā assāti vigatakathaṃkatho. Vesārajjappattoti vesārajjaṃ patto. Kattha? Satthu sāsane. Nāssa paro paccayo, na parassa saddhāya ettha vattatīti aparappaccayo.

The Dhamma of the Noble Truths has been seen by this one, thus he is ‘one who has seen the Dhamma’ (diṭṭhadhammo). This same method is to be understood for the remaining terms as well. Doubt has been crossed over by this one, thus he is ‘one who has crossed over doubt’ (tiṇṇavicikiccho). Questioning is gone for him, thus he is ‘one whose questioning is gone’ (vigatakathaṃkatho). ‘One who has attained confidence’ (vesārajjappatto) means he has attained confidence. Where? In the Teacher’s Dispensation. For him there is no other condition; he does not proceed herein through the faith of another, thus he is ‘one not conditioned by another’ (aparappaccayo).

70. Cittena sampaṭicchamāno abhinanditvā, vācāya pasaṃsamāno anumoditvā. Āvarāmīti thakemi pidahāmi. Anāvaṭanti na āvaritaṃ vivaṭaṃ ugghāṭitaṃ.

70. Accepting with the mind is meant by ‘having greatly rejoiced’ (abhinanditvā); praising with speech is meant by ‘having rejoiced’ (anumoditvā). ‘I close’ (āvarāmi) means I obstruct, I shut. ‘Not closed’ (anāvaṭaṃ) means not obstructed, open, uncovered.

71. Assosi kho dīghatapassīti so kira tassa gatakālato paṭṭhāya – “paṇḍito gahapati[V 3.0067], samaṇo ca gotamo dassanasampanno niyyānikakatho, dassanepi tassa pasīdissati, dhammakathāyapi pasīdissati, pasīditvā saraṇaṃ gamissati, gato nu kho saraṇaṃ gahapati na tāva gato”ti ohitasotova hutvā vicarati. Tasmā paṭhamaṃyeva assosi.

71. ‘Dīghatapassī heard.’ It is said that from the time of his (Upāli's) departure, he had been wandering about with an attentive ear, thinking: ‘The householder is wise, and the ascetic Gotama is pleasing in appearance and a speaker on what leads to liberation. He will be pleased even by seeing him, and he will be pleased by the Dhamma talk. Being pleased, he will go for refuge. Has the householder gone for refuge? Will he go? He has not yet returned.’ Therefore, he heard right away.

72. Tena hi sammāti balavasokena abhibhūto “ettheva tiṭṭhā”ti vacanaṃ sutvāpi atthaṃ asallakkhento dovārikena saddhiṃ sallapatiyeva.

72. Regarding the phrase ‘Then, friend’ (Tena hi samma): Overwhelmed by strong grief, even though he heard the gatekeeper's words, ‘Stay right here,’ the Nigaṇṭha, not comprehending their meaning, just kept conversing with the gatekeeper.

Majjhimāya dvārasālāyānti yassa gharassa satta dvārakoṭṭhakā, tassa sabbaabbhantarato vā sabbabāhirato vā paṭṭhāya catutthadvārakoṭṭhako, yassa pañca, tassa tatiyo, yassa tayo, tassa dutiyo dvārakoṭṭhako majjhimadvārasālā nāma. Ekadvārakoṭṭhakassa pana gharassa majjhaṭṭhāne maṅgalatthambhaṃ nissāya majjhimadvārasālā. Tassa pana gehassa satta dvārakoṭṭhakā, pañcātipi vuttaṃ.

Regarding ‘in the middle gate-hall’ (majjhimāya dvārasālāyā): For a house that has seven gate-chambers, the fourth gate-chamber, counting from either the innermost or the outermost, is called the middle gate-hall. For a house that has five, it is the third; for one that has three, it is the second. As for a house with a single gate-chamber, the middle gate-hall is near the auspicious pillar in the central area. However, regarding that particular house, it is said that it had seven gate-chambers, and also that it had five.

73. Aggantiādīni sabbāni aññamaññavevacanāni. Yaṃ sudanti ettha yanti yaṃ nāṭaputtaṃ. Sudanti nipātamattaṃ. Pariggahetvāti teneva uttarāsaṅgena udare parikkhipanto gahetvā. Nisīdāpetīti [P 3.0094] saṇikaṃ ācariya, saṇikaṃ ācariyāti mahantaṃ telaghaṭaṃ ṭhapento viya nisīdāpeti. Dattosīti kiṃ jaḷosi jātoti attho. Paṭimukkoti sīse parikkhipitvā [M 3.0067] gahito. Aṇḍahārakotiādiṃ duṭṭhullavacanampi samānaṃ upaṭṭhākassa aññathābhāvena uppannabalavasokatāya idaṃ nāma bhaṇāmīti asallakkhetvāva bhaṇati.

73. ‘Foremost’ (aggaṃ) and so on are all synonyms for one another. In ‘yaṃ sudaṃ,’ ‘yaṃ’ refers to Nāṭaputta. ‘Sudaṃ’ is merely a particle. ‘Having embraced’ (pariggahetvā) means having held him, wrapping the upper robe around his belly. ‘He made him sit’ (nisīdāpeti) means, saying, ‘Slowly, teacher, slowly,’ he made him sit as if placing a large pot of oil. ‘You are given’ (dattosi) means ‘What, have you become a fool?’ ‘Held close’ (paṭimukko) means held after being wrapped around the head. Regarding ‘egg-bearer’ (aṇḍahārako) and so on: even though they are coarse words, due to the attendant's (Upāli's) altered state and the arising of strong grief, he (the Nigaṇṭha) speaks without even comprehending, ‘I am saying such a thing.’

74. Bhaddikā, bhante, āvaṭṭanīti nigaṇṭho māyameva sandhāya vadati, upāsako attanā paṭividdhaṃ sotāpattimaggaṃ. Tena hīti nipātamattametaṃ, bhante, upamaṃ te karissāmicceva attho. Kāraṇavacanaṃ vā, yena kāraṇena tumhākaṃ sāsanaṃ aniyyānikaṃ, mama satthu niyyānikaṃ, tena kāraṇena upamaṃ te karissāmīti vuttaṃ hoti.

74. Regarding ‘A good turning back, venerable sir!’ (Bhaddikā, bhante, āvaṭṭanī): The Nigaṇṭha says this referring to this very deception, whereas the lay follower says it referring to the path of stream-entry he himself has penetrated. ‘Therefore’ (Tena hi) is merely a particle, and the meaning should be understood simply as: ‘Venerable sir, I will make a simile for you.’ Alternatively, it is a word indicating a reason: ‘For the reason that your teaching is not liberating, whereas my Teacher's teaching is liberating, for that reason I will make a simile for you’—this is what is meant.

75. Upavijaññāti vijāyanakālaṃ upagatā. Makkaṭacchāpakanti makkaṭapotakaṃ. Kiṇitvā ānehīti mūlaṃ datvāva āhara. Āpaṇesu hi saviññāṇakampi aviññāṇakampi makkaṭādikīḷanabhaṇḍakaṃ [V 3.0068] vikkiṇanti. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ āha. Rajitanti bahalabahalaṃ pītāvalepanaraṅgajātaṃ gahetvā rajitvā dinnaṃ imaṃ icchāmīti attho. Ākoṭitapaccākoṭitanti ākoṭitañceva parivattetvā punappunaṃ ākoṭitañca. Ubhatobhāgavimaṭṭhanti maṇipāsāṇena ubhosu [P 3.0095] passesu suṭṭhu vimaṭṭhaṃ ghaṭṭetvā uppāditacchaviṃ.

75. ‘She is about to give birth’ (upavijāyati) means she has reached the time of delivery. ‘A monkey cub’ (makkaṭacchāpakaṃ) means a young monkey. ‘Having bought it, bring it’ (kiṇitvā ānehi) means ‘Bring it only after giving the price.’ Indeed, in shops they sell playthings like monkeys, both animate and inanimate. It was with reference to this that she spoke. ‘Dyed’ (rajitaṃ): the meaning is, ‘I desire this one, given after being dyed with a thick, yellow-colored coating.’ ‘Pounded and repounded’ (ākoṭitapaccākoṭitaṃ) means pounded, and having been turned over, pounded again and again. ‘Polished on both sides’ (ubhatobhāgavimaṭṭhaṃ) means having a surface made smooth by being well-rubbed on both sides with a gem or stone.

Raṅgakkhamo hi khoti saviññāṇakampi aviññāṇakampi raṅgaṃ pivati. Tasmā evamāha. No ākoṭṭanakkhamoti saviññāṇakassa tāva ākoṭṭanaphalake ṭhapetvā kucchiyaṃ ākoṭitassa kucchi bhijjati, karīsaṃ nikkhamati. Sesī ākoṭitassa sīsaṃ bhijjati, mattaluṅgaṃ nikkhamati. Aviññāṇako khaṇḍakhaṇḍitaṃ gacchati. Tasmā evamāha. No vimajjanakkhamoti saviññāṇako maṇipāsāṇena vimaddiyamāno nillomataṃ nicchavitañca āpajjati, aviññāṇakopi vacuṇṇakabhāvaṃ āpajjati. Tasmā evamāha. Raṅgakkhamo hi kho bālānanti bālānaṃ mandabuddhīnaṃ raṅgakkhamo, rāgamattaṃ janeti, piyo hoti. Paṇḍitānaṃ pana nigaṇṭhavādo vā añño vā bhāratarāmasītāharaṇādi niratthakakathāmaggo appiyova hoti. No anuyogakkhamo, no vimajjanakkhamoti anuyogaṃ vā vīmaṃsaṃ vā na khamati, thuse koṭṭetvā taṇḍulapariyesanaṃ viya kadaliyaṃ sāragavesanaṃ viya ca rittako tucchakova hoti. Raṅgakkhamo ceva paṇḍitānanti [M 3.0068] catusaccakathā hi paṇḍitānaṃ piyā hoti, vassasatampi suṇanto tittiṃ na gacchati. Tasmā evamāha. Buddhavacanaṃ pana yathā yathāpi ogāhissati mahāsamuddo viya gambhīrameva hotīti “anuyogakkhamo ca vimajjanakkhamo cā”ti āha. Suṇohi [P 3.0096] yassāhaṃ sāvakoti tassa guṇe suṇāhīti bhagavato vaṇṇe vattuṃ āraddho.

'Indeed, it is receptive to dye' (raṅgakkhamo hi kho): for both an animate and an inanimate thing 'drinks' dye. Therefore, he said this. 'It is not receptive to pounding' (no ākoṭṭanakkhamo): Firstly, if an animate being is placed on a pounding board and pounded on the belly, its belly bursts and excrement comes out. If it is pounded on the head, its head splits and the brain comes out. An inanimate one goes to pieces. Therefore, he said this. 'It is not receptive to polishing' (no vimajjanakkhamo): An animate being, being polished with a gem or stone, becomes hairless and skinless. An inanimate one is reduced to powder. Therefore, he said this. 'Indeed, it is receptive to dye for fools' (raṅgakkhamo hi kho bālānaṃ): For fools, those of dull intellect, it is receptive to dye; it generates only attachment and is dear to them. But for the wise, the doctrine of the Nigaṇṭhas or other meaningless discourses like the Bhārata, the abduction of Sītā by Rāma, and so on, are not dear at all. 'It is not receptive to questioning, not receptive to investigation' (no anuyogakkhamo, no vimajjanakkhamo): It does not withstand questioning or investigation. Like searching for rice by pounding chaff, or searching for a core in a banana tree, it is empty and void. 'And it is receptive to dye for the wise' (raṅgakkhamo ceva paṇḍitānaṃ): The discourse on the Four Noble Truths is dear to the wise; even listening for a hundred years, one does not reach satiety. Therefore, he said this. Furthermore, the more one delves into the word of the Buddha, the deeper it becomes, just like the great ocean. Therefore, he said, 'It is receptive to questioning and receptive to investigation.' 'Listen, of whom I am a disciple' (suṇohi yassāhaṃ sāvako): Having said, 'Listen to his qualities,' he began to speak of the Blessed One's virtues.

76. Dhīrassāti dhīraṃ vuccati paṇḍiccaṃ, yā paññā pajānanā…pe… sammādiṭṭhi, tena samannāgatassa dhātuāyatanapaṭiccasamuppādaṭṭhānāṭṭhānakusalassa paṇḍitassāhaṃ sāvako, so mayhaṃ satthāti evaṃ sabbapadesu sambandho veditabbo. Pabhinnakhīlassāti bhinnapañcacetokhilassa. Sabbaputhujjane vijiniṃsu vijinanti vijinissanti vāti vijayā. Ke te, maccumārakilesamāradevaputtamārāti? Te vijitā vijayā etenāti vijitavijayo. Bhagavā, tassa vijitavijayassa. Anīghassāti kilesadukkhenapi vipākadukkhenapi niddukkhassa. Susamacittassāti devadattadhanapālakaaṅgulimālarāhulatherādīsupi devamanussesu suṭṭhu samacittassa. Vuddhasīlassāti [V 3.0069] vaḍḍhitācārassa. Sādhupaññassāti sundarapaññassa. Vesamantarassāti rāgādivisamaṃ taritvā vitaritvā ṭhitassa. Vimalassāti vigatarāgādimalassa.

76. 'Of the wise (dhīrassa)': by 'dhīra' is meant the state of being a wise person. I am a disciple of Him who is endowed with that wisdom, skilled in the elements, sense bases, dependent origination, and in what is possible and impossible, of that wise one; He is my Teacher—thus the connection should be understood in all phrases. 'Of Him with stakes destroyed (pabhinnakhīlassa)': of Him who has destroyed the five mental stakes. The three Māras have conquered, are conquering, or will conquer all worldlings; therefore, they are called 'vijayā' (conquerors). Who are they? Māra as death, Māra as defilements, and Māra as a deva's son. By Him, these conquerors ('vijayā') have been conquered ('vijitā'); therefore, He is called 'vijitavijayo' (the conqueror of conquerors). Of that Blessed One, the conqueror of conquerors. 'Of Him without distress (anīghassa)': of Him who is free from suffering, both the suffering of defilements and the suffering of results. 'Of Him with a perfectly balanced mind (susamacittassa)': of Him whose mind is perfectly balanced towards Devadatta, the elephant Dhanapālaka, the robber Aṅgulimāla, the Elder Rāhula, and others, as well as towards devas and humans. 'Of Him with developed virtue (vuddhasīlassa)': of Him whose conduct has been developed. 'Of Him with excellent wisdom (sādhupaññassa)': of Him with excellent wisdom. 'Of Him who has crossed the uneven (vesamantarassa)': of Him who, having crossed and thoroughly crossed beyond the unevenness of lust and so forth, is established. 'Of the Stainless One (vimalassa)': of Him who is free from the stain of lust and so forth.

Tusitassāti tuṭṭhacittassa. Vantalokāmisassāti vantakāmaguṇassa. Muditassāti muditāvihāravasena muditassa, punaruttameva vā etaṃ. Pasādavasena hi ekampi guṇaṃ punappunaṃ vadatiyeva. Katasamaṇassāti [P 3.0097] katasāmaññassa, samaṇadhammassa matthakaṃ pattassāti attho. Manujassāti lokavohāravasena ekassa sattassa. Narassāti punaruttaṃ. Aññathā vuccamāne ekekagāthāya dasa guṇā nappahonti.

'Of the Contented One (tusitassa)': of Him with a pleased mind. 'Of Him who has given up worldly bait (vantalokāmisassa)': of Him who has given up the five strands of sensual pleasure. 'Of the Joyful One (muditassa)': joyful by way of abiding in sympathetic joy; or, this is simply a repetition. Indeed, out of devotion, one may recite even a single quality again and again. 'Of Him who has fulfilled the ascetic's duties (katasamaṇassa)': of Him who has accomplished the duties of an ascetic; the meaning is, of Him who has reached the pinnacle of the ascetic's Dhamma. 'Of a human (manujassa)': by way of worldly convention, of a single being. 'Of a man (narassa)' is a repetition. If the meaning were stated otherwise, ten qualities would not be sufficient for each verse.

Venayikassāti sattānaṃ vināyakassa. Ruciradhammassāti sucidhammassa. Pabhāsakassāti obhāsakassa. Vīrassāti vīriyasampannassa. Nisabhassāti usabhavasabhanisabhesu sabbattha appaṭisamaṭṭhena nisabhassa. Gambhīrassāti gambhīraguṇassa, guṇehi vā gambhīrassa. Monapattassāti ñāṇapattassa. Vedassāti vedo vuccati ñāṇaṃ, tena samannāgatassa. Dhammaṭṭhassāti dhamme ṭhitassa. Saṃvutattassāti pihitattassa.

'Of the Trainer (venayikassa)': of the guide of beings. 'Of Him with a pleasing Dhamma (ruciradhammassa)': of Him with a pure Dhamma. 'Of the Illuminator (pabhāsakassa)': of Him who creates radiance. 'Of the Hero (vīrassa)': of Him endowed with energy. 'Of the Bull-like One (nisabhassa)': like a bull (usabha, vasabha, nisabha), because of the quality of being unshakable in all assemblies, He is like a bull. 'Of the Profound One (gambhīrassa)': of Him with profound qualities, or profound through His qualities. 'Of Him who has attained sagehood (monapattassa)': of Him who has attained knowledge. 'Of the Knower (vedassa)': knowledge is called 'veda'; of Him who is endowed with that. 'Of Him established in Dhamma (dhammaṭṭhassa)': of Him established in the Dhamma. 'Of Him with a restrained self (saṃvutattassa)': of Him whose self is guarded.

Nāgassāti [M 3.0069] catūhi kāraṇehi nāgassa. Pantasenassāti pantasenāsanassa. Paṭimantakassāti paṭimantanapaññāya samannāgatassa. Monassāti monaṃ vuccati ñāṇaṃ, tena samannāgatassa, dhutakilesassa vā. Dantassāti nibbisevanassa.

'Of the Nāga (nāgassa)': of Him who is a Nāga for four reasons. 'Of Him who resorts to remote lodgings (pantasenassa)': of Him who is accustomed to a remote dwelling and seat. 'Of the Respondent (paṭimantakassa)': of Him endowed with the wisdom to respond. 'Of the Sage (monassa)': wisdom is called 'mona'; of Him endowed with that, or of Him who has shaken off the defilements. 'Of the Tamed One (dantassa)': of Him whose faculties are tamed.

Isisattamassāti vipassiādayo cha isayo upādāya sattamassa. Brahmapattassāti [P 3.0098] seṭṭhapattassa. Nhātakassāti nhātakilesassa. Padakassāti akkharādīni samodhānetvā gāthāpadakaraṇakusalassa. Viditavedassāti viditañāṇassa. Purindadassāti sabbapaṭhamaṃ dhammadānadāyakassa. Sakkassāti samatthassa. Pattipattassāti ye pattabbā guṇā, te pattassa. Veyyākaraṇassāti vitthāretvā atthadīpakassa. Bhagavatā hi abyākataṃ nāma tanti padaṃ natthi sabbesaṃyeva attho kathito.

'Of the Seventh Sage (isisattamassa)': the seventh, taking into account the six sages beginning with Vipassī. 'Of Him who has attained the sublime (brahmapattassa)': of Him who has attained the supreme. 'Of the Bathed One (nhātakassa)': of Him who has washed away the defilements. 'Of the Versifier (padakassa)': of Him skilled in composing verses and phrases by combining letters and so on. 'Of Him whose knowledge is known (viditavedassa)': of Him who has known the knowledge. 'Of the Foremost Giver (purindadassa)': of Him who is the very first giver of the gift of the Dhamma. 'Of the Capable One (sakkassa)': of Him who is capable. 'Of Him who has attained the attainable (pattipattassa)': of Him who has attained those qualities that are to be attained. 'Of the Expounder (veyyākaraṇassa)': of Him who explains the meaning in detail. Indeed, by the Blessed One, there is no term in the canon left unexpounded; the meaning of all has been declared.

Vipassissāti [V 3.0070] vipassanakassa. Anabhinatassāti anatassa. No apanatassāti aduṭṭhassa.

'Of the Insightful One (vipassissa)': of Him who practices insight. 'Of Him who is not bent (anabhinatassa)': of Him who is not bent. 'Of Him who is not turned away (no apanatassa)': of Him who is not hostile.

Ananugatantarassāti kilese ananugatacittassa. Asitassāti abaddhassa.

'Of Him whose core is not followed (ananugatantarassa)': of Him whose mind does not follow after defilements. 'Of the Unattached One (asitassa)': of Him who is unbound.

Bhūripaññassāti bhūri vuccati pathavī, tāya pathavīsamāya paññāya vipulāya mahantāya vitthatāya samannāgatassāti attho. Mahāpaññassāti mahāpaññāya samannāgatassa.

'Of Him with vast wisdom (bhūripaññassa)': by the word 'bhūri', the earth is meant. The meaning is: of Him endowed with wisdom that is vast, great, and extensive, like the earth. 'Of Him with great wisdom (mahāpaññassa)': of Him endowed with great wisdom.

Anupalittassāti taṇhādiṭṭhikilesehi alittassa. Āhuneyyassāti āhutiṃ paṭiggahetuṃ yuttassa. Yakkhassāti ānubhāvadassanaṭṭhena ādissamānakaṭṭhena vā bhagavā yakkho nāma. Tenāha “yakkhassā”ti. Mahatoti [P 3.0099] mahantassa. Tassa sāvakohamasmīti tassa evaṃvividhaguṇassa satthussa ahaṃ sāvakoti. Upāsakassa sobhāpattimaggeneva paṭisambhidā āgatā. Iti paṭisambhidāvisaye ṭhatvā padasatena dasabalassa kilesappahānavaṇṇaṃ kathento “kassa taṃ gahapati sāvakaṃ dhāremā”ti pañhassa atthaṃ vissajjesi.

‘Of the Unsullied One’: of Him who is unsmeared by the defilements of craving and wrong views. ‘Of Him worthy of offerings’: of Him who is worthy to receive an offering. ‘Of the Yakkha’: The Blessed One is called ‘yakkha’ either because of His power to show His majesty to the world of beings, or because of His quality of being unseen. Therefore, he said, ‘of the Yakkha.’ ‘Of the Great One’: of the great one. ‘I am His disciple’ means: I am a disciple of that Teacher who possesses such manifold qualities. For the lay follower, the analytical insights arose through the path of stream-entry itself. Thus, standing in the domain of the analytical insights, while speaking with a hundred phrases on the quality of the abandonment of defilements of the One with Ten Powers, he answered the question, ‘Householder, whose disciple are we to take you for?’

77. Kadā [M 3.0070] saññūḷhāti kadā sampiṇḍitā. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi – “ayaṃ idāneva samaṇassa gotamassa santikaṃ gantvā āgato, kadānena ete vaṇṇā sampiṇḍitā”ti. Tasmā evamāha. Vicittaṃ mālaṃ gantheyyāti sayampi dakkhatāya pupphānampi nānāvaṇṇatāya ekatovaṇṭikādibhedaṃ vicitramālaṃ gantheyya. Evameva kho, bhanteti ettha nānāpupphānaṃ mahāpuppharāsi viya nānāvidhānaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ bhagavato sinerumatto vaṇṇarāsi daṭṭhabbo. Chekamālākāro viya upāli gahapati. Mālākārassa vicitramālāganthanaṃ viya gahapatino tathāgatassa vicitravaṇṇaganthanaṃ.

77. ‘When were they gathered?’: when were they compiled? It seems this thought occurred to him: ‘This man has just now gone to the presence of the ascetic Gotama and returned. When were these qualities compiled by him?’ Therefore, he spoke thus. ‘One might weave a variegated garland’: just as one, through one's own skill and because of the various colors of the flowers, might weave a variegated garland distinguished by having a single stalk and so on. ‘So too, venerable sir…’: in this context, just as there is a great heap of various flowers, so the heap of the Blessed One's manifold qualities, as vast as Mount Sineru, should be seen. The householder Upāli should be seen as like a skilled garland-maker. The householder's weaving of the Tathāgata's variegated qualities should be seen as like the garland-maker's weaving of a variegated garland.

Uṇhaṃ lohitaṃ mukhato uggañchīti tassa hi bhagavato sakkāraṃ asahamānassa etadahosi – “anatthiko dāni ayaṃ gahapati amhehi, sve paṭṭhāya paṇṇāsa saṭṭhi jane gahetvā etassa gharaṃ pavisitvā bhuñjituṃ na labhissāmi, bhinnā me bhattakumbhī”ti. Athassa upaṭṭhākavipariṇāmena balavasoko uppajji. Ime hi sattā attano attanova cintayanti. Tassa [V 3.0071] tasmiṃ soke uppanne abbhantaraṃ uṇhaṃ ahosi, lohitaṃ vilīyittha, taṃ mahāvātena samuddharitaṃ kuṭe pakkhittarajanaṃ viya pattamattaṃ mukhato uggañchi. Nidhānagatalohitaṃ vamitvā pana appakā sattā jīvituṃ sakkonti. Nigaṇṭho tattheva jāṇunā patito, atha naṃ pāṭaṅkiyā bahinagaraṃ [P 3.0100] nīharitvā mañcakasivikāya gahetvā pāvaṃ agamaṃsu, so na cirasseva pāvāyaṃ kālamakāsi. Imasmiṃ pana sutte ugghāṭitaññūpuggalassa vasena dhammadesanā pariniṭṭhitāti.

‘Hot blood gushed from his mouth’: Unable to bear the honor shown to the Blessed One, this thought occurred to him: ‘This householder now has no more need of us. From tomorrow, taking fifty or sixty people, I will not be able to enter his house to eat. My meal-pot is broken.’ Then, due to the change of heart of his supporter, intense grief arose in him. Indeed, these beings think only of their own benefit. When that grief arose in him, internal heat arose, his blood liquefied, and a great wind lifted it up. Like dye thrown into a pot, a bowlful gushed from his mouth. Indeed, few beings are able to live after vomiting up stored blood. The Nigaṇṭha fell to his knees right there. Then, they carried him out of the city on a litter, and taking him up on a palanquin, they went to Pāvā. Not long after, he died in Pāvā. In this sutta, however, the Dhamma teaching was concluded by way of a person who understands upon brief explanation.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Upālisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The sixth, the Upāli Sutta, is concluded.

7. Kukkuravatikasuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Kukkuravatika Sutta

78. Evaṃ [V 3.0072] me sutanti kukkuravatikasuttaṃ. Tattha koliyesūti evaṃnāmake janapade. So hi ekopi kolanagare patiṭṭhitānaṃ koliyānaṃ rājakumārānaṃ nivāsaṭṭhānattā evaṃ vuccati. Tasmiṃ koliyesu janapade. Haliddavasananti tassa kira nigamassa māpitakāle pītakavatthanivatthā [M 3.0071] manussā nakkhattaṃ kīḷiṃsu. Te nakkhattakīḷāvasāne nigamassa nāmaṃ āropentā haliddavasananti nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Taṃ gocaragāmaṃ katvā viharatīti attho. Vihāro panettha kiñcāpi na niyāmito, tathāpi buddhānaṃ anucchavike senāsaneyeva vihāsīti veditabbo. Govatikoti samādinnagovato, sīse siṅgāni ṭhapetvā naṅguṭṭhaṃ bandhitvā gāvīhi saddhiṃ tiṇāni khādanto viya carati. Aceloti naggo niccelo. Seniyoti tassa nāmaṃ.

7. ‘Thus have I heard’ begins the Kukkuravatika Sutta. Therein, ‘among the Koliyans’ refers to a country of that name. For though it is one country, it is so called because it was the dwelling place of the Koliyan princes who were established in the city of Koliya. In that country of the Koliyans. ‘Haliddavasana’: it is said that at the time of this town's founding, people dressed in yellow garments played at a festival. At the conclusion of the festival play, when naming the town, they gave it the name Haliddavasana. The meaning is that he dwelt there, having made it his alms-resort village. Although the dwelling is not specified here, it should be understood that he dwelt only in a lodging suitable for Buddhas. ‘An ox-practitioner’ is one who has undertaken the ox-vow; placing horns on his head and tying on a tail, he moves about as if eating grass together with cows. ‘Acela’ means naked, without clothes. ‘Seniya’ is his name.

Kukkuravatikoti samādinnakukkuravato, sabbaṃ sunakhakiriyaṃ karoti. Ubhopete sahapaṃsukīḷikā sahāyakā. Kukkurova palikujjitvāti sunakho nāma sāmikassa santike nisīdanto dvīhi pādehi bhūmiyaṃ vilekhitvā kukkurakūjitaṃ [P 3.0101] kūjanto nisīdati, ayampi “kukkurakiriyaṃ karissāmī”ti bhagavatā saddhiṃ sammoditvā dvīhi hatthehi bhūmiyaṃ vilekhitvā sīsaṃ vidhunanto ‘bhū bhū’ti katvā hatthapāde samiñjitvā sunakho viya nisīdi. Chamānikkhittanti bhūmiyaṃ ṭhapitaṃ. Samattaṃ samādinnanti paripuṇṇaṃ katvā gahitaṃ. Kā gatīti kā nipphatti. Ko abhisamparāyoti abhisamparāyamhi kattha nibbatti. Alanti tassa appiyaṃ bhavissatīti yāvatatiyaṃ paṭibāhati. Kukkuravatanti kukkuravatasamādānaṃ.

78. ‘A dog-practitioner’ is one who has undertaken the dog-vow; he performs all the actions of a dog. Both of these were companions, childhood playmates. Regarding ‘crouching down like a dog’: a dog, when sitting near its master, scratches the ground with its two paws and sits down while whining. This one too, thinking, ‘I will perform the actions of a dog,’ after exchanging friendly greetings with the Blessed One, scratched the ground with both hands, shook his head, made a ‘bhū bhū’ sound, curled up his hands and feet, and sat down like a dog. ‘Placed on the ground’ means placed on the earth. ‘Completely undertaken’ means taken up, having made it complete. ‘What destination?’ means what rebirth? ‘What future state?’ means where will he be reborn in the future life? ‘Enough!’: He prevents him up to the third time, thinking, ‘This will be disagreeable to him.’ ‘The dog-vow’ means the undertaking of the dog-vow.

79. Bhāvetīti vaḍḍheti. Paripuṇṇanti anūnaṃ. Abbokiṇṇanti nirantaraṃ. Kukkurasīlanti kukkurācāraṃ. Kukkuracittanti “ajja paṭṭhāya kukkurehi kātabbaṃ karissāmī”ti evaṃ uppannacittaṃ. Kukkurākappanti kukkurānaṃ gamanākāro atthi, tiṭṭhanākāro atthi, nisīdanākāro atthi, sayanākāro atthi, uccārapassāvakaraṇākāro atthi, aññe kukkure disvā dante vivaritvā gamanākāro atthi, ayaṃ kukkurākappo nāma, taṃ bhāvetīti attho[V 3.0073]. Imināhaṃ sīlenātiādīsu ahaṃ iminā ācārena vā vatasamādānena vā dukkaratapacaraṇena vā methunaviratibrahmacariyena vāti attho. Devoti sakkasuyāmādīsu aññataro. Devaññataroti [P 3.0102] tesaṃ dutiyatatiyaṭṭhānādīsu aññataradevo. Micchādiṭṭhīti adevalokagāmimaggameva devalokagāmimaggoti gahetvā uppannatāya sā assa [M 3.0072] micchādiṭṭhi nāma hoti. Aññataraṃ gatiṃ vadāmīti tassa hi nirayato vā tiracchānayonito vā aññā gati natthi, tasmā evamāha. Sampajjamānanti diṭṭhiyā asammissaṃ hutvā nipajjamānaṃ.

79. 'Develops' means increases. 'Complete' means without deficiency. 'Unbroken' means continuous. 'Dog-like morality' means dog-like conduct. 'A dog-like thought' is a thought that has arisen thus: 'From today onwards, I will do what is to be done by dogs.' 'Dog-like behavior' refers to the mannerisms of dogs: there is a way they go, a way they stand, a way they sit, a way they lie down, a way they defecate and urinate; and when they see other dogs, there is a way they go, baring their teeth—this is called dog-like behavior. The meaning is that one develops this. In the passage beginning 'By this morality...', the meaning is: 'By this conduct, or by this undertaking of a vow, or by this difficult ascetic practice, or by this celibacy which is the abstention from sexual intercourse.' 'A deva' means one among Sakka, Suyāma, and others. 'Some other deva' means a deva of some other rank among their second, third, and other ranks. 'Wrong view' is so called because it arises from taking what is not the path to the deva-world as the path to the deva-world. 'I speak of one of two destinations': for him there is no other destination than either hell or the animal womb; therefore He said thus. 'Being successful' means that, being unmixed with wrong view, it is accomplished.

Nāhaṃ, bhante, etaṃ rodāmi, yaṃ maṃ bhagavā evamāhāti yaṃ maṃ, bhante, bhagavā evamāha, ahametaṃ bhagavato byākaraṇaṃ na rodāmi na paridevāmi, na anutthunāmīti attho. Evaṃ sakammakavasenettha attho veditabbo, na assumuñcanamattena.

'Venerable sir, I do not weep for this, that the Blessed One speaks to me thus' means: 'Venerable sir, regarding what the Blessed One has said to me, I do not weep over this declaration of the Blessed One, nor do I lament, nor do I wail.' Thus the meaning here should be understood by way of the verb's transitive sense, not merely by the shedding of tears.

“Mataṃ vā amma rodanti, yo vā jīvaṃ na dissati;

Jīvantaṃ amma passantī, kasmā maṃ amma rodasī”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.239) –

Mother, they weep for the dead, or for one who, though living, is not seen. Seeing me alive, mother, why do you weep for me?

Ayañcettha payogo. Apica me idaṃ, bhanteti apica kho me idaṃ, bhante, kukkuravataṃ dīgharattaṃ samādinnaṃ, tasmiṃ sampajjantepi vuddhi natthi, vipajjantepi. Iti “ettakaṃ kālaṃ mayā katakammaṃ moghaṃ jāta”nti attano vipattiṃ paccavekkhamāno rodāmi, bhanteti.

'Moreover, venerable sir, this...' means: 'Moreover, venerable sir, this dog-vow has been undertaken by me for a long time. Regarding it, there is no progress whether it is accomplished or whether it fails. Thus, I weep, venerable sir, reflecting on my own ruin: "For such a long time, the deed I have done has become futile."

80. Govatantiādīni kukkuravatādīsu vuttanayeneva veditabbāni. Gavākappanti goākappaṃ. Sesaṃ kukkurākappe vuttasadisameva. Yathā pana tattha aññe kukkure disvā dante vivaritvā gamanākāro, evamidha aññe gāvo disvā kaṇṇe ukkhipitvā gamanākāro veditabbo. Sesaṃ tādisameva.

80. The passage beginning 'The ox-vow' should be understood in the same way as was stated for the passage beginning 'The dog-vow.' 'Ox-like behavior' means the behavior of an ox. The rest is just the same as what was said regarding dog-like behavior.
