However, just as there, upon seeing other dogs, there is a manner of going while baring the teeth, so here, upon seeing other cows, a manner of going while pricking up the ears should be understood. The rest is just the same.

81. Cattārimāni [P 3.0103] puṇṇa kammānīti kasmā imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi? Ayañhi desanā ekaccakammakiriyavasena āgatā, imasmiñca kammacatukke kathite imesaṃ kiriyā pākaṭā bhavissatīti imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi. Apica imaṃ kammacatukkameva desiyamānaṃ ime sañjānissanti[V 3.0074], tato eko saraṇaṃ gamissati, eko pabbajitvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇissatīti ayameva etesaṃ sappāyāti ñatvāpi imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi.

81. “These four are deeds, Puṇṇa”: Why did he begin this discourse? Because this discourse came about by way of the performance of certain deeds. And when this fourfold kamma is spoken of, the practice of these individuals will become manifest; for this reason, he began this discourse. Moreover, when this very fourfold kamma is taught, these individuals will fully understand. From that, one will go for refuge, and one, having gone forth, will attain Arahantship. Knowing thus that this very discourse was suitable for them, he also began this discourse.

Tattha kaṇhanti kāḷakaṃ dasaakusalakammapathakammaṃ. Kaṇhavipākanti apāye nibbattanato kāḷakavipākaṃ. Sukkanti paṇḍaraṃ dasakusalakammapathakammaṃ. Sukkavipākanti sagge nibbattanato paṇḍaravipākaṃ. Kaṇhasukkanti vomissakakammaṃ. Kaṇhasukkavipākanti sukhadukkhavipākaṃ. Missakakammañhi katvā [M 3.0073] akusalena tiracchānayoniyaṃ maṅgalahatthiṭṭhānādīsu uppanno kusalena pavatte sukhaṃ vediyati. Kusalena rājakulepi nibbatto akusalena pavatte dukkhaṃ vediyati. Akaṇhaṃ asukkanti kammakkhayakaraṃ catumaggacetanākammaṃ adhippetaṃ. Tañhi yadi kaṇhaṃ bhaveyya, kaṇhavipākaṃ dadeyya. Yadi sukkaṃ bhaveyya, sukkavipākaṃ dadeyya. Ubhayavipākassa pana adānato akaṇhāsukkavipākattā “akaṇhaṃ asukka”nti vuttaṃ. Ayaṃ tāva uddese attho.

Therein, “dark” means defiled kamma, the kamma of the ten unwholesome courses of action. “Dark result” means a defiled result, because it causes rebirth in the planes of misery. “Bright” means pure kamma, the kamma of the ten wholesome courses of action. “Bright result” means a pure result, because it causes rebirth in heaven. “Dark-bright” means mixed kamma. “Dark-bright result” means a result of pleasure and pain. Indeed, having performed mixed kamma, due to the unwholesome kamma one is born in the animal realm, in a place such as the station of a state elephant, and due to the wholesome kamma one experiences pleasure in the course of that existence. Or, born even in a royal family due to wholesome kamma, one experiences pain in the course of that existence due to unwholesome kamma. By “neither dark nor bright” is intended the kamma that brings about the destruction of kamma, which is the volition of the four paths. Indeed, if that kamma were dark, it would give a dark result. If it were bright, it would give a bright result. However, because it does not give either result, and because its result is neither dark nor bright, it is called “neither dark nor bright.” This, firstly, is the meaning in the summary section.

Niddese pana sabyābajjhanti sadukkhaṃ. Kāyasaṅkhārādīsu kāyadvāre gahaṇādivasena copanappattā dvādasa [P 3.0104] akusalacetanā sabyābajjhakāyasaṅkhāro nāma. Vacīdvāre hanusañcopanavasena vacībhedapavattikā tāyeva dvādasa vacīsaṅkhāro nāma. Ubhayacopanaṃ appattā raho cintayantassa manodvāre pavattā manosaṅkhāro nāma. Iti tīsupi dvāresu kāyaduccaritādibhedā akusalacetanāva saṅkhārāti veditabbā. Imasmiñhi sutte cetanā dhuraṃ, upālisutte kammaṃ. Abhisaṅkharitvāti saṅkaḍḍhitvā, piṇḍaṃ katvāti attho. Sabyābajjhaṃ lokanti sadukkhaṃ lokaṃ upapajjanti. Sabyābajjhā phassā phusantīti sadukkhā vipākaphassā phusanti. Ekantadukkhanti nirantaradukkhaṃ. Bhūtāti hetvatthe nissakkavacanaṃ, bhūtakammato bhūtassa sattassa uppatti hoti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathābhūtaṃ kammaṃ sattā karonti, tathābhūtena kammena kammasabhāgavasena tesaṃ upapatti hoti. Tenevāha “yaṃ karoti tena upapajjatī”ti. Ettha ca tenāti kammena viya vuttā, upapatti ca nāma vipākena hoti. Yasmā pana vipākassa kammaṃ hetu, tasmā tena mūlahetubhūtena kammena nibbattatīti ayamettha attho. Phassā phusantīti yena kammavipākena nibbatto, taṃkammavipākaphassā phusanti. Kammadāyādāti kammadāyajjā kammameva nesaṃ dāyajjaṃ santakanti vadāmi.

In the detailed explanation, however, ‘painful’ means accompanied by suffering. Regarding bodily formations and so on, the twelve unwholesome volitions that arise at the body-door, having attained movement by way of grasping, etc., are called the painful bodily formation. Those same twelve volitions, arising at the speech-door and causing speech to break forth by way of moving the jaw, are called the verbal formation. Those volitions that arise at the mind-door for one thinking in seclusion, not having attained movement of both, are called the mental formation. Thus, it should be known that in all three doors, the unwholesome volitions, classified as bodily misconduct and so on, are the ‘formations.’ Indeed, in this sutta, volition is primary; in the Upāli Sutta, kamma is primary. ‘Having formed’ means having drawn together, having made into a mass; this is the meaning. ‘A painful world’ means they are reborn into a world with suffering. ‘Painful contacts contact’ means resultant contacts accompanied by suffering make contact. ‘Exclusively painful’ means uninterrupted suffering. The word `bhūtā` is an ablative in the sense of cause; from kamma that has come to be, the rebirth of a being that has come to be occurs. This is what is said: just as beings perform kamma that has come to be, so by that kamma that has come to be, their rebirth occurs in accordance with that kamma. Therefore, he said: ‘By what one does, by that one is reborn.’ And here, ‘by that’ is spoken of as if by kamma, but rebirth is by way of result. However, since kamma is the cause of the result, the meaning here is that one is brought into being by that kamma which is the root cause. ‘Contacts contact’ means: by whichever resultant kamma one is brought into being, the resultant contacts of that kamma make contact. ‘Heirs of kamma’ means their inheritance is kamma; I declare that kamma alone is their inheritance, their property.

Abyābajjhanti [V 3.0075] niddukkhaṃ[P 3.0105]. Imasmiṃ vāre kāyadvāre pavattā aṭṭha kāmāvacarakusalacetanā kāyasaṅkhāro nāma. Tāyeva vacīdvāre pavattā vacīsaṅkhāro nāma. Manodvāre pavattā tāyeva aṭṭha, tisso ca heṭṭhimajhānacetanā abyābajjhamanosaṅkhāro nāma. Jhānacetanā tāva hotu, kāmāvacarā kinti abyābajjhamanosaṅkhāro nāma jātāti. Kasiṇasajjanakāle [M 3.0074] ca kasiṇāsevanakāle ca labbhanti. Kāmāvacaracetanā paṭhamajjhānacetanāya ghaṭitā, catutthajjhānacetanā tatiyajjhānacetanāya ghaṭitā. Iti tīsupi dvāresu kāyasucaritādibhedā kusalacetanāva saṅkhārāti veditabbo. Tatiyavāro ubhayamissakavasena veditabbā.

‘Non-painful’ means without suffering. In this section, the eight wholesome sense-sphere volitions that arise at the body-door are called the bodily formation. The same volitions arising at the speech-door are called the verbal formation. The same eight volitions arising at the mind-door, and the three lower jhāna volitions, are called the non-painful mental formation. Let the jhāna volitions be so, but how can the sense-sphere volitions become the non-painful mental formation? They are found at the time of preparing the kasiṇa and at the time of cultivating the kasiṇa. The sense-sphere volitions are connected with the first jhāna volition, and the fourth jhāna volition is connected with the third jhāna volition. Thus, it should be understood that in all three doors, the wholesome volitions, classified as good bodily conduct and so on, are the ‘formations.’ The third section should be understood by way of a mixture of both.

Seyyathāpi manussātiādīsu manussānaṃ tāva kālena sukhaṃ kālena dukkhaṃ pākaṭameva, devesu pana bhummadevatānaṃ, vinipātikesu vemānikapetānaṃ kālena sukhaṃ kālena dukkhaṃ hotīti veditabbaṃ. Hatthiādīsu tiracchānesupi labbhatiyeva.

In the Pāḷi beginning with ‘Just as for humans,’ for humans, at times pleasure and at times pain is indeed manifest. However, it should be understood that among devas, for the earth-deities, and among the fallen, for the Vemanika petas, at times there is pleasure and at times pain. It is indeed found even among animals such as elephants.

Tatrāti tesu tīsu kammesu. Tassa pahānāya yā cetanāti tassa pahānatthāya maggacetanā. Kammaṃ patvāva maggacetanāya añño paṇḍarataro dhammo nāma natthi. Idaṃ pana kammacatukkaṃ patvā dvādasa akusalacetanā kaṇhā nāma, tebhūmakakusalacetanā sukkā nāma, maggacetanā akaṇhā asukkāti āgatā.

‘Therein’ means in those three kammas. ‘The volition for its abandonment’ means the path-volition for the purpose of abandoning it. Having come to the topic of kamma, there is no phenomenon purer than the path-volition. However, having come to this fourfold kamma, the twelve unwholesome volitions are called ‘dark’; the wholesome volitions of the three planes are called ‘bright’; and the path-volition is ‘neither dark nor bright’—thus it has come down.

82. “Labheyyāhaṃ, bhante”ti idaṃ so “ciraṃ vata me aniyyānikapakkhe yojetvā attā kilamito, ‘sukkhanadītīre nhāyissāmī’ti samparivattentena viya thuse koṭṭentena viya ca na koci attho nipphādito, handāhaṃ attānaṃ yoge yojemī”ti cintetvā āha. Atha [P 3.0106] bhagavā yonena khandhake titthiyaparivāso paññatto, yaṃ aññatitthiyapubbo sāmaṇerabhūmiyaṃ ṭhito – “ahaṃ, bhante, itthannāmo aññatitthiyapubbo imasmiṃ dhammavinaye ākaṅkhāmi upasampadaṃ, svāhaṃ, bhante, saṅghaṃ cattāro māse parivāsaṃ yācāmī”tiādinā (mahāva. 86) nayena samādiyitvā parivasati, taṃ sandhāya “yo kho, seniya, aññatitthiyapubbo”tiādimāha.

82. ‘May I receive, venerable sir’: this he said, having thought: ‘Alas, for a long time my self has been wearied by being applied to a path that is not a means of escape, like one rolling about thinking, “I will bathe on a dry riverbank,” or like one pounding chaff, with no benefit whatsoever produced. Come now, I will apply myself to the proper practice.’ Then the Blessed One, with reference to the probationary period for those formerly of other sects that was laid down in the Khandhaka—which one who was formerly of another sect, standing in the position of a novice, undertakes and observes according to the method beginning: ‘Venerable sir, I, of such-and-such a name, formerly of another sect, desire the higher ordination in this Dhamma and Vinaya; I, venerable sir, request from the Saṅgha a probationary period of four months,’ and so on (Mahāvagga 86)—said the words beginning: ‘Whoever, Seniya, was formerly of another sect…’

Tattha pabbajjanti vacanasiliṭṭhatāvaseneva vuttaṃ. Aparivasitvāyeva hi pabbajjaṃ labhati. Upasampadatthikena pana nātikālena gāmappavesanādīni aṭṭha vattāni pūrentena parivasitabbaṃ[V 3.0076]. Āraddhacittāti aṭṭhavattapūraṇena tuṭṭhacittā. Ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthārato panesa titthiyaparivāso samantapāsādikāya vinayaṭṭhakathāya pabbajjakhandhakavaṇṇanāyaṃ (mahāva. aṭṭha. 86) vuttanayeneva veditabbo[M 3.0075]. Apica metthāti apica me ettha. Puggalavemattatā viditāti puggalanānattaṃ viditaṃ. Ayaṃ puggalo parivāsāraho, ayaṃ na parivāsārahoti idaṃ mayhaṃ pākaṭanti dasseti.

Here, 'going forth' is stated merely for verbal smoothness. Indeed, one receives the going forth without having undergone probation. However, one seeking higher ordination must undergo probation, fulfilling the eight duties, such as not entering a village for an excessive time. ‘With aroused minds’ means the monks are pleased by the completion of the eight duties. This is the summary here. In detail, however, this probation for those formerly of other sects should be understood in the very manner stated in the Samantapāsādikā, the Vinaya commentary, in its explanation of the Going-Forth Section. The phrase `apica mettha` is parsed as `apica me ettha` (and moreover for me here). ‘The diversity of individuals is known’ means the variety of individuals is known. He shows: ‘This individual is worthy of probation, this one is not worthy of probation—this is clear to me.’

Tato seniyo cintesi – “aho acchariyaṃ buddhasāsanaṃ, yattha evaṃ ghaṃsitvā koṭṭetvā yuttameva gaṇhanti, ayuttaṃ chaḍḍentī”ti. Tato suṭṭhutaraṃ pabbajjāya sañjātussāho sace, bhantetiādimāha. Atha bhagavā tassa tibbacchandataṃ viditvā na seniyo parivāsaṃ arahatīti aññataraṃ bhikkhuṃ āmantesi – “gaccha tvaṃ, bhikkhu, seniyaṃ nhāpetvā pabbājetvā ānehī”ti. So tathā katvā taṃ pabbājetvā bhagavato santikaṃ ānayi. Bhagavā gaṇe nisīditvā upasampādesi. Tena vuttaṃ – “alattha kho acelo seniyo bhagavato santike pabbajjaṃ alattha upasampada”nti.

Then Seniya thought: 'Oh, how wonderful is the Buddha’s dispensation, where what is appropriate is accepted only after rubbing and pounding, and what is inappropriate is discarded!' Then, with even greater enthusiasm for going forth, he said, 'If so, venerable sir,' and so on. Then the Blessed One, knowing his intense desire, and thinking, 'Seniya does not deserve probation,' addressed a certain monk: 'Go, monk, bathe Seniya, give him the going forth, and bring him here.' He did so, gave him the going forth, and brought him to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, seated in the assembly, conferred higher ordination upon him. Therefore it is said: 'Indeed, the naked ascetic Seniya obtained the going forth in the presence of the Blessed One; he obtained higher ordination.'

Acirūpasampannoti [P 3.0107] upasampanno hutvā nacirameva. Vūpakaṭṭhoti vatthukāmakilesakāmehi kāyena ca cittena ca vūpakaṭṭho. Appamattoti kammaṭṭhāne satiṃ avijahanto. Ātāpīti kāyikacetasikasaṅkhātena vīriyātāpena ātāpī. Pahitattoti kāye ca jīvite ca anapekkhatāya pesitatto vissaṭṭhaattabhāvo. Yassatthāyāti yassa atthāya. Kulaputtāti ācārakulaputtā. Sammadevāti hetunāva kāraṇeneva. Tadanuttaranti taṃ anuttaraṃ. Brahmacariyapariyosānanti maggabrahmacariyapariyosānabhūtaṃ arahattaphalaṃ. Tassa hi atthāya kulaputtā pabbajanti. Diṭṭheva dhammeti imasmiṃyeva attabhāve. Sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvāti attanāyeva paññāya paccakkhaṃ katvā, aparappaccayaṃ ñatvāti attho. Upasampajja vihāsīti pāpuṇitvā sampādetvā vihāsi. Evaṃ viharantova khīṇā jāti…pe… abbhaññāsi.

‘Recently ordained’ means not long after having received the higher ordination. ‘Secluded’ means secluded in body and mind from sensual pleasures as objects and sensual pleasures as defilements. ‘Diligent’ means not abandoning mindfulness on the meditation subject. ‘Ardent’ means possessing the ardour of energy, reckoned as bodily and mental, which torments the defilements. ‘With a resolute self’ means one whose mind is dispatched, one whose individual existence is relinquished, through lack of concern for body and life. ‘For the sake of which’ means for the sake of which fruit of Arahantship. ‘Sons of good families’ means sons of families with good conduct. ‘Rightly’ means by the supporting cause and by the generating cause. The phrase `tadanuttaraṃ` is to be parsed as `taṃ anuttaraṃ`, meaning ‘that unsurpassed’ fruit of Arahantship. ‘The culmination of the holy life’ means the fruit of Arahantship, which is the culmination of the path of the holy life. Indeed, it is for the sake of that fruit that sons of good families go forth. ‘In this very life’ means in this very existence. ‘Having realized by direct knowledge for oneself’ means having made it manifest with one’s own wisdom, knowing it without reliance on another; this is the meaning. ‘Having attained, he dwelt’ means having reached and accomplished it, he dwelt. Dwelling thus, he understood: ‘Birth is destroyed…’ and so on.

Evamassa [V 3.0077] paccavekkhaṇabhūmiṃ dassetvā arahattanikūṭeneva desanaṃ niṭṭhāpetuṃ “aññataro kho panāyasmā seniyo arahataṃ ahosī”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha aññataroti eko. Arahatanti arahantānaṃ, bhagavato sāvakānaṃ arahantānaṃ abbhantaro ahosīti ayamevattha adhippāyo. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

Thus, having shown his ground for reflection, to conclude the discourse with the very pinnacle of Arahantship, it was said: ‘And the Venerable Seniya became one of the Arahants.’ Herein, ‘one’ means one. ‘Of the Arahants’ means he became included among the Arahants, the Arahant disciples of the Blessed One; this is the intended meaning here. The rest is clear everywhere.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Middle Length Discourses.

Kukkuravatikasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Kukkuravatika Sutta is concluded.

8. Abhayarājakumārasuttavaṇṇanā

8. The Explanation of the Discourse to Prince Abhaya.

83. Evaṃ [V 3.0078][P 3.0108][M 3.0076] me sutanti abhayasuttaṃ. Tattha abhayoti tassa nāmaṃ. Rājakumāroti bimbisārassa orasaputto. Vādaṃ āropehīti dosaṃ āropehi. Nerayikoti niraye nibbattako. Kappaṭṭhoti kappaṭṭhitiko. Atekicchoti buddhasahassenāpi tikicchituṃ na sakkā. Uggilitunti dve ante mocetvā kathetuṃ asakkonto uggilituṃ bahi nīharituṃ na sakkhiti. Ogilitunti pucchāya dosaṃ datvā hāretuṃ asakkonto ogilituṃ anto pavesetuṃ na sakkhiti.

83. Thus have I heard—this is the Abhayasutta. Herein, 'Abhaya' is his name. 'Prince' means the legitimate son of King Bimbisāra. 'To bring a charge' means to impute a fault. 'Hell-bound' means one who is fit to be born in hell. 'Fixed for an aeon' means enduring for an aeon. 'Incurable' means unable to be cured even by a thousand Buddhas. 'To vomit it out' means: being unable to speak, having released the two ends, he will not be able to vomit it out, to expel it outward. 'To swallow it down' means: having assigned a fault to the question and being unable to dispel it, he will not be able to swallow it, to cause it to enter within.

Evaṃ, bhanteti nigaṇṭho kira cintesi – “samaṇo gotamo mayhaṃ sāvake bhinditvā gaṇhāti, handāhaṃ ekaṃ pañhaṃ abhisaṅkharomi, yaṃ puṭṭho samaṇo gotamo ukkuṭiko hutvā nisinno uṭṭhātuṃ na sakkhissatī”ti. So abhayassa gehā nīhaṭabhatto siniddhabhojanaṃ bhuñjanto bahū pañhe abhisaṅkharitvā – “ettha samaṇo gotamo imaṃ nāma dosaṃ dassessati, ettha imaṃ nāmā”ti sabbe pahāya cātumāsamatthake imaṃ pañhaṃ addasa. Athassa etadahosi – “imassa pañhassa pucchāya vā vissajjane vā na sakkā doso dātuṃ, ovaṭṭikasāro ayaṃ, ko nu kho imaṃ gahetvā samaṇassa gotamassa vādaṃ āropessatī”ti. Tato “abhayo rājakumāro paṇḍito, so sakkhissatīti taṃ uggaṇhāpemī”ti niṭṭhaṃ gantvā uggaṇhāpesi. So vādajjhāsayatāya tassa vacanaṃ sampaṭicchanto “evaṃ, bhante,”ti āha.

‘Very well, venerable sir.’ The Nigaṇṭha, it is said, thought: ‘The ascetic Gotama, having caused my disciples to break away, takes them. Well then, I shall prepare a question, which when asked, the ascetic Gotama, sitting in a crouching position, will not be able to stand up.’ He, having food brought from Prince Abhaya's house and eating delicate food, prepared many questions. Thinking, ‘Here the ascetic Gotama will show such-and-such a fault, here he will show such-and-such a fault,’ and abandoning all of them, after four months, he saw this question. Then it occurred to him: ‘In the asking or answering of this question, it is not possible to assign a fault. This question is like a treasure carried in one's waistband. Who indeed, taking this, will be able to bring a charge against the ascetic Gotama's doctrine?’ Then, thinking, ‘Prince Abhaya is wise; he will be able,’ he decided, ‘I will make him learn that question,’ and made him learn it. He, due to his inclination for debate, accepting his word, said, ‘Very well, venerable sir.’

84. Akālo [P 3.0109] kho ajjāti ayaṃ pañho catūhi māsehi abhisaṅkhato, tattha idaṃ gahetvā idaṃ vissajjiyamāne divasabhāgo nappahossatīti maññanto evaṃ cintesi. So dānīti sve dāni. Attacatutthoti kasmā bahūhi saddhiṃ na nimantesi? Evaṃ kirassa ahosi – “bahūsu nisinnesu thokaṃ datvā vadantassa aññaṃ suttaṃ aññaṃ kāraṇaṃ aññaṃ tathārūpaṃ vatthuṃ āharitvā dassessati, evaṃ sante kalaho vā kolāhalameva vā bhavissati. Athāpi ekakaṃyeva nimantessāmi, evampi me garahā uppajjissati ‘yāvamaccharī vāyaṃ abhayo, bhagavantaṃ divase divase bhikkhūnaṃ satenapi sahassenapi saddhiṃ carantaṃ disvāpi ekakaṃyeva [V 3.0079][M 3.0077] nimantesī’”ti. “Evaṃ pana doso na bhavissatī”ti aparehi tīhi saddhiṃ attacatutthaṃ nimantesi.

84. ‘Today is not the time,’ he thought. ‘This question was prepared by the Nigaṇṭha over four months. In this matter, if this point is taken up and that point is answered, a portion of the day will not be enough.’ The word `so dāni` should be parsed as `sve dāni` (tomorrow now). ‘With himself as the fourth’—why did he not invite many monks along with him? It is said, it occurred to him thus: ‘If many are seated, after I have given a little and am speaking, he will bring up another sutta, another reason, or another such story to present. This being so, there will be a dispute or just an uproar. Or, if I invite him alone, even so, blame will arise for me: “This Abhaya is extremely miserly indeed! Even having seen the Blessed One traveling day by day with a hundred or a thousand monks, he invites him alone.” Blame will arise thus. However, in this way (inviting four), there will be no fault.’ Thus, he invited him as the fourth with three other monks.

85. Na khvettha, rājakumāra, ekaṃsenāti na kho, rājakumāra, ettha pañhe ekaṃsena vissajjanaṃ hoti. Evarūpañhi vācaṃ tathāgato bhāseyyāpi na bhāseyyāpi. Bhāsitapaccayena atthaṃ passanto bhāseyya, apassanto na bhāseyyāti attho. Iti bhagavā mahānigaṇṭhena catūhi māsehi abhisaṅkhataṃ pañhaṃ asanipātena pabbatakūṭaṃ viya ekavacaneneva saṃcuṇṇesi. Anassuṃ nigaṇṭhāti naṭṭhā nigaṇṭhā.

85. ‘Indeed not in this case, Prince, is it categorical.’ This means: ‘Indeed, Prince, in this question, there is no categorical answer.’ It is true that the Tathāgata might speak such speech, or he might not speak it. Seeing a benefit on account of speaking, he would speak; not seeing a benefit, he would not speak. This is the meaning. And thus the Blessed One, with a single word, crushed the question prepared by the great Nigaṇṭha over four months, as if pulverizing a mountain peak with the fall of a thunderbolt. ‘The Nigaṇṭhas are undone!’ means: The Nigaṇṭhas are ruined.

86. Aṅke nisinno hotīti ūrūsu nisinno hoti. Lesavādino hi vādaṃ paṭṭhapentā kiñcideva phalaṃ vā pupphaṃ vā potthakaṃ vā gahetvā nisīdanti. Te attano jaye sati paraṃ ajjhottharanti, parassa jaye sati phalaṃ khādantā viya pupphaṃ [P 3.0110] ghāyantā viya potthakaṃ vācentā viya vikkhepaṃ dassenti. Ayaṃ pana cintesi – “sammāsambuddho esa osaṭasaṅgāmo paravādamaddano. Sace me jayo bhavissati, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ. No ce bhavissati, dārakaṃ vijjhitvā rodāpessāmi. Tato passatha, bho, ayaṃ dārako rodati, uṭṭhahatha tāva, pacchāpi jānissāmā”ti tasmā dārakaṃ gahetvā nisīdi. Bhagavā pana rājakumārato sahassaguṇenapi satasahassaguṇenapi vādīvarataro, “imamevassa dārakaṃ upamaṃ katvā vādaṃ bhindissāmī”ti cintetvā “taṃ kiṃ maññasi rājakumārā”tiādimāha.

86. 'He was seated on his lap' means he was seated on his thighs. Indeed, those who argue by insinuation, when establishing a debate, sit down having taken some fruit, or a flower, or a book. When they are victorious, they overwhelm the other. When the other is victorious, they show distraction by acting as if eating the fruit, or smelling the flower, or reading the book. But this one (Prince Abhaya) thought: 'This is the Perfectly Enlightened One, experienced in the battle of doctrines, a crusher of others' doctrines. If victory will be mine, that is good. If it will not be, I will strike the child with my fist and make him cry. Then, saying, "Sirs, look, this child is crying! Get up for now; we will find out later," I will bring the matter to an end.' Therefore, he took the child and sat down. But the Blessed One is a more excellent debater than the prince by a thousandfold, by a hundred-thousandfold. Thinking, 'Making this very child of his an example, I will break his argument,' He said, 'What do you think, Prince?' and so on.

Tattha mukhe āhareyyāti mukhe ṭhapeyya. Āhareyyassāhanti apaneyyaṃ assa ahaṃ. Ādikenevāti paṭhamapayogeneva. Abhūtanti abhūtatthaṃ. Atacchanti na tacchaṃ. Anatthasaṃhitanti na atthasaṃhitaṃ na vaḍḍhinissitaṃ. Appiyā amanāpāti neva piyā na manāpā. Iminā nayeneva sabbattha attho daṭṭhabbo.

Herein, 'should put in the mouth' means 'should place in the mouth.' 'I would remove it for him' means: I should remove it for this child. 'From the very beginning' means 'with the very first effort.' 'Unreal' means 'a thing that is not.' 'Untrue' means 'not true.' 'Not connected with benefit' means 'not connected with benefit, not based on growth.' 'Not dear and not pleasing' means 'neither dear nor pleasing to the mind.' In this way, the meaning should be understood in all cases.

Tattha appiyapakkhe paṭhamavācā acoraṃyeva coroti, adāsaṃyeva dāsoti, aduppayuttaṃyeva duppayuttoti pavattā. Na taṃ tathāgato bhāsati. Dutiyavācā coraṃyeva coro ayantiādivasena pavattā. Tampi [M 3.0078] tathāgato na bhāsati. Tatiyavācā “idāni akatapuññatāya duggato dubbaṇṇo appesakkho[V 3.0080], idha ṭhatvāpi puna puññaṃ na karosi, dutiyacittavāre kathaṃ catūhi apāyehi na muccissasī”ti evaṃ mahājanassa atthapurekkhārena [P 3.0111] dhammapurekkhārena anusāsanīpurekkhārena ca vattabbavācā. Tatra kālaññū tathāgatoti tasmiṃ tatiyabyākaraṇe tassā vācāya byākaraṇatthāya tathāgato kālaññū hoti, mahājanassa ādānakālaṃ gahaṇakālaṃ jānitvāva byākarotīti attho.

Therein, on the side of the unpleasant, the first speech is that which proceeds as 'He is a thief' about one who is not a thief, 'He is a slave' about one who is not a slave, or 'He has acted wrongly' about one who has not acted wrongly. The Tathāgata does not speak that. The second speech is that which proceeds by way of saying, 'This one is a thief' about one who is indeed a thief, and so on. That too, the Tathāgata does not speak. The third speech is: 'Now, due to having no merit made, you are unfortunate, of bad appearance, and of little power. Even while here, if you do not make merit again, at the second thought-moment, how will you be freed from the four states of woe?' Thus, this is speech to be spoken to the great populace with benefit as the forerunner, with Dhamma as the forerunner, and with instruction as the forerunner. 'Therein, the Tathāgata is a knower of time' means: in that third utterance, for the sake of uttering that speech, the Tathāgata is a knower of time. Only after knowing the time for the great populace to receive it and the time to grasp it does he declare it. This is the meaning.

Piyapakkhe paṭhamavācā aṭṭhāniyakathā nāma. Sā evaṃ veditabbā – evaṃ kira gāmavāsimahallakaṃ nagaraṃ āgantvā pānāgāre pivantaṃ vañcetukāmā sambahulā dhuttā pītaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā tena saddhiṃ suraṃ pivantā “imassa nivāsanapāvuraṇampi hatthe bhaṇḍakampi sabbaṃ gaṇhissāmā”ti cintetvā katikaṃ akaṃsu – “ekekaṃ attapaccakkhakathaṃ kathema, yo ‘abhūta’nti kathesi, kathitaṃ vā na saddahati, taṃ dāsaṃ katvā gaṇhissāmā”ti. Tampi mahallakaṃ pucchiṃsu “tumhākampi tāta ruccatī”ti. Evaṃ hotu tātāti.

In the category of pleasant speech, the first type of speech is called groundless talk. It should be understood thus: It is said that many rogues, wishing to cheat an old villager who had come to the city and was drinking in a tavern, stood in the drinking place and, while drinking liquor with him, thought, 'We will take this man's lower and upper garments, the goods in his hand, everything.' Having thought thus, they made an agreement: 'Let each of us tell a story that we have personally witnessed. Whoever says, "It is untrue," or does not believe what is said, we will make him a slave and take him.' They also asked that old man, 'Dear sir, is this agreeable to you too?' He replied, 'So be it, sirs.'

Eko dhutto āha – mayhaṃ, bho mātu, mayi kucchigate kapiṭṭhaphaladohalo ahosi. Sā aññaṃ kapiṭṭhahārakaṃ alabbhamānā maṃyeva pesesi. Ahaṃ gantvā rukkhaṃ abhiruhituṃ asakkonto attanāva attānaṃ pāde gahetvā muggaraṃ viya rukkhassa upari khipiṃ; atha sākhato sākhaṃ vicaranto phalāni gahetvā otarituṃ asakkonto gharaṃ gantvā nisseṇiṃ āharitvā oruyha mātu santikaṃ gantvā phalāni mātuyā adāsiṃ; tāni pana mahantāni honti cāṭippamāṇāni. Tato me mātarā ekāsane nisinnāya samasaṭṭhiphalāni [P 3.0112] khāditāni. Mayā ekucchaṅgena ānītaphalesu sesakāni kulasantake gāme khuddakamahallakānaṃ ahesuṃ. Amhākaṃ gharaṃ soḷasahatthaṃ, sesaparikkhārabhaṇḍakaṃ apanetvā kapiṭṭhaphaleheva yāva chadanaṃ pūritaṃ. Tato atirekāni gahetvā gehadvāre rāsiṃ akaṃsu. So asītihatthubbedho pabbato viya ahosi. Kiṃ īdisaṃ, bho sakkā, saddahitunti?

One rogue said: 'Sirs, when I was in my mother's womb, she had a craving for wood-apple fruit. Unable to find another wood-apple gatherer, she sent me. I went, but being unable to climb the tree, I grabbed myself by the feet and threw myself up onto the tree like a mallet. Then, moving from branch to branch, I gathered the fruits, but being unable to descend, I went home, brought a ladder, came down, went to my mother, and gave the fruits to my mother. Furthermore, those fruits were large, the size of large pots. Then my mother, sitting in one seat, ate sixty fruits. Of the fruits I brought in one fold of my garment, the remainder were for the young and old in the family house. Our house was sixteen cubits high; removing the other household goods, it was filled with wood-apple fruits right up to the roof. Taking the excess ones, they made a pile at the house door. It was like a mountain eighty cubits high. Sirs, is it possible to believe such a thing?'

Gāmikamahallako [M 3.0079] tuṇhī nisīditvā sabbesaṃ kathāpariyosāne pucchito āha – “evaṃ bhavissati tātā, mahantaṃ raṭṭhaṃ, raṭṭhamahantatāya sakkā saddahitu”nti. Yathā ca tena, evaṃ sesehipi tathārūpāsu nikkāraṇakathāsu kathitāsu āha – mayhampi tātā suṇātha, na tumhākaṃyeva kulāni, amhākampi kulaṃ mahākulaṃ, amhākaṃ pana avasesakhettehi kappāsakhettaṃ mahantataraṃ[V 3.0081]. Tassa anekakarīsasatassa kappāsakhettassa majjhe eko kappāsarukkho mahā asītihatthubbedho ahosi. Tassa pañca sākhā, tāsu avasesasākhā phalaṃ na gaṇhiṃsu, pācīnasākhāya ekameva mahācāṭimattaṃ phalaṃ ahosi. Tassa cha aṃsiyo, chasu aṃsīsu cha kappāsapiṇḍiyo pupphitā. Ahaṃ massuṃ kāretvā nhātavilitto khettaṃ gantvā tā kappāsapiṇḍiyo pupphitā disvā ṭhitakova hatthaṃ pasāretvā gaṇhiṃ. Tā kappāsapiṇḍiyo thāmasampannā cha dāsā ahesuṃ. Te sabbe maṃ ekakaṃ ohāya palātā. Ettake addhāne te na passāmi, ajja diṭṭhā, tumhe te cha janā. Tvaṃ nando nāma, tvaṃ puṇṇo nāma, tvaṃ vaḍḍhamāno nāma, tvaṃ citto nāma tvaṃ maṅgalo nāma, tvaṃ poṭṭhiyo nāmāti vatvā uṭṭhāya nisinnakeyeva cūḷāsu gahetvā [P 3.0113] aṭṭhāsi. Te “na mayaṃ dāsā”tipi vattuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu. Atha ne kaḍḍhanto vinicchayaṃ netvā lakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā yāvajīvaṃ dāse katvā paribhuñji. Evarūpiṃ kathaṃ tathāgato na bhāsati.

The old villager sat silently, and when asked at the end of everyone's talk, he said: 'It could be so, sirs. The country is very large; due to the country's largeness, it is possible to believe.' And just as that one had spoken, so too when the others had told similar groundless stories, he said: 'Sirs, listen to me too. It is not only your families that are great; our family too is a great family. However, of our fields, the cotton field is much larger. In the middle of that cotton field of many hundreds of karīsas, there was one great cotton tree, eighty cubits high. It had five branches; of these, the other branches bore no fruit, but on the eastern branch, there was just one fruit, the size of a large pot. It had six sections, and in the six sections, six cotton bolls blossomed. Having had my beard trimmed, bathed and anointed, I went to the field, and seeing those cotton bolls blossomed, while still standing, I stretched out my hand and took them. Those cotton bolls became six slaves endowed with strength. They all, leaving me alone, fled. For so long I did not see them; today they are seen. You are those six people. You are named Nanda, you are named Puṇṇa, you are named Vaḍḍhamāna, you are named Citta, you are named Maṅgala, and you are named Poṭṭhiya.' Having said this, he got up and, grabbing them by their topknots while they were still seated, he stood. They were not even able to say, 'We are not slaves.' Then, dragging them, he took them to a judge, had them registered, made them slaves for life, and made use of them. The Tathāgata does not speak such a story.

Dutiyavācā āmisahetucāṭukamyatādivasena nānappakārā paresaṃ thomanavācā ceva, corakathaṃ rājakathanti ādinayappavattā tiracchānakathā ca. Tampi tathāgato na bhāsati. Tatiyavācā ariyasaccasannissitakathā, yaṃ vassasatampi suṇantā paṇḍitā neva tittiṃ gacchanti. Iti tathāgato neva sabbampi appiyavācaṃ bhāsati na piyavācaṃ. Tatiyaṃ tatiyameva pana bhāsitabbakālaṃ anatikkamitvā bhāsati. Tattha tatiyaṃ appiyavācaṃ sandhāya heṭṭhā daharakumāraupamā āgatāti veditabbaṃ.

The second type of speech consists of various kinds of praise of others by way of flattery and so on for the sake of material gain, as well as worldly talk that proceeds in the manner of talk about thieves, talk about kings, and so on. The Tathāgata does not speak that either. The third type of speech is talk connected with the Noble Truths, of which the wise, listening even for a hundred years, never reach satiety. Thus, the Tathāgata speaks neither all unpleasant speech, nor all pleasant speech. Rather, he speaks only the third kind from each category, not transgressing the proper time for speaking. Herein, it should be understood that the simile of the young boy given below was stated with reference to the third kind of unpleasant speech.

87. Udāhu ṭhānasovetanti udāhu ṭhānuppattikañāṇena taṅkhaṇaṃyeva taṃ tathāgatassa upaṭṭhātīti pucchati. Saññātoti ñāto paññāto pākaṭo. Dhammadhātūti dhammasabhāvo. Sabbaññutaññāṇassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ[M 3.0080]. Taṃ bhagavatā suppaṭividdhaṃ, hatthagataṃ bhagavato. Tasmā so yaṃ yaṃ icchati, taṃ taṃ sabbaṃ ṭhānasova paṭibhātīti. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānameva. Ayaṃ pana dhammadesanā neyyapuggalavasena pariniṭṭhitāti.

87. The phrase `udāhu ṭhānaso vetaṃ` means: 'Or does it occur to the Tathāgata at that very moment through knowledge that arises according to the situation?'—thus he asks. `Saññāto` means known, clearly known, manifest. `Dhammadhātu` means the nature of phenomena. This is a synonym for the knowledge of omniscience. It has been well penetrated by the Blessed One; it is in the Blessed One's grasp. Therefore, whatever he wishes, all of that appears to him spontaneously. The rest is clear everywhere. This Dhamma discourse, however, is concluded for the benefit of persons to be guided.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Abhayarājakumārasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Abhayarājakumāra Sutta is concluded.

9. Bahuvedanīyasuttavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Bahuvedanīya Sutta

88. Evaṃ [V 3.0082][P 3.0114] me sutanti bahuvedanīyasuttaṃ. Tattha pañcakaṅgo thapatīti pañcakaṅgoti tassa nāmaṃ. Vāsipharasunikhādanadaṇḍamuggarakāḷasuttanāḷisaṅkhātehi vā aṅgehi samannāgatattā so pañcaṅgoti paññāto. Thapatīti vaḍḍhakījeṭṭhako. Udāyīti paṇḍitaudāyitthero.

9. The sutta beginning 'Thus have I heard' is the Bahuvedanīya Sutta. Therein, regarding the phrase 'Pañcakaṅga the carpenter': 'Pañcakaṅga' is his name. Because he was endowed with the carpenter's tools known as the adze, the axe, the gouge, the handled mallet, and the bamboo tube with black string, he was known as 'Pañcakaṅga'. 'Thapati' means the chief carpenter. 'Udāyī' means the wise Elder Udāyī.

89. Pariyāyanti kāraṇaṃ. Dvepānandāti dvepi, ānanda. Pariyāyenāti kāraṇena. Ettha ca kāyikacetasikavasena dve veditabbā. Sukhādivasena tisso, indriyavasena sukhindriyādikā pañca, dvāravasena cakkhusamphassajādikā cha, upavicāravasena “cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā somanassaṭṭhāniyaṃ rūpaṃ upavicaratī”tiādikā aṭṭhārasa, cha gehassitāni somanassāni, cha nekkhammasitāni somanassāni, cha gehassitāni domanassāni, cha nekkhammasitāni domanassāni, cha gehassitā upekkhā, cha nekkhammasitāti evaṃ chattiṃsa, tā atīte chattiṃsa, anāgate chattiṃsa, paccuppanne chattiṃsāti evaṃ aṭṭhavedanāsataṃ veditabbaṃ.

88. 'Pariyāyaṃ' means reason. 'Dvep'ānanda' means: 'Ānanda, two feelings have been spoken of by me.' 'Pariyāyena' means by reason. And here, two feelings are to be understood by way of the bodily and the mental. By way of pleasure, etc., three are to be understood. By way of faculties, five, beginning with the pleasure faculty, are to be understood. By way of doors, six, beginning with feeling born of eye-contact, are to be understood. By way of close consideration, eighteen, such as, “Having seen a form with the eye, one closely considers a form that is a basis for joy,” are to be understood. There are six joys based on the household life, six joys based on renunciation, six sorrows based on the household life, six sorrows based on renunciation, six kinds of equanimity based on the household life, and six based on renunciation—thus thirty-six. These thirty-six in the past, thirty-six in the future, and thirty-six in the present—thus one hundred and eight feelings are to be understood.

90. Pañca kho ime, ānanda, kāmaguṇāti ayaṃ pāṭiekko anusandhi. Na kevalampi dve ādiṃ katvā vedanā bhagavatā paññattā, pariyāyena ekāpi vedanā kathitā. Taṃ dassento pañcakaṅgassa [P 3.0115] thapatino vādaṃ upatthambhetuṃ imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi.

89. 'These, Ānanda, are the five strands of sensual pleasure'—this is a separate connection. Not only were feelings beginning with two designated by the Blessed One, but by way of explanation, even a single feeling was spoken of. Showing this, in order to support the view of Pañcakaṅga the carpenter, He began this discourse.

Abhikkantataranti sundarataraṃ. Paṇītataranti atappakataraṃ. Ettha ca catutthajjhānato paṭṭhāya adukkhamasukhā vedanā, sāpi santaṭṭhena paṇītaṭṭhena ca sukhanti vuttā. Cha gehassitāni sukhanti vuttāni. Nirodho avedayitasukhavasena [M 3.0081] sukhaṃ nāma jāto. Pañcakāmaguṇavasena hi aṭṭhasamāpattivasena ca uppannaṃ vedayitasukhaṃ nāma. Nirodho avedayitasukhaṃ nāma. Iti vedayitasukhaṃ vā hotu avedayitasukhaṃ vā, taṃ niddukkhabhāvasaṅkhātena sukhaṭṭhena ekantasukhameva jātaṃ.

90. 'More excellent' means more beautiful. 'More refined' means more insatiable. Here, beginning from the fourth jhāna, the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is also called happiness because of its peaceful nature and its refined nature. The six feelings based on the household life are called happiness. Cessation becomes what is called happiness by way of unfelt bliss. Indeed, happiness that has arisen by way of the five strands of sensual pleasure and by way of the eight attainments is called felt happiness. Cessation is called unfelt happiness. Thus, whether it be felt happiness or unfelt happiness, that happiness becomes exclusively happiness because of its nature of happiness, which is described as the state of being without suffering.

91. Yattha [V 3.0083] yatthāti yasmiṃ yasmiṃ ṭhāne. Sukhaṃ upalabbhatīti vedayitasukhaṃ vā avedayitasukhaṃ vā upalabbhati. Taṃ taṃ tathāgato sukhasmiṃ paññapetīti taṃ sabbaṃ tathāgato niddukkhabhāvaṃ sukhasmiṃyeva paññapetīti. Idha bhagavā nirodhasamāpattiṃ sīsaṃ katvā neyyapuggalavasena arahattanikūṭeneva desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesīti.

91. 'Wherever, wherever' means in whatever place. 'Happiness is found' means felt happiness or unfelt happiness is found. 'The Tathāgata designates that as happiness' means: the Tathāgata, on account of its being a state without suffering, designates all that as happiness indeed. Here, the Blessed One, having made the attainment of cessation the main point, by way of the person to be guided, concluded the teaching with the very summit of Arahantship.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Bahuvedanīyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Bahuvedanīya Sutta is concluded.

10. Apaṇṇakasuttavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Apaṇṇaka Sutta

92. Evaṃ [V 3.0084] me sutanti apaṇṇakasuttaṃ. Tattha cārikanti aturitacārikaṃ.

92. The Apaṇṇaka Sutta is that which begins, 'Thus have I heard.' Therein, 'a journey' means an unhurried journey.

93. Atthi pana vo gahapatayoti kasmā āha? So kira gāmo aṭavidvāre niviṭṭho. Nānāvidhā samaṇabrāhmaṇā divasaṃ maggaṃ [P 3.0116] gantvā sāyaṃ taṃ gāmaṃ vāsatthāya upenti, tesaṃ te manussā mañcapīṭhāni pattharitvā pāde dhovitvā pāde makkhetvā kappiyapānakāni datvā punadivase nimantetvā dānaṃ denti. Te pasannacittā tehi saddhiṃ sammantayamānā evaṃ vadanti “atthi pana vo gahapatayo kiñci dassanaṃ gahita”nti? Natthi, bhanteti. “Gahapatayo vinā dassanena loko na niyyāti, ekaṃ dassanaṃ ruccitvā khamāpetvā gahetuṃ vaṭṭati, ‘sassato loko’ti dassanaṃ gaṇhathā”ti vatvā pakkantā. Aparadivase aññe āgatā. Tepi tatheva pucchiṃsu. Te tesaṃ “āma, bhante, purimesu divasesu tumhādisā samaṇabrāhmaṇā āgantvā ‘sassato loko’ti amhe idaṃ dassanaṃ gāhāpetvā gatā”ti ārocesuṃ. “Te bālā kiṃ jānanti? ‘Ucchijjati ayaṃ loko’ti ucchedadassanaṃ gaṇhathā”ti evaṃ tepi ucchedadassanaṃ gaṇhāpetvā pakkantā. Etenupāyena aññe ekaccasassataṃ, aññe antānantaṃ[M 3.0082], aññe amarāvikkhepanti evaṃ dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhiyo uggaṇhāpesuṃ. Te pana ekadiṭṭhiyampi patiṭṭhātuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu. Sabbapacchā bhagavā agamāsi. So tesaṃ hitatthāya pucchanto “atthi pana vo gahapatayo”tiādimāha. Tattha ākāravatīti kāraṇavatī sahetukā. Apaṇṇakoti aviraddho advejjhagāmī ekaṃsagāhiko.

93. “But do you, householders, have any view?” Why did he say this? It is said that the village was situated at the entrance to a forest. Various ascetics and brahmins, after traveling the road by day, would arrive at that village in the evening seeking lodging. The people there would prepare beds and seats, wash their feet, anoint their feet, offer suitable drinks, and on the next day, invite them and give alms. As those people, with pleased minds, conversed with them, the visitors would ask, “But do you, householders, have any view that you have adopted?” “No, venerable sirs.” “Householders, without a view, the world does not find a way out. It is proper to like, approve of, and adopt one view. Adopt the view that ‘the world is eternal.’” Having said this, they departed. On another day, others arrived. They too asked in the same way. The villagers informed them, “Yes, venerable sirs. In previous days, ascetics and brahmins like you came and, having made us adopt this view that ‘the world is eternal,’ they departed.” “Those fools, what do they know? Adopt the annihilationist view that ‘this world is annihilated.’” Thus, they too, having made them adopt the annihilationist view, departed. By this method, others made them adopt partial-eternalism, others finitude and infinitude, others eel-wriggling—thus they were made to adopt the sixty-two views. But they were not able to establish themselves in any single view. Last of all, the Blessed One arrived. For their welfare, he asked, “But do you, householders, have any view?” and so on. Therein, 'ākāravatī' means having a cause, with a reason. 'Apaṇṇaka' means unerring, not leading to a dilemma, taking a single position.

94. Natthi dinnantiādi dasavatthukā micchādiṭṭhi heṭṭhā sāleyyakasutte vitthāritā. Tathā tabbipaccanīkabhūtā sammādiṭṭhi.

94. The wrong view with its ten bases, beginning with 'There is nothing given,' was explained in detail previously in the Sāleyyaka Sutta. Likewise, the right view, which is its opposite.

95. Nekkhamme ānisaṃsanti yo nesaṃ akusalato nikkhantabhāve ānisaṃso, yo ca vodānapakkho visuddhipakkho, taṃ na passantīti attho. Asaddhammasaññattīti [P 3.0117] abhūtadhammasaññāpanā[V 3.0085]. Attānukkaṃsetīti ṭhapetvā maṃ ko añño attano dassanaṃ pare gaṇhāpetuṃ sakkotīti attānaṃ ukkhipati. Paraṃ vambhetīti ettakesu janesu ekopi attano dassanaṃ pare gaṇhāpetuṃ na sakkotīti evaṃ paraṃ heṭṭhā khipati. Pubbeva kho panāti pubbe micchādassanaṃ gaṇhantasseva susīlyaṃ pahīnaṃ hoti, dussīlabhāvo paccupaṭṭhito. Evamassimeti evaṃ assa ime micchādiṭṭhiādayo satta. Aparāparaṃ uppajjanavasena pana teyeva micchādiṭṭhipaccayā aneke pāpakā akusalā dhammā uppajjanti nāma.

95. “The benefit in renunciation” means: they do not see the benefit that exists in the state of having departed from the unwholesome, nor the part that is cleansing, the part that is pure. “A declaration of false doctrine” means making known a doctrine that is not real. “He praises himself” means he elevates himself, thinking, “Besides me, who else is able to make others adopt his view?” “He disparages others” means he puts others down, thinking, “Among so many people, not even one is able to make others adopt his view.” “Even before” means that for one who adopts a wrong view, good morality is already abandoned, and the state of bad morality is established. “Thus for him” means thus for that person are these seven things, beginning with wrong view. Furthermore, by way of successive arising, due to wrong view as a condition, many evil, unwholesome states indeed arise.

Tatrāti tāsu tesaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ laddhīsu. Kaliggahoti parājayaggāho. Dussamatto samādinnoti duggahito dupparāmaṭṭho. Ekaṃsaṃ pharitvā tiṭṭhatīti ekantaṃ ekakoṭṭhāsaṃ sakavādameva pharitvā adhimuccitvā tiṭṭhati, “sace kho natthi paro loko”ti evaṃ santeyeva sotthibhāvāvaho hoti. Riñcatīti vajjeti.

Therein: in those views of those ascetics and brahmins. A losing grasp (kaliggaho): a grasp of defeat. Badly undertaken and adopted (dussamatto samādinno): badly grasped, badly adhered to. He stands pervading one side (ekaṃsaṃ pharitvā tiṭṭhati): he stands pervading and being resolved only upon his own one-sided, partial doctrine; “if there is no other world”—even if it is so, he is one who brings about a state of security. He forsakes (riñcati): he avoids.

96. Saddhammasaññattīti bhūtadhammasaññāpanā.

96. “A declaration of the true doctrine” means making known the true doctrine.

Kaṭaggahoti jayaggāho. Susamatto samādinnoti suggahito suparāmaṭṭho. Ubhayaṃsaṃ [P 3.0118] pharitvā tiṭṭhatīti ubhayantaṃ ubhayakoṭṭhāsaṃ sakavādaṃ paravādañca pharitvā adhimuccitvā tiṭṭhati “sace kho atthi paro loko”ti evaṃ santepi “sace kho natthi paro loko”ti evaṃ santepi sotthibhāvāvaho hoti. Paratopi ekaṃsaubhayaṃsesu imināva nayena attho veditabbo.

“A winning grasp” (kaṭaggāho) means a grasp of victory. “Well undertaken and adopted” (susamatto samādinno) means well-grasped, well-considered. “He stands pervading both sides” (ubhayaṃsaṃ pharitvā tiṭṭhati) means he stands pervading and being resolved upon both extremes, both parts—his own doctrine and the doctrine of others; “if there is another world”—even if it is so, and “if there is no other world”—even if it is so, he is one who brings about a state of well-being. Further on, the meaning in the cases of one side and both sides should be understood by this same method.

97. Karototi [M 3.0083] sahatthā karontassa. Kārayatoti āṇattiyā kārentassa. Chindatoti paresaṃ hatthādīni chindantassa. Pacatoti daṇḍena pīḷentassa vā tajjentassa vā. Socayatoti parassa bhaṇḍaharaṇādīhi sokaṃ sayaṃ karontassapi parehi kārentassapi. Kilamatoti āhārūpaccheda-bandhanāgārappavesanādīhi sayaṃ kilamantassāpi parehi kilamāpentassāpi. Phandato phandāpayatoti paraṃ phandantaṃ phandanakāle sayampi phandato parampi phandāpayato. Pāṇamatipātayatoti pāṇaṃ hanantassapi hanāpentassapi. Evaṃ sabbattha karaṇakārāpanavaseneva attho veditabbo.

97. Doing (karoto): for one who does with their own hand. Causing to do (kārayato): for one who causes it to be done by command. Cutting (chindato): for one who cuts off others' hands, etc. Tormenting (pacato): for one who oppresses with a stick or threatens. Causing grief (socayato): for one who causes grief, whether by oneself stealing another's goods, etc., or by causing others to do so. Causing weariness (kilamato): for one who causes weariness, whether by oneself through cutting off food, imprisonment, etc., or by causing others to be made weary. Trembling and causing to tremble (phandato phandāpayato): for one who trembles oneself when another is trembling, and for one who causes another to tremble. Destroying life (pāṇamatipātayato): for one who kills a living being or causes one to be killed. Thus in all cases, the meaning should be understood by way of doing and causing to be done.

Sandhinti [V 3.0086] gharasandhiṃ. Nillopanti mahāvilopaṃ. Ekāgārikanti ekameva gharaṃ parivāretvā vilumpanaṃ. Paripanthe [P 3.0119] tiṭṭhatoti āgatāgatānaṃ acchindanatthaṃ magge tiṭṭhato. Karoto na karīyati pāpanti yaṃkiñci pāpaṃ karomīti saññāya karotopi pāpaṃ na karīyati, natthi pāpaṃ. Sattā pana karomāti evaṃsaññino hontīti attho. Khurapariyantenāti khuraneminā, khuradhārasadisapariyantena vā. Ekaṃ maṃsakhalanti ekaṃ maṃsarāsiṃ. Puñjanti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Tatonidānanti ekamaṃsakhalakaraṇanidānaṃ. Dakkhiṇatīre manussā kakkhaḷā dāruṇā, te sandhāya hanantotiādi vuttaṃ. Uttaratīre saddhā honti pasannā buddhamāmakā dhammamāmakā saṅghamāmakā, te sandhāya dadantotiādi vuttaṃ.

“Breaking in” (sandhiṃ) means house-breaking. “Plunder” (nillopaṃ) means great plunder. “An attack on a single house” (ekāgārikaṃ) means surrounding just one house and plundering it. “He stands on the highway” (paripanthe tiṭṭhati): for one who stands on the road for the purpose of robbing whoever comes. “For one who acts, no evil is done” means: even for one who acts with the perception, “I am doing something evil,” no evil is done; there is no evil. The meaning is that beings, however, have the perception, “We are doing.” “With a razor-rimmed wheel” (khurapariyantena) means with a razor-rim, or with a boundary like the edge of a razor. “One heap of flesh” (ekaṃ maṃsakhalaṃ) means one mass of flesh. “A pile” (puñjaṃ) is a synonym for that. “Because of that” (tatonidānaṃ) means for the reason of making one heap of flesh. On the southern bank, the people are harsh and cruel; with reference to them, it was said, “killing,” and so on. On the northern bank, they are faithful, serene, devoted to the Buddha, devoted to the Dhamma, devoted to the Saṅgha; with reference to them, it was said, “giving,” and so on.

Tattha yajantoti mahāyāgaṃ karonto. Damenāti indriyadamena uposathakammena. Saṃyamenāti sīlasaṃyamena. Saccavajjenāti saccavacanena. Āgamoti āgamanaṃ, pavattīti attho. Sabbathāpi pāpapuññānaṃ kiriyameva paṭikkhipanti. Sukkapakkhopi vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Sesamettha purimavāre vuttasadisameva.

Therein, `yajanto` means one who performs a great sacrifice. `Damena` means by the taming of the senses, by the act of observing the Uposatha. `Saṃyamena` means by the guarding of virtue. `Saccavajjenāti` means by speaking true speech. `Āgamo` means there is no coming, there is no proceeding; this is the meaning. In all ways, they reject the very doing of demerit and merit. The bright side should also be understood in the way that has been stated. The remainder here is just the same as what was said in the previous section.

100. Natthi hetu natthi paccayoti ettha paccayo hetuvevacanaṃ. Ubhayenāpi vijjamānakameva kāyaduccaritādisaṃkilesapaccayaṃ kāyasucaritādivisuddhipaccayaṃ paṭikkhipanti. Natthi [P 3.0120] balaṃ, natthi vīriyaṃ, natthi purisathāmo, natthi purisaparakkamoti sattānaṃ saṃkilesituṃ vā visujjhituṃ vā [M 3.0084] balaṃ vā vīriyaṃ vā purisena kātabbo nāma purisathāmo vā purisaparakkamo vā natthi.

100. In the phrase 'There is no cause, there is no condition,' `paccayo` is a synonym for `hetu`. By both, they reject the actually existing cause for defilement, such as bodily misconduct, and the actually existing cause for purification, such as good bodily conduct. 'There is no strength, there is no energy, there is no human stamina, there is no human endeavor' means: for beings to be defiled or to be purified, there is no strength, no energy, no so-called human stamina to be enacted by a person, nor human endeavor.

Sabbe sattāti oṭṭhagoṇagadrabhādayo anavasese nidassenti. Sabbe pāṇāti ekindriyo pāṇo dvindriyo pāṇoti ādivasena vadanti. Sabbe bhūtāti aṇḍakosavatthikosesu bhūte sandhāya vadanti. Sabbe jīvāti sāliyavagodhumādayo sandhāya vadanti. Tesu hete viruhanabhāvena jīvasaññino. Avasā abalā avīriyāti tesaṃ attano vaso vā balaṃ vā vīriyaṃ vā natthi. Niyatisaṅgatibhāvapariṇatāti ettha niyatīti niyatatā. Saṅgatīti channaṃ abhijātīnaṃ tattha tattha gamanaṃ. Bhāvoti sabhāvoyeva. Evaṃ niyatiyā ca saṅgatiyā ca bhāvena ca pariṇatā nānappakārataṃ pattā. Yena hi yathā bhavitabbaṃ, so tatheva bhavati. Yena no [V 3.0087] bhavitabbaṃ, so na bhavatīti dassenti. Chasvevābhijātīsūti chasu eva abhijātīsu ṭhatvā sukhañca dukkhañca paṭisaṃvedenti, aññā sukhadukkhabhūmi natthīti dassenti.

By `sabbe sattā` they indicate without remainder beings such as camels, cattle, and donkeys. By `sabbe pāṇā` they speak in terms of beings with one faculty, beings with two faculties, and so on. By `sabbe bhūtā` they speak with reference to beings that have come to be in egg-shells and in wombs. By `sabbe jīvā` they speak with reference to rice, barley, wheat, and so on. Regarding these, they perceive them as living because of their nature of sprouting. `Avasā, abalā, avīriyā` means they have no power of their own, no strength, no energy. Regarding `niyatisaṅgatibhāvapariṇatā`, herein `niyati` is fixedness. `Saṅgati` is the going to this or that destination among the six classes. `Bhāvo` is just its own nature. Thus, they are transformed by fixedness, by class, and by nature, having attained various states. For they show that in whatever way a person is to be, in that very way they become; and in whatever way a person is not to be, in that way they do not become. `Chasvevābhijātīsu` means: established in just the six classes, they experience pleasure and pain; they show that there is no other plane of pleasure and pain.

Tattha cha abhijātiyo [P 3.0121] nāma kaṇhābhijāti nīlābhijāti lohitābhijāti haliddābhijāti sukkābhijāti paramasukkābhijātīti. Tattha sākuṇiko sūkariko luddo macchaghātako coro coraghātako, ye vā panaññepi keci kurūrakammantā, ayaṃ kaṇhābhijāti nāma. Bhikkhū nīlābhijātīti vadanti. Te kira catūsu paccayesu kaṇṭake pakkhipitvā khādanti. “Bhikkhū ca kaṇṭakavuttino”ti ayañhi nesaṃ pāḷiyeva. Atha vā kaṇṭakavuttikā evaṃ nāma eke pabbajitāti vadanti. “Samaṇakaṇṭakavuttikā”tipi hi nesaṃ pāḷi. Lohitābhijāti nāma nigaṇṭhā ekasāṭakāti vadanti. Ime kira purimehi dvīhi paṇḍaratarā. Gihī acelakasāvakā haliddābhijātīti vadanti. Iti attano paccayadāyake nigaṇṭhehipi jeṭṭhakatare karonti. Nando, vaccho, saṅkicco, ayaṃ sukkābhijātīti vadanti. Te kira purimehi catūhi paṇḍaratarā. Ājīvake pana paramasukkābhijātīti vadanti. Te kira sabbehi paṇḍaratarā.

Therein, the six classes are: the black class, the blue class, the red class, the yellow class, the white class, and the supreme white class. Therein, the bird-hunter, the pig-butcher, the hunter, the fisherman, the thief, the executioner of thieves, and whatever other persons who perform cruel actions—this is called the black class. They say that bhikkhus are the blue class. It is said that they eat after putting thorns into the four requisites. 'And bhikkhus are of thorny practice'—this is indeed their own canonical text. Alternatively, they say that some ascetics are called 'those of thorny practice.' Indeed, 'ascetics of thorny practice' is also their canonical text. They say that the Nigaṇṭhas, who wear a single cloth, are called the red class. It is said that these are purer than the previous two. They say that the householders who are disciples of the naked ascetics are the yellow class. Thus they make their own supporters of requisites superior even to the Nigaṇṭhas. They say that Nanda, Vaccha, and Saṅkicca are the white class. It is said that they are purer than the previous four. As for the Ājīvakas, they call them the supreme white class. It is said that they are the purest of all.

Tattha [M 3.0085] sabbe sattā paṭhamaṃ sākuṇikādayova honti, tato visujjhamānā sakyasamaṇā honti, tato visujjhamānā nigaṇṭhā, tato ājīvakasāvakā, tato nandādayo, tato ājīvakāti ayametesaṃ laddhi. Sukkapakkho vuttapaccanīkena veditabbo. Sesamidhāpi purimavāre vuttasadisameva.

Therein, all beings are first bird-hunters and the like; then, being purified, they become Sakyan ascetics; then, being purified, they become Nigaṇṭhas; then, Ājīvaka disciples; then, Nanda and the like; and then, Ājīvakas. This is their doctrine. The bright side should be understood by way of the opposite of what was stated. The remainder here also is just the same as what was said in the previous section.

Imāsu pana tīsu diṭṭhīsu natthikadiṭṭhi vipākaṃ paṭibāhati, akiriyadiṭṭhi kammaṃ paṭibāhati, ahetukadiṭṭhi ubhayampi paṭibāhati. Tattha kammaṃ paṭibāhantenāpi vipāko paṭibāhito hoti, vipākaṃ paṭibāhantenāpi kammaṃ paṭibāhitaṃ. Iti sabbepete [P 3.0122] atthato ubhayapaṭibāhakā natthikavādā ceva ahetukavādā akiriyavādā ca honti. Ye pana tesaṃ laddhiṃ gahetvā rattiṭṭhāne divāṭṭhāne nisinnā sajjhāyanti vīmaṃsanti, tesaṃ – “natthi dinnaṃ natthi yiṭṭhaṃ, karoto na kariyati pāpaṃ, natthi hetu natthi paccayo”ti tasmiṃ ārammaṇe micchāsati santiṭṭhati[V 3.0088], cittaṃ ekaggaṃ hoti, javanāni javanti, paṭhamajavane satekicchā honti, tathā dutiyādīsu. Sattame buddhānampi atekicchā anivattino ariṭṭhakaṇṭakasadisā.

Now, among these three views, the nihilistic view obstructs the result, the view of non-action obstructs action, and the view of causelessness obstructs both. Therein, by one who obstructs action, the result is also obstructed; and by one who obstructs the result, action is also obstructed. Thus, all of these, in essence, become obstructors of both, and are nihilistic doctrines, causeless doctrines, and non-action doctrines. As for those who, having adopted their belief, sit in secluded places by night and by day, reciting and investigating thus: 'There is no fruit of giving, there is no fruit of offering; for one who acts, evil is not done; there is no cause, there is no condition'—for them, wrong mindfulness is established on that object, the mind becomes concentrated, impulsion moments arise. In the first impulsion moment, they are curable, and likewise in the second and so on. At the seventh, they are incurable even for Buddhas, irreversible, like the monk Ariṭṭha and the novice Kaṇṭaka.

Tattha koci ekaṃ dassanaṃ okkamati, koci dve, koci tīṇipi, ekasmiṃ okkantepi dvīsu tīsu okkantesupi niyatamicchādiṭṭhikova hoti, patto saggamaggāvaraṇañceva mokkhamaggāvaraṇañca, abhabbo tassa attabhāvassa anantaraṃ saggampi gantuṃ, pageva mokkhaṃ. Vaṭṭakhāṇu nāmesa satto pathavīgopako. Kiṃ panesa ekasmiṃyeva attabhāve niyato hoti, udāhu aññasmimpīti? Ekasmiññeva niyato, āsevanavasena pana bhavantarepi taṃ taṃ diṭṭhiṃ rocetiyeva. Evarūpassa hi yebhuyyena bhavato vuṭṭhānaṃ nāma natthi.

Therein, someone descends into one view, someone into two, someone into all three. Whether one has descended into one, or into two or three, one becomes one of fixed wrong view, having become an obstruction to the path to heaven and an obstruction to the path to liberation. Immediately after that existence, one is incapable of going even to heaven, let alone to liberation. This being is called a 'saṃsāra-stump,' a 'guardian of the earth.' Now, is this person fixed in just one existence, or also in another? He is fixed in just one existence. However, through the power of cultivation, even in another existence he certainly delights in that same view. For such a one, for the most part, there is no such thing as rising up from existence.

Tasmā akalyāṇajanaṃ, āsīvisamivoragaṃ;

Ārakā parivajjeyya, bhūtikāmo vicakkhaṇoti.

Therefore, one who desires prosperity, being discerning, should avoid the unvirtuous person from afar, like a poisonous snake.

103. Natthi sabbaso āruppāti arūpabrahmaloko nāma sabbākārena natthi. Manomayāti jhānacittamayā. Saññāmayāti arūpajjhānasaññāya saññāmayā. Rūpānaṃyeva nibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya paṭipanno hotīti ayaṃ lābhī vā hoti takkī vā. Lābhī nāma rūpāvacarajjhānalābhī. Tassa rūpāvacare kaṅkhā natthi, arūpāvacaraloke atthi[M 3.0086]. So – “ahaṃ āruppā atthīti vadantānampi [P 3.0123] natthīti vadantānampi suṇāmi, atthi natthīti pana na jānāmi. Catutthajjhānaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ katvā arūpāvacarajjhānaṃ nibbattessāmi. Sace āruppā atthi, tattha nibbattissāmi, sace natthi, rūpāvacarabrahmaloke nibbattissāmi. Evaṃ me apaṇṇako dhammo apaṇṇakova aviraddhova bhavissatī”ti tathā paṭipajjati. Takkī pana appaṭiladdhajjhāno, tassāpi rūpajjhāne kaṅkhā natthi, arūpaloke pana atthi. So – “ahaṃ āruppā atthīti vadantānampi natthīti vadantānampi suṇāmi, atthi natthīti pana na jānāmi. Kasiṇaparikammaṃ katvā catutthajjhānaṃ nibbattetvā taṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ katvā arūpāvacarajjhānaṃ nibbattessāmi. Sace āruppā atthi, tattha nibbattissāmi. Sace natthi, rūpāvacarabrahmaloke nibbattissāmi. Evaṃ me apaṇṇako dhammo apaṇṇakova aviraddhova bhavissatī”ti tathā paṭipajjati.

103. “There are no formless realms whatsoever” means that the formless brahma world does not exist in any way. “Mind-made” means made of the fine-material sphere jhāna-mind. “Perception-made” means made of the perception associated with formless jhāna. “One who practices for disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding forms” means this person is either an attainer or a reasoner. An attainer is one who has attained the fine-material sphere jhāna. For him, there is no doubt about the fine-material sphere, but there is doubt about the formless sphere world. He reflects: “I hear some say the formless realms exist and others say they do not exist, but I do not know for sure whether they exist or not. Making the fourth jhāna the foundation, I will produce the formless-sphere jhāna. If the formless realms exist, I will be reborn there; if they do not exist, I will be reborn in the fine-material sphere brahma world. Thus this practice of mine will be a sure one, certain and unfailing.” So he practices accordingly. A reasoner, however, is one who has not attained jhāna. For him too, there is no doubt about the form jhānas, but there is doubt about the formless world. He reflects: “I hear some say the formless realms exist and others say they do not exist, but I do not know for sure whether they exist or not. After doing the preliminary work on a kasiṇa and attaining the fourth jhāna, making that the foundation, I will produce the formless-sphere jhāna. If the formless realms exist, I will be reborn there; if they do not exist, I will be reborn in the fine-material sphere brahma world. Thus this practice of mine will be a sure one, certain and unfailing.” So he practices accordingly.

104. Bhavanirodhoti [V 3.0089] nibbānaṃ. Sārāgāya santiketi rāgavasena vaṭṭe rajjanassa santike. Saṃyogāyāti taṇhāvasena saṃyojanatthāya. Abhinandanāyāti taṇhādiṭṭhivasena abhinandanāya. Paṭipanno hotīti ayampi lābhī vā hoti takkī vā. Lābhī nāma aṭṭhasamāpattilābhī. Tassa āruppe kaṅkhā natthi, nibbāne atthi. So – “ahaṃ nirodho atthītipi natthītipi suṇāmi, sayaṃ na jānāmi. Samāpattiṃ pādakaṃ katvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhessāmi. Sace nirodho bhavissati, arahattaṃ patvā parinibbāyissāmi. No ce bhavissati, āruppe nibbattissāmī”ti evaṃ paṭipajjati. Takkī pana ekasamāpattiyāpi na lābhī, āruppe panassa kaṅkhā natthi, bhavanirodhe atthi. So – “ahaṃ nirodho atthītipi natthītipi suṇāmi, sayaṃ na jānāmi, kasiṇaparikammaṃ katvā aṭṭhasamāpattiyo nibbattetvā samāpattipadaṭṭhānaṃ vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhessāmi. Sace nirodho bhavissati, arahattaṃ patvā parinibbāyissāmi. No ce bhavissati, āruppe nibbattissāmī”ti evaṃ paṭipajjati. Etthāha [P 3.0124] – “atthi dinnantiādīni tāva apaṇṇakāni bhavantu, natthi dinnantiādīni pana kathaṃ apaṇṇakānī”ti. Gahaṇavasena. Tāni hi apaṇṇakaṃ apaṇṇakanti evaṃ gahitattā apaṇṇakāni nāma jātāni.

104. “The cessation of becoming” is Nibbāna. “Near to those with passion” means near to attachment in the round of existence due to lust. “For the sake of bondage” means for the purpose of being yoked through craving. “For delighting” means for the purpose of greatly delighting through craving and wrong view. “One practices” means this person is also either an attainer or a reasoner. An attainer is one who has attained the eight attainments. For him, there is no doubt about the formless realm, but there is doubt about Nibbāna. He reflects: “I hear that cessation exists and that it does not exist, but I do not know for myself. Having made the attainments a basis, I will develop insight. If cessation exists, having attained Arahantship, I will attain final Nibbāna. If it does not exist, I will be reborn in the formless realm.” Thus, he practices. A reasoner, however, has not attained even a single attainment, but for him there is no doubt about the formless realm; there is doubt only about the cessation of becoming. He reflects: “I hear that cessation exists and that it does not exist, but I do not know for myself. Having done the preliminary work on a kasiṇa and brought into being the eight attainments, I will develop insight that has the attainments as its proximate cause. If cessation exists, having attained Arahantship, I will attain final Nibbāna. If it does not exist, I will be reborn in the formless realm.” Thus, he practices. Here one might say: “Let the views such as ‘There is what is given’ be unerring, but how can views such as ‘There is not what is given’ be unerring?” By way of grasping. For those views have come to be called ‘unerring’ because they are grasped thus: “Unerring, unerring.”

105. Cattārometi [M 3.0087] ayaṃ pāṭiekko anusandhi. Natthikavādo, ahetukavādo akiriyavādo, āruppā natthi nirodho natthīti evaṃvādino ca dveti ime pañca puggalā heṭṭhā tayo puggalāva honti. Atthikavādādayo pañca eko catutthapuggalova hoti. Etamatthaṃ dassetuṃ bhagavā imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi. Tattha sabbaṃ atthato uttānamevāti.

105. The phrase “These four” is a separate connection. The person with the nihilist view, the person with the causelessness view, the person with the inefficacy-of-action view, and the two persons with the views that “the formless realm does not exist” and “cessation does not exist”—these five persons are included in the three types of persons mentioned before. The five persons with the view of existence and so on are just the one fourth person. To show this meaning, the Blessed One began this discourse. Therein, everything is plain in meaning.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Middle Length Discourses.

Apaṇṇakasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Apaṇṇaka Sutta is concluded.

Paṭhamavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the first chapter is concluded.

2. Bhikkhuvaggo

2. The Chapter on Bhikkhus

1. Ambalaṭṭhikarāhulovādasuttavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Ambalaṭṭhika-Rāhulovāda Sutta

107. Evaṃ [V 3.0090][M 3.0088] me sutanti ambalaṭṭhikarāhulovādasuttaṃ. Tattha ambalaṭṭhikāyaṃ viharatīti veḷuvanavihārassa paccante padhānagharasaṅkhepe vivekakāmānaṃ vasanatthāya kate ambalaṭṭhikāti evaṃnāmake pāsāde pavivekaṃ brūhayanto viharati. Kaṇṭako nāma jātakālato paṭṭhāya tikhiṇova hoti, evamevaṃ ayampi āyasmā sattavassikasāmaṇerakāleyeva pavivekaṃ brūhayamāno tattha vihāsi. Paṭisallānā vuṭṭhitoti phalasamāpattito vuṭṭhāya. Āsananti pakatipaññattamevettha āsanaṃ atthi, taṃ papphoṭetvā ṭhapesi. Udakādhāneti [P 3.0125] udakabhājane. “Udakaṭṭhāne”tipi pāṭho.

107. The Ambalaṭṭhikarāhulovāda Sutta is that which begins, 'Thus have I heard.' Therein, 'dwelling at Ambalaṭṭhikā' means: he dwells developing seclusion in a mansion named Ambalaṭṭhikā, which was built on the outskirts of the Veḷuvana monastery in the form of a meditation dwelling for those desiring solitude to reside in. Just as a thorn is sharp from the moment it sprouts, so too this venerable one, even as a seven-year-old novice, dwelt there cultivating seclusion. 'Having arisen from seclusion' means having arisen from the attainment of fruition. 'The seat' means: here there was a seat that is usually appointed; he prepared it by shaking it out. 'In the water container' means in the water vessel. There is also a variant reading: 'udakaṭṭhāne' (in the place for water).

Āyasmantaṃ rāhulaṃ āmantesīti ovādadānatthaṃ āmantesi. Bhagavatā hi rāhulattherassa sambahulā dhammadesanā katā. Sāmaṇerapañhaṃ therasseva vuttaṃ. Tathā rāhulasaṃyuttaṃ mahārāhulovādasuttaṃ cūḷarāhulovādasuttamidaṃ ambalaṭṭhikarāhulovādasuttanti.

'He addressed the Venerable Rāhula' means he addressed him in order to give an exhortation. Indeed, many Dhamma discourses were given by the Blessed One to the Elder Rāhula. The Sāmaṇerapañha (Novice's Questions) was spoken to the Elder himself. Likewise, the Rāhulasaṃyutta, the Mahārāhulovādasutta (Great Discourse of Exhortation to Rāhula), the Cūḷarāhulovādasutta (Shorter Discourse of Exhortation to Rāhula), and this Ambalaṭṭhikarāhulovādasutta.

Ayañhi āyasmā sattavassikakāle bhagavantaṃ cīvarakaṇṇe gahetvā “dāyajjaṃ me samaṇa dehī”ti dāyajjaṃ yācamāno bhagavatā dhammasenāpatisāriputtattherassa niyyādetvā pabbājito. Atha bhagavā daharakumārā nāma yuttāyuttaṃ kathaṃ kathenti, ovādamassa demīti rāhulakumāraṃ āmantetvā “sāmaṇerena nāma, rāhula, tiracchānakathaṃ kathetuṃ na vaṭṭati, tvaṃ kathayamāno evarūpaṃ kathaṃ katheyyāsī”ti sabbabuddhehi avijahitaṃ dasapucchaṃ pañcapaṇṇāsavissajjanaṃ – “eko pañho eko uddeso ekaṃ veyyākaraṇaṃ dve pañhā…pe… dasa pañhā dasa uddesā dasa [V 3.0091] veyyākaraṇāti. Ekaṃ nāma kiṃ? Sabbe sattā āhāraṭṭhitikā…pe… dasa nāma kiṃ? Dasahaṅgehi samannāgato arahāti vuccatī”ti (khu. pā. 4.10) imaṃ sāmaṇerapañhaṃ kathesi. Puna cintesi “daharakumārā nāma piyamusāvādā honti, adiṭṭhameva [P 3.0126] diṭṭhaṃ amhehi, diṭṭhameva na diṭṭhaṃ amhehīti vadanti ovādamassa demī”ti akkhīhi oloketvāpi sukhasañjānanatthaṃ paṭhamameva catasso udakādhānūpamāyo[M 3.0089], tato dve hatthiupamāyo ekaṃ ādāsūpamañca dassetvā imaṃ suttaṃ kathesi. Catūsu pana paccayesu taṇhāvivaṭṭanaṃ pañcasu kāmaguṇesu chandarāgappahānaṃ kalyāṇamittupanissayassa mahantabhāvañca dassetvā rāhulasuttaṃ (su. ni. rāhulasutta) kathesi. Āgatāgataṭṭhāne bhavesu chandarāgo na kattabboti dassetuṃ rāhulasaṃyuttaṃ (saṃ. ni. 2.188 ādayo) kathesi. “Ahaṃ sobhāmi, mama vaṇṇāyatanaṃ pasanna”nti attabhāvaṃ nissāya gehassitachandarāgo na kattabboti mahārāhulovādasuttaṃ kathesi.

Indeed, this venerable one, at the age of seven, took hold of the Blessed One’s robe-corner, and while asking for his inheritance, saying, “Give me my inheritance, recluse!”, he was given the going forth by the Blessed One, who entrusted him to the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma. Then the Blessed One thought, “Young boys speak what is fitting and unfitting. I shall give him an exhortation.” Having called the young Rāhula, he said, “Rāhula, it is not proper for a novice to engage in animal talk. When you speak, you should speak in this way.” He then taught the Novice's Questions, not neglected by any of the Buddhas, with its ten questions and fifty-five answers: 'One question, one recitation, one explanation; two questions... ten questions, ten recitations, ten explanations. What is one? All beings are sustained by food… What is ten? One endowed with ten qualities is called an arahant.' He taught this Novice's Questions. Again, he reflected, “Young boys are fond of lying. They say, ‘We saw what was not seen,’ or ‘We did not see what was seen.’ I shall give him an exhortation.” Having reflected thus, so that he might understand with ease just by looking with his eyes, he first showed him the four similes of the water container, then the two similes of the elephant, and one simile of the mirror, and then taught this sutta. Furthermore, to show the turning away from craving regarding the four requisites, the abandoning of desire and lust regarding the five strands of sensual pleasure, and the great benefit of relying on a good friend, he taught the Rāhula Sutta. To show that desire and lust should not be engaged in with regard to existences wherever one may be reborn, he taught the Rāhula Saṃyutta. To show that, based on one's own person, household-related desire and lust should not be engaged in with thoughts like, 'I am beautiful, my complexion is pleasing,' he taught the Mahārāhulovādasutta.

Tattha rāhulasuttaṃ imasmiṃ nāma kāle vuttanti na vattabbaṃ. Tañhi abhiṇhovādavasena vuttaṃ. Rāhulasaṃyuttaṃ sattavassikakālato paṭṭhāya yāva avassikabhikkhukālā vuttaṃ. Mahārāhulovādasuttaṃ aṭṭhārasa vassasāmaṇerakāle vuttaṃ. Cūḷarāhulovādasuttaṃ avassikabhikkhukāle vuttaṃ. Kumārakapañhañca idañca ambalaṭṭhikarāhulovādasuttaṃ sattavassikasāmaṇerakāle vuttaṃ. Tesu rāhulasuttaṃ abhiṇhovādatthaṃ, rāhulasaṃyuttaṃ, therassa vipassanāgabbhagahaṇatthaṃ, mahārāhulovādaṃ gehassitachandarāgavinodanatthaṃ, cūḷarāhulovādaṃ therassa pañcadasa-vimuttiparipācanīya-dhammaparipākakāle arahattagāhāpanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Idañca [P 3.0127] pana sandhāya rāhulatthero bhikkhusaṅghamajjhe tathāgatassa guṇaṃ kathento idamāha –

Herein, it should not be said that the Rāhula Sutta was spoken at a specific time, for it was spoken by way of frequent exhortation. The Rāhula Saṃyutta was spoken from the time he was seven years old until he was a bhikkhu who had not yet completed a rains-residence. The Mahārāhulovāda Sutta was spoken when he was an eighteen-year-old novice. The Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta was spoken when he was a bhikkhu who had not yet completed a rains-residence. The Kumārakapañha and this Ambalaṭṭhika-Rāhulovāda Sutta were spoken when he was a seven-year-old novice. Among these, the Rāhula Sutta was for the purpose of frequent exhortation; the Rāhula Saṃyutta, for the Elder’s grasping of the embryo of insight; the Mahārāhulovāda, for dispelling household-based desire and lust; and the Cūḷarāhulovāda was spoken to lead the Elder to attain Arahantship at the time when the fifteen qualities that ripen liberation had matured. Moreover, with reference to this, the Elder Rāhula, while speaking of the Tathāgata's virtue in the midst of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, said this:

“Kikīva bījaṃ rakkheyya, cāmarī vālamuttamaṃ;

Nipako sīlasampanno, mamaṃ rakkhi tathāgato”ti. (apa. 1.2.83);

“As the blue jay guards its egg, or the yak its excellent tail; so the Wise One, endowed with virtue, the Tathāgata, protected me.”

Sāmaṇerapañhaṃ ayuttavacanapahānatthaṃ, idaṃ ambalaṭṭhikarāhulovādasuttaṃ sampajānamusāvādassa akaraṇatthaṃ vuttaṃ.

The Sāmaṇerapañha was spoken for the purpose of abandoning unsuitable speech. This Ambalaṭṭhikarāhulovādasutta was spoken for the purpose of not engaging in intentional false speech.

Tattha [V 3.0092] passasi noti passasi nu. Parittanti thokaṃ. Sāmaññanti samaṇadhammo. Nikkujjitvāti adhomukhaṃ katvā. Ukkujjitvāti uttānaṃ katvā.

Therein, 'passasi no' means 'passasi nu' (do you see?). 'Parittaṃ' means a little. 'Sāmaññaṃ' means the state of a recluse. 'Nikkujjitvā' means having turned it upside down. 'Ukkujjitvā' means having turned it right side up.

108. Seyyathāpi, rāhula, rañño nāgoti ayaṃ upamā sampajānamusāvāde saṃvararahitassa opammadassanatthaṃ vuttā. Tattha īsādantoti rathīsāsadisadanto[M 3.0090]. Uruḷhavāti abhivaḍḍhito ārohasampanno. Abhijātoti sujāto jātisampanno. Saṅgāmāvacaroti saṅgāmaṃ otiṇṇapubbo. Kammaṃ karotīti āgatāgate pavaṭṭento ghāteti. Puratthimakāyādīsu pana puratthimakāyena tāva paṭisenāya phalakakoṭṭhakamuṇḍapākārādayo pāteti, tathā pacchimakāyena. Sīsena kammaṃ nāma niyametvā etaṃ padesaṃ maddissāmīti nivattitvā oloketi, ettakena satampi sahassampi dvedhā bhijjati. Kaṇṇehi kammaṃ nāma āgatāgate sare kaṇṇehi paharitvā pātanaṃ. Dantehi kammaṃ nāma paṭihatthiassahatthārohaassārohapadādīnaṃ vijjhanaṃ. Naṅguṭṭhena kammaṃ [P 3.0128] nāma naṅguṭṭhe bandhāya dīghāsilaṭṭhiyā vā ayamusalena vā chedanabhedanaṃ. Rakkhateva soṇḍanti soṇḍaṃ pana mukhe pakkhipitvā rakkhati.

108. “Just as, Rāhula, a king's elephant”—this simile was spoken to show a comparison for one who is devoid of restraint in intentional lying. Therein, 'with tusks like chariot poles' means having tusks that resemble the poles of a chariot. 'Full-grown' means well-developed and fit to be ridden. 'High-born' means well-born, endowed with a noble lineage. 'Battle-hardened' means one who has previously entered battle. 'He performs his task' means he kills oncoming enemies by trampling them. Furthermore, with the front part of his body, he first knocks down the opposing army's plank-huts, watchtowers, and bare ramparts; likewise with the hind part of his body. The work done with the head is this: having resolved, 'I will crush this area,' he turns and looks, and by that alone a hundred or even a thousand are broken in two. The work done with the ears is the knocking down of oncoming arrows by striking them with his ears. The work done with the tusks is the piercing of opposing elephants, horses, elephant riders, horse riders, and foot soldiers. The work done with the tail is the cutting and breaking with a long sword-staff or an iron pestle tied to its tail. 'He protects his trunk' means he protects his trunk by placing it in his mouth.

Tatthāti tasmiṃ tassa hatthino karaṇe. Apariccattanti anissaṭṭhaṃ, paresaṃ jayaṃ amhākañca parājayaṃ passīti maññati. Soṇḍāyapi kammaṃ karotīti ayamuggaraṃ vā khadiramusalaṃ vā gahetvā samantā aṭṭhārasahatthaṭṭhānaṃ maddati. Pariccattanti vissaṭṭhaṃ, idāni hatthiyodhādīsu na kutoci bhāyati, amhākaṃ jayaṃ paresañca parājayaṃ passīti maññati. Nāhaṃ tassa kiñci pāpanti tassa dukkaṭādiāpattivītikkame vā mātughātakādikammesu vā kiñci pāpaṃ akattabbaṃ nāma natthi. Tasmā tiha teti yasmā sampajānamusāvādino akattabbaṃ pāpaṃ nāma natthi, tasmā tayā hasāyapi davakamyatāyapi musā na bhaṇissāmīti sikkhitabbaṃ. Paccavekkhaṇatthoti olokanattho, yaṃ mukhe vajjaṃ hoti, tassa dassanatthoti vuttaṃ hoti. Paccavekkhitvā paccavekkhitvāti oloketvā oloketvā.

Therein: this refers to that action of the elephant. 'Not relinquished' means not given up; the elephant rider thinks, 'He has not given up his life; he sees the victory of others and our defeat.' 'He also performs a task with his trunk' means taking an iron club or a pestle of acacia wood, he crushes the area of eighteen cubits all around. 'Relinquished' means given up; the elephant rider thinks, 'Now my elephant has given up its life. It fears nothing from any elephant-warrior and so on. It sees our victory and the defeat of others.' 'I say that there is no evil that he might not do' means for that person, whether in transgressing offenses starting with wrong-doing or in deeds such as matricide, there is no evil whatsoever that should not be done. Therefore, 'Therefore, you should train' means: since for one who tells a deliberate lie there is no evil that should not be done, therefore you should train yourself, thinking: 'I will not speak a lie, even for the sake of a laugh or for the sake of play.' 'For the purpose of reflection' means for the purpose of looking; it is said for the purpose of seeing whatever blemish is on the face. 'Having reflected again and again' means having looked again and again.

109. Sasakkaṃ na karaṇīyanti ekaṃseneva na kātabbaṃ. Paṭisaṃhareyyāsīti nivatteyyāsi mā kareyyāsi. Anupadajjeyyāsīti anupadeyyāsi upatthambheyyāsi punappunaṃ kareyyāsi. Ahorattānusikkhīti rattiñca divañca sikkhamāno.

109. 'It should not be done with attachment' means it should absolutely not be done. 'You should refrain' means you should turn back, you should not do it. 'You should follow it up' means you should pursue it, you should support it, you should do it again and again. 'Practicing day and night' means training both night and day.

111. Aṭṭīyitabbanti [V 3.0093][P 3.0129] aṭṭena pīḷitena bhavitabbaṃ. Harāyitabbanti lajjitabbaṃ. Jigucchitabbanti gūthaṃ disvā viya jigucchā uppādetabbā. Manokammassa pana adesanāvatthukattā idha desetabbanti na vuttaṃ. Kittake pana ṭhāne kāyakammavacīkammāni [M 3.0091] sodhetabbāni, kittake manokammanti. Kāyakammavacīkammāni tāva ekasmiṃ purebhatteyeva sodhetabbāni. Bhattakiccaṃ katvā divāṭṭhāne nisinnena hi paccavekkhitabbaṃ “aruṇuggamanato paṭṭhāya yāva imasmiṃ ṭhāne nisajjā atthi nu kho me imasmiṃ antare paresaṃ appiyaṃ kāyakammaṃ vā vacīkammaṃ vā”ti.
