Sace atthīti jānāti, desanāyuttaṃ desetabbaṃ, āvikaraṇayuttaṃ āvikātabbaṃ. Sace natthi, teneva pītipāmojjena vihātabbaṃ. Manokammaṃ pana etasmiṃ piṇḍapātapariyesanaṭṭhāne sodhetabbaṃ. Kathaṃ? “Atthi nu kho me ajja piṇḍapātapariyesanaṭṭhāne rūpādīsu chando vā rāgo vā paṭighaṃ vā”ti? Sace atthi, “puna na evaṃ karissāmī”ti citteneva adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ. Sace natthi, teneva pītipāmojjena vihātabbaṃ.

111. 'One should be distressed' means one should be afflicted by suffering. 'One should be ashamed' means one should feel shame. 'One should be disgusted' means disgust should be aroused, as if upon seeing excrement. However, since a mental action is not a basis for confession, it is not stated here that 'it should be confessed.' But in how many instances should bodily and verbal actions be purified, and in how many, mental actions? First, bodily and verbal actions should be purified on one occasion, that is, before the meal. For after finishing the meal and sitting in the daytime resting place, one should reflect: 'From sunrise until now, while sitting in this place, have I committed any bodily or verbal action displeasing to others in this interval?' If one knows there is, what is suitable for confession should be confessed, and what is suitable for disclosure should be disclosed. If there is none, one should dwell with that joy and gladness. Mental actions, however, should be purified in this place of seeking almsfood. How? 'Today, while seeking almsfood, did I have desire, or lust, or aversion toward forms, etc.?' If there was, one should resolve in one's mind: 'I will not do so again.' If there was none, one should dwell with that joy and gladness.

112. Samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vāti buddhā vā paccekabuddhā vā tathāgatasāvakā vā. Tasmātihāti yasmā atītepi evaṃ parisodhesuṃ, anāgatepi parisodhessanti, etarahipi parisodhenti, tasmā tumhehipi tesaṃ anusikkhantehi evaṃ sikkhitabbanti attho. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānameva. Imaṃ pana desanaṃ bhagavā yāva bhavaggā ussitassa ratanarāsino yojaniyamaṇikkhandhena kūṭaṃ gaṇhanto viya neyyapuggalavasena pariniṭṭhāpesīti.

112. Whether ascetics or brahmins—that is, Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, or disciples of the Tathāgata. 'Therefore, you should train' means: since in the past they also purified themselves thus, in the future they will purify themselves, and now also they purify themselves, therefore you too, learning from them, should train yourselves thus. This is the meaning. The rest is clear throughout. Moreover, the Blessed One brought this discourse to its conclusion for the sake of a person who needs guidance, as if placing the pinnacle on a heap of jewels piled as high as the apex of existence with a hundred-yojana-long mass of gems.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Ambalaṭṭhikarāhulovādasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Ambalaṭṭhikā Rāhulovāda Sutta is concluded.

2. Mahārāhulovādasuttavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Great Discourse on the Advice to Rāhula

113. Evaṃ [V 3.0094][P 3.0130] me sutanti mahārāhulovādasuttaṃ. Tattha piṭṭhito piṭṭhito anubandhīti dassanaṃ avijahitvā gamanaṃ abbocchinnaṃ katvā pacchato pacchato iriyāpathānubandhanena anubandhi. Tadā hi bhagavā pade padaṃ nikkhipanto vilāsitagamanena purato purato gacchati, rāhulatthero dasabalassa padānupadiko hutvā pacchato pacchato.

113. Thus have I heard—this is the Great Discourse on the Advice to Rāhula. Therein, 'following closely behind' means he followed in sequence with his mode of deportment from behind, going without abandoning the sight of him and making the movement continuous. Indeed, at that time, the Blessed One, placing one foot after another, went forward with a graceful gait, while the Elder Rāhula, treading in the footsteps of the Ten-Powered One, went closely behind.

Tattha bhagavā supupphitasālavanamajjhagato subhūmiotaraṇatthāya nikkhantamattavaravāraṇo viya virocittha, rāhulabhaddo ca varavāraṇassa pacchato [M 3.0092] nikkhantagajapotako viya. Bhagavā sāyanhasamaye maṇiguhato nikkhamitvā gocaraṃ paṭipanno kesarasīho viya, rāhulabhaddo ca sīhamigarājānaṃ anubandhanto nikkhantasīhapotako viya. Bhagavā maṇipabbatasassirikavanasaṇḍato dāṭhabalo mahābyaggho viya, rāhulabhaddo ca byaggharājānaṃ anubandhabyagghapotako viya. Bhagavā simbalidāyato nikkhantasupaṇṇarājā viya, rāhulabhaddo ca supaṇṇarājassa pacchato nikkhantasupaṇṇapotako viya. Bhagavā cittakūṭapabbatato gaganatalaṃ pakkhandasuvaṇṇahaṃsarājā viya, rāhulabhaddo ca haṃsādhipatiṃ anupakkhandahaṃsapotako viya. Bhagavā [P 3.0131] mahāsaraṃ ajjhogāḷhā suvaṇṇamahānāvā viya, rāhulabhaddo ca suvaṇṇanāvaṃ pacchā anubandhanāvāpotako viya. Bhagavā cakkaratanānubhāvena gaganatale sampayātacakkavattirājā viya, rāhulabhaddo ca rājānaṃ anusampayātapariṇāyakaratanaṃ viya. Bhagavā vigatavalāhakaṃ nabhaṃ paṭipannatārakarājā viya, rāhulabhaddo ca tārakādhipatino anumaggapaṭipannā parisuddhaosadhitārakā viya.

There, the Blessed One, having entered the middle of a fully blossomed sāla grove, shone like a magnificent, rutting, excellent elephant emerging to descend to good ground, and the good Rāhula was like a young elephant emerging behind the excellent elephant. The Blessed One, having emerged from the jewel cave in the evening and set out for his feeding ground, was like a maned lion, and the good Rāhula was like a young lion cub emerging, following the lion, the king of beasts. The Blessed One, from the glorious forest grove of the jewel mountain, was like a great tiger with powerful fangs, and the good Rāhula was like a young tiger following the tiger king. The Blessed One, emerging from the silk-cotton forest, was like the king of supaṇṇas, and the good Rāhula was like a young supaṇṇa emerging behind the supaṇṇa king. The Blessed One, soaring to the expanse of the sky from Cittakūṭa mountain, was like the king of golden haṃsas, and the good Rāhula was like a young haṃsa flying after the lord of haṃsas. The Blessed One, having entered a great lake, was like a great golden ship, and the good Rāhula was like a small boat following behind the golden ship. The Blessed One, traveling through the expanse of the sky by the power of the wheel-treasure, was like a wheel-turning king, and the good Rāhula was like the heir-apparent treasure following the king. The Blessed One, having entered the cloudless sky, was like the king of stars, and the good Rāhula was like the pure morning star following the path of the lord of stars.

Bhagavāpi mahāsammatapaveṇiyaṃ okkākarājavaṃse jāto, rāhulabhaddopi. Bhagavāpi saṅkhe pakkhittakhīrasadiso suparisuddhajātikhattiyakule jāto, rāhulabhaddopi. Bhagavāpi rajjaṃ pahāya pabbajito, rāhulabhaddopi. Bhagavatopi sarīraṃ dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ devanagaresu samussitaratanatoraṇaṃ viya sabbapāliphullo pāricchattako viya ca atimanoharaṇaṃ, rāhulabhaddassāpi. Iti dvepi abhinīhārasampannā, dvepi rājapabbajitā, dvepi khattiyasukhumālā, dvepi [V 3.0095] suvaṇṇavaṇṇā, dvepi lakkhaṇasampannā ekamaggaṃ paṭipannā paṭipāṭiyā gacchantānaṃ dvinnaṃ candamaṇḍalānaṃ dvinnaṃ sūriyamaṇḍalānaṃ dvinnaṃ sakkasuyāmasantusitasunimmitavasavattimahābrahmādīnaṃ siriyā siriṃ abhibhavamānā viya virociṃsu.

The Blessed One was also born in the lineage of the Okkāka kings, in the succession of Mahā Sammata, and so was the good Rāhula. The Blessed One was also born in a supremely pure Khattiya family, like milk placed in a conch shell, and so was the good Rāhula. The Blessed One also, having abandoned the kingdom, went forth, and so did the good Rāhula. The Blessed One's body was adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man, and was exceedingly captivating like a jeweled archway erected in a celestial city and like a pāricchattaka tree in full bloom; and so was the good Rāhula's. Thus, both were endowed with the perfection of aspiration, both were kings who had gone forth, both were delicate Khattiyas, both were of golden complexion, both were endowed with the marks. Having entered upon the same path, as they went in succession, they shone like two moon discs, two sun discs, as if overwhelming with their own glory the glory of two Sakkas, Suyāmas, Santusitas, Sunimmitas, Vasavattis, great Brahmās, and others.

Tatrāyasmā rāhulo bhagavato piṭṭhito piṭṭhito gacchantova pādatalato yāva upari kesantā tathāgataṃ ālokesi. So bhagavato buddhavesavilāsaṃ disvā “sobhati bhagavā dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇavicittasarīro byāmappabhāparikkhittatāya vippakiṇṇasuvaṇṇacuṇṇamajjhagato viya, vijjulatāparikkhitto [P 3.0132] kanakapabbato viya, yantasuttasamākaḍḍhitaratanavicittaṃ suvaṇṇaagghikaṃ viya, rattapaṃsukūlacīvarapaṭicchannopi rattakambalaparikkhittakanakapabbato viya, pavāḷalatāpaṭimaṇḍitaṃ suvaṇṇaagghikaṃ viya[M 3.0093], cīnapiṭṭhacuṇṇapūjitaṃ suvaṇṇacetiyaṃ viya, lākhārasānulitto kanakayūpo viya, rattavalāhakantarato taṅkhaṇabbhuggatapuṇṇacando viya, aho samatiṃsapāramitānubhāvasajjitassa attabhāvassa sirīsampattī”ti cintesi. Tato attānampi oloketvā – “ahampi sobhāmi. Sace bhagavā catūsu mahādīpesu cakkavattirajjaṃ akarissā, mayhaṃ pariṇāyakaṭṭhānantaraṃ adassā. Evaṃ sante ativiya jambudīpatalaṃ asobhissā”ti attabhāvaṃ nissāya gehassitaṃ chandarāgaṃ uppādesi.

There the Venerable Rāhula, while going closely behind the Blessed One, gazed upon the Tathāgata from the sole of his foot up to the tip of his hair. Seeing the graceful beauty of the Blessed One's appearance as a Buddha, he thought: 'The Blessed One is beautiful, his body variegated with the thirty-two marks of a great man, surrounded by a fathom-wide aura, like one in the midst of scattered golden powder, like a golden mountain encircled by lightning creepers, like a golden shrine variegated with jewels and well-drawn by mechanical strings; though covered with a red dust-heap robe, he is like a golden mountain encircled by a red blanket, like a golden shrine adorned with coral creepers, like a golden cetiya honored with powder of China clay and vermilion, like a golden sacrificial post anointed with lac resin, like the full moon just emerged from within a red cloud. Ah, the glorious attainment of a personal existence prepared by the power of the thirty perfections!' Then, looking at himself as well, he thought: 'I too am beautiful. If the Blessed One were to exercise wheel-turning kingship over the four great continents, he would give me the special position of heir-apparent. In that case, the surface of Jambudīpa would be exceedingly splendid!' Thus, based on his own person, he generated desire and lust connected with household life.

Bhagavāpi purato gacchantova cintesi – “paripuṇṇacchavimaṃsalohito dāni rāhulassa attabhāvo. Rajanīyesu rūpārammaṇādīsu hi cittassa pakkhandanakālo jāto, kiṃ bahulatāya nu kho rāhulo vītināmetī”ti. Atha sahāvajjaneneva pasannaudake macchaṃ viya, parisuddhe ādāsamaṇḍale mukhanimittaṃ viya ca tassa taṃ cittuppādaṃ addasa. Disvāva – “ayaṃ rāhulo mayhaṃ atrajo hutvā mama pacchato āgacchanto ‘ahaṃ sobhāmi, mayhaṃ vaṇṇāyatanaṃ pasanna’nti attabhāvaṃ nissāya gehassitachandarāgaṃ uppādeti, atitthe pakkhando uppathaṃ paṭipanno agocare carati, disāmūḷhaaddhiko viya agantabbaṃ disaṃ gacchati. Ayaṃ kho panassa kileso abbhantare vaḍḍhanto attatthampi yathābhūtaṃ passituṃ na dassati, paratthampi, ubhayatthampi. Tato nirayepi paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhāpessati, tiracchānayoniyampi, pettivisayepi, asurakāyepi, sambādhepi mātukucchisminti anamatagge saṃsāravaṭṭe paripātessati. Ayañhi –

The Blessed One, while going in front, also thought: 'Now Rāhula's personal existence is complete with skin, flesh, and blood. Indeed, the time has come for his mind to rush into desirable objects such as visible forms. With what, I wonder, does Rāhula mostly pass his time?' Then, just with that adverting, like seeing a fish in clear water or the reflection of a face in a pure mirror disc, he saw that thought-arising of his. Having seen it, he thought: 'This Rāhula, being my own-born son and coming behind me, is generating desire and lust connected with household life based on his own person, thinking, "I am beautiful, my complexion is pleasing." He is rushing into an improper ford, has entered a wrong path, and wanders in a non-pasturing ground. Like a traveler who has lost their way, he goes in a direction he should not go. Indeed, this defilement of his, growing within, will not allow him to see his own welfare as it really is, nor others' welfare, nor the welfare of both. From that, it will cause him to take rebirth in hell, in the animal realm, in the sphere of ghosts, in the body of asuras, and in a cramped mother's womb, and will cause him to fall into the round of saṃsāra with its unknown beginning. For indeed—'

Anatthajanano [V 3.0096][P 3.0133] lobho, lobho cittappakopano;

Bhayamantarato jātaṃ, taṃ jano nāvabujjhati.

Greed is a generator of harm, greed is a corrupter of the mind; fear is born from within, that the people do not understand.

Luddho atthaṃ na jānāti, luddho dhammaṃ na passati;

Andhatamaṃ tadā hoti, yaṃ lobho sahate naraṃ. (itivu. 88) –

A greedy person does not know what is beneficial, a greedy person does not see the Dhamma; at that time there is blinding darkness, when greed overcomes a person.

Yathā kho pana anekaratanapūrā mahānāvā bhinnaphalakantarena udakaṃ ādiyamānā muhuttampi na ajjhupekkhitabbā hoti, vegenassā vivaraṃ pidahituṃ vaṭṭati, evamevaṃ ayampi na ajjhupekkhitabbo. Yāvassa ayaṃ kileso abbhantare sīlaratanādīni na vināseti, tāvadeva naṃ niggaṇhissāmī”ti ajjhāsayamakāsi. Evarūpesu pana ṭhānesu buddhānaṃ nāgavilokanaṃ [M 3.0094] nāma hoti. Tasmā yantena parivattitasuvaṇṇapaṭimā viya sakalakāyeneva parivattetvā ṭhito rāhulabhaddaṃ āmantesi. Taṃ sandhāya “atha kho bhagavā apaloketvā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Indeed, just as a great ship filled with many treasures, taking in water through a cracked plank, should not be neglected even for a moment, but it is proper to quickly block its opening; even so, this defilement should not be neglected. 'Before this defilement within destroys the treasures of virtue and so forth, I shall restrain it,' thus he made the resolution. Now, in such situations, there is for the Buddhas what is called the 'elephant's glance.' Therefore, like a golden statue turned by a mechanism, having turned with his entire body, he stood and addressed the good Rāhula. With reference to that, it was said: 'Then, indeed, the Blessed One, having looked back...' and so forth.

Tattha yaṃkiñci rūpantiādīni sabbākārena visuddhimagge khandhaniddese vitthāritāni. Netaṃ mamātiādīni mahāhatthipadopame vuttāni. Rūpameva nu kho bhagavāti kasmā pucchati? Tassa kira – “sabbaṃ rūpaṃ netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi na meso attā”ti sutvā – “bhagavā sabbaṃ rūpaṃ vipassanāpaññāya evaṃ daṭṭhabbanti vadati, vedanādīsu nu kho kathaṃ paṭipajjitabba”nti nayo udapādi. Tasmā tasmiṃ naye ṭhito pucchati. Nayakusalo hesa āyasmā rāhulo, idaṃ na kattabbanti [P 3.0134] vutte idampi na kattabbaṃ idampi na kattabbamevāti nayasatenapi nayasahassenapi paṭivijjhati. Idaṃ kattabbanti vuttepi eseva nayo.

Therein, the words beginning with 'whatever form' have been explained in full detail in the Visuddhimagga, in the exposition of the aggregates. The words beginning with 'This is not mine' are stated in the Mahāhatthipadopama Sutta. Why did he ask, 'Is it only form, Blessed One?' It is said that for him, having heard, 'All form is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self,' this line of reasoning arose: 'The Blessed One says all form should be seen thus with insight-wisdom, but how then should one practice with regard to feeling and so forth?' Therefore, standing on that line of reasoning, he asked. For this Venerable Rāhula is skilled in reasoning. When it is said, 'This should not be done,' he penetrates by a hundred or a thousand lines of reasoning that this also should not be done, and that also should not be done. When it is said, 'This should be done,' this is the same line of reasoning.

Sikkhākāmo hi ayaṃ āyasmā, pātova gandhakuṭipariveṇe patthamattaṃ vālikaṃ okirati – “ajja sammāsambuddhassa santikā mayhaṃ upajjhāyassa santikā ettakaṃ ovādaṃ ettakaṃ paribhāsaṃ labhāmī”ti. Sammāsambuddhopi naṃ etadagge ṭhapento – “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhākāmānaṃ yadidaṃ rāhulo”ti (a. ni. 1.209) sikkhāyameva aggaṃ katvā ṭhapesi. Sopi āyasmā bhikkhusaṅghamajjhe tameva sīhanādaṃ nadi –

For this venerable one is indeed desirous of training. Early in the morning, he scatters a measure of sand in the perfumed chamber’s enclosure, thinking, “Today, may I receive this much advice and this much admonishment from the Perfectly Enlightened One and from my preceptor.” The Perfectly Enlightened One, placing him foremost in this, declared, “Monks, among my monk disciples who are desirous of training, Rāhula is the foremost” (AN 1.209), thus establishing him as foremost in the training itself. And that venerable one, amidst the community of monks, uttered that very lion’s roar:

“Sabbametaṃ [V 3.0097] abhiññāya, dhammarājā pitā mama;

Sammukhā bhikkhusaṅghassa, etadagge ṭhapesi maṃ.

“Having known all this through direct knowledge, the King of Dhamma, my father, in the presence of the community of monks, established me in this foremost position.”

Sikkhākāmānahaṃ aggo, dhammarājena thomito;

Saddhāpabbajitānañca, sahāyo pavaro mama.

“I am the foremost of those desirous of training, praised by the King of Dhamma; and among those gone forth through faith, my companion is the most excellent.”

Dhammarājā pitā mayhaṃ, dhammārakkho ca pettiyo;

Sāriputto upajjhāyo, sabbaṃ me jinasāsana”nti.

“The King of Dhamma is my father, the guardian of the Dhamma my paternal uncle, and Sāriputta my preceptor; through them I have the entire teaching of the Victor.”

Athassa bhagavā yasmā na kevalaṃ rūpameva, vedanādayopi evaṃ daṭṭhabbā, tasmā rūpampi rāhulātiādimāha. Ko najjāti ko nu ajja. Therassa kira etadahosi “sammāsambuddho mayhaṃ attabhāvanissitaṃ chandarāgaṃ ñatvā ‘samaṇena nāma evarūpo vitakko na vitakkitabbo’ti neva pariyāyena kathaṃ kathesi, gaccha bhikkhu rāhulaṃ vadehi [M 3.0095] ‘mā puna evarūpaṃ vitakkaṃ vitakkesī’ti na dūtaṃ pesesi. Maṃ sammukkhe ṭhatvāyeva pana sabhaṇḍakaṃ coraṃ cūḷāya gaṇhanto viya sammukhā sugatovādaṃ adāsi. Sugatovādo ca nāma asaṅkheyyehipi kappehi dullabho. Evarūpassa buddhassa sammukhā ovādaṃ labhitvā ko nu [P 3.0135] viññū paṇḍitajātiko ajja gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pavisissatī”ti. Athesa āyasmā āhārakiccaṃ pahāya yasmiṃ nisinnaṭṭhāne ṭhitena ovādo laddho, tatova paṭinivattetvā aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle nisīdi. Bhagavāpi taṃ āyasmantaṃ nivattamānaṃ disvā na evamāha – “mā nivatta tāva, rāhula, bhikkhācārakālo te”ti. Kasmā? Evaṃ kirassa ahosi – “ajja tāva kāyagatāsatiamatabhojanaṃ bhuñjatū”ti.

Then, because not only form, but also feeling and so forth should be seen in this way, the Blessed One said, 'Rāhula, form also...' and so forth. The gloss ‘ko najja’ means ‘ko nu ajja’. It is said that this thought occurred to the elder: “The Perfectly Enlightened One, knowing the lustful desire connected with my personality, did not speak indirectly, saying, ‘Such a thought should not be thought by a monk,’ nor did he send a messenger, saying, ‘Go, monk, tell Rāhula, “Do not think such a thought again.”’ Rather, standing right in my presence, like one seizing a thief with his stolen goods by the topknot, he gave the instruction of the Well-Gone One face to face. And an instruction from the Well-Gone One is difficult to obtain even in countless aeons. Having received such an instruction in the presence of such a Buddha, what wise and intelligent person would today enter the village for alms?” Then this venerable one, having given up the business of food, returned from that very spot where he had received the instruction while he was there, and sat down at the foot of a certain tree. The Blessed One, seeing that venerable one returning, did not say, “Do not return yet, Rāhula, it is time for your alms-round.” Why? It is said that this thought occurred to him: “Today, let him first partake of the deathless food of mindfulness directed to the body.”

Addasā kho āyasmā sāriputtoti bhagavati gate pacchā gacchanto addasa. Etassa kirāyasmato ekakassa viharato aññaṃ vattaṃ, bhagavatā saddhiṃ viharato aññaṃ. Yadā hi dve aggasāvakā ekākino vasanti, tadā pātova senāsanaṃ sammajjitvā sarīrapaṭijagganaṃ katvā samāpattiṃ appetvā sannisinnā attano cittaruciyā bhikkhācāraṃ gacchanti. Bhagavatā saddhiṃ viharantā pana therā evaṃ na karonti. Tadā hi bhagavā bhikkhusaṅghaparivāro paṭhamaṃ bhikkhācāraṃ gacchati. Tasmiṃ gate thero attano senāsanā nikkhamitvā – “bahūnaṃ vasanaṭṭhāne nāma sabbeva pāsādikaṃ [V 3.0098] kātuṃ sakkonti vā, na vā sakkontī”ti tattha tattha gantvā asammaṭṭhaṃ ṭhānaṃ sammajjati. Sace kacavaro achaḍḍito hoti, taṃ chaḍḍeti. Pānīyaṭṭhapetabbaṭṭhānamhi pānīyakūṭe asati pānīyaghaṭaṃ ṭhapeti. Gilānānaṃ santikaṃ gantvā, “āvuso, tumhākaṃ kiṃ āharāmi, kiṃ vo icchitabba”nti? Pucchati. Avassikadaharānaṃ santikaṃ gantvā – “abhiramatha, āvuso, mā ukkaṇṭhittha, paṭipattisārakaṃ buddhasāsana”nti ovadati. Evaṃ katvā sabbapacchā bhikkhācāraṃ gacchati. Yathā [P 3.0136] hi cakkavatti kuhiñci gantukāmo senāya parivārito paṭhamaṃ nikkhamati, pariṇāyakaratanaṃ senaṅgāni saṃvidhāya pacchā nikkhamati, evaṃ saddhammacakkavatti bhagavā bhikkhusaṅghaparivāro paṭhamaṃ nikkhamati, tassa bhagavato pariṇāyakaratanabhūto dhammasenāpati imaṃ kiccaṃ katvā sabbapacchā nikkhamati. So evaṃ nikkhanto tasmiṃ divase aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle nisinnaṃ rāhulabhaddaṃ addasa. Tena vuttaṃ “pacchā gacchanto addasā”ti.

The phrase ‘Addasā kho āyasmā sāriputto’ means: the Venerable Sāriputta, going behind after the Blessed One had departed, saw him. For this venerable one, it is said, there is one set of duties when dwelling alone, and another when dwelling with the Blessed One. When the two chief disciples dwell by themselves, they sweep their lodgings early in the morning, attend to their bodies, enter an attainment, and having sat down together, they go for alms according to their own inclination. But when dwelling with the Blessed One, the Elders do not act thus. For then, the Blessed One, surrounded by the community of monks, goes for alms first. After He has gone, the Elder departs from his own lodging and thinks, “In a place where many reside, are all able to make it pleasant, or are they not?” Going here and there, he sweeps any unswept place. If there is rubbish that has not been discarded, he removes it. If there is no water pitcher in the place where drinking water should be set, he places a water pot there. He approaches the sick monks and asks, “Friends, what shall I bring for you? What do you desire?” He goes to the young monks who have not yet completed a rains-retreat and advises them, “Take delight, friends, do not be discontented. The teaching of the Buddha has practice as its essence.” Having done this, he goes for alms after everyone else. Just as a wheel-turning monarch, wishing to go somewhere, departs first surrounded by his army, while the commander-jewel arranges the army divisions and departs afterwards, so too the Blessed One, the wheel-turning monarch of the true Dhamma, departs first surrounded by the community of monks, while the General of the Dhamma, who is the commander-jewel of the Blessed One, performs these duties and departs after everyone else. He, having departed thus, on that day saw the good Rāhula seated at the foot of a certain tree. Therefore it was said, “going behind, he saw.”

Atha [M 3.0096] kasmā ānāpānassatiyaṃ niyojesi? Nisajjānucchavikattā. Thero kira “etassa bhagavatā rūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ kathita”nti anāvajjitvāva yenākārena ayaṃ acalo anobaddho hutvā nisinno, idamassa etissā nisajjāya kammaṭṭhānaṃ anucchavikanti cintetvā evamāha. Tattha ānāpānassatinti assāsapassāse pariggahetvā tattha catukkapañcakajjhānaṃ nibbattetvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ gaṇhāhīti dasseti.

Then why did he enjoin him in mindfulness of breathing? Because of the suitability of his sitting posture. The Elder, it is said, without reflecting, “The Blessed One has taught him the meditation subject of form,” but simply thinking, “The manner in which this one sits, motionless and unattached—for this sitting posture of his, this meditation subject is suitable,” spoke thus. Therein, by ‘mindfulness of breathing,’ he indicates this meaning: “Having comprehended the in-breaths and out-breaths, and based on them, having produced the fourth jhana of the fourfold system or the fifth of the fivefold system, having developed insight, attain Arahantship.”

Mahapphalā hotīti kīvamahapphalā hoti? Idha bhikkhu ānāpānassatiṃ anuyutto ekāsane nisinnova sabbāsave khepetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, tathā asakkonto maraṇakāle samasīsī hoti, tathā asakkonto devaloke nibbattitvā dhammakathikadevaputtassa dhammaṃ sutvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, tato viraddho anuppanne buddhuppāde paccekabodhiṃ sacchikaroti, taṃ asacchikaronto buddhānaṃ sammukhībhāve bāhiyattherādayo viya khippābhiñño hoti, evaṃ mahapphalā. Mahānisaṃsāti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

When it is said, 'It is of great fruit,' how great is its fruit? Here, a monk devoted to mindfulness of breathing, while still sitting on a single seat, having eradicated all the taints, attains Arahantship. If unable to do so, at the time of death, he becomes a samasīsī. If unable to do so, having been reborn in a deva world, he attains Arahantship after hearing the Dhamma from a Dhamma-preaching devaputta. Failing that, when a Buddha has not arisen, he realizes the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha. Not realizing that, in the presence of Buddhas, he becomes one of swift insight, like the Elder Bāhiya and others. Thus, it is of great fruit. 'Of great benefit' is a synonym for that very term. And this has also been said:

“Ānāpānassatī [P 3.0137] yassa, paripuṇṇā subhāvitā;

Anupubbaṃ paricitā, yathā buddhena desitā;

Somaṃ lokaṃ pabhāseti, abbhā muttova candimā”ti. (theragā. 548; paṭi. ma. 1.1.60) –

“One for whom mindfulness of breathing is complete and well-developed, practiced in sequence as taught by the Buddha—that one illuminates this world like the moon freed from a cloud.”

Imaṃ [V 3.0099] mahapphalataṃ sampassamāno thero saddhivihārikaṃ tattha niyojeti.

Seeing this great fruitfulness, the Elder enjoined his co-resident in that practice.

Iti bhagavā rūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ, thero ānāpānassatinti ubhopi kammaṭṭhānaṃ ācikkhitvā gatā, rāhulabhaddo vihāreyeva ohīno. Bhagavā tassa ohīnabhāvaṃ jānantopi neva attanā khādanīyaṃ bhojanīyaṃ gahetvā agamāsi, na ānandattherassa hatthe pesesi, na pasenadimahārājaanāthapiṇḍikādīnaṃ saññaṃ adāsi. Saññāmattakañhi labhitvā te kājabhattaṃ abhihareyyuṃ. Yathā ca bhagavā, evaṃ sāriputtattheropi na kiñci akāsi. Rāhulatthero nirāhāro chinnabhatto ahosi. Tassa panāyasmato – “bhagavā maṃ vihāre ohīnaṃ jānantopi attanā laddhapiṇḍapātaṃ nāpi sayaṃ gahetvā āgato, na aññassa hatthe pahiṇi[M 3.0097], na manussānaṃ saññaṃ adāsi, upajjhāyopi me ohīnabhāvaṃ jānanto tatheva na kiñci akāsī”ti cittampi na uppannaṃ, kuto tappaccayā omānaṃ vā atimānaṃ vā janessati. Bhagavatā pana ācikkhitakammaṭṭhānameva purebhattampi pacchābhattampi – “itipi rūpaṃ aniccaṃ, itipi dukkhaṃ, itipi asubhaṃ, itipi anattā”ti aggiṃ abhimatthento viya nirantaraṃ manasikatvā sāyanhasamaye cintesi – “ahaṃ upajjhāyena ānāpānassatiṃ bhāvehīti vutto[P 3.0138], tassa vacanaṃ na karissāmi. Ācariyupajjhāyānañhi vacanaṃ akaronto dubbaco nāma hoti. ‘Dubbaco rāhulo, upajjhāyassapi vacanaṃ na karotī’ti ca garahuppattito kakkhaḷatarā pīḷā nāma natthī”ti bhāvanāvidhānaṃ pucchitukāmo bhagavato santikaṃ agamāsi. Taṃ dassetuṃ atha kho āyasmā rāhulotiādi vuttaṃ.

Thus, the Blessed One taught the meditation subject of form, and the Elder taught mindfulness of breathing. Both, having taught a meditation subject, departed, while the good Rāhula was left behind in the monastery. Although the Blessed One knew he had been left behind, he neither went himself taking food, nor sent any by the hand of the Elder Ānanda, nor did he give a sign to King Pasenadi, Anāthapiṇḍika, or others. For had they received just a sign, they would have brought food carried on shoulder poles. And just as the Blessed One did, so too the Elder Sāriputta did nothing. The Elder Rāhula was without food, his meal cut off. Yet for that venerable one, not even the thought arose: “The Blessed One, though knowing I was left behind in the monastery, neither came himself bringing the almsfood he had received, nor sent it by the hand of another, nor gave a sign to the people. My preceptor, too, knowing I was left behind, likewise did nothing.” How, on account of that, could inferiority-conceit or superiority-conceit arise? Rather, both before and after the meal, he continuously gave attention to the very meditation subject taught by the Blessed One—“Thus, form is impermanent; thus, it is suffering; thus, it is non-beautiful; thus, it is not-self”—like one striking fire without pause. In the evening, he thought: “I was told by my preceptor, ‘Develop mindfulness of breathing.’ I shall act on his word. For one who does not follow the word of teachers and preceptors is called ‘one who is difficult to admonish.’ And there is no affliction harsher than the arising of the reproach: ‘Rāhula is difficult to admonish; he does not follow even his preceptor’s word.’” Wishing to ask about the method of development, he went to the Blessed One. To show this, the passage beginning, “Then the Venerable Rāhula…” was spoken.

114. Tattha paṭisallānāti ekībhāvato. Yaṃkiñci rāhulāti kasmā? Bhagavā ānāpānassatiṃ puṭṭho rūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ kathetīti. Rūpe chandarāgappahānatthaṃ. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi – “rāhulassa attabhāvaṃ nissāya chandarāgo uppanno, heṭṭhā cassa saṅkhepena rūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ kathitaṃ. Idānissāpi dvicattālīsāya ākārehi attabhāvaṃ virājetvā visaṅkharitvā taṃnissitaṃ chandarāgaṃ anuppattidhammataṃ āpādessāmī”ti. Atha ākāsadhātuṃ kasmā vitthāresīti? Upādārūpadassanatthaṃ. Heṭṭhā hi cattāri mahābhūtāneva kathitāni, na upādārūpaṃ. Tasmā iminā mukhena taṃ dassetuṃ ākāsadhātuṃ vitthāresi. Apica ajjhattikena ākāsena paricchinnarūpampi pākaṭaṃ hoti.

114. Herein, seclusion means from being solitary. Regarding the words, whatever, Rāhula: Why does the Blessed One, when asked about mindfulness of breathing, teach the meditation subject of form? He teaches for the purpose of abandoning desire and lust for form. It is said that this thought occurred to him: ‘For Rāhula, desire and lust have arisen dependent on his personality. And previously, the meditation subject of form was taught to him in brief. Now, by means of forty-two aspects, having made him dispassionate towards his personality and having dismantled it, I will bring the desire and lust dependent on it to a state where it has the nature of not arising again.’ Then why did he elaborate on the space element? For the purpose of showing derived form. For previously, only the four great elements were taught, not derived form. Therefore, he elaborated on the space element as a means to show that. Moreover, through the internal space element, delimited form also becomes evident.

Ākāsena [V 3.0100] paricchinnaṃ, rūpaṃ yāti vibhūtataṃ;

Tassevaṃ āvibhāvatthaṃ, taṃ pakāsesi nāyako.

Delimited by space, form attains manifestation; for the purpose of its manifestation thus, the Leader revealed that.

Ettha [P 3.0139] pana purimāsu tāva catūsu dhātūsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ mahāhatthipadopame vuttameva.

Here, regarding the first four elements, what needs to be said has already been stated in the Greater Discourse on the Simile of the Elephant's Footprint.

118. Ākāsadhātuyaṃ ākāsagatanti ākāsabhāvaṃ gataṃ. Upādinnantiādinnaṃ gahitaṃ parāmaṭṭhaṃ, sarīraṭṭhakanti attho. Kaṇṇacchiddanti maṃsalohitādīhi asamphuṭṭhakaṇṇavivaraṃ. Nāsacchiddādīsupi eseva nayo. Yena [M 3.0098] cāti yena chiddena. Ajjhoharatīti anto paveseti, jivhābandhanato hi yāva udarapaṭalā manussānaṃ vidatthicaturaṅgulaṃ chiddaṭṭhānaṃ hoti. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Yattha cāti yasmiṃ okāse. Santiṭṭhatīti patiṭṭhāti. Manussānañhi mahantaṃ paṭaparissāvanamattañca udarapaṭalaṃ nāma hoti. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Adhobhāgaṃ nikkhamatīti yena heṭṭhā nikkhamati. Dvattiṃsahatthamattaṃ ekavīsatiyā ṭhānesu vaṅkaṃ antaṃ nāma hoti. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Yaṃ vā panaññampīti iminā sukhumasukhumaṃ cammamaṃsādiantaragatañceva lomakūpabhāvena ca ṭhitaṃ ākāsaṃ dasseti. Sesametthāpi pathavīdhātuādīsu vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

118. In the section on the space element: gone to space means gone to the state of space. Grasped means taken up, grasped, and touched by craving and views; the meaning is the fourfold-originated matter located in the body. The ear-opening means the ear cavity not touched by flesh, blood, and so on. This same method should be understood for the nostril-opening and so on. And by which means by which opening. One swallows means one causes to enter inside; for from the root of the tongue up to the stomach lining, there is for humans an opening-place of a span and four fingers. This was said referring to that. And where means in which place. It remains means it is established. For humans, there is what is called the stomach lining, which is large, about the size of a cloth water-strainer. This was said referring to that. It exits from the lower part means by which it exits downwards. There is what is called the coiled intestine, which is thirty-two cubits long and bent in twenty-one places. This was said referring to that. By the phrase or whatever other, he shows the very subtle space that has gone inside skin, flesh, and so on, and the space that exists as hair-follicles. The remainder here should also be understood in the same way as was stated for the earth element and so on.

119. Idānissa tādibhāvalakkhaṇaṃ ācikkhanto pathavīsamantiādimāha. Iṭṭhāniṭṭhesu hi arajjanto adussanto tādī nāma hoti. Manāpāmanāpāti [P 3.0140] ettha aṭṭha lobhasahagatacittasampayuttā manāpā nāma, dve domanassacittasampayuttā amanāpā nāma. Cittaṃ na pariyādāya ṭhassantīti ete phassā uppajjitvā tava cittaṃ antomuṭṭhigataṃ karonto viya pariyādāya gahetvā ṭhātuṃ na sakkhissanti “ahaṃ sobhāmi, mayhaṃ vaṇṇāyatanaṃ pasanna”nti puna attabhāvaṃ nissāya chandarāgo nuppajjissati. Gūthagatantiādīsu gūthameva gūthagataṃ. Evaṃ sabbattha.

119. Now, explaining to him the characteristic of the state of being steadfast, he spoke the words beginning with like the earth. For one who is not attached to the agreeable and disagreeable, who is not resentful, is called a ‘tādī’ (one who is steadfast). Herein, regarding agreeable and disagreeable contacts: the eight types associated with consciousness accompanied by greed are called ‘agreeable’; the two types associated with consciousness accompanied by displeasure are called ‘disagreeable’. They will not overwhelm and take control of the mind means: these contacts, having arisen, will not be able to overwhelm and seize your mind and remain, as if making it something held inside a fist. Desire and lust, dependent on the personality, will not arise again with the thought, ‘I am beautiful, my complexion is clear.’ In phrases such as gūthagata (related to excrement), it is the excrement itself that is meant. This should be understood similarly in all cases.

Na katthaci patiṭṭhitoti pathavīpabbatarukkhādīsu ekasmimpi na patiṭṭhito, yadi hi pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhito bhaveyya, pathaviyā bhijjamānāya saheva bhijjeyya, pabbate patamāne saheva pateyya, rukkhe chijjamāne saheva chijjeyya.

Not established anywhere means not established in even one thing among earth, mountains, trees, and so on. For if it were established on the earth, when the earth breaks apart, it would break apart together with it. When a mountain falls, it would fall together with it. When a tree is cut, it would be cut together with it.

120. Mettaṃ [V 3.0101] rāhulāti kasmā ārabhi? Tādibhāvassa kāraṇadassanatthaṃ. Heṭṭhā hi tādibhāvalakkhaṇaṃ dassitaṃ, na ca sakkā ahaṃ tādī homīti akāraṇā bhavituṃ, napi “ahaṃ uccākulappasuto bahussuto lābhī, maṃ rājarājamahāmattādayo bhajanti, ahaṃ tādī homī”ti imehi kāraṇehi koci tādī nāma hoti, mettādibhāvanāya pana hotīti tādibhāvassa kāraṇadassanatthaṃ imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi.

120. Why did he begin the teaching with 'Loving-kindness, Rāhula?' To show the cause for the state of being steadfast. For previously, the characteristic of the state of being steadfast was shown, and it is not possible to become steadfast without a cause. Nor does anyone become what is called steadfast by such reasons as, 'I am of high birth, I am very learned, I am a recipient of gains, and kings, royal ministers, and others attend on me; I am steadfast.' Rather, one becomes so through the development of loving-kindness and so on. Thus, to show the cause for the state of being steadfast, he began this teaching.

Tattha [M 3.0099] bhāvayatoti upacāraṃ vā appanaṃ vā pāpentassa. Yo byāpādoti yo satte kopo, so pahīyissati. Vihesāti pāṇiādīhi sattānaṃ vihiṃsanaṃ. Aratīti pantasenāsanesu ceva adhikusaladhammesu ca ukkaṇṭhitatā. Paṭighoti yattha katthaci sattesu saṅkhāresu ca paṭihaññanakileso. Asubhanti [P 3.0141] uddhumātakādīsu upacārappanaṃ. Uddhumātakādīsu asubhabhāvanā ca nāmesā vitthārato visuddhimagge kathitāva. Rāgoti pañcakāmaguṇikarāgo. Aniccasaññanti aniccānupassanāya sahajātasaññaṃ. Vipassanā eva vā esā asaññāpi saññāsīsena saññāti vuttā. Asmimānoti rūpādīsu asmīti māno.

Herein, 'for one who develops' means for one who is attaining either access concentration or absorption concentration. 'Whatever ill will' means whatever anger there is towards beings, that will be abandoned. 'Cruelty' means the harming of beings with one's hands and so on. 'Discontent' means dissatisfaction with remote dwellings and with higher wholesome states. 'Aversion' is the defilement of striking against beings and formations anywhere whatsoever. 'The unlovely' means the access and absorption concentration that occurs in relation to the bloated corpse and so on. And this, the development of the unlovely in relation to the bloated corpse and so on, has already been explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga. 'Lust' is the lust that has the five strands of sensual pleasure as its object. 'The perception of impermanence' is the perception that arises together with the contemplation of impermanence. Or, insight-wisdom itself, although it is not perception, is called 'perception' with perception as the chief factor. 'The conceit “I am”' is the conceit 'I am' in regard to form and so on.

121. Idāni therena pucchitaṃ pañhaṃ vitthārento ānāpānassatintiādimāha. Tattha idaṃ kammaṭṭhānañca kammaṭṭhānabhāvanā ca pāḷiattho ca saddhiṃ ānisaṃsakathāya sabbo sabbākārena visuddhimagge anussatiniddese vitthāritoyeva. Imaṃ desanaṃ bhagavā neyyapuggalavaseneva pariniṭṭhāpesīti.

121. Now, elaborating on the question asked by the Elder, he spoke the words beginning with 'mindfulness of breathing.' Therein, this meditation subject, the development of the meditation subject, the meaning of the Pāli, together with the discourse on its benefits—all this has already been elaborated in every way in the Visuddhimagga, in the section on the recollections. The Blessed One concluded this teaching only on account of a person to be guided.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Māhārāhulovādasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Mahārāhulovāda Sutta is completed.

3. Cūḷamālukyasuttavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Cūḷamālukya Sutta

122. Evaṃ [V 3.0102] me sutanti mālukyasuttaṃ. Tattha mālukyaputtassāti evaṃnāmakassa therassa. Ṭhapitāni paṭikkhittānīti diṭṭhigatāni nāma na byākātabbānīti evaṃ ṭhapitāni ceva paṭikkhittāni ca. Tathāgatoti satto. Taṃ me na ruccatīti taṃ abyākaraṇaṃ mayhaṃ na ruccati. Sikkhaṃ [P 3.0142] paccakkhāyāti sikkhaṃ paṭikkhipitvā.

122. The sutta beginning with 'Thus have I heard' is the Cūḷamālukya Sutta. Therein, 'of Mālukyaputta' means: of the elder of that name. 'Set aside and rejected' means: wrong views should not be declared; thus they are both set aside and rejected. 'The Tathāgata' means: a being. 'That does not please me' means: that non-declaration does not please me. 'Having renounced the training' means: having rejected the training.

125. Ko santo kaṃ paccācikkhasīti yācako vā hi yācitakaṃ paccācikkheyya, yācitako vā yācakaṃ. Tvaṃ neva yācako na yācitako, so dāni tvaṃ ko santo kaṃ paccācikkhasīti attho.

125. 'Being who, whom do you renounce?' means: for a requester might renounce one who is asked, or one who is asked might renounce a requester. You are neither a requester nor one who is asked. So now, being who, whom do you renounce? This is the meaning.

126. Viddho [M 3.0100] assāti parasenāya ṭhitena viddho bhaveyya. Gāḷhapalepanenāti bahalalepanena. Bhisakkanti vejjaṃ. Sallakattanti sallakantanaṃ sallakantiyasuttavācakaṃ. Akkassāti akkavāke gahetvā jiyaṃ karonti. Tena vuttaṃ “akkassā”ti. Saṇhassāti veṇuvilīvassa. Maruvākhīrapaṇṇīnampi vākehiyeva karonti. Tena vuttaṃ yadi vā maruvāya yadi vā khīrapaṇṇinoti. Gacchanti pabbatagacchanadīgacchādīsu jātaṃ. Ropimanti ropetvā vaḍḍhitaṃ saravanato saraṃ gahetvā kataṃ. Sithilahanunoti evaṃnāmakassa pakkhino. Bheravassāti kāḷasīhassa. Semhārassāti makkaṭassa. Evaṃ noti etāya diṭṭhiyā sati na hotīti attho.

126. 'He would be pierced' means: he might be pierced by one standing in the enemy's army. 'With a thick coating of poison' means: with a heavy coating. 'A surgeon' means: a physician. 'An extraction of the dart' means: the cutting of the dart, a term for the thread used for cutting the dart. 'Of akka' means: they take the bark of the akka tree and make a bowstring. Therefore, it is said, 'of akka.' 'Of sanha' means: of bamboo strips. They also make thread from the bark of maruvā and khīrapaṇṇī plants. Therefore, it is said, 'whether from maruvā or from khīrapaṇṇī.' 'From a thicket' means: grown in mountain-thickets, river-thickets, and so on. 'Cultivated' means: grown by being planted; made by taking an arrow from an arrow-bush. 'Of sithilahanu' means: of a bird with that name. 'Of bherava' means: of a black lion. 'Of semhāra' means: of a monkey. 'It is not so' means: when this view is present, the dwelling in the noble practice does not come to be; this is the meaning.

127. Attheva jātīti etāya diṭṭhiyā sati brahmacariyavāsova natthi, jāti pana atthiyeva. Tathā jarāmaraṇādīnīti dasseti. Yesāhanti yesaṃ ahaṃ. Nighātanti upaghātaṃ vināsaṃ. Mama sāvakā hi etesu nibbinnā idheva nibbānaṃ pāpuṇantīti adhippāyo.

127. 'Birth certainly exists' means: when this eternalist view is present, it is only the dwelling in the noble practice that does not exist; but birth certainly does exist. Similarly, it shows that aging, death, and so on exist. The word division of 'yesāhaṃ' is 'yesaṃ ahaṃ' (of whom I). 'Nighātaṃ' means: oppression, destruction. Indeed, my disciples, having become disenchanted with these wrong views, attain Nibbāna in this very life. This is the intention.

128. Tasmātihāti [P 3.0143] yasmā abyākatametaṃ, catusaccameva mayā byākataṃ, tasmāti attho. Na hetaṃ mālukyaputta atthasaṃhitanti etaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ vā etaṃ byākaraṇaṃ vā kāraṇanissitaṃ [V 3.0103] na hoti. Na ādibrahmacariyakanti brahmacariyassa ādimattampi pubbabhāgasīlamattampi na hoti. Na nibbidāyātiādīsu vaṭṭe nibbindanatthāya vā virajjhanatthāya vā vaṭṭanirodhāya vā rāgādivūpasamanatthāya vā abhiññeyye dhamme abhijānanatthāya vā catumaggasaṅkhātasambodhatthāya vā asaṅkhatanibbānasacchikiriyatthāya vā na hoti. Etaṃ hīti etaṃ catusaccabyākaraṇaṃ. Ādibrahmacariyakanti brahmacariyassa ādibhūtaṃ pubbapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Sesaṃ vuttapaṭivipakkhanayena veditabbaṃ. Imampi desanaṃ bhagavā neyyapuggalavasena niṭṭhāpesīti.

128. 'Therefore' means: because this is undeclared, and only the Four Truths have been declared by me, therefore. 'This, Mālukyaputta, is not connected with the goal' means: this wrong view, or the declaration of this wrong view, is not based on a valid reason. 'Not fundamental to the noble practice' means: it is not even the beginning of the noble practice, nor is it even the virtue of the preliminary part. In 'not for disenchantment,' and so on: it does not lead to disenchantment with the round of existence, nor to dispassion, nor to the cessation of the round, nor to the calming of lust and so on, nor to directly knowing the phenomena that are to be directly known, nor to the full awakening which is the four paths, nor to the realization of unconditioned Nibbāna. 'For this' means: this declaration of the Four Truths. 'Fundamental to the noble practice' means: it is the beginning of the noble practice, its preliminary basis. The remainder should be understood in the opposite way to what has been said. The Blessed One also concluded this teaching according to the disposition of the person to be guided.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Middle Length Discourses.

Cūḷamālukyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Cūḷamālukya Sutta is completed.

4. Mahāmālukyasuttavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Mahāmālukya Sutta

129. Evaṃ [V 3.0104][M 3.0101] me sutanti mahāmālukyasuttaṃ. Tattha orambhāgiyānīti heṭṭhā koṭṭhāsikāni kāmabhave nibbattisaṃvattanikāni. Saṃyojanānīti bandhanāni. Kassa [P 3.0144] kho nāmāti kassa devassa vā manussassa vā desitāni dhāresi, kiṃ tvameveko assosi, na añño kocīti? Anusetīti appahīnatāya anuseti. Anusayamāno saṃyojanaṃ nāma hoti.

129. The sutta beginning with 'Thus have I heard' is the Mahāmālukya Sutta. Therein, 'lower fetters' means: pertaining to the lower part, causing rebirth in the sensual realm. 'Fetters' means: bonds. 'For whom, indeed?' means: For which deva or human, do you remember, were these taught by me? Did you alone hear this, and no one else? 'It lies latent' means: it lies latent because it has not been abandoned. That which lies latent is called a fetter.

Ettha ca bhagavatā saṃyojanaṃ pucchitaṃ, therenapi saṃyojanameva byākataṃ. Evaṃ santepi tassa vāde bhagavatā doso āropito. So kasmāti ce? Therassa tathāladdhikattā. Ayañhi tassa laddhi “samudācārakkhaṇeyeva kilesehi saṃyutto nāma hoti, itarasmiṃ khaṇe asaṃyutto”ti. Tenassa bhagavatā doso āropito. Athāyasmā ānando cintesi – “bhagavatā bhikkhusaṅghassa dhammaṃ desessāmīti attano dhammatāyeva ayaṃ dhammadesanā āraddhā, sā iminā apaṇḍitena bhikkhunā visaṃvāditā. Handāhaṃ bhagavantaṃ yācitvā bhikkhūnaṃ dhammaṃ desessāmī”ti. So evamakāsi. Taṃ dassetuṃ “evaṃ vutte āyasmā ānando”tiādi vuttaṃ.

And here, a fetter was asked about by the Blessed One, and the Elder also explained about the fetter itself. Even so, a fault was imputed by the Blessed One to his view. If it is asked, 'Why so?', it is because the Elder held such a view. For this was his view: 'One is said to be conjoined with defilements only at the moment of their occurrence; at other moments, one is unconjoined.' For that reason, a fault was imputed to him by the Blessed One. Then the Venerable Ānanda thought: 'The Blessed One, having intended, "I will teach the Dhamma to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus," began this Dhamma discourse according to his own nature. That discourse has been contradicted by this unwise bhikkhu. Come now, having requested the Blessed One, I will teach the Dhamma to the bhikkhus.' He did so. To show this, the passage beginning, 'When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda...' was spoken.

Tattha sakkāyadiṭṭhipariyuṭṭhitenāti sakkāyadiṭṭhiyā gahitena abhibhūtena. Sakkāyadiṭṭhiparetenāti sakkāyadiṭṭhiyā anugatena. Nissaraṇanti diṭṭhinissaraṇaṃ nāma nibbānaṃ, taṃ yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Appaṭivinītāti avinoditā anīhaṭā. Orambhāgiyaṃ saṃyojananti heṭṭhābhāgiyasaṃyojanaṃ nāma hoti. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Sukkapakkho uttānatthoyeva. “Sānusayā pahīyatī”ti vacanato panettha ekacce “aññaṃ saṃyojanaṃ añño anusayo”ti vadanti. “Yathā hi sabyañjanaṃ bhatta”nti vutte bhattato aññaṃ byañjanaṃ hoti, evaṃ “sānusayā”ti vacanato pariyuṭṭhānasakkāyadiṭṭhito aññena anusayena bhavitabbanti tesaṃ laddhi. Te “sasīsaṃ pārupitvā”tiādīhi [P 3.0145] paṭikkhipitabbā. Na hi sīsato añño puriso atthi. Athāpi siyā – “yadi tadeva saṃyojanaṃ so anusayo, evaṃ sante bhagavatā therassa [M 3.0102] taruṇūpamo upārambho duāropito hotī”ti. Na duāropito, kasmā? Evaṃladdhikattāti [V 3.0105] vitthāritametaṃ. Tasmā soyeva kileso bandhanaṭṭhena saṃyojanaṃ, appahīnaṭṭhena anusayoti imamatthaṃ sandhāya bhagavatā “sānusayā pahīyatī”ti evaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

Therein, 'obsessed with identity view' (sakkāyadiṭṭhipariyuṭṭhitena) means: seized and overwhelmed by identity view. 'Possessed by identity view' (sakkāyadiṭṭhiparetena) means: followed along by identity view. 'Escape' (nissaraṇaṃ) means Nibbāna, which is the escape from views; that he does not know as it really is. 'Unsubdued' (appaṭivinītā) means: not dispelled, not removed. 'A lower fetter' (orambhāgiyaṃ saṃyojanaṃ) means: it is a fetter pertaining to the lower part. In the remaining terms also, this is the method. The white section has an obvious meaning. Here, on account of the statement, 'it is abandoned with its underlying tendency,' some say, 'The fetter is one thing, the underlying tendency is another.' Their view is that just as when it is said, 'rice with curry,' the curry is different from the rice, so too, on account of the statement 'with its underlying tendency,' the underlying tendency must be different from the manifest identity view. They are to be refuted with sayings such as 'covering oneself including the head,' for there is no person other than the head. Furthermore, it might be said: 'If that very fetter is that underlying tendency, in that case, the Blessed One's rebuke to the Elder, which has the simile of something tender, would be wrongly imputed.' It is not wrongly imputed. Why? Because of his having such a view; this has been explained in detail. Therefore, it should be understood that that very defilement is a 'fetter' in the sense of binding, and an 'underlying tendency' in the sense of not being abandoned. It was with reference to this meaning that the Blessed One said, 'it is abandoned with its underlying tendency.'

132. Tacaṃ chetvātiādīsu idaṃ opammasaṃsandanaṃ – tacacchedo viya hi samāpatti daṭṭhabbā, pheggucchedo viya vipassanā, sāracchedo viya maggo. Paṭipadā pana lokiyalokuttaramissakāva vaṭṭati. Evamete daṭṭhabbāti evarūpā puggalā evaṃ daṭṭhabbā.

132. In the passage beginning 'Having cut the skin...,' this is the connection of the simile: for attainment should be seen as like the cutting of the skin, insight as like the cutting of the softwood, and the path as like the cutting of the heartwood. The practice, however, is fitting only as a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane. 'Thus these should be seen' means: such persons should be seen in this way.

133. Upadhivivekāti upadhivivekena. Iminā pañcakāmaguṇaviveko kathito. Akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānāti iminā nīvaraṇappahānaṃ kathitaṃ. Kāyaduṭṭhullānaṃ paṭippassaddhiyāti iminā kāyālasiyapaṭippassaddhi kathitā. Vivicceva kāmehīti upadhivivekena kāmehi vinā hutvā. Vivicca akusalehīti akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānena kāyaduṭṭhullānaṃ paṭippassaddhiyā ca akusalehi vinā hutvā. Yadeva tattha hotīti yaṃ tattha antosamāpattikkhaṇeyeva samāpattisamuṭṭhitañca rūpādidhammajātaṃ hoti. Te [P 3.0146] dhammeti te rūpagatantiādinā nayena vutte rūpādayo dhamme. Aniccatoti na niccato. Dukkhatoti na sukhato. Rogatotiādīsu ābādhaṭṭhena rogato, antodosaṭṭhena gaṇḍato, anupaviddhaṭṭhena dukkhajananaṭṭhena ca sallato, dukkhaṭṭhena aghato, rogaṭṭhena ābādhato, asakaṭṭhena parato, palujjanaṭṭhena palokato, nissattaṭṭhena suññato, na attaṭṭhena anattato. Tattha aniccato, palokatoti dvīhi padehi aniccalakkhaṇaṃ kathitaṃ, dukkhatotiādīhi chahi dukkhalakkhaṇaṃ, parato suññato anattatoti tīhi anattalakkhaṇaṃ.

133. 'Seclusion from the substrates' (upadhiviveka) means: through seclusion from the substrates. By this, seclusion from the five cords of sensual pleasure is taught. By 'for the abandoning of unwholesome states,' the abandoning of the hindrances is taught. By 'through the calming of bodily coarseness,' the calming of bodily sluggishness is taught. 'Secluded from sensual pleasures' means: having become separated from sensual pleasures through seclusion from the substrates. 'Secluded from unwholesome states' means: having become separated from unwholesome states through the abandoning of unwholesome states and the calming of bodily coarseness. 'Whatever is there' means: whatever collection of phenomena such as form, etc., arisen from the attainment, exists right there within the moment of attainment. 'Those phenomena' means: those phenomena, form and so on, spoken of by the method beginning with 'related to form.' 'As impermanent' means: not as permanent. 'As suffering' means: not as pleasant. In 'as a disease,' etc., the meaning should be understood thus: as a disease in the sense of affliction; as a boil in the sense of internal corruption; as a dart in the sense of piercing and causing suffering; as misery in the sense of suffering; as an affliction in the sense of disease; as other in the sense of not being one's own; as perishable in the sense of falling apart; as empty in the sense of being devoid of a being; as not-self in the sense of being the opposite of a self. Therein, with the two terms 'as impermanent' and 'as perishable,' the characteristic of impermanence is taught. With the six terms beginning with 'as suffering,' the characteristic of suffering is taught. With the three terms 'as other,' 'as empty,' and 'as not-self,' the characteristic of not-self is taught.

So tehi dhammehīti so tehi evaṃ tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā diṭṭhehi antosamāpattiyaṃ pañcakkhandhadhammehi. Cittaṃ paṭivāpetīti cittaṃ paṭisaṃharati moceti apaneti. Upasaṃharatīti vipassanācittaṃ tāva savanavasena [M 3.0103] thutivasena pariyattivasena paññattivasena ca etaṃ santaṃ nibbānanti evaṃ asaṅkhatāya amatāya dhātuyā upasaṃharati. Maggacittaṃ nibbānaṃ ārammaṇakaraṇavaseneva etaṃ santametaṃ paṇītanti na evaṃ vadati, iminā pana ākārena taṃ paṭivijjhanto tattha cittaṃ upasaṃharatīti attho. So tattha ṭhitoti tāya tilakkhaṇārammaṇāya vipassanāya ṭhito. Āsavānaṃ khayaṃ pāpuṇātīti anukkamena cattāro magge bhāvetvā pāpuṇāti[V 3.0106]. Teneva dhammarāgenāti samathavipassanādhamme chandarāgena. Samathavipassanāsu hi sabbaso chandarāgaṃ pariyādātuṃ sakkonto arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, asakkonto anāgāmī hoti.

The phrase 'He, by those phenomena' means: he, by those phenomena of the five aggregates within the attainment, which have been seen after applying the three characteristics to them in this way. 'He turns the mind away from them' means: he withdraws the mind, releases it, removes it. 'He directs it' means: the insight-mind, by way of hearing, praise, study, and concept, directs itself to the unconditioned, deathless element, thinking, 'This Nibbāna is peaceful.' The path-mind, however, by the power of making Nibbāna its object, does not say, 'This is peaceful, this is sublime'; rather, the meaning is that, while penetrating it in this manner, he directs the mind there. 'He, established there' means: he is established in that insight which has the three characteristics as its object. 'He reaches the destruction of the taints' means: he reaches it by developing the four paths in sequence. 'Through that very passion for the Dhamma' means: through desire and passion for the dhammas of serenity and insight. For one who is able to completely exhaust desire and passion for serenity and insight attains Arahantship; one who is unable becomes a non-returner.

Yadeva [P 3.0147] tattha hoti vedanāgatanti idha pana rūpaṃ na gahitaṃ. Kasmā? Samatikkantattā. Ayañhi heṭṭhā rūpāvacarajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvā rūpaṃ atikkamitvā arūpāvacarasamāpattiṃ samāpannoti samathavasenapinena rūpaṃ atikkantaṃ, heṭṭhā rūpaṃ sammadeva sammasitvā taṃ atikkamma idāni arūpaṃ sammasatīti vipassanāvasenapinena rūpaṃ atikkantaṃ. Arūpe pana sabbasopi rūpaṃ natthīti taṃ sandhāyapi idha rūpaṃ na gahitaṃ.

In the phrase, 'whatever is included in feeling that is there,' form is not taken here. Why? Because of having been transcended. For this person, having entered into a form-sphere jhāna below and transcended form, has entered a formless attainment; thus, by the power of serenity, form is transcended by this person. Having properly contemplated form below, and having transcended it, one now contemplates the formless; thus, by the power of insight, form is also transcended by this person. Furthermore, in the formless realms, form is entirely absent; therefore, with reference to that, form is not taken here.

Atha kiñcarahīti kiṃ pucchāmīti pucchati? Samathavasena gacchato cittekaggatā dhuraṃ hoti, so cetovimutto nāma. Vipassanāvasena gacchato paññā dhuraṃ hoti, so paññāvimutto nāmāti ettha therassa kaṅkhā natthi. Ayaṃ sabhāvadhammoyeva, samathavaseneva pana gacchantesu eko cetovimutto nāma hoti, eko paññāvimutto. Vipassanāvasena gacchantesupi eko paññāvimutto nāma hoti, eko cetovimuttoti ettha kiṃ kāraṇanti pucchati.

Regarding the phrase 'Then what now?', he asks, 'What is it that I am asking?' For one who proceeds by way of serenity, one-pointedness of mind is the leading factor; such a one is called 'liberated by mind.' For one who proceeds by way of insight, wisdom is the leading factor; such a one is called 'liberated by wisdom.' In this, the Elder has no doubt. This is simply the nature of things. However, among those who proceed solely by way of serenity, one is called 'liberated by mind,' and another 'liberated by wisdom.' And among those who proceed by way of insight, one is called 'liberated by wisdom,' and another 'liberated by mind.' Regarding this, he asks, 'What is the reason?'

Indriyavemattataṃ vadāmīti indriyanānattataṃ vadāmi. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti, na tvaṃ, ānanda, dasa pāramiyo pūretvā sabbaññutaṃ paṭivijjhi, tena te etaṃ apākaṭaṃ. Ahaṃ pana paṭivijjhiṃ, tena me etaṃ pākaṭaṃ. Ettha hi indriyanānattatā kāraṇaṃ. Samathavaseneva hi gacchantesu ekassa bhikkhuno cittekaggatā dhuraṃ hoti, so cetovimutto nāma hoti. Ekassa paññā dhuraṃ hoti, so paññāvimutto nāma hoti. Vipassanāvaseneva ca gacchantesu ekassa paññā dhuraṃ hoti, so paññāvimutto [M 3.0104] nāma hoti. Ekassa cittekaggatā dhuraṃ hoti, so cetovimutto nāma [P 3.0148] hoti. Dve aggasāvakā samathavipassanādhurena arahattaṃ pattā. Tesu dhammasenāpati paññāvimutto jāto, mahāmoggallānatthero cetovimutto. Iti indriyavemattamettha kāraṇanti veditabbaṃ. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

'I declare the diversity of faculties' means 'I declare the difference of faculties.' This is what is meant: 'You, Ānanda, did not penetrate to omniscience after fulfilling the ten perfections; therefore, this is not manifest to you. I, however, have penetrated to it; therefore, this is manifest to me.' Here, the difference of faculties is indeed the reason. For among those who proceed solely by way of serenity, for one bhikkhu, one-pointedness of mind is the leading factor; he is called 'one liberated by mind.' For another, wisdom is the leading factor; he is called 'one liberated by wisdom.' And among those who proceed solely by way of insight, for one bhikkhu, wisdom is the leading factor; he is called 'one liberated by wisdom.' For another, one-pointedness of mind is the leading factor; he is called 'one liberated by mind.' The two chief disciples attained Arahantship through the primary practices of serenity and insight. Of them, the General of the Dhamma became one liberated by wisdom, and the Elder Mahāmoggallāna became one liberated by mind. Thus, it should be understood that the diversity of faculties is the reason here. The rest is clear in all respects.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Mahāmālukyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Mahāmālukya Sutta is concluded.

5. Bhaddālisuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Bhaddāli Sutta

134. Evaṃ [V 3.0107] me sutanti bhaddālisuttaṃ. Tattha ekāsanabhojananti ekasmiṃ purebhatte asanabhojanaṃ, bhuñjitabbabhattanti attho. Appābādhatantiādīni kakacopame vitthāritāni. Na ussahāmīti na sakkomi. Siyā kukkuccaṃ siyā vippaṭisāroti evaṃ bhuñjanto yāvajīvaṃ brahmacariyaṃ carituṃ sakkhissāmi nu kho, na nu khoti iti me vippaṭisārakukkuccaṃ bhaveyyāti attho. Ekadesaṃ bhuñjitvāti porāṇakattherā kira patte bhattaṃ pakkhipitvā sappimhi dinne sappinā uṇhameva thokaṃ bhuñjitvā hatthe dhovitvā avasesaṃ bahi nīharitvā chāyūdakaphāsuke ṭhāne nisīditvā bhuñjanti. Etaṃ sandhāya satthā āha. Bhaddāli, pana cintesi – “sace sakiṃ pattaṃ pūretvā dinnaṃ bhattaṃ bhuñjitvā puna pattaṃ dhovitvā odanassa pūretvā laddhaṃ [P 3.0149] bahi nīharitvā chāyūdakaphāsuke ṭhāne bhuñjeyya, iti evaṃ vaṭṭeyya, itarathā ko sakkotī”ti. Tasmā evampi kho ahaṃ, bhante, na ussahāmīti āha. Ayaṃ kira atīte anantarāya jātiyā kākayoniyaṃ nibbatti. Kākā ca nāma mahāchātakā honti. Tasmā chātakatthero nāma ahosi. Tassa pana viravantasseva bhagavā taṃ madditvā ajjhottharitvā – “yo pana bhikkhu vikāle khādanīyaṃ vā bhojanīyaṃ vā khādeyya vā bhuñjeyya vā pācittiya”nti (pāci. 248) sikkhāpadaṃ paññapesi. Tena vuttaṃ atha kho āyasmā, bhaddāli,…pe… anussāhaṃ pavedesīti.

134. “Thus have I heard”—this is the Bhaddāli Sutta. Therein, ‘eating in one session’ means eating a meal once in the morning; the meaning is ‘the meal that should be eaten.’ The phrases beginning with ‘fewness of illness’ are explained in detail in the Kakacopama Sutta. ‘I am unable’ means ‘I cannot.’ ‘There might be scruples, there might be remorse’ means: ‘For me, eating thus, the scruple and remorse, “Will I be able to practice the holy life for my whole life, or will I not?” would arise.’ ‘Having eaten a portion’—it is said that the ancient elders would place food in their bowls, and when ghee was offered, they would eat a little of the warm food with the ghee, wash their hands, take the remainder outside, and sit and eat in a comfortable place with shade and water. The Teacher spoke with reference to this. Bhaddāli, however, thought: ‘If, after filling the bowl once and eating the offered meal, I were to wash the bowl again, have it filled with rice, take what I received outside, and eat it in a comfortable place with shade and water, in this way it would be allowable. Otherwise, who could do it?’ Therefore, he said, ‘Venerable sir, even in this way I am unable.’ It is said that in his immediately preceding life, he was born in the womb of a crow. And crows are known to be very hungry. Therefore, he was called ‘the hungry elder.’ While he was still protesting, the Blessed One, having subdued and overwhelmed him, laid down the training rule: ‘Whatever monk should chew or consume staple or non-staple food at the wrong time, it is an offense requiring expiation’ (Pācittiya 37). Therefore, it was said: ‘Then the Venerable Bhaddāli… declared his inability.’”

Yathā [M 3.0105] tanti yathā aññopi sikkhāya na paripūrakārī ekavihārepi vasanto satthu sammukhībhāvaṃ na dadeyya, tatheva na adāsīti attho. Neva bhagavato upaṭṭhānaṃ agamāsi, na dhammadesanaṭṭhānaṃ na vitakkamāḷakaṃ, na ekaṃ bhikkhācāramaggaṃ paṭipajji. Yasmiṃ kule bhagavā nisīdati, tassa dvārepi na aṭṭhāsi. Sacassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ bhagavā gacchati, so puretarameva ñatvā aññattha gacchati. Saddhāpabbajito kiresa kulaputto parisuddhasīlo. Tenassa na añño vitakko ahosi, – “mayā nāma udarakāraṇā bhagavato sikkhāpadapaññāpanaṃ paṭibāhitaṃ, ananucchavikaṃ [V 3.0108] me kata”nti ayameva vitakko ahosi. Tasmā ekavihāre vasantopi lajjāya satthu sammukhībhāvaṃ nādāsi.

‘Just as’: just as another who is not a fulfiller of the training, even while dwelling in the same monastery, would not present himself before the Teacher, so too he did not present himself—this is the meaning. He did not go to attend upon the Blessed One, nor to the place of Dhamma teaching, nor to the pavilion for contemplation, nor did he follow the same alms-round path. In whatever family the Blessed One was sitting, he did not stand even at its door. If the Blessed One went to his dwelling place, he, knowing beforehand, would go elsewhere. It is said that this clansman had gone forth out of faith and was of pure virtue. Therefore, he had no other thought than this: ‘By me, for the sake of my belly, the Blessed One's laying down of a training rule has been obstructed. An unseemly thing has been done by me.’ This was the only thought he had. Therefore, even while dwelling in the same monastery, out of shame he did not present himself before the Teacher.

135. Cīvarakammaṃ karontīti manussā bhagavato cīvarasāṭakaṃ adaṃsu, taṃ gahetvā cīvaraṃ karonti. Etaṃ dosakanti etaṃ okāsametaṃ aparādhaṃ, satthu sikkhāpadaṃ paññapentassa paṭibāhitakāraṇaṃ sādhukaṃ manasi karohīti attho. Dukkarataranti [P 3.0150] vassañhi vasitvā disāpakkante bhikkhū kuhiṃ vasitthāti pucchanti, tehi jetavane vasimhāti vutte, “āvuso, bhagavā imasmiṃ antovasse kataraṃ jātakaṃ kathesi, kataraṃ suttantaṃ, kataraṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññapesī”ti pucchitāro honti. Tato “vikālabhojanasikkhāpadaṃ paññapesi, bhaddāli, nāma naṃ eko thero paṭibāhī”ti vakkhanti. Taṃ sutvā bhikkhū – “bhagavatopi nāma sikkhāpadaṃ paññapentassa paṭibāhitaṃ ayuttaṃ akāraṇa”nti vadanti. Evaṃ te ayaṃ doso mahājanantare pākaṭo hutvā duppaṭikārataṃ āpajjissatīti maññamānā evamāhaṃsu. Apica aññepi bhikkhū pavāretvā satthu santikaṃ āgamissanti. Atha tvaṃ “ethāvuso, mama satthāraṃ khamāpentassa sahāyā hothā”ti saṅghaṃ sannipātessasi. Tattha āgantukā pucchissanti, “āvuso, kiṃ imināpi bhikkhunā kata”nti. Tato etamatthaṃ sutvā “bhāriyaṃ kataṃ bhikkhunā, dasabalaṃ nāma paṭibāhissatīti ayuttameta”nti vakkhanti. Evampi te ayaṃ aparādho mahājanantare pākaṭo hutvā duppaṭikārataṃ āpajjissatīti maññamānāpi evamāhaṃsu. Atha vā bhagavā pavāretvā cārikaṃ pakkamissati, atha tvaṃ gatagataṭṭhāne bhagavato khamāpanatthāya saṅghaṃ sannipātessasi. Tatra disāvāsino [M 3.0106] bhikkhū pucchissanti, “āvuso, kiṃ iminā bhikkhunā kata”nti…pe… duppaṭikārataṃ āpajjissatīti maññamānāpi evamāhaṃsu.

135. ‘They are doing robe-work’ means: people gave the Blessed One a robe-cloth, and taking it, they make a robe. ‘This fault’ means: this occasion for blame, this offense—the reason for having obstructed the Teacher as he was laying down a training rule—‘consider it well,’ this is the meaning. ‘More difficult still’: for after spending the rains retreat, when monks have departed to various directions, others will ask them, ‘Where did you spend the rains?’ When they reply, ‘At Jetavana,’ the inquirers will ask, ‘Friend, which Jātaka did the Blessed One relate during this rains retreat? Which Suttanta? Which training rule did he lay down?’ Then they will say, ‘He laid down the training rule concerning eating at the wrong time, but an elder named Bhaddāli obstructed it.’ Hearing this, the monks will say, ‘It is improper and without reason that the Blessed One should be obstructed while laying down a training rule.’ Thinking, ‘Thus this fault of yours will become manifest among the great populace and will become difficult to remedy,’ they spoke thus. Moreover, other monks, having performed the Pavāraṇā, will come to the Teacher. Then you will assemble the Saṅgha, saying, ‘Come, friends, be my companions in asking the Teacher for forgiveness.’ There, the visiting monks will ask, ‘Friend, what has this monk done?’ Then, hearing this matter, they will say, ‘A grave thing has been done by this monk, that he should obstruct the One with Ten Powers! This is improper.’ Thinking that in this way too this offense of yours will become manifest among the great populace and will become difficult to remedy, they also spoke thus. Or else, the Blessed One, having performed the Pavāraṇā, will set out on tour. Then, in whatever place you go, you will assemble the Saṅgha for the purpose of asking the Blessed One for forgiveness. There, monks residing in the regions will ask, ‘Friend, what has this monk done?’… Thinking that it will become difficult to remedy, they also spoke thus.

Etadavocāti appatirūpaṃ mayā kataṃ, bhagavā pana mahantepi aguṇe alaggitvā mayhaṃ accayaṃ paṭiggaṇhissatīti maññamāno etaṃ “accayo maṃ, bhante,”tiādivacanaṃ avoca. Tattha [P 3.0151] accayoti aparādho. Maṃ accagamāti maṃ atikkamma abhibhavitvā pavatto. Paṭiggaṇhātūti khamatu. Āyatiṃ saṃvarāyāti anāgate saṃvaraṇatthāya, puna evarūpassa aparādhassa dosassa khalitassa akaraṇatthāya. Tagghāti ekaṃsena. Samayopi kho te, bhaddālīti, bhaddāli, tayā paṭivijjhitabbayuttakaṃ ekaṃ kāraṇaṃ atthi, tampi te na paṭividdhaṃ na sallakkhitanti dasseti.

‘He said this’: thinking, ‘An improper thing was done by me, but the Blessed One, not clinging even to great faults, will accept my transgression,’ he spoke the words beginning, ‘A transgression has overcome me, venerable sir.’ Therein, ‘transgression’ means offense. ‘It overcame me’ means it occurred having surpassed and overwhelmed me. ‘May he accept’ means may he forgive. ‘For restraint in the future’ means for the sake of restraint in the future, for the sake of not committing such an offense, fault, or failing again. ‘Indeed’ means unequivocally. ‘The time, Bhaddāli’: this shows, ‘Bhaddāli, there is a reason that should have been penetrated by you, but it has not been penetrated by you, not discerned by you.’

136. Ubhatobhāgavimuttotiādīsu [V 3.0109] dhammānusārī, saddhānusārīti dve ekacittakkhaṇikā maggasamaṅgipuggalā. Ete pana sattapi ariyapuggale bhagavatāpi evaṃ āṇāpetuṃ na yuttaṃ, bhagavatā āṇatte tesampi evaṃ kātuṃ na yuttaṃ. Aṭṭhānaparikappavasena pana ariyapuggalānaṃ suvacabhāvadassanatthaṃ [P 3.0152] bhaddālittherassa ca dubbacabhāvadassanatthametaṃ vuttaṃ.

136. In the passages beginning with 'one liberated in both ways,' the Dhamma-follower and the faith-follower are two individuals endowed with the path-mind, possessing a single mind-moment. However, it is not proper for even the Blessed One to command these seven noble individuals in this way, nor is it proper for them to act thus when commanded by the Blessed One. This, however, was said by way of considering an impossible supposition, in order to show the quality of being easy to admonish of the noble individuals, and to show the quality of being difficult to admonish of the Elder Bhaddāli.

Api nu tvaṃ tasmiṃ samaye ubhatobhāgavimuttoti desanaṃ kasmā ārabhi? Bhaddālissa niggahaṇatthaṃ. Ayañhettha adhippāyo – bhaddāli, ime satta ariyapuggalā loke dakkhiṇeyyā mama sāsane sāmino, mayi sikkhāpadaṃ paññapente paṭibāhitabbayutte kāraṇe sati etesaṃ paṭibāhituṃ yuttaṃ. Tvaṃ pana mama sāsanato bāhirako, mayi sikkhāpadaṃ paññapente tuyhaṃ paṭibāhituṃ na yuttanti.

Why then was the discourse 'Were you at that time one liberated in both ways?' initiated? For the purpose of subduing Bhaddāli. This, indeed, is the intention here: 'Bhaddāli, these seven noble individuals are worthy of the highest offerings in the world; they are masters in my Dispensation. When I am laying down a training rule, if there is a reason that ought to be objected to, it is proper for them to object. You, however, are external to my Dispensation; when I am laying down a training rule, it is not proper for you to object.' This is the intention.

Ritto tucchoti anto ariyaguṇānaṃ abhāvena rittako tucchako, issaravacane kiñci na hoti. Yathādhammaṃ paṭikarosīti yathā dhammo ṭhito, tatheva karosi, khamāpesīti vuttaṃ hoti. Taṃ te mayaṃ paṭiggaṇhāmāti taṃ tava aparādhaṃ mayaṃ khamāma. Vuḍḍhi hesā, bhaddāli, ariyassa vinayeti esā, bhaddāli, ariyassa vinaye buddhassa bhagavato sāsane vuḍḍhi nāma. Katamā? Accayaṃ accayato disvā yathādhammaṃ paṭikaritvā āyatiṃ saṃvarāpajjanā. Desanaṃ pana puggalādhiṭṭhānaṃ karonto “yo accayaṃ accayato disvā yathādhammaṃ paṭikaroti, āyatiṃ saṃvaraṃ āpajjatī”ti āha.

‘Empty, hollow’ means: due to the absence of the qualities of noble ones within, he is empty and hollow; there is no heeding of the words of the master. ‘You make amends according to the Dhamma’ means: you act in accordance with how the Dhamma stands; it means that you have asked for forgiveness. ‘We accept that from you’ means: we forgive that offense of yours. ‘This, Bhaddāli, is growth in the Noble One's discipline’ means: this, Bhaddāli, is called growth in the Noble One's discipline, in the Dispensation of the Buddha, the Blessed One. What is that? Seeing a transgression as a transgression, making amends according to the Dhamma, and undertaking restraint for the future. However, giving a discourse established on the individual, He said: ‘Whoever, seeing a transgression as a transgression, makes amends according to the Dhamma, undertakes restraint for the future...’

137. Satthāpi [M 3.0107] upavadatīti “asukavihāravāsī asukassa therassa saddhivihāriko asukassa antevāsiko itthannāmo nāma bhikkhu lokuttaradhammaṃ nibbattetuṃ araññaṃ paviṭṭho”ti sutvā – “kiṃ tassa araññavāsena, yo mayhaṃ pana sāsane sikkhāya aparipūrakārī”ti evaṃ upavadati, sesapadesupi eseva nayo, apicettha devatā na kevalaṃ upavadanti, bheravārammaṇaṃ dassetvā palāyanākārampi karonti. Attanāpi attānanti sīlaṃ āvajjantassa saṃkiliṭṭhaṭṭhānaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti, cittaṃ vidhāvati, na kammaṭṭhānaṃ allīyati. So “kiṃ mādisassa araññavāsenā”ti vippaṭisārī uṭṭhāya pakkamati. Attāpi attānaṃ upavaditoti attanāpi [V 3.0110] attā upavadito, ayameva vā pāṭho. Sukkapakkho vuttapaccanīkanayena veditabbo. So [P 3.0153] vivicceva kāmehītiādi evaṃ sacchikarotīti dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ.

137. ‘The Teacher also reproaches’ means: having heard, ‘A monk named so-and-so, a resident of such-and-such monastery, the co-resident of such-and-such elder, the pupil of such-and-such teacher, has entered the forest to bring forth the supramundane Dhamma,’ He reproaches thus: ‘What is the use of dwelling in the forest for him, who does not fulfill the training in my Dispensation?’ In the remaining passages, this is the same method. Moreover, in this case, the deities do not merely reproach; showing a terrifying object, they also cause an appearance of fleeing. ‘By oneself also oneself’ means: for one reflecting on his virtue, the place of defilement becomes manifest, the mind runs about, and the meditation subject does not adhere. That monk, becoming remorseful and thinking, ‘What is the use of dwelling in the forest for one like me?’, gets up and departs. ‘Oneself also reproaches oneself’ means: by oneself, oneself is reproached; or this is the reading. The bright side should be understood by the method contrary to what has been said. The passage beginning with ‘He, secluded from sensual pleasures...’ was spoken to show that he realizes it in this way.

140. Pasayha pasayha kāraṇaṃ karontīti appamattakepi dose niggahetvā punappunaṃ kārenti. No tathāti mahantepi aparādhe yathā itaraṃ, evaṃ pasayha na kārenti. So kira, “āvuso, bhaddāli, mā cintayittha, evarūpaṃ nāma hoti, ehi satthāraṃ khamāpehī”ti bhikkhusaṅghatopi, kañci bhikkhuṃ pesetvā attano santikaṃ pakkosāpetvā, “bhaddāli, mā cintayittha, evarūpaṃ nāma hotī”ti evaṃ satthusantikāpi anuggahaṃ paccāsīsati. Tato “bhikkhusaṅghenāpi na samassāsito, satthārāpī”ti cintetvā evamāha.

140. ‘Forcibly, forcibly they make him act’ means: having subdued him even for a minor fault, they repeatedly make him undergo punishment. ‘Not so’ means: even for a major offense, they do not forcibly make him undergo punishment as they would for a minor one. It is said that he, Bhaddāli, hoped for support from the community of monks, thinking they would say, ‘Friend Bhaddāli, do not worry, such things happen. Come, ask for the Teacher's forgiveness.’ He also hoped for support from the Teacher, thinking He would have a certain monk sent to summon him to His presence and say, ‘Bhaddāli, do not worry, such things happen.’ Then, thinking, ‘I have not been consoled by the community of monks, nor by the Teacher,’ the Elder Bhaddāli spoke thus.

Atha bhagavā bhikkhusaṅghopi satthāpi ovaditabbayuttameva ovadati, na itaranti dassetuṃ idha, bhaddāli, ekaccotiādimāha. Tattha aññenāññantiādīni anumānasutte vitthāritāni. Na sammā vattatīti sammā vattampi na vattati. Na lomaṃ pātetīti anulomavatte na vattati, vilomameva gaṇhāti. Na nitthāraṃ vattatīti nitthāraṇakavattamhi na vattati, āpattivuṭṭhānatthaṃ turitaturito chandajāto na hoti. Tatrāti tasmiṃ tassa dubbacakaraṇe. Abhiṇhāpattikoti nirantarāpattiko. Āpattibahuloti sāpattikakālovassa bahu, suddho nirāpattikakālo appoti attho. Na khippameva vūpasammatīti khippaṃ na vūpasammati, dīghasuttaṃ hoti. Vinayadharā [M 3.0108] pādadhovanakāle āgataṃ [P 3.0154] “gacchāvuso, vattavelā”ti vadanti. Puna kālaṃ maññitvā āgataṃ “gacchāvuso, tuyhaṃ vihāravelā, gacchāvuso, sāmaṇerādīnaṃ uddesadānavelā, amhākaṃ nhānavelā, therūpaṭṭhānavelā, mukhadhovanavelā”tiādīni vatvā divasabhāgepi rattibhāgepi āgataṃ uyyojentiyeva. “Kāya velāya, bhante, okāso bhavissatī”ti vuttepi “gacchāvuso, tvaṃ imameva ṭhānaṃ jānāsi, asuko nāma vinayadharatthero sinehapānaṃ pivati, asuko virecanaṃ kāreti, kasmā turitosī”tiādīni vatvā dīghasuttameva karonti.

Then the Blessed One, to show that both the community of monks and the Teacher admonish only the individual who is fit to be admonished and not the other, spoke the words beginning with, ‘Here, Bhaddāli, a certain one...’. Therein, the words beginning with ‘one with another’ have been explained in detail in the Anumāna Sutta. ‘He does not conduct himself rightly’ means: he does not conduct himself in the proper practice. ‘He is not compliant’ means: he does not practice in a compliant way; he takes up only the contrary practice. ‘He does not practice for his deliverance’ means: he does not practice the conduct for deliverance; he does not have a swift and eager desire to arise from the offense. ‘Therein’ means: in that act of being difficult to admonish. ‘One who frequently commits offenses’ means: one who has uninterrupted offenses. ‘One who has many offenses’ means: for him, the time with an offense is much, while the pure time without an offense is little; this is the meaning. ‘It is not quickly settled’ means: it is not pacified quickly; it becomes a long-drawn-out affair. The Vinaya-holders, when the difficult monk with an offense comes at the time for washing feet, say, ‘Go, friend, it is time for duties.’ When he comes again, thinking he knows the time, they say, ‘Go, friend, it is time for your dwelling,’ ‘Go, friend, it is time for giving instruction to the novices and others,’ ‘It is our time for bathing,’ ‘It is time for attending to the elders,’ ‘It is time for washing the face.’ Having said these and other things, they send him away when he comes by day or by night. Even when he says, ‘Venerable sirs, at what time will there be an opportunity?’, they say, ‘Go, friend, you only know this one place. A certain Vinaya-holding elder is drinking a fruit tonic; another is taking a purgative. Why are you in a hurry?’ Having said these and other things, they make it a long-drawn-out affair.

141. Khippameva vūpasammatīti lahuṃ vūpasammati, na dīghasuttaṃ hoti. Ussukkāpannā bhikkhū – “āvuso, ayaṃ subbaco bhikkhu, janapadavāsino nāma gāmantasenāsane vasanaṭṭhānanisajjanādīni [V 3.0111] na phāsukāni honti, bhikkhācāropi dukkho hoti, sīghamassa adhikaraṇaṃ vūpasamemā”ti sannipatitvā āpattito vuṭṭhāpetvā suddhante patiṭṭhāpenti.

141. ‘It is quickly settled’ means: it is pacified quickly; it does not become a long-drawn-out affair. The zealous monks, thinking, ‘Friends, this monk is easy to admonish. For those dwelling in the countryside, the places for staying, standing, sitting, and so on, in a monastery near a village are not comfortable, and the alms-round is also difficult. Let us quickly settle his legal issue,’ assemble, make him rise from the offense, and establish him in a state of purity.

142. Adhiccāpattikoti kadāci kadāci āpattiṃ āpajjati. So kiñcāpi lajjī hoti pakatatto, dubbacattā panassa bhikkhū tatheva paṭipajjanti.

142. ‘One who commits an offense occasionally’ means: he sometimes commits an offense. Although that monk is scrupulous and of normal conduct, on account of his being difficult to admonish, the monks treat him in that very same way.
