144. Saddhāmattakena vahati pemamattakenāti ācariyupajjhāyesu appamattikāya gehassitasaddhāya appamattakena gehassitapemena yāpeti. Paṭisandhiggahaṇasadisā hi ayaṃ pabbajjā nāma, navapabbajito pabbajjāya guṇaṃ ajānanto ācariyupajjhāyesu pemamattena yāpeti, tasmā evarūpā saṅgaṇhitabbā. Appamattakampi hi saṅgahaṃ labhitvā pabbajjāya ṭhitā abhiññāpattā mahāsamaṇā bhavissanti. Ettakena kathāmaggena “ovaditabbayuttakaṃ ovadanti, na itara”nti imameva bhagavatā dassitaṃ.

144. ‘He gets by with mere faith, with mere affection’ means: he maintains himself with a little household-based faith and a little household-based affection towards his teachers and preceptors. Indeed, this going forth is like the taking of a new birth. A newly gone-forth one, not knowing the virtue of the going forth, maintains himself with mere affection for his teachers and preceptors. Therefore, such ones should be supported. For, having received even a little support, they, established in the going forth and having attained higher knowledge, will become great ascetics. By this line of discourse, it was shown by the Blessed One that: ‘They advise one who is fit to be advised, not the other.’

145. Aññāya [P 3.0155] saṇṭhahiṃsūti arahatte patiṭṭhahiṃsu. Sattesu hāyamānesūti paṭipattiyā hāyamānāya sattā hāyanti nāma. Saddhamme antaradhāyamāneti paṭipattisaddhamme antaradhāyamāne. Paṭipattisaddhammopi hi paṭipattipūrakesu sattesu asati antaradhāyati nāma[M 3.0109]. Āsavaṭṭhānīyāti āsavā tiṭṭhanti etesūti āsavaṭṭhānīyā. Yesu diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikā parūpavādavippaṭisāravadhabandhanādayo ceva apāyadukkhavisesabhūtā ca āsavā tiṭṭhantiyeva. Yasmā nesaṃ te kāraṇaṃ hontīti attho. Te āsavaṭṭhānīyā vītikkamadhammā yāva na saṅghe pātubhavanti, na tāva satthā sāvakānaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññapetīti ayamettha yojanā.

145. ‘Having understood, they were established’ means: they were established in the fruit of Arahantship. ‘When beings decline’ means: when the practice declines, beings are said to decline. ‘When the true Dhamma disappears’ means: when the true Dhamma of practice disappears. Indeed, the true Dhamma of practice is said to disappear when there are no beings who fulfill the practice. ‘Grounds for the dangers’ (āsavaṭṭhānīyā): the dangers (āsavā) stand in these (transgressions), therefore they are called ‘grounds for the dangers’. In these (transgressions) stand dangers—such as blame from others, remorse, killing, and imprisonment, which pertain to the present life and the next—as well as dangers that are the special cause of suffering in the woeful states. The meaning is: because those (transgressions) are their cause. As long as those things of transgression which are grounds for the dangers do not appear in the Sangha, the Teacher does not lay down a training rule for the disciples. This is the connection here.

Evaṃ akālaṃ dassetvā puna kālaṃ dassetuṃ yato ca kho, bhaddālītiādimāha. Tattha yatoti yadā, yasmiṃ kāleti vuttaṃ hoti. Sesaṃ vuttānusāreneva veditabbaṃ. Ayaṃ vā ettha saṅkhepattho – yasmiṃ kāle āsavaṭṭhānīyā dhammāti saṅkhaṃ gatā vītikkamadosā saṅghe pātubhavanti, tadā satthā sāvakānaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññapeti. Kasmā? Tesaṃyeva āsavaṭṭhānīyadhammasaṅkhātānaṃ vītikkamadosānaṃ paṭighātāya.

Having thus shown the unsuitable time, and again, to show the suitable time, he spoke the words beginning with, ‘And when, Bhaddāli…’. Therein, `yato` means ‘when’, ‘at which time’. The remainder should be understood according to the method already stated. Or, this is the concise meaning here: at the time when the faults of transgression, which are designated as ‘dhammas that are grounds for the dangers,’ appear in the Sangha, then the Teacher lays down a training rule for the disciples. Why? For the removal of those very faults of transgression, which are designated as ‘dhammas that are grounds for the dangers’.

Evaṃ [V 3.0112] āsavaṭṭhānīyānaṃ dhammānaṃ anuppattiṃ sikkhāpadapaññattiyā akālaṃ, uppattiñca kālanti vatvā idāni tesaṃ dhammānaṃ anuppattikālañca uppattikālañca dassetuṃ “na tāva, bhaddāli, idhekacce”tiādimāha. Tattha mahattanti mahantabhāvaṃ. Saṅgho hi yāva na theranavamajjhimānaṃ vasena mahattaṃ patto hoti, tāva senāsanāni pahonti, sāsane ekacce āsavaṭṭhānīyā dhammā [P 3.0156] na uppajjanti. Mahattaṃ patte pana te uppajjanti, atha satthā sikkhāpadaṃ paññapeti. Tattha mahattaṃ patte saṅghe paññattasikkhāpadāni –

Having thus spoken of the non-arising of things that are grounds for the taints as the unsuitable time for laying down a training rule, and their arising as the suitable time, now, to show the time of non-arising and the time of arising of those things, he spoke the words beginning with, ‘Not yet, Bhaddāli, here some…’. Therein, `mahattaṃ` means the state of being numerous. For as long as the Sangha has not attained numerousness by way of elders, middle-status monks, and new monks, the lodgings suffice, and certain things that are grounds for the taints do not arise in the Dispensation. But when numerousness is attained, they arise, and then the Teacher lays down a training rule. Therein, the training rules laid down when the Sangha attained numerousness are:

“Yo pana bhikkhu anupasampannena uttaridvirattatirattaṃ sahaseyyaṃ kappeyya pācittiyaṃ (pāci. 51). Yā pana bhikkhunī anuvassaṃ vuṭṭhāpeyya pācittiyaṃ (pāci. 1171). Yā pana bhikkhunī ekavassaṃ dve vuṭṭhāpeyya pācittiya”nti (pāci. 1175).

‘Whatever bhikkhu should arrange to lie down together with an unordained person for more than two or three nights, it is an offense of expiation.’ ‘Whatever bhikkhunī should give ordination every year, it is an offense of expiation.’ ‘Whatever bhikkhunī should give ordination to two in one year, it is an offense of expiation.’

Iminā nayena veditabbāni.

They should be understood in this way.

Lābhagganti lābhassa aggaṃ. Saṅgho hi yāva na lābhaggapatto hoti, na tāva lābhaṃ paṭicca āsavaṭṭhānīyā dhammā uppajjanti. Patte pana uppajjanti, atha satthā sikkhāpadaṃ paññapeti –

‘The peak of gain’ means: the excellence of gain. For as long as the Sangha has not reached the peak of gain, things that are grounds for the taints do not arise on account of gain. But when it has been reached, they arise. Then the Teacher lays down a training rule:

“Yo [M 3.0110] pana bhikkhu acelakassa vā paribbājakassa vā paribbājikāya vā sahatthā khādanīyaṃ vā bhojanīyaṃ vā dadeyya pācittiya”nti (pāci. 270).

‘Whatever bhikkhu should give, with his own hand, hard food or soft food to a naked ascetic, a male wanderer, or a female wanderer, it is an offense of expiation.’

Idañhi lābhaggapatte saṅghe sikkhāpadaṃ paññattaṃ.

Indeed, this training rule was laid down when the Sangha had reached the peak of gain.

Yasagganti yasassa aggaṃ. Saṅgho hi yāva na yasaggapatto hoti, na tāva yasaṃ paṭicca āsavaṭṭhānīyā dhammā uppajjanti. Patte pana uppajjanti, atha satthā sikkhāpadaṃ paññapeti “surāmerayapāne pācittiya”nti (pāci. 327). Idañhi yasaggapatte saṅghe sikkhāpadaṃ paññattaṃ.

‘The peak of fame’ means: the excellence of retinue and fame. For as long as the Sangha has not reached the peak of fame, things that are grounds for the taints do not arise on account of fame. But when it has been reached, they arise. Then the Teacher lays down the training rule: ‘Drinking spirits and intoxicants is an offense of expiation.’ Indeed, this training rule was laid down when the Sangha had reached the peak of fame.

Bāhusaccanti [V 3.0113] bahussutabhāvaṃ. Saṅgho hi yāva na bāhusaccapatto hoti, na tāva āsavaṭṭhānīyā dhammā uppajjanti. Bāhusaccapatte pana yasmā ekaṃ nikāyaṃ dve nikāye pañcapi nikāye uggahetvā ayoniso ummujjamānā [P 3.0157] puggalā rasena rasaṃ saṃsandetvā uddhammaṃ ubbinayaṃ satthu sāsanaṃ dīpenti, atha satthā – “yo pana bhikkhu evaṃ vadeyya tathāhaṃ bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmi (pāci. 418)…pe… samaṇuddesopi ce evaṃ vadeyyā”tiādinā (pāci. 429) nayena sikkhāpadaṃ paññapeti.

‘Great learning’ means: the state of having heard much. For as long as the Sangha has not attained great learning, things that are grounds for the taints do not arise. But when great learning is attained, because persons, having learned one Nikāya, two Nikāyas, or even five Nikāyas, emerge improperly and, comparing the flavor which is the tangible object of non-appropriated matter with the flavor which is the tangible object of appropriated matter, they present the Teacher's Dispensation as non-Dhamma and non-Vinaya. Then the Teacher lays down the training rule by the method beginning: ‘Whatever bhikkhu should say, “Thus do I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One…” … even if a novice should say thus…’.

Rattaññutaṃ pattoti ettha rattiyo jānantīti rattaññū. Attano pabbajitadivasato paṭṭhāya bahū rattiyo jānanti, cirapabbajitāti vuttaṃ hoti. Rattaññūnaṃ bhāvaṃ rattaññutaṃ. Tatra rattaññutaṃ patte saṅghe upasenaṃ vaṅgantaputtaṃ ārabbha sikkhāpadaṃ paññattanti veditabbaṃ. So hāyasmā ūnadasavasse bhikkhū upasampādente disvā ekavasso saddhivihārikaṃ upasampādesi. Atha bhagavā sikkhāpadaṃ paññapesi – “na, bhikkhave, ūnadasavassena upasampādetabbo, yo upasampādeyya āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (mahāva. 75). Evaṃ paññatte sikkhāpade puna bhikkhū “dasavassamhā dasavassamhā”ti bālā abyattā upasampādenti. Atha bhagavā aparampi sikkhāpadaṃ paññapesi – “na, bhikkhave, bālena abyattena upasampādetabbo, yo upasampādeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, byattena bhikkhunā paṭibalena dasavassena vā atirekadasavassena vā upasampādetu”nti. Iti rattaññutaṃ pattakāle dve sikkhāpadāni paññattāni.

In the passage 'Rattaññutaṃ patto' (attained seniority), 'rattaññū' are those who know the nights. They know many nights from the day of their own ordination; it is said that they have been ordained for a long time. The state of those who know the nights is 'rattaññutaṃ' (seniority). In this context, it should be understood that when the Sangha had attained seniority, the training rule was laid down concerning Upasena, the son of Vaṅganta. That venerable one, seeing monks who were themselves of less than ten vassas giving ordination, himself being of one vassa, gave ordination to his co-resident pupil. Then the Blessed One laid down the training rule: “Monks, one with less than ten vassas should not give ordination. Whoever should give ordination commits an offense of wrongdoing.” When this training rule was laid down, foolish and incompetent monks again gave ordination, thinking, “We are of ten vassas, we are of ten vassas.” Then the Blessed One laid down another training rule: “Monks, a foolish and incompetent one should not give ordination. Whoever should give ordination commits an offense of wrongdoing. I allow, monks, a competent and capable monk of ten vassas or more than ten vassas to give ordination.” Thus, at the time when seniority was attained, two training rules were laid down.

146. Ājānīyasusūpamaṃ [M 3.0111][P 3.0158] dhammapariyāyaṃ desesinti taruṇājānīyaupamaṃ katvā dhammaṃ desayiṃ. Tatrāti tasmiṃ asaraṇe. Na kho, bhaddāli, eseva hetūti na esa sikkhāya aparipūrakārībhāvoyeva eko hetu.

146. ‘I taught the Dhamma discourse, the simile of the young thoroughbred’ means: having made the simile of a young thoroughbred, I taught the Dhamma. ‘Therein’ means in that non-recollection. ‘Not so, Bhaddāli, is this the only reason’ means: this state of not being a fulfiller of the training is not the only reason.

147. Mukhādhāne kāraṇaṃ kāretīti khalīnabandhādīhi mukhaṭṭhapane sādhukaṃ gīvaṃ paggaṇhāpetuṃ kāraṇaṃ kāreti. Visūkāyitānītiādīhi visevanācāraṃ kathesi. Sabbāneva hetāni aññamaññavevacanāni. Tasmiṃ ṭhāneti tasmiṃ visevanācāre. Parinibbāyatīti nibbisevano hoti, taṃ visevanaṃ jahatīti attho. Yugādhāneti yugaṭṭhapane yugassa sādhukaṃ gahaṇatthaṃ.

147. ‘He has it trained in accepting the bit’ means: by means of the bridle and other tack, in placing it in the mouth, he has it trained to raise its neck well. By ‘unruly acts’ and other such terms, he spoke of unruly conduct. All these are synonyms for one another. ‘In that state’ means in that unruly conduct. ‘He is fully extinguished’ means he becomes disciplined; the meaning is that he abandons that unruliness. ‘In accepting the yoke’ means in placing it on the yoke, for the purpose of bearing the yoke well.

Anukkameti [V 3.0114] cattāropi pāde ekappahāreneva ukkhipane ca nikkhipane ca. Parasenāya hi āvāṭe ṭhatvā asiṃ gahetvā āgacchantassa assassa pāde chindanti. Tasmiṃ samaye esa ekappahāreneva cattāropi pāde ukkhipissatīti rajjubandhanavidhānena etaṃ kāraṇaṃ karonti. Maṇḍaleti yathā asse nisinnoyeva bhūmiyaṃ patitaṃ āvudhaṃ gahetuṃ sakkoti, evaṃ karaṇatthaṃ maṇḍale kāraṇaṃ kāreti. Khurakāseti [P 3.0159] aggaggakhurehi pathavīkamane. Rattiṃ okkantakaraṇasmiñhi yathā padasaddo na suyyati, tadatthaṃ ekasmiṃ ṭhāne saññaṃ datvā aggaggakhurehiyeva gamanaṃ sikkhāpenti. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Javeti sīghavāhane. “Dhāve”tipi pāṭho. Attano parājaye sati palāyanatthaṃ, paraṃ palāyantaṃ anubandhitvā gahaṇatthañca etaṃ kāraṇaṃ kāreti. Davatteti davattāya, yuddhakālasmiñhi hatthīsu vā koñcanādaṃ karontesu assesu vā hasantesu rathesu vā nighosantesu yodhesu vā ukkuṭṭhiṃ karontesu tassa ravassa abhāyitvā parasenapavesanatthaṃ ayaṃ kāraṇā karīyati.

'In pacing' means in lifting and in placing down all four feet at the very same instant. For in an enemy army, soldiers standing in a trench and holding a sword cut the feet of an approaching horse. At that time, they perform this training by the method of tying with ropes so that the horse will lift all four feet at the very same instant. 'In circling' means he has it trained in circling for the purpose of being able to pick up a weapon fallen on the ground while still seated on the horse. 'In stepping on the hoof-tips' means in treading the ground with the very tips of the hooves. Indeed, when making an incursion at night, so that the sound of hooves is not heard, for that purpose, having given a signal at one spot, they teach it to go only on the very tips of its hooves. This was said in reference to that. 'In speed' means in swift conveyance. There is also the reading 'Dhāve' (in running). He has this training done for the purpose of fleeing when one's own defeat occurs, and for pursuing and capturing a fleeing enemy. 'In playfulness' means for the sake of playfulness; for at the time of battle, whether elephants are trumpeting, or horses are neighing, or chariots are rumbling, or soldiers are shouting, this training is done so that, unafraid of that noise, it can enter the enemy army.

Rājaguṇeti raññā jānitabbaguṇe. Kūṭakaṇṇarañño kira guḷavaṇṇo nāma asso ahosi. Rājā pācīnadvārena nikkhamitvā cetiyapabbataṃ gamissāmīti [M 3.0112] kalambanadītīraṃ sampatto. Asso tīre ṭhatvā udakaṃ otarituṃ na icchati, rājā assācariyaṃ āmantetvā – “aho tayā asso sikkhāpito udakaṃ otarituṃ na icchatī”ti āha. Ācariyo – “susikkhāpito deva asso, evamassa hi cittaṃ ‘sacāhaṃ udakaṃ otarissāmi, vālaṃ temissati, vāle tinte rañño aṅge udakaṃ pāteyyā’ti evaṃ tumhākaṃ sarīre udakapātanabhayena na otarati, vālaṃ gaṇhāpethā”ti [P 3.0160] āha. Rājā tathā kāresi. Asso vegena otaritvā pāraṃ gato. Etadatthaṃ ayaṃ kāraṇā karīyati. Rājavaṃseti assarājavaṃse. Vaṃso ceso assarājānaṃ, tathārūpena pahārena chinnabhinnasarīrāpi assārohaṃ parasenāya apātetvā bahi nīharantiyeva. Etadatthaṃ kāraṇaṃ kāretīti attho.

'In the royal qualities' means in the qualities to be known by a king. It is said that King Kūṭakaṇṇa had a horse named Guḷavaṇṇa. The king, intending to go to Cetiyapabbata, left through the eastern gate and reached the bank of the Kalamba river. The horse, standing on the bank, did not want to enter the water. The king summoned the horse trainer and said, “Alas, this horse, trained by you, does not want to enter the water!” The trainer replied, “O king, the horse is well-trained. For its thought is thus: ‘If I enter the water, my tail will get wet, and if my tail is wet, water might fall on the king's lap.’ Thus, out of fear of water falling on your body, it does not enter. Have someone hold its tail.” The king did so. The horse swiftly entered the water and went to the other side. This training is done for this purpose. 'In the royal lineage' means in the lineage of kingly horses. And this is the lineage of kingly horses: even though their bodies are cut and broken by such a blow, they carry the horse-rider out of the enemy army without letting him fall. The meaning is that the training is done for this purpose.

Uttame javeti javasampattiyaṃ, yathā uttamajavo hoti, evaṃ kāraṇaṃ kāretīti attho. Uttame hayeti uttamahayabhāve, yathā uttamahayo hoti, evaṃ kāraṇaṃ kāretīti attho. Tattha pakatiyā uttamahayova uttamahayakāraṇaṃ arahati, na añño. Uttamahayakāraṇāya eva ca hayo uttamajavaṃ paṭipajjati, na aññoti.

'In supreme speed' means in the accomplishment of speed; the meaning is, he has it trained in such a way that it has supreme speed. 'In the supreme horse' means in the state of being a supreme horse; the meaning is, he has it trained in such a way that it becomes a supreme horse. Therein, by nature, only a supreme horse is worthy of the training for a supreme horse, not another. And only through the training for a supreme horse does a horse attain supreme speed, not another.

Tatridaṃ [V 3.0115] vatthu – eko kira rājā ekaṃ sindhavapotakaṃ labhitvā sindhavabhāvaṃ ajānitvāva imaṃ sikkhāpehīti ācariyassa adāsi. Ācariyopi tassa sindhavabhāvaṃ ajānanto taṃ māsakhādakaghoṭakānaṃ kāraṇāsu upaneti. So attano ananucchavikattā kāraṇaṃ na paṭipajjati. So taṃ dametuṃ asakkonto “kūṭasso ayaṃ mahārājā”ti vissajjāpesi.

Here is the story: A certain king, it is said, having obtained a young Sindhu horse, and not knowing its quality as a Sindhu horse, gave it to a trainer, saying, “Train this one.” The trainer too, not knowing its quality as a Sindhu horse, subjected it to the trainings of rough, bean-eating horses. Because this was unsuitable for it, it did not undertake the training. He, being unable to tame it, had it sent away, saying, “This is a deceitful horse, O great king.”

Athekadivasaṃ eko assācariyapubbako daharo upajjhāyassa bhaṇḍakaṃ gahetvā gacchanto taṃ parikhāpiṭṭhe carantaṃ disvā – “anaggho, bhante, sindhavapotako”ti upajjhāyassa kathesi. Sace rājā jāneyya, maṅgalassaṃ naṃ kareyyāti. Thero āha – “micchādiṭṭhiko, tāta, rājā appeva nāma buddhasāsane pasīdeyya rañño kathehī”ti. So gantvā, – “mahārāja, anaggho sindhavapotako atthī”ti [P 3.0161] kathesi. Tayā diṭṭho[M 3.0113], tātāti? Āma, mahārājāti. Kiṃ laddhuṃ vaṭṭatīti? Tumhākaṃ bhuñjanakasuvaṇṇathāle tumhākaṃ bhuñjanakabhattaṃ tumhākaṃ pivanakaraso tumhākaṃ gandhā tumhākaṃ mālāti. Rājā sabbaṃ dāpesi. Daharo gāhāpetvā agamāsi.

Then one day, a young monk who had formerly been a horse trainer, while going with his preceptor's requisites, saw that Sindhu colt grazing on the outer edge of the moat and said to his preceptor, 'Venerable sir, this is a priceless Sindhu colt. If the king were to know of it, he would make it the state auspicious horse.' The elder said, 'Dear one, the king holds wrong views. Perhaps he might yet gain faith in the Buddha’s teaching. Tell the king.' So he went and said, 'Great king, there is a priceless Sindhu colt.' 'Have you seen it, dear one?' 'Yes, great king.' 'What is it worthy to receive?' 'Your golden eating bowl, your food for eating, your drink for drinking, your perfumes, and your garlands.' The king had all these given. The young monk had them taken and went to the horse.

Asso gandhaṃ ghāyitvāva “mayhaṃ guṇajānanakaācariyo atthi maññe”ti sīsaṃ ukkhipitvā olokento aṭṭhāsi. Daharo gantvā “bhattaṃ bhuñjā”ti accharaṃ pahari. Asso āgantvā suvaṇṇathāle bhattaṃ bhuñji, rasaṃ pivi. Atha naṃ gandhehi vilimpitvā rājapiḷandhanaṃ piḷandhitvā “purato purato gacchā”ti accharaṃ pahari. So daharassa purato purato gantvā maṅgalassaṭṭhāne aṭṭhāsi. Daharo – “ayaṃ te, mahārāja, anaggho sindhavapotako, imināva naṃ niyāmena katipāhaṃ paṭijaggāpehī”ti vatvā nikkhami.

The horse, just upon smelling the scent, thought, 'It seems there is a trainer who knows my qualities,' and lifting its head, it stood looking. The young monk went and, snapping his fingers, said, 'Eat the rice.' The horse came and ate the rice from the golden plate and drank the juice. Then, after anointing it with perfumes and adorning it with the king's garland, he snapped his fingers, saying, 'Go on ahead.' It went ahead of the young monk and stood in the place of the auspicious horse. The young monk said, 'Great king, this is your priceless Sindhu colt. Look after it in this very manner for a few days,' and then he departed.

Atha katipāhassa accayena āgantvā assassa ānubhāvaṃ passissasi, mahārājāti. Sādhu ācariya kuhiṃ ṭhatvā passāmāti? Uyyānaṃ gaccha, mahārājāti. Rājā assaṃ gāhāpetvā agamāsi. Daharo accharaṃ paharitvā “etaṃ rukkhaṃ anupariyāhī”ti assassa saññaṃ adāsi. Asso pakkhanditvā rukkhaṃ anuparigantvā āgato. Rājā neva gacchantaṃ na āgacchantaṃ addasa. Diṭṭho te, mahārājāti? Na diṭṭho, tātāti. Valañjakadaṇḍaṃ etaṃ rukkhaṃ nissāya ṭhapethāti vatvā accharaṃ pahari “valañjakadaṇḍaṃ gahetvā ehī”ti. Asso pakkhanditvā mukhena gahetvā āgato. Diṭṭhaṃ, mahārājāti. Diṭṭhaṃ, tātāti.

Then, after a few days had passed, he returned and said, 'Great king, do you wish to see the horse's power?' 'Good, teacher. Where shall we stand to see it?' 'Go to the park, great king.' The king had the horse brought and went. The young monk snapped his fingers and gave the horse the signal, 'Circle this tree.' The horse leaped, circled the tree, and returned. The king saw it neither going nor coming. 'Did you see it, great king?' 'I did not see it, dear one.' 'Place your royal staff leaning against this tree,' he said, and snapping his fingers, he gave the command, 'Take the royal staff and come.' The horse leaped, took it in its mouth, and returned. 'Was it seen, great king?' 'It was seen, dear one.'

Puna [V 3.0116] accharaṃ pahari “uyyānassa pākāramatthakena caritvā ehī”ti. Asso tathā akāsi. Diṭṭho, mahārājāti. Na diṭṭho, tātāti. Rattakambalaṃ āharāpetvā assassa pāde bandhāpetvā tatheva saññaṃ adāsi. Asso ullaṅghitvā pākāramatthakena anupariyāyi. Balavatā purisena āviñchanaalātaggisikhā [P 3.0162] viya uyyānapākāramatthake paññāyittha. Asso gantvā samīpe ṭhito. Diṭṭhaṃ, mahārājāti. Diṭṭhaṃ, tātāti. Maṅgalapokkharaṇipākāramatthake anupariyāhīti saññaṃ adāsi.

Again, he snapped his fingers, saying, 'Travel along the top of the garden wall and come.' The horse did so. 'Have you seen, great king?' 'I have not seen, dear one.' He had a red blanket brought and had it tied to the horse's feet, then gave the same signal as before. The horse leaped and circled along the top of the garden wall. It appeared on top of the garden wall like the tip of a firebrand whirled by a strong man. The horse went and stood nearby. 'Have you seen, great king?' 'I have seen, dear one.' He gave the signal, 'Circle along the top of the wall of the auspicious lotus pond.'

Puna “pokkharaṇiṃ otaritvā padumapattesu cārikaṃ carāhī”ti saññaṃ adāsi. Pokkharaṇiṃ otaritvā sabbapadumapatte caritvā agamāsi, ekaṃ pattampi [M 3.0114] anakkantaṃ vā phālitaṃ vā chinditaṃ vā khaṇḍitaṃ vā nāhosi. Diṭṭhaṃ, mahārājāti. Diṭṭhaṃ, tātāti. Accharaṃ paharitvā taṃ hatthatalaṃ upanāmesi. Dhātūpatthaddho laṅghitvā hatthatale aṭṭhāsi. Diṭṭhaṃ, mahārājāti? Diṭṭhaṃ, tātāti. Evaṃ uttamahayo eva uttamakāraṇāya uttamajavaṃ paṭipajjati.

Again, he gave the signal, 'Descend into the pond and tread upon the lotus leaves.' Descending into the pond, it trod upon all the lotus leaves and returned; not a single leaf was untrodden, or split, or severed, or broken. 'Have you seen, great king?' 'I have seen, dear one.' Snapping his fingers, he presented his palm to the horse. Firm in its elements, it leaped and stood upon his palm. 'Have you seen, great king?' 'I have seen, dear one.' Thus, only an excellent horse can achieve excellent speed for an excellent reason.

Uttame sākhalyeti muduvācāya. Muduvācāya hi, “tāta, tvaṃ mā cintayi, rañño maṅgalasso bhavissasi, rājabhojanādīni labhissasī”ti uttamahayakāraṇaṃ kāretabbo. Tena vuttaṃ “uttame sākhalye”ti. Rājabhoggoti rañño upabhogo. Rañño aṅganteva saṅkhaṃ gacchatīti yattha katthaci gacchantena hatthaṃ viya pādaṃ viya anohāyeva gantabbaṃ hoti. Tasmā aṅganti saṅkhaṃ gacchati, catūsu vā senaṅgesu ekaṃ aṅgaṃ hoti.

'In the highest friendliness' means with gentle speech. For with gentle speech, the training of an excellent horse is to be carried out, saying, 'Dear one, do not worry; you will become the king’s auspicious horse, you will receive royal food and so on.' Therefore, it is said, 'in the highest friendliness.' 'Fit for a king's use' means for the king's enjoyment. 'It is counted as a limb of the king' means that wherever one goes, one must go without leaving it behind, just like a hand or a foot. Therefore, it is counted as a 'limb.' Or, it is one of the four limbs of an army.

Asekhāya sammādiṭṭhiyāti arahattaphalasammādiṭṭhiyā. Sammāsaṅkappādayopi taṃsampayuttāva. Sammāñāṇaṃ pubbe vuttasammādiṭṭhiyeva. Ṭhapetvā pana aṭṭha [P 3.0163] phalaṅgāni sesā dhammā vimuttīti veditabbā. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānameva. Ayaṃ pana desanā ugghaṭitaññūpuggalassa vasena arahattanikūṭaṃ gahetvā niṭṭhāpitāti.

'With the right view of a non-learner' means with the right view associated with the fruit of Arahantship. Right intention and the others are also associated with that. Right knowledge is simply the right view mentioned before. However, setting aside the eight factors of the fruit, the remaining states should be known as 'liberation.' The rest is clear everywhere. This discourse, however, was brought to its conclusion for the sake of a person of quick understanding by taking the pinnacle of Arahantship.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Middle-length Discourses.

Bhaddālisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Bhaddāli Sutta is concluded.

6. Laṭukikopamasuttavaṇṇanā

6. The Explanation of the Laṭukikopama Sutta

148. Evaṃ [V 3.0117] me sutanti laṭukikopamasuttaṃ. Tattha yena so vanasaṇḍoti ayampi mahāudāyitthero bhagavatā saddhiṃyeva piṇḍāya pavisitvā saddhiṃ paṭikkami. Tasmā yena so bhagavatā upasaṅkamanto vanasaṇḍo tenupasaṅkamīti veditabbo. Apahattāti apahārako. Upahattāti upahārako. Paṭisallānā vuṭṭhitoti phalasamāpattito vuṭṭhito.

148. The Laṭukikopama Sutta is the one beginning 'Thus have I heard.' Therein, regarding 'to that grove': this Elder Mahā Udāyī, having entered for alms together with the Blessed One, also returned together with him. Therefore, it should be understood thus: he approached that grove which the Blessed One was approaching. 'Apahattā' means one who takes away. 'Upahattā' means one who brings. 'Emerged from seclusion' means having emerged from the attainment of fruition.

149. Yaṃ [M 3.0115] bhagavāti yasmiṃ samaye bhagavā. Iṅghāti āṇattiyaṃ nipāto. Aññathattanti cittassa aññathattaṃ. Tañca kho na bhagavantaṃ paṭicca, evarūpaṃ pana paṇītabhojanaṃ alabhantā kathaṃ yāpessāmāti evaṃ paṇītabhojanaṃ paṭicca ahosīti veditabbaṃ. Bhūtapubbanti iminā rattibhojanassa paṇītabhāvaṃ dasseti. Sūpeyyanti [P 3.0164] sūpena upanetabbaṃ macchamaṃsakaḷīrādi. Samaggā bhuñjissāmāti ekato bhuñjissāma. Saṅkhatiyoti abhisaṅkhārikakhādanīyāni. Sabbā tā rattinti sabbā tā saṅkhatiyo rattiṃyeva honti, divā pana appā parittā thokikā hontīti. Manussā hi divā yāgukañjiyādīhi yāpetvāpi rattiṃ yathāsatti yathāpaṇītameva bhuñjanti.

149. 'When the Blessed One' means: at the time when the Blessed One... 'Iṅgha' is a particle used in the sense of a command. 'A change' means a change of mind. And that did not occur on account of the Blessed One; rather, it should be understood that it occurred on account of the exquisite food, with the thought, 'How shall we subsist if we do not get such exquisite food?' By this phrase 'formerly', he shows the excellent nature of the night-meal. 'With curry' means that which is to be brought with curry, such as fish, meat, bamboo shoots, and so on. 'We will eat together' means: we will eat in one place. 'Prepared foods' means prepared delicacies. 'All that at night' means: all those prepared foods are only for the night; during the day, however, they are few, insignificant, and paltry. For people, having subsisted during the day with gruel, rice-gruel, and so on, at night eat only excellent food according to their ability.

Puna bhūtapubbanti iminā ratti vikālabhojane ādīnavaṃ dasseti. Tattha andhakāratimisāyanti bahalandhakāre. Māṇavehīti corehi. Katakammehīti katacorakammehi. Corā kira katakammā yaṃ nesaṃ devataṃ āyācitvā kammaṃ nipphannaṃ, tassa upahāratthāya manusse māretvā galalohitādīni gaṇhanti. Te aññesu manussesu māriyamānesu kolāhalā uppajjissanti, pabbajitaṃ pariyesanto nāma natthīti maññamānā bhikkhū gahetvā mārenti. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Akatakammehīti aṭavito gāmaṃ āgamanakāle kammanipphannatthaṃ puretaraṃ balikammaṃ kātukāmehi. Asaddhammena nimantetīti “ehi bhikkhu ajjekarattiṃ idheva bhuñjitvā idha vasitvā sampattiṃ anubhavitvā sve gamissasī”ti methunadhammena nimanteti.

Again, by this phrase 'formerly', he shows the danger in eating at the wrong time at night. Therein, 'in the thick darkness' means in dense darkness. 'By young men' means by thieves. 'By those who have done the deed' means by those who have committed an act of thievery. It is said that thieves who have done their deed, having supplicated to a deity of theirs for the accomplishment of their act, kill people to make an offering to that deity and take things like their throat-blood. When other people are being killed, an uproar will arise, so thinking, 'There is no one who will search for a renunciant,' they seize a monk and kill him. It was with reference to this that this was said. 'By those who have not done the deed' means by those who, at the time of coming from the forest to a village, wish to perform a sacrificial offering beforehand for the accomplishment of their act. 'One invites with what is not the true Dhamma' means one invites with the practice of sexual intercourse, saying: 'Come, monk, eat here for one night today, stay here, experience sensual pleasure, and you may go tomorrow.'

Puna bhūtapubbanti iminā attanā diṭṭhakāraṇaṃ katheti. Vijjantarikāyāti [P 3.0165] vijjuvijjotanakkhaṇe[V 3.0118]. Vissaramakāsīti mahāsaddamakāsi. Abhummeti bhū’ti vaḍḍhi, abhū’ti avaḍḍhi, vināso mayhanti attho. Pisāco vata manti pisāco maṃ khādituṃ āgato vata. Ātumārī mātumārīti ettha ātūti pitā, mātūti mātā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yassa pitā vā mātā vā atthi, taṃ mātāpitaro amhākaṃ puttakoti yathā tathā vā uppādetvā yaṃkiñci khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ datvā ekasmiṃ ṭhāne sayāpenti. So evaṃ rattiṃ piṇḍāya na carati. Tuyhaṃ pana mātāpitaro matā maññe, tena evaṃ carasīti.

Again, by this phrase 'formerly', he relates a reason he himself has seen. 'In a flash of lightning' means at the moment of a lightning flash. 'He made a cry' means he made a loud sound. In 'it was my undoing', 'bhū' means growth, 'abhū' means non-growth; the meaning is 'my destruction'. 'A goblin, alas, for me' means: a goblin has indeed come to devour me. In 'father-slayer, mother-slayer', 'ātu' means father, and 'mātu' means mother. This is what is meant: For one who has a father or a mother, the parents, saying, 'This is our little son,' somehow or other procure some hard or soft food, give it to him, and make him sleep in one place. Such a person does not wander for alms at night like this. As for you, I suppose your mother and father are dead; is it for that reason that you wander about like this?

150. Evamevāti [M 3.0116] evameva kiñci ānisaṃsaṃ apassantā nikkāraṇeneva. Evamāhaṃsūti garahanto āha. Tattha āhaṃsūti vadanti. Kiṃ panimassāti imassa appamattakassa hetu kiṃ vattabbaṃ nāma, nanu apassantena viya asuṇantena viya bhavitabbanti. Oramattakassāti parittamattakassa. Adhisallikhatevāyanti ayaṃ samaṇo navanītaṃ pisanto viya padumanāḷasuttaṃ kakacena okkantanto viya atisallekhati, ativāyāmaṃ karoti. Sikkhākāmāti sāriputtamoggallānādayo viya sikkhākāmā, tesu ca appaccayaṃ upaṭṭhapenti. Tesañhi evaṃ hoti “sace [P 3.0166] ete ‘appamattakametaṃ, haratha bhagavā’ti vadeyyuṃ, kiṃ satthā na hareyya. Evaṃ pana avatvā bhagavantaṃ parivāretvā nisinnā ‘evaṃ bhagavā, sādhu bhagavā, paññapetha bhagavā’ti atirekataraṃ ussāhaṃ paṭilabhantī”ti. Tasmā tesu appaccayaṃ upaṭṭhapenti.

150. 'Evamevāti' means: just so, those foolish men, not seeing any benefit, said so without any reason. Thus the Blessed One spoke, wishing to censure. Therein, 'āhaṃsu' means they say. 'Kiṃ panimassa' means: for the sake of this insignificant matter, what is there to be said? Should one not be as if not seeing, as if not hearing? 'Oramattakassa' means of an insignificant fault. 'Adhisallikhatevāyanti' means: this ascetic, like one crushing fresh butter, or like one cutting a lotus stalk with a saw, scrapes excessively, makes excessive effort. 'Sikkhākāmā' means: there are monks desirous of the training, like Sāriputta, Moggallāna, and others, and they cause an offense against them. For this thought occurs to them: 'If these monks were to say, "This is an insignificant matter, remove it, Blessed One," would the Teacher not remove it? But without saying so, having surrounded the Blessed One, they sit and say, "So it is, Blessed One; it is good, Blessed One; may the Blessed One lay it down," and thus they gain even greater enthusiasm.' Therefore, they cause an offense against them.

Tesanti tesaṃ ekaccānaṃ moghapurisānaṃ. Tanti taṃ appamattakaṃ pahātabbaṃ. Thūlo kaliṅgaroti gale baddhaṃ mahākaṭṭhaṃ viya hoti. Laṭukikā sakuṇikāti cātakasakuṇikā. Sā kira ravasataṃ ravitvā naccasataṃ naccitvā sakiṃ gocaraṃ gaṇhāti. Ākāsato bhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhitaṃ pana naṃ disvā vacchapālakādayo kīḷanatthaṃ pūtilatāya bandhanti. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Āgametīti upeti. Tañhi tassāti taṃ pūtilatābandhanaṃ tassā appasarīratāya ceva appathāmatāya ca balavabandhanaṃ nāma, mahantaṃ nāḷikerarajju viya ducchijjaṃ hoti. Tesanti tesaṃ moghapurisānaṃ saddhāmandatāya ca paññāmandatāya ca balavaṃ bandhanaṃ nāma, dukkaṭavatthumattakampi mahantaṃ pārājikavatthu viya duppajahaṃ hoti.

'Tesaṃ' means: for some of those foolish men. 'Taṃ' means: that insignificant thing to be abandoned. 'Thūlo kaliṅgaro' means: it is like a great log tied to the neck. The quail bird (laṭukikā sakuṇikā) is a cātaka bird. It is said that after crying a hundred times and dancing a hundred times, it takes its food just once. But seeing it settled on the ground from the sky, cowherds and others tie it with a pūtilatā creeper for sport. It was with reference to this that this was said. 'Āgameti' means it approaches. 'Tañhi tassā' means: that binding with the pūtilatā creeper, for that bird, on account of its small body and its lack of strength, is indeed a strong binding; it is hard to break, like a great rope of coconut fiber. 'Tesaṃ' means: for those foolish men, on account of their dullness of faith and dullness of wisdom, it is a strong binding; even a mere matter of a dukkaṭa offense becomes as hard to abandon as a great matter of a pārājika offense.

151. Sukkapakkhe pahātabbassāti kiṃ imassa appamattakassa pahātabbassa hetu bhagavatā [V 3.0119] vattabbaṃ atthi, yassa no bhagavā pahānamāha. Nanu evaṃ bhagavato adhippāyaṃ ñatvāpi pahātabbamevāti attho. Appossukkāti anussukkā. Pannalomāti [P 3.0167] patitalomā, na tassa pahātabbabhayena uddhaggalomā. Paradattavuttāti parehi dinnavuttino, parato laddhena yāpentāti attho. Migabhūtena cetasā viharantīti apaccāsīsanapakkhe [M 3.0117] ṭhitā hutvā viharanti. Migo hi pahāraṃ labhitvā manussāvāsaṃ gantvā bhesajjaṃ vā vaṇatelaṃ vā labhissāmīti ajjhāsayaṃ akatvā pahāraṃ labhitvāva agāmakaṃ araññaṃ pavisitvā pahaṭaṭṭhānaṃ heṭṭhā katvā nipatitvā phāsubhūtakāle uṭṭhāya gacchati. Evaṃ migā apaccāsīsanapakkhe ṭhitā. Idaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “migabhūtena cetasā viharantī”ti. Tañhi tassāti taṃ varattabandhanaṃ tassa hatthināgassa mahāsarīratāya ceva mahāthāmatāya ca dubbalabandhanaṃ nāma. Pūtilatā viya suchijjaṃ hoti. Tesaṃ tanti tesaṃ taṃ kulaputtānaṃ saddhāmahantatāya ca paññāmahantatāya ca mahantaṃ pārājikavatthupi dukkaṭavatthumattakaṃ viya suppajahaṃ hoti.

151. Regarding 'sukkapakkhe pahātabbassa': Is there anything to be said by the Blessed One on account of this trifling thing to be abandoned, the abandoning of which our Blessed One has taught? Surely, even knowing the Blessed One’s intention, it is indeed to be abandoned. This is the meaning. 'Appossukkā' means without exertion. 'Pannalomā' means with hair lowered; their hair does not stand on end due to fear of what is to be abandoned. 'Paradattavuttī' means they live on what is given by others; that is, they maintain themselves with what is received from another. This is the meaning. 'Migabhūtena cetasā viharanti' means they dwell, having become established in the state of non-expectation. Indeed, a deer, having been struck, does not form the intention, 'I will go to a human habitation and get medicine or wound-oil.' Rather, having been struck, it enters a village-less forest, lies down with the wounded place underneath, and when it is comfortable, it gets up and goes. Thus, deer are established in the state of non-expectation. Referring to this, it was said: 'they dwell with a mind that has become like a deer's'. Regarding 'tañhi tassa': That binding with a leather strap, for that great elephant, on account of its great body and great strength, is a weak bond. It is as easily broken as a rotten creeper. Regarding 'tesaṃ taṃ': For those sons of good family, on account of their great faith and great wisdom, even a great matter of a Pārājika offense becomes as easy to abandon as a mere matter of a Dukkaṭa offense.

152. Daliddoti dāliddiyena samannāgato. Assakoti nissako. Anāḷhiyoti anaḍḍho. Agārakanti khuddakagehaṃ. Oluggavilugganti yassa gehayaṭṭhiyo piṭṭhivaṃsato muccitvā maṇḍale laggā, maṇḍalato muccitvā bhūmiyaṃ laggā. Kākātidāyinti yattha kiñcideva bhuñjissāmāti anto nisinnakāle visuṃ dvārakiccaṃ nāma natthi, tato tato kākā [P 3.0168] pavisitvā parivārenti. Sūrakākā hi palāyanakāle ca yathāsammukhaṭṭhāneneva nikkhamitvā palāyanti. Naparamarūpanti na puññavantānaṃ gehaṃ viya uttamarūpaṃ. Khaṭopikāti vilīvamañcako. Oluggaviluggāti oṇatuṇṇatā. Dhaññasamavāpakanti dhaññañca samavāpakañca. Tattha dhaññaṃ nāma kudrūsako. Samavāpakanti lābubījakumbhaṇḍabījakādi bījajātaṃ. Naparamarūpanti yathā puññavantānaṃ gandhasālibījādi parisuddhaṃ bījaṃ, na evarūpaṃ. Jāyikāti kapaṇajāyā. Naparamarūpāti pacchisīsā lambatthanī mahodarā pisācā viya bībhacchā. Sāmaññanti samaṇabhāvo. So vatassaṃ, yohanti so vatāhaṃ puriso nāma assaṃ, yo kesamassuṃ ohāretvā pabbajeyyanti.

152. 'Daliddo' means one endowed with poverty. 'Assako' means without property. 'Anāḷhiyo' means not wealthy. 'Agārakaṃ' means a small house. 'Oluggaviluggaṃ' means a house of which the rafters, having slipped from the ridgepole, are caught on the ring-beam, and having slipped from the ring-beam, are caught on the ground. 'Kākātidāyiṃ' means a place where, when one is sitting inside thinking, 'We will eat something,' there is no need to find a separate doorway; from here and there crows enter and surround one. Indeed, bold crows, when it is time to flee, exit and fly away from whatever spot is in front of them. 'Naparamarūpaṃ' means not of excellent form, like the house of meritorious people. 'Khaṭopikā' means a bedstead woven with palm-strips. 'Oluggaviluggā' means being low and high, i.e., uneven. 'Dhaññasamavāpakaṃ' means grain and what is sown with it. Therein, 'dhaññaṃ' is kudrūsaka grain. 'Samavāpakaṃ' means the collection of seeds such as gourd seeds and pumpkin seeds. 'Naparamarūpaṃ' means not of such a form as the pure seeds, such as fragrant sāli rice seeds, of meritorious people. 'Jāyikā' means a wretched wife. 'Naparamarūpā' means having breasts hanging down like a basket on the head, a large belly, and being repulsive like a goblin. 'Sāmaññaṃ' means the state of a recluse. 'So vatassaṃ, yohaṃ' means: 'Indeed, I would be a true man, I who would go forth after shaving off my hair and beard.'

So na sakkuṇeyyāti so evaṃ cintetvāpi gehaṃ gantvā – “pabbajjā nāma lābhagarukā dukkarā durāsadā, sattapi aṭṭhapi gāme piṇḍāya caritvā yathādhoteneva pattena āgantabbampi hoti[V 3.0120], evaṃ yāpetuṃ asakkontassa [M 3.0118] me puna āgatassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ icchitabbaṃ, tiṇavallidabbasambhārā nāma dussamodhāniyā, kinti karomī”ti vīmaṃsati. Athassa taṃ agārakaṃ vejayantapāsādo viya upaṭṭhāti. Athassa khaṭopikaṃ oloketvā – “mayi gate imaṃ visaṅkharitvā uddhanālātaṃ karissanti, puna aṭṭanipādavilīvādīni laddhabbāni honti, kinti [P 3.0169] karissāmī”ti cinteti. Athassa sā sirisayanaṃ viya upaṭṭhāti. Tato dhaññakumbhiṃ oloketvā – “mayi gate ayaṃ gharaṇī imaṃ dhaññaṃ tena tena saddhiṃ bhuñjissati. Puna āgatena jīvitavutti nāma laddhabbā hoti, kinti karissāmī”ti cinteti. Athassa sā aḍḍhateḷasāni koṭṭhāgārasatāni viya upaṭṭhāti. Tato mātugāmaṃ oloketvā – “mayi gate imaṃ hatthigopako vā assagopako vā yo koci palobhessati, puna āgatena bhattapācikā nāma laddhabbā hoti, kinti karissāmī”ti cinteti. Athassa sā rūpinī devī viya upaṭṭhāti. Idaṃ sandhāya “so na sakkuṇeyyā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Regarding 'He would not be able to': Even after thinking thus, he goes home and reflects: 'The going forth is demanding of requisites, difficult, and hard to undertake. After wandering for alms in seven or eight villages, one may have to return with a bowl just as it was washed. For me, unable to maintain myself thus, a place to live will have to be sought upon my return. Grass, vines, and building materials are difficult to gather. What shall I do?' Then that little house appears to him like the Vejayanta palace. Then, looking at his palm-strip bed, he thinks: 'When I am gone, they will dismantle this and make it into firewood for the stove. Again, the frame, legs, palm-strips, and so on will have to be obtained. What shall I do?' Then that bed appears to him like a glorious couch. Next, looking at his grain pot, he thinks: 'When I am gone, this housewife will consume this grain with this man and that. Upon my return, a means of livelihood will have to be found. What shall I do?' Then that grain pot appears to him like twelve hundred and fifty storehouses. Then, looking at the woman, he thinks: 'When I am gone, some elephant keeper or horse keeper or some other person will entice her. Upon my return, a woman to cook rice will have to be found. What shall I do?' Then that woman appears to him like a beautiful goddess. Referring to this, it was said, 'He would not be able to,' and so on.

153. Nikkhagaṇānanti suvaṇṇanikkhasatānaṃ. Cayoti santānato katasannicayo. Dhaññagaṇānanti dhaññasakaṭasatānaṃ.

153. Regarding 'collections of nikkhas': Hundreds of gold nikkhas. Regarding 'a heap': An accumulation made continuously. Regarding 'collections of grain': Hundreds of cartloads of grain.

154. Cattārome, udāyi, puggalāti idha kiṃ dasseti? Heṭṭhā “te tañceva pajahanti, te tañceva nappajahantī”ti pajahanakā ca appajahanakā ca rāsivasena dassitā, na pāṭiyekkaṃ vibhattā. Idāni yathā nāma dabbasambhāratthaṃ gato puriso paṭipāṭiyā rukkhe chinditvā puna nivattitvā vaṅkañca pahāya kamme upanetabbayuttakameva gaṇhāti, evameva appajahanake chaḍḍetvā abbohārike katvā pajahanakapuggalā cattāro hontīti dassetuṃ imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi.

154. Regarding 'These four, Udāyi, are types of persons': What does this show here? Previously, with the words 'some abandon it, and some do not abandon it,' those who abandon and those who do not abandon were shown by way of a group, not distinguished individually. Now, just as a man who has gone for the sake of materials, having cut down trees in succession, turns back and, having discarded the crooked wood, takes only that which is suitable to be brought for his work; in the very same way, this discourse was begun to show that, having discarded those who do not abandon and having rendered them non-referable, there are four types of persons who do abandon.

Upadhipahānāyāti khandhupadhikilesupadhiabhisaṅkhārupadhikāmaguṇūpadhīti imesaṃ upadhīnaṃ pahānāya. Upadhipaṭisaṃyuttāti upadhianudhāvanakā. Sarasaṅkappāti ettha saranti dhāvantīti sarā. Saṅkappentīti [P 3.0170] saṅkappā. Padadvayenapi vitakkāyeva vuttā. Samudācarantīti abhibhavanti ajjhottharitvā vattanti. Saṃyuttoti kilesehi saṃyutto. Indriyavemattatāti indriyanānattatā[M 3.0119]. Kadāci karahacīti bahukālaṃ vītivattetvā. Satisammosāti satisammosena. Nipātoti ayokaṭāhamhi [V 3.0121] patanaṃ. Ettāvatā “nappajahati, pajahati, khippaṃ pajahatī”ti tayo rāsayo dassitā. Tesu cattāro janā nappajahanti nāma, cattāro pajahanti nāma, cattāro khippaṃ pajahanti nāma.

'For the abandoning of attachments' refers to the abandonment of these attachments: the aggregates as attachment, the defilements as attachment, the volitional formations as attachment, and sensual pleasures as attachment. 'Connected with attachments' means thoughts that run after attachments. Regarding 'thoughts that run': herein, `sarā` means they run towards various objects; `saṅkappā` means they conceive of them. By both terms, only sensual thoughts are meant. 'They arise' means they overwhelm; having overwhelmed, they occur. 'Connected' means connected with the defilements. 'Diversity of faculties' means the variety of faculties. 'Occasionally' means after letting a long time pass. 'Through loss of mindfulness' means due to a lapse of mindfulness. 'A fall' means the falling of a raindrop onto an iron pan. By this much, three groups have been shown: 'does not abandon,' 'abandons,' and 'quickly abandons.' Among them, four persons are called 'those who do not abandon,' four are called 'those who abandon,' and four are called 'those who quickly abandon.'

Tattha puthujjano sotāpanno sakadāgāmī anāgāmīti ime cattāro janā nappajahanti nāma. Puthujjanādayo tāva mā pajahantu, anāgāmī kathaṃ na pajahatīti? Sopi hi yāvadevassa bhavalobho atthi, tāva ahosukhaṃ ahosukhanti abhinandati. Tasmā nappajahati nāma. Eteyeva pana cattāro janā pajahanti nāma. Sotāpannādayo tāva pajahantu, puthujjano kathaṃ pajahatīti? Āraddhavipassako hi satisammosena sahasā kilese uppanne “mādisassa nāma bhikkhuno kileso uppanno”ti saṃvegaṃ katvā vīriyaṃ paggayha vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā maggena kilese samugghāteti. Iti so pajahati nāma. Teyeva cattāro khippaṃ pajahanti nāma. Tattha imasmiṃ sutte, mahāhatthipadopame (ma. ni. 1.288 ādayo), indriyabhāvaneti (ma. ni. 3.453 ādayo) imesu suttesu kiñcāpi tatiyavāro gahito, pañho pana dutiyavāreneva kathitoti veditabbo.

Herein, the ordinary person, the stream-enterer, the once-returner, and the non-returner—these four persons are called 'those who do not abandon.' Let the ordinary persons and so on not abandon for now, but for what reason does the non-returner not abandon? Because, for as long as craving for existence exists for him, to that extent he delights. Therefore, he is called 'one who does not abandon.' Furthermore, these same four persons are called 'those who abandon.' Let the stream-enterers and so on abandon, but how does the ordinary person abandon? For an ordinary person who has undertaken insight meditation, when a defilement suddenly arises due to a lapse of mindfulness, having become alarmed, thinking, 'A defilement has arisen in a monk such as myself!', he arouses energy, develops insight, and eradicates the defilements by means of the path. For this reason, he is called 'one who abandons.' These same four persons are called 'those who quickly abandon.' Herein, in this sutta, in the Mahāhatthipadopama Sutta, and in the Indriyabhāvanā Sutta—in these suttas, although the third section, 'quickly abandons,' is taken up, it should be understood that the question is explained only by means of the second section, 'abandons.'

Upadhi [P 3.0171] dukkhassa mūlanti ettha pañca khandhā upadhi nāma. Taṃ dukkhassa mūlanti iti viditvā kilesupadhinā nirupadhi hoti, niggahaṇo nitaṇhoti attho. Upadhisaṅkhaye vimuttoti taṇhakkhaye nibbāne ārammaṇato vimutto.

In the text 'Attachment is the root of suffering,' herein the five aggregates are called attachment. Knowing thus that this is the root of suffering, one becomes free from attachment, that is, the attachment of the defilements; the meaning is: without grasping, without craving. 'Liberated through the destruction of attachment' means liberated from the defilements by taking as object Nibbāna, which is the destruction of craving.

155. Evaṃ cattāro puggale vitthāretvā idāni ye pajahanti, te “ime nāma ettake kilese pajahanti”. Ye nappajahanti, tepi “ime nāma ettake kilese nappajahantī”ti dassetuṃ pañca kho ime udāyi kāmaguṇātiādimāha. Tattha miḷhasukhanti asucisukhaṃ. Anariyasukhanti anariyehi sevitasukhaṃ. Bhāyitabbanti etassa sukhassa paṭilābhatopi vipākatopi bhāyitabbaṃ. Nekkhammasukhanti kāmato nikkhantasukhaṃ. Pavivekasukhanti gaṇatopi kilesatopi pavivittasukhaṃ. Upasamasukhanti rāgādivūpasamatthāya sukhaṃ. Sambodhasukhanti maggasaṅkhātassa sambodhassa nibbattanatthāya [M 3.0120] sukhaṃ. Na bhāyitabbanti etassa sukhassa paṭilābhatopi vipākatopi na bhāyitabbaṃ, bhāvetabbamevetaṃ.

155. Having thus elaborated on the four persons, now, in order to show that 'those who abandon abandon this many defilements of such and such a name,' and 'those who do not abandon do not abandon this many defilements of such and such a name,' He said the passage beginning, 'These five, Udāyi, are strands of sensual pleasure.' Herein, 'filthy pleasure' means impure pleasure. 'Ignoble pleasure' means the pleasure pursued by the ignoble. 'To be feared' means one should fear both the attainment of this pleasure and its result. 'Renunciation pleasure' means the pleasure that has gone forth from sensuality. 'Seclusion pleasure' means the pleasure secluded from company and from defilements. 'Tranquility pleasure' means the pleasure that occurs for the sake of the stilling of passion and so on. 'Enlightenment pleasure' means the pleasure that occurs for the sake of the arising of enlightenment, which is called the path. 'Not to be feared' means one should not fear either the attainment of this pleasure or its result; indeed, it should be cultivated.

156. Iñjitasmiṃ [V 3.0122] vadāmīti iñjanaṃ calanaṃ phandananti vadāmi. Kiñca tattha iñjitasminti kiñca tattha iñjitaṃ. Idaṃ tattha iñjitasminti ye ete aniruddhā vitakkavicārā, idaṃ tattha iñjitaṃ. Dutiyatatiyajjhānesupi eseva nayo. Aniñjitasmiṃ vadāmīti idaṃ catutthajjhānaṃ aniñjanaṃ acalanaṃ nipphandananti vadāmi.

156. When I say, 'In the agitated,' I speak of it as a cause of movement, a cause of trembling. 'And what therein is agitated?' means: what, in that case, is the cause of agitation? 'This therein is agitated' means: those initial and sustained thoughts that are not yet ceased—this is the cause of agitation therein. This same method should be understood in the cases of the second and third jhānas as well. When I say, 'In the unagitated,' I speak of this fourth jhāna as being unagitated, unmoving, and untrembling.

Analanti vadāmīti akattabbaālayanti vadāmi, taṇhālayo [P 3.0172] ettha na uppādetabboti dasseti. Atha vā analaṃ apariyattaṃ, na ettāvatā alametanti sanniṭṭhānaṃ kātabbanti vadāmi. Nevasaññānāsaññāyatanassāpīti evarūpāyapi santāya samāpattiyā pahānameva vadāmi. Aṇuṃ vā thūlaṃ vāti khuddakaṃ vā mahantaṃ vā appasāvajjaṃ vā mahāsāvajjaṃ vā. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānameva. Desanā pana neyyapuggalassa vasena arahattanikūṭeneva niṭṭhāpitāti.

When I say, 'Not enough,' I mean I say that attachment should not be made; this shows that craving-attachment should not be produced herein. Alternatively: 'Not enough' means insufficient. I say that the conclusion, 'By this much, this is enough,' should not be made. 'Even of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception': I speak only of abandoning even such a peaceful attainment as this. 'Subtle or gross' means a small fetter or a great one, one with little fault or one with great fault. The rest is clear everywhere. The teaching, however, is brought to its conclusion crowned with Arahantship, according to the person to be guided.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

The Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Middle Length Discourses.

Laṭukikopamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Laṭukikopama Sutta is finished.

7. Cātumasuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Cātumā Sutta

157. Evaṃ [V 3.0123] me sutanti cātumasuttaṃ. Tattha cātumāyanti evaṃnāmake gāme. Pañcamattāni bhikkhusatānīti adhunā pabbajitānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ pañca satāni. Therā kira cintesuṃ – “ime kulaputtā dasabalaṃ adisvāva pabbajitā, etesaṃ bhagavantaṃ dassessāma, bhagavato santike dhammaṃ sutvā attano attano yathāupanissayena patiṭṭhahissantī”ti. Tasmā te bhikkhū gahetvā āgatā. Paṭisammodamānāti “kaccāvuso, khamanīya”ntiādiṃ paṭisanthārakathaṃ kurumānā. Senāsanāni paññāpayamānāti attano attano ācariyupajjhāyānaṃ vasanaṭṭhānāni pucchitvā dvāravātapānāni [P 3.0173] vivaritvā mañcapīṭhakaṭasārakādīni nīharitvā papphoṭetvā yathāṭṭhāne saṇṭhāpayamānā. Pattacīvarāni paṭisāmayamānāti, bhante, idaṃ [M 3.0121] me pattaṃ ṭhapetha, idaṃ cīvaraṃ, idaṃ thālakaṃ, idaṃ udakatumbaṃ, imaṃ kattarayaṭṭhinti evaṃ samaṇaparikkhāre saṅgopayamānā.

157. 'Thus have I heard' refers to the Cātumā Sutta. Herein, 'at Cātumā' means in a village of that name. 'Five hundred monks' refers to five hundred monks who had recently gone forth. The elders, it is said, thought: 'These sons of good family have gone forth without having seen the Ten-Powered One. We will show them the Blessed One; having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One, they will be established, each according to their own supporting conditions.' Therefore they came, bringing those monks. 'Exchanging greetings' means making courteous talk such as, 'I hope you are well, friend?' and so on. 'Preparing resting places' means asking about the dwelling places of their own teachers and preceptors, opening doors and windows, taking out beds, chairs, mats, and rush-mats, shaking them out, and arranging them in their proper places. 'Putting away bowls and robes' means saying, 'Venerable sirs, please place this bowl for me, this robe, this small bowl, this water gourd, this walking stick,' thus safeguarding the requisites of a recluse.

Uccāsaddā mahāsaddāti uddhaṃ uggatattā uccaṃ, patthaṭattā mahantaṃ avinibbhogasaddaṃ karontā. Kevaṭṭā maññe macchavilopeti kevaṭṭānaṃ macchapacchiṭhapitaṭṭhāne mahājano sannipatitvā – “idha aññaṃ ekaṃ macchaṃ dehi, ekaṃ macchaphālaṃ dehi, etassa te mahā dinno, mayhaṃ khuddako”ti evaṃ uccāsaddaṃ mahāsaddaṃ karonti. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Macchagahaṇatthaṃ jāle pakkhittepi tasmiṃ ṭhāne kevaṭṭā ceva aññe ca “paviṭṭho na paviṭṭho, gahito na gahito”ti mahāsaddaṃ karonti. Tampi sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Paṇāmemīti nīharāmi. Na vo mama santike vatthabbanti tumhe mādisassa buddhassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ āgantvā evaṃ mahāsaddaṃ karotha, attano dhammatāya vasantā kiṃ nāma sāruppaṃ karissatha, tumhādisānaṃ mama santike vasanakiccaṃ natthīti dīpeti. Tesu ekabhikkhupi “bhagavā tumhe mahāsaddamattakena amhe paṇāmethā”ti vā aññaṃ vā kiñci vattuṃ nāsakkhi, sabbe bhagavato vacanaṃ sampaṭicchantā “evaṃ, bhante,”ti vatvā nikkhamiṃsu. Evaṃ pana tesaṃ ahosi “mayaṃ satthāraṃ passissāma, dhammakathaṃ sossāma, satthu santike vasissāmāti [P 3.0174] āgatā. Evarūpassa pana garuno satthu santikaṃ āgantvā mahāsaddaṃ karimhā, amhākameva dosoyaṃ, paṇāmitamhā, na no laddhaṃ bhagavato santike vatthuṃ, na [V 3.0124] suvaṇṇavaṇṇasarīraṃ oloketuṃ, na madhurassarena dhammaṃ sotu”nti. Te balavadomanassajātā hutvā pakkamiṃsu.

'Loud noises, great noises' means they were making a high sound because it rose upwards, and a great sound because it spread out, an indistinguishable clamor. 'Like fishermen, I suppose, at the plundering of fish' refers to how, at the place where fishermen have set down their fish baskets, a great crowd gathers and makes a loud and great noise, saying: 'Give me another fish here! Give me a piece of fish! The one you gave him was large, mine is small!' This is stated in reference to that. Also, when a net is cast for catching fish, at that place the fishermen and others make a great noise, saying: 'It has entered! It has not entered! It is caught! It is not caught!' This too is stated in reference to that. 'I dismiss' means 'I send out.' 'You are not to dwell in my presence' shows this meaning: 'You, having come to the dwelling place of a Buddha such as myself, make such a great noise. When you are living according to your own nature, what suitable conduct will you perform? For those such as you, there is no business of dwelling in my presence.' Among them, not even one monk was able to say, 'Blessed One, you dismiss us merely for making a great noise,' or anything else. All of them, accepting the Blessed One's word, said, 'So be it, venerable sir,' and departed. But this thought occurred to them: 'We came to see the Teacher, to hear a Dhamma discourse, and to dwell in the Teacher's presence. But having come into the presence of such a venerable Teacher, we made a great noise. This is our own fault. We have been dismissed. We have not been able to dwell in the presence of the Blessed One, nor to behold his golden-hued body, nor to hear the Dhamma spoken with his sweet voice.' Having become overcome with strong displeasure, they departed.

158. Tenupasaṅkamiṃsūti te kira sakyā āgamanasamayepi te bhikkhū tattheva nisinnā passiṃsu. Atha nesaṃ etadahosi – “kiṃ nu kho ete bhikkhū pavisitvāva paṭinivattā, jānissāma taṃ kāraṇa”nti cintetvā yena te bhikkhū tenupasaṅkamiṃsu. Handāti vavassaggatthe nipāto. Kahaṃ pana tumheti tumhe idāneva āgantvā kahaṃ gacchatha, kiṃ tumhākaṃ koci upaddavo, udāhu dasabalassāti? Tesaṃ pana bhikkhūnaṃ, – “āvuso, mayaṃ bhagavantaṃ dassanāya āgatā, diṭṭho no bhagavā, idāni attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gacchāmā”ti kiñcāpi evaṃ vacanaparihāro atthi, evarūpaṃ pana lesakappaṃ [M 3.0122] akatvā yathābhūtameva ārocetvā bhagavatā kho, āvuso, bhikkhusaṅgho paṇāmitoti āhaṃsu. Te pana rājāno sāsane dhuravahā, tasmā cintesuṃ – “dvīhi aggasāvakehi saddhiṃ pañcasu bhikkhusatesu gacchantesu bhagavato pādamūlaṃ vigacchissati, imesaṃ nivattanākāraṃ karissāmā”ti. Evaṃ cintetvā tena hāyasmantotiādimāhaṃsu. Tesupi [P 3.0175] bhikkhūsu “mayaṃ mahāsaddamattakena paṇāmitā, na mayaṃ jīvituṃ asakkontā pabbajitā”ti ekabhikkhupi paṭippharito nāma nāhosi, sabbe pana samakaṃyeva, “evamāvuso,”ti sampaṭicchiṃsu.

158. 'They approached them' means: those Sakyans, it is said, even at the time of their arrival, saw those monks sitting right there. Then this thought occurred to them: 'Why have these monks, having just entered, turned back? We will learn the reason.' Having thought thus, they approached those monks. 'Handa' is a particle in the sense of resolving. 'But where are you going?' means: 'You have come just now, where are you going? Is there some affliction for you, or is there for the Ten-Powered One?' Now, although those monks could have made a polite evasion, such as: 'Friends, we came to see the Blessed One, we have seen the Blessed One, and now we are going to our own dwelling place,' without resorting to such a pretense, they related what had actually happened and said: 'Indeed, friends, the community of monks has been dismissed by the Blessed One.' Those kings, however, were bearers of the yoke in the Dispensation. Therefore, they thought: 'When five hundred monks are departing together with the two chief disciples, the Blessed One's presence will become empty. We will arrange for their return.' Having thought thus, they said, 'Well then, venerable sirs,' and so on. Among those monks, not even one was resentful, thinking, 'We have been dismissed for a mere loud noise; we did not go forth because we were unable to make a living.' Instead, all of them unanimously consented, saying, 'So be it, friends.'

159. Abhinandatūti bhikkhusaṅghassa āgamanaṃ icchanto abhinandatu. Abhivadatūti etu bhikkhusaṅghoti evaṃ cittaṃ uppādento abhivadatu. Anuggahitoti āmisānuggahena ca dhammānuggahena ca anuggahito. Aññathattanti dasabalassa dassanaṃ na labhāmāti pasādaññathattaṃ bhaveyya. Vipariṇāmoti pasādaññathattena vibbhamantānaṃ vipariṇāmaññathattaṃ bhaveyya. Bījānaṃ taruṇānanti taruṇasassānaṃ. Siyā aññathattanti udakavārakāle udakaṃ alabhantānaṃ milātabhāvena aññathattaṃ bhaveyya, sussitvā milātabhāvaṃ āpajjanena vipariṇāmo bhaveyya. Vacchakassa pana khīrapipāsāya sussanaṃ aññathattaṃ nāma, sussitvā kālakiriyā vipariṇāmo nāma.

159. 'Let him rejoice' means: desiring the arrival of the community of monks, let him rejoice. 'Let him speak in welcome' means: generating the thought, 'Let the community of monks come,' let him speak. 'Supported' means supported by material support and by Dhamma support. 'Alteration' means there could be an alteration of confidence, thinking, 'We do not get to see the Ten-Powered One.' 'Transformation' means: for those who disrobe due to an alteration of confidence, there could be an alteration that is a transformation. 'Of tender seeds' means of young crops. 'There might be an alteration' means: for crops that do not get water at the time for watering, there could be an alteration through withering. Through drying up and reaching a state of withering, there could be a transformation. Furthermore, for a calf, withering from thirst for milk is called 'alteration'; withering and dying is called 'transformation'.

160. Pasādito bhagavāti thero kira tattha nisinnova dibbacakkhunā brahmānaṃ āgataṃ addasa[V 3.0125], dibbāya sotadhātuyā ca āyācanasaddaṃ suṇi, cetopariyañāṇena bhagavato pasannabhāvaṃ aññāsi. Tasmā – “kañci bhikkhuṃ pesetvā pakkosiyamānānaṃ gamanaṃ nāma na phāsukaṃ, yāva satthā na peseti, tāvadeva gamissāmā”ti maññamāno evamāha. Appossukkoti aññesu kiccesu anussukko hutvā. Diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāranti phalasamāpattivihāraṃ anuyutto maññe bhagavā viharitukāmo, so idāni yathāruciyā viharissatīti evaṃ me ahosīti vadati. Mayampi [P 3.0176] dānīti mayaṃ paraṃ ovadamānā vihārato nikkaḍḍhitā, kiṃ amhākaṃ parovādena. Idāni mayampi diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāreneva viharissāmāti dīpeti. Thero imasmiṃ ṭhāne viraddho attano bhārabhāvaṃ na aññāsi. Ayañhi bhikkhusaṅgho dvinnampi mahātherānaṃ bhāro, tena [M 3.0123] naṃ paṭisedhento bhagavā āgamehītiādimāha. Mahāmoggallānatthero pana attano bhārabhāvaṃ aññāsi. Tenassa bhagavā sādhukāraṃ adāsi.

160. The Blessed One was pleased: The Elder, the Venerable Mahā Moggallāna, it is said, while sitting right there, saw with the divine eye that Brahmā had come, and with the divine ear element heard the sound of the request. With the knowledge of others' minds, he knew the Blessed One’s state of being pleased. Therefore, thinking, “For those who are being summoned after a monk has been sent, the journey is not a comfortable one. As long as the Teacher has not yet sent for us, let us go right now,” he spoke thus. Unconcerned: being without exertion in other matters. Dwelling in happiness in this very life: I think the Blessed One, being devoted to dwelling in the attainment of fruition, wishes to dwell so. Let him now dwell according to his wish. Thus was my thought, he says. We too now: He explains: “We, while admonishing others, were expelled from the monastery. What use is admonishing others to us? Now we too shall dwell only in the happiness of this very life.” The Elder was at fault in this matter; he did not know his own state of having a burden. For this Sangha of monks is the burden of both Great Elders. Therefore the Blessed One, restraining him, said, “Come, Sāriputta,” and so on. The Venerable Mahā Moggallāna, however, knew his own state of having a burden. Therefore, the Blessed One gave him his approval.

161. Cattārimāni, bhikkhaveti kasmā ārabhi? Imasmiṃ sāsane cattāri bhayāni. Yo tāni abhīto hoti, so imasmiṃ sāsane patiṭṭhātuṃ sakkoti. Itaro pana na sakkotīti dassetuṃ imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi. Tattha udakorohanteti udakaṃ orohante puggale. Kumbhīlabhayanti suṃsumārabhayaṃ. Susukābhayanti caṇḍamacchabhayaṃ.

161. These four, O monks: Why was this begun? In this Dispensation, there are four dangers. Whichever monk is unafraid of them is able to be established in this Dispensation. The other, however, is not able. To show this, this discourse was begun. Therein, 'one descending into water' means a person descending into water. 'The danger of crocodiles' means the danger of the suṃsumāra. 'The danger of the susukā' means the danger of fierce fish.

162. Kodhupāyāsassetaṃ adhivacananti yathā hi bāhiraṃ udakaṃ otiṇṇo ūmīsu osīditvā marati, evaṃ imasmiṃ sāsane kodhupāyāse osīditvā vibbhamati. Tasmā kodhupāyāso “ūmibhaya”nti vutto.

162. This is a designation for anger and resentment: Just as one who has entered external water sinks amidst the waves and dies, so too in this Dispensation, one sinks in anger and resentment and disrobes. Therefore, anger and resentment are called 'the danger of waves'.

163. Odarikattassetaṃ adhivacananti yathā hi bāhiraṃ udakaṃ otiṇṇo kumbhīlena khādito marati, evaṃ imasmiṃ sāsane odarikattena khādito vibbhamati. Tasmā odarikattaṃ “kumbhīlabhaya”nti vuttaṃ.

163. This is a designation for gluttony: Just as one who enters external water is eaten by a crocodile and dies, so too in this Dispensation, one eaten by gluttony disrobes. Therefore, gluttony is called 'the danger of crocodiles'.

164. Arakkhiteneva kāyenāti sīsappacālakādikaraṇena arakkhitakāyo hutvā. Arakkhitāya vācāyāti duṭṭhullabhāsanādivasena arakkhitavāco hutvā. Anupaṭṭhitāya [P 3.0177] satiyāti kāyagatāsatiṃ anupaṭṭhāpetvā. Asaṃvutehīti apihitehi. Pañcannetaṃ kāmaguṇānaṃ adhivacananti yathā [V 3.0126] hi bāhiraṃ udakaṃ otiṇṇo āvaṭṭe nimujjitvā marati, evaṃ imasmiṃ sāsane pabbajito pañcakāmaguṇāvaṭṭe nimujjitvā vibbhamati. Tasmā pañca kāmaguṇā “āvaṭṭabhaya”nti vuttā.

164. With an unguarded body: means having an unguarded body by doing things such as shaking the head and so forth. With unguarded speech: means having unguarded speech by way of speaking coarse speech and so forth. With unestablished mindfulness: means not having established mindfulness directed to the body. With unrestrained faculties: means with unclosed faculties. This is a designation for the five strands of sensual pleasure: Just as one who has entered external water sinks in a whirlpool and dies, so too one who has gone forth in this Dispensation, sinking in the whirlpool of the five strands of sensual pleasure, disrobes. Therefore, the five strands of sensual pleasure are called 'the danger of the whirlpool'.

165. Anuddhaṃsetīti kilameti milāpeti. Rāgānuddhaṃsenāti rāgānuddhaṃsitena. Mātugāmassetaṃ adhivacananti yathā hi bāhiraṃ udakaṃ otiṇṇo caṇḍamacchaṃ āgamma laddhappahāro marati, evaṃ imasmiṃ sāsane mātugāmaṃ āgamma uppannakāmarāgo vibbhamati. Tasmā mātugāmo “susukābhaya”nti vutto.

165. Harasses: means it exhausts, it causes to wither. With the harassment of passion: means with a mind harassed by passion. This is a designation for a woman: Just as one who has entered external water, on account of a fierce fish, receives a blow and dies, so too in this Dispensation, on account of a woman, with sensual passion having arisen, one disrobes. Therefore, a woman is called 'the danger of the susukā'.

Imāni [M 3.0124] pana cattāri bhayāni bhāyitvā yathā udakaṃ anorohantassa udakaṃ nissāya ānisaṃso natthi, udakapipāsāya pipāsito ca hoti rajojallena kiliṭṭhasarīro ca, evamevaṃ imāni cattāri bhayāni bhāyitvā sāsane apabbajantassāpi imaṃ sāsanaṃ nissāya ānisaṃso natthi, taṇhāpipāsāya pipāsito ca hoti kilesarajena saṃkiliṭṭhacitto ca. Yathā pana imāni cattāri bhayāni abhāyitvā udakaṃ orohantassa vuttappakāro ānisaṃso hoti, evaṃ imāni abhāyitvā sāsane pabbajitassāpi vuttappakāro ānisaṃso hoti. Thero panāha – “cattāri bhayāni bhāyitvā udakaṃ anotaranto sotaṃ chinditvā paratīraṃ pāpuṇituṃ na sakkoti, abhāyitvā otaranto sakkoti, evamevaṃ bhāyitvā sāsane apabbajantopi taṇhāsotaṃ [P 3.0178] chinditvā nibbānapāraṃ daṭṭhuṃ na sakkoti, abhāyitvā pabbajanto pana sakkotī”ti. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānameva. Ayaṃ pana desanā neyyapuggalassa vasena niṭṭhāpitāti.

But, just as for one who, fearing these four dangers, does not descend into the water, there is no benefit derived from the water, and one is thirsty with thirst for water and has a body soiled with dust and dirt, so too for one who, fearing these four dangers, does not go forth in the Dispensation, there is no benefit derived from this Dispensation, and one is thirsty with the thirst of craving and has a mind soiled with the dust of defilements. And just as for one who, not fearing these four dangers, descends into the water, there is the benefit of the kind already mentioned, so too for one who, not fearing these dangers, has gone forth in the Dispensation, there is the benefit of the kind already mentioned. The Elder, however, said: “One who, fearing the four dangers, does not enter the water is not able to cut the stream and reach the far shore; but one who, not fearing, enters is able to. So too, one who, fearing, does not go forth in the Dispensation is not able to cut the stream of craving and see the far shore of Nibbāna; but one who, not fearing, goes forth is able to.” Thus he said. The rest is clear in every respect. This discourse, however, was concluded for the sake of a person to be guided.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

The Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Cātumasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Cātuma Sutta is concluded.

8. Naḷakapānasuttavaṇṇanā

8. The Explanation of the Naḷakapāna Sutta.

166. Evaṃ [V 3.0127] me sutanti naḷakapānasuttaṃ. Tattha naḷakapāneti evaṃnāmake gāme. Pubbe kira amhākaṃ bodhisatto vānarayoniyaṃ nibbatto, mahākāyo kapirājā anekavānarasahassaparivuto pabbatapāde vicarati. Paññavā kho pana hoti mahāpuñño. So parisaṃ evaṃ ovadati – “imasmiṃ pabbatapāde tātā, visaphalāni nāma honti, amanussapariggahitā pokkharaṇiyo nāma honti, tumhe pubbe khāditapubbāneva phalāni khādatha, pītapubbāneva pānīyāni ca pivatha, ettha vo maṃ paṭipucchitabbakiccaṃ natthi, akhāditapubbāni pana phalāni apītapubbāni ca pānīyāni maṃ apucchitvā mā khādittha mā pivitthā”ti.

166. Thus have I heard—the Naḷakapāna Sutta. There, “at Naḷakapāna” refers to a village of that name. Long ago, it is said, our Bodhisatta was born in a monkey existence, a great-bodied monkey king surrounded by many thousands of monkeys, who roamed at the foot of a mountain. He was wise and of great wisdom. He advised his troop thus: “At this mountain foot, my dears, there are poisonous fruits and ponds possessed by non-humans. Eat only the fruits you have eaten before, and drink only the waters you have drunk before. In this matter, you have no need to consult me. But do not eat any fruits you have not eaten before, and do not drink any waters you have not drunk before without asking me.”

Te [M 3.0125] ekadivasaṃ caramānā aññaṃ pabbatapādaṃ gantvā gocaraṃ gahetvā pānīyaṃ olokentā ekaṃ amanussapariggahitaṃ pokkharaṇiṃ disvā sahasā apivitvā samantā parivāretvā mahāsattassa āgamanaṃ olokayamānā nisīdiṃsu. Mahāsatto āgantvā “kiṃ tātā pānīyaṃ na pivathā”ti āha. Tumhākaṃ [P 3.0179] āgamanaṃ olokemāti. Sādhu tātāti samantā padaṃ pariyesamāno otiṇṇapadaṃyeva addasa, na uttiṇṇapadaṃ, disvā saparissayāti aññāsi. Tāvadeva ca tattha abhinibbattaamanusso udakaṃ dvedhā katvā uṭṭhāsi setamukho nīlakucchi rattahatthapādo mahādāṭhiko vaṅkadāṭho virūpo bībhaccho udakarakkhaso. So evamāha – “kasmā pānīyaṃ na pivatha, madhuraṃ udakaṃ pivatha, kiṃ tumhe etassa vacanaṃ suṇāthā”ti? Mahāsatto āha – “tvaṃ idha adhivattho amanusso”ti? Āmāhanti. Tvaṃ idha otiṇṇe labhasīti? Āma labhāmi, tumhe pana sabbe khādissāmīti. Na sakkhissasi, yakkhāti. Pānīyaṃ pana pivissathāti? Āma pivissāmāti. Evaṃ sante ekopi vo na muccissatīti. Pānīyañca pivissāma, na ca te vasaṃ gamissāmāti ekanaḷaṃ āharāpetvā koṭiyaṃ gahetvā dhami, sabbo ekacchiddo ahosi, tīre nisīditvāva pānīyaṃ pivi, sesavānarānaṃ pāṭiyekke naḷe āharāpetvā [V 3.0128] dhamitvā adāsi. Sabbe yakkhassa passantasseva pānīyaṃ piviṃsu. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

One day, while wandering, they went to another mountain foot, took their feeding ground, and while looking for drinking water, they saw a pond possessed by a non-human. They did not drink from it hastily, but surrounded it on all sides, and sat down watching for the arrival of the Great Being. The Great Being came and asked, “Why, my dears, do you not drink the water?” “We are watching for your arrival,” they replied. “Very well, my dears,” he said, and searching all around for footprints, he saw only descending footprints, and no ascending ones. Seeing this, he knew it was perilous. At that very moment, a non-human who had been born there rose up, splitting the water in two—white-faced, red-bellied, with red hands and feet, with large tusks, crooked tusks, a hideous and terrifying appearance—a water demon. He said, “Why do you not drink the water? Drink the sweet water! Why do you listen to his word?” The Great Being asked, “Are you a non-human dwelling here?” “Yes,” he replied. “Do you seize those who descend here?” “Yes, I do. And I will devour all of you!” “You cannot, O yakkha.” “Then will you drink the water?” “Yes, we will drink.” “In that case, not even one of you will escape.” “We will drink the water, but we will not fall into your power.” He had a single reed brought, took hold of one end, and blew through it, making it entirely one-holed. Sitting right on the bank, he drank the water. For the other monkeys, he had individual reeds brought, blew through them, and gave them. All drank the water while the yakkha watched. And this was said:

“Disvā padamanuttiṇṇaṃ, disvāno’ taritaṃ padaṃ;

Naḷena vāriṃ pissāma, neva maṃ tvaṃ vadhissasī”ti. (jā. 1.1.20);

“Seeing the footprint not come up, seeing the track not ascended; with a reed we shall drink the water, you shall not kill me.”

Tato paṭṭhāya yāva ajjadivasā tasmiṃ ṭhāne naḷā ekacchiddāva honti. Iminā hi saddhiṃ imasmiṃ kappe cattāri kappaṭṭhiyapāṭihāriyāni nāma – cande sasabimbaṃ[P 3.0180], vaṭṭakajātakamhi saccakiriyaṭṭhāne aggissa gamanupacchedo, ghaṭikārakumbhakārassa mātāpitūnaṃ vasanaṭṭhāne devassa avassanaṃ, tassā pokkharaṇiyā tīre naḷānaṃ ekacchiddabhāvoti. Iti sā pokkharaṇī naḷena pānīyassa pītattā naḷakapānāti nāmaṃ labhi. Aparabhāge taṃ pokkharaṇiṃ nissāya gāmo patiṭṭhāsi, tassāpi naḷakapānanteva nāmaṃ jātaṃ. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “naḷakapāne”ti. Palāsavaneti kiṃsukavane.

From that time until this very day, the reeds in that place are single-holed. Indeed, together with this, in this aeon there are four so-called aeon-enduring miracles: the image of the hare in the moon; in the Vaṭṭaka Jātaka, the cessation of the fire's advance at the place of the act of truth; the non-raining of the sky upon the dwelling place of the parents of Ghaṭikāra the potter; and the state of the reeds on the bank of that pond being single-holed. Thus, because the water was drunk with a reed, that pond obtained the name Naḷakapāna. In a later period, a village was established near that pond, and it too came to have the name Naḷakapāna. Referring to that, it was said, “at Naḷakapāna.” Palāsavana means the Kiṃsuka forest.

167. Taggha [M 3.0126] mayaṃ, bhanteti ekaṃseneva mayaṃ, bhante, abhiratā. Aññepi ye tumhākaṃ sāsane abhiramanti, te amhehi sadisāva hutvā abhiramantīti dīpenti.

167. “Assuredly, venerable sir, we are delighted” means: “Venerable sir, we are certainly delighted.” They indicate that others, too, who delight in your Dispensation, delight just as we do.

Neva rājābhinītātiādīsu eko rañño aparādhaṃ katvā palāyati. Rājā kuhiṃ, bho, asukoti? Palāto devāti. Palātaṭṭhānepi me na muccissati, sace pana pabbajeyya, mucceyyāti vadati. Tassa kocideva suhado gantvā taṃ pavattiṃ ārocetvā tvaṃ sace jīvitumicchasi, pabbajāhīti. So pabbajitvā jīvitaṃ rakkhamāno carati. Ayaṃ rājābhinīto nāma.

In the passage “Not driven by a king,” etc., a certain man, having committed an offense against the king, flees. The king asks, “Where, sirs, is so-and-so?” “He has fled, Your Majesty.” “Even in the place he has fled to, he will not escape me; but if he were to go forth, he might be freed,” he says. A certain friend of his goes and reports this news, saying, “If you wish to live, go forth!” He goes forth and lives on, protecting his life. This is called “one driven by a king.”

Eko pana corānaṃ mūlaṃ chindanto carati. Corā sutvā “purisānaṃ atthikabhāvaṃ na jānāti, jānāpessāma na”nti vadanti. So taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā palāyati. Corā palātoti sutvā “palātaṭṭhānepi no na muccissati, sace pana pabbajeyya, mucceyyā”ti vadanti. So taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā pabbajati. Ayaṃ corābhinīto nāma.

Another roams about, cutting the root of thieves. The thieves, hearing this, say, “He does not know of the existence of real men; we will make him know.” Hearing this report, he flees. The thieves, hearing that he has fled, say, “Even in the place he has fled to, he will not escape us; but if he were to go forth, he might escape.” Hearing this report, he goes forth. This is called “one driven by thieves.”

Eko [V 3.0129] pana bahuṃ iṇaṃ khāditvā tena iṇena aṭṭo pīḷito tamhā gāmā palāyati. Iṇasāmikā sutvā “palātaṭṭhānepi no na muccissati, sace pana pabbajeyya, mucceyyā”ti vadanti. So taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā pabbajati. Ayaṃ iṇaṭṭo nāma.

Another, having incurred much debt and being afflicted and oppressed by that debt, flees from that village. The creditors, hearing this, say, “Even in the place he has fled to, he will not escape us; but if he were to go forth, he might escape.” Hearing that news, he goes forth. This is called “one afflicted by debt.”

Rājabhayādīnaṃ [P 3.0181] pana aññatarena bhayena bhīto aṭṭo āturo hutvā nikkhamma pabbajito bhayaṭṭo nāma. Dubbhikkhādīsu jīvituṃ asakkonto pabbajito ājīvikāpakato nāma, ājīvikāya pakato abhibhūtoti attho. Imesu pana ekopi imehi kāraṇehi pabbajito nāma natthi, tasmā “neva rājābhinīto”tiādimāha.

Furthermore, one who, frightened, afflicted, and pained by some fear or other, such as fear of the king, has gone out and gone forth, is called ‘one afflicted by fear.’ One who, unable to sustain life due to famine or the like, goes forth is called ‘one compelled by livelihood,’ the meaning being ‘compelled, overcome by livelihood.’ But among these monks, there is not even one who has gone forth for any of these reasons; therefore, the Blessed One said, “not driven by a king,” etc.

Vivekanti vivicca vivitto hutvā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yaṃ kāmehi ca akusaladhammehi ca vivittena paṭhamadutiyajjhānasaṅkhātaṃ pītisukhaṃ adhigantabbaṃ, sace taṃ vivicca kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi pītisukhaṃ nādhigacchati, aññaṃ vā upari dvinnaṃ jhānānaṃ catunnañca maggānaṃ vasena santataraṃ sukhaṃ nādhigacchati, tassa ime abhijjhādayo cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhantīti. Tattha aratīti adhikusalesu dhammesu ukkaṇṭhitatā. Tandīti ālasiyabhāvo. Evaṃ yo pabbajitvā pabbajitakiccaṃ kātuṃ na sakkoti, tassa ime satta pāpadhammā uppajjitvā [M 3.0127] cittaṃ pariyādiyantīti dassetvā idāni yassa te dhammā cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhanti, soyeva samaṇakiccampi kātuṃ na sakkotīti puna vivekaṃ anuruddhā…pe… aññaṃ vā tato santataranti āha.

“Seclusion” means having become secluded, detached. This is the meaning: the joy and happiness reckoned as the first and second jhānas, which is to be attained by one secluded from sensual pleasures and unwholesome states. If, being secluded from sensual pleasures and unwholesome states, one does not attain that joy and happiness, or does not attain a more peaceful happiness by way of the two higher jhānas or the four paths, then for that person these states—covetousness and the rest—remain overwhelming the mind. Herein, “discontent” means being wearied of superior wholesome states. “Sloth” means a state of laziness. Thus, having shown that for one who, having gone forth, cannot perform the duties of a monastic, these seven evil states arise and overwhelm the mind, it is now shown that for whomever those states remain overwhelming the mind, that very one cannot perform the duties of a contemplative. Therefore, he again says: “Cultivating seclusion… or something more peaceful than that.”
