Evaṃ kaṇhapakkhaṃ dassetvā idāni teneva nayena sukkapakkhaṃ dassetuṃ puna vivekantiādimāha. Tassattho vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

Having thus shown the dark aspect, now in the same way, to show the bright aspect, he again says “seclusion,” etc. Its meaning should be understood in the same manner as stated.

168. Saṅkhāyāti jānitvā. Ekanti [P 3.0182] ekaccaṃ. Paṭisevatīti sevitabbayuttakaṃ sevati. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Upapattīsu byākarotīti sappaṭisandhike tāva byākarotu, appaṭisandhike kathaṃ byākarotīti. Appaṭisandhikassa puna bhave paṭisandhi natthīti vadanto upapattīsu byākaroti nāma.

168. “Having reckoned” means having known. “One” means a certain one. “Associates” means he associates with what is suitable to be associated with. This same method should be seen in the remaining terms as well. As for “declares about rebirths”: one may declare about those with rebirth-linking, but how does one declare about those without? One who says, “For one without rebirth-linking, there is no rebirth-linking in a future existence,” is said to “declare about rebirths.”

Janakuhanatthanti [V 3.0130] janavimhāpanatthaṃ. Janalapanatthanti mahājanassa upalāpanatthaṃ. Na iti maṃ jano jānātūti evaṃ maṃ mahājano jānissati, evaṃ me mahājanassa antare kittisaddo uggacchissatīti imināpi kāraṇena na byākarotīti attho. Uḷāravedāti mahantatuṭṭhino.

“For the sake of deceiving people” means for the purpose of bewildering people. “For the sake of enticing people” means for the purpose of persuading the multitude. “Not so that people may know me” means, thinking, “Thus the multitude will know me; thus the sound of my fame will spread among the multitude.” For this reason too, he does not declare—this is the meaning. “Exalted feeling” means great satisfaction.

169. So kho panassa āyasmāti so parinibbuto āyasmā imassa ṭhitassa āyasmato. Evaṃsīlotiādīsu lokiyalokuttaramissakāva sīlādayo veditabbo. Evaṃdhammoti ettha pana samādhipakkhikā dhammā dhammāti adhippetā. Phāsuvihāro hotīti tena bhikkhunā pūritapaṭipattiṃ pūrentassa arahattaphalaṃ sacchikatvā phalasamāpattivihārena phāsuvihāro hoti, arahattaṃ pattumasakkontassa paṭipattiṃ pūrayamānassa caratopi phāsuvihāroyeva nāma hoti. Iminā nayena sabbavāresu attho veditabboti.

169. And so, “that venerable one”: that venerable one who has attained final Nibbāna is one who has been seen in person or heard about by this venerable one who is still living. In the phrases “of such virtue” and so on, the virtues and other qualities should be understood as a mixture of the mundane and supramundane. Here, in “of such Dhamma,” by “Dhamma” is meant the states that are allied with concentration. “He dwells at ease” means: for a monk who is fulfilling the practice fulfilled by that departed monk, having realized the fruit of Arahantship, there is dwelling at ease through the attainment of fruition. Even for one who is unable to attain Arahantship but is fulfilling the practice, whether striving or dwelling, it is still called dwelling at ease. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all instances.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya

Naḷakapānasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Naḷakapāna Sutta is concluded.

9. Goliyānisuttavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Goliyāni Sutta

173. Evaṃ [V 3.0131][P 3.0183] me sutanti goliyānisuttaṃ. Tattha padasamācāroti dubbalasamācāro oḷārikācāro, paccayesu sāpekkho mahārakkhitatthero [M 3.0128] viya. Taṃ kira upaṭṭhākakule nisinnaṃ upaṭṭhāko āha “asukattherassa me, bhante, cīvaraṃ dinna”nti. Sādhu te kataṃ taṃyeva takketvā viharantassa cīvaraṃ dentenāti. Tumhākampi, bhante, dassāmīti. Sādhu karissasi taṃyeva takkentassāti āha. Ayampi evarūpo oḷārikācāro ahosi. Sappatissenāti sajeṭṭhakena, na attānaṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ katvā viharitabbaṃ. Serivihārenāti sacchandavihārena niraṅkusavihārena.

173. Thus have I heard—the Goliyāni Sutta. Therein, `padasamācāra` means weak conduct, coarse conduct, like the Elder Mahārakkhita, who was attached to the requisites. It is said that while he was sitting in the house of his supporter, the supporter said, 'Venerable sir, I have given a robe to such-and-such an elder.' He replied, 'You have done well by giving a robe to one who dwells constantly scheming for just that.' The supporter then said, 'I will give to you too, venerable sir.' He replied, 'You will do well to give to one who is constantly scheming for just that.' This Goliyāni was also of such coarse conduct. `Sappatissena` means one should have a senior; one should not live making oneself the senior. `Serivihārena` means by living according to one’s own wish, by living without restraint.

Nānūpakhajjāti na anupakhajja na anupavisitvā. Tattha yo dvīsu mahātheresu ubhato nisinnesu te anāpucchitvāva cīvarena vā jāṇunā vā ghaṭṭento nisīdati, ayaṃ anupakhajja nisīdati nāma. Evaṃ akatvā pana attano pattaāsanasantike ṭhatvā nisīdāvusoti vutte nisīditabbaṃ. Sace na vadanti, nisīdāmi, bhanteti āpucchitvā nisīditabbaṃ āpucchitakālato paṭṭhāya nisīdāti vuttepi avuttepi nisīdituṃ vaṭṭatiyeva. Na paṭibāhissāmīti ettha yo attano pattāsanaṃ atikkamitvā navakānaṃ pāpuṇanaṭṭhāne nisīdati, ayaṃ nave bhikkhū [P 3.0184] āsanena paṭibāhati nāma. Tasmiñhi tathā nisinne navā bhikkhū “amhākaṃ nisīdituṃ na detī”ti ujjhāyantā tiṭṭhanti vā āsanaṃ vā pariyesantā āhiṇḍanti. Tasmā attano pattāsaneyeva nisīditabbaṃ. Evaṃ na paṭibāhati nāma.

“Not pushing in” means not intruding, not entering. Therein, if a monk, when two great elders are seated on both sides, sits down without asking them, brushing against them with his robe or knee, this is called “sitting down by pushing in.” However, without doing so, one should stand near the seat allotted to one and sit down when told, “Sit, friend.” If they do not speak, one should ask, “Venerable sirs, I shall sit,” and then sit down. From the time of asking, it is proper to sit whether one is told “Sit” or not. As for “I will not obstruct”: herein, a monk who, passing over the seat allotted to him, sits in the place that junior monks should get, is said to “obstruct the junior monks by means of a seat.” For when he is seated thus, the junior monks complain, “He does not let us sit,” and they either stand or wander about searching for a seat. Therefore, one should sit only in the seat allotted to one. In this way, one is said “not to obstruct.”

Ābhisamācārikampi dhammanti abhisamācārikaṃ vattapaṭipattimattampi. Nātikālenāti na atipāto pavisitabbaṃ, na atidivā paṭikkamitabbaṃ, bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃyeva pavisitabbañca nikkhamitabbañca. Atipāto pavisitvā atidivā nikkhamantassa hi cetiyaṅgaṇabodhiyaṅgaṇavattādīni parihāyanti. Kālasseva mukhaṃ dhovitvā makkaṭakasuttāni chindantena ussāvabindū nipātentena gāmaṃ pavisitvā yāguṃ pariyesitvā yāva bhikkhākālā antogāmeyeva nānappakāraṃ tiracchānakathaṃ kathentena nisīditvā bhattakiccaṃ katvā divā nikkhamma [V 3.0132] bhikkhūnaṃ pādadhovanavelāya vihāraṃ paccāgantabbaṃ hoti. Na purebhattaṃ pacchābhattaṃ kulesu cārittaṃ āpajjitabbanti “yo pana bhikkhu nimantito sabhatto samāno santaṃ bhikkhuṃ anāpucchā purebhattaṃ vā pacchābhattaṃ vā kulesu cārittaṃ āpajjeyya, aññatra samayā pācittiya”nti (pāci. 299) imaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ rakkhantena tassa [M 3.0129] vibhaṅge vuttaṃ purebhattañca pacchābhattañca cārittaṃ na āpajjitabbaṃ. Uddhato hoti capaloti uddhaccapakatiko ceva hoti cīvaramaṇḍana-pattamaṇḍana-senāsanamaṇḍanā imassa vā pūtikāyassa kelāyanā maṇḍanāti evaṃ vuttena ca taruṇadārakāvacāpalyena samannāgato.

'Even the teaching on proper conduct' means even the mere practice of the duties of proper conduct. 'Not at the wrong time' means one should not enter a village too early, and one should not return too late; one should enter and depart only together with the Saṅgha of monks. For one who enters too early and departs too late, the duties concerning the stupa courtyard, the Bodhi tree courtyard, and so on, are neglected. Having washed his face early in the morning, breaking spider-threads and shaking off dewdrops, he enters the village. Having sought rice-gruel, he sits right inside the village until the time for the alms round, speaking various kinds of worldly talk. Having taken his meal, he leaves during the day and has to return to the monastery at the time when the other monks are washing their feet. 'One should not engage in visiting families before or after the meal': observing this training rule—'Whatever monk, having been invited and having eaten a meal, should visit families before or after the meal without having informed a monk who is present, unless it is the proper time, it is an offense of expiation'—one should not engage in the conduct of visiting before the meal and after the meal, as stated in its analysis. 'He is restless and fickle' means he is of a restless nature and is endowed with the frivolity of a young boy, which is expressed as: the adorning of the robe, the adorning of the bowl, the adorning of the lodging, or the cherishing and adorning of this foul body.

Paññavatā [P 3.0185] bhavitabbanti cīvarakammādīsu itikattabbesu upāyapaññāya samannāgatena bhavitabbaṃ. Abhidhamme abhivinayeti abhidhammapiṭake ceva vinayapiṭake ca pāḷivasena ceva aṭṭhakathāvasena ca yogo karaṇīyo. Sabbantimena hi paricchedena abhidhamme dukatikamātikāhi saddhiṃ dhammahadayavibhaṅgaṃ vinā na vaṭṭati. Vinaye pana kammākammavinicchayena saddhiṃ suvinicchitāni dve pātimokkhāni vinā na vaṭṭati.

'One should be possessed of wisdom' means one should be endowed with the wisdom of means in duties that have to be done, such as the work of making robes. 'In the Abhidhamma and in the Vinaya' means effort should be made in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka and the Vinaya Piṭaka, both according to the Pāḷi and according to the commentary. For at the very least, in the Abhidhamma, it is not proper to live in the forest without knowing the Dhammahadayavibhaṅga together with the Duka and Tika mātikās. And in the Vinaya, it is not proper to live in the forest without knowing the two well-mastered Pātimokkhas together with the discrimination of what is and is not a formal act.

Āruppāti ettāvatā aṭṭhapi samāpattiyo vuttā honti. Tā pana sabbena sabbaṃ asakkontena sattasupi yogo karaṇīyo, chasupi…pe… pañcasupi. Sabbantimena paricchedena ekaṃ kasiṇe parikammakammaṭṭhānaṃ paguṇaṃ katvā ādāya vicaritabbaṃ, ettakaṃ vinā na vaṭṭati. Uttarimanussadhammeti iminā sabbepi lokuttaradhamme dasseti. Tasmā arahantena hutvā vihātabbaṃ, arahattaṃ anabhisambhuṇantena anāgāmiphale sakadāgāmiphale sotāpattiphale vā patiṭṭhātabbaṃ. Sabbantimena pariyāyena ekaṃ vipassanāmukhaṃ yāva arahattā paguṇaṃ katvā ādāya vicaritabbaṃ. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānameva. Imaṃ pana desanaṃ āyasmā sāriputto neyyapuggalassa vasena ābhisamācārikavattato paṭṭhāya anupubbena arahattaṃ pāpetvā niṭṭhāpesīti.

'The formless attainments': by this, the eight attainments are also stated. However, by one who is unable to accomplish all of them, effort should be made in seven, or in six... or in five. At the very least, one should make proficient, take up, and practice one preliminary meditation subject on a kasiṇa; without this much, it is not proper. By 'a superior human state', he indicates all the supramundane states. Therefore, one should dwell having become an Arahant. One who does not attain Arahantship should be established in the fruit of non-returning, the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of stream-entry. At the very least, one should make proficient, take up, and practice one entrance to insight up to Arahantship. The rest is clear everywhere. The Venerable Sāriputta concluded this teaching by leading a person capable of being guided, starting from the duties of proper conduct and sequentially causing him to reach Arahantship.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Goliyānisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Goliyāni Sutta is concluded.

10. Kīṭāgirisuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Kīṭāgiri Sutta

174. Evaṃ [V 3.0133][P 3.0186] me sutanti kīṭāgirisuttaṃ. Tattha kāsīsūti evaṃnāmake janapade. Etha tumhepi, bhikkhaveti etha tumhepi, bhikkhave, ime pañca ānisaṃse [M 3.0130] sampassamānā aññatreva rattibhojanā bhuñjatha. Iti bhagavā rattiṃ vikālabhojanaṃ, divā vikālabhojananti imāni dve bhojanāni ekappahārena ajahāpetvā ekasmiṃ samaye divā vikālabhojanameva jahāpesi, puna kālaṃ atināmetvā rattiṃ vikālabhojanaṃ jahāpento evamāha. Kasmā? Imāni hi dve bhojanāni vattamānāni vaṭṭe āciṇṇāni samāciṇṇāni nadiṃ otiṇṇaudakaṃ viya anupakkhandāni, nivātesu ca gharesu subhojanāni bhuñjitvā vaḍḍhitā sukhumālā kulaputtā dve bhojanāni ekappahārena pajahantā kilamanti. Tasmā ekappahārena ajahāpetvā bhaddālisutte divā vikālabhojanaṃ jahāpesi, idha rattiṃ vikālabhojanaṃ. Jahāpento pana na tajjitvā vā niggaṇhitvā vā, tesaṃ pahānapaccayā pana appābādhatañca sañjānissathāti evaṃ ānisaṃsaṃ dassetvāva jahāpesi. Kīṭāgirīti tassa nigamassa nāmaṃ.

174. The sutta beginning with 'Thus have I heard' is the Kīṭāgiri Sutta. Therein, 'in Kāsī' means in the country with that name. In the passage 'Come, you too, O bhikkhus,' the meaning should be understood thus: 'Come, you too, O bhikkhus, seeing these five benefits, eat refraining from the nighttime meal.' Thus the Blessed One, not causing the abandonment of these two meals—eating at the wrong time at night and eating at the wrong time during the day—at one stroke, on one occasion caused the abandonment of only eating at the wrong time during the day. Again, after letting time pass, wishing to cause the abandonment of eating at the wrong time at night, he spoke thus. Why? For these two meals, occurring in the round of existence, practiced, and repeatedly practiced, are things that beings rush into, like water that has flowed down into a river. Furthermore, delicate sons of good families, raised on fine food in windless houses, become weary when abandoning the two meals at one stroke. Therefore, not causing the abandonment at one stroke, in the Bhaddālisutta he caused the abandonment of eating at the wrong time during the day; here he causes the abandonment of eating at the wrong time at night. But in causing the abandonment, he did not do so by threatening or rebuking; rather, only after showing the benefit thus, 'On account of abandoning them, you will know freedom from illness,' did he cause the abandonment. 'Kīṭāgiri' is the name of that market town.

175. Assajipunabbasukāti assaji ca punabbasuko ca chasu chabbaggiyesu dve gaṇācariyā. Paṇḍuko lohitako mettiyo bhummajako [P 3.0187] assaji punabbasukoti ime cha janā chabbaggiyā nāma. Tesu paṇḍukalohitakā attano parisaṃ gahetvā sāvatthiyaṃ vasanti, mettiyabhummajakā rājagahe, ime dve janā kīṭāgirismiṃ āvāsikā honti. Āvāsikāti nibaddhavāsino, taṃnibandhā akataṃ senāsanaṃ karonti, jiṇṇaṃ paṭisaṅkharonti, kate issarā honti. Kālikanti anāgate kāle pattabbaṃ ānisaṃsaṃ.

175. 'Assaji and Punabbasu' means Assaji and Punabbasu, who were two group teachers among the group of six bhikkhus. Paṇḍuka, Lohitaka, Mettiya, Bhummajaka, Assaji, and Punabbasu—these six persons are called the Group of Six. Among them, Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka, taking their own retinue, dwell at Sāvatthī; Mettiya and Bhummajaka dwell at Rājagaha; these two persons are residents in Kīṭāgiri. 'Residents' means those who dwell there regularly; being bound to that place, they build lodgings not previously built, repair old ones, and have authority over those that are built. 'Kālika' means a benefit to be attained in a future time.

178. Mayā cetaṃ, bhikkhaveti idha kiṃ dasseti? Bhikkhave, divasassa tayo vāre bhuñjitvā sukhavedanaṃyeva uppādento na imasmiṃ sāsane kiccakārī nāma hoti, ettakā pana vedanā sevitabbā, ettakā na sevitabbāti etamatthaṃ dassetuṃ imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi. Evarūpaṃ sukhavedanaṃ pajahathāti idañca gehassitasomanassavasena vuttaṃ, upasampajja viharathāti idañca nekkhammasitasomanassavasena[V 3.0134]. Ito paresupi dvīsu vāresu gehassitanekkhammasitānaṃyeva domanassānañca upekkhānañca vasena attho veditabbo.

178. By the phrase, 'And this by me, O bhikkhus'—what does he show here? 'Bhikkhus, one who, eating three times a day, produces only pleasant feeling, is not one called "a doer of what is to be done" in this Dispensation.' To show this meaning—that some feelings are to be cultivated, while others are not to be cultivated—he began this discourse. 'Abandon such a pleasant feeling'—this is said by way of joy connected with the household life. 'Attain and abide'—this is said by way of joy connected with renunciation. Henceforth, in the subsequent two sections as well, the meaning should be understood by way of displeasure and equanimity that are connected with the household life and with renunciation.

181. Evaṃ sevitabbāsevitabbavedanaṃ dassetvā idāni yesaṃ appamādena kiccaṃ kattabbaṃ, yesañca na kattabbaṃ, te dassetuṃ nāhaṃ, bhikkhave[M 3.0131], sabbesaṃyevātiādimāha. Tattha kataṃ tesaṃ appamādenāti tesaṃ yaṃ appamādena kattabbaṃ, taṃ kataṃ. Anulomikānīti paṭipattianulomāni kammaṭṭhānasappāyāni, yattha vasantena sakkā honti maggaphalāni pāpuṇituṃ. Indriyāni [P 3.0188] samannānayamānāti saddhādīni indriyāni samānaṃ kurumānā.

181. Thus, having shown the feelings that are to be cultivated and not to be cultivated, now, to show those for whom a task must be done with diligence and those for whom it must not, he spoke the words beginning with, 'I do not say, O bhikkhus, for all...' Therein, 'For them, what was to be done with diligence has been done' means: for them, that task which was to be done with diligence has been done. 'Conformable' means: conformable to the practice, suitable for the meditation subject; a place wherein, while dwelling, it is possible to attain the paths and fruits. 'Balancing the faculties' means making the faculties, such as faith and so on, equal.

182. Sattime, bhikkhave, puggalāti idha kiṃ dasseti? Yesaṃ appamādena karaṇīyaṃ natthi, te dve honti. Yesaṃ atthi, te pañcāti evaṃ sabbepi ime satta puggalā hontīti imamatthaṃ dasseti.

182. By 'These seven persons, O bhikkhus'—what does he show here? Those for whom there is nothing to be done with diligence are two. Those for whom there is are five. Thus, all these persons are seven—this is the meaning he shows.

Tattha ubhatobhāgavimuttoti dvīhi bhāgehi vimutto. Arūpasamāpattiyā rūpakāyato vimutto, maggena nāmakāyato. So catunnaṃ arūpasamāpattīnaṃ ekekato vuṭṭhāya saṅkhāre sammasitvā arahattaṃ pattānaṃ catunnaṃ, nirodhā vuṭṭhāya arahattaṃ pattaanāgāmino ca vasena pañcavidho hoti. Pāḷi panettha – “katamo ca puggalo ubhatobhāgavimutto, idhekacco puggalo aṭṭha vimokkhe kāyena phusitvā viharati, paññāya cassa disvā āsavā parikkhīṇā hontī”ti (pu. pa. 208) evaṃ abhidhamme aṭṭhavimokkhalābhino vasena āgatā.

Therein, 'liberated in both parts' means liberated from two parts. One is liberated from the form-body through the formless attainments, and from the name-body through the path. That person is of five kinds: by way of the four who, emerging from each of the four formless attainments, contemplate the formations and attain Arahantship, and by way of the non-returner who emerges from cessation and attains Arahantship. The Pāḷi here is: 'And what kind of person is liberated in both parts? Here, a certain person dwells having touched the eight liberations with the body, and for him, having seen with wisdom, the taints are destroyed.' Thus in the Abhidhamma it is presented by way of one who has obtained the eight liberations.

Paññāvimuttoti paññāya vimutto. So sukkhavipassako, catūhi jhānehi vuṭṭhāya arahattaṃ pattā cattāro cāti imesaṃ vasena pañcavidhova hoti. Pāḷi panettha aṭṭhavimokkhapaṭikkhepavaseneva āgatā. Yathāha – “na heva kho aṭṭha vimokkhe kāyena phusitvā viharati, paññāya cassa disvā āsavā parikkhīṇā honti. Ayaṃ vuccati puggalo paññāvimutto”ti.

'Wisdom-liberated' means liberated by wisdom. This person is of five kinds: the dry-insight meditator, and the four who, having emerged from the four jhānas, attain Arahantship. The Pāḷi here is presented by way of the exclusion of the eight liberations, as it is said: 'He does not indeed dwell having touched the eight liberations with the body, but for him, having seen with wisdom, the taints are destroyed. This person is called wisdom-liberated.'

Phuṭṭhantaṃ [P 3.0189] sacchikarotīti kāyasakkhī. Yo jhānaphassaṃ paṭhamaṃ phusati, pacchā nirodhaṃ nibbānaṃ [V 3.0135] sacchikaroti, so sotāpattiphalaṭṭhaṃ ādiṃ katvā yāva arahattamaggaṭṭhā chabbidho hontīti veditabbo. Tenevāha – “idhekacco puggalo aṭṭha vimokkhe kāyena phusitvā viharati, paññāya cassa disvā ekacce āsavā parikkhīṇā honti. Ayaṃ vuccati puggalo kāyasakkhī”ti.

A 'body-witness' is one who realizes that which has been touched. The person who first touches the jhāna-contact, and afterwards realizes Nibbāna, which is cessation—that person should be understood as being of six kinds, beginning with the one established in the fruition of stream-entry up to the one established in the path of Arahantship. Therefore it is said: 'Here, a certain person dwells having touched the eight liberations with the body, and for him, having seen with wisdom, some taints are destroyed. This person is called a body-witness.'

Diṭṭhantaṃ [M 3.0132] pattoti diṭṭhippatto. Tatridaṃ saṅkhepalakkhaṇaṃ – dukkhā saṅkhārā, sukho nirodhoti ñātaṃ hoti diṭṭhaṃ viditaṃ sacchikataṃ phusitaṃ paññāyāti diṭṭhippatto. Vitthārato panesopi kāyasakkhi viya chabbidho hoti. Tenevāha – “idhekacco puggalo idaṃ dukkhanti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti…pe… ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadāti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, tathāgatappaveditā cassa dhammā paññāya vodiṭṭhā honti vocaritā…pe… ayaṃ vuccati puggalo diṭṭhippatto”ti (pu. pa. 208).

‘One who has attained vision’ (diṭṭhippatto) means one who has attained what is seen (diṭṭhaṃ patto). Herein, this is the concise characteristic: ‘Formations are suffering, cessation is bliss’—this is known, seen, understood, realized, and touched by wisdom; therefore, he is one who has attained vision. In detail, this person is also of six kinds, like the body-witness. Therefore, it is said: ‘Here, a certain person understands as it actually is: “This is suffering”... and so on... “This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering,” he understands as it actually is. And for him, the teachings proclaimed by the Tathāgata are well seen and well examined by wisdom... and so on... This person is called one who has attained vision.’

Saddhāvimuttoti saddhāya vimutto. Sopi vuttanayeneva chabbidho hoti. Tenevāha – “idhekacco puggalo idaṃ dukkhanti – yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti…pe… ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadāti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti[P 3.0190]. Tathāgatappaveditā cassa dhammā paññāya vodiṭṭhā honti vocaritā…pe… no ca kho yathā diṭṭhippattassa. Ayaṃ vuccati puggalo saddhāvimutto”ti (pu. pa. 208). Etesu hi saddhāvimuttassa pubbabhāgamaggakkhaṇe saddahantassa viya okappentassa viya adhimuccantassa viya ca kilesakkhayo hoti, diṭṭhippattassa pubbabhāgamaggakkhaṇe kilesacchedakañāṇaṃ adandhaṃ tikhiṇaṃ sūraṃ hutvā vahati. Tasmā yathā nāma nātitikhiṇena asinā kadaliṃ chindantassa chinnaṭṭhānaṃ na maṭṭhaṃ hoti, asi na sīghaṃ vahati, saddo suyyati, balavataro vāyāmo kātabbo hoti, evarūpā saddhāvimuttassa pubbabhāgamaggabhāvanā. Yathā pana nisitaasinā kadaliṃ chindantassa chinnaṭṭhānaṃ maṭṭhaṃ hoti, asi sīghaṃ vahati, saddo na suyyati, balavavāyāmakiccaṃ na hoti, evarūpā paññāvimuttassa pubbabhāgamaggabhāvanā veditabbā.

‘One liberated by faith’ is one liberated through faith. He too is of six kinds, in the way already stated. Therefore it is said: “Here, a certain person understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’... and so on... ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.’ And the teachings proclaimed by the Tathāgata are well seen and well examined by his wisdom... and so on... but not in the same way as for one who has attained vision. This person is called one liberated by faith.” For among these, in the case of the one liberated by faith, at the moment of the preliminary path, the destruction of defilements is slow and not sharp, occurring as for one who is believing, accepting, and resolving. But for one who has attained vision, at the moment of the preliminary path, the knowledge that cuts off defilements proceeds without sluggishness, sharply, and valiantly. Therefore, just as when cutting a banana tree with a not-very-sharp sword, the cut is not smooth, the sword does not proceed swiftly, a sound is heard, and stronger effort must be made—such is the development of the preliminary path for one liberated by faith. But just as when cutting a banana tree with a sharpened sword, the cut is smooth, the sword proceeds swiftly, no sound is heard, and no great effort is needed—so should the development of the preliminary path for one liberated by wisdom be understood.

Dhammaṃ anussaratīti dhammānusārī. Dhammoti paññā, paññāpubbaṅgamaṃ maggaṃ bhāvetīti attho. Saddhānusārimhi ca eseva nayo. Ubho panete sotāpattimaggaṭṭhāyeva. Vuttampi cetaṃ – “yassa [V 3.0136] puggalassa sotāpattiphalasacchikiriyāya paṭipannassa paññindriyaṃ adhimattaṃ hoti, paññāvāhiṃ paññāpubbaṅgamaṃ ariyamaggaṃ bhāveti[P 3.0191]. Ayaṃ vuccati puggalo dhammānusārī”ti (pu. pa. 208). Tathā – “yassa puggalassa sotāpattiphalasacchikiriyāya paṭipannassa saddhindriyaṃ adhimattaṃ hoti, saddhāvāhiṃ saddhāpubbaṅgamaṃ ariyamaggaṃ bhāveti. Ayaṃ vuccati puggalo saddhānusārī”ti. Ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthārato [M 3.0133] panesā ubhatobhāgavimuttādikathā visuddhimagge paññābhāvanādhikāre vuttā. Tasmā tattha vuttanayeneva veditabbā. Yā panesā etesaṃ vibhāgadassanatthaṃ idha pāḷi āgatā, tattha yasmā rūpasamāpattiyā vinā arūpasamāpattiyo nāma natthi, tasmā āruppāti vuttepi aṭṭha vimokkhā vuttāva hontīti veditabbā.

One who follows after the Dhamma is a Dhamma-follower (dhammānusārī). ‘Dhamma’ here is wisdom (paññā); the meaning is that one develops the path that has wisdom as its forerunner. The same method applies in the case of the faith-follower (saddhānusārī). Both of these, however, stand only on the stream-entry path. And this was said: “In the case of a person who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, for whom the faculty of wisdom is predominant, they develop the noble path that is carried by wisdom and has wisdom as its forerunner. This person is called a Dhamma-follower.” Similarly: “In the case of a person who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, for whom the faculty of faith is predominant, they develop the noble path that is carried by faith and has faith as its forerunner. This person is called a faith-follower.” This is the summary here. In detail, however, this discussion on the one liberated in both ways and so forth is stated in the Visuddhimagga, in the section on the development of wisdom. Therefore, it should be understood according to the method explained there. Now, as for the Pāḷi passage that is cited here to show the distinction among these individuals, since there are no formless attainments without the form attainments, it should be understood that even when ‘formless’ is mentioned, the eight liberations are in fact stated.

Kāyena phusitvāti sahajātanāmakāyena phusitvā. Paññāya cassa disvāti paññāya ca etassa ariyasaccadhamme disvā. Ekacce āsavāti paṭhamamaggādīhi pahātabbā ekadesaāsavā. Tathāgatappaveditāti tathāgatena paveditā catusaccadhammā. Paññāya vodiṭṭhā hontīti imasmiṃ ṭhāne sīlaṃ kathitaṃ, imasmiṃ samādhi, imasmiṃ vipassanā, imasmiṃ maggo, imasmiṃ phalanti evaṃ atthena atthe kāraṇena kāraṇe ciṇṇacaritattā maggapaññāya sudiṭṭhā honti. Vocaritāti vicaritā. Saddhā niviṭṭhā hotīti okappanasaddhā patiṭṭhitā hoti. Mattaso nijjhānaṃ khamantīti mattāya olokanaṃ khamanti. Saddhāmattanti saddhāyeva, itaraṃ tasseva vevacanaṃ [P 3.0192]

‘Having touched with the body’ means having touched with the co-arisen mental body. ‘And having seen with wisdom’ means having seen the Dhammas of the Noble Truths with wisdom. ‘Some cankers’ means a portion of the cankers that are to be abandoned by the first path and so on. ‘Proclaimed by the Tathāgata’ means the Dhammas of the Four Truths proclaimed by the Tathāgata. ‘They are well seen by wisdom’ means that because of having practiced the conduct in accordance with the meaning and the reason, they are well seen by the wisdom of the path, as in: ‘In this place, virtue is taught; in this place, concentration; in this place, insight; in this place, the path; in this place, the fruit.’ ‘Well examined’ (vocaritā) means investigated (vicaritā). ‘Faith is established’ means the faith of conviction is established. ‘They endure moderate reflection’ means they endure observation to a certain measure. ‘Mere faith’ (saddhāmattanti) means faith itself; the other term (pemamattaṃ) is a synonym for it.

Iti imesu appamādena karaṇīyesu puggalesu tayo paṭividdhamaggaphalā sekhā. Tesu anulomasenāsanaṃ sevamānā kalyāṇamitte bhajamānā indriyāni samannānayamānā anupubbena arahattaṃ gaṇhanti. Tasmā tesaṃ yathāṭhitova pāḷiattho. Avasāne pana dve sotāpattimaggasamaṅgino. Tehi tassa maggassa anulomasenāsanaṃ sevitaṃ, kalyāṇamittā bhajitā, indriyāni samannānītāni. Upari pana tiṇṇaṃ maggānaṃ atthāya sevamānā bhajamānā samannānayamānā anupubbena arahattaṃ pāpuṇissantīti ayamettha pāḷiattho.

Thus, among these individuals who have a task to be accomplished with diligence, three—the body-witness, the one attained-to-view, and the one liberated by faith—are learners who have penetrated the path and fruit. They, by frequenting suitable lodgings, associating with good friends, and harmonizing their faculties, gradually attain Arahantship. Therefore, for them, the meaning of the Pāḷi is just as it stands. At the end, however, are two—the Dhamma-follower and the faith-follower—who are endowed with the stream-entry path. For the sake of that path, suitable lodgings have been frequented by them, good friends have been associated with, and the faculties have been harmonized. Furthermore, for the sake of the three higher paths, by frequenting suitable lodgings, associating with good friends, and harmonizing their faculties, they will gradually attain Arahantship. This is the meaning of the Pāḷi here.

Vitaṇḍavādī pana imameva pāḷiṃ gahetvā – “lokuttaramaggo na ekacittakkhaṇiko, bahucittakkhaṇiko”ti vadati. So vattabbo – “yadi aññena cittena senāsanaṃ paṭisevati, aññena [V 3.0137] kalyāṇamitte bhajati, aññena indriyāni samannāneti, aññaṃ maggacittanti sandhāya tvaṃ ‘na ekacittakkhaṇiko maggo, bahucittakkhaṇiko’ti vadasi, evaṃ sante senāsanaṃ sevamāno nīlobhāsaṃ pabbataṃ passati, vanaṃ passati, migapakkhīnaṃ [M 3.0134] saddaṃ suṇāti, pupphaphalānaṃ gandhaṃ ghāyati, pānīyaṃ pivanto rasaṃ sāyati, nisīdanto nipajjanto phassaṃ phusati. Evaṃ te pañcaviññāṇasamaṅgīpi lokuttaradhammasamaṅgīyeva bhavissati. Sace panetaṃ sampaṭicchasi, satthārā saddhiṃ paṭivirujjhasi. Satthārā hi pañcaviññāṇakāyā ekantaṃ abyākatāva vuttā, taṃsamaṅgissa kusalākusalaṃ paṭikkhittaṃ, lokuttaramaggo ca ekantakusalo. Tasmā pajahetaṃ vāda”nti paññapetabbo. Sace paññattiṃ na upagacchati, “gaccha pātova vihāraṃ pavisitvā yāguṃ pivāhī”ti uyyojetabbo.

However, a sophist, taking this very Pāḷi text, says: 'The supramundane path is not of a single mind-moment; it is of many mind-moments.' He should be told: 'If, with reference to the idea that with one mind one resorts to a dwelling, with another one associates with good friends, with another one brings the faculties into harmony, and the path-mind is yet another, you say, "The path is not of a single mind-moment; it is of many mind-moments," this being so, a person resorting to a dwelling sees a mountain of blue color, sees a forest, hears the sound of beasts and birds, smells the scent of flowers and fruits, tastes the flavor while drinking water, and experiences contact while sitting or lying down. Thus, one endowed with the five consciousnesses would also be endowed with the supramundane Dhamma. If you accept this, you contradict the Teacher. For the Teacher has declared the five consciousness-bodies to be exclusively indeterminate; for one endowed with them, the wholesome and unwholesome are rejected, whereas the supramundane path is exclusively wholesome. Therefore, abandon this view.' If he does not come to this understanding, he should be dismissed with the words: 'Go! Having entered the monastery early, drink your gruel.'

183. Nāhaṃ[P 3.0193], bhikkhave, ādikenevāti ahaṃ, bhikkhave, paṭhamameva maṇḍūkassa uppatitvā gamanaṃ viya aññārādhanaṃ arahatte patiṭṭhānaṃ na vadāmi. Anupubbasikkhāti karaṇatthe paccattavacanaṃ. Parato padadvayepi eseva nayo. Saddhājātoti okappaniyasaddhāya jātasaddho. Upasaṅkamatīti garūnaṃ samīpaṃ gacchati. Payirupāsatīti santike nisīdati. Dhāretīti sādhukaṃ katvā dhāreti. Chando jāyatīti kattukamyatākusalacchando jāyati. Ussahatīti vīriyaṃ karoti. Tuletīti aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattāti tulayati. Tulayitvā padahatīti evaṃ tīraṇavipassanāya tulayanto maggapadhānaṃ padahati. Pahitattoti pesitacitto. Kāyena ceva paramasaccanti nāmakāyena nibbānasaccaṃ sacchikaroti. Paññāya cāti nāmakāyasampayuttāya maggapaññāya paṭivijjhati passati.

183. Regarding 'Monks, not at the very beginning...': Monks, I do not declare that the attainment, the establishment in Arahantship, is at the very beginning, like the leaping movement of a frog. 'Anupubbasikkhā' (gradual training) is a nominative word used in the instrumental sense. In the two subsequent phrases, this same method should be understood. 'Saddhājāto' (one in whom faith is born) means one in whom faith is born through confident faith. 'Upasaṅkamati' (he approaches) means he goes near the noble teachers. 'Payirupāsati' (he attends on) means he sits in their presence. 'Dhāreti' (he bears in mind) means he bears it in mind well. 'Chando jāyati' (desire arises) means wholesome desire, which is the wish to act, arises. 'Ussahati' (he strives) means he makes an effort. 'Tuleti' (he weighs) means he weighs thus: 'impermanent, suffering, not-self.' 'Tulayitvā padahati' (having weighed, he strives) means: thus weighing with investigative insight, he strives with the striving for the path. 'Pahitatto' (one with a dispatched self) means one whose mind is sent forth towards Nibbāna. 'Kāyena ceva paramasaccaṃ' (with the body, the ultimate truth) means he realizes with the mental body the truth of Nibbāna. 'Paññāya ca' (and with wisdom) means with the wisdom of the path associated with the mental body, he penetrates and sees.

Idāni yasmā te satthu āgamanaṃ sutvā paccuggamanamattampi na akaṃsu, tasmā tesaṃ cariyaṃ garahanto sāpi nāma, bhikkhave, saddhā nāhosītiādimāha. Tattha kīvadūrevimeti kittakaṃ dūre ṭhāne. Yojanasatampi yojanasahassampi apakkantāti vattuṃ vaṭṭati, na pana kiñci āha. Catuppadaṃ veyyākaraṇanti catusaccabyākaraṇaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ.

Now, because those monks, Assaji and Punabbasu, having heard of the Teacher's arrival, did not even go out to meet him, the Teacher, wishing to censure their conduct, said: 'Sāpi nāma, bhikkhave, saddhā nāhosi' ('Monks, even that much faith was not there'), and so on. Therein, 'Kīva dūre vime' ('How far away?') means: in how distant a place? It would be fitting to say that they had departed a hundred yojanas or a thousand yojanas, but he said nothing. 'Catuppadaṃ veyyākaraṇaṃ' (a four-line exposition) was said with reference to the exposition of the Four Truths.

184. Yassuddiṭṭhassāti yassa uddiṭṭhassa. Yopi [P 3.0194] so, bhikkhave, satthāti bāhirakasatthāraṃ dasseti. Evarūpīti evaṃjātikā. Paṇopaṇaviyāti paṇaviyā ca opaṇaviyā ca[V 3.0138]. Na upetīti na hoti. Kayavikkayakāle viya agghavaḍḍhanahāpanaṃ na hotīti attho. Ayaṃ goṇo [M 3.0135] kiṃ agghati, vīsati agghatīti bhaṇanto paṇati nāma. Na vīsati agghati, dasa agghatīti bhaṇanto opaṇati nāma. Idaṃ paṭisedhento āha “paṇopaṇaviyā na upetī”ti. Idāni taṃ paṇopaṇaviyaṃ dassetuṃ evañca no assa, atha naṃ kareyyāma, na ca no evamassa, na naṃ kareyyāmāti āha.

184. 'Yassuddiṭṭhassa' means 'of which teaching pointed out.' By 'Yopi so, bhikkhave, satthā,' He indicates a teacher outside the Dispensation. 'Evarūpī' means 'of such a kind.' 'Paṇopaṇaviyā' means both buying (`paṇaviyā`) and selling (`opaṇaviyā`). 'Na upeti' means 'it is not.' The meaning is: just as at the time of buying and selling, there is no increasing or decreasing of the price. One who says, 'This ox, what is it worth? It is worth twenty,' is called `paṇati`. One who says, 'It is not worth twenty; it is worth ten,' is called `opaṇati`. The Blessed One, wishing to reject this, said, 'There is no buying and selling.' Now, to show that buying and selling, He said: 'If it were to be thus for us, then we would do it; but if it were not thus for us, we would not do it.'

Kiṃ pana, bhikkhaveti, bhikkhave, yaṃ tathāgato sabbaso āmisehi visaṃsaṭṭho viharati, evaṃ visaṃsaṭṭhassa satthuno evarūpā paṇopaṇaviyā kiṃ yujjissati? Pariyogāhiya vattatoti pariyogāhitvā ukkhipitvā gahetvā vattantassa. Ayamanudhammoti ayaṃ sabhāvo. Jānāti bhagavā, nāhaṃ jānāmīti bhagavā ekāsanabhojane ānisaṃsaṃ jānāti, ahaṃ na jānāmīti mayi saddhāya divasassa tayo vāre bhojanaṃ pahāya ekāsanabhojanaṃ bhuñjati. Ruḷahanīyanti rohanīyaṃ. Ojavantanti sinehavantaṃ. Kāmaṃ taco cāti iminā caturaṅgavīriyaṃ dasseti. Ettha hi taco ekaṃ aṅgaṃ, nhāru ekaṃ, aṭṭhi ekaṃ, maṃsalohitaṃ ekanti evaṃ caturaṅgasamannāgataṃ vīriyaṃ adhiṭṭhahitvā arahattaṃ appatvā na vuṭṭhahissāmīti evaṃ paṭipajjatīti [P 3.0195] dasseti. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānameva. Desanaṃ pana bhagavā neyyapuggalassa vasena arahattanikūṭena niṭṭhāpesīti.

'Kiṃ pana, bhikkhave': Monks, since the Tathāgata dwells in every way unmixed with worldly things, for such a Teacher who is unmixed, how could such buying and selling be suitable? 'Pariyogāhiya vattato' means for a disciple who practices having penetrated, borne on the head, and grasped. 'Ayamanudhammo' means this is the suitable nature. 'Jānāti bhagavā, nāhaṃ jānāmi' means: 'The Blessed One knows the benefit of eating in one session; I do not know.' Thus, with faith in me, having abandoned eating three times a day, he eats in one session. 'Ruḷhanīyaṃ' means conducive to growth. 'Ojavantaṃ' means having nutritive essence. By 'Kāmaṃ taco ca,' He shows the four-factored energy. Herein, skin is one factor, sinew is one, bone is one, and flesh and blood is one. Thus He shows that one practices by resolving upon energy endowed with these four factors, thinking: 'Without attaining Arahantship, I will not arise.' The rest is clear everywhere. The Blessed One concluded the discourse, by way of a person to be guided, with Arahantship as its pinnacle.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Kīṭāgirisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Kīṭāgiri Sutta is concluded.

Dutiyavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Second Chapter is concluded.

3. Paribbājakavaggo

3. The Chapter on Wanderers

1. Tevijjavacchasuttavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Tevijjavacchasutta

185. Evaṃ [V 3.0139][M 3.0136] me sutanti tevijjavacchasuttaṃ. Tattha ekapuṇḍarīketi puṇḍarīko vuccati setambarukkho, so tasmiṃ ārāme eko puṇḍarīko atthīti ekapuṇḍarīko. Etadahosīti tattha pavisitukāmatāya ahosi. Cirassaṃ kho, bhanteti pakatiyā āgatapubbataṃ upādāya. Dhammassa cānudhammanti idha sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ dhammo nāma, mahājanassa byākaraṇaṃ anudhammo nāma. Sesaṃ jīvakasutte (ma. ni. 2.51 ādayo) vuttanayameva. Na me teti ananuññāya ṭhatvā anuññampi paṭikkhipati. “Sabbaññū sabbadassāvī aparisesaṃ ñāṇadassanaṃ paṭijānātī”ti hi idaṃ anujānitabbaṃ siyā, – “carato ca me…pe… paccupaṭṭhita”nti idaṃ pana nānujānitabbaṃ. Sabbaññutaññāṇena hi āvajjitvā pajānāti. Tasmā ananuññāya ṭhatvā anuññampi paṭikkhipanto evamāha.

185. The sutta beginning with 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ' is the Tevijjavacchasutta. Therein, as for 'ekapuṇḍarīke', a white mango tree is called 'puṇḍarīka'. Since there was one such white mango tree in that park, it is called 'Ekapuṇḍarīka'. As for 'Etadahosi', this arose from the desire to enter there. As for 'Cirassaṃ kho, bhante', it was said thus with reference to his having come before as a matter of course. In the phrase 'Dhammassa cānudhammaṃ', the knowledge of omniscience is called 'dhamma', and the explanation to the great multitude is called 'anudhamma'. The rest is in the same manner as stated in the Jīvaka Sutta. By the phrase 'Na me te', standing in the position of not granting permission, he rejects even what should be permitted. Indeed, this statement, “He claims to be all-knowing, all-seeing, to possess knowledge and vision without remainder,” should be permitted. But this statement, “While I am walking… it is present,” should not be permitted. Indeed, he knows by reflecting with the knowledge of omniscience. Therefore, standing in the position of not permitting and rejecting even what should be permitted, he spoke thus.

186. Āsavānaṃ khayāti ettha sakiṃ khīṇānaṃ āsavānaṃ puna khepetabbābhāvā yāvadevāti na vuttaṃ. Pubbenivāsañāṇena cettha bhagavā atītajānanaguṇaṃ dasseti, dibbacakkhuñāṇena [P 3.0196] paccuppannajānanaguṇaṃ, āsavakkhayañāṇena lokuttaraguṇanti. Iti imāhi tīhi vijjāhi sakalabuddhaguṇe saṃkhipitvā kathesi.

186. In the phrase 'Āsavānaṃ khayā', 'yāvade' was not said because the taints, having been destroyed once, do not have the nature of needing to be destroyed again. Herein, with the knowledge of previous existences, the Blessed One shows the quality of knowing the past; with the knowledge of the divine eye, the quality of knowing the present; and with the knowledge of the destruction of the taints, the supramundane quality. Thus, with these three kinds of knowledge, having summarized all the qualities of a Buddha, he spoke.

Gihisaṃyojananti gihibandhanaṃ gihiparikkhāresu nikantiṃ. Natthi kho vacchāti gihisaṃyojanaṃ appahāya dukkhassantakaro nāma natthi. Yepi hi santatimahāmatto uggaseno seṭṭhiputto vītasokadārakoti gihiliṅge ṭhitāva arahattaṃ pattā, tepi maggena sabbasaṅkhāresu nikantiṃ [V 3.0140] sukkhāpetvā pattā. Taṃ patvā pana na tena liṅgena aṭṭhaṃsu, gihiliṅgaṃ nāmetaṃ hīnaṃ, uttamaguṇaṃ dhāretuṃ na sakkoti. Tasmā tattha ṭhito arahattaṃ patvā taṃdivasameva pabbajati vā parinibbāti vā. Bhūmadevatā pana tiṭṭhanti. Kasmā? Nilīyanokāsassa atthitāya. Sesakāmabhave manussesu sotāpannādayo tayo tiṭṭhanti, kāmāvacaradevesu [M 3.0137] sotāpannā sakadāgāmino ca, anāgāmikhīṇāsavā panettha na tiṭṭhanti. Kasmā? Tañhi ṭhānaṃ laḷitajanassa āvāso, natthi tattha tesaṃ pavivekārahaṃ paṭicchannaṭṭhānañca. Iti tattha khīṇāsavo parinibbāti, anāgāmī cavitvā suddhāvāse nibbattati. Kāmāvacaradevato upari pana cattāropi ariyā tiṭṭhanti.

‘Gihisaṃyojanaṃ’ means the householder’s fetter, which is craving for a householder's requisites. As for ‘Natthi kho, Vaccha’, it means there is no one called a maker of an end to suffering without having abandoned the householder's fetter. Even those such as Santati the great minister, Uggasena the merchant’s son, and the boy Vītasoka, who attained Arahantship while remaining in the guise of a householder, they too attained it by having dried up craving for all conditioned things by means of the path. However, having attained it, they did not remain in that guise. This guise of a householder is inferior; it is not able to bear the supreme quality. Therefore, one established therein, having attained Arahantship, on that very day either goes forth or attains Parinibbāna. Earth-deities, however, can remain. Why? Because there is a place for concealment. In the remaining sense-sphere existences, among humans, the three types of noble ones, beginning with the Stream-enterer, can remain. Among the sense-sphere devas, Stream-enterers and Once-returners can remain, but Non-returners and Arahants do not remain there. Why? Because that place is the abode of those who delight in sensual pleasures, and there is no suitable place for seclusion and concealment for them there. Thus, therein an Arahant attains Parinibbāna; a Non-returner, having passed away, is reborn in the Pure Abodes. However, above the sense-sphere devas, all four types of noble ones can remain.

Sopāsi kammavādīti sopi kammavādī ahosi, kiriyampi na paṭibāhittha. Tañhi ekanavutikappamatthake attānaṃyeva gahetvā katheti. Tadā kira mahāsatto pāsaṇḍapariggaṇhanatthaṃ pabbajito tassapi pāsaṇḍassa nipphalabhāvaṃ [P 3.0197] jānitvā vīriyaṃ na hāpesi, kiriyavādī hutvā sagge nibbattati. Tasmā evamāha. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

As for 'So'pāsi kammavādī', it means 'he too was a proponent of kamma'. He did not reject the doctrine of action either. For he spoke taking himself as an example from ninety-one aeons ago. It is said that at that time the Great Being went forth to master the views of the sectarians. And though he knew the fruitlessness of that sectarianism, he did not abandon his effort, and becoming a proponent of action, he was reborn in heaven. Therefore, he spoke thus. The rest is clear everywhere.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Tevijjavacchasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Tevijjavacchasutta is concluded.

2. Aggivacchasuttavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Aggivacchasutta

187. Evaṃ [V 3.0141] me sutanti aggivacchasuttaṃ. Tattha na kho ahanti paṭhamavāre nāhaṃ sassatadiṭṭhikoti vadati, dutiye nāhaṃ ucchedadiṭṭhikoti. Evaṃ antānantikādivasena sabbavāresu paṭikkhepo veditabbo. Hoti ca na ca hotīti ayaṃ panettha ekaccasassatavādo. Neva hoti na na hotīti ayaṃ amarāvikkhepoti veditabbo.

187. “Thus I have heard”—this is the Aggivaccha Sutta. Therein, regarding ‘na kho ahaṃ,’ in the first instance, He says, “I am not one with an eternalist view”; in the second, “I am not one with an annihilationist view.” Thus, in all instances that proceed by way of finitude, infinitude, and so on, the rejection should be understood. Among these, the view “it is and it is not” is partial eternalism. The view “it neither is nor is not” should be understood as evasive equivocation.

189. Sadukkhanti kilesadukkhena ceva vipākadukkhena ca sadukkhaṃ. Savighātanti tesaṃyeva dvinnaṃ vasena saupaghātakaṃ. Saupāyāsanti tesaṃyeva vasena saupāyāsaṃ. Sapariḷāhanti tesaṃyeva vasena sapariḷāhaṃ.

189. `Sadukkhaṃ` means with suffering, that is, with the suffering of defilements and the suffering of results. `Savighātaṃ` means with vexation, that is, with oppression by means of those very two. `Saupāyāsaṃ` means with despair, that is, with tribulation by means of those very two. `Sapariḷāhaṃ` means with torment, that is, with anguish by means of those very two.

Kiñci diṭṭhigatanti kāci ekā diṭṭhipi ruccitvā khamāpetvā gahitā atthīti pucchati. Apanītanti nīhaṭaṃ apaviddhaṃ. Diṭṭhanti paññāya diṭṭhaṃ. Tasmāti yasmā pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ udayavayaṃ addasa, tasmā. Sabbamaññitānanti [P 3.0198] sabbesaṃ tiṇṇampi taṇhādiṭṭhimānamaññitānaṃ. Mathitānanti tesaṃyeva vevacanaṃ. Idāni tāni vibhajitvā dassento sabbaahaṃkāra-mamaṃkāra-mānānusayānanti āha. Ettha [M 3.0138] hi ahaṃkāro diṭṭhi, mamaṃkāro taṇhā, mānānusayo māno. Anupādā vimuttoti catūhi upādānehi kañci dhammaṃ anupādiyitvā vimutto.

`Kiñci diṭṭhigataṃ`: he asks, “Is there any single view whatsoever that has been held, having been approved of and consented to?” `Apanītaṃ` means removed, discarded. `Diṭṭhaṃ` means seen by wisdom. `Tasmā`: because he saw the arising and passing away of the five aggregates, therefore. `Sabbamaññitānaṃ` means of all three conceivings: the conceiving of craving, views, and conceit. `Mathitānaṃ` is a synonym for those very same terms. Now, showing them by way of analysis, He said: `sabbaahaṃkāra-mamaṃkāra-mānānusayānaṃ`. Herein, `ahaṃkāra` (I-making) is view, `mamaṃkāra` (mine-making) is craving, and `mānānusayo` (the underlying tendency to conceit) is conceit. `Anupādā vimutto` means liberated through not clinging to any phenomenon by means of the four kinds of clinging.

190. Na upetīti na yujjati. Ettha ca “na upapajjatī”ti idaṃ anujānitabbaṃ siyā. Yasmā pana evaṃ vutte so paribbājako ucchedaṃ gaṇheyya, upapajjatīti pana sassatameva, upapajjati ca na ca upapajjatīti ekaccasassataṃ, neva upapajjati na na upapajjatīti amarāvikkhepaṃ, tasmā bhagavā – “ayaṃ appatiṭṭho anālambo hotu, sukhapavesanaṭṭhānaṃ mā labhatū”ti ananuññāya ṭhatvā anuññampi paṭikkhipi. Alanti samatthaṃ pariyattaṃ[V 3.0142]. Dhammoti paccayākāradhammo. Aññatrayogenāti aññattha payogena. Aññatrācariyakenāti paccayākāraṃ ajānantānaṃ aññesaṃ ācariyānaṃ santike vasantena.

190. `Na upeti` means it is not fitting. And here, this statement “does not arise” (`na upapajjati`) should have been permitted. However, because if it were said thus, that wanderer would grasp the annihilationist view; and if “arises” were said, he would grasp eternalism; if “arises and does not arise” were said, he would grasp partial eternalism; and if “neither arises nor does not arise” were said, he would grasp evasive equivocation; therefore the Blessed One, having considered, “Let this wanderer be without a foothold, without support; may he not obtain a place of easy entry,” stood without giving permission and rejected even what should have been permitted. `Alaṃ` means sufficient, adequate. `Dhamma` means the teaching of the causal structure. `Aññatrayogena` means by one who is making an effort elsewhere. `Aññatrācariyakeṇa` means it is difficult to know for one dwelling in the presence of other teachers who do not know the causal structure.

191. Tena hi vacchāti yasmā tvaṃ sammohamāpādinti vadasi, tasmā taṃyevettha paṭipucchissāmi. Anāhāro [P 3.0199] nibbutoti appaccayo nibbuto.

191. “Then, Vaccha”—because you say, “I have fallen into confusion,” therefore I shall question you in return on this very matter. `Anāhāro nibbuto` means, having become without a condition, it is extinguished.

192. Yena rūpenāti yena rūpena sattasaṅkhātaṃ tathāgataṃ rūpīti paññāpeyya. Gambhīroti guṇagambhīro. Appameyyoti pamāṇaṃ gaṇhituṃ na sakkuṇeyyo. Duppariyogāḷhoti duogāho dujjāno. Seyyathāpi mahāsamuddoti yathā mahāsamuddo gambhīro appameyyo dujjāno, evameva khīṇāsavopi. Taṃ ārabbha upapajjatītiādi sabbaṃ na yujjati. Kathaṃ? Yathā parinibbutaṃ aggiṃ ārabbha puratthimaṃ disaṃ gatotiādi sabbaṃ na yujjati, evaṃ.

192. `Yena rūpena`: by whatever form one might designate the Tathagata, who is reckoned as a being, as ‘possessing form.’ `Gambhīro` means profound in virtue. `Appameyyo` means one is not able to take his measure. `Duppariyogāḷho` means difficult to penetrate, difficult to know. `Seyyathāpi mahāsamuddo`: just as the great ocean is profound, immeasurable, and difficult to know, so too is one whose taints are destroyed. With reference to him, all such statements as “he arises,” and so on, are not fitting. How so? Just as, with reference to an extinguished fire, all such statements as “the fire has gone to the eastern direction” are not fitting, so too it is not fitting here.

Aniccatāti aniccatāya. Sāre patiṭṭhitanti lokuttaradhammasāre patiṭṭhitaṃ. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

`Aniccatā` is said because of impermanence. `Sāre patiṭṭhitaṃ` means established in the essence of the supramundane Dhamma. The remainder is clear everywhere.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Aggivacchasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Aggivaccha Sutta is concluded.

3. Mahāvacchasuttavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Mahāvaccha Sutta

193. Evaṃ [V 3.0143][M 3.0139] me sutanti mahāvacchasuttaṃ. Tattha sahakathīti saddhiṃvādo, bahuṃ mayā tumhehi saddhiṃ kathitapubbanti kathaṃ sāreti mettiṃ ghaṭeti. Purimāni hi dve suttāni etasseva kathitāni, saṃyuttake abyākatasaṃyuttaṃ (saṃ. ni. 4.416 ādayo) nāma etasseva kathitaṃ – “kiṃ nu kho, bho gotama, sassato loko idameva saccaṃ moghamaññanti [P 3.0200] abyākatameta”nti evaṃ ekuttaranikāyepi iminā saddhiṃ kathitaṃ atthiyeva. Tasmā evamāha. Sammāsambuddhopi tassa āgatāgatassa saṅgahaṃ katvā okāsamakāsiyeva. Kasmā? Ayañhi sassatadiṭṭhiko, sassatadiṭṭhikā ca sīghaṃ laddhiṃ na vissajjenti, vasātelamakkhitapilotikā viya cirena sujjhanti. Passati ca bhagavā – “ayaṃ paribbājako kāle gacchante gacchante laddhiṃ vissajjetvā mama santike pabbajitvā cha abhiññāyo sacchikatvā abhiññātasāvako bhavissatī”ti. Tasmā tassa āgatāgatassa saṅgahaṃ katvā okāsamakāsiyeva. Idaṃ panassa pacchimagamanaṃ. So hi imasmiṃ sutte taraṇaṃ vā hotu ataraṇaṃ vā, yaṭṭhiṃ otaritvā udake patamāno viya samaṇassa gotamassa santikaṃ gantvā pabbajissāmīti sanniṭṭhānaṃ katvā āgato. Tasmā dhammadesanaṃ yācanto sādhu me bhavaṃ gotamotiādimāha. Tassa bhagavā mūlavasena saṃkhittadesanaṃ, kammapathavasena vitthāradesanaṃ desesi. Mūlavasena cettha atisaṃkhittā desanā, kammapathavasena saṃkhittā vitthārasadisā. Buddhānaṃ pana nippariyāyena vitthāradesanā nāma natthi. Catuvīsatisamantapaṭṭhānampi hi sattapakaraṇe abhidhammapiṭake ca sabbaṃ saṃkhittameva. Tasmā mūlavasenāpi kammapathavasenāpi saṃkhittameva desesīti veditabbo.

3. “Thus have I heard” begins the Mahāvaccha Sutta. Herein, “having spoken together” means a conversation. “Much have I spoken with you before” is said to recall past conversation and establish friendliness. Indeed, the two previous suttas were spoken to him, and in the Saṃyutta Nikāya, the section called the Abyākatasaṃyutta was spoken to him, beginning: “Venerable Gotama, is the world eternal? Is this alone the truth and anything else foolish?” Thus, in the Aṅguttara Nikāya as well, there is indeed conversation with him. Therefore, he spoke thus. The Perfectly Enlightened One, too, having shown kindness to him on his repeated visits, granted him an opportunity. Why? Because this wanderer held the view of eternalism, and those with eternalist views do not quickly relinquish their beliefs; like a worn cloth smeared with fat and oil, they become clean only after a long time. And the Blessed One saw: “As time passes, this wanderer will relinquish his belief, go forth in my presence, realize the six higher knowledges, and become a renowned disciple.” Therefore, having shown kindness to him on his repeated visits, he granted him an opportunity. This, however, was his final visit. For in this sutta, whether he would cross over or not, like one planting his staff and descending into the water, he came having made the resolution: “I will go to the presence of the ascetic Gotama and go forth.” Therefore, requesting a Dhamma teaching, he said, “It would be good, Venerable Gotama,” and so on. The Blessed One taught him a brief discourse by way of the roots and a detailed discourse by way of the courses of action. Herein, the discourse by way of the roots is extremely brief, and the concise discourse by way of the courses of action resembles a detailed one. For the Buddhas, however, there is no such thing as a detailed discourse in an absolute sense. For even the twenty-fourfold Samantapaṭṭhāna in the seven treatises of the Abhidhamma Piṭaka is all concise. Therefore, it should be understood that he taught concisely both by way of the roots and by way of the courses of action.

194. Tattha pāṇātipātā veramaṇī kusalantiādīsu paṭipāṭiyā sattadhammā kāmāvacarā, anabhijjhādayo tayo catubhūmikāpi vaṭṭanti.

193. Therein, in the passages beginning with “abstinence from the destruction of life is wholesome,” the seven dhammas in sequence are of the sense-sphere, while non-covetousness and the other two may also pertain to the four planes.

Yato [P 3.0201] kho, vaccha, bhikkhunoti kiñcāpi aniyametvā vuttaṃ, yathā pana jīvakasutte ca caṅkīsutte ca, evaṃ imasmiṃ sutte ca attānameva sandhāyetaṃ bhagavatā vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

Regarding “When, Vaccha, a monk...”: although this was spoken without specification, it should be understood that, just as in the Jīvaka Sutta and the Caṅkī Sutta, so too in this sutta the Blessed One spoke referring to himself.

195. Atthi [V 3.0144][M 3.0140] panāti kiṃ pucchāmīti pucchati? Ayaṃ kirassa laddhi – “tasmiṃ tasmiṃ sāsane satthāva arahā hoti, sāvako pana arahattaṃ pattuṃ samattho natthi. Samaṇo ca gotamo ‘yato kho, vaccha, bhikkhuno’ti ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ kathento viya katheti, atthi nu kho samaṇassa gotamassa sāvako arahattappatto”ti. Etamatthaṃ pucchissāmīti pucchati. Tattha tiṭṭhatūti bhavaṃ tāva gotamo tiṭṭhatu, bhavañhi loke pākaṭo arahāti attho. Tasmiṃ byākate uttari bhikkhunīādīnaṃ vasena pañhaṃ pucchi, bhagavāpissa byākāsi.

195. With “But is there...?” what does he ask? This, it seems, was his belief: “In any given teaching, only the teacher is an arahant; a disciple is not capable of attaining arahantship. And the ascetic Gotama, in saying, ‘When, Vaccha, a monk...’ speaks as if of a single monk. Is there, I wonder, any disciple of the ascetic Gotama who has attained arahantship?” He asks intending to ask this. Therein, `tiṭṭhatu` (let that be) means, “Let the Venerable Gotama be for now; for you, venerable sir, are indeed renowned in the world as an arahant.” When that was explained, he further asked questions concerning bhikkhunīs and so on, and the Blessed One also explained it to him.

196. Ārādhakoti sampādako paripūrako.

196. “One who succeeds” means one who accomplishes, one who fulfills.

197. Sekhāya vijjāya pattabbanti heṭṭhimaphalattayaṃ pattabbaṃ. Taṃ sabbaṃ mayā anuppattanti vadati. Vitaṇḍavādī panāha – “katame dhammā sekkhā? Cattāro maggā apariyāpannā heṭṭhimāni ca tīṇi sāmaññaphalānī”ti (dha. sa. 1023) vacanato arahattamaggopi anena pattoyeva. Phalaṃ pana apattaṃ, tassa pattiyā uttari yogaṃ kathāpetīti. So evaṃ saññāpetabbo –

197. “To be attained by the trainee’s knowledge” means the three lower fruits are to be attained. He says, “All of that has been attained by me.” A sophist, however, says: “Based on the statement, ‘What are the states of a trainee? The four paths that are supramundane and the three lower fruits of recluseship’ (Dhs §1023), the path of arahantship has also been attained by him. The fruit, however, has not been attained, and for its attainment, he has him speak of further effort.” That person should be made to understand thus:

“Yo [P 3.0202] ve kilesāni pahāya pañca,

Paripuṇṇasekho aparihānadhammo;

Cetovasippatto samāhitindriyo,

Sa ve ṭhitattoti naro pavuccatī”ti. (a. ni. 4.5);

“That person who, having abandoned the five defilements, is a perfected trainee, not subject to decline, has attained mastery of mind, and has composed faculties—he, indeed, is called one of steadfast self.”

Anāgāmipuggalo hi ekantaparipuṇṇasekho. Taṃ sandhāya “sekhāya vijjāya pattabba”nti āha. Maggassa pana ekacittakkhaṇikattā tattha ṭhitassa pucchā nāma natthi. Iminā suttena maggopi bahucittakkhaṇiko hotūti ce. Etaṃ na buddhavacanaṃ, vuttagāthāya ca attho virujjhati. Tasmā anāgāmiphale ṭhatvā arahattamaggassa vipassanaṃ kathāpetīti veditabbo. Yasmā panassa na kevalaṃ suddhaarahattasseva upanissayo, channampi abhiññānaṃ upanissayo atthi, tasmā bhagavā – “evamayaṃ samathe kammaṃ katvā pañca abhiññā nibbattessati[V 3.0145], vipassanāya kammaṃ katvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇissati. Evaṃ chaḷabhiñño mahāsāvako bhavissatī”ti vipassanāmattaṃ akathetvā samathavipassanā ācikkhi.

For a non-returner is a completely perfected trainee. It was with reference to him that the Blessed One said, “to be attained by the trainee’s knowledge.” But since the path is of a single mind-moment, for one established therein, there is no possibility of questioning. If it is said that, according to this sutta, the path must also have many mind-moments, that is not the word of the Buddha, and the meaning would conflict with the verse cited. Therefore, it should be understood that while he was established in the fruit of non-returning, the Blessed One taught him insight for the path of arahantship. For he had the supporting condition not only for pure arahantship, but also the supporting condition for the six higher knowledges. Therefore, the Blessed One, thinking, “Thus, by undertaking the practice of tranquility, he will produce the five higher knowledges; by undertaking the practice of insight, he will attain arahantship. In this way, he will become a great disciple possessing the six higher knowledges,” did not speak of insight alone, but pointed out both tranquility and insight.

198. Sati [M 3.0141] satiāyataneti sati satikāraṇe. Kiñcettha kāraṇaṃ? Abhiññā vā abhiññāpādakajjhānaṃ vā avasāne pana arahattaṃ vā kāraṇaṃ arahattassa vipassanā vāti veditabbaṃ.

198. The phrase `sati sati āyatane` means 'when there is a cause'. And what here is the cause? It should be understood that the cause is either the higher knowledges, or the jhāna that is the basis for the higher knowledges, or, at the end, arahantship, or the insight for arahantship.

200. Pariciṇṇo me bhagavāti satta hi sekhā bhagavantaṃ paricaranti nāma, khīṇāsavena bhagavā pariciṇṇo hoti. Iti saṅkhepena arahattaṃ byākaronto thero evamāha. Te pana bhikkhū tamatthaṃ na jāniṃsu, ajānantāva tassa vacanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā. Bhagavato ārocesuṃ. Devatāti tesaṃ guṇānaṃ lābhī devatā. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

200. Regarding “The Blessed One has been served by me”: indeed, the seven kinds of trainees are said to attend upon the Blessed One, but it is by one whose cankers are destroyed that the Blessed One is truly served. Thus, briefly declaring arahantship, the Elder spoke in this way. Those monks, however, did not know that meaning, and without knowing it, they accepted his words and reported them to the Blessed One. “A deity” means a deity who is a recipient of those qualities. The rest is clear in all instances.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Mahāvacchasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Mahāvacchasutta is concluded.

4. Dīghanakhasuttavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Dīghanakha Sutta

201. Evaṃ [V 3.0146][P 3.0203] me sutanti dīghanakhasuttaṃ. Tattha sūkarakhatāyanti sūkarakhatāti evaṃnāmake leṇe. Kassapabuddhakāle kira taṃ leṇaṃ ekasmiṃ buddhantare pathaviyā vaḍḍhamānāya antobhūmigataṃ jātaṃ. Athekadivasaṃ eko sūkaro tassa chadanapariyantasamīpe paṃsuṃ khaṇi. Deve vuṭṭe paṃsudhoto chadanapariyanto pākaṭo ahosi. Eko vanacarako disvā – “pubbe sīlavantehi paribhuttaleṇena bhavitabbaṃ, paṭijaggissāmi na”nti samantato paṃsuṃ apanetvā leṇaṃ sodhetvā kuṭṭaparikkhepaṃ katvā dvāravātapānaṃ yojetvā supariniṭṭhita-sudhākammacittakammarajatapaṭṭasadisāya vālukāya santhatapariveṇaṃ leṇaṃ katvā mañcapīṭhaṃ paññāpetvā bhagavato vasanatthāya adāsi. Leṇaṃ gambhīraṃ ahosi otaritvā abhiruhitabbaṃ. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ.

4. “Thus have I heard”—this is the Dīghanakha Sutta. Therein, “at Sūkarakhatā” means in a cave named Sūkarakhatā. It is said that in the time of the Buddha Kassapa, during one interval between Buddhas when the earth was expanding, that cave became situated inside the earth. Then one day, a boar dug the earth near the edge of the cave’s roof. When it rained, the edge of the roof, with the earth washed away, became manifest. A forest-dweller saw it and thought, “This must be a cave used by virtuous ones in the past. I will restore it.” Having removed the earth from all around, he cleaned the cave, made a wall enclosure, fitted a door and a window, did well-finished plaster work and painting, made the enclosure spread with sand that was like a silver plate, prepared a bed and a seat, and gave it to the Blessed One for his residence. The cave was deep; one had to ascend after descending. This was said in reference to that.

Dīghanakhoti tassa paribbājakassa nāmaṃ. Upasaṅkamīti kasmā upasaṅkami? So kira there aḍḍhamāsapabbajite cintesi – “mayhaṃ mātulo aññaṃ pāsaṇḍaṃ gantvā na ciraṃ tiṭṭhati, idāni panassa samaṇassa gotamassa santikaṃ gatassa aḍḍhamāso jāto. Pavattimpissa na suṇāmi, ojavantaṃ [M 3.0142] nu kho sāsanaṃ, jānissāmi na”nti gantukāmo jāto. Tasmā upasaṅkami. Ekamantaṃ ṭhitoti tasmiṃ kira samaye thero bhagavantaṃ bījayamāno ṭhito hoti, paribbājako mātule [P 3.0204] hirottappena ṭhitakova pañhaṃ pucchi. Tena vuttaṃ “ekamantaṃ ṭhito”ti.

201. Dīghanakha was the name of that wanderer. “He approached”: why did he approach? It is said that when the Elder had been ordained for half a month, he (Dīghanakha) thought: “My maternal uncle does not stay long after going to another sect. But now, half a month has passed since he went to the ascetic Gotama. I do not hear any news of him. Is the teaching potent, I wonder? I will find out.” He became desirous of going. Therefore, he approached. “Stood to one side”: it is said that at that time, the Elder was standing, fanning the Blessed One. The wanderer, due to shame and fear of wrongdoing in front of his uncle, asked the question while standing. Therefore, it was said, “stood to one side.”

Sabbaṃ me nakkhamatīti sabbā me upapattiyo nakkhamanti, paṭisandhiyo nakkhamantīti adhippāyena vadati. Ettāvatānena “ucchedavādohamasmī”ti dīpitaṃ hoti. Bhagavā panassa adhippāyaṃ muñcitvā akkhare tāva dosaṃ dassento yāpi kho tetiādimāha. Tattha esāpi te diṭṭhi nakkhamatīti esāpi te paṭhamaṃ ruccitvā khamāpetvā gahitadiṭṭhi nakkhamatīti. Esā ce me, bho gotama, diṭṭhi khameyyāti mayhañhi sabbaṃ nakkhamatīti diṭṭhi, tassa mayhaṃ yā esā sabbaṃ me nakkhamatīti diṭṭhi, esā me khameyya. Yaṃ taṃ “sabbaṃ me nakkhamatī”ti vuttaṃ, tampissa tādisameva. Yathā sabbagahaṇena gahitāpi ayaṃ diṭṭhi khamati, evamevaṃ tampi khameyya[V 3.0147]. Evaṃ attano vāde āropitaṃ dosaṃ ñatvā taṃ pariharāmīti saññāya vadati, atthato panassa “esā diṭṭhi na me khamatī”ti āpajjati. Yassa panesā na khamati na ruccati, tassāyaṃ tāya diṭṭhiyā sabbaṃ me na khamatīti diṭṭhi rucitaṃ. Tena hi diṭṭhiakkhamena arucitena bhavitabbanti sabbaṃ khamatīti ruccatīti āpajjati. Na panesa taṃ sampaṭicchati, kevalaṃ tassāpi ucchedadiṭṭhiyā ucchedameva gaṇhāti. Tenāha bhagavā ato kho te, aggivessana,…pe… aññañca diṭṭhiṃ upādiyantīti. Tattha atoti pajahanakesu nissakkaṃ, ye pajahanti, tehi ye nappajahantīti vucciyanti, teva bahutarāti attho. Bahū hi bahutarāti ettha hikāro nipātamattaṃ, bahū bahutarāti attho. Parato [P 3.0205] tanū hi tanutarāti padepi eseva nayo. Ye evamāhaṃsūti ye evaṃ vadanti. Tañceva diṭṭhiṃ nappajahanti, aññañca diṭṭhiṃ upādiyantīti mūladassanaṃ nappajahanti, aparadassanaṃ upādiyanti.

“Nothing is agreeable to me”: he speaks with the intention, “All future existences are not agreeable to me; rebirths are not agreeable to me.” By this much, it is revealed by him: “I am an annihilationist.” But the Blessed One, setting aside his intention, and wishing first to show the fault in the very words, said the passage beginning, “Yāpi kho te...” Therein, “This view of yours is also not agreeable to you” means: “This view, which was first approved by you and then adopted, is also not agreeable to you.” Regarding the statement, 'If this view of mine were agreeable to me, venerable Gotama...': For me, there is the view 'Nothing is agreeable to me.' For me who holds this, that very view, 'Nothing is agreeable to me,' should be agreeable. What was said, “Nothing is agreeable to me,” for him that too is of the same sort. Just as this view, though encompassed by the word “all,” is agreeable, in the same way that too should be agreeable. Thus, knowing the fault attributed by the Blessed One to his own statement, he speaks with the perception, “I will refute it.” But in meaning, the fault arises for him: “This view is not agreeable to me.” For whom this is not agreeable or approved, for him this view, “Nothing is agreeable to me,” is approved. Therefore, by the non-agreeableness of the view, it should be disapproved. Thus the fault arises that “Everything is agreeable” is approved. But he does not accept that; he only grasps annihilation from that annihilationist view. Therefore the Blessed One said: “In that case, Aggivessana... they adopt another view.” Therein, ‘ato’ is an ablative of comparison with those who abandon. The meaning is: compared to those who abandon, those who are said not to abandon are far more numerous. In “many indeed are more numerous” (bahū hi bahutarā), the particle ‘hi’ is a mere particle; the meaning is “many are more numerous.” Further on, in the phrase “few indeed are fewer” (tanū hi tanutarā), this same method should be understood. “Those who spoke thus” means those who speak thus. “They do not abandon that very view, and they adopt another view” means: they do not abandon the root view; they cling to another view.

Ettha ca sassataṃ gahetvā tampi appahāya ucchedaṃ vā ekaccasassataṃ vā gahetuṃ na sakkā, ucchedampi gahetvā taṃ appahāya sassataṃ vā ekaccasassataṃ vā na sakkā gahetuṃ, ekaccasassatampi gahetvā taṃ appahāya sassataṃ vā ucchedaṃ vā na sakkā gahetuṃ. Mūlasassataṃ pana appahāya [M 3.0143] aññaṃ sassatameva sakkā gahetuṃ. Kathaṃ? Ekasmiñhi samaye “rūpaṃ sassata”nti gahetvā aparasmiṃ samaye “na suddharūpameva sassataṃ, vedanāpi sassatā, viññāṇampi sassata”nti gaṇhāti. Ucchedepi ekaccasassatepi eseva nayo. Yathā ca khandhesu, evaṃ āyatanesupi yojetabbaṃ. Idaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “tañceva diṭṭhiṃ nappajahanti, aññañca diṭṭhiṃ upādiyantī”ti.

Here, having taken up the view of eternalism, without abandoning it, it is not possible to take up the view of annihilation or partial eternalism. Having taken up the view of annihilation, without abandoning it, it is not possible to take up the view of eternalism or partial eternalism. Having taken up the view of partial eternalism, without abandoning it, it is not possible to take up the view of eternalism or annihilation. However, without abandoning a root eternalist view, it is possible to take up another eternalist view. How so? At one time, having taken up the view “form is eternal,” at another time one takes up the view “not only mere form is eternal, feeling also is eternal... consciousness also is eternal.” In the case of annihilationism and partial eternalism too, this same method should be understood. And just as it should be applied to the aggregates, so too should it be applied to the sense bases. With reference to this, it was said: “They do not abandon that very view, and they adopt another view.”

Dutiyavāre atoti appajahanakesu nissakkaṃ, ye nappajahanti, tehi, ye pajahantīti vucciyanti, teva tanutarā appatarāti attho. Tañceva diṭṭhiṃ pajahanti, aññañca diṭṭhiṃ na upādiyantīti tañca mūladassanaṃ pajahanti, aññañca dassanaṃ na gaṇhanti. Kathaṃ? Ekasmiñhi samaye “rūpaṃ sassata”nti gahetvā aparasmiṃ samaye tattha ādīnavaṃ disvā “oḷārikametaṃ mayhaṃ dassana”nti pajahati “na kevalañca rūpaṃ sassatanti dassanameva oḷārikaṃ, vedanāpi sassatā…pe… viññāṇampi sassatanti dassanaṃ oḷārikamevā”ti vissajjeti[V 3.0148]. Ucchedepi ekaccasassatepi eseva nayo. Yathā ca khandhesu, evaṃ āyatanesupi yojetabbaṃ. Evaṃ tañca mūladassanaṃ pajahanti, aññañca dassanaṃ na gaṇhanti.

In the second instance, the word 'ato' is in the ablative case, referring to those who do not abandon. The meaning is that those who are said to abandon are fewer and lesser than those who do not abandon. 'They abandon that very view and do not take up another view' means they abandon that root view and do not grasp another view. How? At one time, having grasped the view "form is eternal," at another time, seeing the danger in it, one abandons it, thinking, "This view of mine is coarse." One rejects it, thinking, "Not only is the view 'form is eternal' coarse, but the view 'feeling is eternal... consciousness is eternal' is also coarse." This same method should be understood for the view of annihilationism and the view of partial eternalism. And as it should be applied to the aggregates, so too should it be applied to the sense bases. In this way, they abandon that root view and do not grasp another view.

Santaggivessanāti [P 3.0206] kasmā ārabhi? Ayaṃ ucchedaladdhiko attano laddhiṃ nigūhati, tassā pana laddhiyā vaṇṇe vuccamāne attano laddhiṃ pātukarissatīti tisso laddhiyo ekato dassetvā vibhajituṃ imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi.

Why did the Blessed One begin the discourse starting with 'Santi, Aggivessana...'? This annihilationist hides his own view. The Blessed One thought, "When the virtues of that view are spoken of, he will reveal his own view." Thus, in order to show the three views together and then analyze them, He began this discourse.

Sārāgāya santiketiādīsu rāgavasena vaṭṭe rajjanassa āsannā taṇhādiṭṭhisaṃyojanena vaṭṭasaṃyojanassa santike. Abhinandanāyāti taṇhādiṭṭhivaseneva gilitvā pariyādiyanassa gahaṇassa ca āsannāti attho. Asārāgāya santiketiādīsu vaṭṭe arajjanassa āsannātiādinā nayena attho veditabbo.

In the phrase 'near to passion' and so on, it means near to attachment in the cycle of rebirth through the power of passion; it is near to being fettered to the cycle by the fetters of craving and views. 'For delighting' means it is near to swallowing, completely seizing, and grasping through the power of craving and views. In the phrase 'not near to passion' and so on, the meaning should be understood by the method of 'near to non-attachment in the cycle of rebirth,' and so on.

Ettha ca sassatadassanaṃ appasāvajjaṃ dandhavirāgaṃ, ucchedadassanaṃ mahāsāvajjaṃ khippavirāgaṃ. Kathaṃ? Sassatavādī hi idhalokaṃ paralokañca atthīti jānāti, sukatadukkaṭānaṃ phalaṃ atthīti jānāti, kusalaṃ karoti, akusalaṃ karonto bhāyati, vaṭṭaṃ assādeti, abhinandati. Buddhānaṃ [M 3.0144] vā buddhasāvakānaṃ vā sammukhībhūto sīghaṃ laddhiṃ jahituṃ na sakkoti. Tasmā taṃ sassatadassanaṃ appasāvajjaṃ dandhavirāganti vuccati. Ucchedavādī pana idhalokaparalokaṃ atthīti jānāti, sukatadukkaṭānaṃ phalaṃ atthīti jānāti, kusalaṃ na karoti, akusalaṃ karonto na bhāyati, vaṭṭaṃ na assādeti, nābhinandati, buddhānaṃ vā buddhasāvakānaṃ vā sammukhībhāve sīghaṃ dassanaṃ pajahati. Pāramiyo pūretuṃ sakkonto buddho hutvā, asakkonto abhinīhāraṃ katvā sāvako hutvā parinibbāyati. Tasmā ucchedadassanaṃ mahāsāvajjaṃ khippavirāganti vuccati.

And here, the view of eternalism has little fault and is slow to fade, while the view of annihilationism has great fault and is quick to fade. How so? An eternalist knows that this world and the next exist, and knows that there is a result of good and bad deeds. He does what is wholesome and fears doing what is unwholesome; he delights in and rejoices in the cycle of rebirth. When he comes face to face with Buddhas or their disciples, he is not able to quickly abandon his view. Therefore, the view of eternalism is said to have little fault and be slow to fade. An annihilationist, on the other hand, knows that this world and the next exist, and knows that there is a result of good and bad deeds. He does not do what is wholesome and does not fear doing what is unwholesome; he does not delight in or rejoice in the cycle of rebirth. When in the presence of Buddhas or their disciples, he quickly abandons his view. One who is able to fulfill the perfections becomes a Buddha and attains parinibbāna; one who is unable, having made an aspiration, becomes a disciple and attains parinibbāna. Therefore, the view of annihilationism is said to have great fault and be quick to fade.

202. So pana paribbājako etamatthaṃ [P 3.0207] asallakkhetvā – “mayhaṃ dassanaṃ saṃvaṇṇeti pasaṃsati, addhā me sundaraṃ dassana”nti sallakkhetvā ukkaṃseti me bhavantiādimāha.

202. But that wanderer, not discerning this meaning, thought, "The Blessed One praises and commends my view; surely my view is excellent!" And so thinking, he said the words beginning with, "The venerable one extols me..."

Idāni yasmā ayaṃ paribbājako kañjiyeneva tittakālābu, ucchedadassaneneva pūrito, so [V 3.0149] yathā kañjiyaṃ appahāya na sakkā lābumhi telaphāṇitādīni pakkhipituṃ, pakkhittānipi na gaṇhāti, evamevaṃ taṃ laddhiṃ appahāya abhabbo maggaphalānaṃ lābhāya, tasmā laddhiṃ jahāpanatthaṃ tatraggivessanātiādi āraddhaṃ. Viggahoti kalaho. Evametāsaṃ diṭṭhīnaṃ pahānaṃ hotīti evaṃ viggahādiādīnavaṃ disvā tāsaṃ diṭṭhīnaṃ pahānaṃ hoti. So hi paribbājako “kiṃ me iminā viggahādinā”ti taṃ ucchedadassanaṃ pajahati.

Now, since this wanderer is like a bitter gourd filled with sour gruel, filled with the view of annihilation, and just as it is not possible to put oil, molasses, and so on, into a gourd without having removed the sour gruel—and even if they were put in, they would not be taken up—so too, without abandoning that view, he is incapable of attaining the path and its fruits. Therefore, in order to have him abandon that view, the passage beginning 'Tatra, Aggivessana...' was commenced. 'Dispute' means quarrel. 'Thus there is the abandoning of these views' means that by seeing the danger in dispute and so on, the abandoning of those views comes about. For that wanderer, thinking, 'What use to me is this dispute and so on?' abandons that view of annihilationism.

205. Athassa bhagavā vamitakañjiye lābumhi sappiphāṇitādīni pakkhipanto viya hadaye amatosadhaṃ pūressāmīti vipassanaṃ ācikkhanto ayaṃ kho pana, aggivessana, kāyotiādimāha. Tassattho vammikasutte vutto. Aniccatotiādīnipi heṭṭhā vitthāritāneva. Yo kāyasmiṃ kāyachandoti yā kāyasmiṃ taṇhā. Snehoti taṇhāsnehova. Kāyanvayatāti kāyānugamanabhāvo, kāyaṃ anugacchanakakilesoti attho.

205. Then the Blessed One, as if putting ghee, molasses, and so on, into a gourd from which the sour gruel had been poured out, thought, "I will fill his heart with the medicine of the deathless." Teaching insight, He said the words beginning with, "Now, Aggivessana, this body..." Its meaning is stated in the Vammika Sutta. The terms 'impermanent' and so on have also been elaborated upon below. 'Desire for the body' means the craving in the body. 'Affection' means the very stickiness of craving. 'Subservience to the body' is the state of following the body; the meaning is the defilement that follows the body.

Evaṃ rūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ dassetvā idāni arūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ dassento tisso khotiādimāha. Puna tāsaṃyeva vedanānaṃ asammissabhāvaṃ dassento yasmiṃ, aggivessana, samayetiādimāha. Tatrāyaṃ saṅkhepattho [M 3.0145][P 3.0208] – yasmiṃ samaye sukhādīsu ekaṃ vedanaṃ vedayati, tasmiṃ samaye aññā vedanā attano vāraṃ vā okāsaṃ vā olokayamānā nisinnā nāma natthi, atha kho anuppannāva honti bhinnaudakapupphuḷā viya ca antarahitā vā. Sukhāpi khotiādi tāsaṃ vedanānaṃ cuṇṇavicuṇṇabhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ.

Having thus shown the meditation subject of material form, now, showing the meditation subject of immaterial form, the Blessed One said the words beginning with, "There are three..." Again, to show the unmixed nature of those very feelings, He said the words beginning with, "At whatever time, Aggivessana..." Here is the summary meaning: at a time when one experiences one feeling among the pleasant and so on, at that time the other feelings are not what is called 'sitting and watching for their turn or opportunity.' Rather, they are simply unarisen, or they have vanished like burst water bubbles. The phrase beginning "Pleasant feeling also..." was spoken to show the crushed and pulverized nature of those feelings.

Na kenaci saṃvadatīti tassataṃ gahetvā “sassatavādī aha”nti ucchedavādināpi saddhiṃ na saṃvadati, tameva gahetvā “sassatavādī aha”nti ekaccasassatavādinā saddhiṃ na vivadati. Evaṃ tayopi vādā parivattetvā yojetabbā. Yañca loke vuttanti yaṃ loke kathitaṃ voharitaṃ, tena voharati aparāmasanto kiñci dhammaṃ parāmāsaggāhena aggaṇhanto. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

'He does not converse with anyone' means that, having grasped the view of eternalism, he does not converse even with an annihilationist, saying, "I am an eternalist." Grasping that very same view, he does not dispute with a partial-eternalist, saying, "I am an eternalist." In this way, all three positions should be interchanged and applied. 'And what is said in the world' means that he makes use of what is spoken and conventionally used in the world without misapprehending it, not grasping any phenomenon with the grasp of misapprehension. And this too has been said:

“Yo hoti bhikkhu arahaṃ katāvī,

Khīṇāsavo antimadehadhārī;

Ahaṃ [V 3.0150] vadāmītipi so vadeyya,

Mamaṃ vadantītipi so vadeyya;

Loke samaññaṃ kusalo viditvā,

Vohāramattena so vohareyyā”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.25);
