A monk who is an Arahant, one who has done what is to be done, one whose taints are destroyed, bearing his final body; he might say, 'I speak,' and he might say, 'They speak of me.' Being skilled in worldly convention, having understood it, he would speak only by way of conventional expression.

Aparampi vuttaṃ – “imā kho citta lokasamaññā lokaniruttiyo lokavohārā lokapaññattiyo, yāhi tathāgato voharati aparāmasa”nti (dī. ni. 1.440).

Furthermore, it is said: 'These, Citta, are worldly designations, worldly expressions, worldly usages, worldly concepts, with which the Tathāgata speaks without misapprehending them.'

206. Abhiññāpahānamāhāti sassatādīsu tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ sassataṃ abhiññāya jānitvā sassatassa pahānamāha, ucchedaṃ, ekaccasassataṃ abhiññāya ekaccasassatassa pahānaṃ vadati. Rūpaṃ abhiññāya rūpassa pahānaṃ vadatītiādinā nayenettha attho veditabbo.

206. As to 'He speaks of abandonment through direct knowledge': among views such as eternalism, regarding those various doctrines, having directly known the view of eternalism, He speaks for the abandonment of the view of eternalism. Having directly known the view of annihilation, He speaks of the abandonment of the view of annihilation. Having directly known the view of partial eternalism, He speaks of the abandonment of the view of partial eternalism. Having directly known form, He speaks of the abandonment of form. In this way and so forth, the meaning here should be understood.

Paṭisañcikkhatoti [P 3.0209] paccavekkhantassa. Anupādāya āsavehi cittaṃ vimuccīti anuppādanirodhena niruddhehi āsavehi aggahetvāva cittaṃ vimucci. Ettāvatā cesa parassa vaḍḍhitaṃ bhattaṃ bhuñjitvā khudaṃ vinodento viya parassa [M 3.0146] āraddhāya dhammadesanāya ñāṇaṃ pesetvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattañceva patto, sāvakapāramīñāṇassa ca matthakaṃ, soḷasa ca paññā paṭivijjhitvā ṭhito. Dīghanakho pana sotāpattiphalaṃ patvā saraṇesu patiṭṭhito.

'Reflecting' means for one who contemplates. 'The mind is liberated from the taints without clinging' means: the mind was liberated by not grasping the taints that had ceased through the cessation of non-re-arising. And by this much, just as one dispels hunger by eating food served for another, so this Elder Sāriputta, by sending forth his wisdom into the Dhamma discourse delivered for the sake of another and developing insight, attained Arahantship, reached the pinnacle of the knowledge of a disciple's perfections, and stood, having penetrated the sixteen kinds of wisdom. As for Dīghanakha, having attained the fruit of stream-entry, he became established in the refuges.

Bhagavā pana imaṃ desanaṃ sūriye dharamāneyeva niṭṭhāpetvā gijjhakūṭā oruyha veḷuvanaṃ gantvā sāvakasannipātamakāsi, caturaṅgasamannāgato sannipāto ahosi. Tatrimāni aṅgāni – māghanakkhattena yutto puṇṇamauposathadivaso, kenaci anāmantitāni hutvā attanoyeva dhammatāya sannipatitāni aḍḍhatelasāni bhikkhusatāni, tesu ekopi puthujjano vā sotāpanna-sakadāgāmi-anāgāmi-sukkhavipassaka-arahantesu vā aññataro natthi, sabbe chaḷabhiññāva, ekopi cettha satthakena kese chinditvā pabbajito nāma natthi, sabbe ehibhikkhunoyevāti.

The Blessed One, having concluded this discourse while the sun was still shining, descended from Vulture Peak, went to the Bamboo Grove, and held an assembly of the disciples. The assembly was one endowed with four factors. Herein, these are the factors: it was the full-moon Uposatha day in conjunction with the Māgha constellation; one thousand two hundred and fifty monks had gathered by their own natural disposition, uninvited by anyone; among them there was not a single ordinary person, nor a stream-enterer, once-returner, non-returner, or any Arahant who was a dry-insight practitioner—all were possessors of the six higher knowledges; and not even one among them was a monk who had gone forth by having his hair cut with a razor—all were 'Come, monk' bhikkhus.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Dīghanakhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Dīghanakha Sutta is concluded.

5. Māgaṇḍiyasuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Explanation of the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta.

207. Evaṃ [V 3.0151] me sutanti māgaṇḍiyasuttaṃ. Tattha agyāgāreti aggihomasālayaṃ. Tiṇasanthāraketi dve māgaṇḍiyā mātulo ca bhāgineyyo ca. Tesu mātulo pabbajitvā arahattaṃ patto, bhāgineyyopi [P 3.0210] saupanissayo nacirasseva pabbajitvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇissati. Athassa bhagavā upanissayaṃ disvā ramaṇīyaṃ devagabbhasadisaṃ gandhakuṭiṃ pahāya tattha chārikatiṇakacavarādīhi uklāpe agyāgāre tiṇasanthārakaṃ paññāpetvā parasaṅgahakaraṇatthaṃ katipāhaṃ vasittha. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Tenupasaṅkamīti na kevalaṃ taṃdivasameva, yasmā pana taṃ agyāgāraṃ gāmūpacāre dārakadārikāhi okiṇṇaṃ avivittaṃ, tasmā bhagavā niccakālampi divasabhāgaṃ tasmiṃ vanasaṇḍe vītināmetvā sāyaṃ vāsatthāya tattha upagacchati.

207. Thus have I heard—the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta. Therein, 'in the fire-offering hut' refers to a hall for fire sacrifices. Regarding 'on a grass mat': there were two Māgaṇḍiyas, an uncle and his nephew. Among them, the uncle went forth and attained Arahantship, and the nephew too, having the requisite supporting conditions, would soon go forth and attain Arahantship. Then the Blessed One, seeing his potential, left the delightful and godlike perfumed chamber and for the sake of helping another, stayed for a few days there in the fire-offering hut, which was messy with ashes, grass, and rubbish, having a grass mat spread out. In reference to this, it was said. 'He approached'—not only on that day alone, but because that fire-offering hut was near the village, crowded with boys and girls, and unsecluded, the Blessed One would regularly spend part of the day in that nearby wood and go there in the evening for his dwelling.

Addasā [M 3.0147] kho…pe… tiṇasanthārakaṃ paññattanti bhagavā aññesu divasesu tiṇasanthārakaṃ saṅgharitvā saññāṇaṃ katvā gacchati, taṃdivasaṃ pana paññapetvāva agamāsi. Kasmā? Tadā hi paccūsasamaye lokaṃ oloketvāva addasa – “ajja māgaṇḍiyo idhāgantvā imaṃ tiṇasanthārakaṃ disvā bhāradvājena saddhiṃ tiṇasanthārakaṃ ārabbha kathāsallāpaṃ karissati, athāhaṃ āgantvā dhammaṃ desessāmi, so dhammaṃ sutvā mama santike pabbajitvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇissati. Paresaṃ saṅgahakaraṇatthameva hi mayā pāramiyo pūritā”ti tiṇasanthārakaṃ paññapetvāva agamāsi.

Then the Blessed One saw… and so on… the grass mat was spread out. On other days, the Blessed One would gather the grass mat, make a sign, and leave. But on that day, having it prepared, he left. Why? Because at dawn, having surveyed the world, he saw: 'Today Māgaṇḍiya will come here, see this grass mat, and engage in conversation with Bhāradvāja about the grass mat. Then I will arrive and teach the Dhamma. Hearing the Dhamma, he will go forth in my presence and attain Arahantship. For it was solely for the purpose of benefiting others that I fulfilled the perfections.' Thus, having had the grass mat prepared, he left.

Samaṇaseyyānurūpaṃ maññeti imaṃ tiṇasanthārakaṃ “samaṇassa anucchavikā seyyā”ti maññāmi. Na ca asaññatasamaṇassa nivutthaṭṭhānametaṃ. Tathāhettha hatthena ākaḍḍhitaṭṭhānaṃ vā pādena ākaḍḍhitaṭṭhānaṃ vā sīsena pahaṭaṭṭhānaṃ vā na paññāyati, anākulo anākiṇṇo abhinno [P 3.0211] chekena cittakārena tūlikāya paricchinditvā paññatto viya. Saññatasamaṇassa vasitaṭṭhānaṃ, kassa bho vasitaṭṭhānanti pucchati. Bhūnahunoti hatavaḍḍhino mariyādakārakassa. Kasmā evamāha? Chasu dvāresu vaḍḍhipaññāpanaladdhikattā. Ayañhi tassa laddhi – cakkhu brūhetabbaṃ vaḍḍhetabbaṃ, adiṭṭhaṃ dakkhitabbaṃ, diṭṭhaṃ samatikkamitabbaṃ. Sotaṃ brūhetabbaṃ vaḍḍhetabbaṃ, asutaṃ [V 3.0152] sotabbaṃ, sutaṃ samatikkamitabbaṃ. Ghānaṃ brūhetabbaṃ vaḍḍhetabbaṃ, aghāyitaṃ ghāyitabbaṃ, ghāyitaṃ samatikkamitabbaṃ. Jivhā brūhetabbā vaḍḍhetabbā, assāyitaṃ sāyitabbaṃ, sāyitaṃ samatikkamitabbaṃ. Kāyo brūhetabbo vaḍḍhetabbo, aphuṭṭhaṃ phusitabbaṃ, phuṭṭhaṃ samatikkamitabbaṃ. Mano brūhetabbo vaḍḍhetabbo, aviññātaṃ vijānitabbaṃ, viññātaṃ samatikkamitabbaṃ. Evaṃ so chasu dvāresu vaḍḍhiṃ paññapeti. Bhagavā pana –

Regarding 'I think it is a bed suitable for an ascetic': this means, 'I consider this grass mat to be a fitting bed for an ascetic.' And it is not the dwelling place of an unrestrained ascetic. For here, no place is apparent that has been pulled by hand, dragged by foot, or struck by the head; it is undisturbed, uncluttered, and unbroken, as if demarcated and prepared by a skilled painter with a brush. He says, 'It is the dwelling place of a restrained ascetic. Sir, whose dwelling place is it?' thus he asks. 'Bhūnahuno' means of the one who destroys growth, the one who sets boundaries. Why did he say this? Because he holds the doctrine of proclaiming growth at the six sense doors. For this is his doctrine: The eye must be cultivated and developed—the unseen must be seen, and the seen must be transcended. The ear must be cultivated and developed—the unheard must be heard, and the heard must be transcended. The nose must be cultivated and developed—the unsmelled must be smelled, and the smelled must be transcended. The tongue must be cultivated and developed—the untasted must be tasted, and the tasted must be transcended. The body must be cultivated and developed—the untouched must be touched, and the touched must be transcended. The mind must be cultivated and developed—the unknown must be known, and the known must be transcended. Thus, he proclaims growth at the six sense doors. But the Blessed One—

“Cakkhunā saṃvaro sādhu, sādhu sotena saṃvaro;

Ghānena saṃvaro sādhu, sādhu jivhāya saṃvaro.

Good is restraint in the eye, good is restraint in the ear; good is restraint in the nose, good is restraint in the tongue.

Kāyena saṃvaro sādhu, sādhu vācāya saṃvaro;

Manasā saṃvaro sādhu, sādhu sabbattha saṃvaro;

Sabbattha saṃvuto bhikkhu, sabbadukkhā pamuccatī”ti. (dha. pa. 360-361) –

Good is restraint in body, good is restraint in speech; good is restraint in mind, good is restraint in all ways. A monk restrained in every way is freed from all suffering.

Chasu [M 3.0148] dvāresu saṃvaraṃ paññapeti. Tasmā so “vaḍḍhihato samaṇo gotamo mariyādakārako”ti maññamāno “bhūnahuno”ti āha.

He teaches restraint at the six sense doors. Therefore, thinking, 'The ascetic Gotama is a destroyer of increase, a maker of limits,' he called him 'Bhūnahuno.'

Ariye ñāye dhamme kusaleti parisuddhe kāraṇadhamme anavajje. Iminā kiṃ dasseti? Evarūpassa nāma uggatassa paññātassa yasassino upari vācaṃ bhāsamānena vīmaṃsitvā upadhāretvā mukhe ārakkhaṃ ṭhapetvā bhāsitabbo [P 3.0212] hoti. Tasmā mā sahasā abhāsi, mukhe ārakkhaṃ ṭhapehīti dasseti. Evañhi no sutte ocaratīti yasmā amhākaṃ sutte evaṃ āgacchati, na mayaṃ mukhāruḷhicchāmattaṃ vadāma, sutte ca nāma āgataṃ vadamānā kassa bhāyeyyāma, tasmā sammukhāpi naṃ vadeyyāmāti attho. Appossukkoti mama rakkhanatthāya anussukko avāvaṭo hutvāti attho. Vuttova naṃ vadeyyāti mayā vuttova hutvā apucchitova kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpetvā ambajambūādīni gahetvā viya apūrayamāno mayā kathitaniyāmena bhavaṃ bhāradvājo vadeyya, vadassūti attho.

Regarding 'skilled in the noble principle, in the Dhamma': this means in the pure, blameless, causal Dhamma. What does this indicate? That when speaking about such a renowned, famous, and respected person, one should speak only after investigating, reflecting, and placing a guard over one's mouth. Therefore, it shows: 'Do not speak rashly; place a guard over your mouth.' Regarding 'For thus it is found in our scripture': Because it is stated thus in our scripture, we do not speak merely what we feel like saying. And when speaking what is found in the scripture, whom should we fear? Therefore, we would say it even to his face—this is the meaning. 'Unconcerned' means: being without exertion and without worry for the sake of protecting me. This is the meaning. 'Let him speak just as told' means: 'Having been told by me, without being asked, without elaborating on the conversation, let the venerable Bhāradvāja speak according to the method I have stated. Speak!' This is the meaning.

208. Assosi [V 3.0153] khoti satthā ālokaṃ vaḍḍhetvā dibbacakkhunā māgaṇḍiyaṃ tattha āgataṃ addasa, dvinnaṃ janānaṃ bhāsamānānaṃ dibbasotena saddampi assosi. Paṭisallānā vuṭṭhitoti phalasamāpattiyā vuṭṭhito. Saṃviggoti pītisaṃvegena saṃviggo calito kampito. Tassa kira etadahosi – “neva māgaṇḍiyena samaṇassa gotamassa ārocitaṃ, na mayā. Amhe muñcitvā añño ettha tatiyopi natthi, suto bhavissati amhākaṃ saddo tikhiṇasotena purisenā”ti. Athassa abbhantare pīti uppajjitvā navanavutilomakūpasahassāni uddhaggāni akāsi. Tena vuttaṃ “saṃviggo lomahaṭṭhajāto”ti. Atha [P 3.0213] kho māgaṇḍiyo paribbājakoti paribbājakassa pabhinnamukhaṃ viya bījaṃ paripākagataṃ ñāṇaṃ, tasmā sannisīdituṃ asakkonto āhiṇḍamāno puna satthu santikaṃ āgantvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Taṃ dassetuṃ “atha kho māgaṇḍiyo”tiādi vuttaṃ.

208. Regarding 'He heard': The Teacher, having extended the light-kasiṇa, saw with the divine eye Māgaṇḍiya arriving there. With the divine ear, he also heard the sound of the two people speaking. 'Having emerged from seclusion' means having emerged from the attainment of fruition. 'Agitated' means agitated, stirred, and shaken by the agitation accompanied by rapture. It is said that this thought occurred to him: 'Neither has Māgaṇḍiya informed the ascetic Gotama, nor have I. Besides us, there is no third person here; our sound must have been heard by the man with a keen ear.' Then, within him, rapture arose, causing the ninety-nine thousand hair follicles to stand on end. Therefore it is said, 'agitated, with hair standing on end.' Regarding 'Then the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya': for the wanderer, his knowledge had reached maturity, like a seed that has split open. Therefore, being unable to sit still, he wandered about and then, returning to the Teacher's presence, sat down to one side. To show this, it was said, 'Then the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya,' and so on.

209. Satthā – “evaṃ kira tvaṃ, māgaṇḍiya, maṃ avacā”ti avatvāva cakkhuṃ kho, māgaṇḍiyāti paribbājakassa dhammadesanaṃ ārabhi. Tattha vasanaṭṭhānaṭṭhena [M 3.0149] rūpaṃ cakkhussa ārāmoti cakkhu rūpārāmaṃ. Rūpe ratanti rūparataṃ. Rūpena cakkhu āmoditaṃ pamoditanti rūpasamuditaṃ. Dantanti nibbisevanaṃ. Guttanti gopitaṃ. Rakkhitanti ṭhapitarakkhaṃ. Saṃvutanti pihitaṃ. Saṃvarāyāti pidhānatthāya.

209. The Teacher, without saying, 'So it seems, Māgaṇḍiya, you spoke of me in this way,' began to deliver a Dhamma discourse to the wanderer, saying: 'The eye, Māgaṇḍiya…' Therein, because form is the dwelling place for the eye, the eye has form as its pleasure-garden; therefore, it is called `rūpārāma`. Because it delights in form, it is called `rūparata`. Because the eye is gladdened and delighted by form, it is called `rūpasamudita`. 'Tamed' (`dantaṃ`) means without attachment. 'Guarded' (`guttaṃ`) means secured. 'Protected' (`rakkhitaṃ`) means having a guard set. 'Restrained' (`saṃvutaṃ`) means closed. 'For restraint' (`saṃvarāya`) means for the purpose of closing.

210. Paricāritapubboti abhiramitapubbo. Rūpapariḷāhanti rūpaṃ ārabbha uppajjanapariḷāhaṃ. Imassa pana te, māgaṇḍiya, kimassa vacanīyanti imassa rūpaṃ pariggaṇhitvā arahattappattassa khīṇāsavassa tayā kiṃ vacanaṃ vattabbaṃ assa, vuḍḍhihato mariyādakārakoti idaṃ vattabbaṃ, na vattabbanti pucchati. Na kiñci, bho gotamāti, bho gotama, kiñci vattabbaṃ natthi. Sesadvāresupi eseva nayo.

210. 'One who has formerly indulged' (`paricāritapubbo`) means one who has formerly delighted (`abhiramitapubbo`). 'The torment of form' (`rūpapariḷāhaṃ`) means the torment that is to arise on account of form. Regarding 'But for this one, Māgaṇḍiya, what is there for you to say?': For this one—an Arahant whose taints are destroyed, who has attained Arahantship by comprehending form—what could be said by you? Should the words 'a destroyer of growth, a maker of limits' be said, or should they not be said? Thus he asks. 'Nothing at all, Venerable Gotama' means: 'Venerable Gotama, there is nothing at all to be said.' This same method should be understood for the remaining sense-doors as well.

211. Idāni yasmā tayā pañcakkhandhe pariggahetvā arahattappattassa khīṇāsavassa kiñci vattabbaṃ natthi, ahañca pañcakkhandhe pariggahetvā [P 3.0214] sabbaññutaṃ patto, tasmā ahampi te na kiñci vattabboti dassetuṃ ahaṃ kho panātiādimāha. Tassa mayhaṃ māgaṇḍiyāti gihikāle attano sampattiṃ dassento āha. Tattha vassikotiādīsu yattha sukhaṃ hoti vassakāle [V 3.0154] vasituṃ, ayaṃ vassiko. Itaresupi eseva nayo. Ayaṃ panettha vacanattho – vassaṃ vāso vassaṃ, vassaṃ arahatīti vassiko. Itaresupi eseva nayo.

211. Now, since there is nothing to be said by you to an Arahant whose taints are destroyed, who has attained Arahantship by comprehending the five aggregates, and since I too have attained omniscience by comprehending the five aggregates, therefore, to show that there is nothing for you to say to me either, he said, 'But I…' and so on. Regarding 'For me, Māgaṇḍiya…': he said this to show his own prosperity during his time as a layman. Therein, regarding terms such as `vassika` (for the rainy season): that in which it is pleasant to dwell during the rainy season is `vassika`. This same method applies to the others as well. Herein, this is the word-analysis: `vassaṃ vāso` means a dwelling for the rainy season. Because it is suitable for the rainy season (`vassaṃ arahati`), it is called `vassiko`. This same method applies to the others as well.

Tattha vassiko pāsādo nātiucco hoti nātinīco, dvāravātapānānipissa nātitanūni nātibahūni, bhūmattharaṇapaccattharaṇakhajjabhojjānipettha missakāneva vaṭṭanti. Hemantike thambhāpi bhittiyopi nīcā honti, dvāravātapānāni tanukāni sukhumacchiddāni. Uṇhapavesanatthāya bhittiniyūhāni nīharīyanti. Bhūmattharaṇapaccattharaṇanivāsanapārupanāni panettha uṇhavīriyāni kambalādīni vaṭṭanti. Khajjabhojjaṃ siniddhaṃ kaṭukasannissitañca. Gimhike thambhāpi bhittiyopi uccā honti. Dvāravātapānāni panettha bahūni vipulajālāni bhavanti. Bhūmattharaṇādīni dukūlamayāni vaṭṭanti, khajjabhojjāni madhurarasasītavīriyāni. Vātapānasamīpesu cettha nava cāṭiyo ṭhapetvā udakassa pūretvā nīluppalādīhi sañchādenti. Tesu tesu padesesu udakayantāni [M 3.0150] karonti, yehi deve vassante viya udakadhārā nikkhamanti.

Therein, the rainy-season palace is neither too high nor too low. Its doors and windows are neither too few nor too many. The floor coverings, seat coverings, and food there are of a mixed nature. In the winter palace, the pillars and walls are low, and the doors and windows are narrow with fine apertures. Wall projections are extended to let in warmth. The floor coverings, seat coverings, undergarments, and cloaks there are of warm potency, such as woolen blankets. The food is rich and based on pungent tastes. In the summer palace, the pillars and walls are high. The doors and windows there are numerous, with wide lattices. Floor coverings and so on made of fine linen are suitable, and food of sweet taste and cool potency. Near the windows, they place new jars, fill them with water, and cover them with blue lotuses and the like. In various places, they set up water-machines from which streams of water flow as if a cloud were raining.

Bodhisattassa pana aṭṭhasatasuvaṇṇaghaṭe ca rajataghaṭe ca gandhodakassa pūretvā nīluppalagacchake katvā sayanaṃ parivāretvā ṭhapayiṃsu. Mahantesu lohakaṭāhesu [P 3.0215] gandhakalalaṃ pūretvā nīluppalapadumapuṇḍarīkāni ropetvā utuggahaṇatthāya tattha tattha ṭhapesuṃ. Sūriyarasmīhi pupphāni pupphanti. Nānāvidhā bhamaragaṇā pāsādaṃ pavisitvā pupphesu rasaṃ gaṇhantā vicaranti. Pāsādo atisugandho hoti. Yamakabhittiyā antare lohanāḷiṃ ṭhapetvā navabhūmikapāsādassa upari ākāsaṅgaṇe ratanamaṇḍapamatthake sukhumacchiddakaṃ jālaṃ baddhaṃ ahosi. Ekasmiṃ ṭhāne sukkhamahiṃsacammaṃ pasāreti. Bodhisattassa udakakīḷanavelāya mahiṃsacamme pāsāṇaguḷe khipanti, meghathanitasaddo viya hoti. Heṭṭhā yantaṃ parivattenti, udakaṃ abhiruhitvā jālamatthake patati, vassapatanasalilaṃ viya hoti. Tadā bodhisatto nīlapaṭaṃ nivāseti, nīlapaṭaṃ pārupati, nīlapasādhanaṃ pasādheti. Parivārāpissa cattālīsanāṭakasahassāni nīlavatthābharaṇāneva nīlavilepanāni hutvā mahāpurisaṃ parivāretvā ratanamaṇḍapaṃ gacchanti. Divasabhāgaṃ udakakīḷaṃ kīḷanto sītalaṃ utusukhaṃ anubhoti.

Furthermore, for the Bodhisatta, they filled one hundred and eight golden jars and one hundred and eight silver jars with fragrant water, arranged them as thickets of blue lotuses, and placed them surrounding his bed. In large bronze cauldrons, they filled fragrant paste, planted blue lotuses, red lotuses, and white lotuses, and placed them here and there to create a suitable atmosphere. The flowers bloomed in the sun’s rays. Various swarms of bees entered the palace and moved among the flowers, gathering nectar. The palace became exceedingly fragrant. Between the double walls, they placed a bronze pipe, and above the nine-storied palace, a fine-meshed net was fastened. In one place, they spread a dry buffalo hide. When the Bodhisatta was playing in the water, they would throw stone balls onto the buffalo hide, and it would sound like the roar of a thundercloud. Below, they turned a machine, and water, having ascended, would fall upon the top of the net, becoming like falling rainwater. At that time, the Bodhisatta would wear a blue lower garment, drape himself in a blue upper garment, and adorn himself with blue ornaments. His retinue of forty thousand female dancers, wearing blue clothes and ornaments, would surround the Great Being and proceed to the jeweled pavilion. Playing in the water for part of the day, he experienced the cool pleasure of the season.

Pāsādassa catūsu disāsu cattāro sarā honti. Divākāle nānāvaṇṇasakuṇagaṇā pācīnasarato [V 3.0155] vuṭṭhāya viravamānā pāsādamatthakena pacchimasaraṃ gacchanti. Pacchimasarato vuṭṭhāya pācīnasaraṃ, uttarasarato dakkhiṇasaraṃ, dakkhiṇasarato uttarasaraṃ gacchanti, antaravassasamayo viya hoti. Hemantikapāsādo pana pañcabhūmiko ahosi, vassikapāsādo sattabhūmiko.

In the four directions of the palace, there are four lakes. During the day, flocks of birds of various colors, rising from the eastern lake and singing joyfully, fly over the top of the palace to the western lake. Rising from the western lake, they fly to the eastern lake; from the northern lake to the southern lake; and from the southern lake to the northern lake. It is like the middle of the rainy season. The winter palace, however, was five-storied, and the rainy-season palace was seven-storied.

Nippurisehīti purisavirahitehi. Na kevalañcettha tūriyāneva nippurisāni, sabbaṭṭhānānipi nippurisāneva[P 3.0216]. Dovārikāpi itthiyova, nhāpanādiparikammakarāpi itthiyova. Rājā kira – “tathārūpaṃ issariyasukhasampattiṃ anubhavamānassa purisaṃ disvā parisaṅkā uppajjati, sā me puttassa [M 3.0151] mā ahosī”ti sabbakiccesu itthiyova ṭhapesi. Tāya ratiyā ramamānoti idaṃ catutthajjhānikaphalasamāpattiratiṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ.

‘Without men’ means devoid of men. Not only were the musical ensembles here without men, but all places were also without men. The doorkeepers were also women, and those who performed services such as bathing were also women. The king, it is said, thought: ‘For one enjoying such sovereign and blissful prosperity, seeing a man might give rise to apprehension; may that not happen to my son.’ Thus, in all matters, he appointed only women. The phrase ‘delighting in that delight’ was said in reference to the delight in the fruition attainment based on the fourth jhāna.

212. Gahapati vā gahapatiputto vāti ettha yasmā khattiyānaṃ setacchattasmiṃyeva patthanā hoti, mahā ca nesaṃ papañco, brāhmaṇā mantehi atittā mante gavesantā vicaranti, gahapatino pana muddāgaṇanamattaṃ uggahitakālato paṭṭhāya sampattiṃyeva anubhavanti, tasmā khattiyabrāhmaṇe aggahetvā “gahapati vā gahapatiputto vā”ti āha. Āvaṭṭeyyāti mānusakakāmahetu āvaṭṭo bhaveyyāti attho. Abhikkantatarāti visiṭṭhatarā. Paṇītatarāti atappakatarā. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

212. Regarding ‘a householder or a householder’s son’: here, because khattiyas aspire only to the white parasol and their path is long and complex, and brahmins, unsatisfied with their mantras, wander seeking more mantras, whereas householders, from the time they learn mere calculation, enjoy prosperity alone. Therefore, leaving aside khattiyas and brahmins, he said, ‘a householder or a householder’s son.’ ‘Would he turn back?’ means: would there be a turning back on account of human sensual pleasures? ‘More excellent’ means more distinguished. ‘More exquisite’ means more insatiable. And this was said:

“Kusaggenudakamādāya, samudde udakaṃ mine;

Evaṃ mānusakā kāmā, dibbakāmāna santike”ti. (jā. 2.21.389) –

‘Taking water with the tip of a kusa grass blade, one might measure the water in the ocean; even so are human sensual pleasures when compared to divine sensual pleasures.’

Samadhigayha tiṭṭhatīti dibbasukhaṃ gaṇhitvā tato visiṭṭhatarā hutvā tiṭṭhati.

‘Stands having surpassed’ means, having taken hold of divine happiness, he stands having become superior to that.

Opammasaṃsandanaṃ panettha evaṃ veditabbaṃ – gahapatissa pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samaṅgībhūtakālo viya bodhisattassa tīsu pāsādesu cattālīsasahassaitthimajjhe modanakālo, tassa sucaritaṃ pūretvā sagge nibbattakālo viya bodhisattassa abhinikkhamanaṃ katvā bodhipallaṅke sabbaññutaṃ paṭividdhakālo[P 3.0217], tassa nandanavane sampattiṃ anubhavanakālo viya tathāgatassa catutthajjhānikaphalasamāpattiratiyā vītivattanakālo, tassa mānusakānaṃ pañcannaṃ kāmaguṇānaṃ [V 3.0156] apatthanakālo viya tathāgatassa catutthajjhānikaphalasamāpattiratiyā vītināmentassa hīnajanasukhassa apatthanakāloti.

Here, the connection of the simile should be understood thus: The time when the householder was endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure is like the time when the Bodhisatta delighted among forty thousand women in the three palaces. The time when that householder, having fulfilled good conduct, was reborn in heaven is like the time when the Bodhisatta, having gone forth in the great renunciation, penetrated to omniscience on the seat of enlightenment. The time when that householder experienced prosperity in the Nandana Grove is like the time when the Tathāgata passed the time in the delight of the fruition attainment based on the fourth jhāna. The time when that householder no longer desired the five strands of human sensual pleasure is like the time when the Tathāgata, while passing the time in the delight of the fruition attainment based on the fourth jhāna, no longer desired the happiness of lowly people.

213. Sukhīti paṭhamaṃ dukkhito pacchā sukhito assa. Serīti paṭhamaṃ vejjadutiyako pacchā serī ekako bhaveyya. Sayaṃvasīti paṭhamaṃ vejjassa vase vattamāno vejjena nisīdāti vutte nisīdi, nipajjāti vutte nipajji, bhuñjāti vutte bhuñji, pivāti vutte pivi, pacchā sayaṃvasī jāto. Yena kāmaṃ [M 3.0152] gamoti paṭhamaṃ icchiticchitaṭṭhānaṃ gantuṃ nālattha, pacchā roge vūpasante vanadassana-giridassana-pabbatadassanādīsupi yenakāmaṃ gamo jāto, yattha yattheva gantuṃ icchati, tattha tattheva gaccheyya.

213. ‘Happy’ means: first he was afflicted with suffering, then he would become happy. ‘Independent’ means: first he had a physician as his companion, then he would become independent and alone. ‘Self-mastered’ means: first he lived under the physician’s control—when the physician said, ‘Sit,’ he sat; when he said, ‘Lie down,’ he lay down; when he said, ‘Eat,’ he ate; when he said, ‘Drink,’ he drank. Later, he became self-mastered. ‘One who goes where he wishes’ means: first he was unable to go to any place he desired, but after the illness subsided, he became one who could go where he wished, even to see forests, hills, and mountains. Wherever he wished to go, there he could go.

Etthāpi idaṃ opammasaṃsandanaṃ – purisassa kuṭṭhikālo viya hi bodhisattassa agāramajjhe vasanakālo, aṅgārakapallaṃ viya ekaṃ kāmavatthu, dve kapallāni viya dve vatthūni, sakkassa pana devarañño aḍḍhateyyakoṭiyāni aṅgārakapallāni viya aḍḍhatiyanāṭakakoṭiyo, nakhehi vaṇamukhāni tacchetvā aṅgārakapalle paritāpanaṃ viya vatthupaṭisevanaṃ, bhesajjaṃ āgamma arogakālo viya kāmesu ādīnavaṃ nekkhamme ca ānisaṃsaṃ disvā nikkhamma buddhabhūtakāle catutthajjhānikaphalasamāpattiratiyā vītivattanakālo, aññaṃ kuṭṭhipurisaṃ disvā apatthanakālo viya tāya ratiyā vītināmentassa hīnajanaratiyā apatthanakāloti.

Here too, this is the connection of the simile: the time the man had leprosy is like the time the Bodhisatta lived in the household; a charcoal pit is like one object of sensual pleasure; two pits are like two objects; for Sakka, king of the devas, two and a half crores of charcoal pits are like two and a half crores of celestial dancers; scraping the openings of the wounds with his nails and heating them over the charcoal pit is like indulging in sensual objects; the time of being free from disease after relying on medicine is like the time when, having seen the danger in sensual pleasures and the benefit in renunciation, he went forth and, upon becoming a Buddha, passed the time in the delight of the fruition attainment based on the fourth jhāna; the time of not desiring it upon seeing another man with leprosy is like the time when, while passing the time in that delight, he did not desire the delight of lowly people.

214. Upahatindriyoti [P 3.0218] kimirakuṭṭhena nāma upahatakāyappasādo. Upahatindriyāti upahatapaññindriyā. Te yathā so upahatakāyindriyo kuṭṭhī dukkhasamphassasmiṃyeva aggismiṃ sukhamiti viparītasaññaṃ paccalattha, evaṃ paññindriyassa upahatattā dukkhasamphassesveva kāmesu sukhamiti viparītasaññaṃ paccalatthuṃ.

214. ‘One with impaired faculties’ means one whose bodily sensitivity is impaired by what is called worm-leprosy. ‘Those with impaired faculties’ means those with an impaired wisdom faculty. Just as that leper with an impaired bodily faculty acquired a perverted perception of pleasure in a fire that is in fact a painful contact, so too, due to the impairment of their wisdom faculty, they have acquired a perverted perception of pleasure in sensual desires that are in fact painful contacts.

215. Asucitarāni cevātiādīsu pakatiyāva tāni asucīni ca duggandhāni ca pūtīni ca, idāni pana asucitarāni ceva duggandhatarāni ca pūtitarāni ca honti. Kācīti tassa hi paritāpentassa ca kaṇḍūvantassa ca pāṇakā anto pavisanti, duṭṭhalohitaduṭṭhapubbā paggharanti. Evamassa kāci assādamattā hoti.

215. Regarding ‘and more impure,’ etc.: by nature, those sores are impure, foul-smelling, and putrid; but now they become even more impure, more foul-smelling, and more putrid. Regarding ‘a certain...’: for him, while heating and scratching it, small creatures enter inside, and corrupted blood and corrupted pus ooze out. In this way, there is for him a certain mere taste of pleasure.

Ārogyaparamāti [V 3.0157] gāthāya ye keci dhanalābhā vā yasalābhā vā puttalābhā vā atthi, ārogyaṃ tesaṃ paramaṃ uttamaṃ, natthi tato uttaritaro lābhoti, ārogyaparamā lābhā. Yaṃkiñci jhānasukhaṃ vā maggasukhaṃ vā phalasukhaṃ vā atthi, nibbānaṃ tattha paramaṃ, natthi tato uttaritaraṃ sukhanti nibbānaṃ paramaṃ sukhaṃ. Aṭṭhaṅgiko maggānanti pubbabhāgamaggānaṃ pubbabhāgagamaneneva amatagāmīnaṃ aṭṭhaṅgiko khemo, natthi tato khemataro [M 3.0153] añño maggo. Atha vā khemaṃ amatagāminanti ettha khemantipi amatantipi nibbānasseva nāmaṃ. Yāvatā puthusamaṇabrāhmaṇā parappavādā khemagāmino ca amatagāmino cāti laddhivasena gahitā, sabbesaṃ tesaṃ khemaamatagāmīnaṃ maggānaṃ aṭṭhaṅgiko paramo uttamoti ayamettha attho.

Regarding the verse beginning with 'Ārogyaparamā': Of whatever gains of wealth, gains of fame, or gains of sons there are, health is supreme, the best among them. There is no gain higher than that; therefore, 'health is the supreme gain.' Of whatever bliss of absorption, bliss of the path, or bliss of fruition there is, Nibbāna is supreme among them. There is no bliss higher than that; therefore, 'Nibbāna is the supreme bliss.' Regarding 'Aṭṭhaṅgiko maggānaṃ': Among the preliminary-part paths that lead to the Deathless by way of the preliminary-part journey, the Eightfold Path is safe. There is no other path safer than that. Alternatively, in the phrase 'khemaṃ amatagāminiṃ', both 'khemaṃ' and 'amataṃ' are names for Nibbāna itself. Insofar as there are many ascetics and brahmins of other doctrines who are held, according to their own tenets, to be followers of paths leading to safety and the Deathless, the Eightfold Path is supreme and the best among all those paths leading to safety and the Deathless. This is the meaning here.

216. Ācariyapācariyānanti ācariyānañceva ācariyācariyānañca. Sametīti [P 3.0219] ekanāḷiyā mitaṃ viya ekatulāya tulitaṃ viya sadisaṃ hoti ninnānākaraṇaṃ. Anomajjatīti pāṇiṃ heṭṭhā otārento majjati – “idaṃ taṃ, bho gotama, ārogyaṃ, idaṃ taṃ nibbāna”nti kālena sīsaṃ kālena uraṃ parimajjanto evamāha.

216. Regarding 'ācariyapācariyānaṃ': of the teachers and of the teachers of the teachers. Regarding 'sameti': it is similar, like something measured with a single 'nāḷi' or weighed with a single scale; it is without difference. Regarding 'anomajjati': lowering his hand, he strokes, and at times stroking his head, at times stroking his chest, he speaks thus: 'This, venerable Gotama, is health; this is Nibbāna.'

217. Chekanti sampannaṃ. Sāhuḷicīrenāti kāḷakehi eḷakalomehi katathūlacīrena. Saṅkāracoḷakenātipi vadanti. Vācaṃ nicchāreyyāti kālena dasāya kālena ante kālena majjhe parimajjanto nicchāreyya, vadeyyāti attho. Pubbakehesāti pubbakehi esā. Vipassīpi hi bhagavā…pe… kassapopi bhagavā catuparisamajjhe nisinno imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsi, “atthanissitagāthā”ti mahājano uggaṇhi. Satthari parinibbute aparabhāge paribbājakānaṃ antaraṃ paviṭṭhā. Te potthakagataṃ katvā padadvayameva rakkhituṃ sakkhiṃsu. Tenāha – sā etarahi anupubbena puthujjanagāthāti.

217. Regarding 'chekaṃ': accomplished. Regarding 'sāhuḷicīrena': with a coarse garment made of black sheep's wool. Some also say 'saṅkāracoḷakena' (with a rag from a rubbish heap). Regarding 'vācaṃ nicchāreyya': stroking at times the fringe, at times the edge, at times the middle, one should utter it, one should speak; this is the meaning. Regarding 'pubbakehesā': the word division should be made as 'pubbakehi esā'. This verse was spoken by the previous Buddhas. Indeed, the Blessed One Vipassī... and the Blessed One Kassapa, seated amidst the fourfold assembly, spoke this verse. The great populace learned it, thinking, 'This is a verse connected with what is beneficial.' After the Teacher attained Parinibbāna, in a later period, it passed into the possession of the wanderers. They, having committed it to books, were able to preserve only two lines. Therefore, He said: 'Now, it has gradually become a verse of the common folk.'

218. Rogova bhūtoti rogabhūto. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Ariyaṃ cakkhunti parisuddhaṃ vipassanāñāṇañceva maggañāṇañca. Pahotīti samattho. Bhesajjaṃ kareyyāti uddhaṃvirecanaṃ adhovirecanaṃ añjanañcāti bhesajjaṃ kareyya.

218. Regarding 'rogova bhūto': disease itself has become manifest; therefore, it is called 'rogabhūto'. This same method should be understood for the remaining terms as well. Regarding 'ariyaṃ cakkhuṃ': the purified insight-knowledge and path-knowledge. Regarding 'pahoti': is capable. Regarding 'bhesajjaṃ kareyya': one should administer medical treatment, such as emetics, purgatives, and eye-salves.

219. Na cakkhūni uppādeyyāti yassa hi antarā pittasemhādipaliveṭhena [P 3.0220] cakkhupasādo [V 3.0158] upahato hoti, so chekaṃ vejjaṃ āgamma sappāyabhesajjaṃ sevanto cakkhūni uppādeti nāma. Jaccandhassa pana [M 3.0154] mātukucchiyaṃyeva vinaṭṭhāni, tasmā so na labhati. Tena vuttaṃ “na cakkhūni uppādeyyā”ti.

219. Regarding 'na cakkhūni uppādeyya': Indeed, for a person whose eye-sensitivity has been damaged in the interim by an envelopment of bile, phlegm, and so on, it is said that by resorting to a skilled physician and using suitable medicine, he produces the eyes. For one blind from birth, however, they were destroyed in the mother's womb itself; therefore, he does not obtain them. For that reason, it was said, 'na cakkhūni uppādeyya'.

220. Dutiyavāre jaccandhoti jātakālato paṭṭhāya pittādipaliveṭhena andho. Amusminti tasmiṃ pubbe vutte. Amittatopi daheyyāti amitto me ayanti evaṃ amittato ṭhapeyya. Dutiyapadepi eseva nayo. Iminā cittenāti vaṭṭe anugatacittena. Tassa me upādānapaccayāti ekasandhi dvisaṅkhepo paccayākāro kathito, vaṭṭaṃ vibhāvitaṃ.

220. In the second instance, regarding 'jaccandho': blind from the time of birth due to being enveloped by bile and so on. Regarding 'amusmiṃ': in that previously mentioned coarse garment made of black sheep's wool. Regarding 'amittato vidaheyyā': one should regard him as an enemy, thinking, 'This one is my enemy.' This same method should be understood for the second term as well. Regarding 'iminā cittena': with a mind that follows along in the round of existence. Regarding 'tassa me upādānapaccayā': the structure of conditionality with one connection and two sections was taught; the round of existence was made manifest.

221. Dhammānudhammanti dhammassa anudhammaṃ anucchavikaṃ paṭipadaṃ. Ime rogā gaṇḍā sallāti pañcakkhandhe dasseti. Upādānanirodhāti vivaṭṭaṃ dassento āha. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

221. Regarding 'dhammānudhammaṃ': the practice that is suitable for and in conformity with the Dhamma, the practice that is the way of escape from the round of existence. With the phrase 'ime rogā gaṇḍā sallā', He indicates the five aggregates of clinging. Regarding the phrase 'upādānanirodhā': wishing to show that which is free from the round of existence, He spoke. The rest is clear everywhere.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

The Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Māgaṇḍiyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta is finished.

6. Sandakasuttavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Sandaka Sutta

223. Evaṃ [V 3.0159] me sutanti sandakasuttaṃ. Tattha pilakkhaguhāyanti tassā guhāya dvāre pilakkharukkho ahosi, tasmā pilakkhaguhātveva saṅkhaṃ gatā. Paṭisallānā vuṭṭhitoti vivekato vuṭṭhito. Devakatasobbhoti vassodakeneva tinnaṭṭhāne jāto mahāudakarahado. Guhādassanāyāti ettha guhāti paṃsuguhā. Sā unname [P 3.0221] udakamuttaṭṭhāne ahosi, ekato umaṅgaṃ katvā khāṇuke ca paṃsuñca nīharitvā anto thambhe ussāpetvā matthake padaracchannagehasaṅkhepena katā, tattha te paribbājakā vasanti. Sā vassāne udakapuṇṇā tiṭṭhati, nidāghe tattha vasanti. Taṃ sandhāya “guhādassanāyā”ti āha. Vihāradassanatthañhi anamataggiyaṃ paccavekkhitvā samuddapabbatadassanatthaṃ vāpi gantuṃ vaṭṭatīti.

223. Thus have I heard—the Sandaka Sutta. There, 'at the Pilakkha cave'—at the entrance of that cave stood a Pilakkha tree; therefore, it was known as the Pilakkha cave. 'Having emerged from seclusion'—having arisen from a secluded place. 'Devakata's pool'—a large water reservoir formed in a place broken open by rainwater. 'To see the cave'—here, 'cave' refers to an earthen cave. It was located on high ground, in a place where the water had receded. Having made a tunnel from one side, having removed stumps and soil, and inside, having erected pillars, it was made on top in the manner of a plank-roofed house. There, those wanderers dwelled. It remains full of water during the rains, and in the hot season, they live there. Referring to this, the Elder Ānanda said, 'to see the cave.' Indeed, for the purpose of seeing a monastery, after reflecting on the beginningless saṃsāra, it is fitting to go even to see the ocean or a mountain.

Unnādiniyāti [M 3.0155] uccaṃ nadamānāya. Evaṃ nadamānāya cassā uddhaṅgamanavasena ucco, disāsu patthaṭavasena mahāsaddoti uccāsaddamahāsaddo, tāya uccāsaddamahāsaddāya. Tesaṃ paribbājakānaṃ pātova uṭṭhāya kattabbaṃ nāma cetiyavattaṃ vā bodhivattaṃ vā ācariyupajjhāyavattaṃ vā yonisomanasikāro vā natthi. Tena te pātova uṭṭhāya bālātape nisinnā, sāyaṃ vā kathāya phāsukatthāya sannipatitā “imassa hattho sobhaṇo imassa pādo”ti evaṃ aññamaññassa hatthapādādīni vā ārabbha itthipurisadārakadārikāvaṇṇe vā aññaṃ vā kāmassādabhavassādādivatthuṃ ārabbha kathaṃ paṭṭhapetvā anupubbena rājakathādianekavidhaṃ tiracchānakathaṃ kathenti. Sā hi aniyyānikattā saggamokkhamaggānaṃ tiracchānabhūtā kathāti tiracchānakathā. Tattha rājānaṃ ārabbha “mahāsammato mandhātā dhammāsoko evaṃmahānubhāvo”tiādinā nayena pavattā kathā rājakathā. Esa nayo corakathādīsu.

With a noisy crowd (unnādiniyā): that is, with one making a loud sound (uccaṃ nadamānāya). For such a noisy assembly, the sound is high (ucco) due to its upward movement and great (mahāsaddo) due to its spreading in all directions; thus it is called 'a high and great sound' (uccāsaddamahāsaddo). For those wanderers, there is nothing to be done upon rising early, such as the duty at a shrine, the duty at the Bodhi tree, the duty towards teachers and preceptors, or wise reflection. Therefore, having risen early, they sit in the morning sun, or in the evening, having gathered for the comfort of conversation, they initiate a discussion concerning one another's hands, feet, and so on, saying, 'This one's hand is beautiful, this one's foot is beautiful,' or concerning the qualities of women, men, boys, and girls, or concerning other topics such as the pleasure of sensual desires and the pleasure of existence. Gradually, they speak various kinds of unprofitable talk, such as talk of kings. Because it does not lead out of saṃsāra, that talk is contrary to the paths to heaven and liberation; therefore, it is called 'unprofitable talk' (tiracchānakathā). Therein, talk that proceeds in the manner of 'Mahāsammata, Mandhātā, and Dhammāsoka were so mighty,' etc., concerning a king, is talk of kings. This same method applies to talk of thieves, and so on.

Tesu “asuko rājā abhirūpo dassanīyo”tiādinā [P 3.0222] nayena gehassitakathāva tiracchānakathā hoti. “Sopi nāma evaṃ mahānubhāvo khayaṃ gato”ti evaṃ pavattā pana kammaṭṭhānabhāve tiṭṭhati. Coresupi “mūladevo evaṃmahānubhāvo, meghamālo evaṃmahānubhāvo”ti tesaṃ [V 3.0160] kammaṃ paṭicca aho sūrāti gehassitakathāva tiracchānakathā. Yuddhepi bhāratayuddhādīsu “asukena asuko evaṃ mārito evaṃ viddho”ti kāmassādavaseneva kathā tiracchānakathā. “Tepi nāma khayaṃ gatā”ti evaṃ pavattā pana sabbattha kathā kammaṭṭhānameva hoti. Apica annādīsu “evaṃ vaṇṇavantaṃ gandhavantaṃ rasavantaṃ phassasampannaṃ khādimha bhuñjimha pivimha paribhuñjimhā”ti kāmassādavasena kathetuṃ na vaṭṭati, sātthakaṃ pana katvā – “pubbe evaṃ vaṇṇādisampannaṃ annaṃ pānaṃ vatthaṃ sayanaṃ mālaṃ gandhaṃ sīlavantānaṃ adamha, cetiye pūjaṃ akarimhā”ti kathetuṃ vaṭṭati.

Among them, talk in the manner of 'Such-and-such a king is handsome and pleasant to look at,' and so on, is worldly talk, which is unprofitable talk. But talk that proceeds like, 'Even he, so mighty, has come to destruction,' stands as a meditation subject. Regarding thieves too, based on their deeds, saying 'Mūladeva was so mighty, Meghamāla was so mighty,' or 'Oh, how brave!' is worldly talk, which is unprofitable talk. In battles too, such as the Bhārata war, talk that proceeds by way of sensual delight, such as 'So-and-so was killed by so-and-so in this way, was pierced in this way,' is unprofitable talk. But talk that proceeds like, 'Even they have come to destruction,' is everywhere just a meditation subject. Furthermore, regarding food and so on, it is not proper to speak by way of sensual delight, saying, 'We have eaten, consumed, drunk, and enjoyed things with such color, scent, taste, and touch.' But, making it meaningful, it is proper to speak thus: 'In the past, we gave food, drink, clothing, bedding, garlands, and scents with such qualities to the virtuous, and we made offerings at shrines.'

Ñātikathādīsupi “amhākaṃ ñātakā sūrā samatthā”ti vā “pubbe mayaṃ evaṃ vicitrehi yānehi carimhā”ti vā assādavasena vattuṃ na vaṭṭati, sātthakaṃ pana katvā “tepi no ñātakā khayaṃ gatā”ti vā “pubbe mayaṃ evarūpā upāhanā saṅghassa adamhā”ti vā kathetabbā. Gāmakathāpi suniviṭṭhadunniviṭṭhasubhikkhadubbhikkhādivasena vā “asukagāmavāsino sūrā samatthā”ti vā evaṃ assādavasena na vaṭṭati, sātthakaṃ pana katvā saddhā pasannāti [M 3.0156] vā khayavayaṃ gatāti vā vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Nigamanagarajanapadakathāsupi eseva nayo. Itthikathāpi vaṇṇasaṇṭhānādīni paṭicca assādavasena na vaṭṭati, saddhā pasannā khayaṃ gatāti evameva vaṭṭati. Sūrakathāpi [P 3.0223] nandimitto nāma yodho sūro ahosīti assādavaseneva na vaṭṭati, saddho pasanno ahosi khayaṃ gatoti evameva vaṭṭati. Visikhākathāpi asukā visikhā suniviṭṭhā dunniviṭṭhā sūrā samatthāti assādavaseneva na vaṭṭati, saddhā pasannā khayaṃ gatā iccevaṃ vaṭṭati.

In discussions about relatives and so on, it is not proper to speak with delight, saying, “Our relatives are brave and capable,” or “In the past, we traveled in such splendid vehicles.” Instead, making it meaningful, one should speak thus: “Those relatives of ours have also passed away,” or “In the past, we offered such sandals to the Saṅgha.” Similarly, in village talk, it is not proper to speak with delight about whether a village is well-established or poorly established, prosperous or famine-stricken, or to say, “The residents of such-and-such village are brave and capable.” Instead, making it meaningful, it is proper to say, “They were faithful and devout,” or “They have come to ruin and destruction.” The same principle applies to discussions about towns, cities, and districts. In talk about women, it is not proper to speak with delight regarding their beauty, appearance, and so on. It is proper only to say, “She was faithful and devout,” or “She has passed away.” In talk about heroes, it is not proper to speak only with delight, saying, “There was a warrior named Nandimitta who was brave.” It is proper only to say, “He was faithful and devout,” or “He has passed away.” Likewise, in talk about streets, it is not proper to speak only with delight, saying, “Such-and-such street is well-established or poorly established, and its people are brave and capable.” It is proper to speak thus: “They were faithful and devout,” or “They have passed away.”

Kumbhaṭṭhānakathāti kumbhaṭṭhānaudakatitthakathā vā vuccati kumbhadāsikathā vā. Sāpi “pāsādikā naccituṃ gāyituṃ chekā”ti assādavasena na vaṭṭati, saddhā pasannātiādinā nayeneva vaṭṭati. Pubbapetakathāti atītañātikathā. Tattha vattamānañātikathāsadisova vinicchayo.

Talk about potters' places (kumbhaṭṭhānakathā) refers to talk about potters' places and water-fords, or talk about potters' female slaves. Regarding her too, it is not proper to speak with delight, saying, 'She is charming, skilled in dancing and singing'; it is proper to speak only in the manner of 'She was faithful and devout,' and so on. Talk about former departed ones (pubbapetakathā) is talk about deceased relatives. Therein, the judgment is just like that for talk about present relatives.

Nānattakathāti purimapacchimakathāvimuttā avasesā nānāsabhāvā niratthakakathā. Lokakkhāyikāti [V 3.0161] ayaṃ loko kena nimmito, asukena nāma nimmito, kākā setā aṭṭhīnaṃ setattā, bakā rattā lohitassa rattattāti evamādikā lokāyatavitaṇḍasallāpakathā.

Talk about diversity (nānattakathā) is the remaining meaningless talk of various natures, apart from the preceding and subsequent talks. Talk about worldly matters (lokakkhāyikā) is like this: 'By whom was this world created? It was created by so-and-so. Crows are white because of the whiteness of their bones. Herons are red because of the redness of their blood.' Such talk as this is the sophistical chatter of the materialists.

Samuddakkhāyikā nāma kasmā samuddo sāgaro, sāgaradevena khaṇitattā sāgaro, khato meti hatthamuddāya niveditattā samuddoti evamādikā niratthakā samuddakkhāyikakathā. Iti bhavo, iti abhavoti yaṃ vā taṃ vā niratthakakāraṇaṃ vatvā pavattitakathā itibhavābhavakathā. Ettha ca bhavoti sassataṃ, abhavoti ucchedaṃ. Bhavoti vaḍḍhi, abhavoti [P 3.0224] hāni. Bhavoti kāmasukhaṃ, abhavoti attakilamatho. Iti imāya chabbidhāya itibhavābhavakathāya saddhiṃ bāttiṃsatiracchānakathā nāma hoti. Evarūpiṃ tiracchānakathaṃ kathentiyā nisinno hoti.

Talk called 'discourse on the sea' (samuddakkhāyikā) is such meaningless talk as: 'Why is the ocean called sāgara? It is called sāgara because it was dug by Prince Sāgara. It is called samudda because it was announced with a hand gesture, saying, "It was dug by me (khato me)!"' Talk that proceeds by stating some meaningless reason, such as 'Thus there is being,' 'thus there is non-being,' is called 'talk of being and non-being' (itibhavābhavakathā). Herein, 'being' is eternalism; 'non-being' is annihilationism. 'Being' is increase; 'non-being' is decrease. 'Being' is indulgence in sensual pleasure; 'non-being' is self-mortification. Thus, together with this six-fold talk of being and non-being, there are thirty-two kinds of unprofitable talk. He is seated in an assembly that is speaking such unprofitable talk.

Tato sandako paribbājako te paribbājake oloketvā – “ime paribbājakā ativiya aññamaññaṃ agāravā appatissā, mayañca samaṇassa [M 3.0157] gotamassa pātubhāvato paṭṭhāya sūriyuggamane khajjopanakūpamā jātā, lābhasakkāropi no parihīno. Sace pana imaṃ ṭhānaṃ samaṇo gotamo gotamasāvako vā gihiupaṭṭhākopi vāssa āgaccheyya, ativiya lajjanīyaṃ bhavissati. Parisadoso kho pana parisajeṭṭhakasseva upari ārohatī”ti ito cito ca vilokento theraṃ addasa. Tena vuttaṃ addasā kho sandako paribbājako…pe… tuṇhī ahesunti.

Then the wanderer Sandaka, observing those wanderers, thought: “These wanderers are extremely disrespectful and lacking deference toward one another. And we, since the appearance of the ascetic Gotama, have become like fireflies at sunrise; our gains and honor have also declined. But if the ascetic Gotama, a disciple of Gotama, or even a lay supporter of his were to come to this place, it would be extremely shameful. Indeed, the fault of an assembly falls upon its elder.” Looking this way and that, he saw the Elder. Therefore it was said: “Sandaka the wanderer saw… they became silent.”

Tattha saṇṭhapesīti sikkhāpesi, vajjamassā paṭicchādesi. Yathā suṭṭhapitā hoti, tathā naṃ ṭhapesi. Yathā nāma parisamajjhaṃ pavisanto puriso vajjapaṭicchādanatthaṃ nivāsanaṃ saṇṭhapeti, pārupanaṃ saṇṭhapeti, rajokiṇṇaṭṭhānaṃ puñchati, evamassā vajjapaṭicchādanatthaṃ “appasaddā bhonto”ti sikkhāpento yathā suṭṭhapitā hoti, tathā naṃ ṭhapesīti attho. Appasaddakāmāti appasaddaṃ icchanti, ekakā nisīdanti, ekakā tiṭṭhanti, na gaṇasaṅgaṇikāya yāpenti. Appasaddavinītāti appasaddena niravena buddhena vinītā. Appasaddassa [P 3.0225] vaṇṇavādinoti yaṃ ṭhānaṃ appasaddaṃ nissaddaṃ. Tassa vaṇṇavādino. Upasaṅkamitabbaṃ maññeyyāti idhāgantabbaṃ maññeyya.

Herein, 'he set them in order' means he instructed them; he concealed the fault of the assembly. He established them in such a way that they were well-established. Just as a man entering an assembly, in order to conceal a flaw, sets his lower garment in order, sets his upper robe in order, and wipes a dusty spot, so too, in order to conceal the fault of this assembly, instructing them, “Be of little sound, sirs,” he established them in such a way that they were well-established; this is the meaning. 'Desiring little sound' means they desire little sound; they sit alone, they stand alone, they do not pass the time in group association. 'Disciplined in little sound' means they were disciplined by the Buddha, who is of little sound, without clamor. 'Praisers of little sound' means they are praisers of a place that has little sound, that is silent. 'They might think it should be approached' means they might think, “One should come here.”

Kasmā panesa therassa upasaṅkamanaṃ paccāsīsatīti. Attano vuddhiṃ patthayamāno. Paribbājakā [V 3.0162] kira buddhesu vā buddhasāvakesu vā attano santikaṃ āgatesu – “ajja amhākaṃ santikaṃ samaṇo gotamo āgato, sāriputto āgato, na kho panete yassa vā tassa vā santikaṃ gacchanti, passatha amhākaṃ uttamabhāva”nti attano upaṭṭhākānaṃ santike attānaṃ ukkhipanti ucce ṭhāne ṭhapenti. Bhagavatopi upaṭṭhāke gaṇhituṃ vāyamanti. Te kira bhagavato upaṭṭhāke disvā evaṃ vadanti – “tumhākaṃ satthā bhavaṃ gotamopi gotamassa sāvakāpi amhākaṃ santikaṃ āgacchanti, mayaṃ aññamaññaṃ samaggā. Tumhe pana amhe akkhīhi passituṃ na icchatha, sāmīcikammaṃ na karotha, kiṃ vo amhehi aparaddha”nti. Appekacce manussā – “buddhāpi etesaṃ santikaṃ gacchanti, kiṃ amhāka”nti tato paṭṭhāya te disvā nappamajjanti. Tuṇhī ahesunti sandakaṃ parivāretvā nissaddā nisīdiṃsu.

But why did he hope for the Elder's approach? Because he was aspiring for his own advancement. It is said that when the Buddha or the Buddha's disciples come to their presence, wanderers boast to their supporters: 'Today, the ascetic Gotama has come to us; Sāriputta has come. Indeed, these ones do not go to just anyone—behold our supreme state!' They elevate themselves in the eyes of their attendants, placing themselves in a high position. They even strive to win over the Blessed One’s supporters. Seeing the Blessed One's attendants, they say: 'Your teacher, the venerable Gotama, and Gotama’s disciples come to us. We are harmonious among ourselves, but you do not wish to even look at us with your eyes or perform respectful duties. What wrong have we done to you?' Some people think: 'Even the Buddhas go to them, what is there for us to say?' From then on, upon seeing them, they are not heedless. 'They became silent' means that surrounding Sandaka, they sat down without a sound.

224. Svāgataṃ bhoto ānandassāti suāgamanaṃ bhoto ānandassa. Bhavante hi no āgate ānando hoti, gate sokoti [M 3.0158] dīpeti. Cirassaṃ khoti piyasamudācāravacanametaṃ. Thero pana kālena kālaṃ paribbājakārāmaṃ cārikatthāya gacchatīti purimagamanaṃ gahetvā evamāha. Evañca pana vatvā na mānatthaddho hutvā nisīdi, attano pana āsanā vuṭṭhāya taṃ āsanaṃ papphoṭetvā theraṃ āsanena nimantento nisīdatu bhavaṃ ānando, idamāsanaṃ paññattanti āha.

224. “Welcome to the venerable Ānanda” means the coming of the venerable Ānanda is a good coming. It indicates: “Indeed, when the venerable one comes, there is joy for us; when he goes, there is sorrow.” “It has been a long time” is a term of affectionate address. The Elder, from time to time, goes to the wanderers' park for the sake of his tour; recalling a previous visit, he spoke thus. And having said this, he did not sit down, being stiff with pride, but rising from his own seat, he dusted off that seat and, inviting the Elder with a seat, said, “Let the venerable Ānanda sit down; this seat is prepared.”

Antarākathā [P 3.0226] vippakatāti nisinnānaṃ vo ārambhato paṭṭhāya yāva mamāgamanaṃ etasmiṃ antare kā nāma kathā vippakatā, mamāgamanapaccayā katamā kathā pariyantaṃ na gatāti pucchati.

“The talk was interrupted” means he asks: “For you who were seated, from the beginning until my arrival, in this interval, what talk was left unfinished? On account of my arrival, what talk did not reach its conclusion?”

Atha paribbājako “niratthakakathāva esā nissārā vaṭṭasannissitā, na tumhākaṃ purato vattabbataṃ arahatī”ti dīpento tiṭṭhatesā, bhotiādimāha. Nesā bhototi sace bhavaṃ sotukāmo bhavissati, pacchāpesā kathā na dullabhā bhavissati, amhākaṃ panimāya attho natthi. Bhoto pana āgamanaṃ labhitvā aññadeva sukāraṇaṃ kathaṃ sotukāmamhāti dīpeti. Tato dhammadesanaṃ yācanto sādhu vata bhavantaṃ ye vātiādimāha. Tattha ācariyaketi ācariyasamaye. Anassāsikānīti assāsavirahitāni. Sasakkanti ekaṃsatthe nipāto, viññū puriso ekaṃseneva [V 3.0163] na vaseyyāti attho. Vasanto ca nārādheyyāti na sampādeyya, na paripūreyyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Ñāyaṃ dhammaṃ kusalanti kāraṇabhūtaṃ anavajjaṭṭhena kusalaṃ dhammaṃ.

Then the wanderer, indicating, 'This talk is indeed meaningless, without essence, dependent on the round of rebirth; it is not fit to be spoken in your presence,' said, 'Let that be, sir,' and so on. 'That is not for you, sir' means: if the venerable one wishes to hear, this talk will not be difficult to hear later. But for us, there is no benefit in this. It indicates: 'Having had the venerable one's arrival, we desire to hear another well-reasoned talk.' Then, requesting a Dhamma discourse, he said, 'It would be good, venerable sir...' and so on. Therein, `ācariyake` means in the teacher's doctrine. `Anassāsikāni` means devoid of solace. `Sasakkaṃ` is a particle in the sense of certainty; the meaning is that a wise person should not commit to it with certainty. 'And abiding, he would not accomplish' means he would not achieve, would not fulfill; this is what is said. `Ñāyaṃ dhammaṃ kusalaṃ` means the Dhamma that is the cause and is wholesome in the sense of being blameless.

225. Idhāti imasmiṃ loke. Natthi dinnantiādīni sāleyyakasutte (ma. ni. 1.440) vuttāni. Cātumahābhūtikoti catumahābhūtamayo. Pathavī pathavīkāyanti ajjhattikā pathavīdhātu bāhirapathavīdhātuṃ. Anupetīti [P 3.0227] anuyāti. Anupagacchatīti tasseva vevacanaṃ, anugacchatītipi attho, ubhayenāpi upeti upagacchatīti dasseti. Āpādīsupi eseva nayo. Indriyānīti manacchaṭṭhāni indriyāni ākāsaṃ pakkhandanti. Āsandipañcamāti nipannamañcena pañcamā, mañco ceva, cattāro mañcapāde gahetvā ṭhitā cattāro purisā cāti attho. Yāvāḷāhanāti yāva susānā. Padānīti ayaṃ evaṃ sīlavā ahosi, evaṃ dussīlotiādinā nayena pavattāni [M 3.0159] guṇapadāni. Sarīrameva vā ettha padānīti adhippetaṃ. Kāpotakānīti kapotakavaṇṇāni, pārāvatapakkhavaṇṇānīti attho.

225. “Here” means in this world. “There is no giving,” and so on, have been stated by me in the Sāleyyaka Sutta. “Composed of the four great elements” means made of the four great elements. “Earth to the earth-body” means the internal earth element follows upon the external earth element. “Follows upon” means it goes after. “Goes along with” is a synonym for that very word; the meaning is also “it follows after.” By both, it shows this meaning: “it approaches,” “it goes to.” The same method applies to water and the other elements. “The faculties” means the faculties with the mind as the sixth leap forth into space. “With the couch as the fifth” means five with the couch for the deceased; the meaning is the couch itself and the four men standing holding the four legs of the couch. “As far as the charnel ground” means as far as the cemetery. “Traces” refers to accounts of qualities that have occurred, in the manner of, “he was virtuous in this way,” or “he was immoral in that way.” Or, here “traces” is intended to mean the body itself. “Pigeon-colored” means having the color of a pigeon; the meaning is having the color of a dove's wings.

Bhassantāti bhasmantā, ayameva vā pāḷi. Āhutiyoti yaṃ paheṇakasakkārādibhedaṃ dinnadānaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ chārikāvasānameva hoti, na tato paraṃ phaladāyakaṃ hutvā gacchatīti attho. Dattupaññattanti dattūhi bālamanussehi paññattaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – bālehi abuddhīhi paññattamidaṃ dānaṃ, na paṇḍitehi. Bālā denti, paṇḍitā gaṇhantīti dasseti. Atthikavādanti atthi dinnaṃ dinnaphalanti imaṃ atthikavādaṃyeva vadanti tesaṃ tucchaṃ vacanaṃ musāvilāpo. Bāle [P 3.0228] ca paṇḍite cāti bālā ca paṇḍitā ca.

"Ending in ashes" means having ash as the end; or this is the reading itself. Regarding "offerings": whatever gift is given, with its various forms such as hospitality gifts and tokens of respect, all of that gift-giving just ends in ashes. The meaning is that it does not proceed beyond that to become fruit-bearing. "Declared by fools" means declared by foolish people. This is what is said: this giving is declared by the foolish, by those without wisdom, not by the wise. It shows that the foolish give and the wise receive. Regarding "the affirmationist view": the speech of those who say, "There is what is given and there is the fruit of what is given," is empty, false, and mere lamentation. "Both the foolish and the wise" means the foolish and the wise.

Akatena me ettha katanti mayhaṃ akateneva samaṇakammena ettha etassa samaye kammaṃ kataṃ nāma hoti, avusiteneva brahmacariyena vusitaṃ nāma hoti. Etthāti etasmiṃ samaṇadhamme. Samasamāti ativiya samā, samena vā guṇena samā. Sāmaññaṃ pattāti samānabhāvaṃ pattā.

"By the undone, for me here it is done" means: by my ascetic duty that has not been done, in this doctrine, the duty is called "done"; and by the holy life that has not been lived, it is called "lived." "Here" means in this ascetic teaching. "Perfectly equal" means exceedingly equal, or equal in quality. "Attained to a state of sameness" means they have reached a state of sameness.

226. Karatotiādīni apaṇṇakasutte vuttāni. Tathā natthi hetūtiādīni.

226. "Of one who does..." and so on have been stated in the Apaṇṇaka Sutta. Likewise, "There is no cause..." and so on.

228. Catutthabrahmacariyavāse [V 3.0164] akaṭāti akatā. Akaṭavidhāti akatavidhānā, evaṃ karohīti kenaci kārāpitā na hontīti attho. Animmitāti iddhiyāpi na nimmitā. Animmātāti animmāpitā. Keci animmitabbāti padaṃ vadanti, taṃ neva pāḷiyaṃ, na aṭṭhakathāyaṃ sandissati. Vañjhāti vañjhapasuvañjhatālādayo viya aphalā, kassaci ajanakāti attho. Etena pathavīkāyādīnaṃ rūpādijanakabhāvaṃ paṭikkhipati. Pabbatakūṭā viya ṭhitāti kūṭaṭṭhā. Īsikaṭṭhāyiṭṭhitāti muñje īsikā viya ṭhitā. Tatrāyamadhippāyo – yamidaṃ jāyatīti vuccati, taṃ muñjato īsikā viya vijjamānameva nikkhamatīti. “Esikaṭṭhāyiṭṭhitā”tipi [P 3.0229] pāṭho, sunikhāto esikatthambho niccalo tiṭṭhati, evaṃ ṭhitāti attho. Ubhayenapi tesaṃ vināsābhāvaṃ dīpeti. Na iñjantīti esikatthambho viya ṭhitattā na calanti. Na vipariṇāmentīti pakatiṃ na jahanti. Na aññamaññaṃ byābādhentīti aññamaññaṃ na upahananti. Nālanti na samatthā.

228. In the fourth holy life-abode, "unmade" means not made. "Of unmade arrangement" means having an unmade arrangement; the meaning is that they are not caused to be made by anyone saying, "Do it thus." "Uncreated" means not created even by psychic power. "Not caused to be created" means not made to be created. Some say the word is "uncreatable," but this is not found in the Pāli nor in the commentary. "Barren" means fruitless, like a barren animal or a fruitless palm tree; the meaning is that they do not generate anything. By this, it rejects the state of being a generator of form, etc., for the earth-body and so on. "Standing like a mountain peak" means they are "peak-standing." "Standing firm like a reed" means standing like the shoot on a muñja grass. Herein, this is the intention: that which is said to be "born" emerges already existing, just like the shoot from the muñja grass. There is also the reading "standing firm like a door-post"; the meaning is that they stand like a well-dug-in, immovable door-post. By both, it shows their state of being without destruction. "They do not stir" means they do not move because they stand like a door-post. "They do not change" means they do not abandon their nature. "They do not obstruct one another" means they do not strike one another. "Not able" means they are not capable.

Pathavīkāyotiādīsu [M 3.0160] pathavīyeva pathavīkāyo, pathavīsamūho vā. Tatthāti tesu jīvasattamesu kāyesu. Natthi hantā vāti hantuṃ vā ghātetuṃ vā sotuṃ vā sāvetuṃ vā jānituṃ vā jānāpetuṃ vā samattho nāma natthīti dīpeti. Sattannaṃtveva kāyānanti yathā muggarāsiādīsu pahaṭaṃ satthaṃ muggarāsiādīnaṃ antarena pavisati, evaṃ sattannaṃ kāyānaṃ antarena chiddena vivarena satthaṃ pavisati. Tattha “ahaṃ imaṃ jīvitā voropemī”ti kevalaṃ saññāmattameva hotīti dasseti. Yonipamukhasatasahassānīti pamukhayonīnaṃ [P 3.0230] uttamayonīnaṃ cuddasasatasahassāni aññāni ca saṭṭhisatāni aññāni ca chasatāni. Pañca ca kammuno satānīti pañca kammasatāni ca, kevalaṃ takkamattakena niratthakaṃ diṭṭhiṃ dīpeti. Pañca ca kammāni tīṇi ca kammānītiādīsupi eseva nayo. Keci panāhu pañca kammānīti pañcindriyavasena bhaṇati. Tīṇīti kāyakammādivasenāti. Kamme ca aḍḍhakamme cāti ettha panassa kāyakammañca vacīkammañca kammanti laddhi, manokammaṃ upaḍḍhakammanti. Dvaṭṭhipaṭipadāti dvāsaṭṭhi paṭipadāti vadati. Dvaṭṭhantarakappāti ekasmiṃ kappe catusaṭṭhi antarakappā nāma honti, ayaṃ pana aññe dve ajānanto evamāha. Chaḷābhijātiyo apaṇṇakasutte vitthāritā.

Regarding "earth-body" and so on: "earth-body" is the earth element itself, or a collection of the earth element. "Therein" means among those bodies which have the soul as the seventh. "There is no killer..." indicates that there is no one so-called who is able to kill or cause to be killed, to hear or cause to be heard, or to know or cause to be known. "Among the seven bodies": just as a weapon struck into a heap of beans, etc., enters through the middle of the heap of beans, etc., so a weapon enters through the interval, the gap, the opening between the seven bodies. Therein, it shows that "I deprive this one of life" is merely a perception. "One million four hundred thousand principal wombs..." refers to one million four hundred thousand principal and superior wombs, and another sixty hundreds, and another six hundreds. "And five hundred actions" means five hundred actions; it shows a useless view based on mere speculation. In "and five actions and three actions," etc., the method is the same. But some say: "five actions" is said in terms of the five faculties; "three" is said in terms of bodily action, etc. Regarding "in an action and in a half-action": here his doctrine is that bodily action and verbal action are "action," and mental action is "half-action." "Sixty-two paths" means he speaks of sixty-two paths. "Sixty-two intermediate eons": in one eon there are sixty-four intermediate eons, but this one, not knowing the other two, says this. The six classes of birth have been explained in detail by me in the Apaṇṇaka Sutta.

Aṭṭha purisabhūmiyoti mandabhūmi khiḍḍābhūmi vīmaṃsakabhūmi ujugatabhūmi sekkhabhūmi samaṇabhūmi [V 3.0165] jinabhūmi pannabhūmīti imā aṭṭha purisabhūmiyoti vadati. Tattha jātadivasato paṭṭhāya sattadivase sambādhaṭṭhānato nikkhantattā sattā mandā honti momūhā. Ayaṃ mandabhūmīti vadati. Ye pana duggatito āgatā honti, te abhiṇhaṃ rodanti ceva viravanti [P 3.0231] ca. Sugatito āgatā taṃ anussaritvā anussaritvā hasanti. Ayaṃ khiḍḍābhūmi nāma. Mātāpitūnaṃ hatthaṃ vā pādaṃ vā mañcaṃ vā pīṭhaṃ vā gahetvā bhūmiyaṃ padanikkhipanaṃ vīmaṃsakabhūmi nāma. Padasāva gantuṃ samatthakālo ujugatabhūmi nāma. Sippānaṃ sikkhanakālo sekkhabhūmi nāma. Gharā nikkhamma pabbajanakālo samaṇabhūmi nāma. Ācariyaṃ sevitvā jānanakālo jinabhūmi nāma. Bhikkhu ca pannako jino na kiñci āhāti evaṃ alābhiṃ samaṇaṃ pannabhūmīti vadati.

"The eight stages of a person": He speaks of these as the eight stages of a person: the dull stage, the playing stage, the investigating stage, the upright-going stage, the learner's stage, the ascetic's stage, the conqueror's stage, and the fallen stage. Among them, from the day of birth for seven days, beings are dull and greatly bewildered because they have come out from a confined place. The heretics call this the dull stage. Furthermore, those who have come from a woeful state constantly weep and wail. Those who have come from a happy state, remembering it again and again, laugh. This is called the playing stage. Taking hold of the mother's or father's hand or foot, or a bed or a chair, and placing a foot on the ground is called the investigating stage. The time when one is able to go by foot alone is called the upright-going stage. The time of learning skills is called the learner's stage. The time of going forth from the home is called the ascetic's stage. The time of knowing after having attended upon a teacher is called the conqueror's stage. He calls the state of a heretical ascetic who receives no alms, as in the saying, “The bhikkhu is fallen, the conqueror takes nothing,” the fallen stage.

Ekūnapaññāsa [M 3.0161] ājīvasateti ekūnapaññāsa ājīvavuttisatāni. Paribbājakasateti paribbājakapabbajjasatāni. Nāgāvāsasateti nāgamaṇḍalasatāni. Vīse indriyasateti vīsa indriyasatāni. Tiṃse nirayasateti tiṃsa nirayasatāni. Rajodhātuyoti rajaokiraṇaṭṭhānāni. Hatthapiṭṭhipādapiṭṭhādīni sandhāya vadati. Satta saññīgabbhāti oṭṭhagoṇagadrabhaajapasumigamahiṃse sandhāya vadati. Asaññīgabbhāti sāliyavagodhumamuggakaṅguvarakakudrūsake sandhāya vadati. Nigaṇṭhigabbhāti nigaṇṭhimhi jātagabbhā, ucchuveḷunaḷādayo sandhāya vadati. Satta devāti bahū devā, so pana sattāti vadati. Mānusāpi [P 3.0232] anantā, so sattāti vadati. Satta pisācāti pisācā mahantā, sattāti vadati.

‘One hundred and forty-nine livelihoods’ means one hundred and forty-nine means of livelihood. ‘One hundred kinds of wandering asceticism’ means one hundred kinds of wandering asceticism. ‘One hundred Nāga-abodes’ means one hundred Nāgas and one hundred herds of elephants. ‘One hundred and twenty faculties’ means one hundred and twenty faculties. ‘One hundred and thirty hells’ means one hundred and thirty hells. ‘The dust elements’ means places where dust is scattered; he speaks with reference to the backs of the hands, the backs of the feet, and so on. ‘Seven conscious wombs’ refers to camels, cattle, donkeys, goats, sheep, deer, and buffalo. ‘Seven unconscious wombs’ refers to rice, barley, wheat, mung beans, millet, panic grass, and kudrūsaka. ‘Seven joint-wombs’ means seeds that grow in a joint; he speaks referring to sugarcane, bamboo, reeds, and so on. ‘Seven devas’: There are many devas, but that person says ‘seven.’ Humans too are countless, but that person says ‘seven.’ ‘Seven pisācas’: Pisācas are numerous, but that person says ‘seven.’

Sarāti mahāsarā. Kaṇṇamuṇḍa-rathakāra-anotatta-sīhapapātakuḷira-mucalinda-kuṇāladahe gahetvā vadati. Pavuṭāti gaṇṭhikā. Papātāti mahāpapātā. Papātasatānīti khuddakapapātasatāni. Supināti mahāsupinā. Supinasatānīti khuddakasupinasatāni. Mahākappinoti mahākappānaṃ. Ettha ekamhā sarā vassasate vassasate kusaggena ekaṃ udakabinduṃ nīharitvā nīharitvā sattakkhattuṃ tamhi sare nirudake kate eko mahākappoti vadati. Evarūpānaṃ mahākappānaṃ caturāsītisatasahassāni khepetvā bālā ca paṇḍitā ca dukkhassantaṃ karontīti ayamassa laddhi. Paṇḍitopi kira antarā sujjhituṃ na sakkoti, bālopi tato uddhaṃ na gacchati.

‘Lakes’ means great lakes. He speaks by taking the lakes Kaṇṇamuṇḍa, Rathakāra, Anotatta, Sīhapapāta, Kuḷira, Mucalinda, and Kuṇālada. ‘Pavuṭā’ means the knots or joints of a mountain. ‘Precipices’ means great precipices. ‘Hundreds of precipices’ means hundreds of small precipices. ‘Dreams’ means great dreams. ‘Hundreds of dreams’ means hundreds of small dreams. ‘Great eons’ refers to the great eons. Here, he says that one great eon is when, from one lake, every hundred years, a single drop of water is taken out with the tip of a kusa grass blade, and after that lake has been emptied seven times by doing this. His doctrine is that both fools and the wise make an end of suffering after having passed through 8,400,000 such great eons. Indeed, even the wise person is not able to be purified in the interim, nor does the fool go beyond that.

Sīlenāti [V 3.0166] acelakasīlena vā aññena vā yena kenaci. Vatenāti tādisena vatena. Tapenāti tapokammena. Aparipakkaṃ paripāceti nāma yo “ahaṃ paṇḍito”ti antarā visujjhati. Paripakkaṃ [P 3.0233] phussa phussa byantiṃ karoti nāma yo “ahaṃ bālo”ti vuttaparimāṇaṃ kālaṃ atikkamitvā yāti. Hevaṃ natthīti evaṃ natthi. Tañhi ubhayampi na sakkā kātunti dīpeti. Doṇamiteti doṇena mitaṃ viya. Sukhadukkheti sukhadukkhaṃ. Pariyantakateti vuttaparimāṇena kālena katapariyanto. Natthi hāyanavaḍḍhaneti natthi hāyanavaḍḍhanāni. Na saṃsāro paṇḍitassa hāyati, na bālassa vaḍḍhatīti attho. Ukkaṃsāvakaṃseti ukkaṃsāvakaṃsā, hāpanavaḍḍhanānamevetaṃ vevacanaṃ. Idāni tamatthaṃ upamāya sādhento [M 3.0162] seyyathāpi nāmātiādimāha. Tattha suttaguḷeti veṭhetvā katasuttaguḷaṃ. Nibbeṭhiyamānameva paletīti pabbate vā rukkhagge vā ṭhatvā khittaṃ suttapamāṇena nibbeṭhiyamānaṃ gacchati, sutte khīṇe tattha tiṭṭhati na gacchati. Evamevaṃ vuttakālato uddhaṃ na gacchatīti dasseti.

‘By virtue’ means by the virtue of the naked ascetics or by any other indiscriminate virtue. ‘By observance’ means by such an observance. ‘By austerity’ means by the act of austerity. He who, thinking ‘I am wise,’ is purified in the interim, is called one who ‘ripens the unripe.’ He who, thinking ‘I am a fool,’ goes on, having exceeded the stated period of time, is called one who ‘makes an end of the ripe, having experienced it again and again.’ ‘It is not so’ means it is not so. This shows that indeed both of these cannot be done. ‘Measured by a doṇa’ means as if measured by a doṇa-basket. ‘Pleasure and pain’ means pleasure and pain. ‘Having a limited end’ means having an end made by the stated period of time. ‘There is no decrease or increase’ means there are no decreases and increases. The meaning is: saṃsāra does not decrease for the wise, nor does it increase for the fool. ‘Excellence and inferiority’ means excellence and inferiority; this is just a synonym for decrease and increase. Now, to establish that meaning with a simile, he says, ‘Just as…’ and so on. Here, ‘a ball of thread’ means a ball of thread made by winding. ‘Unwinding, it just runs out’ means: when a ball of thread is thrown while standing on a mountain or a treetop, it goes, unwinding according to the amount of thread, and when the thread is exhausted, it stops there and does not go further. In just this way, it shows that one does not go beyond the stated period of time.

229. Kimidanti kimidaṃ tava aññāṇaṃ, kiṃ sabbaññu nāma tvanti evaṃ puṭṭho samāno niyativāde pakkhipanto suññaṃ me agārantiādimāha.

229. ‘What is this?’: When asked thus, ‘What is this ignorance of yours? Are you called omniscient?’, he, placing it within the doctrine of determinism, said the words beginning with, ‘Empty is my house...’

230. Anussaviko hotīti anussavanissito hoti. Anussavasaccoti savanaṃ saccato gahetvā ṭhito. Piṭakasampadāyāti vaggapaṇṇāsakāya piṭakaganthasampattiyā.

230. ‘He is one who relies on oral tradition’ means he is dependent on oral tradition. ‘Truth from oral tradition’ means one who stands firm, having taken what has been heard as true. ‘By the transmission of the Piṭaka’ means by the accomplishment of the Piṭaka texts, which consist of groups of fifty chapters.

232. Mandoti mandapañño. Momūhoti atimūḷho. Vācāvikkhepaṃ āpajjatīti vācāya vikkhepaṃ āpajjati. Kīdisaṃ? Amarāvikkhepaṃ, apariyantavikkhepanti attho. Atha [P 3.0234] vā amarā nāma macchajāti. Sā ummujjananimmujjanādivasena udake sandhāvamānā gahetuṃ na sakkāti evameva ayampi vādo ito cito ca sandhāvati, gāhaṃ na upagacchatīti amarāvikkhepoti vuccati. Taṃ amarāvikkhepaṃ.

232. ‘Dull’ means of dull wisdom. ‘Bewildered’ means extremely bewildered. ‘He engages in verbal equivocation’ means he arrives at distraction by way of speech. Of what kind? Amarā-equivocation, the meaning of which is limitless equivocation. Alternatively, there is a species of fish called Amarā. Just as that fish, by means of surfacing and diving in the water, darts about and cannot be caught, in the same way this doctrine also runs here and there and cannot be grasped. Thus it is called Amarā-equivocation. He engages in that Amarā-equivocation.

Evantipi me notiādīsu idaṃ kusalanti puṭṭho “evantipi me no”ti vadati, tato kiṃ akusalanti vutte “tathātipi me no”ti vadati, kiṃ ubhayato aññathāti vutte “aññathātipi me no”ti vadati, tato tividhenāpi na hotīti te laddhīti vutte “notipi me [V 3.0167] no”ti vadati, tato kiṃ no noti te laddhīti vutte “no notipi me no”ti vikkhepamāpajjati, ekasmimpi pakkhe na tiṭṭhati. Nibbijja pakkamatīti attanopi esa satthā avassayo bhavituṃ na sakkoti, mayhaṃ kiṃ sakkhissatīti nibbinditvā pakkamati. Purimesupi anassāsikesu eseva nayo.

In the phrases beginning with “My view is not ‘it is thus’,” when asked, “Is this wholesome?”, he says, “My view is not ‘it is thus’.” Then, when it is said, “Is it unwholesome?”, he says, “My view is not ‘it is like that’ either.” When it is said, “Is it otherwise than both?”, he says, “My view is not ‘it is otherwise’ either.” Then, when it is said, “Is your view that it is not in any of the three ways?”, he says, “My view is not ‘it is not’ either.” Then, when asked, “Is your view ‘it is not not’?”, he says, “My view is not ‘it is not not’ either,” and falls into equivocation, not taking a stand on any single position. As for “disillusioned, he departs”: this teacher is not able to be a refuge even for himself; thinking, “How will he be able to be a refuge for me?”, he becomes disillusioned and departs. In the previous cases of the uncomforting holy lives, this is the same method.

234. Sannidhikārakaṃ kāme paribhuñjitunti yathā pubbe gihibhūto sannidhiṃ katvā vatthukāme paribhuñjati, evaṃ tilataṇḍulasappinavanītādīni sannidhiṃ katvā idāni paribhuñjituṃ abhabboti attho. Nanu ca khīṇāsavassa vasanaṭṭhāne [M 3.0163] tilataṇḍulādayo paññāyantīti. No na paññāyanti, na panesa te attano atthāya ṭhapeti, aphāsukapabbajitādīnaṃ atthāya ṭhapeti. Anāgāmissa [P 3.0235] kathanti. Tassāpi pañca kāmaguṇā sabbasova pahīnā, dhammena pana laddhaṃ vicāretvā paribhuñjati.

234. As for “enjoys sensual pleasures by storing them up”: the meaning is this: just as formerly, having been a householder, one enjoys material sensual pleasures after having stored them, in the same way, he is now unfit to enjoy sesame, rice, ghee, fresh butter, and so on, after having stored them. “But are not sesame, rice, and so on, found in the dwelling place of one whose taints are destroyed?” It is not that they are not found; they are indeed found. However, this one whose taints are destroyed does not keep them for his own sake; he keeps them for the sake of ill monastics and others. “How is it for a non-returner?” For him too, the five strands of sensual pleasure are abandoned in every way. However, he enjoys what has been obtained righteously and properly, after having investigated it.

236. Puttamatāya puttāti so kira imaṃ dhammaṃ sutvā ājīvakā matā nāmāti saññī hutvā evamāha. Ayañhettha attho – ājīvakā matā nāma, tesaṃ mātā puttamatā hoti, iti ājīvakā puttamatāya puttā nāma honti. Samaṇe gotameti samaṇe gotame brahmacariyavāso atthi, aññattha natthīti dīpeti. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

236. As for 'sons of a mother whose sons are dead': it is said that he, having heard this Dhamma and perceiving 'the Ājīvakas are as good as dead,' spoke thus. This is the meaning here: the Ājīvakas are as good as dead; their mother is one whose sons are dead. Thus, the Ājīvakas are called sons of a mother whose sons are dead. As for 'in the ascetic Gotama': it shows that the holy life exists in the ascetic Gotama, and does not exist elsewhere. The remainder is clear everywhere.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

Of the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Middle-Length Discourses.

Sandakasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Sandaka Sutta is finished.

7. Mahāsakuludāyisuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Explanation of the Mahāsakuludāyi Sutta

237. Evaṃ [V 3.0168] me sutanti mahāsakuludāyisuttaṃ. Tattha moranivāpeti tasmiṃ ṭhāne morānaṃ abhayaṃ ghosetvā bhojanaṃ adaṃsu. Tasmā taṃ ṭhānaṃ moranivāpoti saṅkhaṃ gataṃ. Annabhāroti ekassa paribbājakassa nāmaṃ. Tathā varadharoti. Aññe cāti na kevalaṃ ime tayo, aññepi abhiññātā bahū paribbājakā. Appasaddassa vaṇṇavādīti idha appasaddavinītoti avatvāva idaṃ vuttaṃ. Kasmā? Na hi bhagavā aññena vinītoti.

237. “Thus have I heard” is the Mahāsakuludāyi Sutta. Therein, as for “Moranivāpa” (the Peacocks' Feeding Ground): at that place, having proclaimed safety for the peacocks, they gave them food. Therefore, that place came to be known as Moranivāpa. “Annabhāra” is the name of one wanderer. Likewise for “Varadhara.” As for “and others”: not only these three, but also many other well-known wanderers. As for “a proclaimer of the virtue of little sound”: here, this was said without saying “trained to little sound.” Why? Because the Blessed One was not trained by another.

238. Purimānīti hiyyodivasaṃ upādāya purimāni nāma honti, tato paraṃ purimatarāni. Kutūhalasālāyanti kutūhalasālā nāma paccekasālā natthi, yattha pana nānātitthiyā samaṇabrāhmaṇā nānāvidhaṃ kathaṃ pavattenti, sā bahūnaṃ – “ayaṃ kiṃ vadati[P 3.0236], ayaṃ kiṃ vadatī”ti kutūhaluppattiṭṭhānato “kutūhalasālā”ti vuccati. “Kotūhalasālā”tipi pāṭho.
