Lābhāti ye evarūpe samaṇabrāhmaṇe daṭṭhuṃ pañhaṃ pucchituṃ [M 3.0164] dhammakathaṃ vā nesaṃ sotuṃ labhanti, tesaṃ aṅgamagadhānaṃ ime lābhāti attho.

238. As for `purimāni` (previous): beginning from yesterday, they are called `purimāni`; after that, they are `purimatarāni` (even earlier). As for `Kutūhalasālā` (the Hall of Curiosity): there is no separate hall called Kutūhalasālā. But where various ascetics and brahmins of different sects cause diverse talk to arise, that hall is called the “Hall of Curiosity” because it is a place for the arising of curiosity for many, who think, “What does this one say? What does that one say?” There is also the reading `Kotūhalasālā`. As for `lābhā` (gains): the meaning is that for those people of Aṅga and Magadha who get to see such ascetics and brahmins, to ask them questions, or to hear their Dhamma talk, these teachers are a gain.

Saṅghinotiādīsu pabbajitasamūhasaṅkhāto saṅgho etesaṃ atthīti saṅghino. Sveva gaṇo etesaṃ atthīti gaṇino. Ācārasikkhāpanavasena tassa gaṇassa ācariyāti gaṇācariyā. Ñātāti paññātā pākaṭā. Yathābhuccaguṇehi ceva ayathābhūtaguṇehi ca samuggato yaso etesaṃ atthīti yasassino. Pūraṇādīnañhi “appiccho santuṭṭho, appicchatāya vatthampi na nivāsetī”tiādinā nayena yaso samuggato, tathāgatassa “itipi so bhagavā”tiādīhi yathābhūtaguṇehi. Titthakarāti laddhikarā. Sādhusammatāti ime sādhū sundarā sappurisāti evaṃ sammatā. Bahujanassāti assutavato ceva andhabālaputhujjanassa vibhāvino ca paṇḍitajanassa. Tattha titthiyā bālajanassa evaṃ sammatā, tathāgato paṇḍitajanassa. Iminā nayena pūraṇo kassapo saṅghītiādīsu attho veditabbo. Bhagavā pana yasmā aṭṭhatiṃsa ārammaṇāni vibhajanto bahūni nibbānaotaraṇatitthāni akāsi, tasmā “titthakaro”ti vattuṃ vaṭṭati.

In the phrases beginning with `saṅghino`: they are `saṅghino` because they have a `saṅgha`, which is known as an assembly of renunciants. They are `gaṇino` because they have a group (`gaṇa`). They are `gaṇācariyā` because they are teachers of that group by way of instructing in conduct. `Ñātā` means known, manifest. They are `yasassino` because they have fame that has arisen from both true qualities and untrue qualities. For Pūraṇa and others, fame arose by the method of “He has few wishes, is content; due to his fewness of wishes, he does not even wear a cloth,” and so on, whereas for the Tathāgata, fame arose only from true qualities, such as “He is the Blessed One...” `Titthakarā` means creators of a doctrine. `Sādhusammatā` means they are esteemed thus: “These are good, excellent, true persons.” As for `bahujanassa`: of the uninstructed, blind, foolish common person, and of the discerning, wise person. Therein, the sectarians are esteemed thus by the foolish person, while the Tathāgata is esteemed thus by the wise person. By this method, the meaning in phrases like “Pūraṇa Kassapa is a `saṅghī`” should be understood. However, because the Blessed One, by analyzing the thirty-eight meditation objects, created many fords for entering Nibbāna, it is fitting to call him `titthakaro`.

Kasmā [V 3.0169] panete sabbepi tattha osaṭāti? Upaṭṭhākarakkhaṇatthañceva lābhasakkāratthañca. Tesañhi evaṃ hoti – “amhākaṃ upaṭṭhākā samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ saraṇaṃ gaccheyyuṃ, te ca rakkhissāma. Samaṇassa ca gotamassa upaṭṭhāke sakkāraṃ karonte disvā amhākampi upaṭṭhākā amhākaṃ [P 3.0237] sakkāraṃ karissantī”ti. Tasmā yattha yattha bhagavā osarati, tattha tattha sabbe osaranti.

But why did all of them enter and stay there? For the sake of protecting their supporters and for the sake of gain and honor. For this thought occurs to them: “Our supporters might go for refuge to the ascetic Gotama, and we must protect them. And when our supporters see the supporters of the ascetic Gotama paying him respect, they too will pay respect to us.” Therefore, wherever the Blessed One enters and stays, they all enter and stay there.

239. Vādaṃ āropetvāti vāde dosaṃ āropetvā. Apakkantāti, apagatā, keci disaṃ pakkantā, keci gihibhāvaṃ pattā, keci imaṃ sāsanaṃ āgatā. Sahitaṃ meti mayhaṃ vacanaṃ sahitaṃ siliṭṭhaṃ, atthayuttaṃ kāraṇayuttanti attho. Asahitaṃ teti tuyhaṃ vacanaṃ asahitaṃ. Adhiciṇṇaṃ te viparāvattanti yaṃ tuyhaṃ dīgharattāciṇṇavasena suppaguṇaṃ, taṃ mayhaṃ ekavacaneneva viparāvattaṃ viparivattitvā ṭhitaṃ, na kiñci jātanti attho. Āropito te vādoti mayā tava vāde doso [M 3.0165] āropito. Cara vādappamokkhāyāti dosamocanatthaṃ cara vicara, tattha tattha gantvā sikkhāti attho. Nibbeṭhehi vā sace pahosīti atha sayaṃ pahosi, idāneva nibbeṭhehi. Dhammakkosenāti sabhāvakkosena.

239. “Vādaṃ āropetvā” means: having ascribed a fault to the doctrine. “Apakkantā” means: they departed—some went to another direction, some attained the household life, some came to this Dispensation. “Sahitaṃ me” means: my statement is beneficial, smooth, connected with the goal, and connected with reason; this is the meaning. “Asahitaṃ te” means: your statement is not beneficial. “Adhiciṇṇaṃ te viparāvattaṃ” means: that statement of yours, which was well-practiced through long-term habituation, has been overturned by just a single statement of mine; having been overturned, it has come to naught; this is the meaning. “Āropito te vādo” means: by me, a fault has been ascribed to your doctrine. “Cara vādappamokkhāya” means: for the sake of freedom from fault, go, wander; going here and there, learn; this is the meaning. “Nibbeṭhehi vā sace pahosi” means: if you yourself are able, unravel it right now. “Dhammakkosena” means: by a natural reproach.

240. Taṃ no sossāmāti taṃ amhākaṃ desitaṃ dhammaṃ suṇissāma. Khuddamadhunti khuddakamakkhikāhi kataṃ daṇḍakamadhuṃ. Anelakanti niddosaṃ apagatamacchikaṇḍakaṃ. Pīḷeyyāti dadeyya. Paccāsīsamānarūpoti pūretvā nu kho no bhojanaṃ dassatīti bhājanahattho paccāsīsamāno paccupaṭṭhito assa. Sampayojetvāti [P 3.0238] appamattakaṃ vivādaṃ katvā.

240. “Taṃ no sossāma” means: we shall listen to that Dhamma taught to us. “Khuddamadhu” means: honey on a stick made by small bees. “Anelakaṃ” means: faultless, free from bee eggs. “Pīḷeyya” means: he should squeeze it out and give it. “Paccāsīsamānarūpo” means: he would be standing by with a bowl in hand, hoping, “I wonder if he will fill our bowl and give it to us.” “Sampayojetvā” means: having engaged in a small dispute.

241. Itarītarenāti lāmakalāmakena. Pavivittoti idaṃ paribbājako kāyavivekamattaṃ sandhāya vadati, bhagavā pana tīhi vivekehi vivittova.

241. “Itarītarena” means: with a very inferior one. Regarding “Pavivitto,” the wanderer says this with reference only to bodily seclusion, but the Blessed One is secluded by the three kinds of seclusion.

242. Kosakāhārāpīti dānapatīnaṃ ghare aggabhikkhāṭhapanatthaṃ khuddakasarāvā honti, dānapatino aggabhattaṃ vā tattha ṭhapetvā bhuñjanti, pabbajite sampatte taṃ bhattaṃ tassa denti. Taṃ sarāvakaṃ kosakoti vuccati. Tasmā ye ca ekeneva bhattakosakena yāpenti, te kosakāhārāti. Beluvāhārāti beluvamattabhattāhārā. Samatittikanti oṭṭhavaṭṭiyā heṭṭhimalekhāsamaṃ[V 3.0170]. Iminā dhammenāti iminā appāhāratādhammena. Ettha pana sabbākāreneva bhagavā anappāhāroti na vattabbo. Padhānabhūmiyaṃ chabbassāni appāhārova ahosi, verañjāyaṃ tayo māse patthodaneneva yāpesi pālileyyakavanasaṇḍe tayo māse bhisamuḷāleheva yāpesi. Idha [P 3.0239] pana etamatthaṃ dasseti – “ahaṃ ekasmiṃ kāle appāhāro ahosiṃ, mayhaṃ pana sāvakā dhutaṅgasamādānato paṭṭhāya yāvajīvaṃ dhutaṅgaṃ na bhindantī”ti. Tasmā yadi te iminā dhammena sakkareyyuṃ, mayā hi te visesatarā. Añño ceva pana dhammo atthi, yena maṃ te sakkarontīti dasseti. Iminā nayena sabbavāresu yojanā veditabbā.

242. Kosakāhārā means: in the houses of donors, there are small bowls for placing the first portion of the meal. The donors place the first portion of the meal in it and then eat. When a renunciate arrives, they give him that food. That small bowl is called a 'kosaka.' Therefore, those who subsist on just one meal from a kosaka are called 'kosakāhārā' (kosaka-eaters). Beluvāhārā means: those who have food amounting to the size of a beluva fruit. Samatittikaṃ means: level with the lower line of the bowl's rim. Iminā dhammena means: by this principle of being one who has little food. However, in this context, it should not be said that the Blessed One is one of little food in all circumstances. During the period of his striving, he was indeed one of little food for six years. In Verañjā, he subsisted for three months on just horse-fodder. In the Pārileyyaka forest grove, he subsisted for three months on just lotus roots and stalks. But here he shows this meaning: 'I was one of little food at a certain time, but my disciples, from the time they undertake the ascetic practices, do not break them for as long as they live.' Therefore, if they were to honor me for this principle, they are indeed more distinguished than I. He shows that there is, however, another principle by which they honor me. In this way, the application should be understood in all sections.

Paṃsukūlikāti [M 3.0166] samādinnapaṃsukūlikaṅgā. Lūkhacīvaradharāti satthasuttalūkhāni cīvarāni dhārayamānā. Nantakānīti antavirahitāni vatthakhaṇḍāni, yadi hi nesaṃ anto bhaveyya, pilotikāti saṅkhaṃ gaccheyyuṃ. Uccinitvāti phāletvā dubbalaṭṭhānaṃ pahāya thiraṭṭhānameva gahetvā. Alābulomasānīti alābulomasadisasuttāni sukhumānīti dīpeti. Ettāvatā ca satthā cīvarasantosena asantuṭṭhoti na vattabbo. Atimuttakasusānato hissa puṇṇadāsiyā pārupitvā pātitasāṇapaṃsukūlaṃ gahaṇadivase udakapariyantaṃ katvā mahāpathavī akampi. Idha pana etamatthaṃ dasseti – “ahaṃ ekasmiṃyeva kāle paṃsukūlaṃ gaṇhiṃ, mayhaṃ pana sāvakā dhutaṅgasamādānato paṭṭhāya yāvajīvaṃ dhutaṅgaṃ na bhindantī”ti.

Paṃsukūlikā means: those who have undertaken the ascetic practice of the rag-robe wearer. Lūkhacīvaradharā means: those who wear coarse robes. Nantakāni means: pieces of cloth devoid of a border; for indeed, if they had a border, they would be designated as 'old rags'. Uccinitvā means: having split it, discarded the weak part, and taken only the firm part. Alābulomasāni clarifies: fine robes with threads like the hairs of a gourd leaf. And by this much, it should not be said that the Teacher is discontent with regard to contentment with robes. Indeed, on the day he took the hemp rag-robe that had been used to wrap the slave-woman Puṇṇā and was then discarded at the Atimuttaka charnel ground, the great earth shook up to its water-boundary. But here he shows this meaning: 'I took a rag-robe on only one occasion, but my disciples, from the time they undertake the ascetic practices, do not break them for as long as they live.'

Piṇḍapātikāti [P 3.0240] atirekalābhaṃ paṭikkhipitvā samādinnapiṇḍapātikaṅgā. Sapadānacārinoti loluppacāraṃ paṭikkhipitvā samādinnasapadānacārā. Uñchāsake vate ratāti uñchācariyasaṅkhāte bhikkhūnaṃ pakativate ratā, uccanīcagharadvāraṭṭhāyino hutvā kabaramissakaṃ bhattaṃ saṃharitvā paribhuñjantīti attho. Antaragharanti brahmāyusutte ummārato paṭṭhāya antaragharaṃ, idha indakhīlato paṭṭhāya adhippetaṃ. Ettāvatā ca satthā piṇḍapātasantosena asantuṭṭhoti na vattabbo, appāhāratāya vuttaniyāmeneva pana sabbaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ. Idha pana etamatthaṃ dasseti – “ahaṃ ekasmiṃyeva kāle nimantanaṃ na sādayiṃ, mayhaṃ pana sāvakā dhutaṅgasamādānato paṭṭhāya yāvajīvaṃ dhutaṅgaṃ na bhindantī”ti.

Piṇḍapātikā means: those who have undertaken the ascetic practice of eating only almsfood, having rejected extra gain. Sapadānacārino means: those who have undertaken the ascetic practice of going for alms systematically, having rejected greedy wandering. Uñchāsake vate ratā means: they delight in the normal practice of monks known as 'gleaning'; that is, standing at the doors of high and low houses, they collect mixed morsels of food and consume them. Antaragharaṃ: in the Brahmāyu Sutta, 'within the village' is from the threshold onwards; here, it is intended as from the city-post onwards. And by this much, it should not be said that the Teacher is discontent with regard to contentment with almsfood; rather, everything should be elaborated according to the principle already stated for being one of little food. But here he shows this meaning: 'I did not consent to an invitation on only one occasion, but my disciples, from the time they undertake the ascetic practices, do not break them for as long as they live.'

Rukkhamūlikāti channaṃ paṭikkhipitvā samādinnarukkhamūlikaṅgā. Abbhokāsikāti channañca rukkhamūlañca [V 3.0171] paṭikkhipitvā samādinnaabbhokāsikaṅgā. Aṭṭhamāseti hemantagimhike māse. Antovasse pana cīvarānuggahatthaṃ channaṃ pavisanti. Ettāvatā ca satthā senāsanasantosena asantuṭṭhoti na vattabbo, senāsanasantoso [P 3.0241] panassa chabbassikamahāpadhānena ca pālileyyakavanasaṇḍena ca dīpetabbo. Idha pana etamatthaṃ dasseti – “ahaṃ ekasmiṃyeva kāle channaṃ na pāvisiṃ, mayhaṃ pana sāvakā dhutaṅgasamādānato paṭṭhāya yāvajīvaṃ dhutaṅgaṃ na bhindantī”ti.

Rukkhamūlikā means: those who have undertaken the ascetic practice of the tree-root dweller, having rejected a roof. Abbhokāsikā means: those who have undertaken the ascetic practice of the open-air dweller, having rejected both a roof and the root of a tree. This is for eight months, that is, during the winter and summer seasons. But during the rains, for the sake of maintaining their robes, they enter a roofed dwelling. And by this much, it should not be said that the Teacher is discontent with regard to contentment with lodging. His contentment with lodging should be illustrated by the six years of great striving and by his time in the Pārileyyaka forest grove. But here he shows this meaning: 'I did not enter a roofed dwelling on only one occasion, but my disciples, from the time they undertake the ascetic practices, do not break them for as long as they live.'

Āraññikāti [M 3.0167] gāmantasenāsanaṃ paṭikkhipitvā samādinnaāraññikaṅgā. Saṅghamajjhe osarantīti abaddhasīmāya kathitaṃ, baddhasīmāyaṃ pana vasantā attano vasanaṭṭhāneyeva uposathaṃ karonti. Ettāvatā ca satthā no pavivittoti na vattabbo, “icchāmahaṃ, bhikkhave, aḍḍhamāsaṃ paṭisalliyitu”nti (pārā. 162; 565) evañhissa paviveko paññāyati. Idha pana etamatthaṃ dasseti “ahaṃ ekasmiṃyeva tathārūpe kāle paṭisalliyiṃ, mayhaṃ pana sāvakā dhutaṅgasamādānato paṭṭhāya yāvajīvaṃ dhutaṅgaṃ na bhindantī”ti. Mamaṃ sāvakāti maṃ sāvakā.

‘Forest-dweller’ means one who has undertaken the ascetic practice of a forest-dweller, having rejected a dwelling near a village. ‘They enter the midst of the Saṅgha’: this is said regarding an unbounded boundary; but those dwelling in a bounded boundary perform the Uposatha in their own dwelling place. And by this much, it should not be said that the Teacher was not secluded; for his seclusion is apparent from his saying, “Bhikkhus, I wish to go into seclusion for half a month.” Here, however, this meaning is shown: “I went into seclusion on only one such occasion, but my disciples, from the time they undertook the ascetic practices, do not break them for as long as they live.” The phrase `Mamaṃ sāvakā` means 'my disciples'.

244. Sanidānanti sappaccayaṃ. Kiṃ pana appaccayaṃ nibbānaṃ na desetīti. No na deseti, sahetukaṃ pana taṃ desanaṃ katvā deseti, no ahetukanti. Sappāṭihāriyanti purimassevetaṃ vevacanaṃ, sakāraṇanti attho. Taṃ vatāti ettha vatāti nipātamattaṃ.

244. ‘With a basis’ means ‘with a condition’. What then, does he not teach the unconditioned Nibbāna? It is not that he does not teach it; he certainly does teach it. However, he teaches it by presenting that teaching with a cause, not without a cause. ‘With a convincing demonstration’: this is a synonym for the former term; the meaning is ‘with a reason’. In the phrase ‘That indeed,’ the word ‘indeed’ is merely a particle.

245. Anāgataṃ vādapathanti ajja ṭhapetvā sve vā punadivase vā aḍḍhamāse vā māse vā saṃvacchare vā tassa tassa pañhassa upari āgamanavādapathaṃ. Na [P 3.0242] dakkhatīti yathā saccako nigaṇṭho attano niggahaṇatthaṃ āgatakāraṇaṃ visesetvā vadanto na addasa, evaṃ na dakkhatīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Sahadhammenāti sakāraṇena. Antarantarā kathaṃ opāteyyunti mama kathāvāraṃ pacchinditvā antarantare attano kathaṃ paveseyyunti attho. Na kho panāhaṃ, udāyīti, udāyi, ahaṃ ambaṭṭhasoṇadaṇḍakūṭadantasaccakanigaṇṭhādīhi saddhiṃ mahāvāde vattamānepi – “aho vata me ekasāvakopi upamaṃ vā kāraṇaṃ vā āharitvā dadeyyā”ti evaṃ sāvakesu anusāsaniṃ na paccāsīsāmi. Mamayevāti evarūpesu ṭhānesu sāvakā mamayeva anusāsaniṃ ovādaṃ paccāsīsanti.

245. ‘Future paths of speech’ refers to the path of speech concerning the coming of this or that question tomorrow, or the next day, or in half a month, or in a month, or in a year, setting aside today. ‘He does not see’: just as Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha, speaking after specifying the reason for his coming for the sake of his own refutation, did not see, so the ascetic Gotama does not see—such a situation does not exist. ‘With the Dhamma’ means ‘with a reason’. ‘How would they interject their talk intermittently?’ The meaning is: how would they, cutting off my turn to speak, insert their own talk in the intervals? ‘But I, Udāyī’: Udāyī, even when engaged in great debates with Ambaṭṭha, Soṇadaṇḍa, Kūṭadanta, Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha, and others, I do not expect any instruction from disciples, thinking, “Oh, if only even one disciple would bring and offer me a simile or a reason.” ‘From me alone’: in such situations, disciples expect instruction and advice from me alone.

246. Tesāhaṃ [V 3.0172] cittaṃ ārādhemīti tesaṃ ahaṃ tassa pañhassa veyyākaraṇena cittaṃ gaṇhāmi sampādemi paripūremi, aññaṃ puṭṭho aññaṃ na byākaromi, ambaṃ puṭṭho labujaṃ viya labujaṃ vā puṭṭho ambaṃ viya. Ettha ca “adhisīle sambhāventī”ti vuttaṭṭhāne buddhasīlaṃ nāma kathitaṃ, “abhikkante ñāṇadassane [M 3.0168] sambhāventī”ti vuttaṭṭhāne sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ, “adhipaññāya sambhāventī”ti vuttaṭṭhāne ṭhānuppattikapaññā, “yena dukkhenā”ti vuttaṭṭhāne saccabyākaraṇapaññā. Tattha sabbaññutaññāṇañca saccabyākaraṇapaññañca ṭhapetvā [P 3.0243] avasesā paññā adhipaññaṃ bhajati.

246. ‘I please their minds’: By means of the explanation of that question, I capture, satisfy, and fulfill their minds. When asked one thing, I do not explain another, like one who, when asked about a mango, explains about a breadfruit, or when asked about a breadfruit, explains about a mango. And here, in the place where it is said, “they hold him in high esteem for his higher morality,” the morality of a Buddha is spoken of. In the place where it is said, “they hold him in high esteem for his surpassing knowledge and vision,” omniscient knowledge is spoken of. In the place where it is said, “they hold him in high esteem for his higher wisdom,” situational wisdom is spoken of. In the place where it is said, “by which suffering…,” the wisdom of expounding the truths is spoken of. Therein, setting aside omniscient knowledge and the wisdom of expounding the truths, the remaining wisdom is included under higher wisdom.

247. Idāni tesaṃ tesaṃ visesādhigamānaṃ paṭipadaṃ ācikkhanto puna caparaṃ udāyītiādimāha. Tattha abhiññāvosānapāramippattāti abhiññāvosānasaṅkhātañceva abhiññāpāramīsaṅkhātañca arahattaṃ pattā.

247. Now, wishing to explain the path for attaining those various distinctions, he said, “Furthermore, Udāyī,” and so on. Therein, ‘having reached the perfection that culminates in direct knowledge’ means having attained Arahantship, which is reckoned as both the culmination of direct knowledge and the perfection of direct knowledge.

Sammappadhāneti upāyapadhāne. Chandaṃ janetīti kattukamyatākusalacchandaṃ janeti. Vāyamatīti vāyāmaṃ karoti. Vīriyaṃ ārabhatīti vīriyaṃ pavatteti. Cittaṃ paggaṇhātīti cittaṃ ukkhipati. Padahatīti upāyapadhānaṃ karoti. Bhāvanāya pāripūriyāti vaḍḍhiyā paripūraṇatthaṃ. Apicettha – “yā ṭhiti, so asammoso…pe… yaṃ vepullaṃ, sā bhāvanāpāripūrī”ti (vibha. 406) evaṃ purimaṃ purimassa pacchimaṃ pacchimassa atthotipi veditabbaṃ.

‘In the right effort’ means in the effort that is the means. ‘He generates desire’ means he generates wholesome desire, which is the wish to act. ‘He exerts’ means he makes an effort. ‘He initiates energy’ means he brings forth energy. ‘He uplifts the mind’ means he raises the mind. ‘He strives’ means he makes the effort that is the means. ‘For the fulfillment of development’ means for the purpose of completing the growth. Furthermore, here it should also be understood thus: from the passage, “Whatever is stability, that is non-confusion… whatever is abundance, that is the fulfillment of development,” the meaning of the first term corresponds to the first, and the meaning of the last term corresponds to the last.

Imehi pana sammappadhānehi kiṃ kathitaṃ? Kassapasaṃyuttapariyāyena sāvakassa pubbabhāgapaṭipadā kathitā. Vuttañhetaṃ tattha –

But what has been said by these right efforts? By way of the discourse in the Kassapa Saṃyutta, the preliminary-stage practice of a disciple has been described. For it has been said there:

“Cattārome[P 3.0244], āvuso, sammappadhānā. Katame cattāro? Idhāvuso, bhikkhu, anuppannā me pāpakā akusalā dhammā uppajjamānā anatthāya saṃvatteyyunti ātappaṃ karoti. Uppannā me pāpakā akusalā dhammā appahīyamānā anatthāya saṃvatteyyunti ātappaṃ karoti. Anuppannā me kusalā dhammā anuppajjamānā anatthāya saṃvatteyyunti ātappaṃ karoti. Uppannā me kusalā dhammā nirujjhamānā anatthāya saṃvatteyyunti ātappaṃ karotī”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.145).

“Friends, there are these four right efforts. What four? Here, friends, a bhikkhu makes an ardent effort, reflecting: ‘If unarisen evil, unwholesome states were to arise in me, it would lead to my harm.’ He makes an ardent effort, reflecting: ‘If arisen evil, unwholesome states in me were not abandoned, it would lead to my harm.’ He makes an ardent effort, reflecting: ‘If unarisen wholesome states were not to arise in me, it would lead to my harm.’ He makes an ardent effort, reflecting: ‘If arisen wholesome states in me were to cease, it would lead to my harm.’”

Ettha [V 3.0173] ca pāpakā akusalāti lobhādayo veditabbā. Anuppannā kusalā dhammāti samathavipassanā ceva maggo ca, uppannā kusalā nāma samathavipassanāva. Maggo pana sakiṃ uppajjitvā nirujjhamāno anatthāya saṃvattanako [M 3.0169] nāma natthi. So hi phalassa paccayaṃ datvāva nirujjhati. Purimasmimpi vā samathavipassanāva gahetabbāti vuttaṃ, taṃ pana na yuttaṃ.

And here, by ‘evil, unwholesome states,’ greed and so on should be understood. By ‘unarisen wholesome states,’ serenity, insight, and the path are to be understood. ‘Arisen wholesome states’ refers to serenity and insight. But the path, having arisen once, is not something that leads to harm when it ceases, for it ceases only after having given the condition for its fruit. Alternatively, it has been said that in the former case too, only serenity and insight should be taken; but that is not correct.

Tattha “uppannā samathavipassanā nirujjhamānā anatthāya saṃvattantī”ti atthassa āvibhāvatthamidaṃ vatthu – eko kira khīṇāsavatthero “mahācetiyañca mahābodhiñca vandissāmī”ti samāpattilābhinā bhaṇḍagāhakasāmaṇerena saddhiṃ janapadato mahāvihāraṃ āgantvā vihārapariveṇaṃ pāvisi. Sāyanhasamaye mahābhikkhusaṅghe cetiyaṃ vandamāne cetiyaṃ vandanatthāya na nikkhami. Kasmā? Khīṇāsavānañhi tīsu ratanesu mahantaṃ gāravaṃ hoti. Tasmā bhikkhusaṅghe vanditvā paṭikkamante manussānaṃ sāyamāsabhuttavelāyaṃ sāmaṇerampi ajānāpetvā “cetiyaṃ vandissāmī”ti ekakova nikkhami. Sāmaṇero [P 3.0245] – “kiṃ nu kho thero avelāya ekakova gacchati, jānissāmī”ti upajjhāyassa padānupadiko nikkhami. Thero anāvajjanena tassa āgamanaṃ ajānanto dakkhiṇadvārena cetiyaṅgaṇaṃ āruhi. Sāmaṇeropi anupadaṃyeva āruḷho.

Herein, to clarify the meaning of the phrase 'arisen tranquility and insight, in ceasing, conduce to what is not of benefit,' this story is told: A certain elder, one whose taints were destroyed, intending to pay homage to the Great Cetiya and the Great Bodhi Tree, arrived at the Great Monastery from the countryside accompanied by an attendant novice who had attained meditative absorptions. Upon entering a monastic residence, when the great assembly of monks was venerating the cetiya in the evening, he did not go out to pay homage to the cetiya. Why? Because those whose taints are destroyed have great reverence for the Three Jewels. Therefore, after the assembly of monks had paid homage and departed, at the time of the evening meal for the people, without informing the novice, he went out alone to pay homage to the cetiya. The novice thought, 'Why is the elder going out alone at an improper time? I will find out,' and followed in his preceptor's footsteps. The elder, through inattention, was unaware of his arrival and ascended to the cetiya courtyard by the southern gate. The novice also ascended right behind him.

Mahāthero mahācetiyaṃ ulloketvā buddhārammaṇaṃ pītiṃ gahetvā sabbaṃ cetaso samannāharitvā haṭṭhapahaṭṭho cetiyaṃ vandati. Sāmaṇero therassa vandanākāraṃ disvā “upajjhāyo me ativiya pasannacitto vandati, kiṃ nu kho pupphāni labhitvā pūjaṃ kareyyā”ti cintesi. Thero vanditvā uṭṭhāya sirasi añjaliṃ ṭhapetvā mahācetiyaṃ ulloketvā ṭhito. Sāmaṇero ukkāsitvā attano āgatabhāvaṃ jānāpesi. Thero parivattetvā olokento “kadā āgatosī”ti pucchi. Tumhākaṃ cetiyaṃ vandanakāle, bhante. Ativiya pasannā cetiyaṃ vandittha kiṃ nu kho pupphāni labhitvā pūjeyyāthāti? Āma sāmaṇera imasmiṃ cetiye viya aññatra ettakaṃ dhātūnaṃ nidhānaṃ nāma natthi, evarūpaṃ asadisaṃ mahāthūpaṃ pupphāni labhitvā ko na pūjeyyāti. Tena hi, bhante, adhivāsetha, āharissāmīti tāvadeva jhānaṃ samāpajjitvā iddhiyā himavantaṃ gantvā vaṇṇagandhasampannapupphāni parissāvanaṃ pūretvā mahāthere dakkhiṇamukhato pacchimaṃ mukhaṃ asampatteyeva āgantvā pupphaparissāvanaṃ hatthe ṭhapetvā “pūjetha, bhante,”ti āha[V 3.0174]. Thero “atimandāni no sāmaṇera pupphānī”ti āha. Gacchatha, bhante, bhagavato guṇe āvajjitvā pūjethāti.

The great elder, gazing upon the Great Cetiya, took up joy with the Buddha as its object, brought his whole mind to bear, and, greatly delighted, paid homage to the cetiya. Seeing the manner in which the elder paid homage, the novice thought, 'My preceptor is paying homage with an exceedingly serene mind. What if I were to obtain flowers and make an offering?' After paying homage, the elder rose, placed his hands in reverential salutation upon his head, gazed at the Great Cetiya, and stood there. The novice cleared his throat to make his presence known. The elder turned around and, looking at him, asked, 'When did you arrive?' 'At the time you were paying homage to the cetiya, venerable sir. You paid homage with such great serenity of mind—what if you were to obtain flowers and make an offering?' 'Yes, novice. In no other place is there such an enshrinement of relics as in this cetiya. Having obtained flowers, who would not make an offering to such an incomparable Great Stupa?' 'In that case, venerable sir, please consent. I will bring them.' So saying, he immediately entered meditative absorption, traveled by psychic power to the Himalayas, filled a water-strainer with flowers of excellent color and fragrance, and returned before the great elder had passed from the southern face to the western face. Placing the water-strainer of flowers in his hands, he said, 'Please make the offering, venerable sir.' The elder said, 'Novice, our flowers are too few.' 'Go on, venerable sir. Reflect on the virtues of the Blessed One and make the offering,' he said.

Thero [M 3.0170] pacchimamukhanissitena sopāṇena āruyha kucchivedikābhūmiyaṃ [P 3.0246] pupphapūjaṃ kātuṃ āraddho. Vedikābhūmiyaṃ paripuṇṇāni pupphāni patitvā dutiyabhūmiyaṃ jaṇṇupamāṇena odhinā pūrayiṃsu. Tato otaritvā pādapiṭṭhikapantiṃ pūjesi. Sāpi paripūri. Paripuṇṇabhāvaṃ ñatvā heṭṭhimatale vikiranto agamāsi. Sabbaṃ cetiyaṅgaṇaṃ paripūri. Tasmiṃ paripuṇṇe “sāmaṇera pupphāni na khīyantī”ti āha. Parissāvanaṃ, bhante, adhomukhaṃ karothāti. Adhomukhaṃ katvā cālesi, tadā pupphāni khīṇāni. Parissāvanaṃ sāmaṇerassa datvā saddhiṃ hatthipākārena cetiyaṃ tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā catūsu ṭhānesu vanditvā pariveṇaṃ gacchanto cintesi – “yāva mahiddhiko vatāyaṃ sāmaṇero, sakkhissati nu kho imaṃ iddhānubhāvaṃ rakkhitu”nti. Tato “na sakkhissatī”ti disvā sāmaṇeramāha – “sāmaṇera tvaṃ idāni mahiddhiko, evarūpaṃ pana iddhiṃ nāsetvā pacchimakāle kāṇapesakāriyā hatthena madditakañjiyaṃ pivissasī”ti. Daharakabhāvassa nāmesa dosoyaṃ, so upajjhāyassa kathāyaṃ saṃvijjitvā – “kammaṭṭhānaṃ me, bhante, ācikkhathā”ti na yāci, amhākaṃ upajjhāyo kiṃ vadatīti taṃ pana asuṇanto viya agamāsi.

The elder ascended by the stairway connected to the western face and began to make the flower offering on the level of the inner railing. The flowers, having filled the railing level, fell and filled the second level to the measure of a knee's height. Then, descending, he made an offering on the row of the base platform. That too became full. Knowing it was full, he went on, scattering them on the lower ground. The entire cetiya courtyard became full. When it was full, he said, 'Novice, the flowers are not running out.' 'Venerable sir, turn the water-strainer upside down,' said the novice. Having turned it upside down, he shook it; then the flowers were exhausted. Giving the water-strainer to the novice, he circumambulated the cetiya three times together with the elephant-wall, paid homage at the four places, and while going to the monastic dwelling, he thought: 'How very great is the psychic power of this novice! Will he, I wonder, be able to protect this power of iddhi?' Then, seeing 'He will not be able,' he said to the novice: 'Novice, you now have great psychic power. But having destroyed such iddhi, in a later time you will drink rice-gruel kneaded by the hand of a blind weaver woman.' This, indeed, is the fault of youthfulness; though alarmed by his preceptor's words, he did not ask, 'Venerable sir, please teach me a meditation subject.' Instead, thinking, 'What is our preceptor saying?' he went on as if not hearing his words.

Thero mahācetiyañca mahābodhiñca vanditvā sāmaṇeraṃ pattacīvaraṃ gāhāpetvā anupubbena kuṭeḷitissamahāvihāraṃ agamāsi. Sāmaṇero upajjhāyassa padānupadiko hutvā bhikkhācāraṃ na gacchati, “kataraṃ gāmaṃ pavisatha, bhante,”ti [P 3.0247] pucchitvā pana “idāni me upajjhāyo gāmadvāraṃ patto bhavissatī”ti ñatvā attano ca upajjhāyassa ca pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā ākāsena gantvā therassa pattacīvaraṃ datvā piṇḍāya pavisati. Thero sabbakālaṃ ovadati – “sāmaṇera mā evamakāsi, puthujjaniddhi nāma calā anibaddhā, asappāyaṃ rūpādiārammaṇaṃ labhitvā appamattakeneva bhijjati, santāya samāpattiyā parihīnāya brahmacariyavāso santhambhituṃ na sakkotī”ti. Sāmaṇero “kiṃ katheti mayhaṃ upajjhāyo”ti sotuṃ na icchati, tatheva karoti. Thero anupubbena cetiyavandanaṃ karonto kammubinduvihāraṃ nāma gato. Tattha vasantepi there sāmaṇero tatheva karoti.

The elder, having paid homage to the Great Cetiya and the Great Bodhi Tree, had the novice take his bowl and robe, and gradually proceeded to the Kuṭeḷitissa Great Monastery. The novice, following in his preceptor's footsteps, did not go on the alms-round. Instead, after asking, 'Which village will you enter, venerable sir?', and knowing, 'Now my preceptor will have reached the village gate,' he would take both his own and his preceptor's bowl and robe, go through the air, give the elder his bowl and robe, and enter the village for alms. The elder constantly admonished him: 'Novice, do not do so. The psychic power of a worldling is shaky and unstable. Upon encountering an unsuitable object, such as a form, it is broken by a mere trifle. When one has declined from an existing attainment, the holy life cannot be sustained.' The novice, not wishing to hear, thinking, 'What is my preceptor saying?', acted in the very same way. The elder, while gradually making his pilgrimage to the cetiyas, went to a monastery named Kammubinduvihāra. Even while the elder was staying there, the novice acted in the very same way.

Athekadivasaṃ [V 3.0175][M 3.0171] ekā pesakāradhītā abhirūpā paṭhamavaye ṭhitā kammabindugāmato nikkhamitvā padumassaraṃ oruyha gāyamānā pupphāni bhañjati. Tasmiṃ samaye sāmaṇero padumassaramatthakena gacchati, gacchanto pana silesikāya kāṇamacchikā viya tassā gītasadde bajjhi. Tāvadevassa iddhi antarahitā, chinnapakkhakāko viya ahosi. Santasamāpattibalena pana tattheva udakapiṭṭhe apatitvā simbalitūlaṃ viya patamānaṃ anupubbena padumasaratīre aṭṭhāsi. So vegena gantvā upajjhāyassa pattacīvaraṃ datvā nivatti. Mahāthero “pagevetaṃ mayā diṭṭhaṃ, nivāriyamānopi na nivattissatī”ti kiñci avatvā piṇḍāya pāvisi.

Then one day, a weaver's daughter, very beautiful and in her first youth, went out from the village of Kammabindu, descended into the lotus pond, and while singing, plucked flowers. At that time, the novice was passing over the lotus pond, and as he went, like a blind fish caught in a sticky substance, he was ensnared by the sound of her song. At that very moment, his psychic power vanished, and he became like a crow with clipped wings. However, by the power of his existing attainment, he did not fall right there on the surface of the water but, descending like a falling tuft of silk-cotton, he gradually came to stand on the shore of the lotus pond. He went quickly, gave the bowl and robe to his preceptor, and turned back. The great elder, thinking, 'I saw this beforehand. Even if prevented, he will not turn back,' said nothing and entered the village for alms-food.

Sāmaṇero gantvā padumasaratīre aṭṭhāsi tassā paccuttaraṇaṃ āgamayamāno. Sāpi sāmaṇeraṃ ākāsena gacchantañca puna āgantvā ṭhitañca disvā “addhā esa maṃ nissāya ukkaṇṭhito”ti ñatvā “paṭikkama sāmaṇerā”ti āha. So paṭikkami. Itarā paccuttaritvā sāṭakaṃ nivāsetvā taṃ upasaṅkamitvā “kiṃ, bhante,”ti pucchi. So tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Sā bahūhi kāraṇehi gharāvāse ādīnavaṃ brahmacariyavāse ānisaṃsañca dassetvā [P 3.0248] ovadamānāpi tassa ukkaṇṭhaṃ vinodetuṃ asakkontī – “ayaṃ mama kāraṇā evarūpāya iddhiyā parihīno, na dāni yuttaṃ pariccajitu”nti idheva tiṭṭhāti vatvā gharaṃ gantvā mātāpitūnaṃ taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesi. Tepi āgantvā nānappakāraṃ ovadamānā vacanaṃ aggaṇhantaṃ āhaṃsu – “tvaṃ amhe uccakulāti sallakkhesi, mayaṃ pesakārā. Sakkhissasi pesakārakammaṃ kātu”nti sāmaṇero āha – “upāsaka gihibhūto nāma pesakārakammaṃ vā kareyya naḷakārakammaṃ vā, kiṃ iminā sāṭakamattena lobhaṃ karothā”ti. Pesakāro udare baddhasāṭakaṃ datvā gharaṃ netvā dhītaraṃ adāsi.

The novice went and stood on the shore of the lotus pond, waiting for her to ascend. She, seeing the novice both going through the sky and then returning to stand there, and knowing, 'Surely this one is distressed on account of me,' said, 'Step back, novice.' He stepped back. The other came up from the water, put on her garment, approached him, and asked, 'What is it, venerable sir?' He told her the matter. Although she advised him, showing in many ways the drawbacks of the household life and the benefits of the holy life, she was unable to dispel his distress. Thinking, 'On my account, this man has lost such psychic power; it is not right to abandon him now,' she said, 'Stay right here,' and went home to inform her mother and father of the matter. They too came and, while advising him in various ways, said to him when he would not accept their words, 'Do you perceive us to be of a high clan? We are weavers. Will you be able to do the work of a weaver?' The novice said, 'Lay supporter, one who has become a householder might do the work of a weaver or the work of a reed-worker. Why do you show greed for this mere cloth?' The weaver, giving him a cloth to be bound at the waist, took him home and gave him his daughter.

So pesakārakammaṃ uggaṇhitvā pesakārehi saddhiṃ sālāya kammaṃ karoti. Aññesaṃ itthiyo pātova bhattaṃ sampādetvā āhariṃsu, tassa bhariyā na tāva āgacchati. So itaresu kammaṃ vissajjetvā bhuñjamānesu tasaraṃ vaṭṭento nisīdi. Sā pacchā agamāsi. Atha naṃ so “aticirena [M 3.0172] āgatāsī”ti tajjesi. Mātugāmo ca nāma api cakkavattirājānaṃ attani paṭibaddhacittaṃ ñatvā dāsaṃ viya sallakkheti. Tasmā sā evamāha – “aññesaṃ ghare dārupaṇṇaloṇādīni sannihitāni, bāhirato āharitvā dāyakā pesanatakārakāpi atthi, ahaṃ pana [V 3.0176] ekikāva, tvampi mayhaṃ ghare idaṃ atthi idaṃ natthīti na jānāsi. Sace icchasi, bhuñja, no ce icchasi, mā bhuñjā”ti. So “na kevalañca ussūre bhattaṃ āharasi, vācāyapi maṃ ghaṭṭesī”ti kujjhitvā aññaṃ paharaṇaṃ apassanto tameva tasaradaṇḍakaṃ [P 3.0249] tasarato luñcitvā khipi. Sā taṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā īsakaṃ parivatti. Tasaradaṇḍakassa ca koṭi nāma tikhiṇā hoti, sā tassā parivattamānāya akkhikoṭiyaṃ pavisitvā aṭṭhāsi. Sā ubhohi hatthehi vegena akkhiṃ aggahesi, bhinnaṭṭhānato lohitaṃ paggharati. So tasmiṃ kāle upajjhāyassa vacanaṃ anussari – “idaṃ sandhāya maṃ upajjhāyo ‘anāgate kāle kāṇapesakāriyā hatthehi madditakañjiyaṃ pivissasī’ti āha, idaṃ therena diṭṭhaṃ bhavissati, aho dīghadassī ayyo”ti mahāsaddena rodituṃ ārabhi. Tamenaṃ aññe – “alaṃ, āvuso, mā rodi, akkhi nāma bhinnaṃ na sakkā rodanena paṭipākatikaṃ kātu”nti āhaṃsu. So “nāhametamatthaṃ rodāmi, apica kho imaṃ sandhāya rodāmī”ti sabbaṃ paṭipāṭiyā kathesi. Evaṃ uppannā samathavipassanā nirujjhamānā anatthāya saṃvattanti.

He learned the work of a weaver and worked in the workshop with the weavers. The wives of the others prepared their meal early and brought it, but his wife had not yet come. While the others, having set aside their work, were eating, he sat spinning the shuttle. She came later. Then he threatened her, saying, 'You have come very late!' Now, a woman, it is said, knowing a universal monarch is devoted to her, regards him as a mere slave. Therefore, she said this: 'In the homes of others, firewood, greens, salt, and so on are stored up; there are also people to bring things from outside, givers and messengers. But I am all alone, and you do not know what is in my house and what is not. If you wish to eat, eat. If you do not wish to eat, do not eat.' He, becoming angry, said, 'Not only do you bring the meal late, but you also assault me with words!' Not seeing any other weapon, he plucked the shuttle-stick from the shuttle and threw it. Seeing it coming towards her, she turned slightly. The tip of a shuttle-stick is sharp, and as she was turning, it entered the corner of her eye and lodged there. She quickly covered her eye with both hands, and blood flowed from the pierced spot. At that moment, he recalled the words of his preceptor: 'It was with reference to this that my preceptor said, "In the future, you will drink rice-gruel squeezed by the hands of a one-eyed weaver woman." This must have been foreseen by the Elder. Oh, how far-seeing is the noble one!' And he began to weep with a loud voice. The others said to him, 'Enough, friend, do not weep. A pierced eye cannot be made as it was before by weeping.' He said, 'I am not weeping for this matter, but rather I am weeping with reference to this,' and he related the entire story in order. Thus, tranquility and insight, having arisen, when they cease, lead to what is not beneficial.

Aparampi vatthu – tiṃsamattā bhikkhū kalyāṇimahācetiyaṃ vanditvā aṭavimaggena mahāmaggaṃ otaramānā antarāmagge jhāmakhette kammaṃ katvā āgacchantaṃ ekaṃ manussaṃ addasaṃsu. Tassa sarīraṃ masimakkhitaṃ viya ahosi. Masimakkhitaṃyeva ekaṃ kāsāvaṃ kacchaṃ pīḷetvā nivatthaṃ, olokiyamāno jhāmakhāṇuko viya khāyati. So divasabhāge kammaṃ katvā upaḍḍhajjhāyamānānaṃ dārūnaṃ kalāpaṃ ukkhipitvā piṭṭhiyaṃ vippakiṇṇehi kesehi kummaggena āgantvā bhikkhūnaṃ sammukhe aṭṭhāsi. Sāmaṇerā disvā aññamaññaṃ olokayamānā, – “āvuso, tuyhaṃ pitā tuyhaṃ mahāpitā [P 3.0250] tuyhaṃ mātulo”ti hasamānā gantvā “konāmo tvaṃ upāsakā”ti nāmaṃ pucchiṃsu. So nāmaṃ pucchito vippaṭisārī hutvā dārukalāpaṃ chaḍḍetvā [M 3.0173] vatthaṃ saṃvidhāya nivāsetvā mahāthere vanditvā “tiṭṭhatha tāva, bhante,”ti āha. Mahātherā aṭṭhaṃsu.

Another story. About thirty monks, having paid homage at the Kalyāṇī Mahācetiya, were descending by the forest path to the main road when, on the way, they saw a man coming who had been working in a burnt field. His body was as if smeared with soot. He wore a single saffron robe, also smeared with soot, tucked up tightly. When looked at, he appeared like a burnt stump. Having worked during the day, hoisting a bundle of half-burnt firewood, with his hair scattered on his back, he came by a side-path and stood before the monks. The novices, seeing him, looked at one another and, laughing, said, 'Friend, your father, your grandfather, your uncle!' Then they went and asked his name, 'What is your name, lay supporter?' Being asked his name, he became remorseful, threw down the bundle of firewood, arranged his cloth and wore it properly, paid homage to the great elders, and said, 'Please wait a moment, venerable sirs.' The great elders stood still.

Daharasāmaṇerā āgantvā mahātherānaṃ sammukhāpi parihāsaṃ karonti. Upāsako āha – “bhante, tumhe maṃ passitvā parihasatha, ettakeneva matthakaṃ pattamhāti mā sallakkhetha. Ahampi pubbe tumhādisova samaṇo ahosiṃ. Tumhākaṃ pana cittekaggatāmattakampi natthi, ahaṃ imasmiṃ sāsane [V 3.0177] mahiddhiko mahānubhāvo ahosiṃ, ākāsaṃ gahetvā pathaviṃ karomi, pathaviṃ ākāsaṃ. Dūraṃ gaṇhitvā santikaṃ karomi, santikaṃ dūraṃ. Cakkavāḷasatasahassaṃ khaṇena vinivijjhāmi. Hatthe me passatha, idāni makkaṭahatthasadisā, ahaṃ imeheva hatthehi idha nisinnova candimasūriye parāmasiṃ. Imesaṃyeva pādānaṃ candimasūriye pādakathalikaṃ katvā nisīdiṃ. Evarūpā me iddhi pamādena antarahitā, tumhe mā pamajjittha. Pamādena hi evarūpaṃ byasanaṃ pāpuṇanti. Appamattā viharantā jātijarāmaraṇassa antaṃ karonti. Tasmā tumhe maññeva ārammaṇaṃ karitvā appamattā hotha, bhante,”ti tajjetvā ovādamadāsi. Te tassa kathentasseva saṃvegaṃ āpajjitvā vipassamānā tiṃsajanā tattheva arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsūti. Evampi uppannā samathavipassanā nirujjhamānā anatthāya saṃvattantīti veditabbā.

Young novices came and made jokes even in the presence of the senior monks. The lay follower said: “Venerable sirs, seeing me, you jest. Do not think, ‘We have reached the pinnacle with just this much.’ I, too, was formerly a monk like you. But you do not have even a measure of one-pointedness of mind. In this Dispensation, I was of great psychic power, of great might. I could take the sky and make it the earth, and the earth the sky. I could take what is distant and make it near, and what is near, distant. In an instant, I could pierce a hundred thousand world-systems. Look at my hands; now they are like a monkey’s hands. But with these very hands, while sitting right here, I touched the sun and moon. Having made the sun and moon a footstool for these very feet, I sat. Psychic power of such a kind disappeared for me through heedlessness. Do not you be heedless. For through heedlessness, one encounters such a disaster. Dwelling heedfully, they make an end of birth, aging, and death. Therefore, venerable sirs, taking me as your object of reflection, be heedful.” Having thus rebuked them, he gave them this advice. While he was still speaking, thirty of them, feeling a sense of spiritual urgency and developing insight, attained Arahantship right there. Thus, it should be understood that even tranquility and insight, having arisen, if they cease, conduce to what is not for one's welfare.

Anuppannānaṃ pāpakānanti cettha “anuppanno vā kāmāsavo [P 3.0251] na uppajjatī”tiādīsu vuttanayena attho veditabbo. Uppannānaṃ pāpakānanti ettha pana catubbidhaṃ uppannaṃ vattamānuppannaṃ bhutvāvigatuppannaṃ, okāsakatuppannaṃ, bhūmiladdhuppannanti. Tattha ye kilesā vijjamānā uppādādisamaṅgino, idaṃ vattamānuppannaṃ nāma. Kamme pana javite ārammaṇarasaṃ anubhavitvā niruddhavipāko bhutvā vigataṃ nāma. Kammaṃ uppajjitvā niruddhaṃ bhavitvā vigataṃ nāma. Tadubhayampi bhutvāvigatuppannanti saṅkhaṃ gacchati. Kusalākusalaṃ kammaṃ aññassa kammassa vipākaṃ paṭibāhitvā attano vipākassa okāsaṃ karoti, evaṃ kate okāse vipāko uppajjamāno okāsakaraṇato paṭṭhāya uppannoti saṅkhaṃ gacchati. Idaṃ okāsakatuppannaṃ nāma. Pañcakkhandhā pana vipassanāya bhūmi nāma. Te atītādibhedā honti. Tesu anusayitakilesā pana atītā vā anāgatā vā paccuppannā vāti na vattabbā. Atītakhandhesu anusayitāpi hi appahīnāva honti, anāgatakhandhesu, paccuppannakhandhesu [M 3.0174] anusayitāpi appahīnāva honti. Idaṃ bhūmiladdhuppannaṃ nāma. Tenāhu porāṇā – “tāsu tāsu bhūmīsu asamugghātitakilesā bhūmiladdhuppannāti saṅkhaṃ gacchantī”ti.

Herein, regarding ‘of unarisen evil states,’ the meaning should be understood according to the method stated in such passages as, ‘the unarisen canker of sensual desire does not arise.’ Regarding ‘of arisen evil states,’ however, the ‘arisen’ is fourfold: (1) presently arisen, (2) arisen as having been experienced and passed away, (3) arisen by gaining an opportunity, and (4) arisen by obtaining a ground. Therein, those defilements that are existing and endowed with arising, etc., are called ‘presently arisen.’ As for kamma, when the impulsion has run its course, the resultant consciousness that has ceased after having experienced the taste of the object is called ‘having experienced and passed away.’ The kamma that has arisen and ceased is called ‘having been and passed away.’ Both of these are reckoned as ‘arisen as having been experienced and passed away.’ Wholesome or unwholesome kamma, having obstructed the result of another kamma, creates an opportunity for its own result. When this opportunity is thus made, the resultant that is arising is, from the moment of the opportunity's creation, reckoned as ‘arisen.’ This is called ‘arisen by gaining an opportunity.’ The five aggregates are called the ‘ground’ for insight. They are of different kinds, such as past, and so on. The latent defilements within them, however, cannot be said to be past, future, or present. For the latent defilements in past aggregates are indeed unabandoned, and those latent in future aggregates and present aggregates are also unabandoned. This is called ‘arisen by obtaining a ground.’ Therefore, the ancients said: ‘The defilements not eradicated in those various grounds are reckoned as “arisen by obtaining a ground.”’

Aparampi catubbidhaṃ uppannaṃ samudācāruppannaṃ, ārammaṇādhigahituppannaṃ, avikkhambhituppannaṃ asamugghātituppannanti. Tattha sampati vattamānaṃyeva samudācāruppannaṃ nāma. Sakiṃ cakkhūni ummīletvā ārammaṇe nimitte gahite anussaritānussaritakkhaṇe kilesā [P 3.0252] nuppajjissantīti na [V 3.0178] vattabbā. Kasmā? Ārammaṇassa adhigahitattā. Yathā kiṃ? Yathā khīrarukkhassa kuṭhāriyā āhatāhataṭṭhāne khīraṃ na nikkhamissatīti na vattabbaṃ, evaṃ. Idaṃ ārammaṇādhigahituppannaṃ nāma. Samāpattiyā avikkhambhitā kilesā pana imasmiṃ nāma ṭhāne nuppajjissantīti na vattabbā. Kasmā? Avikkhambhitattā. Yathā kiṃ? Yathā sace khīrarukkhe kuṭhāriyā āhaneyyuṃ, imasmiṃ nāma ṭhāne khīraṃ na nikkhameyyāti na vattabbaṃ, evaṃ. Idaṃ avikkhambhituppannaṃ nāma. Maggena asamugghātitakilesā pana bhavagge nibbattassāpi uppajjantīti purimanayeneva vitthāretabbaṃ. Idaṃ asamugghātituppannaṃ nāma.

Furthermore, the ‘arisen’ is fourfold: (1) arisen as active manifestation, (2) arisen by having grasped the object, (3) arisen as unsuppressed, and (4) arisen as uneradicated. Therein, that which is presently occurring is called ‘arisen as active manifestation.’ After opening the eyes once and grasping the sign in an object, it cannot be said that defilements will not arise at every moment of recollection. Why? Because the object has been grasped. Just as it cannot be said that sap will not flow from a milkwood tree at every spot struck by an axe, so it is. This is called ‘arisen by having grasped the object.’ As for defilements not suppressed by meditative attainment, it cannot be said that they will not arise in this or that situation. Why? Because they are unsuppressed. Just as it cannot be said that if one were to strike a milkwood tree with an axe, sap would not flow from this or that spot, so it is. This is called ‘arisen as unsuppressed.’ As for defilements not eradicated by the path, they arise even for one reborn at the peak of existence; this should be elaborated in the same way as before. This is called ‘arisen as uneradicated.’

Imesu uppannesu vattamānuppannaṃ bhutvāvigatuppannaṃ okāsakatuppannaṃ samudācāruppannanti catubbidhaṃ uppannaṃ na maggavajjhaṃ, bhūmiladdhuppannaṃ ārammaṇādhigahituppannaṃ avikkhambhituppannaṃ asamugghātituppannanti catubbidhaṃ maggavajjhaṃ. Maggo hi uppajjamāno ete kilese pajahati. So ye kilese pajahati, te atītā vā anāgatā vā paccuppannā vāti na vattabbā. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

Among these arisen states, the four kinds—(1) presently arisen, (2) arisen as having been experienced and passed away, (3) arisen by gaining an opportunity, and (4) arisen as active manifestation—are not to be destroyed by the path. The four kinds—(1) arisen by obtaining a ground, (2) arisen by having grasped the object, (3) arisen as unsuppressed, and (4) arisen as uneradicated—are to be destroyed by the path. For the path, when arising, abandons these defilements. The defilements that it abandons cannot be said to be past, future, or present. And this has been stated:

“Hañci atīte kilese pajahati, tena hi khīṇaṃ khepeti, niruddhaṃ nirodheti, vigataṃ vigameti atthaṅgataṃ atthaṅgameti. Atītaṃ yaṃ natthi, taṃ pajahati. Hañci anāgate kilese pajahati, tena hi ajātaṃ pajahati, anibbattaṃ, anuppannaṃ, apātubhūtaṃ pajahati. Anāgataṃ yaṃ natthi, taṃ pajahati, hañci paccuppanne kilese pajahati, tena hi ratto rāgaṃ pajahati[P 3.0253], duṭṭho dosaṃ, mūḷho mohaṃ, vinibaddho mānaṃ, parāmaṭṭho diṭṭhiṃ, vikkhepagato uddhaccaṃ, aniṭṭhaṅgato vicikicchaṃ, thāmagato anusayaṃ pajahati. Kaṇhasukkadhammā yuganaddhā samameva vattanti. Saṃkilesikā maggabhāvanā hoti…pe… tena hi natthi maggabhāvanā, natthi phalasacchikiriyā, natthi kilesappahānaṃ, natthi dhammābhisamayoti. Atthi [M 3.0175] maggabhāvanā…pe… atthi dhammābhisamayoti. Yathā kathaṃ viya, seyyathāpi taruṇo rukkho ajātaphalo…pe… apātubhūtāyeva na pātubhavantī”ti.

“If one were to abandon defilements in the past, then one would be exhausting what is exhausted, causing to cease what has ceased, removing what is removed, and causing to disappear what has disappeared. One would be abandoning the past, which does not exist. If one were to abandon defilements in the future, then one would be abandoning what is unborn, unproduced, unarisen, and unmanifested. One would be abandoning the future, which does not exist. If one were to abandon defilements in the present, then one who is lustful would be abandoning lust; one who is hateful, hatred; one who is deluded, delusion; one who is bound, conceit; one who grasps, wrong view; one who is distracted, restlessness; one who is undecided, doubt; one who is strong in defilements, latent tendencies. Dark and bright qualities would proceed yoked together. The development of the path would be defiling... Therefore, is there no development of the path, no realization of the fruit, no abandoning of defilements, and no comprehension of the Dhamma? There is development of the path... there is comprehension of the Dhamma. How so? It is like a young tree that has not yet borne fruit... what has not yet manifested simply does not manifest.”

Iti pāḷiyaṃ ajātaphalarukkho āgato, jātaphalarukkhena pana dīpetabbaṃ. Yathā hi saphalo taruṇambarukkho, tassa phalāni manussā paribhuñjeyyuṃ, sesāni pātetvā pacchiyo pūreyyuṃ[V 3.0179]. Athañño puriso taṃ pharasunā chindeyya, tenassa neva atītāni phalāni nāsitāni honti, na anāgatapaccuppannāni nāsitāni. Atītāni hi manussehi paribhuttāni, anāgatāni anibbattāni, na sakkā nāsetuṃ. Yasmiṃ pana samaye so chinno, tadā phalāniyeva natthīti paccuppannānipi anāsitāni. Sace pana rukkho acchinno, athassa pathavīrasañca āporasañca āgamma yāni phalāni nibbatteyyuṃ, tāni nāsitāni honti. Tāni hi ajātāneva na jāyanti, anibbattāneva na nibbattanti, apātubhūtāneva na pātubhavanti, evameva maggo nāpi atītādibhede kilese pajahati, nāpi na pajahati. Yesañhi kilesānaṃ maggena khandhesu apariññātesu uppatti siyā, maggena uppajjitvā khandhānaṃ pariññātattā te kilesā ajātāva na jāyanti, anibbattāva na nibbattanti, apātubhūtāva na pātubhavanti, taruṇaputtāya itthiyā puna avijāyanatthaṃ, byādhitānaṃ [P 3.0254] rogavūpasamanatthaṃ pītabhesajjehi cāpi ayamattho vibhāvetabbo. Evaṃ maggo ye kilese pajahati, te atītā vā anāgatā vā paccuppannā vāti na vattabbā, na ca maggo kilese na pajahati. Ye pana maggo kilese pajahati, te sandhāya “uppannānaṃ pāpakāna”ntiādi vuttaṃ.

Thus, in the Pāḷi, the simile of the tree that has not yet borne fruit is given, but it should be illustrated with a tree that has borne fruit. For instance, there might be a young, fruit-bearing mango tree. People might enjoy its fruits, and having shaken down the rest, they might fill their baskets. Then another person might cut it down with an axe. By this, neither its past fruits are destroyed, nor are its future and present fruits destroyed. For the past fruits have been consumed by people, and the future fruits are unproduced; they cannot be destroyed. And at the time it is cut, there are simply no fruits, so the present fruits are also not destroyed. But if the tree were not cut, then depending on the nutrients of the earth and water, whatever fruits would have been produced, those fruits are destroyed. For those fruits, being unborn, do not arise; being unproduced, they do not come into being; being unmanifested, they do not manifest. In the very same way, the path neither abandons defilements distinguished as past, future, or present, nor does it not abandon them. For those defilements that would arise if the aggregates were not fully understood by the path—once the path has arisen and the aggregates are fully understood, those defilements, being unborn, do not arise; being unproduced, they do not come into being; being unmanifested, they do not manifest. This meaning should also be clarified by the examples of a woman with a young son for the purpose of not giving birth again, and of medicine drunk by the sick for the calming of disease. Thus, the defilements that the path abandons cannot be said to be past, future, or present. And yet, it is not that the path does not abandon defilements. It is with reference to the defilements that the path does abandon that it is said, ‘of arisen evil states,’ and so on.

Na kevalañca maggo kileseyeva pajahati, kilesānaṃ pana appahīnattā ye ca uppajjeyyuṃ upādinnakakkhandhā, tepi pajahatiyeva. Vuttampi cetaṃ – “sotāpattimaggañāṇena abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇassa nirodhena satta bhave ṭhapetvā anamatagge saṃsāre ye uppajjeyyuṃ nāmañca rūpañca, etthete nirujjhantī”ti (cūḷani. 6) vitthāro. Iti maggo upādinnaanupādinnato vuṭṭhāti. Bhavavasena pana sotāpattimaggo apāyabhavato vuṭṭhāti, sakadāgāmimaggo sugatibhavekadesato, anāgāmimaggo sugatikāmabhavato, arahattamaggo [M 3.0176] rūpārūpabhavato vuṭṭhāti. Sabbabhavehi vuṭṭhātiyevātipi vadanti.

And not only does the path abandon the defilements, but because the defilements have not been abandoned, it also abandons whatever appropriated aggregates would arise. And this has been stated: ‘Through the knowledge of the stream-entry path, with the cessation of karmically formative consciousness, setting aside seven existences, whatever name and form would arise in beginningless saṃsāra, they cease right here.’ This is the detailed explanation. Thus, the path emerges from the appropriated aggregates. In terms of existence, the stream-entry path emerges from existence in the plane of misery; the once-returner path emerges from a part of existence in the happy destinations; the non-returner path emerges from sensual existence in the happy destinations; and the Arahant path emerges from form and formless existence. Some also say that it emerges from all existences whatsoever.

Atha maggakkhaṇe kathaṃ anuppannānaṃ uppādāya bhāvanā hoti, kathaṃ vā uppannānaṃ ṭhitiyāti. Maggappavattiyāyeva. Maggo hi pavattamāno pubbe anuppannapubbattā anuppanno nāma vuccati. Anāgatapubbañhi ṭhānaṃ āgantvā ananubhūtapubbaṃ vā ārammaṇaṃ anubhavitvā vattāro bhavanti “anāgataṭṭhānaṃ āgatamhā, ananubhūtaṃ ārammaṇaṃ anubhavāmā”ti. Yā cassa pavatti, ayameva ṭhiti nāmāti ṭhitiyā bhāvetītipi vattuṃ vaṭṭati.

Then, at the moment of the path, how is there development for the arising of what is unarisen? And how is there development for the stability of what has arisen? It is through the very occurrence of the path. For the path, as it occurs, is called ‘unarisen’ because it has never arisen before. Indeed, having come to a place not come to before, or having experienced an object not experienced before, people say, ‘We have come to a place not come to before; we are experiencing an object not experienced before.’ And whatever occurrence the path has, this very occurrence is called ‘stability.’ Thus, it is also fitting to say that one develops for the sake of stability.

Iddhipādesu [V 3.0180][P 3.0255] saṅkhepakathā cetokhilasutte (ma. ni. 1.185 ādayo) vuttā. Upasamamānaṃ gacchati, kilesūpasamatthaṃ vā gacchatīti upasamagāmī. Sambujjhamānā gacchati, maggasambodhatthāya vā gacchatīti sambodhagāmī.

A brief discussion on the bases of spiritual power is given in the Cetokhila Sutta. It goes while bringing calm, or it goes for the purpose of calming the defilements; therefore, it is called ‘leading to calm.’ It goes while awakening, or it goes for the purpose of awakening to the path; therefore, it is called ‘leading to awakening.’

Vivekanissitādīni sabbāsavasaṃvare vuttāni. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthārato panāyaṃ bodhipakkhiyakathā visuddhimagge vuttā.

‘Based on seclusion,’ and so on, are mentioned in the discourse on the restraint of all taints. This here is the summary. But in detail, this discussion on the requisites of enlightenment is given in the Visuddhimagga.

248. Vimokkhakathāyaṃ vimokkheti kenaṭṭhena vimokkhā, adhimuccanaṭṭhena. Ko panāyaṃ adhimuccanaṭṭho nāma? Paccanīkadhammehi ca suṭṭhu muccanaṭṭho, ārammaṇe ca abhirativasena suṭṭhu muccanaṭṭho, pituaṅke vissaṭṭhaṅgapaccaṅgassa dārakassa sayanaṃ viya aniggahitabhāvena nirāsaṅkatāya ārammaṇe pavattīti vuttaṃ hoti. Ayaṃ panattho pacchimavimokkhe natthi, purimesu sabbesu atthi. Rūpī rūpāni passatīti ettha ajjhattakesādīsu nīlakasiṇādivasena uppāditaṃ rūpajjhānaṃ rūpaṃ, tadassa atthīti rūpī. Bahiddhā rūpāni passatīti bahiddhāpi nīlakasiṇādīni rūpāni jhānacakkhunā passati. Iminā ajjhatta [P 3.0256] bahiddhāvatthukesu kasiṇesu uppāditajjhānassa puggalassa cattāripi rūpāvacarajjhānāni dassitāni.

248. In the discourse on liberations, by what meaning are they 'liberations'? By the meaning of being especially released. And what is this meaning of being especially released? It is the meaning of being thoroughly released from opposing states, and the meaning of being thoroughly inclined towards the object by way of extreme delight. Like the lying down of a child with its major and minor limbs relaxed on its father's lap, it is said that the jhāna proceeds in the object through the absence of suppressed opposing states and through fearlessness. This meaning, however, is not present in the final liberation, but it is present in all the preceding ones. 'One who has form sees forms': here, the form-sphere jhāna produced by means of the blue kasiṇa, etc., on internal objects such as hair, is 'form'. That person has that form; therefore, they are called rūpī (one who has form). 'Sees forms' means one sees external forms, such as the blue kasiṇa, etc., with the eye of jhāna. By this, the four form-sphere jhānas of a person who has produced jhāna in kasiṇas based on internal and external objects are shown.

Ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññīti ajjhattaṃ na rūpasaññī, attano kesādīsu anuppāditarūpāvacarajjhānoti attho. Iminā bahiddhā parikammaṃ katvā bahiddhāva uppāditajjhānassa rūpāvacarajjhānāni dassitāni. Subhanteva adhimutto hotīti iminā suvisuddhesu nīlādīsu vaṇṇakasiṇesu jhānāni dassitāni. Tattha kiñcāpi antoappanāyaṃ subhanti [M 3.0177] ābhogo natthi, yo pana suvisuddhaṃ subhakasiṇaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā viharati, so yasmā subhanti adhimutto hotīti vattabbataṃ āpajjati, tasmā evaṃ desanā katā. Paṭisambhidāmagge pana “kathaṃ subhanteva adhimutto hotīti vimokkho. Idha bhikkhu mettāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharati…pe… mettāya bhāvitattā sattā appaṭikūlā honti. Karuṇāsahagatena, muditāsahagatena, upekkhāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharati…pe… upekkhāya bhāvitattā sattā appaṭikūlā honti. Evaṃ subhanteva adhimutto hotīti vimokkho”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.212) vuttaṃ.

'Internally not percipient of form' means: internally, one is not percipient of form; the meaning is, a person who has not produced a form-sphere jhāna in one's own hair, and so on. By this, the form-sphere jhānas of a person who has produced jhāna externally, having done the preliminary meditation on external objects, are shown. 'One is intent only on the beautiful': by this, the jhānas that have arisen in the very pure color kasiṇas, such as blue, etc., are shown. Therein, although within absorption there is no advertence 'beautiful,' yet since a person who dwells having made a very pure, beautiful kasiṇa the object is intent on 'beautiful,' they come to be spoken of thus. Therefore, the teaching was given in this way. In the Paṭisambhidāmagga, however, it is said: 'How is it a liberation that "one is intent only on the beautiful"? Here, a bhikkhu dwells pervading one direction with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness… because loving-kindness is developed, beings are not repulsive. With a mind accompanied by compassion, with a mind accompanied by altruistic joy, with a mind accompanied by equanimity, one dwells pervading one direction… because equanimity is developed, beings are not repulsive. Thus, one is intent only on the beautiful—this is a liberation.'

Sabbaso [V 3.0181] rūpasaññānantiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ visuddhimagge vuttameva. Ayaṃ aṭṭhamo vimokkhoti ayaṃ catunnaṃ khandhānaṃ sabbaso [P 3.0257] vissaṭṭhattā vimuttattā aṭṭhamo uttamo vimokkho nāma.

Regarding the phrases beginning with 'by the complete overcoming of perceptions of form,' whatever should be said, all of that has already been said in the Visuddhimagga. 'This is the eighth liberation' means: because of the complete relinquishing of and liberation from the four aggregates, this is called the eighth, supreme liberation.

249. Abhibhāyatanakathāyaṃ abhibhāyatanānīti abhibhavanakāraṇāni. Kiṃ abhibhavanti? Paccanīkadhammepi ārammaṇānipi. Tāni hi paṭipakkhabhāvena paccanīkadhamme abhibhavanti, puggalassa ñāṇuttaritāya ārammaṇāni. Ajjhattaṃ rūpasaññītiādīsu pana ajjhattarūpe parikammavasena ajjhattaṃ rūpasaññī nāma hoti. Ajjhattañca nīlaparikammaṃ karonto kese vā pitte vā akkhitārakāya vā karoti, pītaparikammaṃ karonto mede vā chaviyā vā hatthatalapādatalesu vā akkhīnaṃ pītaṭṭhāne vā karoti, lohitaparikammaṃ karonto maṃse vā lohite vā jivhāya vā akkhīnaṃ rattaṭṭhāne vā karoti, odātaparikammaṃ karonto aṭṭhimhi vā dante vā nakhe vā akkhīnaṃ setaṭṭhāne vā karoti. Taṃ pana sunīlaṃ supītakaṃ sulohitakaṃ suodātaṃ na hoti, asuvisuddhameva hoti.

249. In the discourse on the bases of mastery, 'bases of mastery' are the causes of overcoming. What do they overcome? Opposing states and also objects. For they overcome opposing states by being their opposites, and they overcome objects because of the person's superior knowledge. In phrases such as 'internally percipient of form,' one is called 'internally percipient of form' by means of preliminary meditation on internal forms. And when one undertakes the preliminary meditation on blue internally, one does so on the hair, bile, or the pupils of the eyes. When one undertakes the preliminary meditation on yellow, one does so on the fat, skin, palms of the hands and soles of the feet, or the yellow parts of the eyes. When one undertakes the preliminary meditation on red, one does so on the flesh, blood, tongue, or the red parts of the eyes. When one undertakes the preliminary meditation on white, one does so on the bones, teeth, nails, or the white parts of the eyes. However, that is not perfectly blue, perfectly yellow, perfectly red, or perfectly white; it is just impure.

Eko bahiddhā rūpāni passatīti yassetaṃ parikammaṃ ajjhattaṃ uppannaṃ hoti, nimittaṃ pana bahiddhā, so evaṃ ajjhattaṃ parikammassa bahiddhā ca appanāya vasena – “ajjhattaṃ rūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passatī”ti vuccati. Parittānīti avaḍḍhitāni. Suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇānīti suvaṇṇāni vā hontu dubbaṇṇāni vā, parittavaseneva idamabhibhāyatanaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Tāni [M 3.0178][P 3.0258] abhibhuyyāti yathā nāma sampannagahaṇiko kaṭacchumattaṃ bhattaṃ labhitvā “kimettha bhuñjitabbaṃ atthī”ti saṅkaḍḍhitvā ekakabaḷameva karoti, evamevaṃ ñāṇuttariko puggalo visadañāṇo – “kimettha parittake ārammaṇe samāpajjitabbaṃ atthi, nāyaṃ mama bhāro”ti tāni rūpāni abhibhavitvā samāpajjati, saha nimittuppādenevettha appanaṃ pāpetīti attho. Jānāmi passāmīti iminā panassa ābhogo kathito, so ca kho samāpattito vuṭṭhitassa, na antosamāpattiyaṃ. Evaṃsaññī hotīti ābhogasaññāyapi jhānasaññāyapi evaṃsaññī hoti. Abhibhavasaññā hissa antosamāpattiyaṃ atthi, ābhogasaññā pana samāpattito vuṭṭhitasseva.

'One sees forms externally': for a person for whom this preliminary meditation has arisen internally, but the counterpart sign has arisen externally, that person, by means of internal preliminary meditation and external absorption, is called 'one who, being percipient of form internally, sees forms externally.' 'Limited' means undeveloped. 'Of beautiful or ugly color' means: whether they are of beautiful color or of ugly color, it should be understood that this base of mastery is spoken of solely by way of the limited sign. 'Mastering them': just as a person with a large storehouse, having obtained a mere ladleful of food, thinks, 'What is there to eat here?' and gathers it into a single mouthful, so too a person of superior knowledge, of clear knowledge, thinks, 'What is there to attain absorption in, in this limited object? This is no burden for me.' Thinking thus, one masters those forms and attains absorption. The meaning is: one causes the mind to reach absorption here simultaneously with the arising of the sign. 'I know, I see': by this, their advertence is described. And that is described for one who has emerged from the attainment, not while within the attainment. 'Is one of such perception' means: one is of such perception both by the perception of advertence and by the perception of jhāna. Indeed, for them, the perception of mastery exists even within the attainment, but the perception of advertence exists only for one who has emerged from the attainment.

Appamāṇānīti vaḍḍhitappamāṇāni, mahantānīti attho. Abhibhuyyāti ettha pana yathā mahagghaso [V 3.0182] puriso ekaṃ bhattavaḍḍhitakaṃ labhitvā “aññāpi hotu, aññāpi hotu, kimesā mayhaṃ karissatī”ti taṃ na mahantato passati, evameva ñāṇuttaro puggalo visadañāṇo “kimettha samāpajjitabbaṃ, nayidaṃ appamāṇaṃ, na mayhaṃ cittekaggatākaraṇe bhāro atthī”ti tāni abhibhavitvā samāpajjati, saha nimittuppādenevettha appanaṃ pāpetīti attho.

'Immeasurable' means of developed measure, that is, vast; this is the meaning. Here, in 'mastering': just as a big eater, having received one serving of food, says, 'Let there be another, and another! What will this do for me?' and so does not regard it as much, in the same way, a person of superior knowledge, of clear knowledge, thinks: 'What is there to attain absorption in here? This is not immeasurable. There is no burden for me in producing one-pointedness of mind.' Thinking thus, one masters those forms and attains absorption. The meaning is: one causes the mind to reach absorption here simultaneously with the arising of the sign.

Ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññīti alābhitāya vā anatthikatāya vā ajjhattarūpe parikammasaññāvirahito. Eko [P 3.0259] bahiddhā rūpāni passatīti yassa parikammampi nimittampi bahiddhāva uppannaṃ, so evaṃ bahiddhā parikammassa ceva appanāya ca vasena – “ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passatī”ti vuccati. Sesamettha catutthābhibhāyatane vuttanayameva. Imesu pana catūsu parittaṃ vitakkacaritavasena āgataṃ, appamāṇaṃ mohacaritavasena, suvaṇṇaṃ dosacaritavasena, dubbaṇṇaṃ rāgacaritavasena. Etesañhi etāni sappāyāni. Sā ca nesaṃ sappāyatā vitthārato visuddhimaggecariyaniddese vuttā.

One not perceiving form internally means being devoid of the perception of preliminary work regarding internal form, either due to not having obtained the counterpart sign or due to not desiring it. One sees forms externally refers to one for whom both the preliminary work and the sign have arisen only externally. Thus, by means of both the preliminary work and the absorption that have arisen externally, one is called 'one not perceiving form internally, who sees forms externally.' The remainder here is according to the method stated in the fourth base of mastery. Furthermore, among these four, the limited comes by way of one with a discursive temperament; the immeasurable, by way of one with a deluded temperament; the beautiful-colored, by way of one with a hateful temperament; and the ugly-colored, by way of one with a lustful temperament. Indeed, for these persons, these respective objects are suitable. And their suitability is explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga, in the Exposition of Temperaments.

Pañcamaabhibhāyatanādīsu nīlānīti sabbasaṅgāhikavasena vuttaṃ. Nīlavaṇṇānīti vaṇṇavasena. Nīlanidassanānīti nidassanavasena. Apaññāyamānavivarāni asambhinnavaṇṇāni ekanīlāneva hutvā dissantīti vuttaṃ [M 3.0179] hoti. Nīlanibhāsānīti idaṃ pana obhāsavasena vuttaṃ, nīlobhāsāni nīlapabhāyuttānīti attho. Etena nesaṃ suvisuddhataṃ dasseti. Visuddhavaṇṇavaseneva hi imāni cattāri abhibhāyatanāni vuttāni. Umāpupphanti etañhi pupphaṃ siniddhaṃ muduṃ dissamānampi nīlameva hoti. Girikaṇṇikapupphādīni pana dissamānāni setadhātukāni honti. Tasmā idameva gahitaṃ, na tāni. Bārāṇaseyyakanti bārāṇasiyaṃ bhavaṃ. Tattha kira kappāsopi mudu, suttakantikāyopi tantavāyāpi chekā, udakampi suci siniddhaṃ, tasmā vatthaṃ ubhatobhāgavimaṭṭhaṃ hoti, dvīsu passesu maṭṭhaṃ mudu siniddhaṃ khāyati. Pītānītiādīsu [P 3.0260] imināva nayena attho veditabbo. “Nīlakasiṇaṃ uggaṇhanto nīlasmiṃ nimittaṃ gaṇhāti pupphasmiṃ vā vatthasmiṃ vā vaṇṇadhātuyā vā”tiādikaṃ panettha kasiṇakaraṇañceva parikammañca appanāvidhānañca sabbaṃ visuddhimagge vitthārato vuttameva.

In the fifth base of mastery and so forth, nīlāni (blue ones) is said in a comprehensive sense. Nīlavaṇṇāni (blue in color) is said in the sense of color. Nīlanidassanāni (blue in appearance) is said in the sense of appearance. This means that they appear without any discernible gaps, of unmixed color, being purely blue. Nīlanibhāsāni (blue in radiance), however, is said in the sense of luminosity; the meaning is that they have a blue radiance, being endowed with a blue luster. By this, it shows their extreme purity. Indeed, these four bases of mastery are described solely by way of pure color. The umā flower, for instance, though it appears smooth and soft, is purely blue. Flowers like the girikaṇṇikā, however, while appearing blue, have a white element. Therefore, only the former is taken, not the latter. Bārāṇaseyyakaṃ means that which is from Bārāṇasī. There, it is said, the cotton is soft, the spinners and weavers are skilled, and the water is pure and smooth; therefore, the cloth is polished on both sides, appearing smooth, soft, and glossy on both sides. In the case of pītāni (yellow ones) and so forth, the meaning should be understood in this same way. Here, all that pertains to the making of the kasiṇa, the preliminary work, and the method of absorption—such as, 'One apprehending the blue kasiṇa takes the sign in something blue, whether in a flower, a cloth, or a color element'—is explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga.

Abhiññāvosānapāramippattāti ito pubbesu satipaṭṭhānādīsu te dhamme bhāvetvā arahattappattāva [V 3.0183] abhiññāvosānapāramippattā nāma honti, imesu pana aṭṭhasu abhibhāyatanesu ciṇṇavasībhāvāyeva abhiññāvosānapāramippattā nāma.

Those who have reached the perfection culminating in direct knowledge: In contexts prior to this, such as the foundations of mindfulness, only those who have developed those dhammas and attained Arahantship are called 'those who have reached the perfection culminating in direct knowledge.' In the context of these eight bases of mastery, however, they are so called simply through the state of having practiced mastery.

250. Kasiṇakathāyaṃ sakalaṭṭhena kasiṇāni, tadārammaṇānaṃ dhammānaṃ khettaṭṭhena adhiṭṭhānaṭṭhena vā āyatanāni. Uddhanti upari gaganatalābhimukhaṃ. Adhoti heṭṭhā bhūmitalābhimukhaṃ. Tiriyanti khettamaṇḍalamiva samantā paricchinditvā. Ekacco hi uddhameva kasiṇaṃ vaḍḍheti, ekacco adho, ekacco samantato. Tena tena kāraṇena evaṃ pasāreti ālokamiva rūpadassanakāmo. Tena vuttaṃ – “pathavīkasiṇameko sañjānāti uddhaṃadhotiriya”nti. Advayanti disāanudisāsu advayaṃ. Idaṃ pana ekassa aññabhāvānupagamanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Yathā hi udakaṃ paviṭṭhassa sabbadisāsu udakameva [P 3.0261] hoti anaññaṃ, evamevaṃ pathavīkasiṇaṃ pathavīkasiṇameva hoti, natthi tassa añño kasiṇasambhedoti. Esa nayo sabbattha. Appamāṇanti idaṃ tassa tassa pharaṇaappamāṇavasena vuttaṃ. Tañhi cetasā pharanto sakalameva pharati, ayamassa ādi, idaṃ majjhanti pamāṇaṃ gaṇhātīti. Viññāṇakasiṇanti cettha [M 3.0180] kasiṇugghāṭimākāse pavattaṃ viññāṇaṃ. Tattha kasiṇavasena kasiṇugghāṭimākāse, kasiṇugghāṭimākāsavasena tattha pavattaviññāṇe uddhaṃadhotiriyatā veditabbā. Ayamettha saṅkhepo. Kammaṭṭhānabhāvanānayena panetāni pathavīkasiṇādīni vitthārato visuddhimagge vuttāneva. Idhāpi ciṇṇavasibhāveneva abhiññāvosānapāramippattā hontīti veditabbā. Tathā ito anantaresu catūsu jhānesu. Yaṃ panettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ mahāassapurasutte vuttameva.

250. In the discussion on kasiṇas, they are called kasiṇas in the sense of 'whole' or 'entire.' They are called āyatanas (bases) in the sense of being a 'field' or a 'foundation' for the mental states that take them as an object. Uddhaṃ (upward) means above, toward the expanse of the sky. Adho (downward) means below, toward the surface of the earth. Tiriyaṃ (across) means having demarcated all around, like a circular field. For one person expands the kasiṇa only upward, another downward, and another all around. For this or that reason, one expands it thus, like one desiring to see forms with the divine eye spreads light. Therefore it is said: 'One perceives the earth kasiṇa upward, downward, and across.' Advayaṃ (non-dual) means it is not two in the cardinal and intermediate directions. This, however, is said to show that one kasiṇa does not pass into the state of another. For just as for one who has entered water, there is only water and nothing else in all directions, so too, the earth kasiṇa is only the earth kasiṇa; there is no admixture of another kasiṇa for it. This is the method in all cases. Appamāṇaṃ (immeasurable) is said by way of the immeasurability of the pervasion of each respective kasiṇa. For when pervading it with the mind, one pervades it entirely; one does not grasp a measure, thinking, 'This is its beginning, this is its middle.' Regarding viññāṇakasiṇa (consciousness kasiṇa), this is the consciousness that occurs in the space from which the kasiṇa has been removed. Therein, the state of being upward, downward, and across should be understood in the space from which the kasiṇa has been removed (by way of the kasiṇa), and in the consciousness that occurs there (by way of the space from which the kasiṇa has been removed). This is the summary here. However, these meditation subjects, the earth kasiṇa and so on, are explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga according to the method of developing meditation subjects. Here too, it should be understood that through practiced mastery, they are 'those who have reached the perfection culminating in direct knowledge.' The same applies to the four jhānas that follow this. Whatever should be said here has already been stated in the Mahāassapura Sutta.

252. Vipassanāñāṇe pana rūpītiādīnamattho vuttoyeva. Ettha sitamettha paṭibaddhanti ettha cātumahābhūtike kāye nissitañca paṭibaddhañca. Subhoti sundaro. Jātimāti suparisuddhaākarasamuṭṭhito. Suparikammakatoti suṭṭhu kataparikammo apanītapāsāṇasakkharo. Acchoti tanucchavi. Vippasannoti suṭṭhu vippasanno. Sabbākārasampannoti dhovana vedhanādīhi sabbehi ākārehi sampanno. Nīlantiādīhi [P 3.0262] vaṇṇasampattiṃ dasseti. Tādisañhi āvutaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti.

252. Regarding insight knowledge, the meaning of rūpī and so on has already been stated. Here, sitamettha paṭibaddhaṃ (dependent here, bound here) means it is both dependent on and bound to this body composed of the four great elements. Subho means beautiful. Jātimā means arisen from a perfectly pure source. Suparikammakato means well-worked, with stones and gravel removed. Accho means of thin skin. Vippasanno means very clear. Sabbākārasampanno means endowed with all aspects, such as polishing, boring, and so on. By terms like nīlaṃ (blue) and so on, it shows the perfection of the thread's color. Indeed, such a strung thread becomes manifest.

Evameva khoti ettha evaṃ upamāsaṃsandanaṃ veditabbaṃ – maṇi viya hi karajakāyo. Āvutasuttaṃ [V 3.0184] viya vipassanāñāṇaṃ. Cakkhumā puriso viya vipassanālābhī bhikkhu. Hatthe karitvā paccavekkhato “ayaṃ kho maṇī”ti maṇino āvibhūtakālo viya vipassanāñāṇaṃ abhinīharitvā nisinnassa bhikkhuno cātumahābhūtikakāyassa āvibhūtakālo. “Tatridaṃ suttaṃ āvuta”nti suttassa āvibhūtakālo viya vipassanāñāṇaṃ abhinīharitvā nisinnassa bhikkhuno tadārammaṇānaṃ phassapañcamakānaṃ vā sabbacittacetasikānaṃ vā vipassanāñāṇasseva vā āvibhūtakāloti.

Just so, here the connection of the simile should be understood thus: the physical body is like the gem. Insight-knowledge is like the threaded string. The monk who has obtained insight is like the man with sight. Just as the time of the gem's manifestation to one who, having placed it in his hand, reflects, 'This is indeed a gem,' so too is the time of the manifestation of the physical body composed of the four great elements to the monk seated, having directed insight-knowledge. Just as the time of the thread's manifestation is understood in the phrase 'Herein this thread is threaded through it,' so too is the time of the manifestation of either the states which have that as their object, with contact as the fifth, or of all consciousness and mental factors, or of insight-knowledge itself, to the monk seated, having directed insight-knowledge.

Kiṃ panetaṃ ñāṇassa āvibhūtaṃ, puggalassāti. Ñāṇassa, tassa pana āvibhāvattā puggalassa āvibhūtāva honti. Idañca vipassanāñāṇaṃ maggassa anantaraṃ, evaṃ santepi yasmā abhiññāvāre āraddhe etassa antarāvāro natthi, tasmā idheva dassitaṃ. Yasmā ca aniccādivasena akatasammasanassa dibbāya sotadhātuyā bheravasaddaṃ suṇanto pubbenivāsānussatiyā bherave khandhe anussarato dibbena cakkhunā bheravarūpaṃ [M 3.0181] passato bhayasantāso uppajjati, na aniccādivasena katasammasanassa, tasmā abhiññāpattassa bhayavinodakahetusampādanatthampi idaṃ idheva dassitaṃ. Idhāpi arahattavaseneva abhiññāvosānapāramippattatā veditabbā.

But is this manifest to knowledge, or to the person? To knowledge. But because of its manifestation to that knowledge, things are indeed manifest to the person. And this insight-knowledge is immediately after the path. Even so, because when the section on supernormal knowledge is undertaken, there is no intervening turn for this, therefore it is shown right here. And because for one who has not performed comprehension by way of impermanence, etc., fear and terror arise when hearing a terrifying sound with the divine ear-element, or recollecting terrifying aggregates with the recollection of past lives, or seeing a terrifying form with the divine eye, but not for one who has performed comprehension by way of impermanence, etc.; therefore, also for the purpose of accomplishing the cause for dispelling fear for one who has attained supernormal knowledge, this is shown right here. Here too, the attainment of the perfection of the culmination of supernormal knowledge should be known as being by way of Arahantship.
