253. Manomayiddhiyaṃ [P 3.0263] ciṇṇavasitāya. Tattha manomayanti manena nibbattaṃ. Sabbaṅgapaccaṅginti sabbehi aṅgehi ca paccaṅgehi ca samannāgataṃ. Ahīnindriyanti saṇṭhānavasena avikalindriyaṃ. Iddhimatā nimmitarūpañhi sace iddhimā odāto, tampi odātaṃ. Sace aviddhakaṇṇo, tampi aviddhakaṇṇanti evaṃ sabbākārehi tena sadisameva hoti. Muñjamhā īsikantiādi upamattayampi taṃ sadisabhāvadassanatthameva vuttaṃ. Muñjasadisā eva hi tassa anto īsikā hoti. Kosasadisoyeva asi, vaṭṭāya kosiyā vaṭṭaṃ asimeva pakkhipanti, patthaṭāya patthaṭaṃ.

253. In the discourse on mind-made psychic power, this is attained through practiced mastery. Herein, 'mind-made' means produced by the mind. 'Complete in all its major and minor limbs' means endowed with all major limbs and minor limbs. 'With faculties unimpaired' means with faculties unimpaired by way of its form. For a form created by one with psychic power, if the one with psychic power is fair, that form is also fair. If he has unpierced ears, that form also has unpierced ears. Thus, in all aspects, it is just like him. The three similes beginning with 'a reed from muñja grass' are spoken only to show this state of being alike. For the reed within it is just like the muñja grass. The sword is just like the scabbard; into a round scabbard they insert only a round sword, into a flat one, a flat one.

Karaṇḍāti idampi ahikañcukassa nāmaṃ, na vilīvakaraṇḍakassa. Ahikañcuko hi ahinā sadisova hoti. Tattha kiñcāpi “puriso ahiṃ karaṇḍā uddhareyyā”ti hatthena uddharamāno viya dassito, atha kho cittenevassa uddharaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Ayañhi ahi nāma sajātiyaṃ [V 3.0185] ṭhito, kaṭṭhantaraṃ vā rukkhantaraṃ vā nissāya, tacato sarīranikkaḍḍhanapayogasaṅkhātena thāmena, sarīraṃ khādamānaṃ viya purāṇatacaṃ jigucchantoti imehi catūhi kāraṇehi sayameva kañcukaṃ jahāti, na sakkā tato aññena uddharituṃ. Tasmā cittena uddharaṇaṃ sandhāya idaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Iti muñjādisadisaṃ imassa bhikkhuno sarīraṃ, īsikādisadisaṃ nimmitarūpanti idamettha opammasaṃsandanaṃ. Nimmānavidhānaṃ [P 3.0264] panettha parato ca iddhividhādipañcaabhiññākathā sabbākārena visuddhimagge vitthāritāti tattha vuttanayeneva veditabbā. Upamāmattameva hi idha adhikaṃ.

The word 'karaṇḍa' is also a name for a snake’s slough, not for a bamboo basket. For a snake’s slough is just like the snake. Herein, although it is shown as if a man were drawing a snake from its slough with his hand, yet its drawing out should be known as being by the mind. For this snake, being established among its own kind, relying on the space between logs or trees, by the strength called the effort of pulling the body from the skin, and being disgusted with the old skin as if it were biting its body—by these four causes, it sheds the slough by itself. It cannot be drawn out by any means other than these. Therefore, it should be known that this was said in reference to drawing it out with the mind. Thus: 'This monk’s body is like the muñja grass, etc.; the created form is like the reed, etc.'—this is the connection of the simile and its object here. The method of creation, and hereafter the discourse on the five supernormal knowledges beginning with the kinds of psychic power, are elaborated in all aspects in the Visuddhimagga; thus, they should be known by the method stated there. For only the simile is additional here.

Tattha chekakumbhakārādayo viya iddhividhañāṇalābhī bhikkhu daṭṭhabbo. Suparikammakatamattikādayo viya iddhividhañāṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Icchiticchitabhājanavikatiādikaraṇaṃ viya tassa bhikkhuno vikubbanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Idhāpi ciṇṇavasitāvaseneva abhiññāvosānapāramippattatā veditabbā. Tathā ito parāsu catūsu abhiññāsu.

Herein, the monk who has obtained the knowledge of the kinds of psychic power should be regarded as like a skilled potter, etc. The knowledge of the kinds of psychic power should be regarded as like well-prepared clay, etc. That monk's transformation should be regarded as like the making of various vessels, etc., as desired. Here too, the attainment of the perfection of the culmination of supernormal knowledge should be known as being only by way of practiced mastery. Likewise in the four subsequent supernormal knowledges.

255. Tattha [M 3.0182] dibbasotadhātuupamāyaṃ saṅkhadhamoti saṅkhadhamako. Appakasirenevāti niddukkheneva. Viññāpeyyāti jānāpeyya. Tattha evaṃ cātuddisā viññāpente saṅkhadhamake “saṅkhasaddo aya”nti vavatthāpentānaṃ sattānaṃ tassa saṅkhasaddassa āvibhūtakālo viya yogino dūrasantikabhedānaṃ dibbānañceva mānusakānañca saddānaṃ āvibhūtakālo daṭṭhabbo.

255. Therein, in the simile of the divine ear-element, 'saṅkhadhamo' means a conch-blower. 'Appakasireneva' means without difficulty. 'Viññāpeyya' means would cause to know. Therein, just as for beings who determine, 'This is the sound of a conch,' it is the time of the manifestation of that conch sound when the conch-blower thus makes it known in the four directions, so too, for the yogī, the time of the manifestation of sounds, divine and human, distinguished as far and near, should be regarded.

256. Cetopariyañāṇa-upamāyaṃ daharoti taruṇo. Yuvāti yobbanena samannāgato. Maṇḍanakajātikoti yuvāpi samāno na alasiyo kiliṭṭhavatthasarīro, atha kho maṇḍanakapakatiko, divasassa dve tayo vāre nhāyitvā suddhavattha-paridahana-alaṅkārakaraṇasīloti attho. Sakaṇikanti [P 3.0265] kāḷatilakavaṅka-mukhadūsipīḷakādīnaṃ aññatarena sadosaṃ. Tattha yathā tassa mukhanimittaṃ paccavekkhato mukhadoso pākaṭo hoti, evaṃ cetopariyañāṇāya cittaṃ abhinīharitvā nisinnassa bhikkhuno paresaṃ soḷasavidhaṃ cittaṃ pākaṭaṃ hotīti veditabbaṃ. Pubbenivāsaupamādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ mahāassapure vuttameva.

256. In the simile of the knowledge of encompassing minds, 'daharo' means young. 'Yuvā' means endowed with youth. 'Maṇḍanakajātiko' means: though being a youth, he is not lazy with a body clad in soiled garments, but rather is of a decorative nature, having the habit of bathing two or three times a day, wearing clean clothes, and adorning himself—this is the meaning. 'Sakaṇikaṃ' means having a defect with one or another of things like a black mole, a white mole, a freckle, or a pimple. Therein, just as for him, when reflecting on the image of his face, any defect on the face becomes manifest, so too, it should be known that for the monk seated, having directed his mind for the knowledge of encompassing minds, the sixteen-fold mind of others becomes manifest. Whatever is to be said on the similes of recollection of past lives, etc., all that has been said in the Mahā-assapura Sutta.

259. Ayaṃ kho udāyi pañcamo dhammoti ekūnavīsati pabbāni paṭipadāvasena ekaṃ dhammaṃ [V 3.0186] katvā pañcamo dhammoti vutto. Yathā hi aṭṭhakanāgarasutte (ma. ni. 2.17 ādayo) ekādasa pabbāni pucchāvasena ekadhammo kato, evamidha ekūnavīsati pabbāni paṭipadāvasena eko dhammo katoti veditabbāni. Imesu ca pana ekūnavīsatiyā pabbesu paṭipāṭiyā aṭṭhasu koṭṭhāsesu vipassanāñāṇe ca āsavakkhayañāṇe ca arahattavasena abhiññāvosānapāramippattatā veditabbā, sesesu ciṇṇavasibhāvavasena. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

259. This, Udāyi, is the fifth teaching—thus, the nineteen sections, by way of practice, having been made into a single teaching, are called the fifth teaching. For just as in the Aṭṭhakanāgara Sutta, eleven sections were made into a single teaching by way of questions, so here, the nineteen sections are made into a single teaching by way of practice—this should be understood. And among these nineteen sections, in the eight portions in sequence, the state of having reached the ultimate perfection of direct knowledge should be understood in insight knowledge and in the knowledge of the destruction of the taints by way of the fruit of Arahantship; in the remaining sections, it should be understood by way of the state of cultivated mastery. The rest is clear everywhere.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

Of the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary to the Majjhima Nikāya.

Mahāsakuludāyisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Mahāsakuludāyi Sutta is concluded.

8. Samaṇamuṇḍikasuttavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Samaṇamuṇḍika Sutta

260. Evaṃ [V 3.0187][M 3.0183] me sutanti samaṇamuṇḍikasuttaṃ. Tattha uggāhamānoti tassa paribbājakassa nāmaṃ. Sumanoti pakatināmaṃ. Kiñci kiñci pana uggahituṃ uggāhetuṃ samatthatāya uggāhamānoti naṃ sañjānanti. Samayaṃ [P 3.0266] pavadanti etthāti samayappavādakaṃ. Tasmiṃ kira ṭhāne caṅkītārukkhapokkharasātippabhutayo brāhmaṇā nigaṇṭhācelakaparibbājakādayo ca pabbajitā sannipatitvā attano attano samayaṃ pavadanti kathenti dīpenti, tasmā so ārāmo samayappavādakoti vuccati. Sveva tindukācīrasaṅkhātāya timbarūsakarukkhapantiyā parikkhittattā tindukācīraṃ. Yasmā panettha paṭhamaṃ ekā sālā ahosi, pacchā mahāpuññaṃ poṭṭhapādaparibbājakaṃ nissāya bahū sālā katā, tasmā tameva ekaṃ sālaṃ upādāya laddhanāmavasena ekasālakoti vuccati. Mallikāya pana pasenadirañño deviyā uyyānabhūto so pupphaphalasañchanno ārāmoti katvā mallikāya ārāmoti saṅkhaṃ gato. Tasmiṃ samayappavādake tindukācīre ekasālake mallikāya ārāme. Paṭivasatīti vāsaphāsutāya vasati. Divā divassāti divasassa divā nāma majjhanhātikkamo, tasmiṃ divasassapi divābhūte atikkantamatte majjhanhike nikkhamīti attho. Paṭisallīnoti tato tato rūpādigocarato cittaṃ paṭisaṃharitvā līno, jhānaratisevanavasena ekībhāvaṃ gato. Manobhāvanīyānanti manavaḍḍhanakānaṃ, ye [P 3.0267] āvajjato manasikaroto cittaṃ vinīvaraṇaṃ hoti unnamati vaḍḍhati. Yāvatāti yattakā. Ayaṃ tesaṃ aññataroti ayaṃ tesaṃ abbhantaro eko sāvako. Appeva nāmāti tassa upasaṅkamanaṃ patthayamāno āha. Patthanākāraṇaṃ pana sandakasutte vuttameva.

260. Thus have I heard—this is the Samaṇamuṇḍika Sutta. Therein, 'Uggāhamāna' is the name of that wanderer. 'Sumana' is his ordinary name. But because he was capable of learning and teaching whatever little thing, they knew him as Uggāhamāna. 'They proclaim their doctrines there'—hence it is called 'Samayappavādaka' (the Proclamation of Doctrines). At that place, it is said, brahmins such as Caṅkī, Tārukkha, and Pokkharasāti, and renunciants such as Nigaṇṭhas and cloth-wearing wanderers, would gather and each would proclaim, discuss, and explain their own doctrines. Therefore, that park was called 'Samayappavādaka'. That same park, because it was enclosed by a row of Timbarūsaka trees known as Tindukācīra, was also called Tindukācīra. Because at first there was only one hall there, and later, relying on the greatly meritorious wanderer Poṭṭhapāda, many halls were built, it is called 'Ekasālaka' (the Single Hall) by way of the name it received based on that one hall. And because it was a park belonging to Queen Mallikā, the consort of King Pasenadi, a park covered with flowers and fruits, it came to be known as 'Mallikā’s Park'. At that Samayappavādaka, Tindukācīra, Ekasālaka, in Mallikā’s Park. 'He dwells' means he resides there comfortably. 'By day, in the day' means the day's day, that is, the passing of midday. Thus, the meaning is that he would emerge after the midday period had just passed. 'Secluded' means having withdrawn his mind from sense objects such as forms, he remains absorbed, having attained oneness by way of cultivating delight in jhāna. 'Mind-developing' means causing the mind to grow; by attending to which and considering which, the mind becomes free from hindrances, is uplifted, and increases. 'As far as' means to whatever extent. 'This is one of them' means this is one of their inner disciples. 'Perhaps' means he spoke while desiring his approach. The reason for this desire, moreover, is as explained in the Sandaka Sutta.

261. Etadavocāti dandapañño ayaṃ gahapati, dhammakathāya naṃ saṅgaṇhitvā attano sāvakaṃ karissāmīti maññamāno etaṃ “catūhi kho”tiādivacanaṃ avoca. Tattha paññapemīti dassemi ṭhapemi. Sampannakusalanti paripuṇṇakusalaṃ. Paramakusalanti uttamakusalaṃ. Ayojjhanti vādayuddhena yujjhitvā cāletuṃ asakkuṇeyyaṃ acalaṃ nikkampaṃ thiraṃ. Na [M 3.0184] karotīti akaraṇamattameva [V 3.0188] vadati, ettha pana saṃvarappahānaṃ vā paṭisevanappahānaṃ vā na vadati. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo.

261. 'He said this'—thinking, 'This householder is of slow wisdom; I will win him over with a Dhamma discourse and make him my disciple,' he spoke these words beginning with 'By four things...'. Therein, 'I declare' means 'I show' or 'I establish'. 'Perfect in the wholesome' means a person completely perfect in the wholesome. 'Supremely wholesome' means a person of ultimate wholesomeness. 'Unassailable' means one who cannot be shaken by engaging in argumentative debate—immovable, unwavering, firm. 'He does not do' means he speaks only of not doing; here, however, he does not speak of abandonment through restraint or abandonment through use. The same method applies to the remaining phrases.

Neva abhinandīti titthiyā nāma jānitvāpi ajānitvāpi yaṃ vā taṃ vā vadantīti maññamāno nābhinandi. Na paṭikkosīti sāsanassa anulomaṃ viya pasannākāraṃ viya vadatīti maññamāno na paṭisedheti.

'He neither approved'—thinking, 'Sectarians, whether knowing or not, say whatever they please,' he did not approve. 'Nor did he reject'—thinking, 'He speaks as if in conformity with the Teaching, as if with a clear manner,' he did not oppose.

262. Yathā uggāhamānassāti yathā tassa vacanaṃ, evaṃ sante uttānaseyyako kumāro ayojjhasamaṇo thirasamaṇo bhavissati, mayaṃ pana evaṃ na vadāmāti dīpeti. Kāyotipi na hotīti sakakāyo parakāyotipi visesañāṇaṃ na hoti. Aññatra [P 3.0268] phanditamattāti paccattharaṇe valisamphassena vā maṅguladaṭṭhena vā kāyaphandanamattaṃ nāma hoti. Taṃ ṭhapetvā aññaṃ kāyena karaṇakammaṃ nāma natthi. Tampi ca kilesasahagatacitteneva hoti. Vācātipi na hotīti micchāvācā sammāvācātipi nānattaṃ na hoti. Roditamattāti jighacchāpipāsāparetassa pana roditamattaṃ hoti. Tampi kilesasahagatacitteneva. Saṅkappoti micchāsaṅkappo sammāsaṅkappotipi nānattaṃ na hoti. Vikūjitamattāti vikūjitamattaṃ rodanahasitamattaṃ hoti. Daharakumārakānañhi cittaṃ atītārammaṇaṃ pavattati, nirayato āgatā nirayadukkhaṃ saritvā rodanti, devalokato āgatā hasanti, tampi kilesasahagatacitteneva hoti. Ājīvoti micchājīvo sammājīvotipi nānattaṃ na hoti. Aññatra mātuthaññāti thaññacoradārakā nāma honti, mātari khīraṃ pāyantiyā apivitvā aññavihitakāle piṭṭhipassena āgantvā thaññaṃ pivanti. Ettakaṃ muñcitvā añño micchājīvo natthi. Ayampi kilesasahagatacitteneva hotīti dasseti.

262. 'According to Uggāhamāna' means: according to his word, if that were so, an infant lying on its back would be an unassailable ascetic, a steadfast ascetic. But we, however, do not speak thus—this is what he clarifies. 'There is no body either' means there is no discriminating knowledge of 'own body' and 'other's body'. 'Except for mere movement' means there is only the movement of the body due to contact with the folds of the bedding or a bedbug's bite. Apart from that, there is no action to be done by the body. And that too occurs only with a mind accompanied by defilements. 'There is no speech either' means there is no distinction such as 'wrong speech' and 'right speech'. 'Only crying' means for one afflicted by hunger and thirst, there is only crying. That too is only with a mind accompanied by defilements. 'Intention' means there is no distinction such as 'wrong intention' and 'right intention'. 'Only whimpering' means there is only crying and laughing. For the minds of young children operate on past objects: those who have come from hell cry remembering the suffering of hell; those who have come from the heavenly world laugh remembering divine bliss. That too occurs only with a mind accompanied by defilements. 'Livelihood' means there is no distinction such as 'wrong livelihood' and 'right livelihood'. 'Except for mother's milk' means there are children who are milk-thieves: when their mother is giving milk, they do not drink, but when she is otherwise engaged, they come from behind and drink the milk. Apart from this much, there is no other wrong livelihood. This too occurs only with a mind accompanied by defilements—this is shown.

263. Evaṃ paribbājakavādaṃ paṭikkhipitvā idāni sayaṃ sekkhabhūmiyaṃ mātikaṃ ṭhapento catūhi kho ahantiādimāha. Tattha samadhigayha tiṭṭhatīti visesetvā tiṭṭhati. Na [P 3.0269] kāyena pāpa kammantiādīsu na kevalaṃ akaraṇamattameva, bhagavā pana ettha saṃvarappahānapaṭisaṅkhā paññapeti. Taṃ [M 3.0185] sandhāyevamāha. Na ceva sampannakusalantiādi pana khīṇāsavaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ.

263. Thus, having refuted the wanderer's doctrine, now, wishing to establish the matrix in the learner's stage, He Himself said the words beginning with, 'By four things...' Therein, 'stands having comprehended' means 'stands having distinguished.' In 'does no evil deed with the body,' etc., it is not merely a matter of not doing; but indeed, the Blessed One here lays down restraint, abandoning, and reflection. Referring to this, He spoke thus. But the words beginning with 'not accomplished in wholesome qualities' were spoken with reference to one whose taints are destroyed.

Idāni [V 3.0189] asekkhabhūmiyaṃ mātikaṃ ṭhapento dasahi kho ahantiādimāha. Tattha tīṇi padāni nissāya dve paṭhamacatukkā ṭhapitā, ekaṃ padaṃ nissāya dve pacchimacatukkā. Ayaṃ sekkhabhūmiyaṃ mātikā.

Now, wishing to establish the matrix in the non-learner's stage, He said the words beginning with, 'By ten things...' Therein, based on three terms, two first tetrads were established; based on one term, two last tetrads were established. This is the matrix that came in the learner's stage.

264. Idāni taṃ vibhajanto katame ca thapati akusalasīlātiādimāha. Tattha sarāganti aṭṭhavidhaṃ lobhasahagatacittaṃ. Sadosanti paṭighasampayuttacittadvayaṃ. Samohanti vicikicchuddhaccasahagatacittadvayampi vaṭṭati, sabbākusalacittānipi. Moho sabbākusale uppajjatīti hi vuttaṃ. Itosamuṭṭhānāti ito sarāgādicittato samuṭṭhānaṃ uppatti etesanti itosamuṭṭhānā.

264. Now, wishing to analyze it, the Blessed One said the words beginning with, 'And what, householder, are the unwholesome moral disciplines?' Therein, 'with lust' is the eightfold consciousness accompanied by greed. 'With hate' is the pair of consciousnesses associated with aversion. 'With delusion' can mean the pair of consciousnesses accompanied by doubt and restlessness, and it is also suitable for all unwholesome consciousnesses. For indeed, it is said: 'Delusion arises in all that is unwholesome.' As for 'arising from this': because for these unwholesome states, the origin is from this consciousness accompanied by lust, etc., they are called 'arising from this'.

Kuhinti kataraṃ ṭhānaṃ pāpuṇitvā aparisesā nirujjhanti. Ettheteti sotāpattiphale bhummaṃ. Pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlañhi sotāpattiphale paripuṇṇaṃ hoti, taṃ ṭhānaṃ patvā akusalasīlaṃ asesaṃ nirujjhati. Akusalasīlanti ca dussīlassetaṃ adhivacananti veditabbaṃ.

As for 'where?': 'Having reached what state do they cease without remainder?' As for 'here': this is the locative case used in the sense of the fruit of stream-entry. For indeed, the moral discipline of Pātimokkha restraint is perfected in the fruit of stream-entry; having reached that state, unwholesome moral discipline ceases without remainder. And it should be known that 'unwholesome moral discipline' is a designation for one of immoral conduct.

Akusalānaṃ sīlānaṃ nirodhāya paṭipannoti ettha yāva sotāpattimaggā nirodhāya paṭipanno nāma hoti, phalapatte pana te nirodhitā nāma honti.

Herein, in the phrase 'practicing for the cessation of unwholesome moral disciplines': up to the path of stream-entry, one is called 'one practicing for cessation'; but upon attainment of the fruit, they are called 'ceased'.

265. Vītarāgantiādīhi [P 3.0270] aṭṭhavidhaṃ kāmāvacarakusalacittameva vuttaṃ. Etena hi kusalasīlaṃ samuṭṭhāti.

265. By the words beginning with 'free from lust,' only the eightfold wholesome sense-sphere consciousness is spoken of. For by this, wholesome moral discipline arises.

Sīlavā hotīti sīlasampanno hoti guṇasampanno ca. No ca sīlamayoti alamettāvatā, natthi ito kiñci uttari karaṇīyanti evaṃ sīlamayo na hoti. Yatthassa teti arahattaphale bhummaṃ. Arahattaphalañhi patvā akusalasīlaṃ asesaṃ nirujjhati.

'He is virtuous' means he is endowed with virtue and endowed with good qualities. And he is not 'one made of virtue' in the sense of thinking, 'This much is enough; there is nothing further to be done.' As for 'where they...': this is the locative case used in the sense of the fruit of Arahantship. For indeed, having attained the fruit of Arahantship, unwholesome moral discipline ceases without remainder.

Nirodhāya paṭipannoti ettha yāva arahattamaggā nirodhāya paṭipanno nāma hoti, phalapatte pana te nirodhitā nāma honti.

Herein, in the phrase 'practicing for cessation': up to the path of Arahantship, one is called 'one practicing for cessation'; but upon attainment of the fruit, they are called 'ceased'.

266. Kāmasaññādīsu [V 3.0190] kāmasaññā aṭṭhalobhasahagatacittasahajātā, itarā dve domanassasahagatacittadvayena sahajātā.

266. Among the perceptions beginning with sensual perception, sensual perception is co-nascent with the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed; the other two are co-nascent with the pair of consciousnesses accompanied by displeasure.

Paṭhamaṃ [M 3.0186] jhānanti anāgāmiphalapaṭhamajjhānaṃ. Ettheteti anāgāmiphale bhummaṃ. Anāgāmiphalañhi patvā akusalasaṅkappā aparisesā nirujjhanti.

'The first jhāna' means the first jhāna associated with the fruit of non-returning. As for 'here': this is the locative case used in the sense of the fruit of non-returning. For indeed, having attained the fruit of non-returning, unwholesome intentions cease without remainder.

Nirodhāya paṭipannoti ettha yāva anāgāmimaggā nirodhāya paṭipanno nāma hoti, phalapatte pana te nirodhitā nāma honti. Nekkhammasaññādayo hi tissopi aṭṭhakāmāvacarakusalasahajātasaññāva.

Herein, in the phrase 'practicing for cessation': up to the path of non-returning, one is called 'one practicing for cessation'; but upon attainment of the fruit, they are called 'ceased.' For indeed, the three perceptions beginning with the perception of renunciation are themselves perceptions co-nascent with the eight wholesome sense-sphere consciousnesses.

267. Ettheteti arahattaphale bhummaṃ. Dutiyajjhānikaṃ arahattaphalañhi pāpuṇitvā kusalasaṅkappā aparisesā nirujjhanti. Nirodhāya paṭipannoti ettha yāva arahattamaggā nirodhāya paṭipanno nāma hoti, phalapatte pana te nirodhitā nāma honti. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

267. As for 'here': this is the locative case used in the sense of the fruit of Arahantship. For indeed, having reached the fruit of Arahantship associated with the second jhāna, wholesome intentions cease without remainder. Herein, in the phrase 'practicing for cessation': up to the path of Arahantship, one is called 'one practicing for cessation'; but upon attainment of the fruit, they are called 'ceased.' The rest is clear everywhere.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary to the Majjhima Nikāya.

Samaṇamuṇḍikasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Samaṇamuṇḍika Sutta is concluded.

9. Cūḷasakuludāyisuttavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Cūḷasakuludāyi Sutta

270. Evaṃ [V 3.0191][P 3.0271] me sutanti cūḷasakuludāyisuttaṃ. Tattha yadā pana, bhante, bhagavāti idaṃ paribbājako dhammakathaṃ sotukāmo bhagavato dhammadesanāya sālayabhāvaṃ dassento āha.

270. 'Thus have I heard'—this is the Cūḷasakuludāyi Sutta. Therein, the wanderer, desiring to hear a Dhamma talk and showing his fondness for the Blessed One's Dhamma exposition, said the words, 'When, venerable sir, the Blessed One...'

271. Taṃyevettha paṭibhātūti sace dhammaṃ sotukāmo, tuyhevettha eko pañho ekaṃ kāraṇaṃ upaṭṭhātu. Yathā maṃ paṭibhāseyyāti yena kāraṇena mama dhammadesanā upaṭṭhaheyya, etena hi kāraṇena kathāya samuṭṭhitāya sukhaṃ dhammaṃ desetunti dīpeti. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhanteti so kira taṃ disvā – “sace bhagavā idha abhavissā, ayametassa bhāsitassa atthoti dīpasahassaṃ viya ujjalāpetvā ajja me pākaṭaṃ akarissā”ti dasabalaṃyeva anussari. Tasmā tassa mayhaṃ, bhantetiādimāha. Tattha aho nūnāti anussaraṇatthe nipātadvayaṃ. Tena tassa bhagavantaṃ anussarantassa etadahosi “aho nūna bhagavā aho nūna sugato”ti. Yo imesanti yo imesaṃ dhammānaṃ. Sukusaloti suṭṭhu [M 3.0187] kusalo nipuṇo cheko. So bhagavā aho nūna katheyya, so sugato aho nūna katheyya, tassa hi bhagavato pubbenivāsañāṇassa anekāni kappakoṭisahassāni ekaṅgaṇāni pākaṭānīti, ayamettha adhippāyo.

271. The phrase 'Let that itself become clear here' means: 'If you desire to hear the Dhamma, let a single question, a single reason, occur to you in this matter.' The phrase 'So that it may become clear to me' indicates: 'By whatever reason my Dhamma exposition might arise, for indeed, when a talk has arisen from a reason, it is easy for me to teach the Dhamma.' As for 'To me, venerable sir...': it is said that he constantly recollected the Ten-Powered One, thinking: 'If the Blessed One were here, he would illuminate the meaning of this statement like a thousand lamps, making it manifest to me today.' Therefore, he spoke the words beginning with 'To me, venerable sir...' Therein, 'aho nūna' is a pair of particles in the sense of recollection. Through this, as he was recollecting the Blessed One, this thought occurred to him: 'Oh, if only the Blessed One... Oh, if only the Sugata...' As for 'He who among these...': this means 'He who, among these dhammas...' 'Highly skilled' means exceedingly skilled, subtle, expert. 'Oh, if only that Blessed One would speak! Oh, if only that Sugata would speak! For to the knowledge of past abodes of that Blessed One, many thousands of koṭis of kappas are manifest as if in a single courtyard.' This is the intended meaning here.

Tassa vāhaṃ pubbantaṃ ārabbhāti yo hi lābhī hoti, so “pubbe tvaṃ khattiyo ahosi, brāhmaṇo ahosī”ti vutte jānanto [P 3.0272] sakkaccaṃ sussūsati. Alābhī pana – “evaṃ bhavissati evaṃ bhavissatī”ti sīsakampamettameva dasseti. Tasmā evamāha – “tassa vāhaṃ pubbantaṃ ārabbha pañhassa veyyākaraṇena cittaṃ ārādheyya”nti.

As for 'Or I, concerning the past...': For a person who has obtained this knowledge, when it is said, 'Formerly, you were a khattiya; you were a brahmin,' he, knowing this, listens respectfully. But a person who has not obtained it, thinking, 'It might be so, it might be so,' shows only a mere shaking of the head. Therefore, he said: 'I could satisfy his mind with an explanation to a question concerning the past.'

So vā maṃ aparantanti dibbacakkhulābhino hi anāgataṃsañāṇaṃ ijjhati, tasmā evamāha. Itaraṃ pubbe vuttanayameva.

As for 'Or he, concerning the future...': For one who has obtained the divine eye, knowledge of the future is accomplished; therefore, he spoke thus. The other part is according to the method already stated previously.

Dhammaṃ [V 3.0192] te desessāmīti ayaṃ kira atīte desiyamānepi na bujjhissati, anāgate desiyamānepi na bujjhissati. Athassa bhagavā saṇhasukhumaṃ paccayākāraṃ desetukāmo evamāha. Kiṃ pana taṃ bujjhissatīti? Etaṃ pageva na bujjhissati, anāgate panassa vāsanāya paccayo bhavissatīti disvā bhagavā evamāha.

Regarding the statement, 'I will teach you the Dhamma': Indeed, this person will not understand even when taught about the past, nor will he understand when taught about the future. Then the Blessed One, desiring to teach him the gentle and subtle doctrine of dependent origination, spoke thus. But will he understand it? What need is there to say? He will not understand it. Nevertheless, seeing that in a future existence it will become a condition for his latent tendencies, the Blessed One spoke thus.

Paṃsupisācakanti asuciṭṭhāne nibbattapisācaṃ. So hi ekaṃ mūlaṃ gahetvā adissamānakāyo hoti. Tatridaṃ vatthu – ekā kira yakkhinī dve dārake thūpārāmadvāre nisīdāpetvā āhārapariyesanatthaṃ nagaraṃ gatā. Dārakā ekaṃ piṇḍapātikattheraṃ disvā āhaṃsu, – “bhante, amhākaṃ mātā anto nagaraṃ paviṭṭhā, tassā vadeyyātha ‘yaṃ vā taṃ vā laddhakaṃ, gahetvā sīghaṃ gaccha, dārakā te jighacchitaṃ sandhāretuṃ na sakkontī’”ti. Tamahaṃ kathaṃ passissāmīti? Idaṃ, bhante, gaṇhathāti ekaṃ mūlakhaṇḍaṃ adaṃsu. Therassa anekāni yakkhasahassāni paññāyiṃsu, so dārakehi dinnasaññāṇena taṃ yakkhiniṃ addasa virūpaṃ bībhacchaṃ kevalaṃ vīthiyaṃ gabbhamalaṃ paccāsīsamānaṃ. Disvā tamatthaṃ kathesi[P 3.0273]. Kathaṃ maṃ tvaṃ passasīti vutte mūlakhaṇḍaṃ dassesi, sā acchinditvā gaṇhi. Evaṃ paṃsupisācakā ekaṃ mūlaṃ gahetvā adissamānakāyā honti. Taṃ sandhāyesa “paṃsupisācakampi [M 3.0188] na passāmī”ti āha. Na pakkhāyatīti na dissati na upaṭṭhāti.

The term 'paṃsupisācakaṃ' refers to an earth-demon, a demon born in an impure place. For by taking hold of a certain medicinal root, its body becomes invisible. Herein is the story: A certain female yakkha, having seated her two children at the gate of the Thūpārāma, went into the city to search for food. The children, seeing an alms-faring elder, said, 'Venerable sir, our mother has entered the city. Please tell her: "Whatever you have obtained, take it and come quickly. Your children are afflicted by hunger and cannot endure it."' 'How shall I see her?' he asked. 'Venerable sir, take this,' they said, and gave him a piece of a medicinal root. To the elder, many thousands of yakkhas appeared. By the sign given by the children, he saw that female yakkha—deformed, hideous, in the street merely longing for the impurities of the womb. Seeing her, he told her their message. When she asked, 'How do you see me?' he showed her the piece of the root. She snatched it away from him. In this way, earth-demons, by taking hold of a certain root, become invisible. It is with reference to this that he said, 'I do not even see an earth-demon.' 'Na pakkhāyati' means it is not seen, it does not appear.

272. Dīghāpi kho te esāti udāyi esā tava vācā dīghāpi bhaveyya, evaṃ vadantassa vassasatampi vassasahassampi pavatteyya, na ca atthaṃ dīpeyyāti adhippāyo. Appāṭihīrakatanti aniyyānikaṃ amūlakaṃ niratthakaṃ sampajjatīti attho.

272. Regarding 'Dīghāpi kho te esā': Udāyi, this speech of yours could be long. One could go on speaking like this for a hundred years or even a hundred thousand years and still not illuminate the meaning. This is the intention. 'Appāṭihīrakataṃ' means it becomes unleading, baseless, and fruitless. This is the meaning.

Idāni taṃ vaṇṇaṃ dassento seyyathāpi, bhantetiādimāha. Tattha paṇḍukambale nikkhittoti visabhāgavaṇṇe rattakambale ṭhapito. Evaṃvaṇṇo attā hotīti idaṃ so subhakiṇhadevaloke nibbattakkhandhe sandhāya – “amhākaṃ matakāle attā subhakiṇhadevaloke khandhā viya jotetī”ti vadati.

Now, wishing to show that appearance, he spoke the words beginning with 'Seyyathāpi, bhante...' Therein, 'placed on a pale woolen blanket' means placed on a red blanket of a contrasting color. As for the words 'Of such an appearance is the self,' he says this with reference to the aggregates that have arisen in the Subhakiṇha deva-world: 'At the time of our death, the self shines just as the aggregates in the Subhakiṇha deva-world shine.'

273. Ayaṃ [V 3.0193] imesaṃ ubhinnanti so kira yasmā maṇissa bahi ābhā na niccharati, khajjopanakassa aṅguladvaṅgulacaturaṅgulamattaṃ niccharati, mahākhajjopanakassa pana khaḷamaṇḍalamattampi niccharatiyeva, tasmā evamāha.

273. Regarding 'Ayaṃ imesaṃ ubhinnaṃ': It is said that because the radiance of a jewel does not exit outwards, while the radiance of a firefly exits to the measure of one, two, or four finger-breadths, and the radiance of a large firefly indeed exits to the measure of a threshing floor, therefore he spoke thus.

Viddheti ubbiddhe, meghavigamena dūrībhūteti attho. Vigatavalāhaketi apagatameghe. Deveti ākāse. Osadhitārakāti [P 3.0274] sukkatārakā. Sā hi yasmā tassā udayato paṭṭhāya tena saññāṇena osadhāni gaṇhantipi pivantipi, tasmā “osadhitārakā”ti vuccati. Abhido aḍḍharattasamayanti abhinne aḍḍharattasamaye. Iminā gaganamajjhe ṭhitacandaṃ dasseti. Abhido majjhanhikepi eseva nayo.

The word 'viddhe' means 'pierced through'; the meaning is 'become distant due to the dispersal of clouds.' 'Vigatavalāhake' means 'with clouds departed.' 'Deve' means in the sky. 'Osadhitārakā' is the morning star. For it is said that because, from its rising, they gather and drink medicinal herbs by that sign, it is called the 'herb star.' 'Abhido aḍḍharattasamayaṃ' means at the undivided time of midnight. By this is shown the moon standing in the middle of the sky. This same method should be understood for 'abhido majjhanhike' as well.

Ato khoti ye anubhonti, tehi bahutarā, bahū ceva bahutarā cāti attho. Ābhā nānubhontīti obhāsaṃ na vaḷañjanti, attano sarīrobhāseneva ālokaṃ pharitvā viharanti.

Regarding 'Ato kho,' the meaning is: they are more numerous than those who make use of the light; they are many, and they are very many. 'Ābhā nānubhonti' means they do not make use of that radiance; they dwell pervading the space with light solely by means of their own bodily radiance.

274. Idāni yasmā so “ekantasukhaṃ lokaṃ pucchissāmī”ti nisinno, pucchāmūḷho pana jāto, tasmā naṃ bhagavā taṃ pucchaṃ sarāpento kiṃ pana, udāyi, atthi ekantasukho lokotiādimāha. Tattha [M 3.0189] ākāravatīti kāraṇavatī. Aññataraṃ vā pana tapoguṇanti acelakapāḷiṃ sandhāyāha, surāpānaviratīti attho.

274. Now, because he sat down thinking, 'I will ask about the world of exclusive happiness,' but then became confused in his questioning, the Blessed One, reminding him of that question, spoke the words beginning with, 'But, Udāyin, is there a world of exclusive happiness?' Herein, 'ākāravatī' means 'kāraṇavatī,' that is, a practice possessing a cause. The phrase 'or some other ascetic quality' is said with reference to the passage on naked ascetics; the meaning is 'abstinence from intoxicants.'

275. Katamā pana sā, bhante, ākāravatī paṭipadā ekantasukhassāti kasmā pucchati? Evaṃ kirassa ahosi – “mayaṃ sattānaṃ ekantasukhaṃ vadāma, paṭipadaṃ pana kālena sukhaṃ kālena dukkhaṃ vadāma. Ekantasukhassa kho pana attano paṭipadāyapi ekantasukhāya bhavitabbaṃ. Amhākaṃ kathā aniyyānikā, satthu kathāva niyyānikā”ti. Idāni satthāraṃyeva pucchitvā jānissāmīti tasmā pucchati.

275. Why does he ask, 'Venerable sir, what is that practice with its cause for the world of exclusive happiness?' It is said that this occurred to him: 'We speak of exclusive happiness for beings, but as for the practice, we say it is at times pleasant and at times painful. Surely, for that which is exclusively happiness, its practice should also be exclusively for happiness. Our teaching is not a way of escape, whereas the Teacher's teaching is a way of escape.' Thinking, 'Now I will ask the Teacher himself and I will know,' he therefore asks.

Ettha [P 3.0275] mayaṃ anassāmāti etasmiṃ kāraṇe mayaṃ anassāma. Kasmā pana evamāhaṃsu? Te kira pubbe pañcasu dhammesu patiṭṭhāya kasiṇaparikammaṃ katvā tatiyajjhānaṃ nibbattetvā aparihīnajjhānā kālaṃ katvā subhakiṇhesu nibbattantīti jānanti, gacchante gacchante pana kāle [V 3.0194] kasiṇaparikammampi na jāniṃsu, tatiyajjhānampi nibbattetuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu. Pañca pubbabhāgadhamme pana “ākāravatī paṭipadā”ti uggahetvā tatiyajjhānaṃ “ekantasukho loko”ti uggaṇhiṃsu. Tasmā evamāhaṃsu. Uttaritaranti ito pañcahi dhammehi uttaritaraṃ paṭipadaṃ vā tatiyajjhānato uttaritaraṃ ekantasukhaṃ lokaṃ vā na jānāmāti vuttaṃ hoti. Appasadde katvāti ekappahāreneva mahāsaddaṃ kātuṃ āraddhe nissadde katvā.

'Herein we are not satisfied' means 'In this matter, we are not satisfied.' But why did they say so? It is said that they know that formerly, having established themselves in the five qualities and done the preliminary kasiṇa practice, having generated the third jhāna, and having died without falling from that jhāna, they are reborn in the Subhakiṇha realm. But as time went on, they no longer knew even the preliminary kasiṇa practice, nor were they able to generate the third jhāna. However, having learned the five preliminary factors as 'the practice with its cause,' they learned that the third jhāna is 'the world of exclusive happiness.' Therefore, they spoke thus. 'More excellent' means: 'We do not know a practice more excellent than these five qualities, or a world of exclusive happiness more excellent than the third jhāna.' 'Having made them quiet' means: having silenced the assembly that had started to make a great noise all at once.

276. Sacchikiriyāhetūti ettha dve sacchikiriyā paṭilābhasacchikiriyā ca paccakkhasacchikiriyā ca. Tattha tatiyajjhānaṃ nibbattetvā aparihīnajjhāno kālaṃ katvā subhakiṇhaloke tesaṃ devānaṃ samānāyuvaṇṇo hutvā nibbattati, ayaṃ paṭilābhasacchikiriyā nāma. Catutthajjhānaṃ nibbattetvā iddhivikubbanena subhakiṇhalokaṃ gantvā tehi devehi saddhiṃ santiṭṭhati sallapati sākacchaṃ āpajjati, ayaṃ paccakkhasacchikiriyā nāma. Tāsaṃ dvinnampi tatiyajjhānaṃ ākāravatī paṭipadā nāma. Tañhi anuppādetvā neva sakkā subhakiṇhaloke nibbattituṃ, na catutthajjhānaṃ uppādetuṃ. Iti duvidhampetaṃ sacchikiriyaṃ sandhāya – “etassa nūna, bhante, ekantasukhassa lokassa sacchikiriyāhetū”ti āha.

276. Herein, regarding 'for the sake of realization,' there are two kinds of realization: realization by attainment and realization by direct perception. Of these, when one generates the third jhāna and, without falling away from that jhāna, passes away and is reborn in the Subhakiṇha world with the same lifespan and appearance as those devas, this is called realization by attainment. When one generates the fourth jhāna and, by means of psychic transformation, goes to the Subhakiṇha world and stands, converses, and enters into discussion with those devas, this is called realization by direct perception. For both of these, the third jhāna is called the practice possessing the mode. For without having generated it, it is not possible to be reborn in the Subhakiṇha world, nor is it possible to generate the fourth jhāna. Thus, with reference to both these kinds of realization, it was said: 'Surely, venerable sir, this is for the sake of realizing this world of exclusive happiness.'

277. Udañcanikoti [M 3.0190] udakavārako. Antarāyamakāsīti yathā pabbajjaṃ na labhati, evaṃ upaddutamakāsi yathā taṃ upanissayavipannaṃ. Ayaṃ kira kassapabuddhakāle pabbajitvā samaṇadhammamakāsi. Athassa eko sahāyako bhikkhu sāsane anabhirato, “āvuso, vibbhamissāmī”ti [P 3.0276] ārocesi. So tassa pattacīvare lobhaṃ uppādetvā gihibhāvāya vaṇṇaṃ abhāsi. Itaro tassa pattacīvaraṃ datvā vibbhami. Tenassa kammunā idāni bhagavato sammukhā pabbajjāya antarāyo jāto. Bhagavatā panassa purimasuttaṃ atirekabhāṇavāramattaṃ, idaṃ bhāṇavāramattanti ettakāya tantiyā dhammo kathito, ekadesanāyapi maggaphalapaṭivedho na jāto, anāgate panassa paccayo bhavissatīti bhagavā dhammaṃ deseti. Anāgate paccayabhāvañcassa disvā bhagavā dharamāno ekaṃ bhikkhumpi mettāvihārimhi etadagge na ṭhapesi. Passati hi bhagavā – “anāgate ayaṃ mama sāsane pabbajitvā mettāvihārīnaṃ aggo bhavissatī”ti.

277. 'A small water pot' means a water-vessel. 'He made an obstacle' means he created a danger such that he would not receive ordination; he acted in such a way that his supporting condition was destroyed. It is said that this person went forth during the time of the Buddha Kassapa and practiced the ascetic's duties. Then a certain companion monk of his became dissatisfied with the Dispensation and announced, 'Friend, I will disrobe.' Having developed greed for that monk's bowl and robes, he spoke in praise of the lay life. The other monk gave him his bowl and robes and disrobed. Because of that kamma, an obstacle to his ordination has now arisen in the presence of the Blessed One. However, the Dhamma was taught to him by the Blessed One with a text of this much length: the previous sutta being more than a recitation-portion long, and this one being a recitation-portion long. Yet even with a single discourse, the penetration of path and fruit did not occur. But thinking, 'In the future, there will be a condition for him,' the Blessed One taught the Dhamma. And seeing that there would be a condition for him in the future, the Blessed One, while he was living, did not place even a single monk as foremost among those who dwell in loving-kindness. For the Blessed One sees: 'In the future, this one will go forth in my Dispensation and will become the foremost of those who dwell in loving-kindness.'

So bhagavati parinibbute dhammāsokarājakāle pāṭaliputte nibbattitvā pabbajitvā arahattappatto [V 3.0195] assaguttatthero nāma hutvā mettāvihārīnaṃ aggo ahosi. Therassa mettānubhāvena tiracchānagatāpi mettacittaṃ paṭilabhiṃsu, thero sakalajambudīpe bhikkhusaṅghassa ovādācariyo hutvā vattanisenāsane āvasi, tiṃsayojanamattā aṭavī ekaṃ padhānagharaṃ ahosi. Thero ākāse cammakhaṇḍaṃ pattharitvā tattha nisinno kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathesi. Gacchante gacchante kāle bhikkhācārampi agantvā vihāre nisinno kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathesi, manussā vihārameva gantvā dānamadaṃsu. Dhammāsokarājā therassa guṇaṃ sutvā daṭṭhukāmo tikkhattuṃ pahiṇi. Thero bhikkhusaṅghassa ovādaṃ dammīti ekavārampi na gatoti.

After the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna, during the time of King Dhammāsoka, he was reborn in Pāṭaliputta. Having gone forth, he attained arahantship, became known as the Elder Assagutta, and was the foremost of those who dwell in loving-kindness. Through the Elder's power of loving-kindness, even animals gained a mind of loving-kindness. The Elder became the instructing teacher for the Saṅgha of monks in all of Jambudīpa and dwelt in the Vattani monastery. A forest of about thirty yojanas became as a single meditation hall. The Elder would spread a piece of leather in the sky, and sitting there, he taught the meditation subject. As time went on, without even going for alms, he would sit in the monastery and teach the meditation subject. People would go to the monastery itself to give offerings. King Dhammāsoka, hearing of the Elder's virtue and wishing to see him, sent for him three times. The Elder, saying, 'I am giving instruction to the Saṅgha of monks,' did not go even once.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

The Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Cūḷasakuludāyisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Cūḷasakuludāyi Sutta is concluded.

10. Vekhanasasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Vekhanasa Sutta

278. Evaṃ [V 3.0196][P 3.0277][M 3.0191] me sutanti vekhanasasuttaṃ. Tattha vekhanasoti ayaṃ kira sakuludāyissa ācariyo, so “sakuludāyī paribbājako paramavaṇṇapañhe parājito”ti sutvā “mayā so sādhukaṃ uggahāpito, tenāpi sādhukaṃ uggahitaṃ, kathaṃ nu kho parājito, handāhaṃ sayaṃ gantvā samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ paramavaṇṇapañhaṃ pucchitvā jānissāmī”ti rājagahato pañcacattālīsayojanaṃ sāvatthiṃ gantvā yena bhagavā, tenupasaṅkami, upasaṅkamitvā pana ṭhitakova bhagavato santike udānaṃ udānesi. Tattha purimasadisaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

278. The Vekhanasa Sutta begins with 'Thus have I heard.' Therein, as to 'Vekhanasa,' he, it is said, was the teacher of Sakuludāyi. Having heard that 'the wanderer Sakuludāyi was defeated in the question concerning the supreme complexion,' he thought: 'He was well taught by me, and he too learned well. How then was he defeated? Come now, I shall go myself, ask the ascetic Gotama the question concerning the supreme complexion, and find out.' So he traveled from Rājagaha, a distance of forty-five yojanas, to Sāvatthi, and approached the Blessed One. Having approached, while still standing in the Blessed One's presence, he uttered an inspired utterance. Therein, what is similar to the previous sutta should be understood in the same way as was stated.

280. Pañca kho imeti kasmā ārabhi? Agāriyopi ekacco kāmagaruko kāmādhimutto hoti, ekacco nekkhammagaruko nekkhammādhimutto hoti. Pabbajitopi ca ekacco kāmagaruko kāmādhimutto hoti, ekacco nekkhammagaruko nekkhammādhimutto hoti. Ayaṃ pana kāmagaruko kāmādhimutto hoti. So imāya kathāya kathiyamānāya attano kāmādhimuttattaṃ sallakkhessati, evamassāyaṃ desanā sappāyā bhavissatīti imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi. Kāmaggasukhanti nibbānaṃ adhippetaṃ.

280. Why was [the teaching] 'These five...' begun? Among householders, some are devoted to sensual pleasures, intent on sensual pleasures, while others are devoted to renunciation, intent on renunciation. And among those who have gone forth, some are devoted to sensual pleasures, intent on sensual pleasures, while others are devoted to renunciation, intent on renunciation. This one, however, is devoted to sensual pleasures, intent on sensual pleasures. While this discourse is being spoken, he will recognize his own intentness on sensual pleasures, and thus this teaching will be suitable for him. Thinking thus, the Blessed One began this teaching. By the term 'the ultimate sensual happiness' (kāmaggasukhaṃ), Nibbāna is intended.

281. Pāpito [P 3.0278] bhavissatīti ajānanabhāvaṃ pāpito bhavissati. Nāmakaṃyeva sampajjatīti niratthakavacanamattameva sampajjati. Tiṭṭhatu pubbanto tiṭṭhatu aparantoti yasmā tuyhaṃ atītakathāya anucchavikaṃ pubbenivāsañāṇaṃ natthi, anāgatakathāya anucchavikaṃ dibbacakkhuñāṇaṃ natthi, tasmā ubhayampetaṃ tiṭṭhatūti āha. Suttabandhanehīti suttamayabandhanehi. Tassa hi ārakkhatthāya hatthapādesu ceva gīvāya ca suttakāni bandhanti. Tāni sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Mahallakakāle panassa tāni sayaṃ vā pūtīni hutvā muñcanti, chinditvā vā haranti.

281. By 'he will be brought' (pāpito bhavissati) is meant that he will be brought to a state of not knowing. By 'it becomes a mere name' (nāmakaṃyeva sampajjati) is meant that it becomes merely meaningless words. By 'let the past stand, let the future stand' (tiṭṭhatu pubbanto tiṭṭhatu aparanto) is meant: since you have no knowledge of past lives suitable for speaking of the past, nor the divine eye knowledge suitable for speaking of the future, therefore he says, 'Let both of these stand.' By 'with bonds of thread' (suttabandhanehi) is meant with bonds made of thread. For that child's protection, they bind small threads on his hands and feet, and also on his neck. This was said with reference to those. But when he is older, those threads either become rotten and are released by themselves, or they are cut off and removed.

Evameva [V 3.0197] khoti iminā idaṃ dasseti – daharassa kumārassa suttabandhanānaṃ ajānanakālo viya avijjāya purimāya koṭiyā ajānanaṃ, na hi sakkā avijjāya purimakoṭi ñātuṃ, mocanakāle jānanasadisaṃ pana [M 3.0192] arahattamaggena avijjābandhanassa pamokkho jātoti jānanaṃ. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

By 'just so' this is shown: just as for a young boy there is a time of not knowing about his bonds of thread, so too is the not knowing of the prior end of ignorance; for it is not possible to know the prior end of ignorance. At the time of release, however, it is like knowing: 'Through the path of arahantship, release from the bond of ignorance has occurred.' The rest is clear in every case.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Vekhanasasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Vekhanasa Sutta is concluded.

Tatiyavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Third Chapter is concluded.

4. Rājavaggo

4. The Chapter on Kings

1. Ghaṭikārasuttavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Ghaṭikāra Sutta

282. Evaṃ [V 3.0198][M 3.0193] me sutanti ghaṭikārasuttaṃ. Tattha sitaṃ pātvākāsīti mahāmaggena gacchanto aññataraṃ bhūmippadesaṃ oloketvā – “atthi nu kho mayā cariyaṃ caramānena imasmiṃ ṭhāne nivutthapubba”nti āvajjanto addasa [P 3.0279] – “kassapabuddhakāle imasmiṃ ṭhāne vegaḷiṅgaṃ nāma gāmanigamo ahosi, ahaṃ tadā jotipālo nāma māṇavo ahosiṃ, mayhaṃ sahāyo ghaṭikāro nāma kumbhakāro ahosi, tena saddhiṃ mayā idha ekaṃ sukāraṇaṃ kataṃ, taṃ bhikkhusaṅghassa apākaṭaṃ paṭicchannaṃ, handa naṃ bhikkhusaṅghassa pākaṭaṃ karomī”ti maggā okkamma aññatarasmiṃ padese ṭhitakova sitapātukammamakāsi, aggaggadante dassetvā mandahasitaṃ hasi. Yathā hi lokiyamanussā uraṃ paharantā – “kuhaṃ kuha”nti hasanti, na evaṃ buddhā, buddhānaṃ pana hasitaṃ haṭṭhapahaṭṭhākāramattameva hoti.

282. Thus have I heard. This is the Ghaṭikāra Sutta. Herein, by 'manifested a smile' is meant that while proceeding along the great road, he surveyed a certain region of land and reflected: 'While I was practicing the conduct, have I ever dwelt in this place before?' Then he saw: 'During the time of the Buddha Kassapa, there was a village-town named Vegaḷiṅga here. At that time, I was a young man named Jotipāla, and my companion was a potter named Ghaṭikāra. Together with him, a good deed was done by me here. That is not manifest, is concealed, from the Sangha of bhikkhus. Well then, I shall make it manifest to the Sangha of bhikkhus.' Having thus reflected, he stepped off the road, and standing in a certain place, he performed the act of manifesting a smile; he smiled a gentle smile, showing the very tips of his teeth. For just as worldly people laugh, striking their chests and saying, 'Kuhaṃ, kuhaṃ,' Buddhas do not laugh in that way. Rather, the smile of the Buddhas is merely an expression of joy and delight.

Hasitañca nāmetaṃ terasahi somanassasahagatacittehi hoti. Tattha lokiyamahājano akusalato catūhi, kāmāvacarakusalato catūhīti aṭṭhahi cittehi hasati, sekkhā akusalato diṭṭhisampayuttāni dve apanetvā chahi cittehi hasanti, khīṇāsavā catūhi sahetukakiriyacittehi ekena ahetukakiriyacittenāti pañcahi cittehi hasanti. Tesupi balavārammaṇe āpāthagate dvīhi ñāṇasampayuttacittehi hasanti, dubbalārammaṇe duhetukacittadvayena ca ahetukacittena cāti tīhi cittehi hasanti. Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne kiriyāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātusomanassasahagatacittaṃ bhagavato haṭṭhapahaṭṭhākāramattaṃ hasitaṃ uppādesi.

And this act of smiling arises with thirteen types of consciousness accompanied by joy. Herein, the great mass of worldly people laugh with eight types of consciousness: four from the unwholesome and four from the sense-sphere wholesome. Trainees, having removed the two associated with wrong view from the unwholesome, laugh with six types of consciousness. Those whose cankers are destroyed laugh with five types of consciousness: four rooted functional consciousnesses and one rootless functional consciousness. Among these, when a strong object has come into range, they smile with two types of consciousness associated with knowledge; when a weak object has come into range, they smile with three types of consciousness: the pair of two-rooted consciousnesses and the rootless consciousness. In this instance, however, the functional, rootless, mind-consciousness-element accompanied by joy produced the Blessed One's smile, which is merely an expression of delight.

Taṃ [V 3.0199] panetaṃ hasitaṃ evaṃ appamattakampi therassa pākaṭaṃ ahosi. Kathaṃ? Tathārūpe hi kāle tathāgatassa catūhi dāṭhāhi catuddīpikamahāmeghamukhato sateratāvijjulatā viya virocamānā mahātālakkhandhapamāṇā rasmivaṭṭiyo [P 3.0280] uṭṭhahitvā tikkhattuṃ sīsavaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā [M 3.0194] dāṭhaggesuyeva antaradhāyanti. Tena saññāṇena āyasmā ānando bhagavato pacchato gacchamānopi sitapātubhāvaṃ jānāti.

But that smile, even though so slight, became manifest to the Elder. How? For at such a time, from the four canine teeth of the Tathāgata, shining like a sateratā lightning-vine from the mouth of a great cloud covering the four continents, bands of rays the size of a great palmyra trunk arise, circumambulate the excellent head three times to the right, and vanish right at the tips of the canine teeth. By that sign, the Venerable Ānanda, even while walking behind the Blessed One, knows of the smile's manifestation.

Bhagavantaṃ etadavocāti – “ettha kira kassapo bhagavā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ ovadi, catusaccappakāsanaṃ akāsi, bhagavatopi ettha nisīdituṃ ruciṃ uppādessāmi, evamayaṃ bhūmibhāgo dvīhi buddhehi paribhutto bhavissati, mahājano gandhamālādīhi pūjetvā cetiyaṭṭhānaṃ katvā paricaranto saggamaggaparāyaṇo bhavissatī”ti cintetvā etaṃ “tena hi, bhante,”tiādivacanaṃ avoca.

As for 'he said this to the Blessed One': having thought, 'Here, it is said, the Blessed One Kassapa instructed the Sangha of bhikkhus and made the proclamation of the Four Truths. I will cause an inclination to arise in our Blessed One also to sit here. Thus, this portion of the earth will have been used by two Buddhas. The great populace, having made offerings with perfumes, garlands, and so on, and having made it a place for a cetiya, while attending to it, will have the path to heaven as their destination,' he spoke those words beginning with, 'Well then, venerable sir.'

283. Muṇḍakena samaṇakenāti muṇḍaṃ muṇḍoti, samaṇaṃ vā samaṇoti vattuṃ vaṭṭati, ayaṃ pana aparipakkañāṇattā brāhmaṇakule uggahitavohāravaseneva hīḷento evamāha. Sottisināninti sinānatthāya katasottiṃ. Sotti nāma kuruvindapāsāṇacuṇṇāni lākhāya bandhitvā kataguḷikakalāpakā vuccati, yaṃ sandhāya – “tena kho pana samayena chabbaggiyā bhikkhū kuruvindakasuttiyā nahāyantī”ti (cūḷava. 243) vuttaṃ. Taṃ ubhosu antesu gahetvā sarīraṃ ghaṃsanti. Evaṃ sammāti yathā etarahipi manussā “cetiyavandanāya gacchāma, dhammassavanatthāya gacchāmā”ti vuttā ussāhaṃ na karonti, “naṭasamajjādidassanatthāya gacchāmā”ti vuttā pana ekavacaneneva sampaṭicchanti, tatheva [P 3.0281] sinhāyitunti vutte ekavacanena sampaṭicchanto evamāha.

283. As for 'by this shaveling ascetic': it is fitting to call a shaven person 'shaven' or an ascetic 'ascetic,' but this one, due to his immature knowledge and solely by the power of the speech he had learned in a brahmin family, spoke thus, wishing to show contempt. As for 'for a bath with a scrubbing-ball': a sotti made for the purpose of bathing. Sotti is the name for balls or bundles made by binding powder of kuruvinda stone with lac, with reference to which it is said: 'At that time, it is said, the group-of-six bhikkhus were bathing with a kuruvinda-string' (Cv.V.29.4). Holding that at both ends, they rub the body. As for 'So it is, friend': just as even now people, when told, 'Let us go to pay homage at a cetiya; let us go to listen to the Dhamma,' do not make an effort, but when told, 'Let us go to see a show of dancers,' they accept with a single word, just so, when 'Let us go bathe' was said, wishing to accept with a single word, he spoke thus.

284. Jotipālaṃ māṇavaṃ āmantesīti ekapasse ariyaparihārena paṭhamataraṃ nhāyitvā paccuttaritvā ṭhito tassa mahantena issariyaparihārena nhāyantassa nhānapariyosānaṃ āgametvā taṃ nivatthanivāsanaṃ kese vodake kurumānaṃ āmantesi. Ayanti āsannattā dassento āha. Ovaṭṭikaṃ vinivaṭṭhetvāti nāgabalo bodhisatto “apehi sammā”ti īsakaṃ parivattamānova tena gahitagahaṇaṃ vissajjāpetvāti attho. Kesesu parāmasitvā etadavocāti so kira cintesi – “ayaṃ [V 3.0200] jotipālo paññavā, sakiṃ dassanaṃ labhamāno tathāgatassa dassanepi pasīdissati, dhammakathāyapi pasīdissati, pasanno ca pasannākāraṃ kātuṃ sakkhissati, mittā nāma etadatthaṃ honti, yaṃkiñci katvā mama sahāyaṃ gahetvā dasabalassa santikaṃ gamissāmī”ti. Tasmā naṃ kesesu parāmasitvā etadavoca.

284. As for 'he addressed the young man Jotipāla': having first bathed on one side with the attendance befitting a noble one, he came out of the water and stood waiting for the end of the bathing of that one who was bathing with great lordly attendance. He addressed him as he was putting on his lower garment and making his hair free of water. As for 'This': he said this showing that the monastery was near. As for 'having shaken off his grip on the fold of his garment': the meaning is that the Bodhisatta, who had the strength of a royal elephant, saying, 'Away, friend!', while turning slightly, made him release his grip. As for 'having seized him by the hair, he said this': he, it is said, thought: 'This Jotipāla is wise. If he gets to see him once, he will gain confidence in the sight of the Tathāgata and also in the Dhamma talk. And having gained confidence, he will be able to show his confidence. It is for this purpose that friends exist. Having done whatever is necessary, I will take my companion and go to the presence of the Ten-Powered One.' Therefore, having seized him by the hair, he said this.

Ittarajaccoti [M 3.0195] aññajātiko, mayā saddhiṃ asamānajātiko, lāmakajātikoti attho. Na vatidanti idaṃ amhākaṃ gamanaṃ na vata orakaṃ bhavissati na khuddakaṃ, mahantaṃ bhavissati. Ayañhi na attano thāmena gaṇhi, satthu thāmena gaṇhīti gahaṇasmiṃyeva niṭṭhaṃ agamāsi. Yāvatādohipīti ettha dokārahikārapikārā nipātā, yāvatuparimanti attho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “vācāya ālapanaṃ ovaṭṭikāya gahaṇañca atikkamitvā yāva kesaggahaṇampi tattha gamanatthaṃ payogo kattabbo”ti.

As for 'of common birth' (ittarajacco): the meaning is of another birth, of a birth not equal with me, of a low birth. As for 'Surely this...' (na vata idaṃ): This going of ours will surely not be inferior, will not be small; it will be great. Truly, this one did not seize by his own strength; he seized by the Teacher's strength. Thus, he came to this conclusion right at the moment of the seizing. As for 'yāvatā do hi pi': here, the syllables 'do,' 'hi,' and 'pi' are particles. The meaning is 'as far as the utmost.' This is what is meant to be said: 'Having gone beyond calling with the voice and grasping the tucked-in hem of the lower garment, an effort must be made to go there, even up to the point of seizing the hair.'

285. Dhammiyā [P 3.0282] kathāyāti idha satipaṭilābhatthāya pubbenivāsapaṭisaṃyuttā dhammī kathā veditabbā. Tassa hi bhagavā, – “jotipāla, tvaṃ na lāmakaṭṭhānaṃ otiṇṇasatto, mahābodhipallaṅke pana sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ patthetvā otiṇṇosi, tādisassa nāma pamādavihāro na yutto”tiādinā nayena satipaṭilābhāya dhammaṃ kathesi. Parasamuddavāsītherā pana vadanti – “jotipāla, yathā ahaṃ dasapāramiyo pūretvā sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ paṭivijjhitvā vīsatisahassabhikkhuparivāro loke vicarāmi, evamevaṃ tvampi dasapāramiyo pūretvā sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ paṭivijjhitvā samaṇagaṇaparivāro loke vicarissasi. Evarūpena nāma tayā pamādaṃ āpajjituṃ na yutta”nti yathāssa pabbajjāya cittaṃ namati, evaṃ kāmesu ādīnavaṃ nekkhamme ca ānisaṃsaṃ kathesīti.

285. By 'a talk on the Dhamma' is meant: here, a Dhamma talk connected with previous existences for the purpose of gaining mindfulness should be understood. For the Blessed One taught him the Dhamma for the gaining of mindfulness by this method: 'Jotipāla, you are not a being who has descended to a low state; rather, you are one who has descended having aspired to the knowledge of omniscience at the great Bodhi-seat. For one such as you, heedless living is not suitable.' The elders dwelling beyond the sea, however, say: 'Jotipāla, just as I, having fulfilled the ten perfections and penetrated the knowledge of omniscience, wander the world surrounded by twenty thousand monks, so too will you, having fulfilled the ten perfections and penetrated the knowledge of omniscience, wander the world surrounded by a community of ascetics. It is not suitable for one such as you to fall into heedlessness.' Thus, He spoke of the danger in sensual pleasures and the benefit in renunciation in such a way that his mind inclined towards ordination.

286. Alattha kho, ānanda,…pe… pabbajjaṃ alattha upasampadanti pabbajitvā kimakāsi? Yaṃ bodhisattehi kattabbaṃ. Bodhisattā hi buddhānaṃ sammukhe pabbajanti. Pabbajitvā ca pana ittarasattā viya patitasiṅgā na honti, catupārisuddhisīle pana supatiṭṭhāya tepiṭakaṃ buddhavacanaṃ uggaṇhitvā terasa dhutaṅgāni samādāya araññaṃ pavisitvā gatapaccāgatavattaṃ pūrayamānā [V 3.0201] samaṇadhammaṃ karontā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā yāva anulomañāṇaṃ āhacca tiṭṭhanti, maggaphalatthaṃ vāyāmaṃ na karonti. Jotipālopi tatheva akāsi.

286. Regarding 'He obtained, Ānanda… he obtained the going forth, he obtained the higher ordination': Having gone forth, what did he do? He did that which is to be done by Bodhisattas. For Bodhisattas go forth in the presence of Buddhas. And having gone forth, they do not become like inferior beings with fallen horns; rather, being well-established in the fourfold purity of virtue, having learned the Tipiṭaka, the word of the Buddha, having undertaken the thirteen ascetic practices, having entered the forest, fulfilling the duty of going and returning, practicing the ascetic's duties, and developing insight, they reach and stand at the point of conformity-knowledge. They do not strive for the sake of the path and fruition. Jotipāla also did likewise.

287. Aḍḍhamāsupasampanneti kuladārakañhi pabbājetvā aḍḍhamāsampi avasitvā gate mātāpitūnaṃ soko na [P 3.0283] vūpasammati, sopi pattacīvaraggahaṇaṃ [M 3.0196] na jānāti, daharabhikkhusāmaṇerehi saddhiṃ vissāso na uppajjati, therehi saddhiṃ sineho na patiṭṭhāti, gatagataṭṭhāne anabhirati uppajjati. Ettakaṃ pana kālaṃ nivāse sati mātāpitaro passituṃ labhanti. Tena tesaṃ soko tanubhāvaṃ gacchati, pattacīvaraggahaṇaṃ jānāti, sāmaṇeradaharabhikkhūhi saddhiṃ vissāso jāyati, therehi saddhiṃ sineho patiṭṭhāti, gatagataṭṭhāne abhiramati, na ukkaṇṭhati. Tasmā ettakaṃ vasituṃ vaṭṭatīti aḍḍhamāsaṃ vasitvā pakkāmi.

287. Regarding 'having been ordained for half a month': For when a young man of good family is ordained and departs without having stayed for even half a month, the grief of his parents does not subside. He too does not know how to handle the bowl and robe; familiarity with the young monks and novices does not arise; affection with the elders is not established; and discontent arises in whatever place he goes. But when he resides for this much time, his parents get to see him. Because of that, their grief lessens. He learns how to handle the bowl and robe. Familiarity with the novices and young monks arises. Affection with the elders is established. He delights in whatever place he goes and is not dissatisfied. Therefore, thinking, 'It is proper to stay for this long,' he stayed for half a month and then departed.

Paṇḍupuṭakassa sālinoti puṭake katvā sukkhāpitassa rattasālino. Tassa kira sālino vappakālato paṭṭhāya ayaṃ parihāro – kedārā suparikammakatā honti, tattha bījāni patiṭṭhāpetvā gandhodakena siñciṃsu, vappakāle vitānaṃ viya upari vatthakilañjaṃ bandhitvā paripakkakāle vīhisīsāni chinditvā muṭṭhimatte puṭake katvā yottabaddhe vehāsaṃyeva sukkhāpetvā gandhacuṇṇāni attharitvā koṭṭhakesu pūretvā tatiye vasse vivariṃsu. Evaṃ tivassaṃ parivutthassa sugandharattasālino apagatakāḷake suparisuddhe taṇḍule gahetvā khajjakavikatimpi bhattampi paṭiyādiyiṃsu. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ paṇītaṃ khādanīyaṃ bhojanīyaṃ…pe… kālaṃ ārocāpesīti.

Regarding 'of sālī rice in pale bundles': This refers to red sālī rice that has been made into bundles and dried. It is said that from the time of sowing, this sālī rice received this care: the fields were well-prepared, and having established the seeds there, they sprinkled them with fragrant water. At the time of sowing, they tied a cloth mat above like a canopy. When it was ripe, they cut the heads of grain, made them into fist-sized bundles, tied them with cords, and dried them in the open air. Then, having sprinkled them with fragrant powders, they filled them into granaries and opened them in the third year. Thus, taking the perfectly pure grains, free from dark specks, of the fragrant red sālī rice that had been stored for three years, they prepared special hard foods and also boiled rice. Referring to this, it was said: 'excellent hard and soft food... he had the time announced.'

288. Adhivuṭṭho meti kiṃ sandhāya vadati? Vegaḷiṅgato [P 3.0284] nikkhamanakāle ghaṭikāro attano santike vassāvāsaṃ vasanatthāya paṭiññaṃ aggahesi, taṃ sandhāya vadati. Ahudeva aññathattaṃ ahu domanassanti temāsaṃ dānaṃ dātuṃ, dhammañca sotuṃ, iminā ca niyāmena vīsati bhikkhusahassāni paṭijaggituṃ nālatthanti alābhaṃ ārabbha cittaññathattaṃ cittadomanassaṃ ahosi, na tathāgataṃ ārabbha. Kasmā? Sotāpannattā. So kira pubbe brāhmaṇabhatto ahosi. Athekasmiṃ samaye paccante kupite vūpasamanatthaṃ gacchanto uracchadaṃ nāma dhītaramāha – “amma amhākaṃ deve mā pamajjī”ti. Brāhmaṇā taṃ rājadhītaraṃ disvā visaññino ahesuṃ. Ke ime cāti [V 3.0202] vutte tumhākaṃ bhūmidevāti. Bhūmidevā nāma evarūpā hontīti niṭṭhubhitvā pāsādaṃ abhiruhi. Sā ekadivasaṃ vīthiṃ olokentī ṭhitā kassapassa bhagavato aggasāvakaṃ disvā pakkosāpetvā [M 3.0197] piṇḍapātaṃ datvā anumodanaṃ suṇamānāyeva sotāpannā hutvā “aññepi bhikkhū atthī”ti pucchitvā “satthā vīsatiyā bhikkhusahassehi saddhiṃ isipatane vasatī”ti ca sutvā nimantetvā dānaṃ adāsi.

288. With reference to what does he say, 'I have consented'? At the time of his departure from Vegaḷiṅga, Ghaṭikāra obtained a promise from him to dwell for the rains-residence in his presence. He says it with reference to that. Regarding 'There was indeed an alteration, there was dejection': Because he did not get to give alms for the three months, to hear the Dhamma, and in this way to serve twenty thousand monks, on account of this non-acquisition, there was an alteration of mind and mental dejection. It was not on account of the Tathāgata. Why? Because of his being a stream-enterer. It is said that he was formerly a supporter of brahmins. Then, on one occasion, while going to pacify an uprising on the border, he said to his daughter named Uracchadā, 'Dear, do not be heedless regarding our gods.' The brahmins, seeing the royal daughter, became senseless. When she asked, 'Who are these?' it was said, 'Your earth-gods.' Thinking, 'So, earth-gods are of such a kind!', she spat and ascended to the palace. One day, while standing looking out onto the street, she saw the chief disciple of the Blessed One Kassapa, had him summoned, gave him almsfood, and while listening to the words of appreciation, she became a stream-enterer. Having asked, 'Are there other monks?' and having heard, 'The Teacher is dwelling at Isipatana with twenty thousand monks,' she invited them and gave alms.

Rājā paccantaṃ vūpasametvā āgato. Atha naṃ paṭhamatarameva brāhmaṇā āgantvā dhītu avaṇṇaṃ vatvā paribhindiṃsu. Rājā pana dhītu jātakāleyeva varaṃ adāsi. Tassā “satta divasāni rajjaṃ dātabba”nti varaṃ gaṇhiṃsu. Athassā rājā satta divasāni rajjaṃ niyyātesi. Sā satthāraṃ bhojayamānā rājānaṃ pakkosāpetvā bahisāṇiyaṃ nisīdāpesi. Rājā satthu anumodanaṃ sutvāva sotāpanno jāto. Sotāpannassa ca nāma tathāgataṃ ārabbha āghāto natthi. Tena vuttaṃ – “na tathāgataṃ ārabbhā”ti.

The king, having pacified the border region, returned. Then the brahmins came to him first and, speaking dispraise of his daughter, alienated him from her. The king, however, had given a boon at the very time of his daughter's birth. The relatives had accepted the boon that 'the kingdom is to be given to her for seven days.' Then the king handed over the kingdom to her for seven days. She, while feeding the Teacher, had the king summoned and made him sit outside the curtain. The king became a stream-enterer just on hearing the Teacher's words of appreciation. And for a stream-enterer, there is indeed no malice on account of the Tathāgata. Therefore, it was said: 'not on account of the Tathāgata.'

Yaṃ icchati taṃ haratūti so kira bhājanāni pacitvā kayavikkayaṃ [P 3.0285] na karoti, evaṃ pana vatvā dārutthāya vā mattikatthāya vā palālatthāya vā araññaṃ gacchati. Mahājanā “ghaṭikārena bhājanāni pakkānī”ti sutvā parisuddhataṇḍulaloṇadadhitelaphāṇitādīni gahetvā āgacchanti. Sace bhājanaṃ mahagghaṃ hoti, mūlaṃ appaṃ, yaṃ vā taṃ vā datvā gaṇhāmāti taṃ na gaṇhanti. Dhammiko vāṇijo mātāpitaro paṭijaggati, sammāsambuddhaṃ upaṭṭhahati, bahu no akusalaṃ bhavissatīti puna gantvā mūlaṃ āharanti. Sace pana bhājanaṃ appagghaṃ hoti, ābhataṃ mūlaṃ bahu, dhammiko vāṇijo, amhākaṃ puññaṃ bhavissatīti yathābhataṃ gharasāmikā viya sādhukaṃ paṭisāmetvā gacchanti. Evaṃguṇo pana kasmā na pabbajatīti. Rañño vacanapathaṃ pacchindanto andhe jiṇṇe mātāpitaro posetīti āha.

As for 'Let him take what he desires,' it is said that after baking the pots, he does not engage in buying and selling. Instead, having said this, he goes to the forest for firewood, clay, or straw. The people, hearing that 'Ghaṭikāra has baked the pots,' come bringing purified rice, salt, yogurt, oil, molasses, and so on. If a pot is of great value and the price brought is small, they do not take it, thinking, 'Let us take it by giving just any price.' Instead, thinking, 'He is a righteous merchant, he supports his parents, and he attends to the Sammāsambuddha; much demerit will accrue to us,' they go back again and bring the full price. If, however, a pot is of little value and the price brought is much, thinking, 'He is a righteous merchant; merit will accrue to us,' they carefully set aside the full price as brought, as if they were the owners of the house, and depart. Cutting off the king's line of questioning, 'But why does one with such virtues not go forth?', He said: 'He supports his blind and aged parents.'

289. Ko nu khoti kuhiṃ nu kho. Kumbhiyāti ukkhalito. Pariyogāti sūpabhājanato. Paribhuñjāti bhuñja. Kasmā panete evaṃ vadanti? Ghaṭikāro kira bhattaṃ pacitvā sūpaṃ sampādetvā mātāpitaro bhojetvā sayampi bhuñjitvā bhagavato vaḍḍhamānakaṃ bhattasūpaṃ paṭṭhapetvā āsanaṃ paññapetvā ādhārakaṃ upaṭṭhapetvā udakaṃ paccupaṭṭhapetvā mātāpitūnaṃ saññaṃ [V 3.0203] datvā araññaṃ gacchati. Tasmā evaṃ vadanti. Abhivissatthoti [M 3.0198] ativissattho. Pītisukhaṃ [P 3.0286] na vijahatīti na nirantaraṃ vijahati, atha kho rattibhāge vā divasabhāge vā gāme vā araññe vā yasmiṃ yasmiṃ khaṇe – “sadevake nāma loke aggapuggalo mayhaṃ gehaṃ pavisitvā sahatthena āmisaṃ gahetvā paribhuñjati, lābhā vata me”ti anussarati, tasmiṃ tasmiṃ khaṇe pañcavaṇṇā pīti uppajjati. Taṃ sandhāya evaṃ vuttaṃ.

289. 'Ko nu kho' means 'Where indeed has he gone?' 'Kumbhiyā' means from the rice pot. 'Pariyogā' means from the curry pot. 'Paribhuñja' means 'Partake.' But why do they speak thus? It is said that Ghaṭikāra, having cooked rice and prepared curry, fed his parents and then ate himself. Then, having set aside a serving of rice and curry for the Blessed One, prepared a seat, placed a bowl-stand, and set out water, he would give a sign to his parents and go to the forest. Therefore, they speak thus. 'Abhivissaṭṭho' means exceedingly familiar. 'Pītisukhaṃ na vijahati' means that joy and happiness do not leave him; rather, whether by night or by day, in the village or in the forest, at any moment he recollects: 'The foremost person in the world with its devas has entered my home and, taking the almsfood with his own hand, partakes of it. What a gain for me!' At that very moment of recollection, five-colored joy arises. With reference to this, it was said thus.

290. Kaḷopiyāti pacchito. Kiṃ pana bhagavā evamakāsīti. Paccayo dhammiko, bhikkhūnaṃ patte bhattasadiso, tasmā evamakāsi. Sikkhāpadapaññattipi ca sāvakānaṃyeva hoti, buddhānaṃ sikkhāpadavelā nāma natthi. Yathā hi rañño uyyāne pupphaphalāni honti, aññesaṃ tāni gaṇhantānaṃ niggahaṃ karonti, rājā yathāruciyā paribhuñjati, evaṃsampadametaṃ. Parasamuddavāsītherā pana “devatā kira paṭiggahetvā adaṃsū”ti vadanti.

290. 'Kaḷopiyā' means from the basket. But why did the Blessed One act thus? There is a righteous reason: it is like food that is in a bhikkhu's bowl; therefore, He acted thus. Moreover, the laying down of training rules is for the disciples only; for Buddhas, there is no such thing as a boundary of training rules. For instance, in a king's park there are flowers and fruits. They punish others who take them, but the king enjoys them as he pleases. This analogy should be understood in the same way. The elders dwelling across the ocean, however, say: 'It is said that devas received it and then offered it.'

291. Haratha, bhante, haratha bhadramukhāti amhākaṃ putto “kuhiṃ gatosī”ti vutte – “dasabalassa santika”nti vadati, kuhiṃ nu kho gacchati, satthu vasanaṭṭhānassa ovassakabhāvampi na jānātīti putte aparādhasaññino gahaṇe tuṭṭhacittā evamāhaṃsu.

291. As for 'Take, venerable sir, take, O auspicious one!': When their son was asked, 'Where have you been?', he would reply, 'To the presence of the Ten-Powered One.' Thinking, 'Where indeed does our son go? He does not even know that the Teacher's dwelling place is exposed to the rain,' they perceived their son to be at fault. Yet, with minds pleased at the taking of the thatch, they spoke thus.

Temāsaṃ ākāsacchadanaṃ aṭṭhāsīti bhagavā kira catunnaṃ vassikānaṃ māsānaṃ ekaṃ māsaṃ atikkamitvā tiṇaṃ āharāpesi, tasmā evamāha. Ayaṃ panettha padattho – ākāsaṃ chadanamassāti ākāsacchadanaṃ. Na devotivassīti kevalaṃ nātivassi, yathā panettha [P 3.0287] pakatiyā ca nibbakosassa udakapātaṭṭhānabbhantare ekampi udakabindu nātivassi, evaṃ ghanachadanagehabbhantare viya na vātātapāpi ābādhaṃ akaṃsu, pakatiyā utupharaṇameva ahosi. Aparabhāge tasmiṃ nigame chaḍḍitepi taṃ ṭhānaṃ anovassakameva ahosi. Manussā kammaṃ karontā deve vassante tattha sāṭake ṭhapetvā kammaṃ karonti. Yāva kappuṭṭhānā taṃ ṭhānaṃ tādisameva bhavissati. Tañca kho pana na tathāgatassa iddhānubhāvena, tesaṃyeva pana guṇasampattiyā. Tesañhi – “sammāsambuddho kattha na labheyya, amhākaṃ nāma dvinnaṃ andhakānaṃ nivesanaṃ uttiṇaṃ kāresī”ti na tappaccayā domanassaṃ udapādi – “sadevake loke aggapuggalo amhākaṃ [M 3.0199] nivesanā tiṇaṃ āharāpetvā gandhakuṭiṃ chādāpesī”ti pana tesaṃ anappakaṃ [V 3.0204] balavasomanassaṃ udapādi. Iti tesaṃyeva guṇasampattiyā idaṃ pāṭihāriyaṃ jātanti veditabbaṃ.

As for 'For three months it had the sky as its roof': it is said that the Blessed One had the thatch brought after one of the four rainy months had passed; therefore, He said 'for three months.' Herein, this is the meaning of the words: 'It has the sky as its roof,' therefore it is called 'ākāsacchadanaṃ.' As for 'The deva did not rain on it': it was not merely that it did not get wet from rain. Rather, just as by nature not a single drop of water fell within the area of the eavesdrop, so too, as if inside a house with a thick roof, wind and sun caused no affliction; by nature, there was only the pleasant influence of the season. In a later time, even when that market town was abandoned, that place remained unrained upon. People doing their work, when it rained, would place their cloaks there and continue their work. Until the end of the aeon, that place will remain just so. And this was not through the Tathāgata's psychic power, but rather due to their own virtuous accomplishment. Indeed, sorrow did not arise in them on that account, thinking, 'Where could the Sammāsambuddha not obtain thatch? He has caused the dwelling of us two blind people to be unthatched!' Rather, immeasurable, powerful joy arose in them, thinking, 'The foremost person in the world with its devas had thatch brought from our dwelling and had the Perfumed Chamber roofed!' Thus, it should be understood that this marvel arose due to their own virtuous accomplishment.

292. Taṇḍulavāhasatānīti ettha dve sakaṭāni eko vāhoti veditabbo. Tadupiyañca sūpeyyanti sūpatthāya tadanurūpaṃ telaphāṇitādiṃ. Vīsatibhikkhusahassassa temāsatthāya bhattaṃ bhavissatīti kira saññāya rājā ettakaṃ pesesi. Alaṃ me raññova hotūti kasmā paṭikkhipi? Adhigataappicchatāya. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi – “nāhaṃ raññā diṭṭhapubbo, kathaṃ nu kho pesesī”ti. Tato cintesi – “satthā bārāṇasiṃ gato, addhā so rañño vassāvāsaṃ yāciyamāno mayhaṃ paṭiññātabhāvaṃ ārocetvā mama guṇakathaṃ kathesi, guṇakathāya laddhalābho pana naṭena naccitvā laddhaṃ viya [P 3.0288] gāyakena gāyitvā laddhaṃ viya ca hoti. Kiṃ mayhaṃ iminā, kammaṃ katvā uppannena mātāpitūnampi sammāsambuddhassapi upaṭṭhānaṃ sakkā kātu”nti. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

292. Herein, regarding 'hundreds of vāhas of rice,' it should be understood that one vāha is two cartloads. 'And suitable curry ingredients' means oil, molasses, and so on, suitable for that, for the purpose of curry. It is said that the king sent this much, with the thought, 'This will be enough food for twenty thousand bhikkhus for the three months.' Regarding the words, 'Let what is the king's be enough for him,' why did he reject it? Because of his attained quality of having few wishes. It is said this thought occurred to him: 'I have not been seen by the king before. For what reason could he have sent this?' Then he reflected: 'The Teacher has gone to Bārāṇasī. Surely, when being requested by the king for the rains-residence, He must have informed him of His commitment to me and spoken of my virtues. But gain obtained through the speaking of one's virtues is like that obtained by a dancer through dancing or by a singer through singing. What is this to me? It is possible to support my parents and the Sammāsambuddha with what is produced by doing my own work.' The rest is clear everywhere.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Ghaṭikārasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Ghaṭikāra Sutta is concluded.

2. Raṭṭhapālasuttavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Raṭṭhapāla Sutta

293. Evaṃ [V 3.0205] me sutanti raṭṭhapālasuttaṃ. Tattha thullakoṭṭhikanti thullakoṭṭhaṃ paripuṇṇakoṭṭhāgāraṃ. So kira janapado niccasasso sadā bījabhaṇḍaṃ nikkhamati, khalabhaṇḍaṃ pavisati. Tena tasmiṃ nigame koṭṭhā niccapūrāva honti. Tasmā so thullakoṭṭhikanteva saṅkhaṃ gato.

293. Thus have I heard: the Raṭṭhapāla Sutta. Therein, 'Thullakoṭṭhika' means a large granary, a completely full granary. It is said that in that country, there was a constant harvest; the commodity of seeds was always going out, and the commodity of grain from the threshing floor was coming in. Therefore, in that market town, the granaries were always full. Hence, it came to be known as 'Thullakoṭṭhika'.

294. Raṭṭhapāloti kasmā raṭṭhapālo? Bhinnaṃ raṭṭhaṃ sandhāretuṃ pāletuṃ samatthoti raṭṭhapālo. Kadā panassetaṃ nāmaṃ uppannanti. Padumuttarasammāsambuddhakāle. Ito hi pubbe satasahassakappamatthake vassasatasahassāyukesu manussesu padumuttaro nāma satthā uppajjitvā bhikkhusatasahassaparivāro [M 3.0200] lokahitāya cārikaṃ cari, yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ –

294. Why is he called Raṭṭhapāla? Because he was capable of restoring and protecting a broken kingdom, he is called Raṭṭhapāla. But when did this name arise for him? During the time of the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha Padumuttara. For, a hundred thousand aeons ago from this present aeon, among humans whose lifespan was one hundred thousand years, a Teacher named Padumuttara arose and, surrounded by a hundred thousand bhikkhus, wandered for the welfare of the world. It is in reference to him that it was said:

“Nagaraṃ haṃsavatī nāma, ānando nāma khattiyo;

Sujātā nāma janikā, padumuttarassa satthuno”ti. (bu. vaṃ. 12.19);

'The city was named Haṃsavatī, the khattiya was named Ānanda; the mother was named Sujātā, of the Teacher Padumuttara.'

Padumuttare pana anuppanne eva haṃsavatiyā dve kuṭumbikā saddhā pasannā kapaṇaddhikayācakādīnaṃ dānaṃ paṭṭhapayiṃsu. Tadā pabbatavāsino pañcasatā tāpasā haṃsavatiṃ anuppattā. Te dvepi janā tāpasagaṇaṃ majjhe bhinditvā [P 3.0289] upaṭṭhahiṃsu. Tāpasā kiñcikālaṃ vasitvā pabbatapādameva gatā. Dve saṅghattherā ohīyiṃsu. Tadā tesaṃ te yāvajīvaṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ akaṃsu. Tāpasesu bhuñjitvā anumodanaṃ karontesu eko sakkabhavanassa vaṇṇaṃ kathesi, eko bhūmindharanāgarājabhavanassa.

But even before the arising of Padumuttara, two householders in Haṃsavatī, being faithful and devout, established almsgiving for the poor, travelers, beggars, and so on. At that time, five hundred ascetics dwelling in the mountains arrived in Haṃsavatī. Those two people divided the group of ascetics in the middle and attended to them. The ascetics, having stayed for some time, went back to the foot of the mountain. Two elder ascetics remained behind. Then, those two attended to them for as long as they lived. When the ascetics, after eating, were giving their blessings, one spoke of the splendor of Sakka’s abode, and one spoke of the splendor of the abode of the earth-bearing nāga king.

Kuṭumbikesu eko sakkabhavanaṃ patthanaṃ katvā sakko hutvā nibbatto, eko nāgabhavane pālitanāgarājā nāma. Taṃ sakko attano upaṭṭhānaṃ āgataṃ disvā nāgayoniyaṃ abhiramasīti pucchi. So nābhiramāmīti āha. Tena hi padumuttarassa bhagavato dānaṃ datvā imasmiṃ [V 3.0206] ṭhāne patthanaṃ karohi, ubho sukhaṃ vasissāmāti.
