Nāgarājā satthāraṃ nimantetvā bhikkhusatasahassaparivārassa bhagavato sattāhaṃ mahādānaṃ dadamāno padumuttarassa dasabalassa puttaṃ uparevataṃ nāma sāmaṇeraṃ disvā sattame divase buddhappamukhassa saṅghassa dibbavatthāni datvā sāmaṇerassa ṭhānantaraṃ patthesi. Bhagavā anāgataṃ oloketvā – “anāgate gotamassa nāma buddhassa putto rāhulakumāro bhavissatī”ti disvā “samijjhissati te patthanā”ti kathesi. Nāgarājā tamatthaṃ sakkassa kathesi. Sakko tassa vacanaṃ sutvā tatheva sattāhaṃ dānaṃ datvā bhinnaṃ raṭṭhaṃ sandhāretuṃ pāletuṃ samatthakule nibbattitvā saddhāpabbajitaṃ raṭṭhapālaṃ nāma kulaputtaṃ disvā – “ahampi anāgate lokasmiṃ tumhādise buddhe uppanne bhinnaṃ raṭṭhaṃ sandhāretuṃ pāletuṃ samatthakule nibbattitvā ayaṃ kulaputto viya saddhāpabbajito raṭṭhapālo nāma bhaveyya”nti patthanamakāsi. Satthā samijjhanakabhāvaṃ ñatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

Among the householders, one made an aspiration for Sakka's abode and was reborn as Sakka; the other was reborn in the nāga realm as the nāga king named Pālita. Sakka, seeing that nāga king come to attend upon him, asked, 'Do you delight in the nāga birth?' He replied, 'I do not delight.' 'In that case, give alms to the Blessed One Padumuttara and make an aspiration in this place. We shall both live happily.' The nāga king invited the Teacher and, while giving a great offering for seven days to the Blessed One who was surrounded by a hundred thousand bhikkhus, he saw the novice named Uparevata, the son of Padumuttara, the one with Ten Powers. On the seventh day, he gave divine cloths to the Saṅgha with the Buddha at its head and aspired for the special position of the novice. The Blessed One, looking into the future and seeing, 'In the future, there will be the son of the Buddha named Gotama, Prince Rāhula,' said, 'Your aspiration will be fulfilled.' The nāga king related this matter to Sakka. Sakka, hearing his words, likewise gave alms for seven days and, seeing the clansman named Raṭṭhapāla who had gone forth out of faith after being reborn in a family capable of restoring and protecting a broken kingdom, made this aspiration: 'I too, in the future, when a Buddha like you arises in the world, may I be reborn in a family capable of restoring and protecting a broken kingdom and, like this clansman, become one named Raṭṭhapāla who has gone forth out of faith.' The Teacher, knowing that this would be fulfilled, spoke this verse:

“Sarājikaṃ [M 3.0201][P 3.0290] cātuvaṇṇaṃ, posetuṃ yaṃ pahossati;

Raṭṭhapālakulaṃ nāma, tattha jāyissate aya”nti. –

In that family named Raṭṭhapāla, which will be able to nourish the four classes along with the king, there this one will be born.

Evaṃ padumuttarasammāsambuddhakāle tassetaṃ nāmaṃ uppannanti veditabbaṃ.

Thus, it should be understood that this name arose for him in the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Padumuttara.

Etadahosīti kiṃ ahosi? Yathā yathā khotiādi. Tatrāyaṃ saṅkhepakathā – ahaṃ kho yena yena kāraṇena bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmi, tena tena me upaparikkhato evaṃ hoti – “yadetaṃ sikkhattayabrahmacariyaṃ ekadivasampi akhaṇḍaṃ katvā carimakacittaṃ pāpetabbatāya ekantaparipuṇṇaṃ caritabbaṃ, ekadivasampi ca kilesamalena amalīnaṃ katvā carimakacittaṃ pāpetabbatāya ekantaparisuddhaṃ, saṅkhalikhitaṃ vilikhitasaṅkhasadisaṃ dhotasaṅkhasappaṭibhāgaṃ katvā caritabbaṃ, nayidaṃ sukaraṃ agāraṃ ajjhāvasatā agāramajjhe vasantena ekantaparipuṇṇaṃ…pe… carituṃ, yaṃnūnāhaṃ kesañca massuñca ohāretvā kāsāyarasapītatāya kāsāyāni brahmacariyaṃ carantānaṃ anucchavikāni vatthāni acchādetvā agārasmā nikkhamitvā anagāriyaṃ pabbajeyya”nti.

As for 'This thought occurred to him,' what thought was it? It is as stated in the passage beginning 'In whatever way...' Here is the summary explanation: In whatever way I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, as I examine it in that same way, it occurs to me thus: 'This holy life of the threefold training must be practiced completely perfectly, making it unbroken even for a single day, because it must be brought to the final consciousness. It must be practiced completely pure, making it unstained by the defilements even for a single day, because it must be brought to the final consciousness. It must be practiced like a scraped and washed conch shell, like a polished conch shell. It is not easy for one dwelling at home, living in the midst of a household, to practice this holy life completely perfectly... What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, put on the ochre robes—which are suitable for those practicing the holy life—and go forth from the household life into homelessness?'

Acirapakkantesu thullakoṭṭhikesu brāhmaṇagahapatikesu yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamīti raṭṭhapālo anuṭṭhitesu [V 3.0207] tesu na bhagavantaṃ pabbajjaṃ yāci. Kasmā? Tatthassa [P 3.0291] bahū ñātisālohitā mittāmaccā santi, te – “tvaṃ mātāpitūnaṃ ekaputtako, na labbhā tayā pabbajitu”nti bāhāyampi gahetvā ākaḍḍheyyuṃ, tato pabbajjāya antarāyo bhavissatīti saheva parisāya uṭṭhahitvā thokaṃ gantvā puna kenaci sarīrakiccalesena nivattitvā bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamma pabbajjaṃ yāci. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho raṭṭhapālo kulaputto acirapakkantesu thullakoṭṭhikesu…pe… pabbājetu maṃ bhagavā”ti. Bhagavā pana yasmā rāhulakumārassa pabbajitato pabhuti mātāpitūhi ananuññātaṃ puttaṃ na pabbājeti, tasmā naṃ pucchi anuññātosi pana tvaṃ, raṭṭhapāla, mātāpitūhi…pe… pabbajjāyāti.

Raṭṭhapāla did not ask the Blessed One for ordination while the brahmins and householders of Thullakoṭṭhika were still present. Why? Because he thought: 'There are many relatives, kinsmen, friends, and companions of mine here, and they will say, "You are your parents’ only son; it is not permitted for you to go forth!" They might even grab me by the arm and drag me away, and that would be an obstacle to my ordination.' So, rising together with the assembly and going a short distance, he then turned back on some pretext of a bodily need, approached the Blessed One, and asked for ordination. Therefore it is said: 'Then Raṭṭhapāla the clansman, not long after the brahmins and householders of Thullakoṭṭhika had departed... "May the Blessed One ordain me."' But the Blessed One, since the time of Prince Rāhula’s ordination, does not ordain a son who has not been permitted by his parents. Therefore he asked him: 'But have you been permitted by your parents, Raṭṭhapāla, for the going forth?'

295. Ammatātāti ettha ammāti mātaraṃ ālapati, tātāti pitaraṃ. Ekaputtakoti ekova puttako, añño koci jeṭṭho vā kaniṭṭho vā natthi. Ettha ca ekaputtoti vattabbe anukampāvasena ekaputtakoti vuttaṃ. Piyoti pītijanako. Manāpoti manavaḍḍhanako. Sukhedhitoti [M 3.0202] sukhena edhito, sukhasaṃvaḍḍhitoti attho. Sukhaparibhatoti sukhena paribhato, jātakālato pabhuti dhātīhi aṅkato aṅkaṃ āharitvā dhāriyamāno assakarathakādīhi bālakīḷanakehi kīḷayamāno sādurasabhojanaṃ bhojayamāno sukhena parihaṭo. Na tvaṃ, tāta raṭṭhapāla, kassaci dukkhassa jānāsīti tvaṃ[P 3.0292], tāta raṭṭhapāla appamattakampi kalabhāgaṃ dukkhassa na jānāsi na sarasīti attho. Maraṇenapi te mayaṃ akāmakā vinā bhavissāmāti sacepi tava amhesu jīvamānesu maraṇaṃ bhaveyya, tena te maraṇenapi mayaṃ akāmakā anicchakā na attano ruciyā vinā bhavissāma, tayā viyogaṃ pāpuṇissāmāti attho. Kiṃ pana mayaṃ tanti evaṃ sante kiṃ pana kiṃ nāma taṃ kāraṇaṃ, yena mayaṃ taṃ jīvantaṃ anujānissāma. Atha vā kiṃ pana mayaṃ tanti kena pana kāraṇena mayaṃ taṃ jīvantaṃ anujānissāmāti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

295. 'Ammatātā': Here, 'ammā' addresses the mother, and 'tātā' addresses the father. 'Ekaputtako' means the only son; there is no other, either elder or younger. And here, although 'ekaputto' should be said, out of compassion, 'ekaputtako' is said. 'Piyo' means joy-producing. 'Manāpo' means affection-increasing. 'Sukhedhito' means brought up in happiness; the meaning is grown up in happiness. 'Sukhaparibhato' means nurtured in comfort; from the time of birth, carried from lap to lap by nurses, entertained with toys like toy horses and chariots, and fed delicious food—thus he was nurtured in comfort. 'Na tvaṃ, tāta Raṭṭhapāla, kassaci dukkhassa jānāsī'ti: You, dear Raṭṭhapāla, do not know, do not see even the slightest fraction of suffering. This is the meaning. 'Maraṇenapi te mayaṃ akāmakā vinā bhavissāmā'ti: If your death were to occur while we are living, then by that death of yours, we, unwilling and undesiring, not of our own wish, would be separated from you; we would attain separation from you. This is the meaning. 'Kiṃ pana mayaṃ tan'ti: This being so, what reason is there that we should give permission to you while you are living? Alternatively, 'Kiṃ pana mayaṃ tan'ti: For what reason should we give permission to you while you are living? Thus, the meaning here should be understood.

296. Tatthevāti yattha naṃ ṭhitaṃ mātāpitaro nānujāniṃsu, tattheva ṭhāne. Anantarahitāyāti kenaci attharaṇena anatthatāya. Paricārehīti gandhabbanaṭanāṭakādīni paccupaṭṭhapetvā tattha sahāyakehi saddhiṃ yathāsukhaṃ indriyāni cārehi sañcārehi, ito cito ca upanehīti vuttaṃ hoti. Atha vā paricārehīti gandhabbanaṭanāṭakādīni paccupaṭṭhapetvā sahāyakehi saddhiṃ [V 3.0208] laḷa upalaḷa rama, kīḷassūtipi vuttaṃ hoti. Kāme paribhuñjantoti attano puttadārehi saddhiṃ bhoge bhuñjanto. Puññāni karontoti buddhañca dhammañca saṅghañca ārabbha dānappadānādīni sugatimaggasaṃsodhakāni kusalakammāni karonto. Tuṇhī ahosīti kathānuppabandhavicchedanatthaṃ nirālāpasallāpo ahosi.

296. 'Tattheva' means in that very place where his parents did not give him permission. 'Anantarahitāya' means on ground without any covering. 'Paricārehi' means: having arranged for musicians, dancers, and actors, gratify your senses with your companions as you please, summoning them from here and there. This is what is meant. Alternatively, 'Paricārehi' also means: having arranged for musicians, dancers, and actors, enjoy yourself, frolic, delight, and play with your companions. This is what is meant. 'Kāme paribhuñjanto' means enjoying possessions together with his own wives and children. 'Puññāni karonto' means performing wholesome actions such as giving, which purify the path to a good destination, taking the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha as object. 'Tuṇhī ahosī'ti means he became one without speech or reply in order to cut off the sequence of conversation.

Athassa mātāpitaro tikkhattuṃ [P 3.0293] vatvā paṭivacanampi alabhamānā sahāyake pakkosāpetvā “esa vo sahāyako pabbajitukāmo, nivāretha na”nti āhaṃsu. Tepi taṃ upasaṅkamitvā tikkhattuṃ avocuṃ, tesampi tuṇhī ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ – atha kho raṭṭhapālassa kulaputtassa sahāyakā…pe… tuṇhī ahosīti. Athassa sahāyakānaṃ tikkhattuṃ vatvā etadahosi – “sace ayaṃ pabbajjaṃ alabhamāno marissati, na koci guṇo [M 3.0203] labbhati. Pabbajitaṃ pana naṃ mātāpitaropi kālena kālaṃ passissanti, mayampi passissāma, pabbajjāpi ca nāmesā bhāriyā, divase divase mattikāpattaṃ gahetvā piṇḍāya caritabbaṃ, ekaseyyaṃ ekabhattaṃ brahmacariyaṃ atidukkaraṃ, ayañca sukhumālo nāgarikajātiyo, so taṃ carituṃ asakkonto puna idheva āgamissati, handassa mātāpitaro anujānāpessāmā”ti. Te tathā akaṃsu. Mātāpitaropi naṃ “pabbajitena ca pana te mātāpitaro uddassetabbā”ti imaṃ katikaṃ katvā anujāniṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho raṭṭhapālassa kulaputtassa sahāyakā yena raṭṭhapālassa kulaputtassa mātāpitaro…pe… anuññātosi mātāpitūhi…pe… uddassetabbā”ti. Tattha uddassetabbāti uddhaṃ dassetabbā, yathā taṃ kālena kālaṃ passanti, evaṃ āgantvā attānaṃ dassetabbā.

Then his parents, having spoken three times and receiving no reply, summoned his friends and said, 'This friend of yours wishes to go forth; restrain him.' They too approached him and spoke three times, but he remained silent. Hence it is said: 'Then the friends of the clansman Raṭṭhapāla… remained silent.' Then his friends, having spoken three times, thought: 'If he does not get to go forth, he may die, and no good will be gained. But if he goes forth, his parents will see him from time to time, and so will we. Moreover, this going forth is burdensome—going for alms each day with a clay bowl, sleeping alone, eating one meal a day, and the holy life are extremely difficult. And he is delicate, of a refined, city-bred family—unable to sustain it, he will return here. Come, let us get his parents to give him permission.' They did so. His parents also set this condition: 'But having gone forth, you must show yourself to your parents.' They gave their consent. Hence it is said: 'Then the friends of the clansman Raṭṭhapāla went to his parents… you are permitted by your parents… you must show yourself.' Here, 'uddassetabbā' means they must be shown up, that is, he should return and make himself seen so that they might see him from time to time.

299. Balaṃ gahetvāti sappāyabhojanāni bhuñjanto ucchādanādīhi ca kāyaṃ pariharanto kāyabalaṃ janetvā mātāpitaro vanditvā assumukhaṃ ñātiparivaṭṭaṃ pahāya yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami…pe… pabbājetu maṃ, bhante, bhagavāti. Bhagavā samīpe ṭhitaṃ aññataraṃ bhikkhuṃ [P 3.0294] āmantesi – “tena hi bhikkhu raṭṭhapālaṃ pabbājehi ceva upasampādehi cā”ti. Sādhu, bhanteti kho so bhikkhu bhagavato paṭissutvā raṭṭhapālaṃ kulaputtaṃ jinadattiyaṃ saddhivihārikaṃ laddhā pabbājesi ceva upasampādesi ca. Tena vuttaṃ – “alattha kho raṭṭhapālo kulaputto bhagavato santike pabbajjaṃ, alattha upasampada”nti.

299. ‘Having gained strength’: eating suitable food and maintaining his body with anointing and so forth, thereby generating bodily strength, he paid respects to his parents, left his tearful circle of relatives, and approached the Blessed One… “Venerable sir, may the Blessed One give me the going forth.” The Blessed One addressed a certain monk standing nearby: “Well then, monk, give Raṭṭhapāla the going forth and also the full admission.” “Very well, venerable sir,” that monk replied to the Blessed One. Having obtained the clansman Raṭṭhapāla as a co-resident pupil given by the Jina, he gave him the going forth and also the full admission. Thus it is said: “The clansman Raṭṭhapāla obtained the going forth in the presence of the Blessed One; he obtained the full admission.”

Pahitatto [V 3.0209] viharantoti dvādasa saṃvaccharāni evaṃ viharanto. Neyyapuggalo hi ayamāyasmā, tasmā puññavā abhinīhārasampannopi samāno “ajja ajjeva arahatta”nti samaṇadhammaṃ karontopi dvādasame vasse arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

‘He dwells with a resolute mind’: thus he dwelt for twelve years. Indeed, this venerable one was a person to be trained. Therefore, though endowed with merit and a past aspiration, even while practicing the ascetic's duties, thinking, “I will attain Arahantship this very day,” he attained Arahantship in the twelfth year.

Yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamīti mayhaṃ mātāpitaro pabbajjaṃ anujānamānā – “tayā kālena kālaṃ āgantvā amhākaṃ dassanaṃ dātabba”nti vatvā anujāniṃsu, dukkarakārikā kho pana mātāpitaro, ahañca yenajjhāsayena pabbajito, so me matthakaṃ patto, idāni bhagavantaṃ āpucchitvā attānaṃ [M 3.0204] mātāpitūnaṃ dassessāmīti cintetvā āpucchitukāmo upasaṅkami. Manasākāsīti “kiṃ nu kho raṭṭhapāle gate koci upaddavo bhavissatī”ti manasi akāsi. Tato “bhavissatī”ti ñatvā “sakkhissati nu kho raṭṭhapālo taṃ madditu”nti olokento tassa arahattasampattiṃ disvā “sakkhissatī”ti aññāsi. Tena vuttaṃ – yathā bhagavā aññāsi…pe… kālaṃ maññasīti.

‘He approached the Blessed One’: My parents, in permitting me to go forth, said, “You must come from time to time and let us see you,” and then they permitted me. Parents are indeed those who have done what is difficult, and I went forth according to my aspiration, and that has reached its goal. I thought, “I will take leave of the Blessed One and show myself to my parents,” and so, wishing to take leave, I approached him. ‘He turned his mind to it’: He turned his mind to it, thinking, “Will there be any trouble when Raṭṭhapāla is gone?” Then, knowing that there would be, he wondered, “Will Raṭṭhapāla be able to suppress it?” Observing his attainment of arahantship, he understood, “He will be able.” Therefore, it is said: “As the Blessed One understood… you may consider it the right time.”

Migacīreti evaṃnāmake uyyāne. Tañhi raññā – “akāle sampattapabbajitānaṃ dinnameva idaṃ, yathāsukhaṃ paribhuñjantū”ti evamanuññātameva ahosi, tasmā thero – “mama āgatabhāvaṃ mātāpitūnaṃ ārocessāmi, te me pādadhovanauṇhodakapādamakkhanatelādīni [P 3.0295] pesissantī”ti cittampi anuppādetvā uyyānameva pāvisi. Piṇḍāya pāvisīti dutiyadivase pāvisi.

‘In Migacīra’: in a park of that name. For it had been granted by the king thus: “This is given for monastics who have arrived at an unseasonable time; let them enjoy it as they please.” Therefore, the elder, without even the thought arising, “I will inform my parents of my arrival, and they will send me water for washing my feet, warm water, oil for anointing my feet, and so forth,” entered the park. ‘He entered for alms’: on the second day, he entered for alms.

Majjhimāyāti sattadvārakoṭṭhakassa gharassa majjhime dvārakoṭṭhake. Ullikhāpetīti kappakena kese paharāpeti. Etadavocāti – “ime samaṇakā amhākaṃ piyaputtakaṃ pabbājetvā corānaṃ hatthe nikkhipitvā viya ekadivasampi na dassāpenti, evaṃ pharusakārakā ete puna imaṃ ṭhānaṃ upasaṅkamitabbaṃ maññanti, ettova nikaḍḍhitabbā ete”ti cintetvā etaṃ “imehi muṇḍakehī”tiādivacanaṃ avoca. Ñātidāsīti ñātakānaṃ dāsī. Ābhidosikanti pārivāsikaṃ ekarattātikkantaṃ pūtibhūtaṃ. Tatthāyaṃ padattho – pūtibhāvadosena abhibhūtoti abhidoso, abhidosova ābhidosiko. Ekarattātikkantasseva nāmasaññā esā yadidaṃ ābhidosikoti, taṃ ābhidosikaṃ. Kummāsanti yavakummāsaṃ. Chaḍḍetukāmā hotīti yasmā antamaso dāsakammakārānaṃ gorūpānampi aparibhogāraho, tasmā naṃ kacavaraṃ viya bahi chaḍḍetukāmā [V 3.0210] hoti. Sacetanti sace etaṃ. Bhaginīti ariyavohārena attano dhātiṃ ñātidāsiṃ ālapati. Chaḍḍanīyadhammanti chaḍḍetabbasabhāvaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “bhagini etaṃ sace bahi chaḍḍanīyadhammaṃ nissaṭṭhapariggahaṃ, idha me patte ākirāhī”ti. Kiṃ pana evaṃ vattuṃ labbhati[P 3.0296], viññatti vā payuttavācā vā na hotīti. Na hoti. Kasmā? Nissaṭṭhapariggahattā. Yañhi chaḍḍanīyadhammaṃ nissaṭṭhapariggahaṃ, yattha sāmikā anālayā honti, taṃ sabbaṃ “detha āharatha [M 3.0205] ākirathā”ti vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Teneva hi ayamāyasmā aggaariyavaṃsiko samānopi evamāha.

‘The middle’: the middle gateway of a house with seven gateways. ‘Had it shaved’: he had his hair cut by a barber. ‘He said this’: thinking, “These wretched recluses, after making our dear son go forth, have handed him over to thieves, as it were, not showing him even for a single day. They are so harsh! Yet they think they can come back to this place again. They should be dragged away right here,” he spoke these words beginning with “These bald-headed ones…” ‘A slave-girl of the relatives’: a slave belonging to the relatives. ‘Stale overnight’: stale, having passed one night, and become putrid. Here is the meaning of the term: ‘spoiled’ (abhidoso) means overcome by the fault of becoming putrid; that which is spoiled is itself ‘stale overnight’ (ābhidosiko). This is a term for what has been left overnight, that is, ‘stale overnight.’ ‘Gruel’: barley gruel. ‘Wished to throw it away’: since it was not fit for consumption even by slaves, workers, or cattle, she wanted to discard it outside like rubbish. ‘If’: if this. ‘Sister’: he addresses his nurse, the slave-girl of the relatives, with noble speech. ‘Fit to be discarded’: of a nature to be thrown away. This is what is meant: “Sister, if this is fit to be discarded outside, being a relinquished possession, then pour it into my bowl here.” But is it proper to speak thus? Is it not a hint or speech connected to it? No, it is not. Why? Because it is a relinquished possession. Whatever is fit to be discarded and is a relinquished possession—for which the owners have no attachment—it is proper to say of it, “Give, bring, pour.” For that very reason, this venerable one, though of foremost noble lineage, spoke thus.

Hatthānanti bhikkhāgahaṇatthaṃ pattaṃ upanāmayato maṇibandhato pabhuti dvinnampi hatthānaṃ. Pādānanti nivāsanantato paṭṭhāya dvinnampi pādānaṃ. Sarassāti sace taṃ bhaginīti vācaṃ nicchārayato sarassa ca. Nimittaṃ aggahesīti hatthapiṭṭhiādīni olokayamānā – “puttassa me raṭṭhapālassa viya suvaṇṇakacchapapiṭṭhisadisā imā hatthapādapiṭṭhiyo, haritālavaṭṭiyo viya suvaṭṭitā aṅguliyo, madhuro saro”ti gihikāle sallakkhitapubbaṃ ākāraṃ aggahesi sañjāni sallakkhesi. Tassa hāyasmato dvādasavassāni araññāvāsañceva piṇḍiyālopabhojanañca paribhuñjantassa aññādiso sarīravaṇṇo ahosi, tena naṃ sā ñātidāsī disvāva na sañjāni, nimittaṃ pana aggahesīti.

‘Of the hands’: refers to both hands from the wrists onward, as he was presenting the bowl to receive alms. ‘Of the feet’: refers to both feet from the hem of the lower garment downward. ‘Of the voice’: refers to his voice when uttering the words, “If, sister…” ‘She took note of the signs’: while observing the backs of his hands and other features, she grasped the characteristics she had noticed during his household life, thinking, “The backs of his hands and feet are like those of my son Raṭṭhapāla, resembling the shells of golden tortoises; his fingers are well-rounded like sticks of yellow orpiment; his voice is sweet.” She grasped, recognized, and marked the signs. For that venerable one had spent twelve years dwelling in the forest and eating food from alms-gathering, and his complexion was different; therefore, that slave-girl did not recognize him upon seeing him, but she did take note of the signs.

300. Raṭṭhapālassa mātaraṃ etadavocāti therassa aṅgapaccaṅgāni saṇṭhāpetvā thaññaṃ pāyetvā saṃvaḍḍhitadhātīpi samānā pabbajitvā mahākhīṇāsavabhāvappattena sāmiputtena saddhiṃ – “tvaṃ nu kho, me bhante, putto raṭṭhapālo”tiādivacanaṃ vattuṃ avisahantī vegena gharaṃ pavisitvā raṭṭhapālassa mātaraṃ etadavoca. Yaggheti ārocanatthe nipāto. Sace [P 3.0297] je saccanti ettha jeti ālapane nipāto. Evañhi tasmiṃ dese dāsijanaṃ ālapanti, tasmā “tvañhi, bhoti dāsi, sace saccaṃ bhaṇasī”ti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

300. ‘She spoke thus to Raṭṭhapāla’s mother’: Although she was the nurse who had settled the elder’s limbs, given him milk to drink, and nurtured him, she was unable to speak words like “Are you, venerable sir, my son Raṭṭhapāla?” with her master’s son, who had gone forth and attained the state of a great Arahant. She quickly entered the house and spoke thus to Raṭṭhapāla’s mother. ‘Yagghe’: a particle used for announcing. ‘Sace je saccaṃ’: here ‘je’ is a particle used in addressing. For in that region, they address a slave-woman thus; therefore, the meaning here should be understood as, “O good slave-woman, if you speak the truth.”

Upasaṅkamīti kasmā upasaṅkami? Mahākule itthiyo bahi nikkhamantā garahaṃ pāpuṇanti, idañca accāyikakiccaṃ, seṭṭhissa naṃ ārocessāmīti cinteti. Tasmā upasaṅkami. Aññataraṃ kuṭṭamūlanti tasmiṃ kira dese dānapatīnaṃ gharesu sālā honti, āsanāni cettha paññattāni honti, upaṭṭhāpitaṃ udakakañjiyaṃ. Tattha pabbajitā piṇḍāya caritvā nisīditvā bhuñjanti[V 3.0211]. Sace icchanti, dānapatīnampi santakaṃ gaṇhanti. Tasmā tampi aññatarassa kulassa īdisāya sālāya aññataraṃ kuṭṭamūlanti veditabbaṃ. Na hi pabbajitā kapaṇamanussā viya asāruppe ṭhāne nisīditvā bhuñjantīti.

‘She approached’: Why did she approach? Women from great families receive blame when they go outside, and this was an urgent matter; she thought, “I will inform the master.” Therefore, she approached. ‘At the foot of a certain wall’: in that region, it seems, donors’ houses have halls, where seats are arranged, and water and gruel are set out. There, after wandering for alms, monastics sit and eat. If they wish, they may also take what belongs to the donors. Therefore, that place should be understood as ‘at the foot of a certain wall’ of such a hall belonging to a certain family. For monastics do not sit and eat in unseemly places like destitute people.

Atthi [M 3.0206] nāma tātāti ettha atthīti vijjamānatthe, nāmāti pucchanatthe maññanatthe vā nipāto. Idañhi vuttaṃ hoti – atthi nu kho, tāta raṭṭhapāla, amhākaṃ dhanaṃ, nanu mayaṃ niddhanāti vattabbā, yesaṃ no tvaṃ īdise ṭhāne nisīditvā ābhidosikaṃ kummāsaṃ paribhuñjissasi. Tathā atthi nu kho, tāta raṭṭhapāla, amhākaṃ jīvitaṃ, nanu mayaṃ matāti vattabbā, yesaṃ no tvaṃ īdise ṭhāne nisīditvā ābhidosikaṃ kummāsaṃ paribhuñjissasi. Tathā atthi maññe, tāta raṭṭhapāla, tava abbhantare sāsanaṃ nissāya paṭiladdho samaṇaguṇo, yaṃ tvaṃ subhojanarasasaṃvaḍḍhitopi imaṃ jigucchaneyyaṃ ābhidosikaṃ kummāsaṃ amatamiva nibbikāro paribhuñjissasīti. So pana gahapati dukkhābhitunnatāya etamatthaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ katvā vattumasakkonto – “atthi nāma, tāta raṭṭhapāla, ābhidosikaṃ kummāsaṃ paribhuñjissasī”ti ettakameva avaca. Akkharacintakā panettha idaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ vadanti – anokappanāmarisanatthavasenetaṃ [P 3.0298] atthisadde upapade “paribhuñjissasī”ti anāgatavacanaṃ kataṃ. Tassāyamattho – “atthi nāma…pe… paribhuñjissasi, idaṃ paccakkhampi ahaṃ na saddahāmi na marisayāmī”ti. Idaṃ ettakaṃ vacanaṃ gahapati therassa pattamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ gahetvā ṭhitakova kathesi. Theropi pitari pattamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ gahetvā ṭhiteyeva taṃ pūtikummāsaṃ paribhuñji sunakhavantasadisaṃ pūtikukkuṭaṇḍamiva bhinnaṭṭhāne pūtikaṃ vāyantaṃ. Puthujjanena kira tathārūpaṃ kummāsaṃ paribhuñjituṃ na sakkā. Thero pana ariyiddhiyaṃ ṭhatvā dibbojaṃ amatarasaṃ paribhuñjamāno viya paribhuñjitvā dhamakaraṇena udakaṃ gahetvā pattañca mukhañca hatthapāde ca dhovitvā kuto no gahapatītiādimāha.

Herein, regarding “Atthi nāma, tāta,” the particle “atthi” is in the sense of existence, and the particle “nāma” is in the sense of questioning or, alternatively, supposition. For this is what is meant: “Is it not so, dear Raṭṭhapāla, that we have wealth? Should we not then be called destitute, if you, our son, sitting in such a place, are to eat this stale, putrid barley-meal?” Likewise: “Is it not so, dear Raṭṭhapāla, that we are still alive? Should we not then be called dead, if you, our son, sitting in such a place, are to eat this stale, putrid barley-meal?” And likewise: “I suppose, dear Raṭṭhapāla, that there is within you a quality of a recluse, attained by relying on the Teaching, that you, though raised on fine, flavorful food, are to eat this repulsive, stale, putrid barley-meal without any change in expression, as if it were the deathless nectar.” However, that householder, being overwhelmed by sorrow and unable to express this meaning in full, said only this much: “Is it really so, dear Raṭṭhapāla, that you will eat stale, putrid barley-meal?” Herein, grammarians state this rule: due to the sense of disbelief and unacceptance, with the word “atthi” present, the future tense verb “paribhuñjissasi” is used. This is its meaning: “That you will eat… this, even seeing it with my own eyes, I do not believe, I cannot accept.” The householder spoke just this much while standing there holding the rim of the Elder’s bowl. The Elder, even while his father stood holding the rim of the bowl, consumed that putrid barley-meal, which was like a dog’s vomit and like a rotten chicken egg emitting a putrid smell from where it is broken. It is said that an ordinary person would be unable to eat such barley-meal. The Elder, however, abiding in noble power, consumed it as if consuming divine nutriment, the deathless nectar. Having consumed it, he took water with a water-strainer, washed his bowl, his mouth, and his hands and feet, and then said, “From where, householder…?” and so on.

Tattha kuto noti kuto nu. Neva dānanti deyyadhammavasena neva dānaṃ alatthamha. Na paccakkhānanti “kiṃ, tāta raṭṭhapāla, kacci te khamanīyaṃ, kaccisi appakilamathena āgato, na tāva tāta gehe bhattaṃ sampādiyatī”ti evaṃ paṭisanthāravasena paccakkhānampi na alatthamha. Kasmā pana thero evamāha? Pitu anuggahena. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi – “yathā esa maṃ vadati[V 3.0212], aññepi pabbajite evaṃ vadati maññe. Buddhasāsane ca pattantare padumaṃ viya bhasmāchanno aggi viya pheggupaṭicchanno candanasāro viya suttikāpaṭicchannaṃ muttaratanaṃ viya valāhakapaṭicchanno [P 3.0299] candimā viya mādisānaṃ [M 3.0207] paṭicchannaguṇānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ anto natthi, tesupi na evarūpaṃ vacanaṃ pavattessati, saṃvare ṭhassatī”ti anuggahena evamāha.

Herein, “kuto no” means “kuto nu” (from where indeed?). “Neva dānaṃ” means: in terms of things to be given, we received no gift. “Na paccakkhānaṃ” means: we did not even receive a polite refusal by way of a friendly greeting, such as: “What, dear Raṭṭhapāla, are you well? Did you arrive without much fatigue? Dear son, the meal is not yet ready in the house.” But why did the Elder speak thus? For the benefit of his father. For it occurred to him thus: “Just as he speaks to me, so too, I suppose, he speaks to other monastics. And in the Dispensation of the Buddha, there is no end of monks like me whose virtues are concealed—like a lotus among leaves, like a fire covered by ashes, like sandalwood heartwood concealed by sapwood, like a pearl concealed in an oyster shell, like the moon concealed by a cloud. Towards them also, he will not utter such words; he will abide in restraint.” For his father's benefit, he spoke thus.

Ehi tātāti tāta tuyhaṃ gharaṃ mā hotu, ehi gharaṃ gamissāmāti vadati. Alanti thero ukkaṭṭhaekāsanikatāya paṭikkhipanto evamāha. Adhivāsesīti thero pana pakatiyā ukkaṭṭhasapadānacāriko svātanāyabhikkhaṃ nāma nādhivāseti, mātu anuggahena pana adhivāsesi. Mātu kirassa theraṃ anussaritvā mahāsoko uppajji, rodaneneva pakkakkhi viya jātā, tasmā thero “sacāhaṃ taṃ apassitvā gamissāmi, hadayampissā phāleyyā”ti anuggahena adhivāsesi. Kārāpetvāti ekaṃ hiraññassa, ekaṃ suvaṇṇassāti dve puñje kārāpetvā. Kīvamahantā pana puñjā ahesunti. Yathā orato ṭhito puriso pārato ṭhitaṃ majjhimappamāṇaṃ purisaṃ na passati, evaṃmahantā.

“Ehi, tāta” means the father says: “Dear son, let this not be your home. Come, let us go to our home.” “Alaṃ” (Enough!): the Elder, refusing on account of his strict practice of eating in one session, spoke thus. “Adhivāsesi” (He consented): The Elder, being by nature a strict practitioner of the alms-round without omission, does not normally accept an invitation for the next day's meal. However, for the benefit of his mother, he consented. For it is said that great sorrow arose in his mother as she constantly remembered the Elder, and from weeping her eyes had become as if inflamed. Therefore, the Elder, thinking, “If I go without seeing her, her heart might even break,” consented for her benefit. “Kārāpetvā” (Having had made): Having had two piles made, one of silver and one of gold. And how large were the piles? They were so large that a person standing on this side could not see a person of medium height standing on the other side.

301. Idaṃ te tātāti kahāpaṇapuñjañca suvaṇṇapuñjañca dassento āha. Mattikanti mātito āgataṃ, idaṃ te mātāmahiyā mātu imaṃ gehaṃ āgacchantiyā gandhamālādīnaṃ atthāya dinnaṃ dhananti attho. Aññaṃ pettikaṃ aññaṃ pitāmahanti yaṃ pana te pitu ca pitāmahānañca santakaṃ, taṃ aññaṃyeva, nihitañca payuttañca ativiya bahu. Ettha ca “pitāmaha”nti taddhitalopaṃ katvā vuttanti veditabbaṃ. “Petāmaha”nti vā pāṭho. Sakkā [P 3.0300]tatonidānanti dhanahetu dhanapaccayā. Taṃ taṃ dhanaṃ rakkhantassa ca rājādīnaṃ vasena dhanaparikkhayaṃ pāpuṇantassa kassaci uppajjamānasokādayo sandhāya evamāha. Evaṃ vutte seṭṭhi gahapati – “ahaṃ imaṃ uppabbājessāmīti ānesiṃ, so dāni me dhammakathaṃ kātuṃ āraddho, ayaṃ na me vacanaṃ karissatī”ti uṭṭhāya gantvā assa orodhānaṃ dvāraṃ vivarāpetvā – “ayaṃ vo sāmiko, gacchatha yaṃ kiñci katvā naṃ gaṇhituṃ vāyamathā”ti uyyojesi. Suvaye ṭhitā nāṭakitthiyo nikkhamitvā theraṃ parivārayiṃsu[M 3.0208], tāsu dve jeṭṭhakitthiyo sandhāya purāṇadutiyikātiādi vuttaṃ. Paccekaṃ pādesu gahetvāti ekekamhi pāde naṃ gahetvā.

301. “Idaṃ te, tāta” (This is for you, dear son): He spoke while showing the pile of coins and the pile of gold. “Mattikaṃ” (maternal inheritance) means what came from the mother's side. The meaning is: “This is the wealth given to your mother by your maternal grandmother for the purpose of perfumes, garlands, and so on, when she came to this house.” “Aññaṃ pettikaṃ, aññaṃ pitāmahaṃ” (The paternal is separate, the grandparental is separate) means: “That which belongs to your father and your grandfathers is entirely separate; the wealth that is buried and that which is loaned out is also exceedingly abundant.” And here, it should be understood that “pitāmahaṃ” is stated with the elision of a Taddhita suffix. Or, the reading is “petāmahaṃ.” Regarding the phrase 'It is possible, based on that...': he spoke thus in reference to the sorrow and so on that arises for someone on account of wealth, both while protecting that wealth and when one experiences the destruction of wealth due to kings and so on. When this was said, the merchant householder thought: “I brought him here to make him disrobe, but now he has begun to give me a Dhamma talk; he will not do as I say.” Getting up and going, he had the door to the women's quarters opened and dispatched them, saying: “This is your master. Go and try to win him over by whatever means you can.” The dancing girls, standing in their youth, came out and surrounded the Elder. In reference to the two senior women among them, the words “former wives,” and so on, were said. “Paccekaṃ pādesu gahetvā” (Taking hold of each foot) means taking hold of him at each foot.

Kīdisā [V 3.0213] nāma tā ayyaputta accharāyoti kasmā evamāhaṃsu? Tadā kira sambahule khattiyakumārepi brāhmaṇakumārepi seṭṭhiputtepi mahāsampattiyo pahāya pabbajante disvā pabbajjāguṇaṃ ajānantā kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpenti “kasmā ete pabbajantī”ti. Athaññe vadanti “devaccharādevanāṭakānaṃ kāraṇā”ti. Sā kathā vitthārikā ahosi. Taṃ gahetvā sabbā evamāhaṃsu. Atha thero paṭikkhipanto na kho mayaṃ bhaginītiādimāha. Samudācaratīti [P 3.0301] voharati vadati. Tattheva mucchitā papatiṃsūti taṃ bhaginivādena samudācarantaṃ disvā “mayaṃ ajja āgamissati, ajja āgamissatī”ti dvādasa vassāni bahi na nikkhantā, etaṃ nissāya no dārakā na laddhā, yesaṃ ānubhāvena jīveyyāma, ito camhā parihīnā aññato ca. Ayaṃ loko nāma attanova cintesi, tasmā tāpi “idāni mayaṃ anāthā jātā”ti attanova cintayamānā – “anatthiko dāni amhehi ayaṃ, so amhe pajāpatiyo samānā attanā saddhiṃ ekamātukucchiyā sayitadārikā viya maññatī”ti samuppannabalavasokā hutvā tasmiṃyeva padese mucchitā papatiṃsu, patitāti attho.

“Noble son, what kind of celestial nymphs are these?” Why did they say this? At that time, it is said, upon seeing many young nobles, young brahmins, and sons of merchants renounce great fortunes and go forth into homelessness, those who did not know the benefit of going forth raised the topic: ‘Why do these men go forth?’ Then others would say, ‘It is for the sake of celestial nymphs, the divine attendants.’ This talk became widespread. Taking up this talk, all of his former wives spoke thus. Then the Elder, rejecting this, said the words beginning with, ‘Indeed, sisters…’ ‘He addressed’ (samudācarati) means he spoke to, he called. ‘There they fainted and fell down’ means that upon seeing him address them with the term ‘sisters,’ they—who for twelve years had not gone outside, thinking, ‘Today he will come, today he will come,’ and who, relying on him, had not obtained children by whose power they might live—thought, ‘We are bereft both here and elsewhere. This world thinks only of its own interest.’ Therefore, they too, thinking only of themselves—‘Now we have become helpless. This man now has no need of us. Though we are his wives, he regards us as if we were young girls who had slept in the same mother’s womb as himself’—being overcome by intense sorrow, fainted and fell down in that very place. ‘Fell down’ is the meaning.

Mā no viheṭhethāti mā amhe dhanaṃ dassetvā mātugāme ca uyyojetvā viheṭhayittha, vihesā hesā pabbajitānanti. Kasmā evamāha? Mātāpitūnaṃ anuggahena. So kira seṭṭhi – “pabbajitaliṅgaṃ nāma kiliṭṭhaṃ, pabbajjāvesaṃ hāretvā nhāyitvā tayo janā ekato bhuñjissāmā”ti maññamāno therassa bhikkhaṃ na deti. Thero – “mādisassa khīṇāsavassa āhārantarāyaṃ katvā ete bahuṃ apuññaṃ pasaveyyu”nti tesaṃ anuggahena evamāha.

‘Do not harass us’ means: do not harass us by displaying wealth and by presenting women. This is a harassment for renunciants. Why did he say this? For the benefit of his parents. It is said that the merchant, thinking, ‘The sign of a renunciant is impure; having him discard the renunciant’s attire and bathe, the three of us shall eat together,’ did not give almsfood to the Elder. The Elder, for their benefit, spoke thus, thinking, ‘By creating an obstacle to the meal of a canker-free one like myself, they would produce much demerit.’

302. Gāthā abhāsīti gāthāyo abhāsi. Tattha passāti santike ṭhitajanaṃ sandhāya vadati. Cittanti cittavicittaṃ. Bimbanti attabhāvaṃ. Arukāyanti [P 3.0302] navannaṃ vaṇamukhānaṃ vasena vaṇakāyaṃ. Samussitanti tīṇi aṭṭhisatāni navahi nhārusatehi bandhitvā navahi maṃsapesisatehi limpitvā samantato ussitaṃ. Āturanti jarāturatāya rogāturatāya kilesāturatāya ca niccāturaṃ. Bahusaṅkappanti paresaṃ uppannapatthanāsaṅkappehi bahusaṅkappaṃ[M 3.0209]. Itthīnañhi kāye purisānaṃ saṅkappā uppajjanti, tesaṃ kāye itthīnaṃ. Susāne chaḍḍitakaḷevarabhūtampi cetaṃ kākakulalādayo patthayantiyevāti bahusaṅkappo nāma hoti. Yassa natthi [V 3.0214] dhuvaṃ ṭhitīti yassa kāyassa māyāmarīcipheṇapiṇḍa udakapupphuḷādīnaṃ viya ekaṃseneva ṭhiti nāma natthi, bhijjanadhammatāva niyatā.

302. ‘He spoke verses’ (gāthā abhāsi) means he uttered stanzas. Therein, ‘Behold’ (passa) is said in reference to the people standing nearby. ‘Decorated’ (cittaṃ) means variegated and adorned. ‘Image’ (bimbaṃ) means this individual existence. ‘A body of sores’ (arukāyaṃ) means a body of wounds, by way of the nine wound-like orifices. ‘Built up’ (samussitaṃ) means erected all around, being constructed of three hundred bones bound by nine hundred sinews and plastered with nine hundred pieces of flesh. ‘Afflicted’ (āturaṃ) means constantly afflicted by the affliction of aging, the affliction of disease, and the affliction of defilements. ‘Much-thought-of’ (bahusaṅkappaṃ) means it is the object of many thoughts due to the thoughts of longing and desire that arise in others. For in a woman’s body, thoughts of lust arise in men; and in their bodies, thoughts of lust arise in women. And even when this body has become a corpse discarded in the charnel ground, crows, vultures, and the like still desire it; thus it is called ‘much-thought-of.’ ‘For which there is no lasting stability’ (yassa natthi dhuvaṃ ṭhiti) means that for this body, just as for a magical illusion, a mirage, a lump of foam, a water bubble, and so on, there is absolutely no such thing as stability; its nature is certain to break apart.

Tacena onaddhanti allamanussacammena onaddhaṃ. Saha vatthebhi sobhatīti gandhādīhi maṇikuṇḍalehi ca cittakatampi rūpaṃ vatthehi saheva sobhati, vinā vatthehi jegucchaṃ hoti anolokanakkhamaṃ.

‘Enveloped in skin’ (tacena onaddhaṃ) means it is covered with moist human skin. ‘It shines with its garments’ (saha vatthebhi sobhati) means that this form, though adorned with perfumes and so on, and with jeweled earrings, shines only together with its clothes. Without clothes, it is repulsive, unfit to be looked at.

Alattakakatāti alattakena rañjitā. Cuṇṇakamakkhitanti sāsapakakkena mukhapīḷakādīni nīharitvā loṇamattikāya duṭṭhalohitaṃ viliyāpetvā tilapiṭṭhena lohitaṃ pasādetvā haliddiyā vaṇṇaṃ sampādetvā cuṇṇakagaṇḍikāya mukhaṃ paharanti, tenesa ativiya virocati. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ.

‘Dyed with lac’ (alattakakatā) means the feet are colored with lac-dye. ‘Smeared with powder’ (cuṇṇakamakkhitaṃ) refers to when they remove facial blemishes like pimples with mustard paste, dissolve impure blood with salt-earth, clarify the blood with sesame powder, perfect the complexion with turmeric, and then rub the face with fragrant powder, by which it shines exceedingly. This was said in reference to that.

Aṭṭhāpadakatāti [P 3.0303] rasodakena makkhitvā nalāṭapariyante āvattanaparivatte katvā aṭṭhapadakaracanāya racitā. Añjanīti añjananāḷikā.

‘Styled in a checkerboard pattern’ (aṭṭhāpadakatā) means the hair is arranged in a checkerboard design, made by smearing it with water mixed with resin, creating forward and surrounding curls at the edge of the forehead. ‘With kohl’ (añjanī) refers to the kohl-tube.

Odahīti ṭhapesi. Pāsanti vākarājālaṃ. Nāsadāti na ghaṭṭayi. Nivāpanti nivāpasutte vuttanivāpatiṇasadisabhojanaṃ. Kandanteti viravamāne paridevamāne. Imāya hi gāthāya thero mātāpitaro migaluddake viya katvā dassesi, avasesañātake migaluddakaparisaṃ viya, hiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ vākarājālaṃ viya, attanā bhuttabhojanaṃ nivāpatiṇaṃ viya, attānaṃ mahāmigaṃ viya katvā dassesi. Yathā hi mahāmigo yāvadatthaṃ nivāpatiṇaṃ khāditvā pānīyaṃ pivitvā gīvaṃ ukkhipitvā disaṃ oloketvā “imaṃ nāma ṭhānaṃ gatassa sotthi bhavissatī”ti migaluddakānaṃ paridevantānaṃyeva vākaraṃ aghaṭṭayamānova uppatitvā araññaṃ pavisitvā ghanacchāyassa chattassa viya gumbassa heṭṭhā mandamandena vātena bījayamāno āgatamaggaṃ olokento tiṭṭhati, evameva thero imā gāthā bhāsitvā ākāseneva gantvā migacīre paccupaṭṭhāsi.

‘He set’ (odahi) means he placed. ‘The snare’ (pāsaṃ) means a deer-net. ‘I was not caught’ (nāsadaṃ) means I was not ensnared. ‘The bait’ (nivāpaṃ) means food similar to the bait-grass mentioned in the Nivāpa Sutta. ‘As they wept’ (kandante) means while they were crying out and lamenting. Indeed, with this verse, the Elder showed his parents as deer hunters, his remaining relatives as the hunters’ party, the gold and silver as the deer-net, the food he had eaten as the bait-grass, and himself as a great deer. For just as a great deer, having eaten its fill of bait-grass and drunk water, lifts its neck, looks to the directions, and thinks, ‘Going to such-and-such a place will be safe for me,’ and then, while the deer hunters are still lamenting, without getting caught in the net, leaps up, enters the forest, and stands under a dense thicket that is like an umbrella, being fanned by a gentle breeze while looking back at the path he came from; even so, the Elder, after reciting these verses, went through the sky and appeared in the Migacīra park.

Kasmā pana thero ākāsena gatoti. Pitā kirassa seṭṭhi sattasu dvārakoṭṭhakesu aggaḷaṃ [V 3.0215] dāpetvā malle āṇāpesi – “sace nikkhamitvā [M 3.0210] gacchati[P 3.0304], hatthapādesu naṃ gahetvā kāsāyāni haritvā gihivesaṃ gaṇhāpethā”ti. Tasmā thero – “ete mādisaṃ mahākhīṇāsavaṃ hatthe vā pāde vā gahetvā apuññaṃ pasaveyyuṃ, taṃ nesaṃ mā ahosī”ti cintetvā ākāsena agamāsi. Parasamuddavāsittherānaṃ pana – “ṭhitakova imā gāthā bhāsitvā vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā rañño korabyassa migacīre paccupaṭṭhāsī”ti ayaṃ vācanāmaggoyeva.

But why did the Elder go through the sky? It is said that his father, the merchant, had bolts placed on the seven gatehouses and commanded his wrestlers, saying, ‘If he tries to leave, seize him by his hands and feet, strip him of his saffron robes, and make him assume the layman’s attire.’ Therefore the Elder, thinking, ‘If these men were to seize a great canker-free one like myself by the hand or foot, they would produce much demerit; may that not happen to them,’ departed through the sky. However, according to the Elders from across the sea, this is simply the line of recitation: ‘Standing right there, he recited these verses, rose up into the air, and appeared in King Korabya’s Migacīra park.’

303. Migavoti tassa uyyānapālassa nāmaṃ. Sodhentoti uyyānamaggaṃ samaṃ kāretvā antouyyāne tacchitabbayuttaṭṭhānāni tacchāpento sammajjitabbayuttāni ṭhānāni sammajjāpento vālukāokiraṇa-pupphavikiraṇa-puṇṇaghaṭaṭṭhapana-kadalikkhandhaṭhapanādīni ca karontoti attho. Yena rājā korabyo tenupasaṅkamīti amhākaṃ rājā sadā imassa kulaputtassa vaṇṇaṃ kathesi, passitukāmo etaṃ, āgatabhāvaṃ panassa na jānāti, mahā kho panāyaṃ paṇṇākāro, gantvā rañño ārocessāmīti cintetvā yena rājā korabyo tenupasaṅkami.

303. 'Migava' is the name of that park keeper. 'Sodhento' means: having caused the park path to be made level, and inside the park, causing places that should be planed to be planed, causing places that should be swept to be swept, and doing things such as scattering sand, strewing flowers, placing full water pots, and setting up banana tree trunks—this is the meaning. 'Yena rājā Korabyo tenupasaṅkami' means: having thought, 'Our king always spoke of the virtues of this clansman. He is desirous of seeing him, but he does not know of his arrival. Indeed, this is a great gift. I will go and inform the king,' he approached the place where King Korabya was.

Kittayamāno ahosīti so kira rājā theraṃ anussaritvā balamajjhepi nāṭakamajjhepi – “dukkaraṃ kataṃ kulaputtena tāva mahantaṃ sampattiṃ pahāya pabbajitvā punanivattitvā anapalokentenā”ti guṇaṃ kathesi, taṃ gahetvā ayaṃ evamāha. Vissajjethāti [P 3.0305] vatvāti orodhamahāmattabalakāyādīsu yassa yaṃ anucchavikaṃ, tassa taṃ dāpetvāti attho. Ussaṭāya ussaṭāyāti ussitāya ussitāya, mahāmattamahāraṭṭhikādīnaṃ vasena uggatuggatameva parisaṃ gahetvā upasaṅkamīti attho. Idha bhavaṃ raṭṭhapālo hatthatthare nisīdatūti hatthattharo tanuko bahalapupphādiguṇaṃ katvā atthato abhilakkhito hoti, tādise anāpucchitvā nisīdituṃ na yuttanti maññamāno evamāha.

'Kittayamāno ahosi' means: it is said that the king, constantly remembering the Elder, spoke of his virtue both in the midst of his army and in the midst of his court ladies, saying, 'A difficult thing was done by the clansman, who went forth after abandoning such great fortune, not returning again, and without looking back.' Taking these words, this park keeper spoke thus. 'Vissajjetha' means: having caused to be given to whomever among the court ladies, great ministers, troops, and so on, whatever was appropriate for them—this is the meaning. 'Ussaṭāya ussaṭāya' means: by way of those who were renowned and distinguished, such as great ministers and great provincial governors, he approached, taking only that assembly which had become prominent—this is the meaning. 'Idha bhavaṃ Raṭṭhapālo hatthatthare nisīdatu' means: the king, thinking, 'The elephant saddle-cloth is soft; having been made with qualities such as thick flowers, it is laid out and marked as excellent. It is not proper to sit on such a thing without being invited,' spoke thus.

304. Pārijuññānīti pārijuññabhāvā parikkhayā. Jiṇṇoti jarājiṇṇo. Vuḍḍhoti vayovuḍḍho. Mahallakoti jātimahallako. Addhagatoti addhānaṃ atikkanto. Vayoanuppattoti pacchimavayaṃ anuppatto. Pabbajatīti dhuravihāraṃ gantvā bhikkhū vanditvā, – “bhante, mayā daharakāle [M 3.0211] bahuṃ kusalaṃ kataṃ, idāni mahallakomhi, mahallakassa cesā pabbajjā nāma, cetiyaṅgaṇaṃ sammajjitvā appaharitaṃ katvā jīvissāmi, pabbājetha maṃ, bhante,”ti kāruññaṃ uppādento [V 3.0216] yācati, therā anukampāya pabbājenti. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Dutiyavārepi eseva nayo.

304. 'Pārijuññāni' means the states of being worn out, the states of exhaustion. 'Jiṇṇo' means one aged by old age. 'Vuḍḍho' means one senior in age. 'Mahallako' means one senior by birth. 'Addhagato' means one who has passed a long time. 'Vayoanuppatto' means one who has reached the final age. 'Pabbajati' means: having gone to the main monastery and paid homage to the monks, he requests, arousing compassion, saying, 'Venerable sirs, I did much that was meritorious in my youth. Now I have become old. For an old person, this is what is called "going forth": I will make a living by sweeping the stupa courtyard and making it free of green things. Venerable sirs, please give me, an old man, the going forth.' The elder monks, out of compassion, give the going forth. This was said in reference to that. In the second instance, this is the same method.

Appābādhoti arogo. Appātaṅkoti [P 3.0306] niddukkho. Samavepākiniyāti samavipācaniyā. Gahaṇiyāti kammajatejodhātuyā. Tattha yassa bhuttabhutto āhāro jīrati, yassa vā pana puṭabhattaṃ viya tatheva tiṭṭhati, ubhopete na samavepākiniyā gahaṇiyā samannāgatā. Yassa pana bhuttakāle bhattacchando uppajjateva, ayaṃ samavepākiniyā samannāgato. Nātisītāya naccuṇhāyāti teneva kāraṇena nātisītāya naccuṇhāya. Anupubbenāti rājāno vā harantītiādinā anukkamena. Dutiyavāre rājabhayacorabhayachātakabhayādinā anukkamena.

'Appābādho' means without illness. 'Appātaṅko' means without suffering. 'Samavepākiniyā' means with even digestion. 'Gahaṇiyā' means with a digestive faculty born of kamma. Therein, one for whom food, whenever eaten, is digested, or one for whom it remains just so, like food placed in a bundle—both these two are not endowed with a digestive faculty that digests evenly. But one for whom the desire for food arises at mealtime, this one is endowed with a digestive faculty that digests evenly. 'Nātisītāya naccuṇhāya' means: for that very reason, it is neither too cold nor too hot. 'Anupubbena' means by the sequence beginning with 'kings carry away.' In the second instance, it means by the sequence of fear of kings, fear of thieves, fear of hunger, and so on.

305. Dhammuddesā uddiṭṭhāti dhammaniddesā uddiṭṭhā. Upaniyyatīti jarāmaraṇasantikaṃ gacchati, āyukkhayena vā tattha niyyati. Addhuvoti dhuvaṭṭhānavirahito. Atāṇoti tāyituṃ samatthena virahito. Anabhissaroti asaraṇo abhisaritvā abhigantvā assāsetuṃ samatthena virahito. Assakoti nissako sakabhaṇḍavirahito. Sabbaṃ pahāya gamanīyanti sakabhaṇḍanti sallakkhitaṃ sabbaṃ pahāya lokena gantabbaṃ. Taṇhādāsoti taṇhāya dāso.

305. 'The summaries of the Dhamma have been pointed out' means the detailed expositions of the Dhamma have been pointed out. 'It is led near' means it goes to the vicinity of old age and death, or it is led there by the exhaustion of the lifespan. 'Not permanent' means devoid of a permanent state. 'Without protection' means devoid of one who is capable of protecting. 'Without a master' means without a refuge, devoid of one who is capable of giving comfort by being approached and gone to. 'Without ownership' means not one's own, devoid of one's own property. 'One must go, abandoning everything' means having abandoned all that is considered 'one's own property', the world must go on. 'A slave to craving' means a slave of craving.

306. Hatthisminti hatthisippe. Katāvīti [P 3.0307] katakaraṇīyo, sikkhitasikkho paguṇasippoti attho. Esa nayo sabbattha. Ūrubalīti ūrubalasampanno. Yassa hi phalakañca āvudhañca gahetvā parasenaṃ pavisitvā abhinnaṃ bhindato bhinnaṃ sandhārayato parahatthagataṃ rajjaṃ āharituṃ ūrubalaṃ atthi, ayaṃ ūrubalī nāma. Bāhubalīti bāhubalasampanno. Sesaṃ purimasadisameva. Alamattoti samatthaattabhāvo.

306. 'In elephants' means in the art of elephants. 'Accomplished' means one who has done what should be done, one who has learned what should be learned, one who has mastered the skill—this is the meaning. This is the method everywhere. 'Strong-thighed' means endowed with thigh-strength. Indeed, one who, taking shield and weapon, enters the enemy's army, breaking the unbroken and rallying the broken, and has the thigh-strength to bring back a kingdom that has fallen into the hands of another—such a one is called 'strong-thighed.' 'Strong-armed' means endowed with arm-strength. The rest is just like the preceding. 'Sufficient' means a capable physical frame.

Pariyodhāya vattissantīti uppannaṃ uppaddavaṃ odhāya avattharitvā vattissantīti sallakkhetvā gahitā.

'They will live, having set a boundary' means: they were chosen with the consideration that 'they will live by guarding against and overcoming any danger that arises.'

Saṃvijjati [M 3.0212] kho, bho raṭṭhapāla, imasmiṃ rājakule pahūtaṃ hiraññasuvaṇṇanti idaṃ so rājā upari dhammuddesassa kāraṇaṃ āharanto āha.

The king said this statement—'Indeed, friend Raṭṭhapāla, in this royal family there is much gold and silver'—as he was bringing forth a reason for the summary of the Dhamma above.

Athāparaṃ [V 3.0217] etadavocāti etaṃ “passāmi loke”tiādinā nayena catunnaṃ dhammuddesānaṃ anugītiṃ avoca.

'Then he further said this' means: he spoke this recitation corresponding to the four summaries of the Dhamma, in the manner beginning with 'I see in the world...'

307. Tattha bhiyyova kāme abhipatthayantīti ekaṃ labhitvā dve patthayanti, dve labhitvā cattāroti evaṃ uttaruttari vatthukāmakilesakāme patthayantiyeva.

307. Therein, 'they desire sensual pleasures even more' means: having obtained one, they desire two; having obtained two, they desire four. Thus, ever higher and higher, they just keep desiring material sensual pleasures and defilement-sensual pleasures.

Pasayhāti sapattagaṇaṃ abhibhavitvā. Sasāgarantanti saddhiṃ sāgarantena. Oraṃ samuddassāti yaṃ samuddassa orato sakaraṭṭhaṃ, tena atittarūpoti attho. Na hatthīti na hi atthi.

'By force' means having overcome the host of enemies. 'Up to the ocean's end' means together with the ocean's boundary. 'The near shore of the ocean' means: he is of a nature not satisfied with his own kingdom which is on this side of the ocean—this is the meaning. In the phrase 'na hatthi', the division of words is 'na hi atthi' (indeed, there is not).

Aho vatā noti aho vata nu, ayameva vā pāṭho. Amarāti [P 3.0308] cāhūti amaraṃ iti ca āhu. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yaṃ mataṃ ñātī parivāretvā kandanti, taṃ – “aho vata amhākaṃ bhātā mato, putto mato”tiādīnipi vadanti.

'Aho vatā no' means 'aho vata nu', or this itself is the reading. 'Amarāti cāhu' means 'amaraṃ iti ca āhu' (and they say 'immortal'). This is what is meant: when relatives, having surrounded a dead person, weep, they also say of him such things as, 'Alas, our brother is dead,' 'our son is dead.'

Phusanti phassanti maraṇaphassaṃ phusanti. Tatheva phuṭṭhoti yathā bālo, dhīropi tatheva maraṇaphassena phuṭṭho, aphuṭṭho nāma natthi, ayaṃ pana viseso. Bālo ca bālyā vadhitova setīti bālo bālabhāvena maraṇaphassaṃ āgamma vadhitova seti abhihatova sayati. Akataṃ vata me kalyāṇantiādivippaṭisāravasena calati vedhati vipphandati. Dhīro ca na vedhatīti dhīro sugatinimittaṃ passanto na vedhati na calati.

“They experience” means they are touched, they experience the touch of death. “Just as he is touched” means just as the fool, so too the wise one is touched by the touch of death; there is no one called ‘untouched.’ But this is the difference: “And the fool, because of foolishness, lies as if struck down” means the fool, because of his foolishness, on account of the touch of death, lies as if afflicted, lies as if greatly afflicted. By way of regret, such as, “Alas, I have not done good!” he moves, trembles, and quivers. “But the wise one does not tremble” means the wise one, seeing the sign of a good destiny, does not tremble, does not waver.

Yāya vosānaṃ idhādhigacchatīti yāya paññāya imasmiṃ loke sabbakiccavosānaṃ arahattaṃ adhigacchati, sāva dhanato uttamatarā. Abyositattāti apariyositattā, arahattapattiyā, abhāvenāti attho. Bhavābhavesūti hīnappaṇītesu bhavesu.

“By which one here attains completion” means by which wisdom one in this world attains Arahantship, the completion of all duties; that very wisdom is a wealth more excellent than any other. “Due to not being completed” means because of not having reached the end, due to the absence of the attainment of Arahantship—this is the meaning. “In various existences” means in inferior and superior existences.

Upeti gabbhañca parañca lokanti tesu pāpaṃ karontesu yo koci satto paramparāya saṃsāraṃ āpajjitvā gabbhañca parañca lokaṃ upeti. Tassappapaññoti tassa tādisassa appapaññassa añño appapañño abhisaddahanto.

“He approaches the womb and the next world” means: among those who do evil, any being who, having reached saṃsāra through a succession of existences, approaches the womb and another world, the next world. “Of one with little wisdom” means: another person of little wisdom who, having heard the words of such a one with little wisdom, believes.

Sakammunā [V 3.0218][M 3.0213] haññatīti attanā katakammavasena “kasāhipi tāletī”tiādīhi kammakāraṇāhi haññati. Pecca paramhi loketi ito gantvā paramhi apāyaloke.

“By one’s own deed one is tormented” means one is tormented by the power of the deed done by oneself, by the instruments of kamma, such as “he strikes with whips,” and so on. “After departing, in the next world” means having gone from this state of existence, in the next world, the plane of misery.

Virūparūpenāti [P 3.0309] vividharūpena, nānāsabhāvenāti attho. Kāmaguṇesūti diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikesu sabbakāmaguṇesu ādīnavaṃ disvā. Daharāti antamaso kalalamattabhāvaṃ upādāya taruṇā. Vuḍḍhāti vassasatātikkantā. Apaṇṇakaṃ sāmaññameva seyyoti aviruddhaṃ advajjhagāmiṃ ekantaniyyānikaṃ sāmaññameva “seyyo, uttaritarañca paṇītatarañcā”ti upadhāretvā pabbajitosmi mahārājāti. Tasmā yaṃ tvaṃ vadasi – “kiṃ disvā vā sutvā vā”ti, idaṃ disvā ca sutvā ca pabbajitosmīti maṃ dhārehīti desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesīti.

“By a diverse form” means by various forms, by various natures—this is the meaning. “In the strands of sensual pleasure” means having seen the danger in all the five strands of sensual pleasure, both in the present existence and in the next. “The young” means, at the very least, taking into account the state of being a mere embryo, they are called young. “The old” means those who have passed one hundred years. “The certain ascetic life is indeed better” means having investigated and reflected that the ascetic life itself—which is unopposed, unambiguous, and certainly a means of release from the suffering of the cycle—is indeed “better, more excellent, and more sublime.” [He said,] “I have gone forth, great king.” Therefore, regarding what you ask, “Having seen what, or having heard what?”—[he said,] “Remember me as one who has gone forth having seen and heard this.” Thus he concluded the discourse.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Middle Length Discourses.

Raṭṭhapālasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the Raṭṭhapāla Sutta is finished.

3. Maghadevasuttavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Maghadeva Sutta

308. Evaṃ [V 3.0219] me sutanti maghadevasuttaṃ. Tattha maghadevaambavaneti pubbe maghadevo nāma rājā taṃ ambavanaṃ ropesi. Tesu rukkhesu palujjamānesu aparabhāge aññepi rājāno ropesuṃyeva. Taṃ pana paṭhamavohāravasena maghadevambavananteva saṅkhaṃ gataṃ. Sitaṃ pātvākāsīti sāyanhasamaye vihāracārikaṃ caramāno ramaṇīyaṃ bhūmibhāgaṃ disvā – “vasitapubbaṃ nu kho me imasmiṃ okāse”ti āvajjanto – “pubbe ahaṃ maghadevo nāma rājā hutvā imaṃ ambavanaṃ ropesiṃ, ettheva [P 3.0310] pabbajitvā cattāro brahmavihāre bhāvetvā brahmaloke nibbattiṃ. Taṃ kho panetaṃ kāraṇaṃ bhikkhusaṅghassa apākaṭaṃ, pākaṭaṃ karissāmī”ti aggaggadante dassento sitaṃ pātu akāsi.

308. Thus have I heard—this is the Maghadeva Sutta. Therein, regarding 'in Maghadeva's mango grove': In the past, a king named Maghadeva had that mango grove planted. When those trees were decaying, in a later period, other kings also had them planted. However, by the power of its first designation, that mango grove came to be known only as 'Maghadeva's mango grove.' As for 'He manifested a smile': While walking around the monastery in the evening, seeing a delightful portion of land, and reflecting, 'Have I lived in this place before?', he recalled: 'In the past, having been a king named Maghadeva, I planted this mango grove. Right here, having gone forth, I developed the four divine abidings and was reborn in the Brahma world. Indeed, this matter is not manifest to the community of bhikkhus. I shall make it manifest.' Thus resolving, while showing the very tips of his teeth, he made a smile manifest.

Dhammo assa atthīti dhammiko. Dhammena rājā jātoti dhammarājā. Dhamme ṭhitoti dasakusalakammapathadhamme ṭhito. Dhammaṃ caratīti samaṃ carati[M 3.0214]. Tatra brāhmaṇagahapatikesūti yopi so pubbarājūhi brāhmaṇānaṃ dinnaparihāro, taṃ ahāpetvā pakatiniyāmeneva adāsi, tathā gahapatikānaṃ. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Pakkhassāti iminā pāṭihārikapakkhopi saṅgahito. Aṭṭhamīuposathassa hi paccuggamanānuggamanavasena sattamiyañca navamiyañca, cātuddasapannarasānaṃ paccuggamanānuggamanavasena terasiyañca pāṭipade cāti ime divasā pāṭihārikapakkhāti veditabbā. Tesupi uposathaṃ upavasi.

“Righteous” (dhammiko) means he possesses righteousness (dhammo). “A righteous king” (dhammarājā) means he became a king through righteousness. “Established in righteousness” (dhamme ṭhito) means he was established in the Dhamma of the ten wholesome courses of action. “He practiced righteousness” (dhammaṃ carati) means he acted impartially. Therein, as for “among brahmins and householders”: Whatever provisions were given to brahmins by former kings, he gave them without diminishing them, according to the traditional rule, and likewise for householders. This was said with reference to that. By “of the fortnight” (pakkhassa), the “special observance fortnight” (pāṭihārikapakkha) is also included. For the eighth-day Uposatha, by way of the preceding and following days, the seventh and ninth days are included; and for the fourteenth and fifteenth days, by way of the preceding and following days, the thirteenth and the first day of the next fortnight are included. These days are to be known as the “special observance fortnight.” On these days too, he observed the Uposatha.

309. Devadūtāti devoti maccu, tassa dūtāti devadūtā. Sirasmiñhi palitesu pātubhūtesu maccurājassa santike ṭhito viya hoti, tasmā palitāni maccudevassa dūtāti vuccanti. Devā viya dūtātipi devadūtā. Yathā hi alaṅkatapaṭiyattāya devatāya ākāse ṭhatvā “asukadivase marissatī”ti vutte taṃ tatheva hoti, evaṃ sirasmiṃ palitesu pātubhūtesu devatābyākaraṇasadisameva [P 3.0311] hoti. Tasmā palitāni devasadisā dūtāti vuccanti. Visuddhidevānaṃ dūtātipi devadūtā. Sabbabodhisattā hi jiṇṇabyādhitamatapabbajite disvāva saṃvegamāpajjitvā nikkhamma pabbajanti. Yathāha –

309. “Divine messengers” (devadūtā): “Deva” is death (maccu), and “dūtā” are its messengers; therefore, they are called “devadūtā.” Indeed, when gray hairs have appeared on the head, it is as if one is standing in the presence of the King of Death. Therefore, gray hairs are called the messengers of the death-deva. Also, “messengers like devas” (devā viya dūtā) are “devadūtā.” Just as when a deity, adorned and prepared, stands in the sky and says, “On such-and-such a day, he will die,” and that comes to be true, so too, when gray hairs have appeared on the head, it is just like a pronouncement by a deity. Therefore, gray hairs are called messengers similar to devas. Also, “messengers of the pure deities” (visuddhidevānaṃ dūtā) are “devadūtā.” For all Bodhisattas, only upon seeing the aged, the sick, the dead, and one gone forth, do they attain a sense of urgency, leave home, and go forth. As it is said:

“Jiṇṇañca [V 3.0220] disvā dukhitañca byādhitaṃ,

Matañca disvā gatamāyusaṅkhayaṃ;

Kāsāyavatthaṃ pabbajitañca disvā,

Tasmā ahaṃ pabbajitomhi rājā”ti.

“Having seen the aged, and the sick and afflicted one, and having seen the dead who has reached the exhaustion of their life-span, and having seen one gone forth in ochre robes, therefore, O king, I have gone forth.”

Iminā pariyāyena palitāni visuddhidevānaṃ dūtattā devadūtāti vuccanti.

By this line of reasoning, gray hairs are called 'divine messengers' because of their being messengers of the pure deities.

Kappakassa gāmavaraṃ datvāti satasahassuṭṭhānakaṃ jeṭṭhakagāmaṃ datvā. Kasmā adāsi? Saṃviggamānasattā. Tassa hi añjalismiṃ ṭhapitāni palitāni disvāva saṃvego uppajjati. Aññāni caturāsītivassasahassāni āyu atthi, evaṃ santepi maccurājassa santike ṭhitaṃ viya attānaṃ maññamāno saṃviggo pabbajjaṃ roceti. Tena vuttaṃ –

As for 'Having given the best village to the barber': It means having given the chief village that yields a revenue of one hundred thousand. Why did he give it? Because his mind was stirred with urgency. Indeed, for him, a sense of urgency arose just upon seeing the gray hairs placed in his cupped hands. Although another eighty-four thousand years of life remained, even so, considering himself as if standing in the presence of the King of Death, being stirred with urgency, he found delight in going forth. Therefore it was said:

“Sire [M 3.0215] disvāna palitaṃ, maghadevo disampati;

Saṃvegaṃ alabhī dhīro, pabbajjaṃ samarocayī”ti.

“Having seen a gray hair on his head, Maghadeva, lord of the realm, the wise one, attained a sense of urgency; he greatly delighted in going forth.”

Aparampi vuttaṃ –

And further it was said:

“Uttamaṅgaruhā mayhaṃ, ime jātā vayoharā;

Pātubhūtā devadūtā, pabbajjāsamayo mamā”ti.

“These hairs on my highest limb, stealers of youth, have grown for me. The divine messengers have appeared; it is the time for my going forth.”

Purisayugeti vaṃsasambhave purise. Kesamassuṃ ohāretvāti tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajantāpi hi paṭhamaṃ kesamassuṃ ohāretvā pabbajanti, tato paṭṭhāya vaḍḍhite kese bandhitvā jaṭākalāpadharā hutvā vicaranti. Bodhisattopi tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbaji. Pabbajito pana anesanaṃ [P 3.0312] ananuyuñjitvā rājagehato āhaṭabhikkhāya yāpento brahmavihāraṃ bhāvesi. Tasmā so mettāsahagatenātiādi vuttaṃ.

As for ‘a generation of men’: it means a man born into the lineage. As for ‘having shaved off his hair and beard’: for even those who go forth into the ascetic life first shave off their hair and beard and then go forth. From that time onward, having tied up their grown hair, becoming wearers of matted locks, they wander about. The Bodhisatta also went forth into the ascetic life. However, having gone forth, without engaging in improper seeking, maintaining himself on almsfood brought from the royal palace, he developed the divine abidings. Therefore, the words beginning with ‘He, with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness…’ were spoken.

Kumārakīḷitaṃ kīḷīti aṅkena aṅkaṃ parihariyamāno kīḷi. Mālākalāpaṃ viya hi naṃ ukkhipitvāva [V 3.0221] vicariṃsu. Rañño maghadevassa putto…pe… pabbajīti imassa pabbajitadivase pañca maṅgalāni ahesuṃ. Maghadevarañño matakabhattaṃ, tassa rañño pabbajitamaṅgalaṃ, tassa puttassa chattussāpanamaṅgalaṃ, tassa puttassa uparajjamaṅgalaṃ, tassa puttassa nāmakaraṇamaṅgalanti ekasmiṃyeva samaye pañca maṅgalāni ahesuṃ, sakalajambudīpatale unnaṅgalamahosi.

As for ‘He played the child’s game’: it means he played while being carried from one lap to another. Indeed, they carried him about, lifting him up just like a garland of flowers. As for ‘The son of King Maghadeva… went forth’: on the day this king went forth, five auspicious ceremonies occurred. The funeral meal for King Maghadeva, the auspicious going forth of that king, the raising of the umbrella for his son, the appointment of his son as viceroy, and the naming ceremony for his son—thus, at one and the same time, five auspicious ceremonies occurred. Throughout the entire land of Jambudīpa, it became a time of festival.

311. Puttapaputtakāti puttā ca puttaputtā cāti evaṃ pavattā tassa paramparā. Pacchimako ahosīti pabbajjāpacchimako ahosi. Bodhisatto kira brahmaloke nibbatto – “pavattati nu kho taṃ mayā manussaloke nihataṃ kalyāṇavatta”nti āvajjanto addasa – “ettakaṃ addhānaṃ pavattati, idāni na pavattissatī”ti. Na kho panāhaṃ mayhaṃ paveṇiyā ucchijjituṃ dassāmīti attano vaṃse jātaraññoyeva aggamahesiyā kucchismiṃ paṭisandhiṃ gahetvā attano vaṃsassa nemiṃ ghaṭento viya nibbatto, tenevassa nimīti nāmaṃ ahosi. Iti so pabbajitarājūnaṃ [M 3.0216] sabbapacchimako hutvā pabbajitoti pabbajjāpacchimako ahosi. Guṇehi pana atirekataro. Tassa hi sabbarājūhi atirekatarā dve guṇā ahesuṃ[P 3.0313]. Catūsu dvāresu satasahassaṃ satasahassaṃ vissajjetvā devasikaṃ dānaṃ adāsi, anuposathikassa ca dassanaṃ nivāresi. Anuposathikesu hi rājānaṃ passissāmāti gatesu dovāriko pucchati “tumhe uposathikā no vā”ti. Ye anuposathikā honti, te nivāreti “anuposathikānaṃ rājā dassanaṃ na detī”ti. “Mayaṃ janapadavāsino kāle bhojanaṃ kuhiṃ labhissāmā”tipi tattha vacanokāso natthi. Catūsu hi dvāresu rājaṅgaṇe ca anekāni bhattacāṭisahassāni paṭiyattāneva honti. Tasmā mahājano icchiticchitaṭṭhāne massuṃ kāretvā nhāyitvā vatthāni parivattetvā yathārucitaṃ bhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā uposathaṅgāni adhiṭṭhāya rañño gehadvāraṃ gacchati. Dovārikena “uposathikā tumhe”ti pucchitapucchitā “āma āmā”ti vadanti. Tena hi āgacchathāti pavesetvā rañño dasseti. Iti imehi dvīhi guṇehi atirekataro ahosi.

311. ‘Sons and grandsons’ means his lineage continued with sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons. ‘He was the last’ means he was the last among the kings who went forth. It is said that the Bodhisatta, having been reborn in the Brahma world, reflected, “Does that virtuous practice established by me in the human world still continue?” He saw, “It has continued for this long, but now it will cease.” “Indeed, I will not allow my lineage to be cut off.” Having thus resolved, taking conception in the womb of the chief queen of a king born in his own lineage, he was reborn as if joining the rim of his lineage. For that very reason, his name became Nimī. Thus, being the very last of the kings who went forth, he went forth; thus he was the last to go forth. Moreover, he was more exceedingly endowed with virtues. Indeed, he possessed two virtues that were more exceeding than all other kings: daily, he gave alms by distributing one hundred thousand at each of the four gates, and he prevented an audience for those who had not observed the Uposatha. For when those who had not observed the Uposatha went, thinking, “We will see the king,” the gatekeeper would ask, “Are you observers of the Uposatha or not?” Those who were not observers of the Uposatha were prevented with the words, “The king does not grant an audience to those who do not observe the Uposatha.” There was no opportunity even to say, “We are country-dwellers—where shall we get food at the proper time?” For at the four gates and in the royal courtyard, many thousands of large pots of rice were always prepared. Therefore, the great populace, at any place they wished, had their beards attended to, bathed, changed their clothes, ate food as they desired, undertook the Uposatha precepts, and then went to the king’s palace gate. When asked repeatedly by the gatekeeper, “Are you observers of the Uposatha?” they would reply, “Yes, yes.” Then he would say, “In that case, come,” and admitting them, would show them to the king. Thus, by these two virtues, he was more exceedingly endowed.

312. Devānaṃ tāvatiṃsānanti tāvatiṃsabhavane nibbattadevānaṃ. Te kira devā videharaṭṭhe mithilanagaravāsino rañño ovāde ṭhatvā pañca sīlāni rakkhitvā uposathakammaṃ katvā tattha nibbattā rañño guṇakathaṃ kathenti. Te sandhāya vuttaṃ “devānaṃ tāvatiṃsāna”nti.

312. ‘Of the Tāvatiṃsa devas’ refers to the devas born in the Tāvatiṃsa realm. It is said that these devas, having been residents of the city of Mithilā in the Videha country, having abided in the king’s exhortation, observed the five precepts, performed the Uposatha observance, and were reborn there. They then spoke of the king’s virtues. Referring to them, it was said, ‘of the Tāvatiṃsa devas’.

Nisinno [V 3.0222] hotīti pāsādavarassa uparigato dānañca sīlañca upaparikkhamāno nisinno hoti. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi – “dānaṃ nu kho mahantaṃ udāhu sīlaṃ, yadi dānaṃ mahantaṃ, ajjhottharitvā dānameva dassāmi. Atha sīlaṃ, sīlameva pūrissāmī”ti. Tassa “idaṃ mahantaṃ idaṃ mahanta”nti nicchituṃ asakkontasseva sakko gantvā purato pāturahosi. Tena vuttaṃ atha kho, ānanda,…pe… sammukhe pāturahosīti. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi – “rañño kaṅkhā uppannā, tassa kaṅkhacchedanatthaṃ pañhañca kathessāmi, idhāgamanatthāya paṭiññañca gaṇhissāmī”ti[P 3.0314]. Tasmā gantvā sammukhe pāturahosi. Rājā adiṭṭhapubbaṃ rūpaṃ disvā bhīto ahosi lomahaṭṭhajāto. Atha naṃ sakko – “mā bhāyi, mahārāja, vissattho pañhaṃ puccha, kaṅkhaṃ te paṭivinodessāmī”ti āha.

‘He was seated’ means that having gone to the upper part of his excellent palace, he was seated, investigating generosity and virtue. It is said that this occurred to him: “Which, I wonder, is greater: generosity or virtue? If generosity is greater, then overwhelming all else, I will give only generosity. But if it is virtue, I will fulfill only virtue.” While he was thus unable to decide, “This is great, this is great,” Sakka went and appeared before him. Therefore it was said: “Then, indeed, Ānanda… he appeared before him.” It is said that this occurred to Sakka: “A doubt has arisen for the king. For the sake of cutting off his doubt, I will both answer his question and take a promise for his coming here.” Therefore, he went and appeared before him. The king, seeing a form never seen before, was frightened, and his hair stood on end. Then Sakka said to him, “Do not be afraid, great king. Ask your question confidently. I will dispel your doubt.”

Rājā [M 3.0217] –

The king:

“Pucchāmi taṃ mahārāja, sabbabhūtānamissara;

Dānaṃ vā brahmacariyaṃ vā, katamaṃ su mahapphala”nti. –

“I ask you, great king, lord of all beings: between generosity and the holy life, which indeed has great fruit?”

Pañhaṃ pucchi. Sakko – “dānaṃ nāma kiṃ, sīlameva guṇavisiṭṭhatāya mahantaṃ. Ahañhi pubbe, mahārāja, dasavassasahassāni dasannaṃ jaṭilasahassānaṃ dānaṃ datvā pettivisayato na mutto, sīlavantā pana mayhaṃ dānaṃ bhuñjitvā brahmaloke nibbattā”ti vatvā imā gāthā avoca –

He asked the question. Sakka replied: “What is generosity? Virtue alone is great due to its superior quality. Indeed, great king, in a former existence, I, having given alms to ten thousand matted-hair ascetics for ten thousand years, was not freed from the realm of the petas. But the virtuous ones, having partaken of my alms, were reborn in the Brahma world.” Having said this, he spoke these verses:

“Hīnena brahmacariyena, khattiye upapajjati;

Majjhimena ca devattaṃ, uttamena visujjhati.

“With an inferior holy life, one is reborn among the Khattiyas; with a middling one, into the state of a deva; with the supreme, one is purified.

Na hete sulabhā kāyā, yācayogena kenaci;

Ye kāye upapajjanti, anāgārā tapassino”ti. (jā. 2.22.429-430);

Indeed, these bodies are not easily obtained by any act of giving. Those who are reborn in these bodies are the homeless, the ascetics.”

Evaṃ [V 3.0223] rañño kaṅkhaṃ vinodetvā devalokagamanāya paṭiññāgahaṇatthaṃ lābhā te mahārājātiādimāha. Tattha avikampamānoti abhāyamāno. Adhivāsesīti ahaṃ mahājanaṃ kusalaṃ samādapemi, puññavantānaṃ pana vasanaṭṭhānaṃ disvā āgatena manussapathe sukhaṃ kathetuṃ hotīti adhivāsesi.

Thus, having dispelled the king's doubt, in order to obtain his promise for the journey to the world of the devas, he spoke the words beginning with, 'It is a gain for you, great king.' Therein, 'unwavering' (avikampamāno) means not being afraid. 'He consented' (adhivāsesi) means he consented, thinking, 'I am causing the great populace to undertake wholesome deeds. Moreover, having seen the dwelling place of the meritorious and returned, it will be easy to speak of the fruit of merit on the human path.'

313. Evaṃ bhaddantavāti evaṃ hotu bhaddakaṃ tava vacananti vatvā. Yojetvāti ekasmiṃyeva yuge sahassaassājānīye [P 3.0315] yojetvā. Tesaṃ pana pāṭiyekkaṃ yojanakiccaṃ natthi, manaṃ āgamma yuttāyeva honti. So pana dibbaratho diyaḍḍhayojanasatiko hoti, naddhito paṭṭhāya rathasīsaṃ paññāsayojanāni, akkhabandho paṇṇāsayojanāni, akkhabandhato paṭṭhāya pacchābhāgo paṇṇāsayojanāni, sabbo sattavaṇṇaratanamayo. Devaloko nāma uddhaṃ, manussaloko adho, tasmā heṭṭhāmukhaṃ rathaṃ pesesīti na sallakkhetabbaṃ. Yathā pana pakatimaggaṃ peseti, evameva manussānaṃ sāyamāsabhatte niṭṭhite candena saddhiṃ yuganaddhaṃ katvā pesesi, yamakacandā uṭṭhitā viya ahesuṃ. Mahājano disvā “yamakacandā uggatā”ti āha. Āgacchante āgacchante na yamakacandā, ekaṃ vimānaṃ, na vimānaṃ, eko rathoti. Rathopi āgacchanto āgacchanto [M 3.0218] pakatirathappamāṇova, assāpi pakatiassappamāṇāva ahesuṃ. Evaṃ rathaṃ āharitvā rañño pāsādaṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pācīnasīhapañjaraṭṭhāne rathaṃ nivattetvā āgatamaggābhimukhaṃ katvā sīhapañjare ṭhatvāva ārohanasajjaṃ ṭhapesi.

313. “So be it, venerable sir” means, having said, “May your words be auspicious; so be it.” “Yoked” means having yoked a thousand thoroughbred horses to a single yoke. For them, however, there was no task of yoking each one individually; they become yoked simply by relying on the mind. That divine chariot was one hundred and fifty yojanas in dimension: from the base of the pole to the front of the chariot was fifty yojanas, the axle-span was fifty yojanas, and from the axle to the rear was fifty yojanas. The entire chariot was made of seven-colored gems. The world of the devas is above and the world of humans is below; therefore, it should not be assumed that he sent the chariot facing downwards. Just as one would send it along a normal path, so too, after the evening meal of the humans was finished, he sent it yoked together with the moon, so it was as if twin moons had risen. The great crowd, seeing this, said, “Twin moons have risen!” As it drew nearer and nearer, they said, “It is not twin moons, but a single celestial mansion,” and then, “It is not a celestial mansion, but a single chariot.” The chariot, too, as it came closer and closer, became the size of an ordinary chariot, and the horses also became the size of ordinary horses. Having brought the chariot thus, and having circumambulated the king's palace to the right, he turned the chariot at the place of the eastern lion-window, made it face the path by which it had come, and stopping right at the lion-window, he positioned it ready for mounting.

Abhiruha mahārājāti rājā – “dibbayānaṃ me laddha”nti na tāvadeva abhiruhi, nāgarānaṃ pana ovādaṃ adāsi “passatha tātā, yaṃ me sakkena devaraññā dibbaratho pesito, so ca kho na jātigottaṃ vā kulappadesaṃ vā paṭicca pesito, mayhaṃ [P 3.0316] pana sīlācāraguṇe pasīditvā pesito. Sace tumhepi sīlaṃ rakkhissatha, tumhākampi pesessati, evaṃ rakkhituṃ yuttaṃ nāmetaṃ sīlaṃ. Nāhaṃ devalokaṃ gantvā cirāyissāmi, appamattā hothā”ti mahājanaṃ ovaditvā pañcasu sīlesu patiṭṭhāpetvā rathaṃ abhiruhi. Tato mātali saṅgāhako “ahampi mahārājassa mamānucchavikaṃ karissāmī”ti ākāsamhi dve magge dassetvā apica mahārājātiādimāha.

“Mount, great king,”—the king, thinking, “I have obtained a divine vehicle,” did not immediately mount. Instead, he first advised the townsfolk: “See, fathers, this divine chariot sent to me by Sakka, the king of gods. It was not sent on account of birth, lineage, or family origin, but sent because he was pleased with my virtue and good conduct. If you too maintain virtue, he will send one for you as well. Thus, this virtue is worth maintaining. I shall not remain in the world of the devas for long; be diligent.” After admonishing the great multitude and establishing them in the five precepts, he mounted the chariot. Then Mātali, the supporter, thinking, “I too shall perform what is fitting for the great king,” showed two paths in the sky and spoke the words beginning with, “Moreover, great king...”

Tattha [V 3.0224] katamenāti, mahārāja, imesu maggesu eko nirayaṃ gacchati, eko devalokaṃ, tesu taṃ katamena nemi. Yenāti yena maggena gantvā yattha pāpakammantā pāpakānaṃ kammānaṃ vipākaṃ paṭisaṃvediyanti, taṃ ṭhānaṃ sakkā hoti passitunti attho. Dutiyapadepi eseva nayo. Jātakepi –

Therein, “By which” means, “Great king, of these paths, one leads to hell, the other to the world of the devas. By which of these shall I lead you?” “By which” means the path by which, having gone, one can see that place where evildoers experience the results of their evil deeds. This is the meaning. The same method applies to the second phrase. In the Jātaka also:

“Kena taṃ nemi maggena, rājaseṭṭha disampati;

Yena vā pāpakammantā, puññakammā ca ye narā”ti. (jā. 2.22.450) –

“By which path shall I lead you, O best of kings, lord of the directions? The path of those who do evil deeds, or of those men who do meritorious deeds?”

Gāthāya ayamevattho. Tenevāha –

This is the meaning of the verse. Therefore, he said:

“Niraye tāva passāmi, āvāse pāpakamminaṃ;

Ṭhānāni luddakammānaṃ, dussīlānañca yā gatī”ti. (jā. 2.22.451);

“Let me first see hell, the abode of evildoers, the places of those who do cruel deeds, and the destination of the immoral.”
