Ubhayeneva maṃ mātali nehīti mātali dvīhi maggehi maṃ nehi, ahaṃ nirayaṃ passitukāmo devalokampīti. Paṭhamaṃ katamena nemīti. Paṭhamaṃ nirayamaggena nehīti. Tato mātali attano ānubhāvena rājānaṃ pañcadasa mahāniraye dassesi. Vitthārakathā panettha –

“Lead me by both, Mātali,” means, “Mātali, lead me by both paths; I wish to see hell and the world of the devas as well.” When asked, “By which shall I lead you first?” the reply was, “First, lead me by the path to hell.” Then Mātali, by his own power, showed the king the fifteen great hells. The detailed account here is:

“Dassesi [M 3.0219][P 3.0317] mātali rañño, duggaṃ vetaraṇiṃ nadiṃ;

Kuthitaṃ khārasaṃyuttaṃ, tattaṃ aggisikhūpama”nti. (jā. 2.22.452) –

“Mātali showed the king the Vetaraṇī river, difficult to traverse, boiling, filled with caustic water, burning hot, and like a flame of fire.”

Jātake vuttanayena veditabbā. Nirayaṃ dassetvā rathaṃ nivattetvā devalokābhimukhaṃ gantvā bīraṇīdevadhītāya soṇadinnadevaputtassa gaṇadevaputtānañca vimānāni dassento devalokaṃ nesi. Tatrāpi vitthārakathā –

This is to be understood in the manner stated in the Jātaka. Having shown hell, he turned the chariot around and, heading towards the world of the devas, he led him there while showing the celestial mansions of the deva-daughter Bīraṇī, the deva-son Soṇadinna, and the Gaṇa devas. There too, the detailed account is:

“Yadi te sutā bīraṇī jīvaloke,

Āmāyadāsī ahu brāhmaṇassa;

Sā pattakāle atithiṃ viditvā,

Mātāva [V 3.0225] puttaṃ sakimābhinandī;

Saṃyamā saṃvibhāgā ca,

Sā vimānasmi modatī”ti. (jā. 2.22.507) –

“If you have heard of Bīraṇī: in the world of the living, she was a home-born slave girl of a brahmin. She, recognizing a guest at mealtime, rejoiced as a mother rejoices in her son. Through her restraint and sharing, she now delights in her celestial mansion.”

Jātake vuttanayeneva veditabbā.

This is to be understood in the very manner stated in the Jātaka.

Evaṃ gacchato pana tassa rathanemi vaṭṭiyā cittakūṭadvārakoṭṭhakassa ummāre pahatamatteva devanagare kolāhalaṃ ahosi. Sakkaṃ devarājānaṃ ekakaṃyeva ohāya devasaṅgho mahāsattaṃ paccuggamanamakāsi, taṃ devatānaṃ ādaraṃ disvā sakko cittaṃ sandhāretuṃ asakkonto – “abhirama, mahārāja, devesu devānubhāvenā”ti āha. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi – “ayaṃ rājā ajja āgantvā ekadivaseneva devagaṇaṃ attano abhimukhamakāsi. Sace ekaṃ dve divase vasissati, na maṃ devā olokessantī”ti. So usūyamāno, “mahārāja, tuyhaṃ imasmiṃ devaloke vasituṃ puññaṃ natthi, aññesaṃ puññena vasāhī”ti iminā adhippāyena evamāha. Bodhisatto – “nāsakkhi jarasakko manaṃ sandhāretuṃ, paraṃ nissāya laddhaṃ kho pana yācitvā laddhabhaṇḍakaṃ [P 3.0318] viya hotī”ti paṭikkhipanto alaṃ mārisātiādimāha. Jātakepi vuttaṃ –

As he was thus traveling, the rim of his chariot wheel had just struck the threshold of the gatehouse of Cittakūṭa when a great uproar arose in the city of the devas. Leaving Sakka, the king of the devas, all alone, the assembly of devas went forth to welcome the Great Being. Seeing this reverence from the deities, Sakka was unable to contain his mind and said, “Enjoy, O great king, among the devas by the power of the devas.” It is said that this thought occurred to him: “This king, having arrived today, has in a single day turned the host of devas to face him. If he stays for one or two days, the devas will no longer look at me.” So, being jealous, he spoke with this intention: “Great king, you have no merit of your own to dwell in this world of the devas; dwell here by the merit of others.” The Bodhisatta, thinking, “Old Sakka was unable to contain his mind. Indeed, what is obtained by depending on another is like borrowed goods,” rejected this, saying the words beginning with, “Enough, my friend...” In the Jātaka, it is also said:

“Yathā yācitakaṃ yānaṃ, yathā yācitakaṃ dhanaṃ;

Evaṃsampadameve taṃ, yaṃ parato dānapaccayā;

Na cāhametamicchāmi, yaṃ parato dānapaccayā”ti. (jā. 2.22.585-586) –

“Just as a borrowed vehicle, just as borrowed wealth, so too is this success which is due to a gift from another. And I do not desire that which is due to a gift from another.”

Sabbaṃ [M 3.0220] vattabbaṃ. Bodhisatto pana manussattabhāvena kativāre devalokaṃ gatoti. Cattāro – mandhāturājakāle sādhinarājakāle guttilavīṇāvādakakāle nimimahārājakāleti. So mandhātukāle devaloke asaṅkhyeyyaṃ kālaṃ vasi, tasmiñhi vasamāneyeva chattiṃsa sakkā caviṃsu. Sādhinarājakāle sattāhaṃ vasi, manussagaṇanāya satta vassasatāni honti. Guttilavīṇāvādakakāle ca nimirājakāle ca muhuttamattaṃ vasi, manussagaṇanāya satta divasāni honti.

All that is to be said should be stated. However, it should be known thus: 'How many times did the Bodhisatta, in a human existence, go to the deva world?' Four times: during the time of King Mandhātu, during the time of King Sādhina, during the time of the lute-player Guttila, and during the time of King Nimi. During the time of Mandhātu, he dwelt in the deva world for an incalculable period. Indeed, while he was dwelling there, thirty-six Sakkas passed away. During the time of King Sādhina, he dwelt for seven days, which by human reckoning is seven hundred years. During the time of the lute-player Guttila and during the time of King Nimi, he dwelt for only a moment, which by human reckoning is seven days.

314. Tattheva [V 3.0226] mithilaṃ paṭinesīti paṭinetvā pakatisirigabbheyeva patiṭṭhāpesi.

314. As for the phrase 'he brought him back to Mithilā right there,' it means: having brought him back, he established him in the very royal apartment of usual splendor.

315. Kaḷārajanakoti tassa nāmaṃ. Kaḷāradantatāya pana kaḷārajanakoti vutto. Na so agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajīti ettakamattameva na akāsi, sesaṃ sabbaṃ pākatikameva ahosi.

315. Kaḷārajanaka was his name. However, he was called Kaḷārajanaka because of his mottled teeth. He did not do even this much, that is, go forth from the household life into homelessness; all the remaining traditional practices of the good kings of the past were just as usual.

316. Samucchedo hotīti ettha kalyāṇavattaṃ ko samucchindati, kena samucchinnaṃ, ko pavatteti, kena pavattitaṃ nāma hotīti ayaṃ vibhāgo veditabbo. Tattha sīlavā bhikkhu [P 3.0319] “na sakkā mayā arahattaṃ laddhu”nti vīriyaṃ akaronto samucchindati. Dussīlena samucchinnaṃ nāma hoti. Satta sekhā pavattenti. Khīṇāsavena pavattitaṃ nāma hoti. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

316. In the passage 'There is a cutting off,' this analysis should be understood: who is cutting off the noble practice? By whom has it been cut off? Who is causing it to continue? By whom is it said to have been made to continue? Therein, a virtuous monk, not making an effort, thinking, 'I am not able to attain Arahantship,' is cutting it off. By an immoral person, it is said to have been cut off. The seven trainees cause it to continue. By one whose taints are destroyed, it is said to have been made to continue. The rest is clear everywhere.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

Of the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Maghadevasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Maghadevasutta is finished.

4. Madhurasuttavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Madhura Sutta

317. Evaṃ [V 3.0227] me sutanti madhurasuttaṃ. Tattha mahākaccānoti gihikāle ujjenikarañño purohitaputto abhirūpo dassanīyo pāsādiko suvaṇṇavaṇṇo ca. Madhurāyanti evaṃnāmake nagare. Gundāvaneti kaṇhakagundāvane[M 3.0221]. Avantiputtoti avantiraṭṭhe rañño dhītāya putto. Vuddho ceva arahā cāti daharaṃ arahantampi na tathā sambhāventi yathā mahallakaṃ, thero pana vuddho ceva ahosi arahā ca. Brāhmaṇā, bho kaccānāti so kira rājā brāhmaṇaladdhiko, tasmā evamāha. Brāhmaṇova seṭṭho vaṇṇotiādīsu jātigottādīnaṃ paññāpanaṭṭhāne brāhmaṇāva seṭṭhāti dasseti. Hīno añño vaṇṇoti itare tayo vaṇṇā hīnā lāmakāti vadati. Sukkoti [P 3.0320] paṇḍaro. Kaṇhoti kāḷako. Sujjhantīti jātigottādipaññāpanaṭṭhānesu sujjhanti. Brahmuno puttāti mahābrahmuno puttā. Orasā mukhato jātāti ure vasitvā mukhato nikkhantā, ure katvā saṃvaddhitāti vā orasā. Brahmajāti brahmato nibbattā. Brahmanimmitāti brahmunā nimmitā. Brahmadāyādāti brahmuno dāyādā. Ghosoyeva kho esoti vohāramattamevetaṃ.

317. ‘Thus have I heard’ begins the Madhurasutta. Therein, Mahākaccāna, during his lay life, was the son of the chaplain to the king of Ujjeni; he was handsome, pleasant to behold, inspiring confidence, and had a golden complexion. ‘In Madhurā’ means in the city of that name. ‘In Gundāvana’ means in the Kaṇhakagundā forest. ‘Avantiputta’ means the son of the daughter of the king in the Avanti country. As for ‘both elder and an Arahant’: they do not honor a young Arahant as they do an elder one, but the Thera was both elder and an Arahant. As for ‘Brahmin, good Kaccāna’: it seems that king held the brahmin doctrine, therefore he spoke thus. In ‘The brahmin is the highest caste,’ etc., it shows that in the matter of designating birth, lineage, and so on, brahmins are the highest. ‘The other caste is inferior’ means he says the other three castes are inferior and base. ‘White’ means pure. ‘Black’ means dark. ‘They are purified’ means they are purified in the matter of designating birth, lineage, and so on. ‘Sons of Brahmā’ means sons of the Great Brahmā. ‘Legitimate sons, born from the mouth’ means having dwelt in the chest, they came out from the mouth; or, having been placed in the chest, they were nurtured, therefore they are called legitimate sons. ‘Born of Brahmā’ means produced from Brahmā. ‘Created by Brahmā’ means fashioned by Brahmā. ‘Heirs of Brahmā’ means heirs of Brahmā. ‘This is merely a sound’ means this is just a matter of designation.

318. Ijjheyyāti samijjheyya, yattakāni dhanādīni pattheyya, tattakehissa manoratho pūreyyāti attho. Khattiyopissāssāti khattiyopi assa issariyasampattassa pubbuṭṭhāyī assa. Nesaṃ ettha kiñcīti na etesaṃ ettha kiñci.

318. ‘May he prosper’ means may he be successful. The meaning is this: by as much wealth and so on as he might desire, by that much his heart's desire would be fulfilled. As for ‘a khattiya also would be his’: another khattiya would be an early-riser for him who has attained sovereignty and prosperity. As for ‘among them in this,’ it means: ‘not among them in this, anything.’

322. Āsanena vā nimanteyyāmāti nisinnāsanaṃ papphoṭetvā idha nisīdāti vadeyyāma. Abhinimanteyyāmapi nanti abhiharitvā taṃ nimanteyyāma. Tattha duvidho abhihāro vācāya ceva kāyena ca. “Tumhākaṃ icchiticchitakkhaṇe mamaṃ cīvarādīhi vadeyyātha yenattho”ti vadanto hi vācāya abhiharitvā nimanteti nāma. Cīvarādivekallaṃ sallakkhetvā “idaṃ gaṇhathā”ti tāni dento pana kāyena abhiharitvā nimanteti nāma. Tadubhayampi [P 3.0321] sandhāya “abhinimanteyyāmapi na”nti āha. Rakkhāvaraṇaguttinti rakkhāsaṅkhātañceva āvaraṇasaṅkhātañca [V 3.0228] guttiṃ. Yā panesā āvudhahatthe purise ṭhapentena rakkhā, sā dhammikā nāma saṃvihitā na hoti. Yathā pana avelāya kaṭṭhahārikāpaṇṇahārikādayo vihāraṃ na pavisanti, migaluddakādayo vihārasīmāya mige vā macche vā na gaṇhanti, evaṃ saṃvidahantena dhammikā nāma saṃvihitā hoti. Taṃ sandhāyāha “dhammika”nti.

322. ‘Or we might invite with a seat’ means, having dusted off the prepared seat, we would say, ‘Please sit here.’ As for ‘we would not even specially invite them,’ it means we would not invite them by making a special approach. Therein, the special approach is twofold: by speech and by body. One who says, ‘At any moment you desire, you may ask me for whatever requisite you need, such as robes,’ is said to invite by making a special approach with speech. But one who, having noticed a lack of robes or other requisites, says, ‘Please accept this,’ and gives them, is said to invite by making a special approach with the body. Referring to both of these, it is said, ‘we would not even specially invite them.’ ‘Protection, guarding, and security’ means security that is known as protection and guarding. But that protection which consists of stationing men with weapons in hand is not called protection that is righteously arranged. However, when it is arranged so that, for instance, female wood-gatherers, leaf-gatherers, and so on do not enter the monastery at an improper time, and hunters and so on do not catch deer or fish within the monastery boundary, in this way it is called protection that is righteously arranged. Referring to that, he said ‘righteous.’

Evaṃ [M 3.0222] santeti evaṃ catunnampi vaṇṇānaṃ pabbajitānaṃ pabbajitasakkārena same samāne. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

As for 'this being so': thus, when those who have gone forth from all four castes are equal with respect to the honor shown to one who has gone forth. The rest is clear everywhere.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

Of the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Madhurasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Madhurasutta is finished.

5. Bodhirājakumārasuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Bodhirājakumāra Sutta

324. Evaṃ [V 3.0229] me sutanti bodhirājakumārasuttaṃ. Tattha kokanadoti kokanadaṃ vuccati padumaṃ. So ca maṅgalapāsādo olokanakapadumaṃ dassetvā kato, tasmā kokanadoti saṅkhaṃ labhi.

324. The sutta beginning with 'Thus have I heard' is the Bodhirājakumāra Sutta. Therein, as for 'Kokanada,' a lotus is called 'kokanada.' And that auspicious palace was made displaying a lotus for viewing; therefore, it received the designation 'Kokanada'.

325. Yāva pacchimasopānakaḷevarāti ettha pacchimasopānakaḷevaranti paṭhamaṃ sopānaphalakaṃ vuttaṃ. Addasā [P 3.0322] khoti olokanatthaṃyeva dvārakoṭṭhake ṭhito addasa. Bhagavā tuṇhī ahosīti “kissa nu kho atthāya rājakumārena ayaṃ mahāsakkāro kato”ti āvajjanto puttapatthanāya katabhāvaṃ aññāsi. So hi rājakumāro aputtako, sutañcānena ahosi – “buddhānaṃ kira adhikāraṃ katvā manasā icchitaṃ labhantī”ti. So – “sacāhaṃ puttaṃ labhissāmi, sammāsambuddho mama celappaṭikaṃ akkamissati. No ce labhissāmi, na akkamissatī”ti patthanaṃ katvā santharāpesi. Atha bhagavā “nibbattissati nu kho etassa putto”ti āvajjetvā “na nibbattissatī”ti addasa.

325. Herein, in the phrase 'up to the frame of the last step,' by 'the frame of the last step' the first plank of the staircase is meant. 'He saw' means that he, standing at the gateway just for the sake of looking, saw. As for 'The Blessed One remained silent,' while reflecting, 'For what purpose has this great honor been done by the prince?' he understood that it was done out of a desire for a son. For that prince was childless, and he had heard: 'It is said that by making an aspiration to the Buddhas, one obtains what is desired in mind.' He, having made the aspiration, 'If I obtain a son, the Perfectly Enlightened One will step on my cloth. If I do not obtain one, he will not step on it,' had the cloth spread. Then the Blessed One, reflecting, 'Will a son be born to him?' saw, 'A son will not be born.'

Pubbe kira so ekasmiṃ dīpe vasamāno samacchandena sakuṇapotake khādi. Sacassa mātugāmo aññova bhaveyya, puttaṃ labheyya. Ubhohi pana samānacchandehi hutvā pāpakammaṃ kataṃ, tenassa putto na nibbattissatīti aññāsi. Dusse pana akkante – “buddhānaṃ adhikāraṃ katvā patthitapatthitaṃ labhantīti loke anussavo, mayā ca mahāabhinīhāro kato, na ca puttaṃ labhāmi, tucchaṃ idaṃ vacana”nti micchāgahaṇaṃ gaṇheyya. Titthiyāpi – “natthi samaṇānaṃ akattabbaṃ nāma, celappaṭikaṃ maddantā āhiṇḍantī”ti ujjhāyeyyuṃ[M 3.0223]. Etarahi ca akkamantesu bahū bhikkhū paracittaviduno, te bhabbaṃ jānitvā akkamissanti, abhabbaṃ jānitvā na akkamissanti. Anāgate pana upanissayo mando bhavissati, anāgataṃ na jānissanti. Tesu akkamantesu sace patthitaṃ ijjhissati, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ[P 3.0323]. No ce ijjhissati, – “pubbe bhikkhusaṅghassa abhinīhāraṃ katvā icchiticchitaṃ labhanti, taṃ idāni na labhanti[V 3.0230]. Teyeva maññe bhikkhū paṭipattipūrakā ahesuṃ, ime paṭipattiṃ pūretuṃ na sakkontī”ti manussā vippaṭisārino bhavissantīti imehi kāraṇehi bhagavā akkamituṃ anicchanto tuṇhī ahosi. Sikkhāpadaṃ paññapesi “na, bhikkhave, celappaṭikā akkamitabbā”ti (cūḷava. 268). Maṅgalatthāya paññattaṃ anakkamantesu pana akkamanatthāya anupaññattiṃ ṭhapesi – “gihī, bhikkhave, maṅgalikā, anujānāmi, bhikkhave, gihīnaṃ maṅgalatthāyā”ti (cūḷava. 268).

It is said that in a past life, while living on an island, he ate young birds with a woman of like desire. If his wife had been another, he would have obtained a son. But since both, having a like desire, committed an evil deed, the Buddha knew that a son would not be born to him. Furthermore, if He were to step on the cloth, the prince might take up the wrong view: 'There is a saying in the world that by making an aspiration to the Buddhas, one obtains what is wished for. I have made a great aspiration, yet I do not obtain a son. This saying is empty.' The sectarians, too, might censure them: 'There is nothing the ascetics will not do; they wander about trampling on cloths.' Also, at present, there are many monks who know the minds of others; they, knowing one who is worthy, will step, and knowing one who is not worthy, will not step. But in the future, the supporting condition will be weak, and they will not know the future. If those future monks step and the aspiration is fulfilled, that is good. If it is not fulfilled, people will become regretful, thinking: 'Formerly, by making an aspiration to the Sangha of monks, people obtained what they wished for, but now they do not. We think only those monks fulfilled the practice; these are unable to fulfill the practice.' For these reasons, the Blessed One, not wishing to step, remained silent. He laid down the training rule: 'Monks, a cloth is not to be stepped upon.' But when they did not step on a cloth laid out for auspiciousness, He established a supplementary allowance for the purpose of stepping: 'Monks, householders are fond of auspicious things. I allow it, monks, for the sake of the householders' auspiciousness.'

326. Pacchimaṃ janataṃ tathāgato anukampatīti idaṃ thero vuttesu kāraṇesu tatiyaṃ kāraṇaṃ sandhāyāha. Na kho sukhena sukhanti kasmā āha? Kāmasukhallikānuyogasaññī hutvā sammāsambuddho na akkami, tasmā ahampi satthārā samānacchando bhavissāmīti maññamāno evamāha.

326. 'The Tathāgata has compassion for future generations'—this the Elder said, referring to the third of the reasons stated. Why did he say, 'Not through pleasure is pleasure attained'? The Perfectly Enlightened One, perceiving it as an indulgence in sensual pleasures, did not step; therefore, thinking, 'I too shall be of like desire with the Teacher,' he spoke thus.

327. So kho ahantiādi “yāva rattiyā pacchime yāme”ti tāva mahāsaccake (ma. ni. 1.364 ādayo) vuttanayena veditabbaṃ. Tato paraṃ yāva pañcavaggiyānaṃ āsavakkhayā pāsarāsisutte (ma. ni. 1.272 ādayo) vuttanayena veditabbaṃ.

327. 'So kho ahaṃ' and so on, up to 'in the last watch of the night,' should be understood according to the method stated in the Mahāsaccaka Sutta (MN 1.364 ff.). After that, up to the destruction of the taints of the group of five, it should be understood according to the method stated in the Pāsarāsi Sutta (MN 1.272 ff.).

343. Aṅkusagayhe sippeti aṅkusagahaṇasippe. Kusalo ahanti cheko ahaṃ. Kassa [P 3.0324] panāyaṃ santike sippaṃ uggaṇhīti? Pitu santike, pitāpissa pitu santikeva uggaṇhi. Kosambiyaṃ kira parantaparājā nāma rajjaṃ kāresi. Rājamahesī garubhārā ākāsatale raññā saddhiṃ bālātapaṃ tappamānā rattakambalaṃ pārupitvā nisinnā hoti, eko hatthiliṅgasakuṇo “maṃsapesī”ti maññamāno gahetvā ākāsaṃ pakkhandi. Sā “chaḍḍeyya ma”nti bhayena nissaddā ahosi, so taṃ pabbatapāde rukkhaviṭape ṭhapesi. Sā pāṇissaraṃ karontī mahāsaddamakāsi. Sakuṇo [M 3.0224] palāyi, tassā tattheva gabbhavuṭṭhānaṃ ahosi. Tiyāmarattiṃ deve vassante kambalaṃ pārupitvā nisīdi. Tato ca avidūre tāpaso vasati. So tassā saddena aruṇe uggate rukkhamūlaṃ āgato jātiṃ pucchitvā nisseṇiṃ bandhitvā otāretvā attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ netvā yāguṃ pāyesi. Dārakassa meghautuñca pabbatautuñca gahetvā jātattā udenoti nāmaṃ akāsi. Tāpaso phalāphalāni āharitvā dvepi jane posesi.

343. 'Aṅkusagayhe sippe' means in the skill of handling the elephant goad. 'Kusalo ahaṃ' means 'I am skilled' or 'I am clever.' From whom did he learn this skill? From his father, and his father too learned it from his father. It is said that in Kosambī, a king named Parantapa ruled. His chief queen, heavy with child, was sitting with the king in the open air, warming herself in the morning sun, wrapped in a red blanket. A hatthiliṅga bird, thinking it was a piece of meat, seized her and flew into the sky. Fearing that it might drop her, she remained silent. The bird placed her on a tree branch at the foot of a mountain. Clapping her hands, she made a loud noise. The bird fled, and right there she gave birth. For the three watches of the night, while it rained, she sat wrapped in the blanket. Not far from there lived an ascetic. Hearing her sound at the break of dawn, he came to the foot of the tree, asked about her lineage, fashioned a ladder, helped her down, took her to his dwelling, and gave her rice-gruel to drink. Because the boy was born in connection with the rain-season and the mountain-season, he gave him the name Udena. The ascetic brought various fruits and nourished them both.

Sā [V 3.0231] ekadivasaṃ tāpasassa āgamanavelāya paccuggamanaṃ katvā itthikuttaṃ dassetvā tāpasaṃ sīlabhedaṃ āpādesi. Tesaṃ ekato vasantānaṃ kāle gacchante parantaparājā kālaṃ akāsi. Tāpaso rattibhāge nakkhattaṃ oloketvā rañño matabhāvaṃ ñatvā – “tuyhaṃ rājā mato, putto te kiṃ idha vasituṃ icchati, udāhu pettike rajje chattaṃ ussāpetu”nti pucchi. Sā puttassa ādito paṭṭhāya sabbaṃ pavattiṃ ācikkhitvā chattaṃ ussāpetukāmatañcassa ñatvā tāpasassa ārocesi. Tāpaso ca hatthiganthasippaṃ jānāti, kutonena laddhaṃ? Sakkassa [P 3.0325] santikā. Pubbe kirassa sakko upaṭṭhānaṃ āgantvā “kena kilamathā”ti pucchi. So “hatthiparissayo atthī”ti ārocesi. Tassa sakko hatthiganthañceva vīṇakañca datvā “palāpetukāmatāya sati imaṃ tantiṃ vādetvā imaṃ silokaṃ vadeyyātha, pakkositukāmatāya sati imaṃ silokaṃ vadeyyāthā”ti āha. Tāpaso taṃ sippaṃ kumārassa adāsi. So ekaṃ vaṭarukkhaṃ abhiruhitvā hatthīsu āgatesu tantiṃ vādetvā silokaṃ vadati, hatthī bhītā palāyiṃsu.

One day, at the time of the ascetic's arrival, she went out to meet him, displayed feminine wiles, and caused him to break his virtue. While they were living together, as time passed, King Parantapa died. The former ascetic, having observed the stars in the night and realized that the king had died, asked, 'Your king is dead. Does your son wish to stay here, or to raise the white parasol in his paternal kingdom?' She recounted the entire story of her son from the very beginning and, knowing his desire to raise the parasol, informed the former ascetic. Now, the ascetic knew the art of elephant lore; from where had he obtained it? From Sakka. It is said that formerly, Sakka had come to attend on him and asked, 'What causes you weariness?' He replied, 'There is danger from elephants.' Sakka gave him the art of elephant lore and a lute, saying, 'If you wish to drive them away, play this string and recite this verse. If you wish to summon them, recite this verse.' The ascetic gave this skill to the prince. Climbing a banyan tree, when the elephants came, he played the string and recited the verse, and the elephants fled in fear.

So sippassa ānubhāvaṃ ñatvā punadivase pakkosanasippaṃ payojesi. Jeṭṭhakahatthī āgantvā khandhaṃ upanāmesi. So tassa khandhagato yuddhasamatthe taruṇahatthī uccinitvā kambalañca muddikañca gahetvā mātāpitaro vanditvā nikkhanto anupubbena taṃ taṃ gāmaṃ pavisitvā – “ahaṃ rañño putto, sampattiṃ atthikā āgacchantū”ti janasaṅgahaṃ katvā nagaraṃ parivāretvā – “ahaṃ rañño putto, mayhaṃ chattaṃ dethā”ti asaddahantānaṃ kambalañca muddikañca dassetvā chattaṃ ussāpesi. So hatthivittako hutvā “asukaṭṭhāne sundaro hatthī atthī”ti vutte gantvā gaṇhāti. Caṇḍapajjoto [M 3.0225] “tassa santike sippaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti kaṭṭhahatthiṃ payojetvā tassa anto yodhe nisīdāpetvā taṃ hatthiṃ gahaṇatthāya āgataṃ gaṇhitvā tassa santike sippaṃ gahaṇatthāya dhītaraṃ uyyojesi. So tāya saddhiṃ saṃvāsaṃ kappetvā taṃ gahetvā attano nagaraṃyeva agamāsi. Tassā kucchiyaṃ uppanno ayaṃ bodhirājakumāro attano pitu santike sippaṃ uggaṇhi.

Knowing the power of the skill, on the next day he employed the skill of summoning. The chief elephant came and lowered its neck. He, being situated on its neck, selected young elephants capable of battle, took the blanket and the ring, paid homage to his mother and father, and departed. Gradually entering various villages, he gathered the people, saying, 'I am the king’s son; let those who desire wealth come!' Having surrounded the city, he proclaimed, 'I am the king’s son; give me the white parasol!' To those who did not believe, he showed the blanket and the ring and had the white parasol raised. Having become fond of elephants, whenever it was said, 'In such-and-such a place there is a fine elephant,' he would go and capture it. Caṇḍapajjota, thinking, 'I will get the skill from him,' employed a wooden elephant, had soldiers sit inside it, and captured him when he came to seize that elephant. In order to learn the skill from him, he sent his daughter. He, having cohabited with her, took her and fled to his own city. This Prince Bodhi, who arose in her womb, learned the skill from his father.

344. Padhāniyaṅgānīti padhānaṃ vuccati padahanabhāvo, padhānamassa atthīti padhāniyo. Padhāniyassa bhikkhuno aṅgānīti padhāniyaṅgāni. Saddhoti saddhāya samannāgato. Sā panesā [P 3.0326] āgamanasaddhā [V 3.0232] adhigamasaddhā okappanasaddhā pasādasaddhāti catubbidhā. Tattha sabbaññubodhisattānaṃ saddhā abhinīhārato paṭṭhāya āgatattā āgamanasaddhā nāma. Ariyasāvakānaṃ paṭivedhena adhigatattā adhigamasaddhā nāma. Buddho dhammo saṅghoti vutte acalabhāvena okappanaṃ okappanasaddhā nāma. Pasāduppatti pasādasaddhā nāma, idha pana okappanasaddhā adhippetā. Bodhinti catumaggañāṇaṃ. Taṃ suppaṭividdhaṃ tathāgatenāti saddahati, desanāsīsameva cetaṃ, iminā pana aṅgena tīsupi ratanesu saddhā adhippetā. Yassa hi buddhādīsu pasādo balavā, tassa padhānaṃ vīriyaṃ ijjhati.

344. The factors of striving: 'Striving' is said to be the state of exertion; one who has striving is a 'striver'. The 'factors of a striver' are the 'factors of striving'. 'Faithful' means one endowed with faith. Furthermore, this faith is fourfold: faith of arrival, faith of attainment, faith of conviction, and faith of confidence. Therein, the faith of omniscient Bodhisattas is called 'faith of arrival' because it has come about starting from their aspiration. The faith of noble disciples is called 'faith of attainment' because it is attained through penetration. The unshaken conviction that arises when it is said, 'the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha,' is called 'faith of conviction.' The arising of confidence is called 'faith of confidence.' Here, however, 'faith of conviction' is intended. 'Enlightenment' means the knowledge of the four paths. One has faith that 'It is well-penetrated by the Tathāgata.' And this is merely the heading of the discourse; in fact, by this factor, faith in the Three Jewels is intended. For one whose confidence in the Buddha and so forth is strong, their striving effort succeeds.

Appābādhoti arogo. Appātaṅkoti niddukkho. Samavepākiniyāti samavipācaniyā. Gahaṇiyāti kammajatejodhātuyā. Nātisītāya nāccuṇhāyāti atisītagahaṇiko hi sītabhīrū hoti, accuṇhagahaṇiko uṇhabhīrū, tesaṃ padhānaṃ na ijjhati. Majjhimagahaṇikassa ijjhati. Tenāha “majjhimāya padhānakkhamāyā”ti. Yathābhūtaṃ attānaṃ āvikattāti yathābhūtaṃ attano aguṇaṃ pakāsetā. Udayatthagāminiyāti udayañca atthañca gantuṃ paricchindituṃ samatthāya, etena paññāsalakkhaṇapariggāhikaṃ udayabbayañāṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Ariyāyāti parisuddhāya. Nibbedhikāyāti anibbiddhapubbe lobhakkhandhādayo nibbijjhituṃ samatthāya. Sammādukkhakkhayagāminiyāti [P 3.0327] tadaṅgavasena kilesānaṃ pahīnattā yaṃ dukkhaṃ khīyati, tassa dukkhassa khayagāminiyā. Iti sabbehipi imehi padehi vipassanāpaññāva kathitā. Duppaññassa hi padhānaṃ na ijjhati. Imāni ca pañca padhāniyaṅgāni lokiyāneva veditabbāni.

'With few illnesses' means free from sickness. 'With few afflictions' means free from suffering. 'With balanced digestion' means that which digests evenly. 'With a digestive faculty' refers to the fire element born of kamma. 'Not too cold, not too hot': indeed, one with a very cold digestive faculty is fearful of the cold, and one with a very hot digestive faculty is fearful of the heat; for them, striving does not succeed. It succeeds for one with a moderate digestive faculty. Therefore, it is said, 'moderate, conducive to striving.' 'One who reveals oneself as one truly is' means one who reveals one's own faults as they really are. 'Leading to arising and passing away' refers to wisdom capable of comprehending arising and passing away; by this is meant the knowledge of arising and passing away which comprehends the fifty characteristics. 'Noble' means purified. 'Penetrative' refers to wisdom capable of piercing the previously unpierced aggregates of greed and so on. 'Leading to the right destruction of suffering' refers to wisdom leading to the destruction of that suffering which is destroyed due to the abandonment of defilements by way of substitution. Thus, by all these terms, only insight wisdom is spoken of. Indeed, for one lacking wisdom, striving does not succeed. And these five factors of striving should be understood as being only mundane.

345. Sāyamanusiṭṭho [M 3.0226] pāto visesaṃ adhigamissatīti atthaṅgate sūriye anusiṭṭho aruṇuggamane visesaṃ adhigamissati. Pātamanusiṭṭho sāyanti aruṇuggamane anusiṭṭho sūriyatthaṅgamanavelāyaṃ. Ayañca pana desanā neyyapuggalavasena vuttā. Dandhapañño hi neyyapuggalo sattahi divasehi arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, tikkhapañño ekadivasena, sesadivase majjhimapaññāvasena veditabbaṃ. Aho buddho aho dhammo aho dhammassa svākkhātatāti yasmā buddhadhammānaṃ uḷāratāya dhammassa ca svākkhātatāya pāto kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathāpetvā sāyaṃ arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, tasmā pasaṃsanto evamāha. Yatra hi nāmāti vimhayatthe nipāto.

345. One who is instructed in the evening will attain distinction in the morning: this means one who is instructed when the sun has set will attain distinction at the rising of the dawn. One who is instructed in the morning will attain distinction in the evening: this means one who is instructed at the rising of the dawn will attain distinction at the time of sunset. This teaching, moreover, was given with reference to an individual who is to be guided. Indeed, a person to be guided who has dull wisdom attains arahantship in seven days; one of sharp wisdom attains it in a single day; for the remaining days, it should be understood in relation to those of medium wisdom. 'Ah, the Buddha! Ah, the Dhamma! Ah, the well-proclaimed nature of the Dhamma!': Since, due to the magnificence of the Buddha and the Dhamma, and due to the well-proclaimed nature of the Dhamma, one who has the meditation subject taught in the morning attains arahantship in the evening, therefore, praising, he spoke thus. The particle 'Yatra hi nāma' is used in the sense of astonishment.

346. Kucchimatīti [V 3.0233] āpannasattā. Yo me ayaṃ, bhante, kucchigatoti kiṃ panevaṃ saraṇaṃ gahitaṃ hotīti. Na hoti. Acittakasaraṇagamanaṃ nāma natthi, ārakkho panassa paccupaṭṭhitova hoti. Atha naṃ yadā mahallakakāle mātāpitaro, – “tāta, kucchigatameva taṃ saraṇaṃ gaṇhāpayimhā”ti sārenti, so ca sallakkhetvā “ahaṃ saraṇaṃ gato upāsako”ti satiṃ uppādeti, tadā saraṇaṃ gahitaṃ nāma hoti. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

346. 'Kucchimatī' means a pregnant woman. 'This one in my womb, venerable sir'—is refuge thus taken? It is not. There is no such thing as taking refuge without consciousness, but protection is indeed established for him. Then, when he is grown up, his parents remind him, saying, 'Dear son, we had you take the refuges while you were still in the womb.' And he, having noted this, generates the mindfulness, 'I am a lay follower who has gone for refuge.' At that time, it is called 'having taken refuge'. The rest is clear in all respects.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary to the Majjhima Nikāya.

Bodhirājakumārasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Bodhirājakumāra Sutta is concluded.

6. Aṅgulimālasuttavaṇṇanā

6. The Explanation of the Aṅgulimāla Sutta

347. Evaṃ [V 3.0234][P 3.0328] me sutanti aṅgulimālasuttaṃ. Tattha aṅgulīnaṃ mālaṃ dhāretīti kasmā dhāreti? Ācariyavacanena. Tatrāyaṃ anupubbikathā –

347. The sutta beginning 'Thus have I heard' is the Aṅgulimāla Sutta. Therein, regarding 'he wears a garland of fingers': why does he wear it? Because of his teacher's word. Herein, this is the sequential story:

Ayaṃ kira kosalarañño purohitassa mantāṇiyā nāma brāhmaṇiyā kucchismiṃ paṭisandhiṃ aggahesi. Brāhmaṇiyā rattibhāge gabbhavuṭṭhānaṃ ahosi. Tassa mātukucchito nikkhamanakāle sakalanagare āvudhāni pajjaliṃsu, rañño maṅgalasakuntopi sirisayane ṭhapitā asilaṭṭhipi [M 3.0227] pajjali. Brāhmaṇo nikkhamitvā nakkhattaṃ olokento coranakkhattena jātoti rañño santikaṃ gantvā sukhaseyyabhāvaṃ pucchi.

It is said that this one took conception in the womb of the brahmin woman named Mantānī, the wife of the King of Kosala's chaplain. For the brahmin woman, labor occurred during the night. At the time of his emergence from his mother's womb, all the weapons in the entire city blazed. The king's auspicious small sword, placed on the glorious bed, also blazed. The brahmin, having gone out and observing the constellation, knew, 'He is born under the thief constellation,' and went to the king's presence and inquired about his comfortable sleep.

Rājā “kuto, me ācariya, sukhaseyyā? Mayhaṃ maṅgalāvudhaṃ pajjali, rajjassa vā jīvitassa vā antarāyo bhavissati maññe”ti. Mā bhāyi, mahārāja, mayhaṃ ghare kumāro jāto, tassānubhāvena na kevalaṃ tuyhaṃ nivesane, sakalanagarepi āvudhāni pajjalitānīti. Kiṃ bhavissati ācariyāti? Coro bhavissati mahārājāti. Kiṃ ekacorako, udāhu rajjadūsako coroti? Ekacorako devāti. Evaṃ vatvā ca pana rañño manaṃ gaṇhitukāmo āha – “māretha naṃ devā”ti. Ekacorako samāno kiṃ karissati? Karīsasahassakhette ekasālisīsaṃ viya hoti, paṭijaggatha nanti. Tassa nāmaggahaṇaṃ gaṇhantā sayane ṭhapitamaṅgalaasilaṭṭhi, chadane ṭhapitā sarā, kappāsapicumhi [P 3.0329] ṭhapitaṃ tālavaṇṭakaraṇasatthakanti ete pajjalantā kiñci na hiṃsiṃsu, tasmā ahiṃsakoti nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Taṃ sippuggahaṇakāle takkasīlaṃ pesayiṃsu.

The king said, 'Teacher, how could I have comfortable sleep? My auspicious weapon blazed; I think there will be danger to the kingdom or to my life.' 'Do not be afraid, great king. A boy has been born in my house. By his power, not only in your palace but throughout the entire city have the weapons blazed.' 'What will he become, teacher?' 'He will become a thief, great king.' 'Will he be a lone thief, or a thief who corrupts the kingdom?' 'A lone thief, Your Majesty.' Having said this, and wishing to win the king's favor, the chaplain said, 'Your Majesty, have him killed.' 'Being a lone thief, what can he do? He is like a single ear of paddy in a field of a thousand karīsas. You should raise him.' When giving him a name, they noted that the auspicious sword-stick placed on the bed, the arrows placed on the roof, and the small knife for making palm-leaf fans placed in a cotton ball—these, while blazing, harmed no one. Therefore, they gave him the name Ahiṃsaka. When it was time for him to learn a craft, they sent him to Takkasīla.

So dhammantevāsiko hutvā sippaṃ paṭṭhapesi. Vattasampanno kiṃkārapaṭissāvī manāpacārī piyavādī ahosi. Sesaantevāsikā bāhirakā ahesuṃ. Te – “ahiṃsakamāṇavakassa āgatakālato paṭṭhāya mayaṃ na paññāyāma, kathaṃ naṃ bhindeyyāmā”ti? Nisīditvā mantayantā [V 3.0235] – “sabbehi atirekapaññattā duppaññoti. Na sakkā vattuṃ, vattasampannattā dubbattoti. Na sakkā vattuṃ, jātisampannattā dujjātoti na sakkā vattuṃ, kinti karissāmā”ti? Tato ekaṃ kharamantaṃ mantayiṃsu “ācariyassa antaraṃ katvā naṃ bhindissāmā”ti tayo rāsī hutvā paṭhamaṃ ekacce ācariyaṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā aṭṭhaṃsu. Kiṃ tātāti? Imasmiṃ gehe ekā kathā suyyatīti. Kiṃ tātāti? Ahiṃsakamāṇavo tumhākaṃ antare dubbhatīti maññāmāti. Ācariyo santajjetvā – “gacchatha vasalā, mā me puttaṃ mayhaṃ antare paribhindathā”ti niṭṭhubhi. Tato itare, atha itarehi tayopi koṭṭhāsā āgantvā tatheva vatvā – “amhākaṃ asaddahantā upaparikkhitvā jānāthā”ti āhaṃsu.

Having become an inner disciple, he commenced his training in the craft. He was accomplished in his duties, responsive to requests, pleasing in conduct, and a speaker of kind words. The other disciples became outsiders. They, sitting and conspiring, said: 'Since the arrival of the youth Ahiṃsaka, we are not recognized. How can we create a rift with him?' 'Because he is of superior wisdom to all, it is not possible to say he is of dull wisdom. Because he is accomplished in his duties, it is not possible to say he is ill-behaved. Because he is of noble birth, it is not possible to say he is of low birth. What shall we do?' Then they devised a harsh plan: 'We will create a division with the teacher and cause him to be broken.' Having formed three groups, at first some of them approached the teacher, paid respects, and stood by. 'What is it, dear ones?' 'In this house, we hear a certain talk.' 'What is it, dear ones?' 'We think that the youth Ahiṃsaka is misbehaving in your inner circle.' The teacher, rebuking them, said, 'Go away, you wretches! Do not create a rift between me and my son!' and he spat. Then the others, and then the others after them—all three groups—came and spoke in the very same way, saying, 'If you do not believe us, investigate and find out.'

Ācariyo [M 3.0228] sinehena vadante disvā “atthi maññe santhavo”ti paribhijjitvā cintesi “ghātemi na”nti. Tato cintesi – “sace ghātessāmi ‘disāpāmokkho ācariyo attano santikaṃ sippuggahaṇatthaṃ āgate māṇavake dosaṃ uppādetvā jīvitā voropetī’ti. Puna koci sippuggahaṇatthaṃ na āgamissati, evaṃ me lābho parihāyissati, atha [P 3.0330] naṃ sippassa pariyosānupacāroti vatvā jaṅghasahassaṃ ghātehīti vakkhāmi. Avassaṃ ettha eko uṭṭhāya taṃ ghātessatī”ti.

The teacher, seeing them speaking as if with affection and becoming divided in his mind, thought, 'I suppose there is intimacy.' He thought, 'I will kill him.' Then he thought again: 'If I kill him, people will say, "The world-renowned teacher, having generated an offense towards a youth who came to him to learn a craft, deprived him of life." Hearing this, no one else will come to learn a craft, and thus my gain will diminish. Instead, saying to him, "This is the concluding rite of the craft," I will say, "Kill a thousand foot-travelers." Surely, among them, someone will rise up and kill him.'

Atha naṃ āha – “ehi tāta jaṅghasahassaṃ ghātehi, evaṃ te sippassa upacāro kato bhavissatī”ti. Mayaṃ ahiṃsakakule jātā, na sakkā ācariyāti. Aladdhupacāraṃ sippaṃ phalaṃ na deti tātāti. So pañcāvudhaṃ gahetvā ācariyaṃ vanditvā aṭaviṃ paviṭṭho. Aṭaviṃ pavisanaṭṭhānepi aṭavimajjhepi aṭavito nikkhamanaṭṭhānepi ṭhatvā manusse ghāteti. Vatthaṃ vā veṭhanaṃ vā na gaṇhāti. Eko dveti gaṇitamattameva karonto gacchati, gaṇanampi na uggaṇhāti. Pakatiyāpi paññavā esa, pāṇātipātino pana cittaṃ na patiṭṭhāti, tasmā anukkamena gaṇanampi na sallakkhesi, ekekaṃ aṅguliṃ chinditvā ṭhapeti. Ṭhapitaṭṭhāne aṅguliyo vinassanti, tato vijjhitvā aṅgulīnaṃ mālaṃ katvā dhāresi, teneva cassa aṅgulimāloti saṅkhā udapādi. So sabbaṃ araññaṃ nissañcāramakāsi, dāruādīnaṃ atthāya araññaṃ gantuṃ samattho nāma natthi.

Then he said to him: 'Come, dear son, kill a thousand people; thus the homage to your craft will be performed.' 'Teacher, we are born in a non-violent family; it cannot be done.' 'Dear son, a craft for which the homage has not been performed does not bear fruit.' Taking the five weapons, he paid respects to his teacher and entered the forest. Standing at the entrance to the forest and at the exit from the forest, he killed people. He took nothing. He went about, just making a count, 'one,' 'two,' but he had not learned how to count. Though naturally intelligent, the mind of one who takes life is not steady; therefore, in due course, he did not even keep track of the count. He cut off each finger one by one and set them aside. In the place where they were set, the fingers perished. Therefore, he strung them, made a garland of fingers, and wore it. For that very reason, the designation 'Aṅgulimāla' arose for him. He made the entire forest devoid of human traffic; there was no one capable of entering the forest for the sake of wood or other things.

Rattibhāge [V 3.0236] antogāmampi āgantvā pādena paharitvā dvāraṃ ugghāteti. Tato sayiteyeva māretvā eko ekoti gahetvā gacchati. Gāmo osaritvā nigame aṭṭhāsi, nigamo nagare. Manussā tiyojanato paṭṭhāya gharāni pahāya dārake hatthesu gahetvā āgamma sāvatthiṃ parivāretvā khandhāvāraṃ bandhitvā rājaṅgaṇe sannipatitvā – “coro, te deva, vijite aṅgulimālo nāmā”tiādīni [P 3.0331] vadantā kandanti. Bhaggavo “mayhaṃ putto bhavissatī”ti ñatvā brāhmaṇiṃ āha – bhoti aṅgulimālo nāma coro uppanno, so na añño, tava putto ahiṃsakakumāro. Idāni rājā taṃ gaṇhituṃ nikkhamissati, kiṃ kattabbanti? Gaccha [M 3.0229] sāmi, puttaṃ me gahetvā ehīti. Nāhaṃ bhadde ussahāmi, catūsu hi janesu vissāso nāma natthi, coro me purāṇasahāyoti avissāsanīyo, sākhā me purāṇasanthatāti avissāsanīyā, rājā maṃ pūjetīti avissāsanīyo, itthī me vasaṃ gatāti avissāsanīyāti. Mātu hadayaṃ pana mudukaṃ hoti. Tasmā ahaṃ pana gantvā mayhaṃ puttaṃ ānessāmīti nikkhantā.

During the night, he would even enter a village, kick open the door with his foot, and then kill people while they were still asleep, taking them one by one as he went. The village fled and was re-established in a market town; the market town fled and was re-established in a city. People, starting from a distance of three yojanas, abandoned their homes, took their children in their arms, and came to Sāvatthī. Surrounding it, they set up an encampment, assembled in the royal courtyard, and cried out, saying: 'Your Majesty, in your kingdom there is a robber named Aṅgulimāla!' Bhaggava, knowing, 'This must be my son,' said to the brahmin woman: 'Madam, a robber named Aṅgulimāla has arisen. He is no other than your son, Ahiṃsaka-kumāra. Now the king will set out to capture him. What is to be done?' 'Go, my lord, take my son and come back.' 'I do not dare, good lady. For there is no trust to be placed in four kinds of beings: a robber is not to be trusted, even if he is an old companion of mine; a tree branch is not to be trusted, even if it was my old resting place; a king is not to be trusted, even if he honors me; a woman is not to be trusted, even if she is under my authority.' A mother's heart, however, is tender. Therefore, she set out, thinking, 'I will go and bring my son back.'

Taṃdivasañca bhagavā paccūsasamaye lokaṃ volokento aṅgulimālaṃ disvā – “mayi gate etassa sotthi bhavissati. Agāmake araññe ṭhito catuppadikaṃ gāthaṃ sutvā mama santike pabbajitvā cha abhiññā sacchikarissati. Sace na gamissāmi, mātari aparajjhitvā anuddharaṇīyo bhavissati, karissāmissa saṅgaha”nti pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā piṇḍāya pavisitvā katabhattakicco taṃ saṅgaṇhitukāmo vihārā nikkhami. Etamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “atha kho bhagavā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

And on that day, the Blessed One, surveying the world at dawn, saw Aṅgulimāla and thought: 'If I go, there will be well-being for him. Standing in the villageless wilderness, upon hearing a four-line verse, he will go forth in my presence and realize the six higher knowledges. If I do not go, he will commit an offense against his mother and become irredeemable. I shall take him under my care.' In the morning, having dressed, entered for alms-food, and finished his meal, he departed from the monastery, desiring to extend his guidance to him. To show this meaning, the passage beginning 'Then the Blessed One...' was spoken.

348. Saṅkaritvā saṅkaritvāti saṅketaṃ katvā vaggavaggā hutvā. Hatthatthaṃ gacchantīti hatthe atthaṃ vināsaṃ gacchanti. Kiṃ pana te bhagavantaṃ sañjānitvā evaṃ vadanti asañjānitvāti? Asañjānitvā. Aññātakavesena hi bhagavā [P 3.0332] ekakova agamāsi. Coropi tasmiṃ samaye dīgharattaṃ dubbhojanena ca dukkhaseyyāya ca ukkaṇṭhito hoti. Kittakā panānena manussā māritāti? Ekenūnasahassaṃ. So pana idāni ekaṃ labhitvā sahassaṃ pūressatīti saññī hutvā yameva paṭhamaṃ passāmi, taṃ ghātetvā gaṇanaṃ pūretvā sippassa upacāraṃ katvā kesamassuṃ ohāretvā nhāyitvā vatthāni parivattetvā mātāpitaro passissāmīti aṭavimajjhato aṭavimukhaṃ [V 3.0237] āgantvā ekamantaṃ ṭhitova bhagavantaṃ addasa. Etamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “addasā kho”tiādi vuttaṃ.

348. The phrase `Saṅkaritvā saṅkaritvā` means: having made a plan, they formed into groups. The phrase 'they fall into his hands' means they go to destruction in his hands. Did they speak thus recognizing the Blessed One, or not recognizing him? Not recognizing him. For the Blessed One went all alone in an unknown guise. The robber, too, at that time, was discontented from long-term poor food and uncomfortable lodging. But how many people had been killed by him? A thousand less one. He, having formed the intention, 'Whomever I see first, I will kill that person to complete the count of a thousand, perform the homage to my craft, and then, having shaved my hair and beard, bathed, and changed my clothes, I will see my parents,' came from the middle of the forest to the edge of the forest, and standing to one side, he saw the Blessed One. To show this meaning, the passage beginning 'He saw...' was spoken.

Iddhābhisaṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkhāsīti mahāpathaviṃ ummiyo uṭṭhapento viya saṃharitvā aparabhāge akkamati, orabhāge valiyo nikkhamanti, aṅgulimālo sarakkhepamattaṃ muñcitvā gacchati. Bhagavā purato mahantaṃ aṅgaṇaṃ dassetvā sayaṃ majjhe hoti, coro ante. So “idāni naṃ pāpuṇitvā gaṇhissāmī”ti sabbathāmena dhāvati. Bhagavā aṅgaṇassa pārimante [M 3.0230] hoti, coro majjhe. So “ettha naṃ pāpuṇitvā gaṇhissāmī”ti vegena dhāvati. Bhagavā tassa purato mātikaṃ vā thalaṃ vā dasseti, etenupāyena tīṇi yojanāni gahetvā agamāsi. Coro kilami, mukhe kheḷo sussi, kacchehi sedā mucciṃsu. Athassa “acchariyaṃ vata bho”ti etadahosi. Migampīti migaṃ kasmā gaṇhāti? Chātasamaye āhāratthaṃ. So kira ekaṃ gumbaṃ ghaṭṭetvā mige uṭṭhāpeti. Tato cittaruciyaṃ migaṃ anubandhanto gaṇhitvā pacitvā khādati. Puccheyyanti yena kāraṇenāyaṃ gacchantova ṭhito nāma[P 3.0333], ahañca ṭhitova aṭṭhito nāma, yaṃnūnāhaṃ imaṃ samaṇaṃ taṃ kāraṇaṃ puccheyyanti attho.

'He performed a feat of psychic power' means this: as if causing waves to rise on the great earth, he contracted it, stepping on the far side while folds of earth appeared on the near side. Aṅgulimāla, running, covered only the distance of a bow-shot. The Blessed One showed a large open space ahead and was in the middle, while the robber was at the edge. Thinking, 'Now I will overtake and catch him,' he ran with all his might. The Blessed One was at the far edge of the open space, while the robber was in the middle. Thinking, 'Here I will overtake and catch him,' he ran swiftly. The Blessed One showed him a water-course or high ground ahead; by this means, he led him for three yojanas. The robber grew weary, the saliva in his mouth dried up, and sweat poured from his armpits. Then this thought occurred to him: 'Oh, how astonishing!' This is to say, he was swift enough to catch a deer. How does one catch a deer? For food when hungry. It is said that he would strike a bush to startle the deer, then pursue one that pleased his eye, catch it, cook it, and eat it. The meaning of 'I should ask' is this: 'For what reason is this ascetic, though walking, said to be standing, while I, though standing still, am not standing? Indeed, I should ask this ascetic the reason for that.'

349. Nidhāyāti yo vihiṃsanatthaṃ bhūtesu daṇḍo pavattayitabbo siyā, taṃ nidhāya apanetvā mettāya khantiyā paṭisaṅkhāya avihiṃsāya sāraṇīyadhammesu ca ṭhito ahanti attho. Tuvamaṭṭhitosīti pāṇesu asaññatattā ettakāni pāṇasahassāni ghātentassa tava mettā vā khanti vā paṭisaṅkhā vā avihiṃsā vā sāraṇīyadhammo vā natthi, tasmā tuvaṃ aṭṭhitosi, idāni iriyāpathena ṭhitopi niraye dhāvissasi, tiracchānayoniyaṃ pettivisaye asurakāye vā dhāvissasīti vuttaṃ hoti.

349. Nidhāya means: whatever rod should be wielded for the purpose of harming beings, having laid aside that rod, having removed it, I am established in loving-kindness, patience, reflection, non-harming, and in the six states of conciliation. This is the meaning. Tuvaṃ aṭṭhito si means: because of being unrestrained towards beings, for you who have killed so many thousands of beings, there is no loving-kindness, or patience, or reflection, or non-harming, or state of conciliation. Therefore, you are not established. Now, even while standing in posture, you will have to run in hell; you will have to run in the animal realm, the ghost realm, or the asura realm. Thus it is said.

Tato coro – “mahā ayaṃ sīhanādo, mahantaṃ gajjitaṃ, na idaṃ aññassa bhavissati, mahāmāyāya puttassa siddhatthassa samaṇarañño etaṃ gajjitaṃ, diṭṭho vatamhi maññe tikhiṇacakkhunā sammāsambuddhena, saṅgahakaraṇatthaṃ me bhagavā āgato”ti cintetvā cirassaṃ vata metiādimāha. Tattha mahitoti devamanussādīhi catupaccayapūjāya pūjito. Paccupādīti cirassaṃ [V 3.0238] kālassa accayena mayhaṃ saṅgahatthāya imaṃ mahāvanaṃ paṭipajji. Pahāya pāpanti pajahitvā pāpaṃ.

Then the robber thought: "This is a great lion's roar, a mighty roaring. This will not be of another; this is the roaring of the ascetic king Siddhattha, son of Mahāmāyā. Surely, I think I have been seen by the sharp-eyed Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. The Blessed One has come to bestow favor upon me." Thinking thus, he spoke the words beginning with, "After a long time indeed..." Therein, mahito means: honored by gods, humans, and others with the offering of the four requisites. Paṭipajji means: after a long time has passed, for the sake of bestowing favor upon me, he has come to this great forest. Pahāya pāpaṃ means: having abandoned evil.

Itvevāti evaṃ vatvāyeva. Āvudhanti [P 3.0334] pañcāvudhaṃ. Sobbheti samantato chinne. Papāteti ekato chinne. Naraketi phalitaṭṭhāne. Idha pana tīhipi imehi padehi araññameva vuttaṃ. Akirīti khipi chaḍḍesi.

Itveva means: having spoken thus. Āvudhaṃ means: the five weapons. Sobbhe means: in a chasm cut off all around. Papāte means: in a precipice cut off on one side. Narake means: in a place that is split open. Here, however, by these three terms, only the forest is meant. Akiri means: he threw, he discarded.

Tamehi [M 3.0231] bhikkhūti tadā avocāti bhagavato imaṃ pabbājento kuhiṃ satthakaṃ labhissāmi, kuhiṃ pattacīvaranti pariyesanakiccaṃ natthi, kammaṃ pana olokesi. Athassa pubbe sīlavantānaṃ aṭṭhaparikkhārabhaṇḍakassa dinnabhāvaṃ ñatvā dakkhiṇahatthaṃ pasāretvā – “ehi bhikkhu svākkhāto dhammo, cara brahmacariyaṃ sammā dukkhassa antakiriyāyā”ti āha. So saha vacaneneva iddhimayapattacīvaraṃ paṭilabhi. Tāvadevassa gihiliṅgaṃ antaradhāyi, samaṇaliṅgaṃ pāturahosi.

Regarding the words, "To him, 'Come, bhikkhu,' He then said": For the Blessed One, while ordaining this man, there was no task of searching, thinking, "Where will I get a razor? Where will I get a bowl and robes?" But rather, He looked at his kamma. Then, having known that in the past he had given the eight requisites to virtuous persons, He extended His right hand and said: "Come, bhikkhu. The Dhamma is well-proclaimed. Practice the holy life for the right ending of suffering." Together with that very utterance, he obtained a bowl and robes created by psychic power. At that very moment, his lay appearance vanished, and the appearance of a monk manifested.

“Ticīvarañca patto ca, vāsi sūci ca bandhanaṃ;

Parissāvanena aṭṭhete, yuttayogassa bhikkhuno”ti. –

The three robes and the bowl, a razor, a needle, and a girdle; together with a water strainer—these eight are for a monk devoted to the practice.

Evaṃ vuttā aṭṭha parikkhārā sarīrapaṭibaddhāva hutvā nibbattiṃsu. Eseva tassa ahu bhikkhubhāvoti esa ehibhikkhubhāvo tassa upasampannabhikkhubhāvo ahosi, na hi ehibhikkhūnaṃ visuṃ upasampadā nāma atthi.

Thus, the eight requisites spoken of arose as if attached to his body. Regarding "This itself was his state as a bhikkhu": this "ehi bhikkhu" state became his state as a fully ordained bhikkhu. For indeed, for "ehi bhikkhus," there is no such thing as a separate ordination.

350. Pacchāsamaṇenāti bhaṇḍaggāhakena pacchāsamaṇena, teneva attano pattacīvaraṃ gāhāpetvā taṃ pacchāsamaṇaṃ katvā gatoti attho. Mātāpissa aṭṭhausabhamattena ṭhānena antaritā, – “tāta, ahiṃsaka kattha ṭhitosi, kattha nisinnosi, kuhiṃ gatosi? Mayā saddhiṃ na kathesi tātā”ti vadantī āhiṇḍitvā apassamānā ettova gatā.

350. Pacchāsamaṇena means: with a following monk who carries the requisites. The meaning is: having had that very person carry His own bowl and robes, and having made him the following monk, He departed. His mother, being separated by a distance of about eight usabhas, wandered about, lamenting, "Dear Ahiṃsaka, where are you standing? Where are you sitting? Where have you gone? Dear one, you do not speak with me." Not seeing him, she departed from that very forest place.

Pañcamattehi [P 3.0335] assasatehīti sace corassa parājayo bhavissati, anubandhitvā naṃ gaṇhissāmi. Sace mayhaṃ parājayo bhavissati, vegena palāyissāmīti sallahukena balena nikkhami[V 3.0239]. Yena ārāmoti kasmā ārāmaṃ agamāsi? So kira corassa bhāyati, cittena gantukāmo na gacchati, garahābhayena nikkhami. Tenassa etadahosi – “sammāsambuddhaṃ vanditvā nisīdissāmi, so pucchissati ‘kasmā balaṃ gahetvā nikkhantosī’ti. Athāhaṃ ārocessāmi, bhagavā hi maṃ na kevalaṃ samparāyikeneva atthena saṅgaṇhāti, diṭṭhadhammikenapi saṅgaṇhātiyeva. So sace mayhaṃ jayo bhavissati, adhivāsessati. Sace parājayo bhavissati ‘kiṃ te, mahārāja, ekaṃ coraṃ ārabbha gamanenā’ti vakkhati. Tato [M 3.0232] maṃ jano evaṃ sañjānissati – ‘rājā coraṃ gahetuṃ nikkhanto, sammāsambuddhena pana nivattito’ti” garahamokkhaṃ sampassamāno agamāsi.

Regarding "with about five hundred horsemen": thinking, "If the robber is defeated, I will pursue and capture him. If I am defeated, I will flee quickly," he set out with a light and swift force. Regarding "to where the monastery was": why did he go to the monastery? It is said that he feared the robber; though wishing to go in his mind, he did not. He went out due to fear of blame. For this reason, this thought occurred to him: "I will pay homage to the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One and sit down. He will ask, 'Why have you set out with a force?' Then I will inform him. Indeed, the Blessed One supports me not only with benefits pertaining to the next life, but also with benefits in this very life. If I am to be victorious, He will consent. If I am to be defeated, He will say, 'Great King, what is the use of going on account of a single robber?' Then the people will know of me thus: 'The king set out to capture the robber, but was turned back by the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.'" Foreseeing this escape from blame, he went to the monastery.

Kuto panassāti kasmā āha? Api nāma bhagavā tassa upanissayaṃ oloketvā taṃ ānetvā pabbājeyyāti bhagavato parigaṇhanatthaṃ āha. Raññoti na kevalaṃ raññoyeva bhayaṃ ahosi, avasesopi mahājano bhīto phalakāvudhāni chaḍḍetvā sammukhasammukhaṭṭhāneva palāyitvā nagaraṃ pavisitvā dvāraṃ pidhāya aṭṭālake āruyha olokento aṭṭhāsi. Evañca avoca – “aṅgulimālo ‘rājā mayhaṃ santikaṃ āgacchatī’ti ñatvā paṭhamataraṃ āgantvā jetavane nisinno, rājā tena gahito, mayaṃ pana palāyitvā muttā”ti. Natthi te ito bhayanti ayañhi idāni kunthakipillikaṃ jīvitā na voropeti, natthi te imassa santikā bhayanti attho.

Why did he say, "But whence to him?" He said it to probe the Blessed One's intention, thinking, "Perhaps the Blessed One, having seen his potential for the path and fruit, might bring him and ordain him." Regarding "the king's": it was not only the king who was afraid. The rest of the populace, being afraid, discarded their shields and weapons, fled from wherever they were facing, entered the city, closed the gates, climbed up the watchtowers, and stood looking out. And they spoke thus: "Aṅgulimāla, knowing 'The king is coming to me,' came first and is sitting in Jetavana. The king has been captured by him, but we, having been able to flee, are saved." Regarding "There is no fear for you from here": for this one now does not deprive even a louse or an ant of life. The meaning is: "There is no fear for you from this one's presence."

Kathaṃ gottoti? Kasmā pucchati? Pabbajitaṃ dāruṇakammena [P 3.0336] uppannanāmaṃ gahetvā voharituṃ na yuttaṃ, mātāpitūnaṃ gottavasena naṃ samudācarissāmīti maññamāno pucchi. Parikkhārānanti etesaṃ atthāya ahaṃ ussukkaṃ karissāmīti attho. Kathentoyeva ca udare baddhasāṭakaṃ muñcitvā therassa pādamūle ṭhapesi.

"Of what clan are you?" Why did he ask this? It is not proper to address one who has gone forth by a name that arose from a cruel deed. Thinking, "I will address him according to the clan of his mother and father," he asked. Regarding "for the requisites": the meaning is, "For the sake of these, I will make an effort." And while still speaking, he loosened the cloth tied at his waist and placed it at the elder's feet.

351. Āraññikotiādīni cattāri dhutaṅgāni pāḷiyaṃ āgatāni. Therena pana terasapi samādinnāneva ahesuṃ, tasmā alanti āha. Yañhi mayaṃ, bhanteti kiṃ sandhāya vadati? “Hatthimpi dhāvantaṃ anubandhitvā gaṇhāmī”ti āgataṭṭhāne raññā pesitahatthādayo so evaṃ aggahesi. Rājāpi – “hatthīhiyeva naṃ parikkhipitvā gaṇhatha, asseheva, rathehevā”ti evaṃ [V 3.0240] anekavāraṃ bahū hatthādayo pesesi. Evaṃ gatesu pana tesu – “ahaṃ are aṅgulimālo”ti tasmiṃ uṭṭhāya saddaṃ karonte ekopi āvudhaṃ parivattetuṃ nāsakkhi, sabbeva koṭṭetvā māresi. Hatthī araññahatthī, assā araññaassā, rathāpi tattheva bhijjantīti idaṃ sandhāya rājā evaṃ vadati.

351. The four ascetic practices, beginning with being a forest-dweller, are found in the Pāḷi Canon. However, the elder had indeed undertaken all thirteen, hence he said, 'It is enough.' With reference to what does the king say, 'Indeed, venerable sir, as for us...'? At the place where it is stated, 'I pursue and seize even a running elephant,' he seized in this way the elephant-riders and others sent by the king. The king also sent many elephant-riders and others many times, saying, 'Surround and seize him with elephants,' 'with horses,' 'with chariots.' However, when they had gone thus, and he stood up and made a sound, saying, 'Hey, I am Aṅgulimāla!' not even one was able to turn his weapon; he cut them all down and killed them. The elephants became wild elephants, the horses became wild horses, and the chariots also broke right there. It is with reference to this that the king speaks thus.

Piṇḍāya pāvisīti na idaṃ paṭhamaṃ pāvisi. Itthidassanadivasaṃ sandhāya panetaṃ vuttaṃ. Devasikampi panesa pavisateva, manussā ca naṃ disvā uttasantipi palāyantipi dvārampi thakenti, ekacce aṅgulimāloti sutvāva palāyitvā araññaṃ vā pavisanti, gharaṃ vā pavisitvā dvāraṃ thakenti. Palāyituṃ [M 3.0233] asakkontā piṭṭhiṃ datvā tiṭṭhanti[P 3.0337]. Thero uḷuṅgayāgumpi kaṭacchubhikkhampi na labhati, piṇḍapātena kilamati. Bahi alabhanto nagaraṃ sabbasādhāraṇanti nagaraṃ pavisati. Yena dvārena pavisati, tattha aṅgulimālo āgatoti kūṭasahassānaṃ bhijjanakāraṇaṃ hoti. Etadahosīti kāruññappattiyā ahosi. Ekena ūnamanussasahassaṃ ghātentassa ekadivasampi kāruññaṃ nāhosi, gabbhamūḷhāya itthiyā dassanamatteneva kathaṃ uppannanti? Pabbajjābalena, pabbajjābalañhi etaṃ.

Regarding 'He entered for alms,' this was not the first time he entered. However, this was said with reference to the day he saw the woman. Moreover, he entered daily, and people, upon seeing him, were terrified, fled, and shut their doors. Some, just on hearing 'Aṅgulimāla,' would flee and enter the forest, or enter their homes and shut the door. Those unable to flee would stand with their backs turned. The elder did not receive even a mouthful of gruel or a ladleful of alms-food; he grew weary from seeking alms-food. Not obtaining anything outside, he entered the city, thinking, 'The city is common to all.' By whichever gate he entered, there, the cry 'Aṅgulimāla has come!' became the cause for the shattering of a thousand water pots. Regarding 'This occurred to him,' it occurred through the attainment of compassion. For him who was killing a thousand people less one, not even for a single day had there been compassion. How then did it arise merely by seeing a woman with an obstructed birth? It arose through the power of ordination; for this is indeed the power of ordination.

Tena hīti yasmā te kāruññaṃ uppannaṃ, tasmāti attho. Ariyāya jātiyāti, aṅgulimāla, etaṃ tvaṃ mā gaṇhi, nesā tava jāti. Gihikālo esa, gihī nāma pāṇampi hananti, adinnādānādīnipi karonti. Idāni pana te ariyā nāma jāti. Tasmā tvaṃ “yato ahaṃ, bhagini, jāto”ti sace evaṃ vattuṃ kukkuccāyasi, tena hi “ariyāya jātiyā”ti evaṃ visesetvā vadāhīti uyyojesi.

'Therefore' means: because compassion has arisen in you, therefore. Regarding 'by the noble birth': Aṅgulimāla, do not take that to be your birth; that is not your birth. That was the time of being a householder. Householders, by name, kill living beings and commit theft and other such things. But now, your birth is called the noble birth. Therefore, if you are scrupulous about saying, 'Sister, since I was born,' then, this being so, specify it thus, saying, 'by the noble birth.' Having said this, He sent him.

Taṃ itthiṃ etadavocāti itthīnaṃ gabbhavuṭṭhānaṭṭhānaṃ nāma na sakkā purisena upasaṅkamituṃ. Thero kiṃ karosīti? Aṅgulimālatthero saccakiriyaṃ katvā sotthikaraṇatthāya āgatoti ārocāpesi. Tato te sāṇiyā parikkhipitvā therassa bahisāṇiyaṃ pīṭhakaṃ paññāpesuṃ. Thero tattha nisīditvā – “yato ahaṃ bhagini sabbaññubuddhassa ariyāya jātiyā jāto”ti saccakiriyaṃ akāsi, saha saccavacaneneva dhamakaraṇato muttaudakaṃ viya dārako nikkhami. Mātāputtānaṃ sotthi ahosi. Imañca pana parittaṃ na kiñci parissayaṃ na maddati, mahāparittaṃ nāmetanti [V 3.0241] vuttaṃ. Therena [P 3.0338] nisīditvā saccakiriyakataṭṭhāne pīṭhakaṃ akaṃsu. Gabbhamūḷhaṃ tiracchānagatitthimpi ānetvā tattha nisajjāpenti, tāvadeva sukhena gabbhavuṭṭhānaṃ hoti. Yā dubbalā hoti na sakkā ānetuṃ, tassā pīṭhakadhovanaudakaṃ netvā sīse siñcanti, taṅkhaṇaṃyeva gabbhavuṭṭhānaṃ hoti, aññampi rogaṃ vūpasameti. Yāva kappā tiṭṭhanakapāṭihāriyaṃ kiretaṃ.

Regarding 'He said this to that woman': it is not possible for a man to approach the place where a woman gives birth. When asked, 'What is the elder doing?', he had it announced: 'The Elder Aṅgulimāla has come to bring about well-being by making an asseveration of truth.' Then they, having enclosed the area with a curtain, prepared a seat for the elder outside the curtain. The elder sat there and made the asseveration of truth: 'Sister, from when I was born by the noble birth in the Dispensation of the Omniscient Buddha...' Together with the words of truth, the child came out like water released from a water-strainer. There was well-being for mother and child. Moreover, this protective chant crushes every single danger; it is called the Great Protective Chant. They made a seat at the place where the elder sat and performed the asseveration of truth. Bringing even a female animal with an obstructed birth and making it sit there, immediately the delivery from the womb happens with ease. For a woman who is weak and cannot be brought, they take the water from washing the seat and sprinkle it on her head; at that very moment, the delivery from the womb happens, and it also pacifies other diseases. It is said this is a miracle that will last for an eon.

Kiṃ pana bhagavā theraṃ vejjakammaṃ kārāpesīti? Na kārāpesi. Therañhi disvā manussā bhītā palāyanti. Thero bhikkhāhārena kilamati, samaṇadhammaṃ kātuṃ na sakkoti. Tassa anuggahena saccakiriyaṃ kāresi. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi – “idāni kira aṅgulimālatthero mettacittaṃ [M 3.0234] paṭilabhitvā saccakiriyāya manussānaṃ sotthibhāvaṃ karotīti manussā theraṃ upasaṅkamitabbaṃ maññissanti, tato bhikkhāhārena akilamanto samaṇadhammaṃ kātuṃ sakkhissatī”ti anuggahena saccakiriyaṃ kāresi. Na hi saccakiriyā vejjakammaṃ hoti. Therassāpi ca “samaṇadhammaṃ karissāmī”ti mūlakammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhāne nisinnassa cittaṃ kammaṭṭhānābhimukhaṃ na gacchati, aṭaviyaṃ ṭhatvā manussānaṃ ghātitaṭṭhānameva pākaṭaṃ hoti. “Duggatomhi, khuddakaputtomhi, jīvitaṃ me dehi sāmīti maraṇabhītānaṃ vacanākāro ca hatthapādavikāro ca āpāthaṃ āgacchati, so vippaṭisārī hutvā tatova uṭṭhāya gacchati, athassa bhagavā taṃ jātiṃ abbohārikaṃ katvāvāyaṃ vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ gaṇhissatīti ariyāya jātiyā saccakiriyaṃ kāresi. Eko vūpakaṭṭhotiādi vatthasutte (ma. ni. 1.80) vitthāritaṃ.

But did the Blessed One have the elder perform a medical act? He did not. For, seeing the elder, people were frightened and fled. The elder grew weary from seeking alms-food and was unable to practice the ascetic's duties. Out of compassion for him, the Blessed One had him perform the asseveration of truth. It is said that this occurred to Him: 'Now the Elder Aṅgulimāla, having gained a mind of loving-kindness, brings about a state of well-being for people through an asseveration of truth. Thus, people will think that the elder should be approached. Then, no longer weary from seeking alms-food, he will be able to practice the ascetic's duties.' Thus, out of compassion, He had him perform the asseveration of truth. For an asseveration of truth is not a medical act. Moreover, for the elder himself, having thought, 'I will practice the ascetic's duties,' and having taken up his foundational meditation subject, while sitting in his places for day and night, his mind would not go towards the meditation subject. The very place where he stood in the forest and killed people would become manifest to him. The manner of speech of those afraid of death—'Master, I am wretched, I am a young son, grant me my life!'—and the contortions of their hands and feet would come into his mental range. Becoming remorseful, he would get up from that very spot and go away. Then the Blessed One, thinking, 'Having made that former birth something not to be transacted with, this one will develop insight and attain Arahantship,' had him perform the asseveration of truth by means of his noble birth. The passage beginning with 'Alone, secluded...' is elaborated in the Vatthu Sutta.

352. Aññenapi leḍḍu khittoti kākasunakhasūkarādīnaṃ paṭikkamāpanatthāya samantā sarakkhepamatte ṭhāne yena kenaci [P 3.0339] disābhāgena khitto āgantvā therasseva kāye patati. Kittake ṭhāne evaṃ hoti? Gaṇṭhikaṃ paṭimuñcitvā piṇḍāya caritvā paṭinivattetvā yāva gaṇṭhikapaṭimukkaṭṭhānaṃ āgacchati, tāva hoti. Bhinnena sīsenāti mahācammaṃ chinditvā yāva aṭṭhimariyādā bhinnena.

352. ‘Even when a clod is thrown by another’ means: a clod thrown from any direction whatsoever within the range of an arrow’s throw for the purpose of driving away crows, dogs, pigs, and so on, comes and falls only on the elder’s body. Over what distance does this happen? From when he puts on his girdle, goes for alms, and returns, until he reaches the place where the girdle is taken off, so long does it happen. ‘With a broken head’ means with the thick skin split open, up to the limit of the bone.

Brāhmaṇāti khīṇāsavabhāvaṃ sandhāya āha. Yassa kho tvaṃ, brāhmaṇa, kammassa vipākenāti idaṃ sabhāgadiṭṭhadhammavedanīyakammaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Kammañhi kariyamānameva tayo koṭṭhāse pūreti. Sattasu [V 3.0242] cittesu kusalā vā akusalā vā paṭhamajavanacetanā diṭṭhadhammavedanīyakammaṃ nāma hoti. Taṃ imasmiṃyeva attabhāve vipākaṃ deti. Tathā asakkontaṃ ahosikammaṃ, nāhosi kammavipāko, na bhavissati kammavipāko, natthi kammavipākoti imassa tikassa vasena ahosikammaṃ nāma hoti. Atthasādhikā sattamajavanacetanā upapajjavedanīyakammaṃ nāma. Taṃ anantare attabhāve vipākaṃ deti. Tathā asakkontaṃ vuttanayeneva taṃ ahosikammaṃ nāma hoti. Ubhinnamantare pañcajavanacetanā aparāpariyavedanīyakammaṃ nāma hoti. Taṃ anāgate yadā okāsaṃ labhati, tadā [M 3.0235] vipākaṃ deti. Sati saṃsārappavattiyā ahosikammaṃ nāma na hoti. Therassa pana upapajjavedanīyañca aparāpariyavedanīyañcāti imāni dve kammāni kammakkhayakarena arahattamaggena samugghāṭitāni, diṭṭhadhammavedanīyaṃ atthi[P 3.0340]. Taṃ arahattappattassāpi vipākaṃ detiyeva. Taṃ sandhāya bhagavā “yassa kho tva”ntiādimāha. Tasmā yassa khoti ettha yādisassa kho tvaṃ, brāhmaṇa, kammassa vipākenāti evaṃ attho veditabbo.

By ‘brāhmaṇa’, he spoke referring to the state of one whose cankers are destroyed. The phrase, ‘By the result of which kamma, O brāhmaṇa, you…’ was spoken in reference to kamma that is to be experienced in this very life. For kamma, while being performed, fulfills three portions. Among the seven javana consciousnesses, the volition of the first javana, whether wholesome or unwholesome, is called ‘kamma to be experienced in this very life.’ It gives its result in this very existence. When it is unable to do so, by means of this triad—‘the kamma was, but its result was not; its result will not be; its result is not’—it becomes what is called ‘defunct kamma.’ The volition of the seventh javana, which accomplishes the purpose, is called ‘kamma to be experienced in the next existence.’ It gives its result in the immediately following existence. When it is unable to do so, by the method already stated, it becomes what is called ‘defunct kamma.’ The five javana volitions in between are called ‘kamma to be experienced in subsequent existences.’ It gives its result in the future when it finds an opportunity. As long as the process of saṃsāra exists, it does not become ‘defunct kamma.’ For the Elder, however, these two kammas—that to be experienced in the next existence and that to be experienced in subsequent existences—have been completely uprooted by the path of Arahantship, which brings about the destruction of kamma. The kamma to be experienced in this very life remains. It gives its result even to one who has attained Arahantship. It was with reference to this that the Blessed One said, ‘By the result of which kamma, you…’ and so forth. Therefore, here in the phrase ‘yassa kho’, the meaning should be understood as: ‘By the result of whatever kamma, O brāhmaṇa, you…’

Abbhā muttoti desanāsīsamattametaṃ, abbhā mahikā dhūmo rajo rāhūti imehi pana upakkilesehi mutto candimā idha adhippeto. Yathā hi evaṃ nirupakkileso candimā lokaṃ pabhāseti, evaṃ pamādakilesavimutto appamatto bhikkhu imaṃ attano khandhāyatanadhātulokaṃ pabhāseti, vihatakilesandhakāraṃ karoti.

‘Freed from clouds’ is merely the heading of the discourse. Rather, what is intended here is the moon freed from these defilements: clouds, mist, smoke, dust, and Rāhu. For just as the moon, thus undefiled, illuminates the world, so too a diligent monk, freed from all defilements rooted in negligence, illuminates this world of his own aggregates, sense bases, and elements; he dispels the darkness of the defilements.

Kusalena pidhīyatīti maggakusalena pidhīyati appaṭisandhikaṃ karīyati. Yuñjati buddhasāsaneti buddhasāsane kāyena vācāya manasā ca yuttappayutto viharati. Imā tisso therassa udānagāthā nāma.

‘Is covered by the wholesome’ means it is obstructed by the wholesome path; it is made to be without rebirth-linking. ‘One engages in the Buddha’s teaching’ means one dwells strenuously engaged in the Buddha’s teaching with body, speech, and mind. These three are called the Elder’s verses of inspired utterance.

Disā hi meti idaṃ kira thero attano parittāṇākāraṃ karonto āha. Tattha disā hi meti mama sapattā. Ye maṃ evaṃ upavadanti – “yathā mayaṃ aṅgulimālena māritānaṃ ñātakānaṃ vasena dukkhaṃ vediyāma, evaṃ aṅgulimālopi vediyatū”ti, te mayhaṃ disā catusaccadhammakathaṃ suṇantūti attho. Yuñjantūti kāyavācāmanehi yuttappayuttā viharantu. Ye dhammamevādapayanti [V 3.0243] santoti ye santo sappurisā dhammaṃyeva ādapenti samādapenti gaṇhāpenti, te manujā mayhaṃ sapattā bhajantu sevantu payirupāsantūti attho.

It is said the Elder spoke the words ‘Disā hi me’ while making a protective utterance for himself. Therein, ‘disā hi me’ means 'my adversaries'. The meaning is: ‘Those who reproach me thus—“Just as we experience suffering on account of the relatives killed by Aṅgulimāla, so too may Aṅgulimāla experience it”—let those enemies of mine listen to the discourse on the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths.’ ‘Let them apply themselves’ means: let them dwell strenuously engaged with body, speech, and mind. ‘Those peaceful ones who only encourage the Dhamma’ means: ‘Those good people who only accept, undertake, and grasp the Dhamma of true persons—let my adversaries associate with, serve, and attend upon those good people’—this is the meaning.

Avirodhappasaṃsīnanti [P 3.0341] avirodho vuccati mettā, mettāpasaṃsakānanti attho. Suṇantu dhammaṃ kālenāti khaṇe khaṇe khantimettāpaṭisaṅkhāsāraṇīyadhammaṃ suṇantu. Tañca anuvidhīyantūti tañca dhammaṃ anukarontu pūrentu.

‘Those who praise non-opposition’ means: non-opposition is called loving-kindness; the meaning is 'those who praise loving-kindness'. ‘Let them listen to the Dhamma at the right time’ means: let them listen at every moment to the Dhamma that should be constantly remembered, which consists of patience and loving-kindness. ‘And let them follow it’ means: let them imitate and fulfill that Dhamma.

Na hi jātu so mamaṃ hiṃseti yo mayhaṃ diso, so maṃ ekaṃseneva na hiṃseyya. Aññaṃ vā pana kiñci nanti na kevalaṃ maṃ, aññampi pana [M 3.0236] kañci puggalaṃ mā hiṃsantu mā viheṭhentu. Pappuyya paramaṃ santinti paramaṃ santibhūtaṃ nibbānaṃ pāpuṇitvā. Rakkheyya tasathāvareti tasā vuccanti sataṇhā, thāvarā nittaṇhā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yo nibbānaṃ pāpuṇāti, so sabbaṃ tasathāvaraṃ rakkhituṃ samattho hoti. Tasmā mayhampi disā nibbānaṃ pāpuṇantu, evaṃ maṃ ekaṃseneva na hiṃsissantīti. Imā tisso gāthā attano parittaṃ kātuṃ āha.

‘For that one would never harm me’ means: my enemy would surely not harm me. ‘Nor any other being’ means: not only me, but may they not harm or afflict any other person. ‘Having attained the highest peace’ means: having attained Nibbāna, which is the supreme peace. ‘May they protect the trembling and the steadfast’ means: ‘trembling’ refers to those with craving, and ‘steadfast’ to those without craving. This is what is said: whoever attains Nibbāna is capable of protecting all beings, both trembling and steadfast. Therefore, may my enemies also attain Nibbāna; in this way, they will surely not harm me. He spoke these three verses to make a protection for himself.

Idāni attanova paṭipattiṃ dīpento udakañhi nayanti [P 3.0342] nettikāti āha. Tattha nettikāti ye mātikaṃ sodhetvā bandhitabbaṭṭhāne bandhitvā udakaṃ nayanti. Usukārāti usukārakā. Namayantīti telakañjikena makkhetvā kukkuḷe tāpetvā unnatunnataṭṭhāne namentā ujuṃ karonti. Tejananti kaṇḍaṃ. Tañhi issāso tejaṃ karoti, parañca tajjeti, tasmā tejananti vuccati. Attānaṃ damayantīti yathā nettikā ujumaggena udakaṃ nayanti, usukārā tejanaṃ, tacchakā ca dāruṃ ujuṃ karonti, evamevaṃ paṇḍitā attānaṃ damenti ujukaṃ karonti nibbisevanaṃ karonti.

Now, explaining his own practice, he said: ‘For irrigators lead the water.’ Therein, ‘irrigators’ are those who, having cleared the channels and dammed them where they should be dammed, lead the water. ‘Fletchers straighten the shaft.’ ‘They straighten’ means they make it straight by anointing it with oil and rice-gruel, heating it in hot embers, and bending the high and low places. ‘The shaft’ means an arrow. For an archer makes it sharp, and it also pierces another; therefore, it is called a ‘shaft.’ ‘The wise tame themselves’ means that just as irrigators lead water along a straight path, fletchers straighten the shaft, and carpenters straighten wood, even so, the wise tame themselves, make themselves upright, and make themselves free from coarseness.

Tādināti iṭṭhāniṭṭhādīsu nibbikārena – “pañcahākārehi bhagavā tādī, iṭṭhāniṭṭhe tādī, vantāvīti tādī, cattāvīti tādī, tiṇṇāvīti tādī, tanniddesāti tādī”ti (mahāni. 38; 192) evaṃ tādilakkhaṇappattena satthārā. Bhavanettīti bhavarajju, taṇhāyetaṃ nāmaṃ. Tāya hi goṇā viya gīvāya rajjuyā, sattā hadaye baddhā taṃ taṃ bhavaṃ nīyanti, tasmā bhavanettīti vuccati. Phuṭṭho [P 3.0343] kammavipākenāti maggacetanāya phuṭṭho. Yasmā hi maggacetanāya [V 3.0244] kammaṃ paccati vipaccati ḍayhati, parikkhayaṃ gacchati, tasmā sā kammavipākoti vuttā. Tāya hi phuṭṭhattā esa aṇaṇo nikkileso jāto, na dukkhavedanāya aṇaṇo. Bhuñjāmīti cettha theyyaparibhogo iṇaparibhogo dāyajjaparibhogo sāmiparibhogoti cattāro paribhogā veditabbā. Tattha dussīlassa paribhogo theyyaparibhogo nāma. So hi cattāro paccaye thenetvā bhuñjati. Vuttampi cetaṃ “theyyāya vo, bhikkhave, raṭṭhapiṇḍo bhutto”ti (pārā. 195). Sīlavato pana apaccavekkhaṇaparibhogo iṇaparibhogo nāma. Sattannaṃ sekkhānaṃ paribhogo dāyajjaparibhogo nāma. Khīṇāsavassa paribhogo sāmiparibhogo [M 3.0237] nāma. Idha kilesaiṇānaṃ abhāvaṃ sandhāya “aṇaṇo”ti vuttaṃ. “Aniṇo”tipi pāṭho. Sāmiparibhogaṃ sandhāya “bhuñjāmi bhojana”nti vuttaṃ.

'Such' (Tādinā) means: by the Teacher who has attained the characteristic of being 'such' through being without alteration in regard to desirable and undesirable objects, etc. The Blessed One is 'such' (tādī) in five ways: He is 'such' in regard to the desirable and undesirable; He is 'such' because He has vomited defilements; He is 'such' because He has abandoned defilements; He is 'such' because He has crossed over saṃsāra; He is 'such' because He is truly indicated by those qualities. 'The guide to existence' (Bhavanetti) is the rope of existence; this is a name for craving. For by that craving, beings, bound in the heart, are led to this or that existence, just as oxen are by a rope at the neck. Therefore, it is called 'the guide to existence.' 'Touched by the result of kamma' means touched by the volition associated with the path. Because by the volition associated with the path, kamma ripens, matures, is burned, and goes to destruction, therefore that volition is called 'the result of kamma.' Because of being touched by that, this person has become debt-free and without defilements; he is not debt-free on account of painful feeling. And in the phrase 'I partake' (bhuñjāmi), four kinds of partaking should be understood: partaking by theft, partaking by debt, partaking by inheritance, and partaking as a master. Among these, the partaking of an immoral person is called partaking by theft. For he partakes of the four requisites by stealing them. And this was said: 'Monks, the country's almsfood is partaken of by you through theft.' For a virtuous person, however, partaking without reflection is called partaking by debt. The partaking of the seven trainees is called partaking by inheritance. The partaking of one whose taints are destroyed is called partaking as a master. Here, 'debt-free' (aṇaṇo) is said with reference to the absence of the debts which are the defilements. There is also the reading 'without debt' (aniṇo). With reference to partaking as a master, it is said, 'I partake of the meal.'

Kāmaratisanthavanti duvidhesupi kāmesu taṇhāratisanthavaṃ mā anuyuñjatha mā karittha. Nayidaṃ dummantitaṃ mamāti yaṃ mayā sammāsambuddhaṃ disvā pabbajissāmīti mantitaṃ, taṃ mama mantitaṃ na dummantitaṃ. Saṃvibhattesu dhammesūti ahaṃ satthāti evaṃ loke uppannehi ye dhammā saṃvibhattā, tesu dhammesu yaṃ seṭṭhaṃ nibbānaṃ, tadeva ahaṃ upagamaṃ upagato sampatto, tasmā mayhaṃ idaṃ āgamanaṃ svāgataṃ nāma gatanti. Tisso vijjāti pubbenivāsadibbacakkhuāsavakkhayapaññā. Kataṃ [P 3.0344] buddhassa sāsananti yaṃ buddhassa sāsane kattabbakiccaṃ atthi, taṃ sabbaṃ mayā kataṃ. Tīhi vijjāhi navahi ca lokuttaradhammehi desanaṃ matthakaṃ pāpesīti.

'Do not pursue sensual pleasure and intimacy' (Kāmaratisanthavaṃ) means: do not exert yourselves in, do not engage in, delight and association through craving in both kinds of sensual pleasures.
