'This was not an ill-advised counsel of mine' (nayidaṃ dummantitaṃ mama) means: the counsel I made, that 'Having seen the Perfectly Enlightened One, I shall go forth,' that counsel of mine was not ill-advised. 'Among the well-analyzed Dhammas' (saṃvibhattesu dhammesu) means: by the arising in the world of one who says 'I am the Teacher,' the Dhammas were well-analyzed. Among those Dhammas, I have reached and well attained that which is supreme, Nibbāna itself. Therefore, this coming of mine has been a good coming. 'The three knowledges' (tisso vijjā) are: the knowledge of previous existences, the divine eye, and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints. 'The Buddha’s instruction has been fulfilled' (kataṃ buddhassa sāsanaṃ) means: whatever duty was to be done in the Buddha’s Dispensation, all of it has been done by me. He brought the teaching to its culmination with the three knowledges and the nine supramundane Dhammas.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Aṅgulimālasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Aṅgulimāla Sutta is concluded.

7. Piyajātikasuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Explanation of the Piyajātika Sutta

353. Evaṃ [V 3.0245] me sutanti piyajātikasuttaṃ. Tattha neva kammantā paṭibhantīti na sabbena sabbaṃ paṭibhanti, pakatiniyāmena pana na paṭibhanti. Dutiyapadepi eseva nayo. Ettha ca na paṭibhātīti na ruccati. Āḷāhananti susānaṃ. Aññathattanti vivaṇṇatāya aññathābhāvo. Indriyāni nāma manoviññeyyā dhammā, patiṭṭhitokāsaṃ pana sandhāya idaṃ vuttaṃ. Piyajātikāti piyato jāyanti. Piyappabhāvikāti piyato pabhavanti.

353. 'Thus have I heard' introduces the Piyajātika Sutta. Therein, 'neither do tasks appear' means it is not that tasks do not appear at all; rather, they do not appear in their normal way. The same method applies to the second phrase. And here, 'does not appear' means it is not pleasing. 'Āḷāhana' means a charnel ground. 'Aññathatta' means a different state due to disfigurement. 'Indriyāni' (faculties) are phenomena cognizable by the mind, but this is said with reference to their established basis. 'Piyajātikā' means they are born from the beloved. 'Piyappabhāvikā' means they spring from the beloved.

355. Sace taṃ, mahārājāti tassa atthaṃ asallakkhayamānāpi satthari saddhāya evaṃ vadati. Cara pireti apehi amhākaṃ pare, anajjhattikabhūteti attho. Atha vā cara pireti parato gaccha, mā idha tiṭṭhātipi attho.

355. Regarding 'If, O great king'—though not discerning its meaning, she speaks thus out of faith in the Teacher. 'Cara pire' (Go away, stranger) means “Go away, you who are other, not one of us.” Alternatively, 'Cara pire' also means “Go elsewhere, do not stay here.”

356. Dvidhā [M 3.0238] chetvāti asinā dve koṭṭhāse karonto chinditvā. Attānaṃ [P 3.0345] upphālesīti teneva asinā attano udaraṃ phālesi. Yadi hi tassa sā appiyā bhaveyya, idāni aññaṃ mātugāmaṃ gaṇhissāmīti attānaṃ na ghāteyya. Yasmā panassa sā piyā ahosi, tasmā paralokepi tāya saddhiṃ samaṅgibhāvaṃ patthayamāno evamakāsi.

356. 'Having cut in two' (Dvidhā chetvā) means having cut with a sword, making two portions. 'He split himself open' (Attānaṃ upphālesi) means he split open his own belly with that same sword. For if she had been displeasing to him, he would not have killed himself, thinking, “Now I will take another woman.” But because she was dear to him, desiring to attain union with her even in the next world, he acted thus.

357. Piyā te vajirīti evaṃ kirassā ahosi – “sacāhaṃ, ‘bhūtapubbaṃ, mahārāja, imissāyeva sāvatthiyaṃ aññatarissā itthiyā’tiādikathaṃ katheyyaṃ, ‘ko te evaṃ akāsi, apehi natthi eta’nti maṃ paṭisedheyya, vattamāneneva naṃ saññāpessāmī”ti cintetvā evamāha. Vipariṇāmaññathābhāvāti ettha maraṇavasena vipariṇāmo, kenaci saddhiṃ palāyitvā gamanavasena aññathābhāvo veditabbo.

357. Regarding 'Is Vajirī dear to you?', this thought, it seems, occurred to her: “If I were to relate a story beginning, ‘Once upon a time, great king, in this very Sāvatthī, there was a certain woman,’ he might reject me, saying, ‘Who did this to you? Go away, this is not so.’ I will make him understand by means of a present event.” Thinking thus, she spoke thus. Regarding 'change and alteration,' herein, 'change' should be understood as change by way of death, and 'alteration' as a different state by way of fleeing and going away with someone.

Vāsabhāyāti vāsabhā nāma rañño ekā devī, taṃ sandhāyāha.

Regarding 'Vāsabhāya,' Vāsabhā was the name of one of the king's queens; it is with reference to her that this is said.

Piyā [V 3.0246] te ahanti kasmā sabbapacchā āha? Evaṃ kirassā ahosi – “ayaṃ rājā mayhaṃ kupito, sacāhaṃ sabbapaṭhamaṃ ‘piyā te aha’nti puccheyyaṃ, ‘na me tvaṃ piyā, cara pire’ti vadeyya, evaṃ sante kathā patiṭṭhānaṃ na labhissatī”ti kathāya patiṭṭhānatthaṃ sabbapacchā pucchi. Kāsikosalesu chaḍḍitabhāvena vipariṇāmo, paṭirājūnaṃ hatthagamanavasena aññathābhāvo veditabbo.

Why did she ask 'Am I dear to you?' last of all? It seems this thought occurred to her: “This king is angry with me. If I were to ask first, ‘Am I dear to you?’, he might say, ‘You are not dear to me, go away, stranger!’ In that case, the conversation would not find a footing.” Therefore, to establish a footing for the conversation, she asked last of all. In the case of Kāsī and Kosala, 'change' should be understood as change due to being abandoned, and 'alteration' as a different state by way of falling into the hands of rival kings.

Ācamehīti [P 3.0346] ācamanodakaṃ dehi. Ācamitvā hatthapāde dhovitvā mukhaṃ vikkhāletvā satthāraṃ namassitukāmo evamāha. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

'Ācamehi' means 'Give water for rinsing.' Wishing to pay homage to the Teacher after rinsing, washing his hands and feet, and cleansing his mouth, he spoke thus. The rest is clear everywhere.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Piyajātikasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Piyajātika Sutta is concluded.

8. Bāhitikasuttavaṇṇanā

8. The Explanation of the Bāhitika Sutta

358. Evaṃ [V 3.0247] me sutanti bāhitikasuttaṃ. Tattha ekapuṇḍarīkaṃ nāganti evaṃnāmakaṃ hatthiṃ. Tassa kira phāsukānaṃ upari tālaphalamattaṃ paṇḍaraṭṭhānaṃ atthi[M 3.0239], tenassa ekapuṇḍarīkoti nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Sirivaḍḍhaṃ mahāmattanti paccekahatthiṃ abhiruhitvā kathāphāsukatthaṃ saddhiṃ gacchantaṃ evaṃnāmakaṃ mahāmattaṃ. Āyasmānoti ettha noti pucchāya nipāto. Mahāmatto therassa saṅghāṭipattadhāraṇākāraṃ sallakkhetvā “evaṃ, mahārājā”ti āha.

358. The sutta beginning with 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ' is the Bāhitika Sutta. Therein, 'ekapuṇḍarīkaṃ nāgaṃ' means an elephant with that name. It is said that on its ribs there was a white spot the size of a palm fruit; for that reason, they gave it the name Ekapuṇḍarīka. 'Sirivaḍḍhaṃ mahāmattaṃ' means the great minister of that name who, having mounted a separate elephant, was going along for the sake of comfortable conversation. In 'āyasmāno', 'no' is a particle used in a question. The great minister, having observed the Elder's manner of carrying his outer robe and bowl, said, 'So it is, great king.'

359. Opārambhoti upārambhaṃ dosaṃ āropanāraho. Kiṃ pucchāmīti rājā pucchati. Sundarivatthusmiṃ uppannamidaṃ suttaṃ, taṃ pucchāmīti pucchati. Yañhi mayaṃ, bhanteti, bhante, yaṃ mayaṃ viññūhīti idaṃ padaṃ gahetvā pañhena paripūretuṃ nāsakkhimhā, taṃ kāraṇaṃ āyasmatā evaṃ vadantena paripūritaṃ.

359. 'Opārambho' means worthy of having fault ascribed to it. 'What shall I ask?' Thus the king asks. This sutta arose in the context of the Sundarī affair; 'I ask about that,' thus he asks. 'Yañhi mayaṃ, bhante': 'Venerable sir, that matter which we were unable to complete by means of a question, taking this phrase 'by the wise' (viññūhi), has been completed by the venerable one speaking thus.'

360. Akusaloti akosallasambhūto. Sāvajjoti [P 3.0347] sadoso. Sabyābajjhoti sadukkho. Dukkhavipākoti idha nissandavipāko kathito. Tassāti tassa evaṃ attabyābādhādīnaṃ atthāya pavattakāyasamācārassa.

360. 'Akusalo' means arisen from unskillfulness. 'Sāvajjo' means with fault. 'Sabyāpajjho' means with suffering. 'Dukkhavipāko' means: in this present life, the result of the outflow is spoken of. 'Tassa' refers to that person whose bodily conduct occurs for the sake of self-affliction and so on.

Sabbākusaladhammapahīno kho, mahārāja, tathāgato kusaladhammasamannāgatoti ettha sabbesaṃyeva akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānaṃ vaṇṇetīti. Āma vaṇṇetīti vutte yathā pucchā, tathā attho vutto bhaveyya. Evaṃ byākaraṇaṃ pana na bhāriyaṃ. Appahīnaakusalopi hi pahānaṃ vaṇṇeyya, bhagavā pana pahīnākusalatāya yathākārī tathāvādīti dassetuṃ evaṃ byākāsi. Sukkapakkhepi eseva nayo.

Regarding the passage, 'The Tathāgata, great king, has abandoned all unwholesome states and is endowed with wholesome states': if, when asked, 'Does he praise the abandonment of all unwholesome states?' one were to reply, 'Yes, he praises it,' the meaning would have been spoken in accordance with the question. However, such an answer is not weighty. Indeed, even one who has not abandoned unwholesome states could praise their abandonment. But the Blessed One, because he has abandoned unwholesome states, is one who acts as he speaks and speaks as he acts; to show this meaning, he answered thus. Regarding the wholesome side also, this same method should be understood.

362. Bāhitikāti bāhitiraṭṭhe uṭṭhitavatthassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Soḷasasamā āyāmenāti āyāmena samasoḷasahatthā. Aṭṭhasamā vitthārenāti vitthārena samaaṭṭhahatthā.

362. 'Bāhitikā' is the name of a cloth that arose in the Bāhiti country. 'Soḷasasamā āyāmena' means: in length, equal to sixteen cubits. 'Aṭṭhasamā vitthārena' means: in width, equal to eight cubits.

363. Bhagavato [V 3.0248] pādāsīti bhagavato niyyātesi. Datvā ca pana gandhakuṭiyaṃ vitānaṃ katvā bandhi. Tato paṭṭhāya gandhakuṭi bhiyyosomattāya [M 3.0240] sobhi. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānameva. Neyyapuggalassa pana vasena ayaṃ desanā niṭṭhitāti.

363. 'Bhagavato pādāsi' means he dedicated it to the Blessed One. And having given it, he had a canopy made in the perfumed chamber and fastened it. From that time onwards, the perfumed chamber shone with excessive beauty. The remainder is clear everywhere. Furthermore, this discourse was concluded for the sake of a person who is to be guided.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Bāhitikasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Bāhitika Sutta is concluded.

9. Dhammacetiyasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Dhammacetiya Sutta

364. Evaṃ [V 3.0249][P 3.0348] me sutanti dhammacetiyasuttaṃ. Tattha medāḷupanti nāmetaṃ tassa, tassa hi nigamassa medavaṇṇā pāsāṇā kirettha ussannā ahesuṃ, tasmā medāḷupanti saṅkhaṃ gataṃ. Senāsanaṃ panettha aniyataṃ, tasmā na taṃ vuttaṃ. Nagarakanti evaṃnāmakaṃ sakyānaṃ nigamaṃ. Kenacideva karaṇīyenāti na aññena karaṇīyena, ayaṃ pana bandhulasenāpatiṃ saddhiṃ dvattiṃsāya puttehi ekadivaseneva gaṇhathāti āṇāpesi, taṃdivasañcassa bhariyāya mallikāya pañcahi bhikkhusatehi saddhiṃ bhagavā nimantito, buddhappamukhe bhikkhusaṅghe gharaṃ āgantvā nisinnamatte “senāpati kālaṅkato”ti sāsanaṃ āharitvā mallikāya adaṃsu. Sā paṇṇaṃ gahetvā mukhasāsanaṃ pucchi. “Raññā ayye senāpati saddhiṃ dvattiṃsāya puttehi ekappahāreneva gahāpito”ti ārocesuṃ. Mahājanagataṃ mā karitthāti ovaṭṭikāya paṇṇaṃ katvā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ parivisi. Tasmiṃ samaye ekā sappicāṭi nīharitā, sā ummāre āhacca bhinnā, taṃ apanetvā aññaṃ āharāpetvā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ parivisi.

364. The sutta beginning with 'Thus have I heard' is the Dhammacetiya Sutta. Therein, 'Medāḷupa' is the name of that town. For it is said that the stones of that town were abundant and had a color like fat, so it came to be called Medāḷupa. The dwelling place there was not fixed; therefore, it was not mentioned. 'Nagaraka' is a town of the Sakyans with that name. 'For some reason' means not for any other reason, but rather this: the king had ordered, 'Seize and kill General Bandhula, together with his thirty-two sons, in a single day.' On that very day, his wife Mallikā had invited the Blessed One together with five hundred monks. When the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, had come to the house and had just sat down, they brought the message, 'The general is dead,' and gave it to Mallikā. She took the letter and asked for the oral message. They informed her, 'Noble lady, the king has had the general seized and killed, together with his thirty-two sons, in a single stroke.' Saying, 'Do not let this become public talk,' she placed the letter in the fold of her garment and served the community of monks. At that time, a pot of ghee that was brought out struck the threshold and broke. Having it removed and having another brought, she served the community of monks.

Satthā katabhattakicco kathāsamuṭṭhāpanatthaṃ – “sappicāṭiyā bhinnapaccayā na cintetabba”nti āha. Tasmiṃ samaye mallikā paṇṇaṃ nīharitvā [P 3.0349] bhagavato purato ṭhapetvā – “bhagavā imaṃ dvattiṃsāya puttehi saddhiṃ senāpatino matasāsanaṃ, ahaṃ etampi na cintayāmi, sappicāṭipaccayā kiṃ cinteyyāmī”ti āha. Bhagavā – “mallike, mā cintayi, anamatagge saṃsāre nāma vattamānānaṃ hoti eta”nti aniccatādipaṭisaṃyuttaṃ dhammakathaṃ katvā agamāsi. Mallikā dvattiṃsasuṇisāyo pakkosāpetvā ovādaṃ adāsi. Rājā mallikaṃ pakkosāpetvā “senāpatino amhākaṃ antare [M 3.0241] bhinnadoso atthi natthī”ti pucchi. Natthi sāmīti. So tassā vacanena tassa niddosabhāvaṃ ñatvā vippaṭisārī balavadomanassaṃ uppādesi. So – “evarūpaṃ nāma adosakārakaṃ maṃ sambhāvayitvā āgataṃ sahāyakaṃ vināsesi”nti tato paṭṭhāya pāsāde vā nāṭakesu vā rajjasukhesu vā cittassādaṃ alabhamāno tattha tattha vicarituṃ āraddho. Etadeva kiccaṃ ahosi. Idaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “kenacideva karaṇīyenā”ti.

The Teacher, having finished his meal, said, in order to initiate a Dhamma talk, 'One should not be concerned on account of the broken ghee pot.' At that time, Mallikā took out the letter, placed it before the Blessed One, and said, 'Blessed One, this is the message of the death of the general along with his thirty-two sons. I do not worry even about this; why should I worry on account of a ghee pot?' The Blessed One said, 'Mallikā, do not worry. For beings faring in this saṃsāra with its unknown beginning, such things happen.' Having given a Dhamma talk connected with impermanence and so on, he departed. Mallikā summoned her thirty-two daughters-in-law and gave them advice. The king summoned Mallikā and asked, 'Was there any fault causing a rift between us and the general, or not?' 'There was not, lord.' Having known his faultlessness from her words, he became remorseful and generated strong mental displeasure. He thought, 'I have destroyed such a companion, a doer of no wrong, who came having confidence in me.' From then on, finding no delight of mind in the palace, or in dramas, or in the pleasures of kingship, he began to wander here and there. This became his sole preoccupation. It was with reference to this that it was said, 'for some reason.'

Dīghaṃ [V 3.0250] kārāyananti dīghakārāyano nāma bandhulasenāpatissa bhāgineyyo “etassa me mātulo adosakārako nikkāraṇena ghātito”ti raññā senāpatiṭṭhāne ṭhapito. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Mahaccā rājānubhāvenāti mahatā rājānubhāvena[P 3.0350], dharaṇitalaṃ bhindanto viya sāgaraṃ parivattento viya vicittavesasobhena mahatā balakāyenāti attho. Pāsādikānīti dassaneneva saha rañjanakāni. Pasādanīyānīti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Atha vā pāsādikānīti pasādajanakāni. Appasaddānīti nissaddāni. Appanigghosānīti avibhāvitatthena nigghosena rahitāni. Vijanavātānīti vigatajanavātāni. Manussarāhasseyyakānīti manussānaṃ rahassakammānucchavikāni, rahassamantaṃ mantentānaṃ anurūpānīti attho. Paṭisallānasāruppānīti nilīyanabhāvassa ekībhāvassa anucchavikāni. Yattha sudaṃ mayanti na tena tattha bhagavā payirupāsitapubbo, tādisesu pana payirupāsitapubbo, tasmā yādisesu sudaṃ mayanti ayamettha attho.

'Dīghaṃ kārāyana' means Dīghakārāyana, the nephew of General Bandhula. He was appointed to the position of general by the king, who thought, 'By me, his maternal uncle, who had done no wrong, was killed without reason.' It is with reference to this that this was said. 'By the great royal power' means by the great power of the king, with a great army, splendid with various attires, as if splitting the surface of the earth, as if overturning the ocean—this is the meaning. 'Delightful' means inspiring affection upon sight. 'Inspiring confidence' is a synonym for that. Alternatively, 'delightful' means producing confidence. 'With little sound' means without sound. 'Without clamor' means devoid of indistinct shouting. 'Free from the passage of people' means where the coming and going of people has ceased. 'Fit for human privacy' means suitable for people's secret actions, appropriate for those discussing secret counsel—this is the meaning. 'Suitable for seclusion' means suitable for a state of being hidden and a state of being alone. As for 'in which places we...', he had not previously attended upon the Blessed One there, but he had attended upon him in similar places. Therefore, 'in what sort of places we...'—this is the meaning here.

Atthi, mahārājāti paṇḍito senāpati “rājā bhagavantaṃ mamāyatī”ti jānāti, so sace maṃ rājā “kahaṃ bhagavā”ti vadeyya, adandhāyantena ācikkhituṃ yuttanti carapurise payojetvā bhagavato nivāsanaṭṭhānaṃ ñatvāva viharati. Tasmā evamāha. Ārāmaṃ pāvisīti bahinigame khandhāvāraṃ bandhāpetvā kārāyanena saddhiṃ pāvisi.

'Yes, great king.' The wise general knows, 'The king esteems the Blessed One.' Thinking, 'If the king should ask me, "Where is the Blessed One?", it would be proper to inform him without delay,' he employed spies, and having learned the Blessed One's dwelling place, he remains prepared. Therefore, he spoke thus. 'He entered the park' means that having had a camp set up outside the town, he entered together with Kārāyana.

366. Vihāroti gandhakuṭiṃ sandhāyāhaṃsu. Āḷindanti [P 3.0351] pamukhaṃ. Ukkāsitvāti ukkāsitasaddaṃ katvā. Aggaḷanti kavāṭaṃ. Ākoṭehīti agganakhena īsakaṃ kuñcikacchiddasamīpe koṭehīti vuttaṃ hoti. Dvāraṃ kira atiupari amanussā, atiheṭṭhā dīghajātikā koṭenti. Tathā akoṭetvā [M 3.0242] majjhe chiddasamīpe koṭetabbaṃ, idaṃ dvārakoṭṭakavattanti dīpentā vadanti. Tatthevāti bhikkhūhi vuttaṭṭhāneyeva. Khaggañca uṇhīsañcāti desanāmattametaṃ,

366. 'Vihāra'—they said this referring to the Fragrant Chamber. 'Āḷinda' means the front porch. 'Having cleared his throat' means having made the sound of clearing the throat. 'Bar' refers to the door leaf. 'Knock' means 'tap lightly with the tip of a fingernail near the keyhole'—this is what is meant. It is said that non-humans knock on the door too high up, while the long-lived species knock too low down. Not knocking in that way, one should knock in the middle, near the keyhole. Explaining, they say, 'This is the custom of knocking on a door.' 'The sword and the turban'—this is merely a part of the discourse.

Vālabījanimuṇhīsaṃ, khaggaṃ chattañcupāhanaṃ;

Oruyha rājā yānamhā, ṭhapayitvā paṭicchadanti. –

The yak-tail fan, the turban, the sword, the umbrella, and the footwear; the king, having descended from his vehicle, set them aside and handed them over.

Āgatāni pana pañcapi rājakakudhabhaṇḍāni adāsi. Kasmā pana adāsīti. Atigaruno sammāsambuddhassa [V 3.0251] santikaṃ uddhatavesena gantuṃ na yuttanti ca, ekakova upasaṅkamitvā attano rucivasena sammodissāmi cāti. Pañcasu hi rājakakudhabhaṇḍesu nivattitesu tvaṃ nivattāti vattabbaṃ na hoti, sabbe sayameva nivattanti. Iti imehi dvīhi kāraṇehi adāsi. Rahāyatīti rahassaṃ karoti nigūhati. Ayaṃ kirassa adhippāyo “pubbepi ayaṃ rājā samaṇena gotamena saddhiṃ catukkaṇṇamantaṃ mantetvā mayhaṃ mātulaṃ saddhiṃ dvattiṃsāya puttehi gaṇhāpesi, idānipi catukkaṇṇamantaṃ mantetukāmo, kacci nu kho maṃ gaṇhāpessatī”ti. Evaṃ kopavasenassa etadahosi.

Then he gave the five royal regalia that had been brought. And why did he give them? Because it was not proper to go into the presence of the very venerable Perfectly Enlightened One with an arrogant appearance, and also because he thought, 'I will approach alone and converse according to my own inclination.' For when the five royal regalia are sent back, it is not necessary to say, 'You, turn back'; all turn back by themselves. For these two reasons, he gave them. 'He acts in secret' means he does something secretly, he conceals. This, it seems, was his intention: 'Previously, this king, after holding a private consultation with the ascetic Gotama, had my maternal uncle seized along with his thirty-two sons. Now too, he wishes to hold a private consultation; I wonder, will he have me seized?' Thus, this occurred to him through the power of anger.

Vivari [P 3.0352] bhagavā dvāranti na bhagavā uṭṭhāya dvāraṃ vivari, vivaratūti pana hatthaṃ pasāresi. Tato – “bhagavā tumhehi anekesu kappakoṭīsu dānaṃ dadamānehi na sahatthā dvāravivaraṇakammaṃ kata”nti sayameva dvāraṃ vivaṭaṃ. Taṃ pana yasmā bhagavato manena vivaṭaṃ, tasmā “vivari bhagavā dvāra”nti vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Vihāraṃ pavisitvāti gandhakuṭiṃ pavisitvā. Tasmiṃ pana paviṭṭhamatteyeva kārāyano pañca rājakakudhabhaṇḍāni gahetvā khandhāvāraṃ gantvā viṭaṭūbhaṃ āmantesi “chattaṃ samma ussāpehī”ti. Mayhaṃ pitā kiṃ gatoti? Pitaraṃ mā puccha, sace tvaṃ na ussāpesi, taṃ gaṇhitvā ahaṃ ussāpemīti. “Ussāpemi sammā”ti sampaṭicchi. Kārāyano rañño ekaṃ assañca asiñca ekameva ca paricārikaṃ itthiṃ ṭhapetvā – “sace rājā jīvitena atthiko, mā āgacchatū”ti viṭaṭūbhassa chattaṃ ussāpetvā taṃ gahetvā sāvatthimeva gato.

Regarding 'The Blessed One opened the door': it was not that the Blessed One got up and opened the door, but rather, thinking, 'Let it open,' he extended his hand. Then, as if to say, 'O Blessed One, by you who have given gifts for many crores of aeons, the act of opening a door with your own hand has never been done,' the door opened by itself. However, since it opened by the Blessed One's mind, it is therefore proper to say, 'The Blessed One opened the door.' 'Having entered the monastery' means having entered the Fragrant Chamber. But just as he entered, Kārāyana took the five royal regalia, went to the army camp, and addressed Viṭaṭūbha, saying, 'Friend, raise the parasol!' When asked, 'Where has my father gone?' he replied, 'Do not ask about your father. If you do not raise it, I will seize you and raise the parasol myself.' Viṭaṭūbha agreed, saying, 'I will raise it, friend.' Kārāyana, having left for the king only one horse, a sword, and a single female attendant, said, 'If the king is desirous of his life, let him not come.' Then, having had Viṭaṭūbha raise the parasol, he took him and went right to Sāvatthī.

367. Dhammanvayoti [M 3.0243] paccakkhañāṇasaṅkhātassa dhammassa anunayo anumānaṃ, anubuddhīti attho. Idāni yenassa dhammanvayena “sammāsambuddho bhagavā”tiādi hoti, taṃ dassetuṃ idha panāhaṃ, bhantetiādimāha. Tattha āpāṇakoṭikanti pāṇoti jīvitaṃ, taṃ mariyādaṃ anto karitvā, maraṇasamayepi carantiyeva, taṃ na vītikkamantīti vuttaṃ hoti. “Apāṇakoṭika”ntipi pāṭho, ājīvitapariyantanti attho. Yathā [P 3.0353] ekacce jīvitahetu atikkamantā pāṇakoṭikaṃ katvā caranti, na evanti attho. Ayampi kho me, bhanteti buddhasubuddhatāya dhammasvākkhātatāya saṅghasuppaṭipannatāya ca etaṃ evaṃ hoti, evañhi me, bhante, ayaṃ bhagavati dhammanvayo hotīti dīpeti. Eseva nayo sabbattha.

367. 'Consequential reasoning' means the deduction, the inference, the corresponding understanding of the Dhamma reckoned as direct knowledge; this is the meaning. Now, to show by which consequential reasoning it comes to be for him that 'The Blessed One is a Perfectly Enlightened One,' and so on, he spoke the words beginning, 'But here, venerable sir.' Therein, 'up to the end of life' means: 'pāṇa' is life; making that the boundary, even at the time of death they continue to practice and do not transgress it. This is what is said. There is also the reading 'apāṇakoṭikaṃ', meaning 'until the end of life.' The meaning is that they are not like some who, transgressing for the sake of life, do not practice up to the end of life. 'And this too for me, venerable sir' shows: 'Because of the Buddha's perfect enlightenment, the Dhamma's being well-expounded, and the Sangha's good practice, this is so. Indeed, venerable sir, in this way this consequential reasoning regarding the Blessed One occurs for me.' This is the method in all cases.

369. Na [V 3.0252] viya maññe cakkhuṃ bandhanteti cakkhuṃ abandhante viya. Apāsādikañhi disvā puna olokanakiccaṃ na hoti, tasmā so cakkhuṃ na bandhati nāma. Pāsādikaṃ disvā punappunaṃ olokanakiccaṃ hoti, tasmā so cakkhuṃ bandhati nāma. Ime ca apāsādikā, tasmā evamāha. Bandhukarogo noti kularogo. Amhākaṃ kule jātā evarūpā hontīti vadanti. Uḷāranti mahesakkhaṃ. Pubbenāparanti pubbato aparaṃ visesaṃ. Tattha kasiṇaparikammaṃ katvā samāpattiṃ nibbattento uḷāraṃ pubbe visesaṃ sañjānāti nāma, samāpattiṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ katvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ gaṇhanto uḷāraṃ pubbato aparaṃ visesaṃ sañjānāti nāma.

369. The phrase 'It is as if, I think, they do not bind the eye' means 'as if not binding the eye.' For having seen an uninspiring person, there is no need to look again; therefore, such a one is said 'not to bind the eye.' Having seen an inspiring person, there is a need to look again and again; therefore, such a one is said 'to bind the eye.' And these are uninspiring; therefore, he spoke thus. 'A family disease' means a hereditary disease. They say, 'Those born in our family are of such a kind.' 'Uḷāraṃ' means of great power. 'Pubbenāparaṃ' means a later distinction from a former state. Therein, one who produces an attainment after doing the preliminary work on a kasiṇa is said to know a great, later distinction from the former state. One who attains arahantship by developing insight, having made the attainment a basis, is said to know a great, later distinction from the former state.

370. Ghātetāyaṃ vā ghātetunti ghātetabbayuttakaṃ ghātetuṃ. Jāpetāyaṃ vā jāpetunti dhanena vā jāpetabbayuttakaṃ jāpetuṃ jānituṃ adhanaṃ kātuṃ. Pabbājetāyaṃ vā pabbājetunti raṭṭhato vā pabbājetabbayuttakaṃ pabbājetuṃ.

370. 'To kill one fit to be killed' means to kill one who is suitable to be killed. 'To ruin one fit to be ruined' means to ruin with wealth one who is suitable to be ruined, to cause loss, to make destitute. 'To banish one fit to be banished' means to banish from the country one who is suitable to be banished.

373. Isidattapurāṇāti [P 3.0354] isidatto ca purāṇo ca. Tesu eko brahmacārī, eko sadārasantuṭṭho. Mamabhattāti mama santakaṃ bhattaṃ [M 3.0244] etesanti mamabhattā. Mamayānāti mama santakaṃ yānaṃ etesanti mamayānā. Jīvikāya dātāti jīvitavuttiṃ dātā. Vīmaṃsamānoti upaparikkhamāno. Tadā kira rājā niddaṃ anokkantova okkanto viya hutvā nipajji. Atha te thapatayo “katarasmiṃ disābhāge bhagavā”ti pucchitvā “asukasmiṃ nāmā”ti sutvā mantayiṃsu – “yena sammāsambuddho, tena sīse kate rājā pādato hoti. Yena rājā, tena sīse kate satthā pādato hoti, kiṃ karissāmā”ti? Tato nesaṃ etadahosi – “rājā kuppamāno yaṃ amhākaṃ deti, taṃ acchindeyya. Na kho pana mayaṃ sakkoma jānamānā satthāraṃ pādato kātu”nti rājānaṃ pādato katvā nipajjiṃsu. Taṃ sandhāya ayaṃ rājā evamāha.

373. 'Isidatta and Purāṇa' means Isidatta and Purāṇa. Among them, one was a celibate, the other was content with his own wife. 'My dependents for food' means 'they for whom my own food exists,' thus they are my dependents for food. 'My dependents for transport' means 'they for whom my own vehicle exists,' thus they are my dependents for transport. 'Giver of livelihood' means a giver of the means of living. 'Vīmaṃsamāno' means investigating. At that time, it is said, the king, without yet having fallen asleep, lay down as if he had. Then those two carpenters asked, 'In which direction is the Blessed One?' and having heard, 'In such-and-such a direction,' they consulted: 'If we place our heads in the direction of the Perfectly Enlightened One, the king is at our feet. If we place our heads in the direction of the king, the Teacher is at our feet. What shall we do?' Then this occurred to them: 'If the king gets angry, he might take away what he gives us. But we, knowing, are not able to place the Teacher at our feet.' So, having placed the king at their feet, they lay down. It was with reference to this that the king spoke thus.

374. Pakkāmīti gandhakuṭito nikkhamitvā kārāyanassa ṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ gato, taṃ tattha adisvā khandhāvāraṭṭhānaṃ gato, tatthāpi aññaṃ adisvā taṃ itthiṃ pucchi. Sā sabbaṃ pavattiṃ ācikkhi. Rājā – “na idāni mayā ekakena tattha gantabbaṃ, rājagahaṃ gantvā bhāgineyyena saddhiṃ āgantvā mayhaṃ rajjaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti rājagahaṃ gacchanto antarāmagge kaṇājakabhattañceva [V 3.0253] bhuñji, bahalaudakañca pivi. Tassa sukhumālapakatikassa āhāro na sammā pariṇāmi. So rājagahaṃ pāpuṇantopi vikāle dvāresu pihitesu [P 3.0355] pāpuṇi. “Ajja sālāyaṃ sayitvā sve mayhaṃ bhāgineyyaṃ passissāmī”ti bahinagare sālāya nipajji. Tassa rattibhāge uṭṭhānāni pavattiṃsu, katipayavāre bahi nikkhami. Tato paṭṭhāya padasā gantuṃ asakkonto tassā itthiyā aṅke nipajjitvā balavapaccūse kālamakāsi. Sā tassa matabhāvaṃ ñatvā – “dvīsu rajjesu rajjaṃ kāretvā idāni parassa bahinagare anāthasālāya anāthakālakiriyaṃ katvā nipanno mayhaṃ sāmi kosalarājā”tiādīni vadamānā uccāsaddena paridevituṃ ārabhi. Manussā sutvā rañño ārocesuṃ. Rājā āgantvā disvā sañjānitvā āgatakāraṇaṃ ñatvā mahāparihārena sarīrakiccaṃ karitvā “viṭaṭūbhaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti bheriṃ carāpetvā balakāyaṃ sannipātesi. Amaccā pādesu patitvā – “sace, deva, tumhākaṃ mātulo arogo assa, tumhākaṃ gantuṃ yuttaṃ bhaveyya, idāni pana viṭaṭūbhopi tumhe [M 3.0245] nissāya chattaṃ ussāpetuṃ arahatiyevā”ti saññāpetvā nivāresuṃ.

374. He departed, leaving the Fragrant Chamber and going to the place where Dīghakārāyana was staying. Not seeing him there, he went to the military camp. Not seeing anyone else there either, he questioned that woman. She related the entire matter. The king thought, 'Now I should not go there alone. I will go to Rājagaha and return with my nephew to reclaim my kingdom.' On his way to Rājagaha, he ate broken rice and drank turbid water. For one of his delicate constitution, the food was not properly digested. By the time he reached Rājagaha, it was late, and the gates were closed. Thinking, 'Today I will sleep in the hall and see my nephew tomorrow,' he lay down in a hall outside the city. During the night, he had bouts of dysentery and went outside several times. From then on, unable to walk, he lay down in that woman’s lap and passed away at early dawn. Realizing he had died, she began to lament loudly, saying, 'After having ruled in two kingdoms, now my lord, the king of Kosala, lies in another's city, in a hall for the destitute, having died an unsupported death.' Hearing her, people informed the king. The king came, saw and recognized him, and having learned the reason for his arrival, had the funeral rites performed with great honor. Then, thinking, 'I will capture Viṭaṭūbha,' he had the drum beaten to assemble the army. The ministers fell at his feet and, having made him understand, restrained him, saying, 'Your Majesty, if your uncle were healthy, it would be fitting for you to go. But now, Viṭaṭūbha also, relying on you, is indeed worthy to raise the umbrella.'

Dhammacetiyānīti dhammassa cittīkāravacanāni. Tīsu hi ratanesu yattha katthaci cittīkāre kate sabbattha katoyeva hoti, tasmā bhagavati cittīkāre kate dhammopi katova hotīti bhagavā “dhammacetiyānī”ti āha. Ādibrahmacariyakānīti maggabrahmacariyassa ādibhūtāni, pubbabhāgapaṭipattibhūtānīti attho. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

'Monuments to the Dhamma' means expressions of reverence for the Dhamma. For when reverence is shown to any of the three jewels, it is shown to all. Therefore, when reverence is shown to the Blessed One, reverence is also shown to the Dhamma. For that reason, the Blessed One said, 'Monuments to the Dhamma'. 'Pertaining to the beginning of the holy life' means those things that are the beginning of the holy life of the path, that is, the practices that constitute the preliminary part. The rest is clear in all instances.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Dhammacetiyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Dhammacetiya Sutta is concluded.

10. Kaṇṇakatthalasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Kaṇṇakatthala Sutta.

375. Evaṃ [V 3.0254][P 3.0356] me sutanti kaṇṇakatthalasuttaṃ. Tattha uruññāyanti uruññāti tassa raṭṭhassapi nagarassapi etadeva nāmaṃ, bhagavā uruññānagaraṃ upanissāya viharati. Kaṇṇakatthale migadāyeti tassa nagarassa avidūre kaṇṇakatthalaṃ nāma eko ramaṇīyo bhūmibhāgo atthi, so migānaṃ abhayatthāya dinnattā migadāyoti vuccati, tasmiṃ kaṇṇakatthale migadāye. Kenacideva karaṇīyenāti na aññena, anantarasutte vuttakaraṇīyeneva. Somā ca bhaginī sakulā ca bhaginīti imā dve bhaginiyo rañño pajāpatiyo. Bhattābhihāreti bhattaṃ abhiharaṇaṭṭhāne. Rañño bhuñjanaṭṭhānañhi sabbāpi orodhā kaṭacchuādīni gahetvā rājānaṃ upaṭṭhātuṃ gacchanti, tāpi tatheva agamaṃsu.

375. 'Thus have I heard' begins the Kaṇṇakatthala Sutta. Therein, 'at Uruññā': Uruññā is the name of both that country and that city. The Blessed One was dwelling in dependence on the city of Uruññā. 'At Kaṇṇakatthala, the deer park': not far from that city, there is a delightful plot of land named Kaṇṇakatthala. Because it was given for the safety of the deer, it is called a deer park; it was in that Kaṇṇakatthala deer park. 'For some business or other': not for any other, but for the very business mentioned in the immediately preceding sutta. 'Sister Somā and Sister Sakulā': these two sisters were the king's consorts. 'At the presentation of the meal': at the place where food is brought. For at the king's eating place, all the women of the inner quarters, taking ladles and so forth, go to attend upon the king; they too came in that very same way.

376. Kiṃ pana, mahārājāti kasmā evamāha? Rañño garahaparimocanatthaṃ. Evañhi parisā cinteyya – “ayaṃ rājā āgacchamānova mātugāmānaṃ sāsanaṃ āroceti, mayaṃ attano dhammatāya bhagavantaṃ daṭṭhuṃ āgatoti maññāma, ayaṃ pana mātugāmānaṃ sāsanaṃ gahetvā āgato, mātugāmadāso maññe, esa pubbepi imināva kāraṇena āgacchatī”ti. Pucchito pana so attano āgamanakāraṇaṃ kathessati, evamassa ayaṃ garahā na uppajjissatīti garahamocanatthaṃ evamāha.

376. “But what is it, great king?”—why did he say this? To free the king from reproach. For if he had not asked, the assembly might think: “This king, just as he arrives, announces a message from the womenfolk. We thought he had come to see the Blessed One of his own accord, but he has come bringing a message from the womenfolk—a slave to women, it seems! Previously, too, he must have come for this very reason.” But when asked, he would state his reason for coming, and thus this reproach would not arise for him. To free him from reproach, he spoke thus.

378. Abbhudāhāsīti [M 3.0246] kathesi. Sakideva [P 3.0357] sabbaṃ ussati sabbaṃ dakkhitīti yo ekāvajjanena ekacittena atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ sabbaṃ ussati vā dakkhiti vā, so natthīti attho. Ekena hi cittena atītaṃ sabbaṃ jānissāmīti āvajjitvāpi atītaṃ sabbaṃ jānituṃ na sakkā, ekadesameva jānāti. Anāgatapaccuppannaṃ pana tena cittena sabbeneva sabbaṃ na jānātīti. Esa nayo itaresu. Evaṃ ekacittavasenāyaṃ pañho kathito. Heturūpanti hetusabhāvaṃ kāraṇajātikaṃ. Saheturūpanti sakāraṇajātikaṃ. Samparāyikāhaṃ, bhanteti samparāyaguṇaṃ ahaṃ, bhante, pucchāmi.

378. “Abbhudāhāsi” means he stated. As for “at one and the same time will know all, will see all”: the meaning is that there is no person who, with a single advertence, with a single mind, will know or will see everything of the past, future, and present. For even having adverted, “With a single mind I will know all of the past,” it is not possible to know all of the past; one knows only a part. Furthermore, with that same mind, one does not know all of the future and present in every way. This is the method in the other cases. Thus this question was stated in terms of a single mind. “Heturūpaṃ” means having the nature of a cause, being of the nature of a reason. “Saheturūpaṃ” means being of the nature of having a cause. “Samparāyikāhaṃ, bhante” means “I, venerable sir, ask about the quality concerning the future life.”

379. Pañcimānīti [V 3.0255] imasmiṃ sutte pañca padhāniyaṅgāni lokuttaramissakāni kathitāni. Kathinaṅgaṇavāsīcūḷasamuddatthero pana “tumhākaṃ, bhante, kiṃ ruccatī”ti vutte “mayhaṃ lokuttarānevāti ruccatī”ti āha. Padhānavemattatanti padhānanānattaṃ. Aññādisameva hi puthujjanassa padhānaṃ, aññādisaṃ sotāpannassa, aññādisaṃ sakadāgāmino, aññādisaṃ anāgāmino, aññādisaṃ arahato, aññādisaṃ asītimahāsāvakānaṃ, aññādisaṃ dvinnaṃ aggasāvakānaṃ, aññādisaṃ paccekabuddhānaṃ, aññādisaṃ sabbaññubuddhānaṃ. Puthujjanassa padhānaṃ sotāpannassa padhānaṃ na pāpuṇāti…pe… paccekabuddhassa padhānaṃ sabbaññubuddhassa padhānaṃ na pāpuṇāti. Imamatthaṃ sandhāya “padhānavemattataṃ vadāmī”ti āha. Dantakāraṇaṃ gaccheyyunti yaṃ akūṭakaraṇaṃ, anavacchindanaṃ[P 3.0358], dhurassa acchindananti dantesu kāraṇaṃ dissati, taṃ kāraṇaṃ upagaccheyyunti attho. Dantabhūminti dantehi gantabbabhūmiṃ. Assaddhotiādīsu puthujjanasotāpannasakadāgāmianāgāmino cattāropi assaddhā nāma. Puthujjano hi sotāpannassa saddhaṃ appattoti assaddho, sotāpanno sakadāgāmissa, sakadāgāmī anāgāmissa, anāgāmī arahato saddhaṃ appattoti assaddho, ābādho arahatopi uppajjatīti pañcapi bahvābādhā nāma honti. Ariyasāvakassa pana saṭho māyāvīti nāmaṃ natthi. Teneva thero – “pañca padhāniyaṅgāni lokuttarāni kathitānīti mayhaṃ ruccatī”ti āha. Assakhaḷuṅkasuttante pana – “tayo ca, bhikkhave, assakhaḷuṅke tayo ca purisakhaḷuṅke desessāmī”ti (a. ni. 3.141) ettha ariyasāvakassāpi sambodhināmaṃ āgataṃ[M 3.0247], tassa vasena lokuttaramissakā kathitāti vuttaṃ. Puthujjano pana sotāpattimaggavīriyaṃ asampatto…pe… anāgāmī arahattamaggavīriyaṃ asampattoti kusītopi assaddho viya cattārova honti, tathā duppañño.

379. As for “these five”: in this sutta, five factors of striving mixed with the supramundane are taught. However, the Elder Cūḷasamudda, the resident of Kathinaṅgaṇa, when asked, “Venerable sir, what is your preference?” said, “My preference is that they are purely supramundane.” “Padhānavemattataṃ” means the diversity of striving. For the striving of a worldling is of one kind, that of a stream-enterer is of another kind, that of a once-returner is of another kind, that of a non-returner is of another kind, that of an arahant is of another kind, that of the eighty great disciples is of another kind, that of the two chief disciples is of another kind, that of the paccekabuddhas is of another kind, and that of the all-knowing Buddhas is of another kind. The striving of a worldling does not reach the striving of a stream-enterer… (and so on) … the striving of a paccekabuddha does not reach the striving of an all-knowing Buddha. Referring to this meaning, he said, “I speak of the diversity of striving.” As for “they should go to the state of the tamed”: the meaning is that they should approach that state which is seen in the tamed, which is the state of not being crooked, not cutting off, not cutting off the yoke. “Dantabhūmiṃ” means the ground to be gone to by the tamed. In “faithless,” etc., the four—the worldling, the stream-enterer, the once-returner, and the non-returner—are all called “faithless.” For a worldling, not having attained the faith of a stream-enterer, is “faithless”; a stream-enterer, not having attained the faith of a once-returner; a once-returner, not having attained the faith of a non-returner; a non-returner, not having attained the faith of an arahant, is “faithless.” And since illness arises even for an arahant, all five are called “of many illnesses.” But for a noble disciple, there is no such name as “deceitful and fraudulent.” For that reason the Elder said, “My preference is that the five factors of striving are taught as purely supramundane.” But in the Assakhaḷuṅka Sutta, in the passage “Monks, I will teach the three untamed colts and the three untamed men,” the name “sambodhi” has come up even for a noble disciple, and on account of that, it is said that they are taught as mixed with the supramundane. Furthermore, a worldling has not attained the energy of the stream-entry path… (and so on) … a non-returner has not attained the energy of the path of arahantship; thus the “lazy” ones are also four in number, just like the “faithless”; likewise for the “unwise.”

Evaṃ panettha opammasaṃsandanaṃ veditabbaṃ – adantahatthiādayo viya hi maggapadhānarahito puggalo. Dantahatthiādayo viya maggapadhānavā. Yathā adantā hatthiādayo kūṭākāraṃ akatvā avicchinditvā dhuraṃ apātetvā dantagamanaṃ vā gantuṃ dantabhūmiṃ vā pattuṃ na sakkonti, evamevaṃ maggapadhānarahito maggapadhānavatā pattabbaṃ pāpuṇituṃ nibbattetabbaṃ guṇaṃ nibbattetuṃ na sakkoti. Yathā pana dantahatthiādayo kūṭākāraṃ akatvā avicchinditvā dhuraṃ apātetvā dantagamanaṃ vā gantuṃ dantabhūmiṃ vā pattuṃ sakkonti[P 3.0359], evamevaṃ maggapadhānavā maggapadhānavatā pattabbaṃ [V 3.0256] pāpuṇituṃ nibbattetabbaṃ guṇaṃ nibbattetuṃ sakkoti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “sotāpattimaggapadhānavā sotāpattimaggapadhānavatā pattokāsaṃ pāpuṇituṃ nibbattetabbaṃ guṇaṃ nibbattetuṃ sakkoti…pe… arahattamaggapadhānavā arahattamaggapadhānavatā pattokāsaṃ pāpuṇituṃ nibbattetabbaṃ guṇaṃ nibbattetuṃ sakkotī”ti.

Herein, the comparison of the simile should be understood thus: a person devoid of path-exertion is like an untamed elephant and so forth. A person possessing path-exertion is like a tamed elephant and so forth. Just as untamed elephants and so forth, without acting deceitfully, without breaking off, without casting off the yoke, are unable to go the way of the tamed or to reach the ground of the tamed, even so, a person devoid of path-exertion is unable to attain what is to be attained by one with path-exertion, or to bring into being the quality that is to be brought into being. But just as tamed elephants and so forth, without acting deceitfully, without breaking off, without casting off the yoke, are able to go the way of the tamed or to reach the ground of the tamed, even so, a person possessing path-exertion is able to attain what is to be attained by one with path-exertion, and to bring into being the quality that is to be brought into being. This is what is said: “One possessing the exertion of the stream-entry path is able to reach the state to be attained by one with the exertion of the stream-entry path, and to bring into being the quality that is to be brought into being… (and so on) … one possessing the exertion of the Arahantship path is able to reach the state to be attained by one with the exertion of the Arahantship path, and to bring into being the quality that is to be brought into being.”

380. Sammappadhānāti maggapadhānena sammappadhānā. Na kiñci nānākaraṇaṃ vadāmi yadidaṃ vimuttiyā vimuttinti yaṃ ekassa phalavimuttiyā itarassa phalavimuttiṃ ārabbha nānākaraṇaṃ vattabbaṃ siyā, taṃ na kiñci vadāmīti attho. Acciyā vā accinti acciyā vā accimhi. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo, bhummatthe hi etaṃ upayogavacanaṃ. Kiṃ pana tvaṃ, mahārājāti, mahārāja, kiṃ tvaṃ? “Santi devā cātumahārājikā, santi devā tāvatiṃsā…pe… santi devā paranimmitavasavattino, santi devā tatuttari”nti evaṃ devānaṃ atthibhāvaṃ na jānāsi, yena evaṃ vadesīti. Tato atthibhāvaṃ jānāmi, manussalokaṃ pana āgacchanti [P 3.0360] nāgacchantīti idaṃ pucchanto yadi vā te, bhantetiādimāha. Sabyābajjhāti sadukkhā, samucchedappahānena appahīnacetasikadukkhā. Āgantāroti upapattivasena āgantāro. Abyābajjhāti samucchinnadukkhā. Anāgantāroti upapattivasena anāgantāro.

380. 'Right efforts' means they are of equal exertion by means of path-exertion. 'I declare no distinction whatsoever with regard to liberation from liberation' means: whatever distinction might be stated concerning the fruition-liberation of one person and the fruition-liberation of another, I declare no such distinction whatsoever; this is the meaning. 'By a flame or in a flame' means 'by a flame' (instrumental) or 'in a flame' (locative). In the remaining two phrases, this is the same method, for this is an accusative case-ending used in the sense of the locative. 'But what of you, great king?' means: 'Great king, what of you? Do you not know of the existence of the gods, that you speak thus, saying: "There are the Cātumahārājika devas, there are the Tāvatiṃsa devas... and so on... there are the Paranimmitavasavattī devas, there are devas beyond that"?' Therefore, [the king, thinking,] 'I know of their existence, but do they come to the human world or not?' and asking this, said, 'Or, venerable sir...' and so on. 'With affliction' means with suffering, with mental suffering not yet abandoned by eradication. 'Comers' means they are comers by way of rebirth. 'Without affliction' means with suffering completely cut off. 'Non-comers' means they are non-comers by way of rebirth.

381. Pahotīti [M 3.0248] sakkoti. Rājā hi puññavantampi lābhasakkārasampannaṃ yathā na koci upasaṅkamati, evaṃ karonto tamhā ṭhānā cāvetuṃ sakkoti. Taṃ apuññavantampi sakalagāmaṃ piṇḍāya caritvā yāpanamattaṃ alabhantaṃ yathā lābhasakkārasampanno hoti, evaṃ karonto tamhā ṭhānā cāvetuṃ sakkoti. Brahmacariyavantampi itthīhi saddhiṃ sampayojetvā sīlavināsaṃ pāpento balakkārena vā uppabbājento tamhā ṭhānā cāvetuṃ sakkoti. Abrahmacariyavantampi sampannakāmaguṇaṃ amaccaṃ bandhanāgāraṃ pavesetvā itthīnaṃ mukhampi passituṃ adento tamhā ṭhānā cāveti nāma. Raṭṭhato pana yaṃ icchati, taṃ pabbājeti nāma.

381. 'Is capable' means is able. For a king is able to displace from his position even a meritorious person endowed with gain and honor by acting in such a way that no one approaches him. He is able to displace from his state even an unmeritorious person who, having wandered the entire village for alms, does not receive enough to subsist on, by acting in such a way that he becomes endowed with gain and honor. He is able to displace from his state even one who lives the holy life by associating him with women and causing the destruction of his virtue, or by forcibly disrobing him. And a minister who does not live the holy life but is endowed with sense-pleasures, the king is said to displace from that state by having him enter a prison and not allowing him to even see the faces of women. Furthermore, whomever he wishes, he is said to banish from the country.

Dassanāyapi nappahontīti kāmāvacare tāva abyābajjhe deve sabyābajjhā devā cakkhuviññāṇadassanāyapi nappahonti. Kasmā? Arahato tattha ṭhānābhāvato. Rūpāvacare pana ekavimānasmiṃyeva tiṭṭhanti ca nisīdanti cāti cakkhuviññāṇadassanāya pahonti, etehi diṭṭhaṃ [V 3.0257] pana sallakkhitaṃ paṭividdhaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ daṭṭhuṃ sallakkhituṃ paṭivijjhituṃ [P 3.0361] na sakkontīti ñāṇacakkhunā dassanāya nappahonti, uparideve ca cakkhuviññāṇadassanenāpīti.

'They are not capable even of seeing' means: in the sense-sphere, to begin with, the devas with affliction are not capable of seeing the devas without affliction even with the seeing of eye-consciousness. Why? Because there is no standing-place for an Arahant there. In the form-sphere, however, since they stand and sit in the very same celestial mansion, they are capable of seeing with the seeing of eye-consciousness. But they are not able to see, mark, or penetrate the characteristic seen, marked, and penetrated by these [unafflicted devas]; thus they are not capable of seeing with the eye of knowledge. And they are not capable of seeing the devas in the higher realms even with the seeing of eye-consciousness.

382. Ko nāmo ayaṃ, bhanteti rājā theraṃ jānantopi ajānanto viya pucchati. Kasmā? Pasaṃsitukāmatāya. Ānandarūpoti ānandasabhāvo. Brahmapucchāpi vuttanayeneva veditabbā. Atha kho aññataro purisoti sā kira kathā viṭaṭūbheneva kathitā, te “tayā kathitā, tayā kathitā”ti kupitā aññamaññaṃ imasmiṃyeva ṭhāne attano attano balakāyaṃ uṭṭhāpetvā kalahampi kareyyunti nivāraṇatthaṃ so rājapuriso etadavoca. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānameva. Ayaṃ pana desanā neyyapuggalassa vasena niṭṭhitāti.

382. 'What is this one's name, venerable sir?' The king, though knowing the Elder, asked as if not knowing. Why? From a desire to praise him. 'Of delightful form' means of a delightful nature. The question about Brahmā should also be understood in the way that has been stated. 'Then a certain man': it seems that story was told by Viṭaṭūbha himself. To prevent them—[Viṭaṭūbha and the other man]—from becoming angry and saying to each other, "You said it!", "You said it!", and then, right in this place, raising their respective armies and starting a quarrel, that royal man said this. The rest is clear everywhere. This discourse, however, was concluded for the sake of a person to be guided.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Middle Length Discourses.

Kaṇṇakatthalasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Kaṇṇakatthala Sutta is concluded.

Catutthavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Fourth Chapter is concluded.

5. Brāhmaṇavaggo

5. The Brahmin Chapter

1. Brahmāyusuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Brahmāyu Sutta

383. Evaṃ [V 3.0258][M 3.0249] me sutanti brahmāyusuttaṃ. Tattha mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhinti mahatāti guṇamahattenapi mahatā, saṅkhyāmahattenapi. So hi bhikkhusaṅghe guṇehipi mahā ahosi appicchatādiguṇasamannāgatattā, saṅkhyāyapi mahā pañcasatasaṅkhyattā. Bhikkhūnaṃ saṅghena bhikkhusaṅghena, diṭṭhisīlasāmaññasaṅghātasaṅkhātena samaṇagaṇenāti attho. Saddhinti ekato. Pañcamattehi bhikkhusatehīti pañca mattā etesanti pañcamattāni. Mattāti pamāṇaṃ vuccati, tasmā yathā bhojane [P 3.0362] mattaññūti vutte bhojane mattaṃ jānāti pamāṇaṃ jānātīti attho hoti, evamidhāpi tesaṃ bhikkhusatānaṃ pañcamattā pañcapamāṇanti evamattho daṭṭhabbo. Bhikkhūnaṃ satāni bhikkhusatāni. Tehi pañcamattehi bhikkhusatehi.

383. Thus have I heard—this is the Brahmāyu Sutta. Therein, regarding 'with a great assembly of bhikkhus': 'great' means great in terms of virtue and also great in terms of number. For that assembly of bhikkhus was great in virtues, as they were endowed with qualities such as having few desires, and it was also great in number, as they numbered five hundred. 'With an assembly of bhikkhus' means with a group of ascetics designated as a community by their commonality of view and virtue. 'With' (`saddhiṃ`) means together. Regarding 'with five-measured hundreds of bhikkhus' (`pañcamattehi bhikkhusatehi`): 'five measures are theirs' (`pañca mattā etesaṃ`), hence they are `pañcamattāni`. The word `mattā` means 'measure' (`pamāṇaṃ`). Therefore, just as when it is said 'one who knows the measure in food' (`bhojane mattaññū`), it means one who knows the measure or quantity, so too here, for those hundreds of bhikkhus, 'five-measured' means having a measure of five. This is how the meaning should be understood. 'Hundreds of bhikkhus' (`bhikkhusatāni`) are hundreds of bhikkhus. With those five-measured hundreds of bhikkhus.

Vīsavassasatikoti vīsādhikavassasatiko. Tiṇṇaṃ vedānanti iruvedayajuvedasāmavedānaṃ. Oṭṭhapahatakaraṇavasena pāraṃ gatoti pāragū. Saha nighaṇḍunā ca keṭubhena ca sanighaṇḍukeṭubhānaṃ, nighaṇḍūti nāmanighaṇṭurukkhādīnaṃ vevacanappakāsakaṃ satthaṃ. Keṭubhanti kiriyākappavikappo kavīnaṃ upakārāya satthaṃ. Saha akkharappabhedena sakkharappabhedānaṃ. Akkharappabhedoti sikkhā ca nirutti ca. Itihāsapañcamānanti āthabbaṇavedaṃ catutthaṃ katvā “itiha āsa itiha āsā”ti īdisavacanappaṭisaṃyutto purāṇakathāsaṅkhāto itihāso pañcamo etesanti itihāsapañcamā, tesaṃ itihāsapañcamānaṃ. Padañca tadavasesañca byākaraṇaṃ adhīyati pavedeti cāti padako veyyākaraṇo. Lokāyataṃ vuccati vitaṇḍavādasatthaṃ. Mahāpurisalakkhaṇanti [P 3.0363] mahāpurisānaṃ buddhādīnaṃ lakkhaṇadīpakaṃ dvādasasahassaganthappamāṇaṃ satthaṃ, yattha soḷasasahassagāthāparimāṇāya [V 3.0259] buddhamantā nāma ahesuṃ, yesaṃ vasena “iminā lakkhaṇena samannāgatā buddhā nāma honti, iminā paccekabuddhā nāma honti, iminā dve aggasāvakā, asītimahāsāvakā, buddhamātā, buddhapitā, aggupaṭṭhāko, aggupaṭṭhāyikā, rājā cakkavattī”ti ayaṃ viseso [M 3.0250] ñāyati. Anavayoti imesu lokāyatamahāpurisalakkhaṇesu anūno paripūrakārī, avayo na hotīti vuttaṃ hoti. Avayo nāma yo tāni atthato ca ganthato ca sandhāretuṃ na sakkoti. Assosi khotiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ siyā, taṃ sāleyyakasutte (ma. ni. 1.439 ādayo) vuttameva.

'One hundred and twenty years old' (`vīsavassasatiko`) means one hundred years plus twenty. 'Of the three Vedas' (`tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ`) means of the Irubeda (Ṛgveda), Yajubeda (Yajurveda), and Sāmaveda. 'One who has gone to the far shore' (`pāragū`) means one who has gone to the far shore by means of the striking of the lips. 'With the Nighaṇḍu and Keṭubha' (`sanighaṇḍukeṭubhānaṃ`): `nighaṇḍu` is the name of a treatise that explains the synonyms for things like trees. `keṭubha` is a treatise for the benefit of poets concerning the arrangement and modification of rites. 'With the analysis of syllables' (`sakkharappabhedānaṃ`): 'analysis of syllables' (`akkharappabhedo`) means phonetics (`sikkhā`) and etymology (`nirutti`). 'With the Itihāsa as the fifth' (`itihāsapañcamānaṃ`): making the Āthabbana Veda the fourth, the Itihāsa—a collection of ancient stories connected with sayings like 'thus it was' (`iti ha āsa`)—is the fifth of these. 'A master of words and a grammarian' (`padako veyyākaraṇo`): he studies and makes known the words (`pada`) and the grammar (`byākaraṇa`). 'Lokāyata' is the name for the treatise on sophistry (`vitaṇḍavādasatthaṃ`). 'The marks of a great man' (`mahāpurisalakkhaṇaṃ`) refers to a treatise of twelve thousand sections that illuminates the marks of great men such as the Buddhas. In it, there were sixteen thousand verses of what are called Buddha-mantras, by means of which this distinction is known: 'Those endowed with this mark are called Buddhas; with this, Paccekabuddhas; with this, the two chief disciples, the eighty great disciples, the Buddha's mother, the Buddha's father, the chief male attendant, the chief female attendant, and a wheel-turning king.' 'Not deficient' (`anavayo`) means he is not lacking in these treatises on Lokāyata and the marks of a great man; he is one who fulfills them completely. He is not deficient (`avayo`), is what is said. A deficient person (`avayo`) is one who is unable to retain those treatises in terms of both meaning and text. As for what should be said regarding 'He heard, indeed...' and so on, that has already been stated in the Sāleyyaka Sutta.

384. Ayaṃ tātāti ayaṃ mahallakatāya gantuṃ asakkonto māṇavaṃ āmantetvā evamāha. Apica esa brāhmaṇo cintesi “imasmiṃ loke ‘ahaṃ buddho ahaṃ buddho’ti uggatassa nāmaṃ gahetvā bahū janā vicaranti, tasmā na me anussavamatteneva upasaṅkamituṃ yuttaṃ. Ekaccañhi upasaṅkamantassa apakkamanampi garu hoti, anatthopi uppajjati. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ mama antevāsikaṃ pesetvā ‘buddho vā no vā’ti jānitvā upasaṅkameyya”nti tasmā māṇavaṃ āmantetvā “ayaṃ tātā”tiādimāha. Taṃ bhavantanti tassa bhavato. Tathā santaṃyevāti tathā satoyeva. Idañhi itthambhūtākhyānatthe upayogavacanaṃ. Yathā [P 3.0364] kathaṃ panāhaṃ, bhoti ettha kathaṃ panāhaṃ, bho, taṃ bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ jānissāmi, yathā sakkā so ñātuṃ, tathā me ācikkhāti attho. Yathāti vā nipātamattamevetaṃ. Kathanti ayaṃ ākārapucchā, kenākārenāhaṃ bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ jānissāmīti attho.

384. 'This, dear one...' (`ayaṃ tāta`): This one, being unable to go on account of old age, addressed the young man and spoke thus. Moreover, this brahmin thought: 'In this world, many people wander about, taking up the name of a famous person and saying, "I am a Buddha, I am a Buddha." Therefore, it is not proper for me to approach based merely on hearsay. For one who approaches a certain person, even having to retreat is burdensome, and disadvantage can also arise. What if I were to send my resident pupil, find out whether he is a Buddha or not, and then approach?' Therefore, he addressed the young man and said, 'This, dear one...' and so on. 'That venerable one' (`taṃ bhavantaṃ`) means 'of that venerable one' (`tassa bhavato`). 'Just as he truly is' (`tathā santaṃ yeva`) means 'being truly thus' (`tathā sato yeva`). This is a term in the accusative case used to describe a state. Regarding 'But how, sir, shall I...?' (`yathā kathaṃ panāhaṃ bho`): the meaning is, 'But how, sir, shall I know that venerable Gotama? In what way it is possible to know him, please explain to me.' Alternatively, `yathā` is merely a particle. `kathaṃ` is a question about the manner. The meaning is: 'In what manner shall I know the venerable Gotama?'

Evaṃ vutte kira naṃ upajjhāyo – “kiṃ tvaṃ, tāta, pathaviyaṃ ṭhito pathaviṃ na passāmīti viya candimasūriyānaṃ obhāse ṭhito candimasūriye na passāmīti viya vadasī”tiādīni vatvā jānanākāraṃ dassento āgatāni kho tātātiādimāha. Tattha mantesūti vedesu. Tathāgato kira uppajjissatīti paṭikacceva suddhāvāsā devā vedesu lakkhaṇāni pakkhipitvā “buddhamantā nāma ete”ti brāhmaṇavesena vede vācenti “tadanusārena mahesakkhā sattā tathāgataṃ jānissantī”ti. Tena pubbe vedesu mahāpurisalakkhaṇāni āgacchanti. Parinibbute pana tathāgate anukkamena antaradhāyanti, tena etarahi natthi. Mahāpurisassāti paṇidhisamādānañāṇakaruṇādiguṇamahato purisassa. Dveyeva gatiyoti dve eva niṭṭhā[V 3.0260]. Kāmañcāyaṃ gatisaddo – “pañca kho imā[M 3.0251], sāriputta, gatiyo”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.153) bhavabhede vattati, “gati migānaṃ pavana”ntiādīsu (pari. 339) nivāsaṭṭhāne, “evaṃ adhimattagatimanto”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.161) paññāya, “gatigata”ntiādīsu visaṭabhāve, idha pana niṭṭhāyaṃ vattatīti veditabbo. Tattha kiñcāpi yehi samannāgato [P 3.0365] rājā hoti, na teheva buddho hoti, jātisāmaññato pana tāniyeva tānīti vuccanti. Tena vuttaṃ – “yehi samannāgatassā”ti. Sace agāraṃ ajjhāvasatīti yadi agāre vasati, rājā hoti cakkavattī. Catūhi acchariyadhammehi saṅgahavatthūhi ca lokaṃ rañjanato rājā. Cakkaratanaṃ vatteti, catūhi sampatticakkehi vatteti, tehi ca paraṃ vatteti, parahitāya ca iriyāpathacakkānaṃ vatto etasmiṃ atthīti cakkavattī. Ettha ca rājāti sāmaññaṃ, cakkavattīti visesanaṃ. Dhammena caratīti dhammiko, ñāyena samena vattatīti attho. Dhammena rajjaṃ labhitvā rājā jātoti dhammarājā. Parahitadhammakaraṇena vā dhammiko, attahitadhammakaraṇena dhammarājā. Caturantāya issaroti cāturanto, catusamuddantāya catubbidhadīpabhūsitāya ca pathaviyā issaroti attho. Ajjhattaṃ kopādipaccatthike bahiddhā ca sabbarājāno vijesīti vijitāvī. Janapadatthāvariyappattoti janapade thāvarabhāvaṃ dhuvabhāvaṃ patto, na sakkā kenaci cāletuṃ, janapado vā tamhi thāvariyappatto anussukko sakammanirato acalo asampavedhīti janapadatthāvariyappatto. Seyyathidanti nipāto, tassa tāni katamānīti attho. Cakkaratanantiādīsu cakkañca taṃ ratijananatthena ratanañcāti cakkaratanaṃ. Eseva nayo sabbattha.

When this was said, his preceptor replied, it is said: 'Why, my son, do you speak as if, standing on the earth, you do not see the earth, or as if, standing in the light of the moon and sun, you do not see the moon and sun?' Having said this and showing the manner of knowing, he spoke the words beginning with 'These, my son, have come.' Therein, 'in the mantras' means in the Vedas. It is said that the Tathāgata will arise. Indeed, beforehand, the Suddhāvāsa devas inserted the characteristics into the Vedas, proclaiming them as 'Buddha-mantras' in the guise of brahmins, so that 'beings of great power may recognize the Tathāgata accordingly.' Thus, the marks of a Great Man appeared in the Vedas in the past. However, after the Tathāgata’s Parinibbāna, they gradually disappear, which is why they are not found now. 'Of a Great Man' refers to a man great through qualities such as aspiration, undertaking, knowledge, and compassion. 'Only two destinies' means precisely two outcomes. Although this word 'gati' is used in various senses such as a state of existence, a dwelling place, wisdom, and soundlessness, here it should be understood as referring to an outcome. Therein, although one endowed with certain marks becomes a king, he does not with those same marks become a Buddha; yet, due to the commonality of the class of marks, the very same ones are spoken of as those. Hence it is said, 'for one endowed with which.' If he lives the household life, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch. A king (rājā) delights (rañjeti) the world with the four marvelous qualities and the four bases of sympathy. He is a wheel-turner (cakkavattī) because he turns the wheel-gem; he turns with the four wheels of prosperity; with them he turns others; and in him there is the turning of the wheels of the postures for the welfare of others. And here, 'king' is a general term, and 'wheel-turner' is a specific one. 'He acts by Dhamma' means he is righteous (dhammiko), meaning he acts with justice and fairness. Having obtained kingship by Dhamma, he has become a king, thus he is a righteous king (dhammarājā). Or, he is righteous (dhammiko) by acting for the welfare of others, and a righteous king (dhammarājā) by acting for his own welfare. 'Lord of the four ends' makes him one whose rule extends to the four quarters (cāturanto), meaning he is the lord of the earth bounded by the four oceans and adorned with the four great continents. He has conquered (vijesī) internal enemies such as anger and all external kings, thus he is a conqueror (vijitāvī). 'He has attained the stability of the country' means he has attained a state of stability and permanence in the country, unshakable by anyone; or, the country under him has attained stability—untroubled, devoted to its own work, unshaken, and undisturbed—thus, he has attained the stability of the country. 'Seyyathidaṃ' is a particle meaning 'which are those?' In 'wheel-gem' and so on, it is both a wheel and a gem (ratana) because it generates delight (rati), thus it is a wheel-gem (cakkaratana). This same method applies everywhere.

Imesu [P 3.0366] pana ratanesu ayaṃ cakkavattirājā cakkaratanena ajitaṃ jināti, hatthiassaratanehi vijite yathāsukhaṃ anuvicarati, pariṇāyakaratanena vijitamanurakkhati, sesehi upabhogasukhamanubhavati. Paṭhamena cassa ussāhasattiyogo, hatthiassagahapatiratanehi pabhusattiyogo, pacchimena mantasattiyogo suparipuṇṇo hoti, itthimaṇiratanehi tividhasattiyogaphalaṃ. So itthimaṇiratanehi bhogasukhamanubhavati, sesehi [M 3.0252] issariyasukhaṃ. Visesato cassa purimāni tīṇi adosakusalamūlajanitakammānubhāvena sampajjanti, majjhimāni alobhakusalamūlajanitakammānubhāvena, pacchimamekaṃ amohakusalamūlajanitakammānubhāvenāti veditabbaṃ. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana bojjhaṅgasaṃyutte [V 3.0261] ratanasuttassa (saṃ. ni. 5.222-223) upadesato gahetabbo. Apica bālapaṇḍitasuttepi (ma. ni. 3.255) imesaṃ ratanānaṃ uppattikkamena saddhiṃ vaṇṇanā āgamissati.

Furthermore, concerning these gems, this wheel-turning monarch conquers the unconquered with the wheel-gem. With the elephant and horse gems, he roams at will through the conquered territories. He protects his conquests with the heir-apparent gem, and enjoys the pleasure of consumption with the remaining gems. Through the first gem, he is endowed with the power of initiative; through the elephant, horse, and householder gems, with the power of sovereignty; and through the last gem, his endowment with the power of counsel becomes fully complete. Through the woman and jewel gems, he experiences the fruit of the endowment of these three powers. He enjoys the pleasure of consumption through the woman and jewel gems, and the pleasure of sovereignty through the others. Specifically, it should be understood that the first three gems arise through the power of kamma generated by the wholesome root of non-hatred; the middle ones—the woman, jewel, and householder gems—arise through the power of kamma generated by the wholesome root of non-greed; and the last one, the heir-apparent gem, arises through the power of kamma generated by the wholesome root of non-delusion. This is the summary here; the detailed explanation should be taken from the instruction in the Ratana Sutta of the Bojjhaṅga Saṃyutta. Moreover, a description together with the order of arising of these gems will also be found in the Bālapaṇḍita Sutta.

Parosahassanti atirekasahassaṃ. Sūrāti abhīrukajātikā. Vīraṅgarūpāti devaputtasadisakāyā, evaṃ tāva eke vaṇṇayanti, ayaṃ panettha sabhāvo – vīrāti uttamasūrā vuccanti. Vīrānaṃ aṅgaṃ vīraṅgaṃ, vīrakāraṇaṃ vīriyanti vuttaṃ hoti. Vīraṅgaṃ rūpaṃ etesanti vīraṅgarūpā, vīriyamayasarīrā viyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Parasenappamaddanāti [P 3.0367] sace paṭimukhaṃ tiṭṭheyya parasenā, taṃ maddituṃ samatthāti adhippāyo. Dhammenāti “pāṇo na hantabbo”tiādinā pañcasīladhammena.

'More than a thousand' means exceeding a thousand. 'Valiant' (sūrā) means those of a fearless nature. 'Of heroic form' (vīraṅgarūpā) means having bodies like those of devaputtas; thus do some explain it. But here is the intrinsic meaning: 'heroes' (vīrā) refers to the most excellent valiant ones. The 'constituent' (aṅga) of heroes is vīraṅga; it is said that the cause of heroism is energy (vīriya). They have a form (rūpa) that is of this heroic constituent (vīraṅga), therefore they are 'of heroic form' (vīraṅgarūpā); it is said they are as if having bodies made of energy. 'Crushers of others' armies' means that if another's army were to stand opposing them, the intention is that they are capable of crushing it. 'By the Dhamma' means by the Dhamma of the five precepts beginning with 'a living being is not to be killed.'

Arahaṃ hoti sammāsambuddho loke vivaṭṭacchadoti ettha rāgadosamohamānadiṭṭhiavijjāduccaritachadanehi sattahi paṭicchanne kilesandhakāraloke taṃ chadanaṃ vivaṭṭetvā samantato sañjātāloko hutvā ṭhitoti vivaṭṭacchado. Tattha paṭhamena padena pūjārahatā, dutiyena tassā hetu yasmā sammāsambuddhoti, tatiyena buddhattahetubhūtā vivaṭṭacchadatā vuttāti veditabbā. Atha vā vivaṭṭo ca vicchado cāti vivaṭṭacchado, vaṭṭarahito chadanarahito cāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tena arahaṃ vaṭṭābhāvena, sammāsambuddho chadanābhāvenāti evaṃ purimapadadvayasseva hetudvayaṃ vuttaṃ hoti. Dutiyavesārajjena cettha purimasiddhi, paṭhamena dutiyasiddhi, tatiyacatutthehi tatiyasiddhi hoti. Purimañca dhammacakkhuṃ, dutiyaṃ buddhacakkhuṃ, tatiyaṃ samantacakkhuṃ sādhetītipi veditabbaṃ. Tvaṃ mantānaṃ paṭiggahetāti imināssa sūrabhāvaṃ janeti.

Regarding the text: 'He is an Arahant, a Sammāsambuddha in the world, one with the covering rolled back.' Herein, in the world which is a dark abode of defilements, covered by the seven coverings—greed, hatred, delusion, conceit, wrong view, ignorance, and misconduct—having rolled back that covering, he stands, having become one with light arisen all around; therefore, he is called 'one with the covering rolled back.' Therein, by the first term, worthiness of offerings is stated; by the second, the cause for that worthiness, because he is a Sammāsambuddha; by the third, the state of having the covering rolled back, which is the cause of Buddhahood, is stated—thus it should be known. Alternatively, he is free from the round of rebirth (vivaṭṭa) and free from the covering (vicchada), thus he is 'one free from the round of rebirth and the covering.' It is meant that he is without the round of rebirth and without the covering. Due to that absence of the round of rebirth, he is an Arahant; due to the absence of the covering, he is a Sammāsambuddha. Thus, the pair of causes for the preceding two terms is stated. Herein, by the second ground of self-confidence, the accomplishment of the first term is established; by the first, the accomplishment of the second is established; by the third and fourth, the accomplishment of the third is established. And it should also be known that the first term accomplishes the Dhamma-eye, the second the Buddha-eye, and the third the all-seeing eye. By this phrase, 'You are the recipient of the sacred texts,' it generates his heroic nature.

385. Sopi tāya ācariyakathāya lakkhaṇesu vigatasammoho ekobhāsajāto viya buddhamante sampassamāno evaṃ, bhoti āha. Tassattho – yathā, bho, maṃ tvaṃ vadasi, evaṃ karissāmīti. Samannesīti [P 3.0368] gavesi, ekaṃ dveti vā gaṇayanto samānayi. Addasā khoti [M 3.0253] kathaṃ addasa? Buddhānañhi nisinnānaṃ vā nipannānaṃ vā koci lakkhaṇaṃ pariyesituṃ na sakkoti, ṭhitānaṃ pana caṅkamantānaṃ vā sakkoti. Tasmā lakkhaṇapariyesanatthaṃ āgataṃ disvā buddhā uṭṭhāyāsanā tiṭṭhanti vā caṅkamaṃ vā adhiṭṭhahanti. Iti lakkhaṇadassanānurūpe iriyāpathe vattamānassa [V 3.0262] addasa. Yebhuyyenāti pāyena, bahukāni addasa, appāni na addasāti attho. Tato yāni na addasa, tesaṃ dīpanatthaṃ vuttaṃ ṭhapetvā dveti. Kaṅkhatīti “aho vata passeyya”nti patthanaṃ uppādeti. Vicikicchatīti tato tato tāni vicinanto kicchati na sakkoti daṭṭhuṃ. Nādhimuccatīti tāya vicikicchāya sanniṭṭhānaṃ na gacchati. Na sampasīdatīti tato “paripuṇṇalakkhaṇo aya”nti bhagavati pasādaṃ nāpajjati. Kaṅkhāya vā dubbalā vimati vuttā, vicikicchāya majjhimā, anadhimuccanatāya balavatī, asampasādena tehi tīhi dhammehi cittassa kālussiyabhāvo. Kosohiteti vatthikosena paṭicchanne. Vatthaguyheti aṅgajāte. Bhagavato hi vāraṇasseva kosohitavatthaguyhaṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ padumagabbhasamānaṃ, taṃ so vatthapaṭicchannattā, antomukhagatāya [P 3.0369] ca jivhāya pahūtabhāvaṃ asallakkhento tesu dvīsu lakkhaṇesu kaṅkhī ahosi vicikicchī.

385. He too, by that speech of his teacher, having his confusion regarding the marks dispelled and perceiving the Buddha's sacred knowledge as if a single light had arisen, said, 'So it is, sir.' Its meaning is: 'Sir, just as you tell me, so I will do.' 'He investigated' means he searched; counting 'one,' 'two,' thus he compared them. 'He indeed saw.' How did he see? For no one is able to investigate the marks of Buddhas who are sitting or lying down, but one is able to do so for those who are standing or walking. Therefore, seeing one who has come to investigate the marks, Buddhas, rising from their seats, either stand or undertake walking meditation. Thus, he saw the marks of the Blessed One, who was engaged in a posture suitable for seeing them. 'For the most part' means mostly; the meaning is that he saw many marks, but did not see a few. Then, to show those which he did not see, it is said, 'except for two.' 'He doubts' means he gives rise to the aspiration, 'Oh, that I might see!' 'He is perplexed' means, while investigating them here and there, he becomes weary and is not able to see. 'He is not convinced' means, due to that perplexity, he does not arrive at a conclusion. 'He does not become serene' means, because of that, he does not attain confidence in the Blessed One, thinking, 'This one has the complete marks.' Alternatively, by 'doubt,' a weak uncertainty is meant; by 'perplexity,' a medium one; by 'non-conviction,' a strong one; by 'non-serenity,' the state of the mind's turbidity is meant. 'Concealed in a sheath' means concealed in a fleshy sheath. 'Private parts' means the male organ. For the Blessed One's male organ, concealed in a sheath like that of a royal elephant, is of golden hue, similar to the pericarp of a lotus. He, not perceiving that organ due to its being covered by the robe, and the great extent of the tongue due to its being inside the mouth, became doubtful and perplexed about those two marks.

Atha kho bhagavāti atha bhagavā cintesi – “sacāhaṃ imassa etāni dve lakkhaṇāni na dassessāmi, nikkaṅkho na bhavissati. Etassa kaṅkhāya sati ācariyopissa nikkaṅkho na bhavissati, atha maṃ dassanāya na āgamissati, anāgato dhammaṃ na sossati, dhammaṃ asuṇanto tīṇi sāmaññaphalāni na sacchikarissati. Etasmiṃ pana nikkaṅkhe ācariyopissa nikkaṅkho maṃ upasaṅkamitvā dhammaṃ sutvā tīṇi sāmaññaphalāni sacchikarissati. Etadatthaṃyeva ca mayā pāramiyo pūritā. Dassessāmissa tāni lakkhaṇānī”ti.

Then the Blessed One thought: 'If I do not show this one these two marks, he will not become free from doubt. While he has doubt, his teacher also will not become free from doubt. Then he will not come to see me. Not having come, he will not hear the Dhamma. Not hearing the Dhamma, he will not realize the three lower fruits of recluseship. But when this one is free from doubt, his teacher also, being free from doubt, will approach me, hear the Dhamma, and realize the three lower fruits of recluseship. It is for this very purpose that the perfections were fulfilled by me. I will show him those marks.'

Tathārūpaṃ iddhābhisaṅkhāramakāsi. Kathaṃrūpaṃ? Kimettha aññena vattabbaṃ? Vuttametaṃ nāgasenatthereneva milindaraññā puṭṭhena –

He performed a psychic feat of such a kind. What kind? What more needs to be said here? This was stated by the Elder Nāgasena himself when questioned by King Milinda—

Āha ca dukkaraṃ, bhante nāgasena, bhagavatā katanti. Kiṃ mahārājāti? Mahājanena hirikaraṇokāsaṃ brahmāyubrāhmaṇassa ca antevāsiuttarassa ca bāvariyassa antevāsīnaṃ soḷasabrāhmaṇānañca selassa ca brāhmaṇassa antevāsīnaṃ tisatamāṇavānañca dassesi, bhanteti. Na, mahārāja, bhagavā guyhaṃ [M 3.0254] dasseti, chāyaṃ bhagavā dasseti, iddhiyā abhisaṅkharitvā nivāsananivatthaṃ kāyabandhanabaddhaṃ cīvarapārutaṃ chāyārūpakamattaṃ dassesi mahārājāti. Chāyaṃ diṭṭhe sati [V 3.0263] diṭṭhoyeva. Nanu, bhanteti? Tiṭṭhatetaṃ, mahārāja, hadayarūpaṃ disvā bujjhanakasatto bhaveyya, hadayamaṃsaṃ [P 3.0370] nīharitvā dasseyya sammāsambuddhoti. Kallosi, bhante nāgasenāti.

And he said, 'Venerable Nāgasena, a difficult thing was done by the Blessed One.' 'What, great king?' 'Venerable sir, before a great assembly, he showed a cause for shame to Brahmāyu the brahmin and his disciple Uttara, to the sixteen brahmin disciples of Bāvari, and to the three hundred young men, disciples of Sela the brahmin.' 'No, great king, the Blessed One does not show his private part; the Blessed One shows an illusory image. Great king, having fashioned it by psychic power, he showed merely an illusory form, wearing the lower robe, bound with a belt, and draped in the outer robe.' 'Venerable sir, when an image is seen, it is indeed seen, is it not?' 'Let that be, great king. If there were a being capable of awakening by seeing the physical heart, the Sammāsambuddha would extract his heart-flesh and show it.' 'You are clever, venerable Nāgasena.'

Ninnāmetvāti nīharitvā. Anumasīti kathinasūciṃ viya katvā anumajji. Tathā karaṇena cettha mudubhāvo, kaṇṇasotānumasanena dīghabhāvo, nāsikasotānumasanena tanubhāvo, nalāṭacchādanena puthulabhāvo pakāsitoti veditabbo. Ubhopi kaṇṇasotānītiādīsu cettha buddhānaṃ kaṇṇasotesu malaṃ vā jallikā vā natthi, dhovitvā ṭhapitarajatapanāḷikā viya honti, tathā nāsikasotesu, tānipi hi suparikammakatakañcanapanāḷikā viya ca maṇipanāḷikā viya ca honti. Tasmā jivhaṃ nīharitvā kathinasūciṃ viya katvā mukhapariyante upasaṃharanto dakkhiṇakaṇṇasotaṃ pavesetvā tato nīharitvā vāmakaṇṇasotaṃ pavesesi, tato nīharitvā dakkhiṇanāsikasotaṃ pavesetvā tato nīharitvā vāmanāsikasotaṃ pavesesi, tato nīharitvā puthulabhāvaṃ dassento rattavalāhakena aḍḍhacandaṃ viya ca suvaṇṇapattaṃ viya ca rattakambalapaṭalena vijjujotasadisāya jivhāya kevalakappaṃ nalāṭamaṇḍalaṃ paṭicchādesi.

‘Having extended’ means having drawn it out. ‘He stroked’ means having made it like a firm needle, he stroked it repeatedly. And here, by that action, its softness was revealed; by stroking the ear canals, its length was revealed; by stroking the nasal passages, its thinness was revealed; and by covering the forehead, its breadth was revealed—thus it should be understood. And here, in phrases such as ‘both ear canals,’ there is no dirt or grime in the ear canals of the Buddhas; they are like silver tubes that have been washed and set down. Similarly for the nasal passages, for they are indeed like well-wrought golden tubes and like jeweled tubes. Therefore, having extended his tongue, making it like a firm needle and bringing it to the edge of his mouth, he inserted it into the right ear canal, and drawing it out from there, he inserted it into the left ear canal. Drawing it out from there, he inserted it into the right nasal passage, and drawing it out from there, he inserted it into the left nasal passage. Drawing it out from there, wishing to show its breadth, just as a red cloud might cover a half-moon, and as a red woolen blanket might cover a golden plate, with his tongue that was like a flash of lightning, he covered the entire orb of his forehead.

Yaṃnūnāhanti kasmā cintesi? Ahañhi mahāpurisalakkhaṇāni samannesitvā gato “diṭṭhāni te, tāta, mahāpurisalakkhaṇānī”ti ācariyena pucchito “āma, ācariyā”ti vattuṃ sakkhissāmi. Sace pana maṃ “kiriyākaraṇamassa kīdisa”nti pucchissati[P 3.0371], taṃ vattuṃ na sakkhissāmi, na jānāmīti vutte pana ācariyo kujjhissati “nanu tvaṃ mayā sabbampetaṃ jānanatthāya pesito, kasmā ajānitvā āgatosī”ti, tasmā yannūnāhanti cintetvā anubandhi. Bhagavā nhānaṭṭhānaṃ mukhadhovanaṭṭhānaṃ sarīrapaṭijagganaṭṭhānaṃ rājarājamahāmattādīnaṃ orodhehi saddhiṃ parivāretvā nisinnaṭṭhānanti imāni cattāri ṭhānāni ṭhapetvā sesaṭṭhānesu antamaso ekagandhakuṭiyampi okāsamakāsi.

Why did he think, ‘What if I were to…’? ‘Having gone and investigated the marks of a Great Man, when asked by my teacher, “Dear one, have you seen the marks of a Great Man?” I will be able to say, “Yes, teacher.” But if he asks me, “What is his conduct like?” I will not be able to say. And when I say, “I do not know,” my teacher will become angry, thinking, “Were you not sent by me for the purpose of knowing all this? Why have you returned without knowing?”’ Therefore, thinking, ‘What if I were to…’, he followed him. The Blessed One, excepting these four places—the bathing place, the face-washing place, the body-tending place, and the place where he sits surrounded by the ladies of the court of kings, great ministers, and others—granted him access in the remaining places, even into the single perfumed chamber.

Gacchante [M 3.0255] gacchante kāle – “ayaṃ kira brahmāyubrāhmaṇassa māṇavo uttaro nāma ‘buddho vā no vā’ti tathāgatassa buddhabhāvaṃ vīmaṃsanto carati, buddhavīmaṃsako nāmāya”nti pākaṭo jāto. Yamhi yamhi ṭhāne buddhā vasanti, pañca kiccāni katāneva honti, tāni heṭṭhā dassitāneva[V 3.0264]. Tattha pacchābhattaṃ alaṅkatadhammāsane nisīditvā dantakhacitaṃ cittabījaniṃ gahetvā mahājanassa dhammaṃ desente bhagavati uttaropi avidūre nisīdati. Dhammassavanapariyosāne saddhā manussā svātanāya bhagavantaṃ nimantetvā māṇavampi upasaṅkamitvā evaṃ vadanti – “tāta, amhehi bhagavā nimantito, tvampi bhagavatā saddhiṃ āgantvā amhākaṃ gehe bhattaṃ gaṇheyyāsī”ti. Punadivase tathāgato bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto gāmaṃ pavisati, uttaropi padavāre padavāre pariggaṇhanto padānupadiko anubandhati. Kulagehaṃ paviṭṭhakāle dakkhiṇodakaggahaṇaṃ ādiṃ katvā sabbaṃ olokento nisīdati. Bhattakiccāvasāne tathāgatassa pattaṃ bhūmiyaṃ ṭhapetvā nisinnakāle māṇavakassa pātarāsabhattaṃ sajjenti. So ekamante nisinno bhuñjitvā puna āgantvā satthu santike ṭhatvā bhattānumodanaṃ sutvā bhagavatā saddhiṃyeva vihāraṃ gacchati.

As time went on, it became well-known: ‘This young man named Uttara, of the brahmin Brahmāyu, is reportedly going about investigating the Tathāgata’s state of Buddhahood, asking, “Is he a Buddha or not?” He is called the Buddha-investigator.’ In whatever place the Buddhas dwell, the five duties are always performed; these have been shown below. There, in the afternoon, while the Blessed One was seated on the decorated Dhamma-seat, holding a variegated fan inlaid with ivory and teaching the Dhamma to the great assembly, Uttara also sat not far away. At the conclusion of the Dhamma hearing, faithful people would invite the Blessed One for the next day, and approaching the young man, they would speak thus: ‘Dear one, the Blessed One has been invited by us. You too, coming with the Blessed One, should accept a meal at our house.’ On the next day, the Tathāgata, surrounded by the community of monks, would enter the village. Uttara also would follow closely in his footsteps, taking note at every stride. At the time of entering a patron’s house, he would sit observing everything, beginning with the receiving of the dedication water.
