At the conclusion of the meal-duty, at the time when the Tathāgata had placed his bowl on the ground and was seated, they would prepare the morning meal for the young man. He, having sat to one side and eaten, would come again, and standing in the Teacher’s presence and hearing the blessing for the meal, he would go to the monastery together with the Blessed One.

Tattha bhagavā bhikkhūnaṃ bhattakiccapariyosānaṃ āgamento gandhamaṇḍalamāḷe nisīdati. Bhikkhūhi bhattakiccaṃ [P 3.0372] katvā pattacīvaraṃ paṭisāmetvā āgamma vanditvā kāle ārocite bhagavā gandhakuṭiṃ pavisati, māṇavopi bhagavatā saddhiṃyeva gacchati. Bhagavā parivāretvā āgataṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ gandhakuṭippamukhe ṭhito ovaditvā uyyojetvā gandhakuṭiṃ pavisati, māṇavopi pavisati. Bhagavā khuddakamañce appamattakaṃ kālaṃ nisīdati, māṇavopi avidūre olokento nisīdati. Bhagavā muhuttaṃ nisīditvā sīsokkamanaṃ dasseti, – “bhoto gotamassa vihāravelā bhavissatī”ti māṇavo gandhakuṭidvāraṃ pidahanto nikkhamitvā ekamantaṃ nisīdati. Manussā purebhattaṃ dānaṃ datvā bhuttapātarāsā samādinnauposathaṅgā suddhuttarāsaṅgā mālāgandhādihatthā dhammaṃ suṇissāmāti vihāraṃ āgacchanti, cakkavattino khandhāvāraṭṭhānaṃ viya hoti.

There, the Blessed One, awaiting the conclusion of the monks' meal-duty, would sit in the perfumed circular pavilion. When the monks, having completed their meal-duty, put away their bowls and robes, approached, paid homage, and announced the time, the Blessed One would enter the perfumed chamber, and the young man would go right along with the Blessed One. The Blessed One, standing at the entrance of the perfumed chamber, would admonish and dismiss the community of monks that had come surrounding him, and then enter the perfumed chamber; the young man would also enter. The Blessed One would sit for a short time on a small couch, and the young man would sit not far away, observing. Having sat for a moment, the Blessed One would show a movement of his head. Thinking, 'It must be the time for the venerable Gotama's private abiding,' the young man, while closing the door to the perfumed chamber, went out and sat to one side. People who had given alms in the forenoon, had eaten their morning meal, had undertaken the Uposatha precepts, wore pure upper garments, and held garlands, perfumes, and so on in their hands, would come to the monastery thinking, 'We will listen to the Dhamma.' It would become like the encampment of a wheel-turning monarch.

Bhagavā muhuttaṃ sīhaseyyaṃ kappetvā vuṭṭhāya pubbabhāgena paricchinditvā samāpattiṃ samāpajjati. Samāpattito vuṭṭhāya mahājanassa āgatabhāvaṃ ñatvā [M 3.0256] gandhakuṭito nikkhamma mahājanaparivuto gandhamaṇḍalamāḷaṃ gantvā paññattavarabuddhāsanagato parisāya dhammaṃ deseti. Māṇavopi avidūre nisīditvā – “kiṃ nu kho samaṇo gotamo gehassitavasena parisaṃ ussādento vā apasādento vā dhammaṃ deseti, udāhu no”ti akkharakkharaṃ padaṃ padaṃ pariggaṇhāti. Bhagavā tathāvidhaṃ kathaṃ akathetvāva kālaṃ ñatvā desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi. Māṇavo iminā [V 3.0265] niyāmena pariggaṇhanto satta māse ekato vicaritvā bhagavato kāyadvārādīsu aṇumattampi avakkhalitaṃ na addasa. Anacchariyañcetaṃ, yaṃ buddhabhūtassa [P 3.0373] manussabhūto māṇavo na passeyya, yassa bodhisattabhūtassa chabbassāni padhānabhūmiyaṃ amanussabhūto māro devaputto gehassitavitakkamattampi adisvā buddhabhūtaṃ ekasaṃvaccharaṃ anubandhitvā kiñci apassanto –

The Blessed One, having rested for a moment in the lion's posture, arose, and having determined the time in the earlier part of the day, entered into attainment. Emerging from attainment, knowing that the great multitude had arrived, he departed from the perfumed chamber and, surrounded by the great multitude, went to the perfumed pavilion. Having gone to the excellent, prepared Buddha-seat, he taught the Dhamma to the assembly. The young man, sitting not far away, scrutinized every letter and every word, thinking: “Does the ascetic Gotama teach the Dhamma while praising or disparaging the assembly by way of what pertains to the household life, or not?” The Blessed One, without speaking any such talk, knowing the time, concluded the discourse. The young man, scrutinizing in this manner, wandered together with him for seven months and did not see even a minute fault in the Blessed One’s bodily conduct and so forth. And this is not surprising, that a human youth would not see a fault in one who has become a Buddha, for when he was a Bodhisatta for six years on the ground of exertion, the non-human Māra, the deity, did not see even a mere thought connected with the household life; and after he had become a Buddha, Māra followed him for a whole year, but seeing nothing—

“Satta vassāni bhagavantaṃ, anubandhiṃ padāpadaṃ;

Otāraṃ nādhigacchissaṃ, sambuddhassa satīmato”ti. (su. ni. 448) –

“For seven years I followed the Blessed One step by step; yet I could not find an opening in the mindful Fully Enlightened One.”

Ādigāthāyo vatvā pakkāmi. Tato māṇavo cintesi – “ahaṃ bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ satta māse anubandhamāno kiñci vajjaṃ na passāmi. Sace panāhaṃ aññepi satta māse satta vā vassāni vassasataṃ vā vassasahassaṃ vā anubandheyyaṃ, nevassa vajjaṃ passeyyaṃ. Ācariyo kho panassa me mahallako, yogakkhemaṃ nāma na sakkā jānituṃ. Samaṇassa gotamassa sabhāvaguṇeneva buddhabhāvaṃ vatvā mayhaṃ ācariyassa ārocessāmī”ti bhagavantaṃ āpucchitvā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ vanditvā nikkhami.

Having spoken the foregoing verses, he departed. Then the young man thought: “For seven months I have been following the Venerable Gotama, yet I see no blemish in him. Even if I were to follow him for another seven months, or seven years, or a hundred years, or a thousand years, I would still see no blemish in him. But my teacher is old, and it is not possible to know of his security from bondage. I will declare the ascetic Gotama's Buddhahood to my teacher based on his inherent qualities.” Having taken leave of the Blessed One and paid homage to the community of bhikkhus, he departed.

Ācariyassa santikañca pana gantvā – “kacci, tāta uttara, taṃ bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ tathāsantaṃyeva saddo abbhuggato”ti pucchito, “ācariya, kiṃ vadesi? Cakkavāḷaṃ atisambādhaṃ, bhavaggaṃ atinīcaṃ, tassa hi, bhoto gotamassa ākāsaṃ viya apariyanto guṇagaṇo. Tathāsantaṃyeva, bho, taṃ bhavantaṃ gotama”ntiādīni vatvā yathādiṭṭhāni dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇāni paṭipāṭiyā ācikkhitvā kiriyasamācāraṃ ācikkhi. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho uttaro māṇavo…pe… ediso ca ediso ca bhavaṃ gotamo tato ca bhiyyo”ti.

Having gone to his teacher, he was asked, “My dear Uttara, has the report concerning the Venerable Gotama arisen based on what is truly so?” He replied, “Teacher, what are you saying? The universe is too confined, the peak of existence too low; for the multitude of the Venerable Gotama's qualities is boundless, like the sky. Indeed, sir, the report concerning the Venerable Gotama has arisen based on what is truly so.” Having said this and more, he described in order the thirty-two marks of a great man as he had seen them, and he described his conduct and deportment. Therefore it was said: “Then the young man Uttara... such and such is the Venerable Gotama, and even more than that.”

386. Tattha [M 3.0257][P 3.0374] suppatiṭṭhitapādoti yathā hi aññesaṃ bhūmiyaṃ pādaṃ ṭhapentānaṃ aggatalaṃ vā paṇhi vā passaṃ vā paṭhamaṃ phusati, vemajjhaṃ vā pana chiddaṃ hoti, ukkhipantānampi aggatalādīsu ekakoṭṭhāsova paṭhamaṃ uṭṭhahati, na evaṃ tassa. Tassa pana suvaṇṇapādukatalaṃ viya ekappahāreneva sakalaṃ pādatalaṃ bhūmiṃ phusati, bhūmito uṭṭhahati. Tasmā “suppatiṭṭhitapādo kho pana so bhavaṃ gotamo”ti vadati.

386. Therein, ‘well-established feet’ means this: Whereas for others, when placing a foot on the ground, either the forefoot, the heel, or the side touches first, or there is a gap in the middle, and even when lifting it, only one part, such as the forefoot, rises first—it is not so for him. For him, like the sole of a golden sandal, the entire sole of the foot touches the ground at a single stroke and lifts from the ground. Therefore, he says, “The Venerable Gotama has well-established feet.”

Tatridaṃ [V 3.0266] bhagavato suppatiṭṭhitapādatāya – sacepi hi bhagavā anekasataporisaṃ narakaṃ akkamissāmīti pādaṃ nīharati, tāvadeva ninnaṭṭhānaṃ vātapūritaṃ viya kammārabhastaṃ unnamitvā pathavīsamaṃ hoti, unnataṭṭhānampi anto pavisati. Dūre akkamissāmīti abhinīharantassa sineruppamāṇopi pabbato seditavettaṅkuro viya namitvā pādasamīpaṃ āgacchati. Tathā hissa yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ katvā yugandharapabbataṃ akkamissāmīti pāde abhinīharato pabbato namitvā pādasamīpaṃ āgato, so taṃ akkamitvā dutiyapādena tāvatiṃsabhavanaṃ akkami. Na hi cakkalakkhaṇena patiṭṭhātabbaṭṭhānaṃ visamaṃ bhavituṃ sakkoti. Khāṇu vā kaṇḍako vā sakkharakathalā vā uccārapassāvo vā kheḷasiṅghāṇikādīni vā purimatarāva apagacchanti, tattha tattheva ca pathaviṃ pavisanti. Tathāgatassa hi sīlatejena paññātejena dhammatejena dasannaṃ pāramīnaṃ ānubhāvena ayaṃ [P 3.0375] mahāpathavī samā mudu pupphābhikiṇṇā hoti. Tatra tathāgato samaṃ pādaṃ nikkhipati, samaṃ uddharati, sabbāvantehi pādatalehi bhūmiṃ phusati.

Herein is this power due to the Blessed One's well-established feet: If the Blessed One, intending to step over a chasm many hundreds of men deep, were to extend his foot, that very low ground would swell up like a blacksmith’s bellows filled with air, becoming level with the earth, and even high ground would sink down. If he extends his foot, intending to step far, even a mountain as large as Sineru bends like a softened cane shoot and comes near his foot. For a place that is to be trod upon by one with the wheel-mark cannot be uneven. Stumps, thorns, gravel, potsherds, excrement, urine, spit, mucus, and so forth, all vanish beforehand, sinking into the earth right where they are. By the power of the Tathāgata’s virtue, wisdom, and Dhamma, and by the influence of the ten perfections, this great earth becomes level, soft, and strewn with flowers. There, the Tathāgata places his foot evenly, lifts it evenly, and touches the ground with the entire soles of his feet.

Cakkānīti dvīsu pādesu dve cakkāni. Tesaṃ arā ca nemi ca nābhi ca pāḷiyaṃ vuttāva. Sabbākāraparipūrānīti iminā pana ayaṃ viseso veditabbo – tesaṃ kira cakkānaṃ pādatalassa majjhe nābhi dissati, nābhiparicchinnā vaṭṭalekhā dissati, nābhimukhaparikkhepapaṭṭo dissati, panāḷimukhaṃ dissati, arā dissanti, aresu vaṭṭalekhā dissanti, nemī dissanti, nemimaṇikā dissanti. Idaṃ tāva pāḷiāgatameva.

The Wheels: On the two feet are two wheels. Their spokes, rims, and hubs are as stated in the Pāli canon. By the phrase ‘complete in all aspects,’ this distinction should be understood: it is said that in the middle of the sole of the foot, the hub of those wheels is seen; a circular line defining the hub is seen; a band encircling the mouth of the hub is seen; the mouth of a conduit is seen; the spokes are seen; circular lines on the spokes are seen; the rims are seen; and jewels on the rims are seen. This much is indeed from the Pāli canon.

Sambahulavāro pana anāgato, so evaṃ daṭṭhabbo – satti siri vaccho nandi sovattiko vaṭaṃsako vaḍḍhamānakaṃ macchayugalaṃ bhaddapīṭhaṃ aṅkusaṃ [M 3.0258] tomaro pāsādo toraṇaṃ setacchattaṃ khaggo tālavaṇṭaṃ morahatthako vāḷabījanī uṇhīsaṃ patto maṇi kusumadāmaṃ nīluppalaṃ rattuppalaṃ setuppalaṃ padumaṃ puṇḍarīkaṃ puṇṇaghaṭo puṇṇapāti samuddo cakkavāḷo himavā sineru candimasūriyā nakkhattāni cattāro mahādīpā dveparittadīpasahassāni, antamaso cakkavattirañño parisaṃ upādāya sabbo cakkalakkhaṇasseva parivāro.

Furthermore, the section of many things, which has not come in the Pāli, should be understood thus: a spear, an auspicious face, a nandi flower, the three lines on the neck, a head-ornament, a vaḍḍhamānaka, a pair of fish, an auspicious throne, a goad, a forked spear, a tiered palace, a gateway, a white parasol, a sword, a palm-leaf fan, a bunch of peacock feathers, a yak-tail whisk, a diadem, an alms-bowl, a jewel, a flower garland, a blue water lily, a red water lily, a white water lily, a lotus, a white lotus, a full vessel, a full bowl, the ocean, the world-system, the Himālaya mountain, Mount Sineru, the moon and sun, the constellations, the four great continents, and the two thousand minor surrounding islands—even down to the assembly of a wheel-turning monarch—all this is the retinue of the Wheel-mark alone.

Āyatapaṇhīti [P 3.0376] dīghapaṇhi, paripuṇṇapaṇhīti attho. Yathā hi aññesaṃ aggapādo dīgho hoti, paṇhimatthake jaṅghā patiṭṭhāti, paṇhi tacchetvā ṭhapitā viya hoti, na evaṃ tathāgatassa[V 3.0267]. Tathāgatassa pana catūsu koṭṭhāsesu dve koṭṭhāsā aggapādo hoti, tatiye koṭṭhāse jaṅghā patiṭṭhāti, catutthe koṭṭhāse āraggena vaṭṭetvā ṭhapitā viya rattakambale geṇḍukasadisā paṇhi hoti.

‘Long-heeled’ means having long heels; the meaning is having full heels. For whereas with other people the forefoot is long, the lower leg is established on top of the heel, and the heel is as if carved and placed, it is not so for the Tathāgata. For the Tathāgata, of four parts, two parts are the forefoot; in the third part, the lower leg is established; and in the fourth part is the heel, which is like a ball on a red woolen blanket, as if rounded with the tip of an awl and set in place.

Dīghaṅgulīti yathā aññesaṃ kāci aṅguli dīghā hoti, kāci rassā, na evaṃ tathāgatassa. Tathāgatassa pana makkaṭasseva dīghahatthapādaṅguliyo mūle thūlā anupubbena gantvā agge tanukā niyyāsatelena madditvā vaṭṭitaharitālavaṭṭisadisā honti. Tena vuttaṃ “dīghaṅgulī”ti.

‘Long-fingered’ means that whereas for other people some fingers or toes are long and some are short, it is not so for the Tathāgata. The Tathāgata's long fingers and toes are like those of a monkey: being thick at the base, they proceed gradually, becoming slender at the tips, and are like rounded sticks of yellow orpiment that have been massaged with resinous oil. Therefore, it is said, ‘long-fingered’.

Mudutalunahatthapādoti sappimaṇḍe osādetvā ṭhapitaṃ satavāravihatakappāsapaṭalaṃ viya mudū, jātamattakumārassa viya ca niccakālaṃ talunā ca hatthapādā assāti mudutalunahatthapādo.

‘One with soft and tender hands and feet’ means: His hands and feet are soft like a layer of cotton wool that has been carded a hundred times and steeped in the cream of ghee, and they are always tender like the hands and feet of a newborn infant. Therefore, he is called ‘one with soft and tender hands and feet’.

Jālahatthapādoti na cammena paṭibaddhaaṅgulantaro. Ediso hi phaṇahatthako purisadosena upahato pabbajjampi na labhati. Tathāgatassa pana catasso hatthaṅguliyo pañcapi pādaṅguliyo ekappamāṇā honti, tāsaṃ ekappamāṇattāya yavalakkhaṇaṃ aññamaññaṃ paṭivijjhitvā tiṭṭhati. Athassa hatthapādā kusalena vaḍḍhakinā yojitajālavātapānasadisā honti. Tena vuttaṃ “jālahatthapādo”ti.

‘One with net-like hands and feet’ means that the spaces between his fingers are not connected by skin. For such a person, called ‘cobra-handed’, is afflicted by a physical defect and cannot even obtain the going forth. For the Tathāgata, the four fingers and the five toes are of equal length. Solely because of their equal length, the characteristic mark stands as if piercing from one to another. Then, His hands and feet are like a net-like lattice window fitted by a skilled carpenter. Therefore, it is said, ‘one with net-like hands and feet’.

Uddhaṃ patiṭṭhitagopphakattā ussaṅkhā pādā assāti [P 3.0377] ussaṅkhapādo. Aññesañhi piṭṭhipāde gopphakā honti. Tena tesaṃ pādā āṇibaddhā viya thaddhā honti, na yathāsukhaṃ parivattanti, gacchantānaṃ pādatalāni na dissanti[M 3.0259]. Tathāgatassa pana abhiruhitvā upari gopphakā patiṭṭhahanti. Tenassa nābhito paṭṭhāya uparimakāyo nāvāya ṭhapitasuvaṇṇapaṭimā viya niccalo hoti, adhokāyova iñjati. Sukhena pādā parivattanti. Puratopi pacchatopi ubhayapassesupi ṭhatvā passantānaṃ pādatalāni paññāyanti, na hatthīnaṃ viya pacchatoyeva.

He is ‘one with high insteps’ because his ankles are established high up. For other people, the ankles are on the top of the foot. Therefore, their feet are stiff as if fastened with pegs; they do not turn with ease, and when they walk, the soles of their feet are not seen. For the Tathāgata, however, the ankles, having ascended, are established high up. Because of this, His upper body from the navel upwards is motionless like a golden statue placed in a boat; only the lower body moves. The feet turn with ease. The soles of his feet are visible to those who stand and look from the front, from behind, and from both sides, not like those of elephants, which are visible only from behind.

Eṇijaṅghoti eṇimigasadisajaṅgho maṃsussadena paripuṇṇajaṅgho, na ekato baddhapiṇḍikamaṃso[V 3.0268], samantato samasaṇṭhitena maṃsena parikkhittāhi suvaṭṭitāhi sāligabbhasadisāhi jaṅghāhi samannāgatoti attho.

‘One with antelope-like calves’ means he has calves like those of an eṇī deer; he has full calves due to an abundance of flesh. He does not have the calf muscle bound in a lump on one side, but is endowed with well-rounded calves surrounded on all sides by evenly established flesh, like sheaves of rice. This is the meaning.

Anonamantoti anamanto. Etenassa akhujjaavāmanabhāvo dīpito. Avasesajanā hi khujjā vā honti vāmanā vā, khujjānaṃ uparimakāyo aparipuṇṇo hoti, vāmanānaṃ heṭṭhimakāyo. Te aparipuṇṇakāyattā na sakkonti anonamantā jaṇṇukāni parimajjituṃ. Tathāgato pana paripuṇṇaubhayakāyattā sakkoti.

‘Not bending down’ means not bending. By this is shown his state of being neither hunchbacked nor dwarfish. For other people are either hunchbacked or dwarfish. For the hunchbacked, the upper body is incomplete; for the dwarfish, the lower body is incomplete. Because they have incomplete bodies, they are not able to stroke their knees without bending down. The Tathāgata, however, is able to do so because he has a complete body in both parts.

Usabhavāraṇādīnaṃ viya suvaṇṇapadumakaṇṇikasadise kose ohitaṃ paṭicchannaṃ vatthaguyhaṃ assāti kosohitavatthaguyho. Vatthaguyhanti vatthena gūhitabbaṃ aṅgajātaṃ vuccati.

He is called ‘one whose private part is concealed in a sheath’ because He has a private part that is withdrawn inside and concealed in a sheath, like that of a bull, a noble elephant, and so on, and which is like the pericarp of a golden lotus. ‘Private part’ refers to the generative organ that ought to be hidden by a cloth.

Suvaṇṇavaṇṇoti jātihiṅgulakena majjitvā dīpidāṭhāya ghaṃsitvā gerukaparikammaṃ katvā ṭhapitaghanasuvaṇṇarūpakasadisoti attho. Etenassa ghanasiniddhasaṇhasarīrataṃ dassetvā chavivaṇṇadassanatthaṃ kañcanasannibhattacoti vuttaṃ, purimassa vā vevacanameva etaṃ.

‘One of golden complexion’ means he is like a figure of solid gold that has been polished with genuine cinnabar, smoothed with a leopard's tooth, prepared with red ochre, and set in place. By this, having shown his state of having a solid, smooth, and fine body, to show the color of his skin it is said, ‘his skin is like gold.’ Or, this is merely a synonym for the former.

Rajojallanti [P 3.0378] rajo vā malaṃ vā. Na upalimpatīti na laggati, padumapalāsato udakabindu viya vivaṭṭati. Hatthadhovanapādadhovanādīni pana utuggahaṇatthāya ceva dāyakānaṃ puññaphalatthāya ca buddhā karonti, vattasīsenāpi ca karontiyeva. Senāsanaṃ pavisantena hi bhikkhunā pāde dhovitvā pavisitabbanti vuttametaṃ.

‘Dust and dirt’ means fine dust or grime. ‘Is not smeared’ means it does not stick; it rolls off like a drop of water from a lotus leaf. However, the Buddhas do things like washing their hands and feet both for the sake of physical well-being and for the sake of the fruit of merit for donors. And they do so also as a matter of observance. For indeed, it has been said: ‘A monk entering a lodging should enter after having washed his feet’.

Uddhaggalomoti āvaṭṭapariyosāne uddhaggāni hutvā mukhasobhaṃ ullokayamānāni viya ṭhitāni lomāni assāti uddhaggalomo.

‘One with upward-pointing body-hairs’ means: He has body-hairs that, at the end of each right-turning whorl, become upward-pointing and stand as if gazing up at the beauty of his face. Therefore, he is called ‘one with upward-pointing body-hairs’.

Brahmujugattoti [M 3.0260] brahmā viya ujugatto, ujumeva uggatadīghasarīro. Yebhuyyena hi sattā khandhe kaṭiyaṃ jāṇūsūti tīsu ṭhānesu namanti. Te kaṭiyaṃ namantā pacchato namanti, itaresu dvīsu ṭhānesu purato. Dīghasarīrā paneke passavaṅkā honti, eke mukhaṃ unnāmetvā nakkhattāni gaṇayantā [V 3.0269] viya caranti, eke appamaṃsalohitā sūlasadisā honti, pavedhamānā gacchanti. Tathāgato pana ujumeva uggantvā dīghappamāṇo devanagare ussitasuvaṇṇatoraṇaṃ viya hoti.

‘One with a body straight like Brahmā’s’ means he has a straight body like Brahmā; his body is perfectly straight, risen up, and tall. For the most part, beings bend in three places: at the shoulders, at the waist, and at the knees. Bending at the waist, they bend backwards; at the other two places, they bend forwards. Furthermore, some with tall bodies are crooked at the sides; some walk with their faces raised as if counting the constellations; some, having little flesh and blood, are like stakes and go along trembling. The Tathāgata, however, having risen up perfectly straight, is of a tall measure, like a golden gateway erected in a celestial city.

Sattussadoti dve hatthapiṭṭhiyo dve pādapiṭṭhiyo dve aṃsakūṭāni khandhoti imesu sattasu ṭhānesu paripuṇṇamaṃsussado assāti sattussado. Aññesaṃ pana hatthapādapiṭṭhīsu nhārujālā paññāyanti, aṃsakūṭakhandhesu [P 3.0379] aṭṭhikoṭiyo, te manussapetā viya khāyanti, na tathāgato. Tathāgato pana sattasu ṭhānesu paripuṇṇamaṃsussadattā nigūḷhanhārujālehi hatthapiṭṭhādīhi vaṭṭetvā ṭhapitasuvaṇṇavaṇṇāliṅgasadisena khandhena silārūpakaṃ viya cittakammarūpakaṃ viya ca khāyati.

He has seven convex surfaces: Because he has full and convex flesh on the two backs of his hands, the two backs of his feet, his two shoulder-tops, and his nape—these seven places—he is called `sattussada`. For others, however, networks of sinews are visible on the backs of their hands and feet, and the tips of their bones are visible on their shoulder-tops and napes; they appear like ghosts, but not so the Tathāgata. The Tathāgata, however, because of having full and convex flesh in these seven places, with his networks of sinews concealed on the backs of his hands and so forth, and with a nape like a well-rounded, placed, golden-hued drum, appears like a stone statue or a painted image.

Sīhassa pubbaddhaṃ viya kāyo assāti sīhapubbaddhakāyo. Sīhassa hi puratthimakāyova paripuṇṇo hoti, pacchimakāyo aparipuṇṇo. Tathāgatassa pana sīhassa pubbaddhakāyova sabbo kāyo paripuṇṇo. Sopi sīhasseva na tattha tattha vinatunnatādivasena dussaṇṭhitavisaṇṭhito, dīghayuttaṭhāne pana dīgho, rassakisathūlaanuvaṭṭitayuttaṭṭhānesu tathāvidhova hoti. Vuttañhetaṃ –

His body is like the forepart of a lion: This means his body is like the forepart of a lion; thus, he is `sīhapubbaddhakāyo`. For a lion, only the front part of its body is full, while the rear part is not full. But for the Tathāgata, his entire body is full, like the forepart of a lion. Furthermore, his body is not ill-formed or misshapen with depressions and elevations here and there; rather, where it should be long, it is long, and in places where it should be short, slender, thick, or rounded, it is just so. For it has been said:

“Manāpiye ca kho, bhikkhave, kammavipāke paccupaṭṭhite yehi aṅgehi dīghehi sobhati, tāni aṅgāni dīghāni saṇṭhahanti. Yehi aṅgehi rassehi sobhati, tāni aṅgāni rassāni saṇṭhahanti. Yehi aṅgehi thūlehi sobhati, tāni aṅgāni thūlāni saṇṭhahanti. Yehi aṅgehi kisehi sobhati, tāni aṅgāni kisāni saṇṭhahanti. Yehi aṅgehi vaṭṭehi sobhati, tāni aṅgāni vaṭṭāni saṇṭhahantī”ti.

“O bhikkhus, when the pleasing result of kamma is present, by whichever long limbs he is beautiful, those limbs are established as long. By whichever short limbs he is beautiful, those limbs are established as short. By whichever thick limbs he is beautiful, those limbs are established as thick. By whichever slender limbs he is beautiful, those limbs are established as slender. By whichever round limbs he is beautiful, those limbs are established as round.”

Iti [M 3.0261] nānācittena puññacittena cittito dasahi pāramīhi sajjito tathāgatassa attabhāvo, tassa loke sabbasippino vā iddhimanto vā paṭirūpakampi kātuṃ na sakkonti.

Thus, the Tathāgata's being is adorned by various and manifold meritorious deeds and prepared by the ten perfections; of him, all the artisans or those with psychic power in the world are not able to create even a replica.

Citantaraṃsoti [P 3.0380] antaraṃsaṃ vuccati dvinnaṃ koṭṭānamantaraṃ, taṃ citaṃ paripuṇṇamassāti citantaraṃso. Aññesañhi taṃ ṭhānaṃ ninnaṃ hoti, dve piṭṭhikoṭṭā pāṭiyekkaṃ paññāyanti. Tathāgatassa pana kaṭito paṭṭhāya maṃsapaṭalaṃ yāva khandhā uggamma samussitasuvaṇṇaphalakaṃ viya piṭṭhiṃ chādetvā patiṭṭhitaṃ.

Full between the shoulders: The space between the two shoulder-blades is called `antaraṃsa`. That space of his is filled up and full; thus, he is `citantaraṃso`. For others, that place is hollow, and the two shoulder-blades appear separately. But for the Tathāgata, a sheet of flesh, starting from the waist, rises up to the nape of the neck and is established, covering the back like a raised golden plank.

Nigrodhaparimaṇḍaloti [V 3.0270] nigrodho viya parimaṇḍalo. Yathā paṇṇāsahatthatāya vā satahatthatāya vā samakkhandhasākho nigrodho dīghatopi vitthāratopi ekappamāṇova hoti, evaṃ kāyatopi byāmatopi ekappamāṇo. Yathā aññesaṃ kāyo vā dīgho hoti byāmo vā, na evaṃ visamappamāṇoti attho. Teneva “yāvatakvassa kāyo”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yāvatako assāti yāvatakvassa.

His proportions are like a banyan tree: This means he is perfectly proportioned like a banyan tree. Just as a banyan tree with a trunk and branches of equal measure, whether fifty or a hundred cubits, is of the same measure in height and in breadth, so too is he of the same measure in his body's height and his arm-span. The meaning is that he is not of unequal proportions, as is the case with others for whom either the body is tall or the arm-span is long. Therefore it was said, “As is his body…” and so on. Therein, `yāvatakvassa` means `yāvatako assa`.

Samavaṭṭakkhandhoti samavaṭṭitakkhandho. Yathā eke koñcā viya bakā viya varāhā viya ca dīghagalā vaṅkagalā puthulagalā ca honti, kathanakāle sirājālaṃ paññāyati, mando saro nikkhamati, na evaṃ tassa. Tathāgatassa pana suvaṭṭitasuvaṇṇāliṅgasadiso khandho hoti, kathanakāle sirājālaṃ na paññāyati, meghassa viya gajjato saro mahā hoti.

Evenly rounded neck: This means having an evenly rounded neck. Unlike some who, like cranes, herons, or boars, have long, crooked, or thick necks, and for whom a network of veins appears and a weak sound emerges when they speak—it is not so for him. Rather, the Tathāgata's neck is like a well-rounded golden drum; when he speaks, no network of veins appears, and his voice is great, like that of a thundering cloud.

Rasaggasaggīti ettha rasaṃ gasantīti rasaggasā[P 3.0381], rasaharaṇīnametaṃ adhivacanaṃ, tā aggā assāti rasaggasaggī. Tathāgatassa hi satta rasaharaṇisahassāni uddhaggāni hutvā gīvāyameva paṭimukkāni. Tilaphalamattopi āhāro jivhagge ṭhapito sabbaṃ kāyaṃ anupharati, teneva mahāpadhānaṃ padahantassa ekataṇḍulādīhipi kāḷāyayūsapasatenāpi kāyassa yāpanaṃ ahosi. Aññesaṃ pana tathā abhāvā na sakalakāyaṃ ojā pharati, tena te bahvābādhā honti. Idaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ appābādhatāsaṅkhātassa nissandaphalassa vasena pākaṭaṃ hoti.

Supreme in taste: Herein, `rasaggasā` means 'they consume taste'; this is a designation for the taste-conducting nerves. Because those nerves are supreme for him, he is called `rasaggasaggī`. For the Tathāgata, seven thousand taste-conducting nerves, with tips pointing upwards, are located in his neck. Even a piece of food the size of a sesame seed, when placed on the tip of his tongue, pervades his entire body. For that reason, while undertaking the Great Exertion, his body was sustained even by a single grain of rice and so forth, or by a handful of bean soup. For others, however, due to the absence of this quality, nutritive essence does not pervade the entire body, and thus they have many illnesses. This characteristic becomes manifest by way of the resultant fruit known as 'fewness of ailments'.

Sīhasseva [M 3.0262] hanu assāti sīhahanu. Tattha sīhassa heṭṭhimahanumeva paripuṇṇaṃ hoti, na uparimaṃ. Tathāgatassa pana sīhassa heṭṭhimaṃ viya dvepi paripuṇṇāni dvādasiyaṃ pakkhassa candasadisāni honti.

Lion-like jaw: This means he has a jaw like a lion's; thus, he is `sīhahanu`. For a lion, only the lower jaw is full, not the upper one. But for the Tathāgata, both jaws are full like a lion's lower jaw, and they are like the moon on the twelfth day of the lunar fortnight.

Cattālīsadantotiādīsu uparimahanuke patiṭṭhitā vīsati, heṭṭhime vīsatīti cattālīsa dantā assāti cattālīsadanto. Aññesañhi paripuṇṇadantānampi dvattiṃsa dantā honti, tathāgatassa cattālīsaṃ.

Forty teeth: This means twenty teeth are established in the upper jaw and twenty in the lower; because he has forty teeth, he is called `cattālīsadanto`. For others, even those with a full set of teeth, there are thirty-two teeth, but the Tathāgata has forty.

Aññesañca [V 3.0271] keci dantā uccā keci nīcāti visamā honti, tathāgatassa pana ayapaṭṭachinnasaṅkhapaṭalaṃ viya samā.

And for others, some teeth are high and some are low, thus they are uneven. But the Tathāgata's teeth are even, like a slice of conch shell cut with an iron saw.

Aññesaṃ kumbhīlānaṃ viya dantā viraḷā honti, macchamaṃsādīni khādantānaṃ dantantaraṃ pūrati. Tathāgatassa pana kanakalatāya samussāpitavajirapanti viya aviraḷā tulikāya dassitaparicchedā viya dantā honti.

For others, their teeth have gaps like those of crocodiles, and for those who eat fish, meat, and so on, the spaces between the teeth get filled. The Tathāgata’s teeth, however, are without gaps, like a row of diamonds set on a golden vine, and are as if their divisions were delineated with a painter's brush.

Susukkadāṭhoti aññesañca pūtidantā uṭṭhahanti, tena kāci dāṭhā kāḷāpi vivaṇṇāpi honti. Tathāgato susukkadāṭho [P 3.0382] osadhitārakampi atikkamma virocamānāya pabhāya samannāgatadāṭho, tena vuttaṃ “susukkadāṭho”ti.

Exceedingly white eye-teeth: For others, decayed teeth arise, and because of that, some of their eye-teeth are black or discolored. The Tathāgata has exceedingly white eye-teeth; he possesses eye-teeth endowed with a radiance that shines, surpassing even the morning star. Therefore, it was said, `susukkadāṭho`.

Pahūtajivhoti aññesaṃ jivhā thūlāpi hoti kisāpi rassāpi thaddhāpi visamāpi, tathāgatassa pana mudu dīghā puthulā vaṇṇasampannā hoti. So taṃ lakkhaṇaṃ pariyesituṃ āgatānaṃ kaṅkhāvinodanatthaṃ mudukattā taṃ jivhaṃ kathinasūciṃ viya vaṭṭetvā ubho nāsikasotāni parāmasati, dīghattā ubho kaṇṇasotāni parāmasati, puthulattā kesantapariyosānaṃ kevalampi nalāṭaṃ paṭicchādeti. Evaṃ tassā mududīghaputhulabhāvaṃ pakāsento kaṅkhaṃ vinodeti. Evaṃ tilakkhaṇasampannaṃ jivhaṃ sandhāya “pahūtajivho”ti vuttaṃ.

“Having a large tongue” means that while the tongues of others may be thick, thin, short, stiff, or uneven, the Tathāgata's tongue is soft, long, broad, and beautifully colored. To dispel the doubts of those who come seeking this characteristic, because of its softness, he rolls his tongue up like a hard needle and touches both nostrils; because of its length, he touches both ears; and because of its breadth, he covers his entire forehead up to the hairline. In this way, by displaying its softness, length, and breadth, he dispels their doubt. Thus, with reference to a tongue endowed with these three characteristics, it is said, “having a large tongue.”

Brahmassaroti aññe chinnassarāpi bhinnassarāpi kākassarāpi honti, tathāgato pana mahābrahmuno sarasadisena sarena samannāgato. Mahābrahmuno hi pittasemhehi apalibuddhattā saro visuddho hoti. Tathāgatenāpi katakammaṃ vatthuṃ sodheti, vatthussa suddhattā nābhito paṭṭhāya samuṭṭhahanto saro visuddho aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgatova samuṭṭhāti. Karaviko viya bhaṇatīti karavikabhāṇī, mattakaravikarutamañjughosoti attho.

“Having a voice like Brahma” means that while the voices of others may be broken, cracked, or crow-like, the Tathāgata is endowed with a voice similar to that of the great Brahma. Indeed, the voice of the great Brahma is especially pure because it is not obstructed by bile and phlegm. For the Tathāgata, too, the kamma that was done purifies the physical basis of speech; because the basis is pure, the voice that arises, starting from the navel, is especially pure and endowed with eight qualities. He speaks like a karavika bird, hence he is called 'Karavikabhāṇī'. The meaning is: having a sweet and melodious voice like the cry of an intoxicated karavika bird.

Tatridaṃ [M 3.0263] karavikarutassa mañjutāya – karavikasakuṇe kira madhurarasaṃ ambapakkaṃ mukhatuṇḍakena paharitvā paggharitaṃ rasaṃ sāyitvā [P 3.0383] pakkhena tālaṃ datvā vikūjamāne catuppadādīni mattāni viya laḷituṃ ārabhanti. Gocarappasutāpi catuppadā mukhagatānipi tiṇāni [V 3.0272] chaḍḍetvā taṃ saddaṃ suṇanti, vāḷamigā khuddakamige anubandhamānā ukkhittapādaṃ anukkhipitvāva tiṭṭhanti, anubaddhamigāpi maraṇabhayaṃ hitvāpi tiṭṭhanti, ākāse pakkhandapakkhinopi pakkhe pasāretvā tiṭṭhanti, udake macchāpi kaṇṇapaṭalaṃ apphoṭentā taṃ saddaṃ suṇamānāva tiṭṭhanti. Evaṃ mañjurutā karavikā.

Herein is a story on the sweetness of the karavika's cry: It is said that when the karavika bird strikes a sweet, ripe mango with its beak, licks the juice that flows out, and then sings while beating time with its wing, four-footed creatures begin to frolic as if intoxicated. Even four-footed creatures intent on grazing drop the grass from their mouths and listen to that sound. Predatory animals pursuing smaller prey stand still without putting down their raised paws. Even the pursued animals, abandoning their fear of death, stand still. Birds flying in the sky spread their wings and stand still. Fish in the water, without flapping their gills, stand still, just listening to that sound. So sweet-crying are the karavika birds.

Asandhimittāpi dhammāsokassa devī – “atthi nu kho, bhante, buddhasaddena sadiso kassaci saddo”ti saṅghaṃ pucchi. Atthi karavikasakuṇassāti. Kuhiṃ, bhante, sakuṇāti? Himavanteti. Sā rājānaṃ āha, – “deva, karavikasakuṇaṃ daṭṭhukāmā”ti. Rājā “imasmiṃ pañjare nisīditvā karaviko āgacchatū”ti suvaṇṇapañjaraṃ vissajjesi. Pañjaro gantvā ekassa karavikassa purato aṭṭhāsi. So “rājāṇāya āgato pañjaro, na sakkā agantu”nti tattha nisīdi. Pañjaro āgantvā rañño puratova aṭṭhāsi. Karavikaṃ saddaṃ kārāpetuṃ na sakkonti. Atha rājā “kathaṃ bhaṇe ime saddaṃ karontī”ti āha? Ñātake disvā devāti. Atha naṃ rājā ādāsehi parikkhipāpesi. So attanova chāyaṃ disvā “ñātakā me āgatā”ti maññamāno pakkhena tāḷaṃ datvā mañjussarena maṇivaṃsaṃ dhamamāno viya viravi. Sakalanagare manussā mattā viya laḷiṃsu. Asandhimittā cintesi – “imassa tāva tiracchānassa evaṃ madhuro saddo, kīdiso nu kho sabbaññutaññāṇasirippattassa bhagavato [P 3.0384] ahosī”ti pītiṃ uppādetvā taṃ pītiṃ avijahitvā sattahi jaṅghasatehi saddhiṃ sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāsi. Evaṃ madhuro karavikasaddo. Tato satabhāgena sahassabhāgena ca madhurataro tathāgatassa saddo, loke pana karavikato aññassa madhurarassa abhāvato “karavikabhāṇī”ti vuttaṃ.

Queen Asandhimittā, the consort of King Dhammāsoka, asked the Saṅgha, “Venerable sirs, is there any sound comparable to the Buddha's voice?” They replied, “There is the sound of the karavika bird.” “Where are these birds, venerable sirs?” she asked. “In the Himavanta,” they answered. She then told the king, “Your Majesty, I wish to see the karavika bird.” The king sent forth a golden cage, saying, “Let a karavika come and sit in this cage.” The cage went and stood before a karavika bird. The bird, thinking, “This cage has come by the king's command; it is not possible not to go,” sat in it. The cage returned and stood before the king. They could not make the karavika produce a sound. Then the king asked, “Tell me, how do these birds make their sound?” They replied, “Upon seeing their kin, Your Majesty.” The king then had it surrounded by mirrors. Seeing its own reflection and thinking, “My kin have come,” the bird beat time with its wing and sang with a sweet voice, as if blowing on a jeweled flute. The people in the entire city frolicked as if intoxicated. Asandhimittā reflected, “If the sound of this mere animal is so sweet, what must the voice of the Blessed One, who attained the glory of omniscience, have been like?” Generating rapture, and without abandoning that rapture, she, together with seven hundred ladies-in-waiting, was established in the fruit of stream-entry. So sweet is the sound of the karavika. The Tathāgata's voice is a hundred times, a thousand times sweeter than that. However, because in the world there is no other sweet sound than the karavika's, it is said, 'He speaks like a karavika'.

Abhinīlanettoti na sakalanīlanettova, nīlayuttaṭṭhāne panassa umāpupphasadisena ativisuddhena nīlavaṇṇena samannāgatāni akkhīni honti. Pītayuttaṭṭhāne kaṇikārapupphasadisena pītavaṇṇena, lohitayuttaṭṭhāne [M 3.0264] bandhujīvakapupphasadisena lohitavaṇṇena, setayuttaṭṭhāne osadhitārakasadisena setavaṇṇena, kāḷayuttaṭṭhāne addāriṭṭhakasadisena kāḷavaṇṇena samannāgatāni suvaṇṇavimāne ugghāṭitamaṇisīhapañjarasadisāni khāyanti.

His eyes being “deep blue” does not mean his entire eyes are blue. Rather, in the areas appropriate for blue, his eyes possess an extremely pure blue color like that of a flax flower. In the areas appropriate for yellow, they have a yellow color like that of a kaṇikāra flower; in the areas appropriate for red, a red color like that of a bandhujīvaka flower; in the areas appropriate for white, a white color like that of the morning star; and in the areas appropriate for black, a black color like that of a soap nut seed. They appear like an opened, jewel-studded lion-window in a golden celestial mansion.

Gopakhumoti ettha pakhumanti sakalaṃ cakkhubhaṇḍaṃ adhippetaṃ. Taṃ kāḷavacchakassa bahaladhātukaṃ [V 3.0273] hoti, rattavacchakassa vippasannaṃ, taṃmuhuttajātarattavacchasadisacakkhubhaṇḍoti attho. Aññesañhi akkhibhaṇḍā aparipuṇṇā honti, hatthimūsikakākādīnaṃ akkhisadisehi viniggatehi gambhīrehipi akkhīhi samannāgatā honti. Tathāgatassa pana dhovitvā majjitvā ṭhapitamaṇiguḷikā viya mudusiniddhanīlasukhumapakhumācitāni akkhīni.

Herein, in the phrase “having eyelashes like a cow's” (gopakhumo), “eyelashes” (pakhuma) refers to the entire eyelash structure. For a black calf, this is thick; for a red calf, it is very clear. The meaning is that he has an eyelash structure like that of a newly born red calf. The eyelash structures of others are incomplete; they are endowed with protruding or deep-set eyes, similar to the eyes of elephants, mice, crows, and so on. But the Tathāgata's eyes are like jewel-beads that have been washed, polished, and set, fringed with eyelashes that are soft, smooth, dark blue, and delicate.

Uṇṇāti uṇṇalomaṃ. Bhamukantareti [P 3.0385] dvinnaṃ bhamukānaṃ vemajjhe nāsikamatthakeyeva jātā. Uggantvā pana nalāṭamajjhajātā. Odātāti parisuddhā osadhitārakavaṇṇā. Mudūti sappimaṇḍe osādetvā ṭhapitasatavāravihatakappāsapaṭalasadisā. Tūlasannibhāti simbalitūlalatātūlasamānā, ayamassā odātatāya upamā. Sā panesā koṭiyaṃ gahetvā ākaḍḍhiyamānā upaḍḍhabāhuppamāṇā hoti, vissaṭṭhā dakkhiṇāvaṭṭavasena āvaṭṭitvā uddhaggā hutvā santiṭṭhati, suvaṇṇaphalakamajjhe ṭhapitarajatapupphuḷakā viya suvaṇṇaghaṭato nikkhamamānā khīradhārā viya aruṇappabhārañjite gamanatale osadhitārakā viya ca atimanoharāya siriyā virocati.

The 'uṇṇā' means the noble hair (uṇṇaloma). 'Between the eyebrows' means it grows in the middle of the two eyebrows, just above the nose. Furthermore, having ascended, it is situated in the middle of the forehead. 'White' means it is pure, having the color of the morning star. 'Soft' means it is like a layer of cotton that has been teased a hundred times, dipped in ghee, and set down. 'Resembling cotton' means it is like silk-cotton or creeper-cotton; this is a simile for its whiteness. Furthermore, when it is grasped at the tip and pulled, it is half an arm's length. When released, it coils clockwise, stands with its tip pointing upwards, and remains settled. It shines with an exceedingly captivating splendor, like a silver bubble placed in the middle of a golden plank, like a stream of milk flowing from a golden pot, and like the morning star in the expanse of the sky tinted with the radiance of dawn.

Uṇhīsasīsoti idaṃ paripuṇṇanalāṭatañceva paripuṇṇasīsatañcāti dve atthavase paṭicca vuttaṃ. Tathāgatassa hi dakkhiṇakaṇṇacūḷikato paṭṭhāya maṃsapaṭalaṃ uṭṭhahitvā sakalaṃ nalāṭaṃ chādayamānaṃ pūrayamānaṃ gantvā vāmakaṇṇacūḷikāya patiṭṭhitaṃ, rañño baddhauṇhīsapaṭṭo viya virocati. Pacchimabhavikabodhisattānaṃ kira imaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ viditvā rājūnaṃ uṇhīsapaṭṭaṃ akaṃsu, ayaṃ tāva eko attho. Aññe pana janā aparipuṇṇasīsā honti, keci [P 3.0386] kappasīsā, keci phalasīsā, keci aṭṭhisīsā, keci tumbasīsā, keci pabbhārasīsā. Tathāgatassa pana āraggena vaṭṭetvā ṭhapitaṃ viya suparipuṇṇaṃ udakapupphuḷasadisaṃ sīsaṃ hoti. Tattha purimanayena uṇhīsaveṭhitasīso [M 3.0265] viyāti uṇhīsasīso. Dutiyanayena uṇhīsaṃ viya sabbattha parimaṇḍalasīsoti uṇhīsasīso.

'Head with an uṇhīsa' (uṇhīsasīsa) is stated in dependence on two special meanings: having a perfectly full forehead and having a perfectly complete head. Indeed, for the Tathāgata, a layer of flesh, arising from the tip of the right ear-lobe, goes on to cover and fill the entire forehead, and is established at the tip of the left ear-lobe; it shines like a king's bound royal headband. It is said that, having known this characteristic of Bodhisattas in their final existence, they made royal headbands for kings in imitation. This, for now, is the first meaning. Other people, however, have incomplete heads: some have monkey-like heads, some have fruit-like heads, some have bony heads, some have gourd-like heads, and some have heads with a sloping back. The Tathāgata's head, however, is perfectly complete and like a water bubble, as if turned with the point of an awl and set down. Therein, according to the first method, because his head is like one bound with a royal headband, he is called 'uṇhīsasīsa'. According to the second method, because his head is perfectly round in all aspects like a royal headband, he is called 'uṇhīsasīsa'.

Imāni pana mahāpurisalakkhaṇāni kammaṃ kammasarikkhakaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ lakkhaṇānisaṃsanti ime cattāro koṭṭhāse ekekasmiṃ lakkhaṇe dassetvā kathitāni sukathitāni honti. Tasmā bhagavatā lakkhaṇasutte (dī. ni. 3.200-202) vuttāni imāni kammādīni dassetvā kathetabbāni[V 3.0274]. Suttavasena vinicchituṃ asakkontena sumaṅgalavilāsiniyā dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāya tasseva suttassa vaṇṇanāya vuttanayena gahetabbāni.

Furthermore, these characteristics of a great man are well-explained when they are shown and spoken of for each individual characteristic according to these four aspects: the kamma that causes the characteristic, the correspondence with the kamma, the characteristic itself, and the benefit of the characteristic. Therefore, these four aspects beginning with kamma, as stated by the Blessed One in the Lakkhaṇa Sutta, should be shown and explained by one who wishes to commentate. By a teacher of the Dhamma who is unable to decide based on the Sutta, they should be understood according to the method stated in the commentary on that very Sutta in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the commentary to the Dīghanikāya.

Imehi kho, bho, so bhavaṃ gotamoti, bho ācariya, imehi dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇehi so bhavaṃ gotamo samannāgato devanagare samussitaratanavicittaṃ suvaṇṇatoraṇaṃ viya yojanasatubbedho sabbapāliphullo pāricchattako viya selantaramhi supupphitasālarukkho viya tārāgaṇapaṭimaṇḍitagaganatalamiva ca attano sirivibhavena lokaṃ ālokaṃ kurumāno viya caratīti imatthampi dīpetvā kiriyācāraṃ ācikkhituṃ gacchanto kho panātiādimāha.

'Indeed, venerable sir, with these is the venerable Gotama endowed' means: O teacher, that venerable Gotama is endowed with these thirty-two characteristics of a great man; he moves about as if illuminating the world with the splendor of his own majesty, like a golden archway, variegated with jewels, erected in the city of the devas; like a Pāricchattaka tree, a hundred yojanas high, in full bloom; like a sāla tree, well-blossomed, amidst the mountains; and like the expanse of the sky adorned with a host of stars. Having thus illustrated this meaning as well, in order to declare his conduct and deportment, the young man Uttara spoke the words beginning with 'gacchanto kho pana...'

387. Dakkhiṇenāti buddhānañhi ṭhatvā vā nisīditvā vā nipajjitvā vā gamanaṃ abhinīharantānaṃ dakkhiṇapādova purato hoti. Satatapāṭihāriyaṃ kiretaṃ. Nātidūre [P 3.0387] pādaṃ uddharatīti taṃ dakkhiṇapādaṃ na atidūre ṭhapessāmīti uddharati. Atidūrañhi abhihariyamāne dakkhiṇapādena vāmapādo ākaḍḍhiyamāno gaccheyya, dakkhiṇapādopi dūraṃ gantuṃ na sakkuṇeyya, āsanneyeva patiṭṭhaheyya, evaṃ sati padavicchedo nāma hoti. Dakkhiṇapāde pana pamāṇeneva uddhate vāmapādopi pamāṇeneva uddhariyati, pamāṇena uddhato patiṭṭhahantopi pamāṇeyeva patiṭṭhāti. Evamanena tathāgatassa dakkhiṇapādakiccaṃ vāmapādena niyamitaṃ, vāmapādakiccaṃ dakkhiṇapādena niyamitanti veditabbaṃ.

387. 'With the right' means: indeed, for the Buddhas, whether setting out to go from a standing, sitting, or lying position, it is only the right foot that is foremost. This, it is said, is a constant miracle. 'He does not lift his foot too far' means: he lifts that right foot with the thought, 'I will place it not too far away.' For if it were carried too far, the left foot would be dragged by the right foot, and the right foot too would not be able to go far but would be set down close by. This being so, there would be what is called a break in the stride. But when the right foot is lifted by just the right measure, the left foot is also lifted by just the right measure; and being lifted by the right measure, when it is set down, it is also set down by just the right measure. Thus it should be understood: for the Tathāgata, the function of the right foot is regulated by the left foot, and the function of the left foot is regulated by the right foot.

Nātisīghanti divā vihārabhattatthāya gacchanto bhikkhu viya na atisīghaṃ gacchati. Nātisaṇikanti yathā pacchato āgacchanto okāsaṃ na labhati, evaṃ na atisaṇikaṃ gacchati. Adduvena adduvanti jaṇṇukena jaṇṇukaṃ, na [M 3.0266] satthiṃ unnāmetīti gambhīre udake gacchanto viya na ūruṃ unnāmeti. Na onāmetīti rukkhasākhāchedanadaṇḍaṅkusapādo viya na pacchato osakkāpeti. Na sannāmetīti obaddhānābaddhaṭṭhānehi pādaṃ koṭṭento viya na thaddhaṃ karoti. Na [P 3.0388] vināmetīti yantarūpakaṃ kīḷāpento viya na ito cito ca cāleti. Adharakāyovāti heṭṭhimakāyova iñjati, uparimakāyo nāvāya ṭhapitasuvaṇṇapaṭimā viya niccalo hoti. Dūre ṭhatvā olokento hi buddhānaṃ ṭhitabhāvaṃ vā gamanabhāvaṃ vā na jānāti[V 3.0275]. Kāyabalenāti bāhā khipanto sarīrato sedehi muccantehi na kāyabalena gacchati. Sabbakāyenevāti gīvaṃ aparivattetvā rāhulovāde vuttanāgāpalokitavaseneva apaloketi.

'Not too quickly' means: he does not go too quickly, like a monk going for the monastery meal during the day. 'Not too slowly' means: he does not go so slowly that one coming from behind does not get an opportunity to pass. 'He does not strike his knees together.' 'He does not lift up the thigh' means: he does not lift up his thigh like a person walking in deep water. 'He does not lower it' means: he does not let his foot fall back behind him, like the trailing foot of a man striking tree branches with a long pole. 'He does not bring them together' means: he does not make his feet joined, as if striking them against each other at the ankles. 'He does not bend it' means: he does not move it here and there like one making a mechanical puppet play. 'Only the lower body' means: only the lower part of his body moves; the upper part of his body is motionless, like a golden statue placed on a boat. Indeed, one looking from a distance does not know whether the Buddhas are standing or walking. 'Not by bodily strength' means: he does not go by bodily strength, swinging his arms and with sweat being released from his body. 'He looks around with the whole body' means: without turning his neck, he looks around only in the manner of the 'elephant's look' spoken of in the Rāhulovāda Sutta.

Na uddhantiādīsu nakkhattāni gaṇento viya na uddhaṃ ulloketi, naṭṭhaṃ kākaṇikaṃ vā māsakaṃ vā pariyesanto viya na adho oloketi, na hatthiassādayo passanto viya ito cito ca vipekkhamāno gacchati. Yugamattanti navavidatthimatte cakkhūni ṭhapetvā gacchanto yugamattaṃ pekkhati nāma, bhagavāpi yuge yutto sudantaājānīyo viya ettakaṃ passanto gacchati. Tato cassa uttarīti yugamattato paraṃ na passatīti na vattabbo. Na hi kuṭṭaṃ vā kavāṭaṃ vā gaccho vā latā vā āvarituṃ sakkoti, atha khvassa anāvaraṇañāṇassa anekāni cakkavāḷasahassāni ekaṅgaṇāneva honti. Antaragharanti heṭṭhā mahāsakuludāyisutte indakhīlato paṭṭhāya antaragharaṃ, idha gharaummārato paṭṭhāya veditabbaṃ. Na [P 3.0389] kāyantiādi pakatiiriyapatheneva pavisatīti dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Daliddamanussānaṃ nīcagharakaṃ pavisantepi hi tathāgate chadanaṃ vā uggacchati, pathavī vā ogacchati, bhagavā pana pakatigamaneneva gacchati. Nātidūreti atidūre parivattantena hi ekaṃ dve padavāre piṭṭhibhāgena gantvā nisīditabbaṃ hoti. Nāccāsanneti accāsanne parivattantena ekaṃ dve padavāre purato gantvā nisīditabbaṃ hoti. Tasmā yasmiṃ padavāre ṭhitena purato vā pacchato vā agantvā nisīditabbaṃ hoti, tattha parivattati.

Regarding the phrase 'He does not look up,' and so on, the meaning should be understood in the following way. He does not look up as if counting the stars; he does not look down as if searching for a lost kākaṇika or māsaka coin; he does not go along glancing distractedly here and there as if looking at wild elephants and horses. 'A yoke's length' means that one who walks with their eyes fixed on a spot nine spans ahead is said to be looking a yoke's length; and the Blessed One, like a well-trained thoroughbred yoked to a chariot, walks seeing just that far. It should not be said that he does not see beyond that yoke's length, for no wall, door, bush, or vine can obstruct him. Indeed, for his unobstructed knowledge, many thousands of world-systems are like a single courtyard. 'Within the house'—whereas in the Mahāsakuludāyi Sutta this is to be understood as starting from the city gatepost, here it is to be understood as starting from the threshold of a house. The phrase beginning 'Not with the body...' is stated to show that he enters with a natural posture. For even when the Tathāgata enters the low-roofed houses of poor people, the roof rises and the earth sinks, but the Blessed One for his part walks in his natural manner. 'Not too far'—for one turning around too far from the seat would have to take a step or two backward to sit down. 'Not too close'—for one turning around too close to the seat would have to take a step or two forward to sit down. Therefore, he turns around at the very spot from which he can sit down without having to move forward or backward.

Pāṇināti kaṭivātābādhiko viya na āsanaṃ hatthehi gahetvā nisīdati. Pakkhipatīti yo kiñci kammaṃ katvā kīḷanto ṭhitakova patati, yopi orimaṃ aṅgaṃ nissāya nisinno ghaṃsanto yāva pārimaṅgā gacchati, pārimaṅgaṃ [M 3.0267] vā nissāya nisinno tatheva yāva orimaṅgā āgacchati, sabbo so āsane kāyaṃ pakkhipati nāma. Bhagavā pana evaṃ akatvā āsanassa majjhe olambakaṃ dhārento viya tūlapicuṃ ṭhapento viya saṇikaṃ nisīdati. Hatthakukkuccanti pattamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ udakabinduṭhapanaṃ makkhikabījaniyā paṇṇacchedanaphālanādi hatthena asaṃyatakaraṇaṃ. Pādakukkuccanti pādena bhūmighaṃsanādi asaṃyatakaraṇaṃ.

'With the hands' means he does not sit down by grasping the seat with his hands, like one afflicted with a back ailment. 'To throw the body down' means: whoever, being tired after doing some work, just falls down where they stand; or whoever, sitting leaning on one side, shuffles along rubbing against the seat until they reach the other side; or sitting leaning on the other side, similarly shuffles back to the first side—all this is called 'throwing the body down onto the seat.' The Blessed One, however, does not do so; he sits down gently, as if lowering a plumb line in the middle of the seat or placing down a tuft of cotton. 'Fidgeting with the hands' is unrestrained action with the hands, such as placing drops of water on the rim of the bowl, cutting or splitting leaves with a fan, and so on. 'Fidgeting with the feet' is unrestrained action with the feet, such as scraping the ground, and so on.

Na chambhatīti na bhāyati. Na kampatīti na osīdati. Na vedhatīti na calati. Na [P 3.0390] paritassatīti bhayaparitassanāyapi taṇhāparitassanāyapi na paritassati. Ekacco hi dhammakathādīnaṃ atthāya [V 3.0276] āgantvā manussesu vanditvā ṭhitesu “sakkhissāmi nu kho tesaṃ cittaṃ gaṇhanto dhammaṃ vā kathetuṃ, pañhaṃ vā pucchito vissajjetuṃ, bhattānumodanaṃ vā kātu”nti bhayaparitassanāya paritassati. Ekacco “manāpā nu kho me yāgu āgacchissati, manāpaṃ antarakhajjaka”nti vā taṇhāparitassanāya paritassati. Tadubhayampi tassa natthīti na paritassati. Vivekāvaṭṭoti viveke nibbāne āvaṭṭamānaso hutvā. Vivekavattotipi pāṭho, vivekavattayutto hutvāti attho. Vivekavattaṃ nāma katabhattakiccassa bhikkhuno divāvihāre samathavipassanāvasena mūlakammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā nisīdanaṃ. Evaṃ nisinnassa hi iriyāpatho upasanto hoti.

'He is not terrified' means he is not afraid. 'He does not tremble' means he does not sink down. 'He does not quiver' means he does not stir. 'He is not agitated' means he is not agitated by the agitation of fear, nor is he agitated by the agitation of craving. For a certain person, having come for the purpose of a Dhamma talk or the like, when people are standing paying respects, becomes agitated with the agitation of fear, thinking: 'Will I be able to capture their minds and teach the Dhamma, or answer a question if asked, or give the meal-blessing?' Another person becomes agitated with the agitation of craving, thinking: 'I wonder if some nice gruel will come to me, or some nice solid food?' Both of these are absent for him; therefore, he is not agitated. 'Turned towards seclusion' means having his mind turned towards Nibbāna, which is seclusion from formations. There is also the reading `vivekavatto`, which means 'endowed with the practice of seclusion.' The practice of seclusion is this: a monk who has finished the business of his meal takes up his root meditation subject by way of serenity and insight during his day-sojourn, and sits with his legs crossed. For one sitting thus, his posture is calmed.

Na pattaṃ unnāmetītiādīsu ekacco pattamukhavaṭṭiyā udakadānaṃ āharanto viya pattaṃ unnāmeti, eko pādapiṭṭhiyaṃ ṭhapento viya onāmeti, eko baddhaṃ katvā gaṇhāti, eko ito cito ca phandāpeti, evaṃ akatvā ubhohi hatthehi gahetvā īsakaṃ nāmetvā udakaṃ paṭiggaṇhātīti attho. Na samparivattakanti parivattetvā paṭhamameva pattapiṭṭhiṃ na dhovati. Nātidūreti yathā nisinnāsanato dūre patati, na evaṃ chaḍḍeti. Nāccāsanneti pādamūleyeva na chaḍḍeti. Vicchaḍḍayamānoti [P 3.0391] vikiranto, yathā paṭiggāhako temati, na evaṃ chaḍḍeti.

Regarding the phrase 'He does not lift up the bowl,' and so on: one person lifts up the bowl as if fetching a water pot with the rim of his bowl; another lowers it as if placing it on the top of his foot; another grasps it tightly; another shakes it here and there. Not doing so, he receives the water by taking the bowl with both hands and lowering it slightly—this is the meaning. 'Not turning it all around' means he does not turn the bowl over and wash the outside first. 'Not too far' means he does not discard the water in such a way that it lands far from where he is seated. 'Not too close' means he does not discard it right at his feet. 'Not scattering' means not discarding the water by scattering it, in such a way that the person receiving the bowl back would get wet.

Nātithokanti [M 3.0268] yathā ekacco pāpiccho appicchataṃ dassento muṭṭhimattameva gaṇhāti, na evaṃ. Atibahunti yāpanamattato atirekaṃ. Byañjanamattāyāti byañjanassa mattā nāma odanato catuttho bhāgo. Ekacco hi bhatte manāpe bhattaṃ bahuṃ gaṇhāti, byañjane manāpe byañjanaṃ bahuṃ. Satthā pana tathā na gaṇhāti. Na ca byañjanenāti amanāpañhi byañjanaṃ ṭhapetvā bhattameva bhuñjanto, bhattaṃ vā ṭhapetvā byañjanameva khādanto byañjanena ālopaṃ atināmeti nāma. Satthā ekantarikaṃ byañjanaṃ gaṇhāti, bhattampi byañjanampi ekatova niṭṭhanti. Dvattikkhattunti tathāgatassa hi puthujivhāya dantānaṃ upanītabhojanaṃ dvattikkhattuṃ dantehi phuṭṭhamattameva saṇhakaraṇīyapiṭṭhavilepanaṃ viya hoti, tasmā evamāha. Na mukhe avasiṭṭhāti pokkharapatte patitaudakabindu viya vinivattitvā paragalameva yāti, tasmā avasiṭṭhā na hoti. Rasapaṭisaṃvedīti madhuratittakadukādirasaṃ jānāti. Buddhānañhi antamaso pānīyepi dibbojā pakkhittāva hoti, tena nesaṃ sabbattheva raso pākaṭo hoti, rasagedho pana natthi.

Not too little means: Just as a certain monk of evil desires, wishing to show that he has few wishes, takes only a handful, He does not take in that way. Not too much means: He does not take in excess of what is just enough for sustenance. With a suitable amount of curry means: The measure of curry is a fourth part of the rice. For a certain monk, when the rice is pleasing, takes much rice; when the curry is pleasing, he takes much curry. But the Teacher does not take in that way. And not overwhelming the morsel with curry means: A monk who, setting aside an unpleasing curry, eats only the rice, or setting aside unpleasing rice, eats only the curry, is said to overwhelm the morsel with curry. The Teacher does not take curry on alternate morsels; both the rice and the curry are finished together. Two or three times means: For the Tathāgata, with his broad tongue, the food brought to his teeth, merely upon being touched by the teeth two or three times, becomes like an ointment made of fine flour. Therefore, it was said thus. Nothing remains in the mouth means: Like a drop of water that has fallen on a lotus leaf, it rolls and goes right down the throat. Therefore, no morsel of food remains. Experiencing the taste means: He knows tastes such as sweet, bitter, and pungent. Truly, for the Buddhas, at the very least, even in drinking water, divine nutritive essence is as if infused. Therefore, for them, the taste in all suitable things is manifest. But there is no greed for taste.

Aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgatanti [P 3.0392] “neva davāyā”ti vuttehi aṭṭhahi aṅgehi samannāgataṃ. Visuddhimagge panassa [V 3.0277] vinicchayo āgatoti sabbāsavasutte vuttametaṃ. Hatthesu dhotesūti satthā kiṃ karoti? Paṭhamaṃ pattassa gahaṇaṭṭhānaṃ dhovati. Tattha pattaṃ gahetvā sukhumajālahatthaṃ pesetvā dve vāre sañcāreti. Ettāvatā pokkharapatte patitaudakaṃ viya vinivattitvā gacchati. Na ca anatthikoti yathā ekacco pattaṃ ādhārake ṭhapetvā patte udakaṃ na puñchati, raje patante ajjhupekkhati, na evaṃ karoti. Na ca ativelānurakkhīti yathā ekacco pamāṇātikkantaṃ ārakkhaṃ ṭhapeti, bhuñjitvā vā patte udakaṃ puñchitvā cīvarabhogantaraṃ pavesetvā pattaṃ udarena akkamitvā gaṇhāti, na evaṃ karoti.

Endowed with eight factors means: Endowed with the eight factors spoken of as 'not for amusement...'. Its analysis is found in the Visuddhimagga; this is stated in the Sabbāsava Sutta. When the hands are washed means: What does the Teacher do? First, he washes the place for holding the bowl. Therein, having taken the bowl, he extends his finely-meshed hand and moves it twice. By just that much, the water rolls off and goes away like water that has fallen on a lotus leaf. And not unconcerned means: Just as a certain monk, having placed the bowl on a stand, does not wipe the water in the bowl and is indifferent when dust falls in, He does not act in that way. And not excessively protective means: Just as a certain monk establishes protection that exceeds the limit; or, having eaten, wipes the water in the bowl, inserts it into the fold of his robe, and takes the bowl by pressing it with his belly, He does not act in that way.

Na ca anumodanassāti yo hi bhuttamattova dārakesu bhattatthāya rodantesu chātajjhattesu manussesu bhuñjitvā anāgatesveva anumodanaṃ ārabhati, tato sabbakammāni chaḍḍetvā ekacce āgacchanti, ekacce anāgatāva honti, ayaṃ kālaṃ atināmeti. Yopi manussesu [M 3.0269] āgantvā anumodanatthāya vanditvā nisinnesu anumodanaṃ akatvāva “kathaṃ tissa, kathaṃ phussa, kathaṃ sumana, kathaṃ tisse, kathaṃ phusse, kathaṃ sumane, kaccittha arogā, sassaṃ sampanna”ntiādiṃ pāṭiyekkaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti, ayaṃ anumodanassa kālaṃ atināmeti, manussānaṃ pana okāsaṃ ñatvā āyācitakāle karonto nātināmeti nāma, satthā tathā karoti.

And not transgressing the time for the anumodanā means: A monk who, having just eaten, begins the anumodanā while children are crying for food and before the people afflicted by hunger have eaten and arrived. Because of this, some people, having abandoned all their work, come, while others have not yet arrived. This monk is said to transgress the time. Also, a monk who, when people have come, paid respects for the sake of the anumodanā, and are seated, without yet giving the anumodanā, starts up other worldly talk such as, 'How are you, Tissa? How are you, Phussa? How are you, Sumana? How are you, Tissā? How are you, Phussā? Are you well? Is the harvest plentiful?' and so on—this monk is said to transgress the time for the anumodanā. But a monk who, having known the people's opportunity to listen, gives it at the requested time, is said not to transgress the time. The Teacher acts in that way.

Na taṃ bhattanti kiṃ bhattaṃ nāmetaṃ uttaṇḍulaṃ atikilinnantiādīni vatvā na garahati. Na [P 3.0393] aññaṃ bhattanti svātanāya vā punadivasāya vā bhattaṃ uppādessāmīti hi anumodanaṃ karonto aññaṃ bhattaṃ paṭikaṅkhati. Yo vā – “yāva mātugāmānaṃ bhattaṃ paccati, tāva anumodanaṃ karissāmi, atha me anumodanāvasāne attano pakkabhattatopi thokaṃ dassantī”ti anumodanaṃ vaḍḍheti, ayampi paṭikaṅkhati nāma. Satthā na evaṃ karoti. Na ca muccitukāmoti ekacco hi paṭisaṃmuñcitvā gacchati, vegena anubandhitabbo hoti. Satthā pana na evaṃ gacchati, parisāya majjhe ṭhitova gacchati. Accukkaṭṭhanti yo hi yāva hanukaṭṭhito ukkhipitvā pārupati, tassa accukkaṭṭhaṃ nāma hoti. Yo yāva gopphakā otāretvāva pārupati, tassa accukkaṭṭhaṃ hoti. Yopi ubhato ukkhipitvā udaraṃ vivaritvā yāti, tassapi accukkaṭṭhaṃ hoti. Yo ekaṃsaṃ katvā thanaṃ vivaritvā yāti, tassapi accukkaṭṭhaṃ. Satthā taṃ sabbaṃ na karoti.

He does not disparage that food means: He does not disparage the offered food by saying such things as, 'What kind of food is this? It is undercooked. It is too soft.' Not another meal means: A monk who gives the anumodanā while thinking, 'I will cause food to arise for tomorrow or for the next day,' is said to desire another meal. Or, a monk who extends the anumodanā, thinking, 'I will give the anumodanā for as long as the women are cooking the food. Then, at the end of my anumodanā, they will give me a little even from their own cooked food'—this monk too is said to desire a meal. The Teacher does not act in this way. And not wishing to be released means: A certain monk, having dismissed the assembly, goes quickly and has to be followed swiftly. The Teacher, however, does not go in this way; he departs while standing in the midst of the assembly. Worn improperly high or low means: For a monk who wears his robe lifted up to his chin, this is called 'worn too high.' For one who wears it lowered to the ankles, this is called 'worn too low.' For one who lifts it on both sides, exposing his belly as he walks, this too is 'worn too high.' For one who makes it one-shouldered, exposing his chest as he walks, this too is 'worn too high.' The Teacher does none of these things.

Allīnanti [V 3.0278] yathā aññesaṃ sedena tintaṃ allīyati, na evaṃ satthu. Apakaṭṭhanti khalisāṭako viya kāyato muccitvāpi na tiṭṭhati. Vātoti verambhavātopi uṭṭhahitvā cāletuṃ na sakkoti. Pādamaṇḍanānuyoganti iṭṭhakāya ghaṃsanādīhi pādasobhānuyogaṃ. Pakkhāletvāti pādeneva pādaṃ dhovitvā. So neva attabyābādhāyātiādīni na pubbenivāsacetopariyañāṇānaṃ atthitāya vadati, iriyāpathasantataṃ pana disvā anumānena vadati. Dhammanti pariyattidhammaṃ. Na ussādetīti [P 3.0394] kiṃ mahāraṭṭhika, kiṃ mahākuṭumbikātiādīni vatvā gehassitavasena na ussādeti. Na apasādetīti “kiṃ, upāsaka, kathaṃ te vihāramaggo ñāto? Kiṃ bhayena nāgacchasi? Na hi bhikkhū kiñci acchinditvā gaṇhanti, mā bhāyī”ti [M 3.0270] vā “kiṃ tuyhaṃ evaṃ macchariyajīvitaṃ nāmā”ti vā ādīni vatvā gehassitapemena na apasādeti.

Not clinging means: Just as for others, the robe, being wet with sweat, clings to the body, it is not so for the Teacher; his robe does not cling. Not standing apart means: Like a starched cloth, his robe does not stand apart from his body even when released. By the wind means: Even a Verambha wind, having arisen, is not able to shake it. The practice of adorning the feet means: The practice of beautifying the feet by such means as rubbing with a brick. Having washed means: Having washed one foot with the other foot. He (Uttara) does not say the words 'not for the affliction of self...' because of possessing the knowledge of past lives or the knowledge of others' minds; rather, having seen the tranquility of His deportment, he speaks by inference. 'Dhamma' means the Dhamma of the scriptures. 'He does not exalt' means: He does not exalt by way of household connection, saying things like, 'Are you a great provincial ruler? Are you a great householder?' 'He does not disparage' means: He does not disparage with affection based on the household life, saying things like, 'What, lay follower, how did you know the way to the monastery? Why do you not come out of fear? Truly, the monks do not snatch anything, do not be afraid,' or 'Why this miserly life of yours?'

Vissaṭṭhoti siniddho apalibuddho. Viññeyyoti viññāpanīyo pākaṭo, vissaṭṭhattāyeva cesa viññeyyo hoti. Mañjūti madhuro. Savanīyoti sotasukho, madhurattāyeva cesa savanīyo hoti. Bindūti sampiṇḍito. Avisārīti avisaṭo, binduttāyeva cesa avisārī hoti. Gambhīroti gambhīrasamuṭṭhito. Ninnādīti ninnādavā, gambhīrattāyeva cesa ninnādī hoti. Yathāparisanti cakkavāḷapariyantampi ekābaddhaparisaṃ viññāpeti. Bahiddhāti aṅgulimattampi parisato bahiddhā na gacchati. Tasmā? So evarūpo madhurassaro akāraṇā mā nassīti. Iti bhagavato ghoso parisāya matthakeneva carati.

“Vissaṭṭha” means smooth, unobstructed. “Viññeyya” means intelligible, manifest; and it is precisely because of its smoothness that this voice is intelligible. “Mañju” means sweet. “Savanīya” means pleasant to the ear; and it is precisely because of its sweetness that this voice is pleasant to hear. “Bindu” means compact. “Avisārī” means not scattered; and it is precisely because of its compactness that this voice is not scattered. “Gambhīra” means originating from a depth. “Ninnādī” means resonant; and it is precisely because of its depth that this voice is resonant. “Yathāparisaṃ” means it makes itself understood to the assembly, which is as one, even to the confines of the universe. “Bahiddhā” means the voice does not go outside the assembly even by a finger's breadth. Why is that? So that such a sweet voice may not perish without cause. Thus, the Blessed One's voice travels only over the heads of the assembly.

Avalokayamānāti [P 3.0395] sirasmiṃ añjaliṃ ṭhapetvā bhagavantaṃ olokentāva paccosakkitvā dassanavijahanaṭṭhāne vanditvā gacchanti. Avijahitattāti yo hi kathaṃ sutvā vuṭṭhito aññaṃ diṭṭhasutādikaṃ kathaṃ kathento gacchati, esa sabhāvena vijahati nāma. Yo pana sutadhammakathāya vaṇṇaṃ kathentova gacchati, ayaṃ na vijahati nāma, evaṃ avijahantabhāvena pakkamanti. Gacchantanti rajjuyantavasena ratanasattubbedhaṃ suvaṇṇagghikaṃ viya gacchantaṃ. Addasāma ṭhitanti samussitakañcanapabbataṃ viya ṭhitaṃ addasāma. Tato ca bhiyyoti vitthāretvā guṇe kathetuṃ asakkonto avasese guṇe saṃkhipitvā kalāpaṃ viya suttakabaddhaṃ viya ca katvā vissajjento evamāha. Ayamettha adhippāyo – mayā kathitaguṇehi akathitāva bahutarā. Mahāpathavimahāsamuddādayo viya hi tassa bhoto anantā appameyyā guṇā ākāsamiva vitthāritāti.

“Avalokayamānā” means: having placed their hands in añjali at their heads and gazing upon the Blessed One, they withdrew, paid homage at the place where they lost sight of him, and then departed. “Avijahitattā” means: for one who, having heard a discourse, rises and departs while discussing other things seen, heard, and so on, is said to abandon it by nature. But one who departs while speaking of the excellence of the Dhamma discourse just heard, is said not to abandon it. Thus, they depart with the quality of not abandoning. “Gacchantaṃ” means: him going, like a great golden stupa one hundred cubits high moving by means of a rope-machine. “Addasāma ṭhitaṃ” means: we saw him standing like a well-erected golden mountain. “Tato ca bhiyyo” means: unable to speak of the qualities in detail, he condensed the remaining qualities, making them like a bundle or like something bound with thread, and releasing them, spoke thus. This is the intention here: the qualities unspoken by me are far more numerous than those spoken. For, like the great earth, the great ocean, and so on, the endless, immeasurable qualities of that venerable one are spread out like the sky.

390. Appaṭisaṃviditoti [V 3.0279] aviññātaāgamano. Pabbajite upasaṅkamantena hi cīvaraparikammādisamaye vā ekaṃ nivāsetvā sarīrabhañjanasamaye vā upasaṅkamitvā tatova paṭinivattitabbaṃ hoti, paṭisanthāramattampi na jāyati. Puretaraṃ pana okāse kārite divāṭṭhānaṃ sammajjitvā cīvaraṃ pārupitvā bhikkhu vivitte ṭhāne nisīdati, taṃ āgantvā passantā dassanenapi [M 3.0271] pasīdanti, paṭisanthāro jāyati, pañhabyākaraṇaṃ [P 3.0396] vā dhammakathā vā labbhati. Tasmā paṇḍitā okāsaṃ kārenti. So ca nesaṃ aññataro, tenassa etadahosi. Jiṇṇo vuḍḍhoti attano uggatabhāvaṃ akathetvā kasmā evamāha? Buddhā nāma anuddayasampannā honti, mahallakabhāvaṃ ñatvā sīghaṃ okāsaṃ karissatīti evamāha.

390. “Appaṭisaṃvidito” means one whose arrival is not made known. For if a layperson approaches a monk at an improper time, such as when he is preparing his robes or, having put on a single robe, is anointing his body, one must turn back right from there; not even a mere greeting arises. But if an opportunity is made beforehand, a monk sweeps the day-resting place, dons his robe, and sits in a secluded place. When visitors come and see him, they are pleased even by the sight, a greeting arises, and they receive answers to questions or a Dhamma talk. Therefore, the wise make an opportunity. And he was one of them, which is why this thought occurred to him. “Jiṇṇo vuḍḍho”: Why did he speak thus, without mentioning his own eminence? He spoke thus thinking: “Buddhas are endowed with compassion. Knowing my old age, He will quickly make an opportunity for me.”

391. Oramiya okāsamakāsīti vegena uṭṭhāya dvidhā bhijjitvā okāsamakāsi.

391. “Oramiya okāsamakāsi” means: the assembly, quickly rising, parted into two and made an opportunity.

Ye meti ye mayā. Nārīsamānasavhayāti nārīsamānanāmaṃ itthiliṅgaṃ, tena avhātabbāti nārīsamānasavhayā, itthiliṅgena vattabbāti vohārakusalatāya evaṃ vadati. Pahūtajivhoti puthulajivho. Ninnāmayetanti nīhara etaṃ.

“Ye me” means “which by me.” “Nārīsamānasavhayā”: The name “nārīsamāna” is a feminine noun. Because it should be addressed with a term similar to “woman,” it is called “nārīsamānasavhayā.” It should be spoken of with the feminine gender; he speaks thus due to skill in conventional speech. “Pahūtajivho” means having a broad tongue. “Ninnāmayetaṃ” means “Please bring it out and show it.”

393. Kevalīti sakalaguṇasampanno.

393. “Kevalī” means one endowed with all qualities.

394. Paccabhāsīti ekappahārena pucchite aṭṭha pañhe byākaronto patiabhāsi. Yo vedīti yo vidati jānāti, yassa pubbenivāso pākaṭo. Saggāpāyañca passatīti dibbacakkhuñāṇaṃ kathitaṃ. Jātikkhayaṃ [P 3.0397] pattoti arahattaṃ patto. Abhiññā vositoti taṃ arahattaṃ abhijānitvā vosito vosānappatto. Munīti arahattañāṇamoneyyena samannāgato.

394. “Paccabhāsi” means: replying, he answered the eight questions that were asked all at once. “Yo vedi” means: one who knows, one for whom past lives are manifest. “Saggāpāyañca passatī” refers to the knowledge of the divine eye. “Jātikkhayaṃ patto” means one who has attained Arahantship. “Abhiññā vosito” means: having directly known that Arahantship, one has reached the culmination, the end. “Muni” means one endowed with the sagehood that is the knowledge of Arahantship.

Visuddhanti paṇḍaraṃ. Muttaṃ rāgehīti kilesarāgehi muttaṃ. Pahīnajātimaraṇoti jātikkhayappattattā pahīnajātiko, jātipahāneneva pahīnamaraṇo. Brahmacariyassa kevalīti yaṃ brahmacariyassa kevalī sakalabhāvo, tena samannāgato, sakalacatumaggabrahmacariyavāsoti attho. Pāragū sabbadhammānanti sabbesaṃ lokiyalokuttaradhammānaṃ abhiññāya pāraṃ gato, sabbadhamme abhijānitvā ṭhitoti attho. Pāragūti vā ettāvatā pariññāpāragū pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ, pahānapāragū sabbakilesānaṃ[V 3.0280], bhāvanāpāragū catunnaṃ maggānaṃ, sacchikiriyāpāragū nirodhassa, samāpattipāragū sabbasamāpattīnanti ayamattho vutto. Puna sabbadhammānanti iminā abhiññāpāragū vuttoti. Buddho tādī pavuccatīti tādiso chahi [M 3.0272] ākārehi pāraṃ gato sabbākārena catunnaṃ saccānaṃ buddhattā buddhoti pavuccatīti.

“Visuddhaṃ” means pure, white. “Muttaṃ rāgehi” means freed from the defilements of lust. “Pahīnajātimaraṇo” means: because one has attained the destruction of birth, birth is abandoned; and precisely by the abandoning of birth, death is abandoned. “Brahmacariyassa kevalī” means: one who is complete in the holy life, endowed with the entirety of the holy life; the meaning is one who dwells in the complete holy life of the four paths. “Pāragū sabbadhammānaṃ” means: one who has gone to the far shore of all worldly and supramundane phenomena through direct knowledge; the meaning is one who stands firm having directly known all phenomena. Alternatively, “pāragū” means: one who has gone to the far shore of full understanding of the five aggregates, gone to the far shore of abandoning all defilements, gone to the far shore of developing the four paths, gone to the far shore of realizing cessation, and gone to the far shore of attaining all meditative attainments—this is the meaning spoken of. Then, by “sabbadhammānaṃ,” one who has gone to the far shore of direct knowledge is spoken of. “Buddho tādī pavuccati” means: such a one, having gone to the far shore in six ways, is called “Buddha” because of having awakened to the four truths in every way.

Kiṃ pana ettāvatā sabbe pañhā vissajjitā hontīti? Āma vissajjitā, cittaṃ visuddhaṃ jānāti, muttaṃ rāgehīti iminā tāva bāhitapāpattā brāhmaṇoti paṭhamapañho vissajjito hoti. Pāragūti iminā vedehi gatattā vedagūti dutiyapañho vissajjito hoti. Pubbenivāsantiādīhi imāsaṃ tissannaṃ vijjānaṃ [P 3.0398] atthitāya tevijjoti tatiyapañho vissajjito hoti. Muttaṃ rāgehi sabbasoti imināva nissaṭattā pāpadhammānaṃ sottiyoti catutthapañho vissajjito hoti. Jātikkhayaṃ pattoti iminā pana arahattasseva vuttattā pañcamapañho vissajjito hoti. Vositoti ca brahmacariyassa kevalīti ca imehi chaṭṭhapañho vissajjito hoti. Abhiññā vosito munīti iminā sattamapañho vissajjito hoti. Pāragū sabbadhammānaṃ, buddho tādī pavuccatīti iminā aṭṭhamapañho vissajjito hoti.

Now then, by this much have all the questions been answered? Yes, they have been answered. By this text, 'One knows the mind is pure, freed from lusts,' firstly, because of having expelled evil, the first question regarding the brahmin is answered. By this text, 'One who has gone beyond,' because of having gone by means of the path-knowledges, the second question regarding the vedagū is answered. By the texts beginning with 'knowledge of past lives,' because of the existence of these three knowledges, the third question regarding the tevijjo is answered. By this very text, 'Freed from lusts entirely,' because of being released from evil qualities, the fourth question regarding the sotthiya is answered. Now, by this text, 'Having reached the destruction of birth,' because only Arahantship is spoken of, the fifth question is answered. By these two phrases, 'Accomplished' and 'perfected in the holy life,' the sixth question is answered. By this text, 'Accomplished in direct knowledge, the sage,' the seventh question is answered. By this text, 'One who has gone beyond all phenomena, the Buddha is called "Such a One",' the eighth question is answered.

395. Dānakathantiādīni heṭṭhā sutte vitthāritāneva. Paccapādīti paṭipajji. Dhammassānudhammanti imasmiṃ sutte dhammo nāma arahattamaggo, anudhammo nāma heṭṭhimā tayo maggā tīṇi ca sāmaññaphalāni, tāni paṭipāṭiyā paṭilabhīti attho. Na ca maṃ dhammādhikaraṇaṃ vihesesīti mañca dhammakāraṇā na kilamesi, na punappunaṃ kathāpesīti vuttaṃ hoti. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānameva. Tattha parinibbāyīti pana padena desanāya arahatteneva kūṭaṃ gahitanti.

395. The topics beginning with the talk on giving have been elaborated upon in the previous sutta. 'He practiced' means he undertook the practice. As for 'the Dhamma and what conforms to the Dhamma': in this sutta, 'Dhamma' means the path to Arahantship, and 'what conforms to the Dhamma' means the three lower paths and the three fruits of recluseship. The meaning is that he attained them in sequence. As for 'And he did not trouble me regarding the Dhamma,' it means: he did not weary me for the sake of the Dhamma, he did not make me speak again and again. The rest is clear everywhere. Furthermore, by the phrase 'one who attains final Nibbāna there,' the summit of the teaching was taken with Arahantship itself.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Brahmāyusuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Brahmāyu Sutta is concluded.

2. Selasuttavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Sela Sutta

396. Evaṃ [V 3.0281] me sutanti selasuttaṃ. Tattha aṅguttarāpesūtiādi potaliyasutte vitthāritameva. Aḍḍhateḷasehīti aḍḍhena teḷasehi, dvādasahi [M 3.0273] satehi [P 3.0399] paññāsāya ca bhikkhūhi saddhinti vuttaṃ hoti. Te pana sāvakasannipāte sannipatitā bhikkhūyeva sabbe ehibhikkhupabbajjāya pabbajitā khīṇāsavā. Keṇiyoti tassa nāmaṃ, jaṭiloti tāpaso. So kira brāhmaṇamahāsālo, dhanarakkhaṇatthāya pana tāpasapabbajjaṃ samādāya rañño paṇṇākāraṃ datvā bhūmibhāgaṃ gahetvā tattha assamaṃ kāretvā vasati pañcahi sakaṭasatehi vaṇijjaṃ payojetvā kulasahassassa nissayo hutvā, assamepi cassa eko tālarukkho divase divase ekaṃ sovaṇṇamayaṃ tālaphalaṃ muñcatīti vadanti. So divā kāsāyāni dhāreti, jaṭā ca bandhati, rattiṃ kāmasampattiṃ anubhavati. Dhammiyā kathāyāti pānakānisaṃsapaṭisaṃyuttāya dhammiyā kathāya. Ayañhi keṇiyo tucchahattho bhagavato dassanāya gantuṃ lajjāyamāno – “vikālabhojanā viratānampi pānakaṃ kappatī”ti cintetvā susaṅkhatabadarapānaṃ pañcahi kājasatehi gāhāpetvā agamāsi. Evaṃ gatabhāvo cassa – “atha kho keṇiyassa jaṭilassa etadahosi kiṃ nu kho ahaṃ samaṇassa gotamassa harāpeyya”nti bhesajjakkhandhake (mahāva. 300) pāḷiāruḷhoyeva.

396. 'Thus have I heard'—this is the Sela Sutta. Therein, the passage beginning 'In Aṅguttarāpa' has been elaborated upon in the Potaliya Sutta. 'With twelve and a half hundred' means with twelve hundred and fifty bhikkhus. Furthermore, all those bhikkhus gathered in the assembly of disciples were Arahants, ordained with the 'Come, bhikkhu' ordination. 'Keṇiya' was his name; 'jaṭila' means a matted-hair ascetic. He, it is said, was a brahmin of great wealth. However, for the sake of protecting his wealth, he undertook the life of an ascetic, gave tribute to the king, received a portion of land, had a hermitage built there, and dwelt there. Engaging in trade with five hundred carts, he became a support for a thousand families. It is also said that in his hermitage, a single palm tree would daily release one golden palm fruit.
