By day, he wore saffron robes and tied his matted hair, but at night, he enjoyed sensual pleasures. 'With a talk on the Dhamma' means with a talk on the Dhamma connected to the benefits of drinks. For this Keṇiya, being ashamed to go see the Blessed One empty-handed, thought, 'A drink is allowable even for those who abstain from eating at the wrong time.' Having had five hundred shoulder-poles of well-prepared drink brought, he went. The fact of his having gone thus is recorded in the Pali of the Bhesajjakkhandhaka: 'Then this thought occurred to Keṇiya the matted-hair ascetic: "What now should I have brought for the recluse Gotama?"'

Dutiyampi kho bhagavāti kasmā punappunaṃ paṭikkhipi? Titthiyānaṃ paṭikkhepapasannatāya, akāraṇametaṃ, natthi buddhānaṃ paccayahetu evarūpaṃ kohaññaṃ. Ayaṃ pana aḍḍhateḷasāni bhikkhusatāni disvā ettakānaṃyeva [P 3.0400] bhikkhaṃ paṭiyādessati, sveva selo tīhi purisasatehi saddhiṃ pabbajissati. Ayuttaṃ kho pana navake aññato pesetvā imeheva saddhiṃ gantuṃ, ime vā aññato pesetvā navakehi saddhiṃ gantuṃ. Athāpi sabbe gahetvā gamissāmi, bhikkhāhāro nappahossati. Tato bhikkhūsu piṇḍāya carantesu manussā ujjhāyissanti – “cirassāpi keṇiyo samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ nimantetvā yāpanamattaṃ dātuṃ nāsakkhī”ti, sayampi vippaṭisārī bhavissati. Paṭikkhepe pana kate “samaṇo gotamo punappunaṃ ‘tvañca brāhmaṇesu abhippasanno’ti [V 3.0282] brāhmaṇānaṃ nāmaṃ gaṇhātī”ti cintetvā brāhmaṇepi nimantetukāmo bhavissati, tato brāhmaṇe pāṭiyekkaṃ nimantessati[M 3.0274], te tena nimantitā bhikkhū hutvā bhuñjissanti. Evamassa saddhā anurakkhitā bhavissatīti punappunaṃ paṭikkhipi. Kiñcāpi kho, bhoti iminā idaṃ dīpeti, – “bho gotama, kiṃ jātaṃ yadi ahaṃ brāhmaṇesu abhippasanno, adhivāsetu bhavaṃ gotamo, ahaṃ brāhmaṇānampi dātuṃ sakkomi tumhākampī”ti.

Why did the Blessed One refuse again and again? Is it because he is pleased by refusal, as sectarians are? That is not the reason. For Buddhas, there is no such craftiness on account of requisites. Rather, seeing the twelve hundred and fifty bhikkhus, he thought: 'He will prepare almsfood for only this many. But tomorrow, Sela will go forth with three hundred men. It is not proper to send the new ones elsewhere and go only with these, nor to send these elsewhere and go with the new ones. And if I go taking all of them, the almsfood will not be sufficient. Then, when the bhikkhus go about for alms, people will complain, saying: "After such a long-awaited invitation, Keṇiya was not able to give even enough to subsist on." He himself will also become remorseful. On the other hand, when the refusal is made, he will think, "The recluse Gotama repeatedly takes the name of the brahmins, saying, 'And you are very devoted to the brahmins'," and he will become desirous of inviting the brahmins also. Then he will invite the brahmins separately. They, having been invited by him, will eat after becoming bhikkhus. In this way, his faith will be protected.' Having considered this, he refused again and again. By the phrase 'Even so, venerable sir,' this is shown: 'Venerable Gotama, what does it matter if I am devoted to the brahmins? Let the venerable Gotama accept. I am able to give to the brahmins also.'

Kāyaveyyāvaṭikanti kāyaveyyāvaccaṃ. Maṇḍalamāḷanti dussamaṇḍapaṃ.

'Bodily duty' means service with the body. 'Circular hall' means a cloth pavilion.

397. Āvāhoti kaññāgahaṇaṃ. Vivāhoti kaññādānaṃ. So me nimantitoti so mayā nimantito. Atha brāhmaṇo paripakkopanissayattā buddhasaddaṃ sutvāva amatenevābhisitto pasādaṃ āvikaronto buddhoti[P 3.0401], bho keṇiya, vadesīti āha. Keṇiyo yathābhūtaṃ ācikkhanto buddhoti, bho sela, vadāmīti āha. Tato naṃ punapi daḷhīkaraṇatthaṃ pucchi, itaropi tatheva ārocesi.

397. 'Bringing a bride' is the taking of a maiden. 'Giving in marriage' is the giving of a maiden. 'He is invited by me' means 'He has been invited by me.' Then the brahmin, because his supporting condition was mature, just upon hearing the word 'Buddha,' was as if sprinkled with the deathless. Manifesting his faith, he said: 'Venerable Keṇiya, do you say, "Buddha"?' Keṇiya, speaking in accordance with reality, said: 'Venerable Sela, I do say, "Buddha".' Then he asked him again in order to make it firm, and the other informed him in the same way.

398. Athassa kappasatasahassehipi buddhasaddasseva dullabhabhāvaṃ sampassato. Etadahosīti. Etaṃ “ghosopi kho”tiādi ahosi. Nīlavanarājīti nīlavaṇṇarukkhapanti. Pade padanti padappamāṇe padaṃ. Accāsanne hi atidūre vā pāde nikkhipamāne saddo uṭṭhāti, taṃ paṭisedhento evamāha. Sīhāva ekacarāti gaṇavāsī sīho sīhapotakādīhi saddhiṃ pamādaṃ āpajjati, ekacaro appamatto hoti. Iti appamādavihāraṃ dassento ekacarasīhena opammaṃ karoti. Mā me bhontoti ācāraṃ sikkhāpento āha. Ayañhettha adhippāyo – sace tumhe kathāvāraṃ alabhitvā mama kathāya antare kathaṃ pavesessatha, “antevāsike sikkhāpetuṃ nāsakkhī”ti mayhaṃ garahā uppajjissati, tasmā okāsaṃ passitvā manteyyāthāti. No ca kho naṃ jānāmīti vipassīpi bodhisatto caturāsītisahassattherapabbajitaparivāro satta māsāni bodhisattacārikaṃ cari, buddhuppādakālo viya ahosi. Amhākampi bodhisatto chabbassāni bodhisattacārikaṃ cari. Evaṃ paripuṇṇasarīralakkhaṇehi [P 3.0402] samannāgatāpi buddhā na honti. Tasmā brāhmaṇo “no ca kho naṃ jānāmī”ti āha.

398. Then, for that brahmin Sela, who clearly saw that even in hundreds of thousands of eons the very sound 'Buddha' was difficult to obtain, this thought arose, beginning with: 'This sound indeed...' `Nīlavanarāji` means a line of dark green-colored trees. `Pade padaṃ` means placing the foot in the space the size of a footstep. For, when placing the foot either too near or too far, a loud sound arises; wishing to prevent this, he spoke thus. Regarding 'like a solitary lion': a lion that dwells in a group, together with lion cubs and others, falls into heedlessness; one who wanders alone is heedful. Thus, wishing to show the state of dwelling in heedfulness, he makes a comparison with a solitary lion. He spoke, teaching proper conduct, saying, 'Sirs, do not...' This is the intention here: 'If you, without getting a turn to speak, were to insert speech in the middle of my talk, the blame, "He was not able to train his resident pupils," would arise for me. Therefore, having seen a suitable opportunity, you should speak.' As for 'But I do not know him': The Bodhisatta Vipassī, with a retinue of eighty-four thousand great elder renunciates, wandered the Bodhisatta's wandering for seven months; it was as if it were the time of a Buddha's arising. Our Bodhisatta also wandered the Bodhisatta's wandering for six years. Thus, even those endowed with complete bodily marks are not necessarily Buddhas. Therefore, the brahmin said, 'But I do not know him.'

399. Paripuṇṇakāyoti [V 3.0283][M 3.0275] lakkhaṇehi paripuṇṇatāya ahīnaṅgatāya ca paripuṇṇasarīro. Surucīti sundarasarīrappabho. Sujātoti ārohapariṇāhasampattiyā saṇṭhānasampattiyā ca sunibbatto. Cārudassanoti sucirampi passantānaṃ atittijanako manoharadassano. Suvaṇṇavaṇṇoti suvaṇṇasadisavaṇṇo. Susukkadāṭhoti suṭṭhu sukkadāṭho. Mahāpurisalakkhaṇāti paṭhamaṃ vuttabyañjanāneva vacanantarena nigamento āha.

399. 'Perfect in body' means having a complete body on account of the completeness of the characteristics and the absence of any deficient limbs. 'Radiant' means having the splendor of a beautiful body. 'Well-born' means well-formed on account of perfection in height and girth, and perfection in form. 'Pleasing to behold' means producing non-satiation for those who look even for a very long time, having a sight that captivates the heart. 'Golden-colored' means having a complexion similar to gold. 'With very white teeth' means having exceedingly white canine teeth. Concluding with a different expression the very marks that were spoken of before, he spoke of 'the marks of a great man'.

Idāni tesu lakkhaṇesu attano cittarucitāni gahetvā thomento pasannanettotiādimāha. Bhagavā hi pañcavaṇṇapasādasampattiyā pasannanetto, puṇṇacandasadisamukhatāya sumukho, ārohapariṇāhasampattiyā brahā, brahmujugattatāya uju, jutimantatāya patāpavā. Yampi cettha pubbe vuttaṃ, taṃ “majjhe samaṇasaṅghassā”ti iminā pariyāyena thomayatā puna vuttaṃ. Ediso hi evaṃ virocati. Uttaragāthāyapi eseva nayo. Uttamavaṇṇīnoti uttamavaṇṇasampannassa. Rathesabhoti uttamasārathi. Jambusaṇḍassāti jambudīpassa. Pākaṭena issariyaṃ [P 3.0403] issaro hoti.

Now, praising by selecting from among those characteristics the ones that were pleasing to his own mind, he spoke the words beginning with 'with serene eyes.' Indeed, the Blessed One has serene eyes due to the perfection of the five-colored sensitive substance of the eye; he has a beautiful face because of having a face like the full moon; he is great like Brahmā because of perfection in height and girth; he is upright because of having a body as straight as Brahmā's; he is majestic because of his radiance. And what was said before was spoken again by him as he praised with the phrase, 'in the midst of the community of ascetics.' For such a one shines thus. In the subsequent verse, this same method should be understood. 'Of supreme complexion' refers to one endowed with a supreme complexion. 'Bull among chariot-riders' means a supreme charioteer. `Jambusaṇḍassa` means of Jambudīpa. Although the verse mentions the prominent isle of Jambu to praise his sovereignty, a wheel-turning monarch is in fact the lord of all four continents.

Khattiyāti jātikhattiyā. Bhogīti bhogiyā. Rājānoti ye keci rajjaṃ kārentā. Rājābhirājāti rājūnaṃ pūjanīyo, adhirājā hutvā, cakkavattīti adhippāyo. Manujindoti manussādhipati paramissaro hutvā.

'Warrior-noble' means warrior-nobles by birth. 'Wealthy' means possessors of wealth. 'Kings' means whoever exercises rule. 'King of kings' means one worthy of veneration by kings, having become a superior king, a wheel-turning monarch; this is the intention. 'Lord of men' means having become the lord of humans, the supreme sovereign.

Evaṃ vutte bhagavā – “ye te bhavanti arahanto sammāsambuddhā, te sakavaṇṇe bhaññamāne attānaṃ pātukarontī”ti imaṃ selassa manorathaṃ pūrento rājāhamasmītiādimāha. Tatrāyamadhippāyo – yaṃ maṃ tvaṃ sela “rājā arahasi bhavitu”nti yācasi, ettha appossukko hoti rājāhamasmi. Sati ca rājatte yathā añño rājā yojanasataṃ vā anusāsati yojanasahassaṃ vā, cakkavattī hutvāpi catudīpapariyantamattaṃ vā, nāhamevaṃ paricchinnavisayo, ahañhi dhammarājā anuttaro bhavaggato avīcipariyantaṃ katvā tiriyaṃ appamāṇalokadhātuyo anusāsāmi. Yāvatā [M 3.0276] hi apadadvipadādibhedā sattā, ahaṃ tesaṃ aggo. Na hi me koci sīlena vā…pe… vimuttiñāṇadassanena vā paṭibhāgo atthi, svāhaṃ evaṃ dhammarājā anuttaro anuttareneva catusatipaṭṭhānādibhedena dhammena cakkaṃ vattemi. Idaṃ pajahatha, idaṃ upasampajja viharathāti āṇācakkaṃ, idaṃ kho pana, bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ ariyasaccantiādinā pariyattidhammena [V 3.0284] dhammacakkameva vā. Cakkaṃ appaṭivattiyanti [P 3.0404] yaṃ cakkaṃ appaṭivattiyaṃ hoti samaṇena vā…pe… kenaci vā lokasminti.

When this was said, the Blessed One, fulfilling this heart's desire of Sela—'Those who are Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, reveal themselves when their own excellent qualities are spoken of'—spoke the words beginning with 'I am a king.' Therein, this is the intention: Sela, regarding the request you make, 'You are fit to be a king,' be unconcerned about this. I am a king. And although there is kingship, just as another king might rule over a hundred or a thousand yojanas, or a wheel-turning monarch might rule over just the extent of the four continents, my domain is not limited in this way. Indeed, I, the unsurpassed Dhamma King, instruct the immeasurable world-systems across, from the peak of existence down to Avīci. For, among all beings, whether footless, two-footed, or otherwise, I am the chief. There is no one who is my counterpart in virtue... or in the knowledge and vision of liberation. I, being thus the unsurpassed Dhamma King, turn the wheel with the unsurpassed Dhamma, distinguished as the four foundations of mindfulness, etc. I turn the wheel of authority, saying, 'Abandon this; dwell having attained this.' And with the Dhamma of the scriptures, beginning with, 'This, O monks, is the noble truth of suffering,' I turn the wheel of authority, or rather the Dhamma-wheel itself. A wheel that cannot be turned back means a wheel that cannot be turned back in the world by an ascetic... or by anyone whatsoever.

Evaṃ attānaṃ āvikarontaṃ bhagavantaṃ disvā pītisomanassajāto selo puna daḷhīkaraṇatthaṃ sambuddho paṭijānāsīti gāthādvayamāha. Tattha ko nu senāpatīti rañño bhoto dhammena pavattitassa cakkassa anupavattako senāpati ko nūti pucchi.

Seeing the Blessed One thus revealing himself, Sela, in whom joy and gladness had arisen, again spoke a pair of verses beginning with 'The Enlightened One acknowledges,' for the purpose of confirmation. Therein, regarding 'Who then is the general?', he asked: 'For you, the venerable king, who is the general that continues to turn the wheel that you have set in motion righteously?'

Tena ca samayena bhagavato dakkhiṇapasse āyasmā sāriputto nisinno hoti suvaṇṇapuñjo viya siriyā sobhamāno, taṃ dassento bhagavā mayā pavattitanti gāthamāha. Tattha anujāto tathāgatanti tathāgataṃ hetuṃ anujāto, tathāgatena hetunā jātoti attho. Apica avajāto anujāto atijātoti tayo vuttā. Tesu avajāto dussīlo, so tathāgatassa putto nāma na hoti. Atijāto nāma pitarā uttaritaro, tādisopi tathāgatassa putto natthi. Tathāgatassa pana eko anujātova putto hoti, taṃ dassento evamāha.

And at that time, on the Blessed One's right side, the Venerable Sāriputta was seated, shining with splendor like a heap of gold. The Blessed One, pointing him out, spoke the verse beginning with 'Set in motion by me.' Therein, 'born after the Tathāgata' means born into the noble caste through the Tathāgata as cause, or born fittingly because of the Tathāgata; this is the meaning. Moreover, three types of sons are spoken of: the inferior-born, the conforming-born, and the superior-born. Among these, the inferior-born is the immoral one; he is not truly called a son of the Tathāgata. The superior-born is one who surpasses his father; for the Tathāgata, there is no such son. For the Tathāgata, however, there is only the conforming-born son. Pointing him out, he spoke thus.

Evaṃ “ko nu senāpatī”ti pañhaṃ byākaritvā yaṃ selo āha “sambuddho paṭijānāsī”ti, tatra naṃ nikkaṅkhaṃ kātukāmo “nāhaṃ paṭiññāmatteneva paṭijānāmi, apicāhaṃ iminā kāraṇena buddho”ti ñāpetuṃ abhiññeyyanti gāthamāha. Tatra abhiññeyyanti vijjā ca vimutti ca. Bhāvetabbaṃ maggasaccaṃ. Pahātabbaṃ samudayasaccaṃ. Hetuvacanena pana phalasiddhito tesaṃ phalāni nirodhasaccadukkhasaccānipi vuttāneva honti. Evaṃ sacchikātabbaṃ sacchikataṃ pariññātabbaṃ pariññātanti idampettha saṅgahitanti catusaccabhāvanāphalañca vimuttiñca [P 3.0405] dassento “bujjhitabbaṃ bujjhitvā buddho jātosmī”ti yuttahetunā buddhabhāvaṃ sādheti.

Having thus answered the question, 'Who then is the general?', with regard to what Sela said, 'You profess to be a Fully Enlightened One,' the Blessed One, wishing to make him free from doubt on that point and to make known that, 'I do not profess this merely by assertion, but rather, I am a Buddha for this reason,' spoke the verse beginning 'What should be directly known.' Therein, 'what should be directly known' refers to knowledge (the path) and liberation (the fruit). The truth of the path, which is to be developed, has been developed. The truth of the origin, which is to be abandoned, has been abandoned. Furthermore, by stating the causes, due to the accomplishment of the result, their fruits—the truth of cessation and the truth of suffering—are also said to have been spoken of. Thus, it is included herein that 'what is to be realized has been realized; what is to be fully understood has been fully understood.' Therefore, showing this development of the four truths and the fruit of developing the truths, which is liberation, he establishes his state of Buddhahood with the valid reason: 'Having understood what is to be understood, I have become a Buddha.'

Evaṃ [M 3.0277] nippariyāyena attānaṃ āvikatvā attani kaṅkhāvitaraṇatthaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ aticāriyamāno vinayassūti gāthattayamāha. Tattha sallakattoti rāgādisallakantano. Anuttaroti yathā bāhiravejjena vūpasamitarogo imasmiññevattabhāve kuppati, na evaṃ. Mayā vūpasamitassa [V 3.0285] pana rogassa bhavantarepi uppatti natthi, tasmā ahaṃ anuttaroti attho. Brahmabhūtoti seṭṭhabhūto. Atituloti tulaṃ atīto, nirupamoti attho. Mārasenappamaddanoti kāmā te paṭhamā senāti evaṃ āgatāya mārasenāya pamaddano. Sabbāmitteti khandhakilesābhisaṅkhāramaccudevaputtamārasaṅkhāte sabbapaccatthike. Vasīkatvāti attano vase vattetvā. Akutobhayoti kutoci abhayo.

Having thus revealed himself directly, wishing to help the brahmin overcome doubt in him and to guide him to a higher practice, the Blessed One spoke the three verses beginning 'Train.' Therein, 'the dart-extractor' means one who cuts off the darts of lust and so forth. 'Unsurpassed' means: just as a disease pacified by an external physician recurs in this very existence, it is not so with me. Furthermore, for the disease pacified by me, there is no arising even in a future existence; therefore, the meaning is 'I am unsurpassed.' 'Brahmā-become' means having become the best. 'Beyond comparison' means having surpassed any equal, incomparable. 'Trampler of Māra’s army' means the crusher of Māra’s army which is described as 'Sensual desires are your first army.' 'Having mastered all enemies' refers to all adversaries, namely, the Māras of the aggregates, defilements, formations, death, and the deva's son. 'Having mastered' means having brought them under his own control. 'Fearless from any quarter' means having no fear from anywhere.

Evaṃ vutte selo brāhmaṇo tāvadeva bhagavati sañjātapasādo pabbajjāpekkho hutvā imaṃ bhontoti gāthattayamāha. Tattha kaṇhābhijātikoti caṇḍālādinīcakule jāto. Tato tepi māṇavakā pabbajjāpekkhā hutvā evañce ruccati, bhototi gāthamāhaṃsu. Atha selo tesu māṇavakesu tuṭṭhacitto te ca dassento pabbajjaṃ yācanto “brāhmaṇā”ti gāthamāha.

When this was said, the brahmin Sela, at that very moment, his confidence in the Blessed One having arisen, became one who aspired for ordination and spoke the three verses beginning 'Sirs.' Therein, 'of dark birth' means born in a low family such as the Caṇḍālas. Then those young men, also aspiring for ordination, spoke the verse beginning 'And if this pleases you, sir.' Then Sela, pleased with those young men, presenting them and also requesting ordination, spoke the verse beginning 'Brahmins.'

Tato [P 3.0406] bhagavā yasmā selo atīte padumuttarassa bhagavato sāsane tesaṃyeva tiṇṇaṃ purisasatānaṃ gaṇaseṭṭho hutvā tehi saddhiṃ pariveṇaṃ kāretvā dānādīni puññāni katvā tena kammena devamanussasampattiṃ anubhavamāno pacchime bhave tesaṃyeva ācariyo hutvā nibbatto, tañca tesaṃ kammaṃ vimuttiparipākāya paripakkaṃ ehibhikkhubhāvassa ca upanissayabhūtaṃ, tasmā te sabbeva ehibhikkhupabbajjaṃ pabbājento svākkhātanti gāthamāha. Tattha sandiṭṭhikanti sayameva daṭṭhabbaṃ paccakkhaṃ. Akālikanti maggānantaraphaluppattiyā na kālantaraṃ pattabbaphalaṃ. Yattha amoghāti yasmiṃ maggabrahmacariye appamattassa sikkhattayapūraṇena sikkhato pabbajjā amoghā hoti, saphalāti attho. Evañca vatvā “etha bhikkhavo”ti bhagavā avoca. Te sabbe pattacīvaradharā hutvā ākāsenāgantvā vassasatikattherā viya suvinītā bhagavantaṃ abhivādayiṃsu. Evamimaṃ tesaṃ ehibhikkhubhāvaṃ sandhāya “alattha kho selo”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Then the Blessed One, because Sela in the past, during the dispensation of the Blessed One Padumuttara, had become the leader of those same three hundred men, had a monastery built with them, performed meritorious deeds such as giving, and through that kamma experienced the prosperity of devas and humans, and in his final existence was reborn as their teacher—and because that kamma of theirs had ripened for the maturation of liberation and had become a supporting condition for the state of 'Come, bhikkhu'—therefore, ordaining all of them with the 'Come, bhikkhu' ordination, he spoke the verse beginning 'Well-proclaimed.' Therein, 'directly visible' means to be seen by oneself, directly. 'Timeless' means that due to the arising of the fruit immediately after the path, the fruit is not one to be attained at another time. 'Where it is not in vain' means: in which path of the holy life, for one who is diligent and trains by fulfilling the three trainings, the ordination is not in vain; it is fruitful, that is the meaning. And having said this, the Blessed One said, 'Come, bhikkhus.' They all, becoming bearers of bowl and robes, came through the air and, like well-trained elders of a hundred rains, paid homage to the Blessed One. Thus, with reference to this 'Come, bhikkhu' state of theirs, it was said, 'Sela has indeed obtained,' and so on.

400. Imāhīti [M 3.0278] imāhi keṇiyassa cittānukūlāhi gāthāhi. Tattha aggiparicariyaṃ vinā brāhmaṇānaṃ yaññābhāvato “aggihuttamukhā yaññā”ti vuttaṃ. Aggihuttaseṭṭhā aggijuhanappadhānāti attho. Vede sajjhāyantehi paṭhamaṃ sajjhāyitabbato, sāvittī, “chandaso mukha”nti vutto. Manussānaṃ [P 3.0407] seṭṭhato rājā “mukha”nti vutto. Nadīnaṃ ādhārato paṭisaraṇato ca sāgaro “mukha”nti vutto. Candayogavasena “ajja kattikā ajja rohiṇī”ti saññāṇato [V 3.0286] ālokakaraṇato sommabhāvato ca “nakkhattānaṃ mukhaṃ cando”ti vuttaṃ. Tapantānaṃ aggattā ādicco “tapataṃ mukha”nti vutto. Dakkhiṇeyyānaṃ pana aggattā visesena tasmiṃ samaye buddhappamukhaṃ saṅghaṃ sandhāya “puññaṃ ākaṅkhamānānaṃ, saṅgho eva yajataṃ mukha”nti vuttaṃ. Tena saṅgho puññassa āyamukhanti dasseti.

400. 'By these' means by these verses that were pleasing to the mind of Keṇiya. Therein, because for brahmins there is no sacrifice without tending the fire, it is said, 'Sacrifices have the fire-offering as their head.' The meaning is that they have the offering into the fire as their primary feature. Because it is to be recited first by those who recite the Vedas, the Sāvitrī is called 'the head of the hymns.' Because he is the foremost among humans, the king is called 'the head.' Because it is the receptacle and refuge for rivers, the ocean is called 'the head.' Because of the recognition based on conjunction with the moon, such as 'today is Kattikā, today is Rohiṇī,' and because it provides light and has a soothing quality, it is said, 'the moon is the head of the constellations.' Because it is the chief among those that shine, the sun is called 'the head of those that shine.' Furthermore, because the Sangha is the chief among those worthy of offerings, with special reference to the Sangha headed by the Buddha at that time, it is said, 'For those aspiring for merit, the Sangha is indeed the head of those who sacrifice.' By this, it is shown that the Sangha is the source of merit.

Yaṃ taṃ saraṇanti aññaṃ byākaraṇagāthamāha. Tassattho – pañcahi cakkhūhi cakkhumā bhagavā yasmā mayaṃ ito aṭṭhame divase taṃ saraṇaṃ āgatamhā, tasmā attanā tava sāsane anuttarena damathena dantāmhā, aho te saraṇassa ānubhāvoti.

With the words 'That refuge which,' he spoke another verse of declaration. Its meaning is: O Blessed One, possessor of the five eyes, since on the eighth day from today we went to you for refuge, therefore we ourselves have been tamed in your dispensation by your unsurpassed taming. Ah, the power of your refuge!

Tato paraṃ bhagavantaṃ dvīhi gāthāhi thometvā tatiyāya vandanaṃ yācanto bhikkhavo tisatā imetiādimāhāti.

After that, having praised the Blessed One with two verses, requesting to pay homage with a third verse, he spoke the words beginning, 'These three hundred bhikkhus...'

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Selasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Sela Sutta is concluded.

3. Assalāyanasuttavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Assalāyana Sutta

401. Evaṃ [V 3.0287][P 3.0408] me sutanti assalāyanasuttaṃ. Tattha nānāverajjakānanti aṅgamagadhādīhi nānappakārehi verajjehi āgatānaṃ, tesu vā raṭṭhesu jātasaṃvaḍḍhānantipi attho. Kenacidevāti yaññupāsanādinā aniyamitakiccena. Cātuvaṇṇinti catuvaṇṇasādhāraṇaṃ. Mayaṃ pana nhānasuddhiyā bhāvanāsuddhiyāpi brāhmaṇāva sujjhantīti vadāma, ayuttampi samaṇo gotamo karotīti maññamānā evaṃ cintayiṃsu. Vuttasiroti vāpitasiro.

3. 'Thus have I heard' refers to the Assalāyana Sutta. Therein, 'of various foreign lands' means those who have come from various different countries, such as Aṅga and Magadha, or it means those who were born and raised in those countries. 'By some means' refers to an unfixed duty, such as seeking alms by reciting mantras for receiving offerings. 'Of the four castes' means common to the four castes. 'But we say, "Brahmins alone are purified by purification through bathing and by purification through mental cultivation,"' and thinking, 'The ascetic Gotama does what is improper,' they considered thus. 'Shaven-headed' means one with a shaven head.

Dhammavādīti [M 3.0279] sabhāvavādī. Duppaṭimantiyāti amhādisehi adhammavādīhi dukkhena paṭimantitabbā honti. Dhammavādino nāma parājayo na sakkā kātunti dasseti. Paribbājakanti pabbajjāvidhānaṃ, tayo vede uggahetvā sabbapacchā pabbajantā yehi mantehi pabbajanti, pabbajitā ca ye mante pariharanti, yaṃ vā ācāraṃ ācaranti, taṃ sabbaṃ bhotā caritaṃ sikkhitaṃ. Tasmā tuyhaṃ parājayo natthi, jayova bhavissatīti maññantā evamāhaṃsu.

“Speaker of Dhamma” means one who speaks of reality. “Hard to counter” means they are to be debated with difficulty by those like us who speak what is not reality. It shows that it is not possible to inflict defeat upon a speaker of Dhamma. “The state of a wanderer” means the procedure of going forth. Having learned the three Vedas, they go forth after all others. The mantras by which they go forth, the mantras they maintain after having gone forth, and the conduct they practice—all that has been practiced and learned by the venerable one. Therefore, thinking, “For you there is no defeat, there will only be victory,” they spoke thus.

402. Dissanti kho panātiādi tesaṃ laddhibhindanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha brāhmaṇiyoti brāhmaṇānaṃ puttapaṭilābhatthāya āvāhavivāhavasena kulā ānītā brāhmaṇiyo dissanti[P 3.0409]. Tā kho panetā aparena samayena utuniyopi honti, sañjātapupphāti attho. Gabbhiniyoti sañjātagabbhā. Vijāyamānāti puttadhītaro janayamānā. Pāyamānāti dārake thaññaṃ pāyantiyo. Yonijāva samānāti brāhmaṇīnaṃ passāvamaggena jātā samānā. Evamāhaṃsūti evaṃ vadanti. Kathaṃ? Brāhmaṇova seṭṭho vaṇṇo…pe… brahmadāyādāti. Yadi pana nesaṃ saccavacanaṃ siyā, brāhmaṇīnaṃ kucchi mahābrahmuno uro bhaveyya, brāhmaṇīnaṃ passāvamaggo mahābrahmuno mukhaṃ bhaveyya, ettāvatā “mayaṃ mahābrahmuno ure vasitvā mukhato nikkhantā”ti vattuṃ mā labhantūti ayaṃ mukhato jātacchedakavādo vutto.

402. The passage beginning with “But they are seen...” was spoken to destroy their view. Therein, “brahmin women” means brahmin women who are seen to be brought from other families by means of giving and taking in marriage for the purpose of obtaining sons for brahmins. And these women, at a later time, also become menstruous; the meaning is that the flower of menstruation has arisen. “Pregnant women” means those who have conceived. “Those giving birth” means those who are bearing sons and daughters. “Those nursing” means those who are suckling milk to children. “Being born from the womb” means being born through the birth canal of brahmin women. “They spoke thus” means they say thus. How? “The brahmin is the highest caste... heirs of Brahmā.” But if their words were true, the womb of a brahmin woman would be the chest of Mahābrahmā, and the birth canal of a brahmin woman would be the mouth of Mahābrahmā. By this much, let them not get to say, “We, having dwelt in the chest of Mahābrahmā, are born from his mouth.” Thus this section which refutes the claim of being born from the mouth was spoken.

403. Ayyo hutvā dāso hoti, dāso hutvā ayyo hotīti brāhmaṇo sabhariyo vaṇijjaṃ [V 3.0288] payojento yonakaraṭṭhaṃ vā kambojaraṭṭhaṃ vā gantvā kālaṃ karoti, tassa gehe vayappatte putte asati brāhmaṇī dāsena vā kammakarena vā saddhiṃ saṃvāsaṃ kappeti. Ekasmiṃ dārake jāte so puriso dāsova hoti, tassa jātadārako pana dāyajjasāmiko hoti. Mātito suddho pitito asuddho so vaṇijjaṃ payojento majjhimapadesaṃ gantvā brāhmaṇadārikaṃ gahetvā tassā kucchismiṃ puttaṃ paṭilabhati, sopi mātitova suddho hoti pitito asuddho. Evaṃ brāhmaṇasamayasmiññeva jātisambhedo hotīti dassanatthametaṃ vuttaṃ. Kiṃ [P 3.0410] balaṃ, ko assāsoti yattha tumhe [M 3.0280] dāsā hontā sabbeva dāsā hotha, ayyā hontā sabbeva ayyā hotha, ettha vo ko thāmo, ko avassayo, yaṃ brāhmaṇova seṭṭho vaṇṇoti vadathāti dīpeti.

403. The meaning of “Having been a master, one becomes a slave; having been a slave, one becomes a master” is as follows: A brahmin, together with his wife, while engaging in trade, goes to the country of the Yonas or the country of the Kambojas and dies. In his house, there being no son who has come of age, the brahmin woman cohabits with a slave or a worker. When a child is born, that man is only a slave, but the child born of him becomes the owner of the inheritance. Pure from the mother's side and impure from the father's side, he, engaging in trade, goes to the middle country, takes a brahmin girl, and obtains a son in her womb. That son, too, is pure only from the mother's side and impure from the father's side. This was spoken to show this meaning: “Thus, even within the brahmin tradition itself, there is a mixing of birth.” It reveals the meaning of “What is your strength? What is your support?” as: “Wherein, you being slaves, are all slaves, and being masters, are all masters—herein, what is your power, what is your reliance, that you say, ‘The brahmin is the highest caste’?”

404. Khattiyova nu khotiādayo suttacchedakavādā nāma honti.

404. The statements beginning with “Is it only the Khattiya...” are called sections that cut off the discourse.

408. Idāni cātuvaṇṇisuddhiṃ dassento idha rājātiādimāha. Sāpānadoṇiyāti sunakhānaṃ pivanadoṇiyā. Aggikaraṇīyanti sītavinodanaandhakāravidhamanabhattapacanādi aggikiccaṃ. Ettha assalāyanāti ettha sabbasmiṃ aggikiccaṃ karonte.

408. Now, wishing to show the purity of the four castes, he spoke the words beginning with “Here, O king...”. “A dog's trough” means a drinking trough for dogs. “What is to be done with fire” means the duty of fire, such as dispelling cold, dispelling darkness, and cooking food. “Herein, Assalāyana” means herein, while performing all the duties of fire.

409. Idāni yadetaṃ brāhmaṇā cātuvaṇṇisuddhīti vadanti, ettha cātuvaṇṇāti niyamo natthi. Pañcamo hi pādasikavaṇṇopi atthīti saṃkhittena tesaṃ vāde dosadassanatthaṃ idha khattiyakumārotiādimāha. Tatra amutra ca panesānanti amusmiñca pana purimanaye etesaṃ māṇavakānaṃ kiñci nānākaraṇaṃ na passāmīti vadati. Nānākaraṇaṃ pana tesampi atthiyeva. Khattiyakumārassa hi brāhmaṇakaññāya uppanno khattiyapādasiko nāma, itaro brāhmaṇapādasiko nāma, ete hīnajātimāṇavakā.

409. Now, regarding what the brahmins call “the purity of the four castes,” herein there is no fixed rule of “four castes.” Indeed, there is also a fifth caste, the Pādasika caste. Thus, to briefly show the fault in their doctrine, he spoke the words beginning with “Here, a Khattiya youth...”. The phrase “among them, in this world and the next” means: “In that former method of teaching, I see no difference whatsoever among these young men,” thus he says. However, there is indeed a difference among them. Indeed, a son born to a brahmin maiden from a Khattiya youth is called a Khattiya-pādasika. The other, born to a Khattiya maiden from a brahmin youth, is called a Brāhmaṇa-pādasika. These are young men of low birth.

Evaṃ pañcamassa vaṇṇassa atthitāya cātuvaṇṇisuddhīti etesaṃ vāde dosaṃ dassetvā idāni puna cātuvaṇṇisuddhiyaṃ ovadanto taṃ kiṃ maññasītiādimāha. Tattha [P 3.0411] saddheti matakabhatte. Thālipāketi paṇṇākārabhatte. Yaññeti yaññabhatte. Pāhuneti āgantukānaṃ katabhatte. Kiṃ hīti kiṃ mahapphalaṃ bhavissati, no bhavissatīti dīpeti.

Thus, having shown the fault in their doctrine of “the purity of the four castes” due to the existence of a fifth caste, now, wishing to admonish regarding the purity of the four castes, he spoke the words beginning with “What do you think of that?”. Therein, `saddhe` means at a funeral meal. `Thālipāke` means at a meal made as a gift. `Yaññe` means at a meal made for a sacrifice. `Pāhunake` means at a meal made for guests. `Kiṃ hi` shows this meaning: “From what will it be of great fruit? It will not be of great fruit.”

410. Bhūtapubbanti [V 3.0289] assalāyana pubbe mayi jātiyā hīnatare tumhe seṭṭhatarā samānāpi mayā jātivāde pañhaṃ puṭṭhā sampādetuṃ na sakkhittha, idāni tumhe hīnatarā hutvā mayā seṭṭhatarena buddhānaṃ sake jātivādapañhaṃ puṭṭhā kiṃ sampādessatha? Na ettha cintā kātabbāti māṇavaṃ upatthambhento imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi. Tattha asitoti kāḷako. Devaloti [M 3.0281] tassa nāmaṃ, ayameva bhagavā tena samayena. Paṭaliyoti gaṇaṅgaṇupāhanā. Patthaṇḍileti paṇṇasālapariveṇe. Ko nu khoti kahaṃ nu kho. Gāmaṇḍalarūpo viyāti gāmadārakarūpo viya. So khvāhaṃ, bho, homīti so ahaṃ, bho, asitadevalo homīti vadati. Tadā kira mahāsatto koṇḍadamako hutvā vicarati. Abhivādetuṃ upakkamiṃsūti vandituṃ upakkamaṃ akaṃsu. Tato paṭṭhāya ca vassasatikatāpasopi tadahujātaṃ brāhmaṇakumāraṃ avandanto koṇḍito hoti.

410. Bhūtapubbaṃ means this: Assalāyana, formerly, when I was of a much lower birth and you were of a much higher birth, though you were asked a question by me on the matter of birth, you were not able to answer it fully. Now, you being of a much lower birth and I being of a much higher state, when asked by me a question on the matter of birth, which is the own domain of the Buddhas, how will you be able to answer? Regarding this, no thought should be given. Thus, wishing to encourage the young man, he began this discourse. Therein, ‘asito’ means ‘kāḷako’ (the dark one). ‘Devalo’ was his name. At that time, the Blessed One was this very person. ‘Paṭaliyo’ means layered sandals. ‘Patthaṇḍile’ means in the precinct of a leaf-hut. ‘Ko nu kho’ means ‘where indeed have they gone?’ ‘Gāmaṇḍalarūpo viya’ means ‘like the form of a village boy.’ ‘So khvāhaṃ, bho, homi’ means he says, ‘Bho, I am that Asita Devala.’ At that time, it is said, the Great Being wandered about as a tamer of the untamed. ‘Abhivādetuṃ upakkamiṃsu’ means they made an effort to pay homage. Furthermore, from that time onwards, even a hundred-year-old ascetic who does not pay respects to a brahmin youth born on that very day is called ‘koṇḍito’ (uncivilized).

411. Janikā [P 3.0412] mātāti yāya tumhe janitā, sā vo janikā mātā. Janikāmātūti janikāya mātu. Yo janakoti yo janako pitā. “Yo janiko pitāteva” vā pāṭho.

411. ‘Janikā mātā’ means: the mother by whom you were born, she is your birth-giving mother. ‘Janikāmātū’ means of the birth-giving mother. ‘Yo janako’ means: he who begets is the father. Alternatively, the reading is ‘Yo janiko pitā’tveva’ (the one who begets is indeed the father).

Asitenāti pañcābhiññena asitena devalena isinā imaṃ gandhabbapañhaṃ puṭṭhā na sampāyissanti. Yesanti yesaṃ sattannaṃ isīnaṃ. Na puṇṇo dabbigāhoti tesaṃ sattannaṃ isīnaṃ dabbiṃ gahetvā paṇṇaṃ pacitvā dāyako puṇṇo nāma eko ahosi, so dabbigahaṇasippaṃ jānāti. Tvaṃ sācariyako tesaṃ puṇṇopi na hoti, tena ñātaṃ dabbigahaṇasippamattampi na jānāsīti. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

'Asitena' means: by the seer Asita Devala, who possessed the five higher knowledges; the brahmins, being asked this question about the gandhabbas, will not be able to answer it fully. 'Yesaṃ' means: of which seven seers. 'Na puṇṇo dabbigāho' means: for those seven seers, there was an attendant named Puṇṇa, a donor who, taking a ladle, would cook leafy greens; he knew the skill of handling a ladle. You, together with your teacher, are not even their attendant Puṇṇa, and you do not know even the mere skill of handling a ladle that was known by him. The rest is clear everywhere.

Ayaṃ pana assalāyano saddho ahosi pasanno, attano antonivesaneyeva cetiyaṃ kāresi. Yāvajjadivasā assalāyanavaṃse jātā nivesanaṃ kāretvā antonivesane cetiyaṃ karontevāti.

Furthermore, this Assalāyana became faithful and devoted; he had a cetiya built right inside his own house. Even to this day, those born in the lineage of Assalāyana, having had a house built, continue to build a cetiya inside the house.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

Of the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Middle Length Discourses.

Assalāyanasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Assalāyana Sutta is finished.

4. Ghoṭamukhasuttavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Ghoṭamukha Sutta

412. Evaṃ [V 3.0290] me sutanti ghoṭamukhasuttaṃ. Tattha khemiyambavaneti evaṃnāmake ambavane. Dhammiko paribbajoti dhammikā pabbajjā. Adassanāti tumhādisānaṃ [M 3.0282] vā paṇḍitānaṃ adassanena. Yo vā panettha dhammoti yo vā pana ettha dhammo [P 3.0413] sabhāvo, tasseva vā adassanena. Iminā “amhākaṃ kathā appamāṇaṃ, dhammova pamāṇa”nti dasseti. Tato thero “navauposathāgāre viya bahunā kammena idha bhavitabba”nti cintetvā caṅkamā oruyha paṇṇasālaṃ pavisitvā nisīdi. Taṃ dassetuṃ evaṃ vuttetiādi vuttaṃ.

412. The sutta beginning with 'Thus have I heard' is the Ghoṭamukha Sutta. Therein, 'in the Khemiya mango grove' means in the mango grove of that name. 'A righteous wanderer' means a righteous going-forth. 'By not seeing' means by not seeing wise ones like you. 'Or whatever Dhamma is here' means whatever true nature there is in this going-forth, or by not seeing that very thing. By this, he shows: 'Our talk is not the standard; the Dhamma alone is the standard.' Then the elder, thinking, 'There should not be much work here, as there would be in a new Uposatha hall,' descended from his walkway, entered the leaf-hut, and sat down. To show that, the passage beginning 'When this was said...' was spoken.

413. Cattārome brāhmaṇāti therassa kira etadahosi – “ayaṃ brāhmaṇo ‘dhammikaṃ pabbajjaṃ upagato samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā natthī’ti vadati. Imassa cattāro puggale dve ca parisā dassetvā ‘catutthaṃ puggalaṃ katarāya parisāya bahulaṃ passasī’ti pucchissāmi, jānamāno ‘anāgāriyaparisāya’nti vakkhati. Evametaṃ sakamukheneva ‘dhammiko paribbajo atthī’ti vadāpessāmī”ti imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi.

413. Regarding 'These four, O brahmin,' it is said this thought occurred to the elder: 'This brahmin says, “There is no ascetic or brahmin who has undertaken a righteous going-forth.” I will show him four individuals and two assemblies and ask, “In which assembly do you see the fourth individual much?” Knowing, he will say, “In the assembly of the homeless.” In this way, I will make him state with his own mouth, “There is a righteous wanderer.”’ Having thought thus, he began this discourse.

414. Tattha sārattarattāti suṭṭhu rattarattā. Sānuggahā vācā bhāsitā sakāraṇā vācā bhāsitā. Vuttañhetaṃ mayā “amhākaṃ kathā appamāṇaṃ, dhammova pamāṇa”nti.

414. Therein, 'intensely passionate' means exceedingly impassioned and attached. 'Words spoken with support' means words spoken with reason. For this was said by me: 'Our talk is not the standard; the Dhamma alone is the standard.'

421. Kiṃ pana teti gihi nāma kappiyampi akappiyampi vadeyyāti vivecanatthaṃ pucchi. Kārāpesīti māpesi. Kārāpetvā ca pana kālaṃ katvā sagge nibbatto. Etassa kira jānanasippe mātarampi pitarampi ghātetvā attāva ghātetabboti āgacchati. Etaṃ sippaṃ jānanto ṭhapetvā etaṃ añño sagge nibbatto nāma natthi, esa pana theraṃ upanissāya puññaṃ katvā tattha nibbattitvā ca pana “kenāhaṃ kammena idha nibbatto”ti āvajjetvā yathābhūtaṃ [P 3.0414] ñatvā ekadivasaṃ jiṇṇāya bhojanasālāya paṭisaṅkharaṇatthaṃ saṅghe sannipatite manussavesena āgantvā pucchi – “kimatthaṃ, bhante, saṅgho sannipatito”ti? Bhojanasālāya [V 3.0291] paṭisaṅkharaṇatthanti. Kenesā kāritāti? Ghoṭamukhenāti. Idāni so kuhinti? Kālaṅkatoti. Atthi panassa koci ñātakoti? Atthi ekā bhaginīti. Pakkosāpetha nanti. Bhikkhū pakkosāpesuṃ. So taṃ upasaṅkamitvā – “ahaṃ, tava bhātā, ghoṭamukho nāma imaṃ sālaṃ kāretvā sagge nibbatto, asuke ca asuke ca ṭhāne mayā ṭhapitaṃ dhanaṃ [M 3.0283] atthi, taṃ gahetvā imañca bhojanasālaṃ kārehi, dārake ca posehī”ti vatvā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ vanditvā vehāsaṃ uppatitvā devalokameva agamāsi. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

421. Regarding 'But what of those...', this was asked to clarify whether a householder might speak what is allowable and what is not. 'He had it built' means he caused it to be created. And having had it built, he passed away and was reborn in a heavenly world. It is said that in his particular craft, it is taught that one must kill one's mother and father, and then kill oneself. Apart from him, no one else knowing this craft was reborn in a heavenly world. But he, by relying on the elder and making merit, was reborn there. And having been reborn there, reflecting, 'By what kamma was I reborn here?' and knowing it as it really was, one day, when the Saṅgha had gathered to repair the old dining hall, he came in human form and asked, 'For what purpose, venerable sirs, has the Saṅgha gathered?' 'For the repair of the dining hall.' 'By whom was it built?' 'By Ghoṭamukha.' 'Where is he now?' 'He has passed away.' 'Does he have any relatives?' 'He has one sister.' 'Please summon her.' The bhikkhus had her summoned. Approaching her, he said, 'I am your brother, Ghoṭamukha. Having had this hall built, I was reborn in a heavenly world. In such and such places, there is wealth placed by me. Take it and have this dining hall built, and also raise the children.' Having said this, he paid homage to the Bhikkhu-Saṅgha, rose into the sky, and went to the deva world. The rest is clear everywhere.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Middle Length Discourses.

Ghoṭamukhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Ghoṭamukha Sutta is finished.

5. Caṅkīsuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Caṅkī Sutta

422. Evaṃ [V 3.0292] me sutanti caṅkīsuttaṃ. Tattha devavane sālavaneti tasmiṃ kira devatānaṃ balikammaṃ karīyati, tena taṃ devavanantipi sālavanantipi vuccati. Opāsādaṃ ajjhāvasatīti opāsādanāmake brāhmaṇagāme vasati, abhibhavitvā vā āvasati, tassa sāmī hutvā yāya mariyādāya tattha vasitabbaṃ, tāya mariyādāya vasati. Upasaggavasena panettha bhummatthe upayogavacanaṃ veditabbaṃ, tathassa anuppayogattāva sesapadesu. Tattha lakkhaṇaṃ saddasatthato pariyesitabbaṃ. Sattussadanti [P 3.0415] sattehi ussadaṃ ussannaṃ, bahujanaṃ ākiṇṇamanussaṃ posāvaniyahatthiassamoramigādianekasattasamākiṇṇañcāti attho. Yasmā pana so gāmo bahi āvijjhitvā jātena hatthiassādīnaṃ ghāsatiṇena ceva gehacchadanatiṇena ca sampanno, tathā dārukaṭṭhehi ceva gehasambhārakaṭṭhehi ca, yasmā cassa abbhantare vaṭṭacaturassādisaṇṭhānā bahū pokkharaṇiyo, jalajakusumavicittāni ca bahi anekāni taḷākāni vā udakassa niccabharitāneva honti, tasmā satiṇakaṭṭhodakanti vuttaṃ.

422. The sutta beginning with 'Thus have I heard' is the Caṅkī Sutta. Therein, regarding 'in Devavana, the Sāla-grove': it is said that in that grove, offerings are made to the deities; for that reason, it is called both Devavana and Sālavana. Regarding 'he dwells at Opāsāda': he dwells in the brahmin village named Opāsāda; or, he dwells there having dominated it. Having become its master, he dwells there according to the custom by which one ought to dwell there. Here, by the power of the prefix, the accusative case should be understood in the sense of the locative; and because they are its qualifiers, the same applies to the remaining words. The grammatical rule for this should be sought from the grammar texts. Regarding 'teeming with beings': the meaning is that it is teeming with beings, populous, crowded with people, and crowded with many kinds of domesticated creatures such as elephants, horses, peacocks, and deer. And because that village is endowed with grass for fodder for elephants, horses, and so on, that grows around its outskirts, and with grass for roofing houses, and also with firewood and timber for house construction; and because within it there are many circular, quadrangular, and other shaped ponds, and outside there are many reservoirs adorned with aquatic flowers that are always full of water, therefore it is called 'endowed with grass, wood, and water'.

Saha dhaññena sadhaññaṃ, pubbaṇṇāparaṇṇādibhedaṃ bahudhaññasannicayanti attho. Ettāvatā yasmiṃ gāme brāhmaṇo setacchattaṃ ussāpetvā rājalīlāya vasati. Tassa samiddhisampatti dīpitā hoti. Rājato laddhaṃ bhoggaṃ rājabhoggaṃ. Kena dinnanti ce, raññā pasenadinā kosalena dinnaṃ. Rājadāyanti rañño dāyabhūtaṃ, dāyajjanti attho. Brahmadeyyanti seṭṭhadeyyaṃ, chattaṃ ussāpetvā rājasaṅkhepena bhuñjitabbanti attho. Atha vā rājabhogganti sabbaṃ chejjabhejjaṃ anusāsantena titthapabbatādīsu suṅkaṃ [M 3.0284] gaṇhantena setacchattaṃ ussāpetvā raññā hutvā bhuñjitabbaṃ. Tattha raññā pasenadinā kosalena dinnaṃ rājadāyanti. Ettha raññā dinnattā rājadāyaṃ, dāyakarājadīpanatthaṃ panassa “raññā pasenadinā kosalena dinna”nti idaṃ vuttaṃ. Brahmadeyyanti seṭṭhadeyyaṃ, yathā dinnaṃ na puna gahetabbaṃ hoti nissaṭṭhapariccattaṃ, evaṃ dinnanti attho.

Because it is 'with grain' (saha dhaññena), it is called 'endowed with grain' (sadhaññaṃ); the meaning is that it has a great accumulation of various kinds of grain, such as early and late crops. By this much, the prosperous fortune of the brahmin who dwells in that village with royal splendor, having raised a white parasol, is described. A fief received from the king is a 'royal fief' (rājabhoggaṃ). If it is asked, 'By whom was it given?' It was given by King Pasenadi of Kosala. Regarding 'a royal gift' (rājadāyaṃ): the meaning is that it is a gift from the king, an inheritance. Regarding 'a supreme gift' (brahmadeyyaṃ): the meaning is that it is a supreme gift, to be enjoyed in the manner of a king, having raised a parasol. Alternatively, 'royal fief' (rājabhoggaṃ) means it is to be enjoyed by one who, having become a king, rules over all matters of punishment and execution, collects taxes at river-crossings, mountain passes, and so on, and has raised a white parasol. Therein, 'a royal gift given by King Pasenadi of Kosala': here, it is a 'royal gift' because it was given by the king. To indicate the king who was the giver, the phrase 'given by King Pasenadi of Kosala' was stated. Regarding 'a supreme gift' (brahmadeyyaṃ): a supreme gift. The meaning is: it is given in such a way that what is given is not to be taken back again; it is relinquished and abandoned. It is given thus.

423. Bahū [P 3.0416] bahū hutvā saṃhatāti saṅghā. Ekekissā disāya saṅgho tesaṃ atthīti saṅghī. Pubbe [V 3.0293] gāmassa anto agaṇā bahi nikkhamitvā gaṇā sampannāti gaṇībhūtā. Uttarenamukhāti uttaradisābhimukhā. Khattaṃ āmantesīti khattā vuccati pucchitapañhabyākaraṇasamattho mahāmatto, taṃ āmantesi. Āgamentūti muhuttaṃ paṭimānentu, acchantūti vuttaṃ hoti.

423. They are called 'groups' (saṅghā) because, being many, they are assembled together. They are called 'members of a group' (saṅghī) because they have a group from each direction. They are said to have 'formed into a group' (gaṇībhūtā) because previously, inside the village, they were not in a group, but having gone outside, they formed a group. 'Facing north' (uttarenamukhā) means facing the northern direction. Regarding 'he addressed his chamberlain' (khattaṃ āmantesi): a great minister who is capable of answering questions that are asked is called a 'chamberlain' (khattā); he addressed him. Regarding 'let them wait' (āgamentu): it means 'let them wait a moment, let them stay'.

424. Nānāverajjakānanti nānāvidhesu rajjesu aññesu kāsikosalādīsu jātā vā nivasanti vā, tato vā āgatāti nānāverajjakā, tesaṃ nānāverajjakānaṃ. Kenacidevāti aniyamitena yaññupāsanādinā kenaci kiccena. Te tassa gamanaṃ sutvā cintesuṃ – “ayaṃ, caṅkī, uggatabrāhmaṇo, yebhuyyena ca aññe brāhmaṇā samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ saraṇaṃ gatā, ayameva na gato. Svāyaṃ sace tattha gamissati, addhā samaṇassa gotamassa āvaṭṭaniyā māyāya āvaṭṭito saraṇaṃ gamissati. Tato etassāpi gehadvāre brāhmaṇānaṃ asannipāto bhavissati. Handassa gamanantarāyaṃ karomā”ti sammantayitvā tattha agamaṃsu. Taṃ sandhāya “atha kho te brāhmaṇā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

424. Regarding 'from various kingdoms' (nānāverajjakānaṃ): they are called nānāverajjakā because they were born or reside in various other kingdoms such as Kāsi and Kosala, or because they have come from those various kingdoms; this refers to those from various kingdoms. Regarding 'for some reason' (kenacideva): by some unspecified business, such as attending a sacrifice. Hearing of his going, they thought: 'This Caṅkī is a prominent brahmin. For the most part, other brahmins have gone for refuge to the ascetic Gotama, but he alone has not gone. If he goes there, he will surely be converted by the ascetic Gotama's converting magic and will go for refuge. Then, at his house-door too, there will be no gathering of brahmins. Come, let us create an obstacle to his going.' Having thus conferred, they went there. In reference to that, the passage beginning 'Then those brahmins...' was spoken.

Tattha ubhatoti dvīhi pakkhehi. Mātito [P 3.0417] ca pitito cāti, bhoto mātā brāhmaṇī, mātumātā brāhmaṇī, tassāpi mātā brāhmaṇī. Pitā brāhmaṇo, pitupitā brāhmaṇo, tassapi pitā brāhmaṇoti. Evaṃ bhavaṃ ubhato sujāto, mātito ca pitito ca. Saṃsuddhagahaṇikoti [M 3.0285] saṃsuddhā te mātu gahaṇī, saṃsuddhā te mātu kucchīti attho. Yāva sattamā pitāmahayugāti ettha pitu pitā pitāmaho, pitāmahassa yugaṃ pitāmahayugaṃ. Yuganti āyuppamāṇaṃ vuccati. Abhilāpamattameva cetaṃ, atthato pana pitāmahova pitāmahayugaṃ. Tato uddhaṃ sabbepi pubbapurisā pitāmahaggahaṇeneva gahitā. Evaṃ yāva sattamo puriso, tāva saṃsuddhagahaṇiko. Atha vā akkhitto anupakuṭṭho jātivādenāti dasseti. Akkhittoti apanetha etaṃ, kiṃ imināti evaṃ akkhitto anavakkhitto. Anupakkuṭṭhoti na upakuṭṭho, na akkosaṃ vā nindaṃ vā pattapubbo. Kena kāraṇenāti. Jātivādena, itipi hīnajātiko esoti evarūpena vacanenāti attho. Imināpaṅgenāti imināpi kāraṇena.

Therein, 'on both sides' (ubhato) means from two sides. From the mother's side and the father's side: your mother is a brahmin woman, your mother's mother was a brahmin woman, and her mother was also a brahmin woman. Your father is a brahmin, your father's father was a brahmin, and his father was also a brahmin. Thus, you are well-born on both sides, from the mother's and the father's side. Regarding 'of pure maternal descent' (saṃsuddhagahaṇiko): the meaning is 'your mother's womb is pure'. Regarding 'up to the seventh ancestral generation' (yāva sattamā pitāmahayugā): here, the father's father is the grandfather (pitāmaha); the generation (yuga) of the grandfather is the ancestral generation (pitāmahayugaṃ). By 'generation' (yuga), the measure of a lifetime is meant. But this is just a figure of speech; in meaning, the grandfather himself is the 'ancestral generation'. Beyond that, all previous ancestors are included by the term 'grandfather'. Thus, as far as the seventh ancestor, he is of pure maternal descent. Alternatively, it shows that he is 'unreproached and uncensured in regard to birth'. Regarding 'unreproached' (akkhitto): he is not cast off or rejected with words like, 'Remove this one! What is he for?' Regarding 'uncensured' (anupakuṭṭho): not censured; he has never before been subject to abuse or blame. For what reason? In regard to birth; the meaning is: by words such as, 'This one is of low birth'. Regarding 'by this attribute' (imināpaṅgena): for this reason also.

Aḍḍhoti issaro. Mahaddhanoti mahatā dhanena samannāgato. Bhoto hi gehe pathaviyaṃ paṃsuvālikā viya bahu dhanaṃ, samaṇo pana gotamo adhano bhikkhāya udaraṃ pūretvā yāpetīti dassenti[V 3.0294]. Mahābhogoti pañcakāmaguṇavasena mahāupabhogo. Evaṃ yaṃ yaṃ guṇaṃ vadanti, tassa tassa paṭipakkhavasena [P 3.0418] bhagavato aguṇaṃyeva dassemāti maññamānā vadanti.

"Wealthy" (aḍḍho) means a master. "Possessing great wealth" (mahaddhano) means endowed with great wealth. Truly, in the venerable one's house, there is much wealth, like the dust and sand on the earth, whereas the ascetic Gotama is without wealth; he maintains himself by filling his belly through alms-gathering—this is what they point out. "Of great possessions" (mahābhogo) means having great enjoyment by way of the five strands of sensual pleasure. Thus, for whatever virtue they speak of, they speak thinking, "By way of its opposite, we will show only the Blessed One's lack of virtue."

Abhirūpoti aññehi manussehi adhikarūpo. Dassanīyoti divasampi passantānaṃ atittikaraṇato dassanayoggo, dassaneneva cittapasādajananato pāsādiko. Pokkharatā vuccati sundarabhāvo, vaṇṇassa pokkharatā vaṇṇapokkharatā, tāya vaṇṇapokkharatāya, vaṇṇasampattiyāti attho. Porāṇā pana pokkharanti sarīraṃ vadanti, vaṇṇaṃ vaṇṇameva. Tesaṃ matena vaṇṇo ca pokkharañca vaṇṇapokkharāni, tesaṃ bhāvo vaṇṇapokkharatā. Iti paramāya vaṇṇapokkharatāyāti uttamaparisuddhena vaṇṇena ceva sarīrasaṇṭhānasampattiyā cāti attho. Brahmavaṇṇīti seṭṭhavaṇṇī, parisuddhavaṇṇesupi seṭṭhena suvaṇṇavaṇṇeneva samannāgatoti attho. Brahmavacchasīti mahābrahmuno sarīrasadisena sarīrena samannāgato. Akhuddāvakāso dassanāyāti bhoto sarīre dassanassa okāso na khuddako mahā. Sabbāneva te aṅgapaccaṅgāni dassanīyāneva, tāni cāpi mahantānevāti dīpeti.

"Handsome" (abhirūpo) means he has a form superior to other humans. "Inspiring to see" (dassanīyo) means he is worthy of being seen because he does not cause satiety for those who look at him even for a whole day; he is inspiring (pāsādiko) because he is able to cause serenity of mind merely by being seen. By "excellence" (pokkharatā) is meant the state of being beautiful. The excellence of complexion is vaṇṇapokkharatā; he is endowed with that excellence of complexion. The meaning is: with the accomplishment of complexion. The ancient teachers, however, say that pokkhara means the body, and vaṇṇa is simply complexion. According to their view, vaṇṇapokkharāni means both complexion and body, and their state is vaṇṇapokkharatā. Thus, "with the highest excellence of complexion" (paramāya vaṇṇapokkharatāya) means endowed with a supreme and very pure complexion and with the accomplishment of bodily form. "Of brahma-like complexion" (brahmavaṇṇī) means having an excellent complexion; the meaning is that even among pure complexions, he is endowed with the excellent complexion that is like the color of gold. "Of brahma-like body" (brahmavacchasī) means endowed with a body similar to the body of a Mahābrahmā. "Not of limited opportunity for viewing" (akhuddāvakāso dassanāya) means the opportunity for seeing the venerable one's body is not small, but great. It indicates that all his major and minor limbs are indeed worthy of being seen, and those limbs are also large.

Sīlamassa [M 3.0286] atthīti sīlavā. Vuddhaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ sīlamassāti vuddhasīlī. Vuddhasīlenāti vuddhena vaḍḍhitena sīlena. Samannāgatoti yutto, idaṃ vuddhasīlīpadasseva vevacanaṃ. Sabbametaṃ pañcasīlamattameva sandhāya vadanti.

He has virtue, therefore he is called sīlavā. He has mature and developed virtue, therefore he is called vuddhasīlī. Vuddhasīlena means with mature and developed virtue. Samannāgato means endowed; this is a synonym for the term vuddhasīlī. All this is said by the brahmins referring merely to the five precepts.

Kālyāṇavācotiādīsu kalyāṇā sundarā parimaṇḍalapadabyañjanā vācā assāti kalyāṇavāco. Kalyāṇaṃ madhuraṃ vākkaraṇaṃ assāti kalyāṇavākkaraṇo. Vākkaraṇanti udāharaṇaghoso. Guṇaparipuṇṇabhāvena [P 3.0419] pure bhavāti porī. Pure vā bhavattā porī. Nāgarikitthiyā sukhumālattanena sadisātipi porī. Tāya poriyā. Vissaṭṭhāyāti apalibuddhāya, sandiṭṭhavilambitādidosarahitāya. Anelagalāyāti elagalena virahitāya. Ekaccassa hi kathentassa elaṃ galati, lālā vā paggharati, kheḷaphusitāni vā nikkhamanti, tassa vācā elagalā nāma hoti. Tabbiparitāyāti attho. Atthassa viññāpaniyātiādimajjhapariyosānaṃ pākaṭaṃ katvā bhāsitatthassa viññāpanasamatthāya. Sesamettha brāhmaṇavaṇṇe uttānameva.

In kalyāṇavāco and other such terms, the analysis should be understood in the following way. He has good speech with well-rounded words and syllables, therefore he is called kalyāṇavāco. He has pleasant spoken words, therefore he is called kalyāṇavākkaraṇo. Vākkaraṇa is the sound of utterance. Because it is complete with qualities, it is speech that is foremost (pure bhavā), therefore it is called porī. Alternatively, because it exists in a great city (pure bhavattā), it is called porī. It is also called porī because it is similar to the refined and gentle speech of a woman born in a great city. By that porī speech, vissaṭṭhāya means unhindered, free from faults such as speaking in fragments or speaking too slowly. Anelagalāya means free from drooling. For when a certain person speaks, saliva flows, or spittle drips, or flecks of phlegm come out; his speech is called elagalā. The meaning here is the opposite of that. Atthassa viññāpanīya means capable of making known the meaning of what is said by making the beginning, middle, and end clear. The rest here in this description of the brahmins' qualities is self-evident.

425. Evaṃ [V 3.0295] vutteti evaṃ tehi brāhmaṇehi vutte, caṅkī, “ime brāhmaṇā attano vaṇṇe vuccamāne atussanakasatto nāma natthi, vaṇṇamassa bhaṇitvā nivāressāmāti jātiādīhi mama vaṇṇaṃ vadanti, na kho pana me yuttaṃ attano vaṇṇe rajjituṃ. Handāhaṃ etesaṃ vādaṃ bhinditvā samaṇassa gotamassa mahantabhāvaṃ ñāpetvā etesaṃ tattha gamanaṃ karomī”ti cintetvā tena hi, bho, mamāpi suṇāthātiādimāha. Tattha yepi “ubhato sujāto”tiādayo attano guṇehi sadisā guṇā, tepi “ko cāhaṃ, ke ca samaṇassa gotamassa jātisampattiādayo guṇā”ti attano guṇehi uttaritareyeva maññamāno, itare pana ekanteneva bhagavato mahantabhāvadīpanatthaṃ pakāseti. Mayameva arahāmāti evaṃ niyamento cettha idaṃ [P 3.0420] dīpeti – yadi guṇamahantatāya upasaṅkamitabbo nāma hoti, yathā sineruṃ upanidhāya sāsapo, mahāsamuddaṃ upanidhāya gopadakaṃ, sattasu mahāsaresu udakaṃ upanidhāya ussāvabindu paritto lāmako, evamevaṃ samaṇassa gotamassa jātisampattiādayo guṇe upanidhāya amhākaṃ guṇā [M 3.0287] parittā lāmakā, tasmā mayameva arahāma taṃ bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ dassanāya upasaṅkamitunti.

425. When it was thus said by those brahmins, Caṅkī thought: "When their own qualities are praised, there is no being who is not pleased. Thinking, 'Having praised his qualities, we will prevent him from going,' they speak of my qualities, such as birth. But indeed, it is not proper for me to be attached to my own qualities. Now, I will break their argument, make known the greatness of the recluse Gotama, and cause them to go to him." Having thought thus, he said, "Well then, sirs, listen to me too." Therein, even regarding those qualities such as "well-born on both sides," which are somewhat similar to his own, Caṅkī, thinking, "What am I, and what are the qualities of the recluse Gotama, such as his accomplishment of birth?" and considering the Buddha's qualities as far superior to his own, reveals them. As for the other qualities, he reveals them entirely for the purpose of showing the greatness of the Blessed One. In determining "It is we who are worthy," he indicates this: If one should approach another on account of greatness in qualities, then just as a mustard seed is small and insignificant when compared to Mount Sineru, as the water in a cow's hoofprint is small and insignificant when compared to the great ocean, and as a dewdrop is small and insignificant when compared to the water in the seven great lakes, even so, when compared to the qualities of the recluse Gotama, such as his accomplishment of birth, our qualities are small and insignificant. Therefore, it is we who are worthy to approach the venerable Gotama for an audience.

Bhūmigatañca vehāsaṭṭhañcāti ettha rājaṅgaṇe ceva uyyāne ca sudhāmaṭṭhā pokkharaṇiyo sattaratanapūriṃ katvā bhūmiyaṃ ṭhapitaṃ dhanaṃ bhūmigataṃ nāma, pāsādaniyūhādayo pana pūretvā ṭhapitaṃ vehāsaṭṭhaṃ nāma. Evaṃ tāva kulapariyāyena āgataṃ. Tathāgatassa pana jātadivaseyeva saṅkho elo uppalo puṇḍarīkoti cattāro nidhayo upagatā. Tesu saṅkho gāvutiko, elo aḍḍhayojaniko, uppalo tigāvutiko puṇḍarīko yojanikoti. Tesupi gahitagahitaṭṭhānaṃ pūratiyeva. Iti bhagavā pahūtaṃ hiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ ohāya pabbajitoti veditabbo. Daharo vātiādīni heṭṭhā vitthāritāneva.

Regarding bhūmigatañca vehāsaṭṭhañca (on the ground and in the air), the meaning should be understood. Wealth placed on the ground—having filled stuccoed ponds in the royal courtyard and in the park with the seven kinds of gems—is called bhūmigata (on the ground). But wealth placed having filled palaces, projecting windows, and so on, is called vehāsaṭṭha (in the air). Such was the wealth that had come down through his lineage. Moreover, on the very day of the Tathāgata's birth, four treasure troves appeared: Saṅkha, Elo, Uppala, and Puṇḍarika. Among them, Saṅkha was a gāvuta in size, Elo was half a yojana, Uppala was three gāvutas, and Puṇḍarika was a yojana. In those treasures, too, whatever place was taken from was immediately refilled. Thus, it should be understood that the Blessed One went forth, having renounced abundant silver and gold. The phrases beginning with daharo vā have already been explained in detail previously.

Akhuddāvakāsoti ettha bhagavati aparimāṇoyeva dassanāvakāsoti veditabbo. Tatridaṃ vatthuṃ – rājagahe kira aññataro brāhmaṇo “samaṇassa kira gotamassa pamāṇaṃ gahetuṃ na sakkā”ti sutvā bhagavato piṇḍāya pavisanakāle saṭṭhihatthaṃ veḷuṃ gahetvā nagaradvārassa bahi ṭhatvā sampatte bhagavati veḷuṃ gahetvā samīpe aṭṭhāsi, veḷu bhagavato jāṇumattaṃ pāpuṇi. Punadivase dve veḷū ghaṭetvā samīpe aṭṭhāsi[P 3.0421], bhagavā dvinnaṃ veḷūnaṃ upari dviveṇumattameva paññāyamāno, “brāhmaṇa, kiṃ karosī”ti āha? Tumhākaṃ pamāṇaṃ gaṇhāmīti. “Brāhmaṇa, sacepi tvaṃ sakalacakkavāḷagabbhaṃ pūretvā ṭhitaveḷuṃ ghaṭetvā āgamissasi, neva me pamāṇaṃ gahetuṃ [V 3.0296] sakkhissasi. Na hi mayā cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni kappasatasahassañca tathā pāramiyo pūritā, yathā me paro pamāṇaṃ gaṇheyya, atulo brāhmaṇa, tathāgato appameyyo”ti vatvā dhammapade gāthamāha. Gāthāpariyosāne caturāsītipāṇasahassāni amataṃ piviṃsu.

“Not of limited opportunity”—herein, it should be understood that with regard to the Blessed One, there is an immeasurable opportunity for seeing. In that regard, this is the story: In Rājagaha, it is said, a certain brahmin, having heard, “It is not possible to take the measure of the ascetic Gotama,” took a sixty-cubit bamboo pole at the time the Blessed One was entering for alms-food, and stood outside the city gate. When the Blessed One arrived, he took the bamboo pole and stood nearby. The bamboo pole reached only to the Blessed One's knee. On the next day, he joined two bamboo poles and stood nearby. The Blessed One, appearing to be just two bamboo-lengths above the two bamboos, said, “Brahmin, what are you doing?” “I am taking your measure.” “Brahmin, even if you were to come having joined bamboo poles that stand filling the entire Cakkavāḷa-sphere, you would not be able to take my measure. For I did not fulfill the perfections for four incalculable aeons and one hundred thousand kappas in such a way that another could take my measure. The Tathāgata is incomparable, immeasurable, O brahmin.” Having said this, he spoke a verse that comes in the Dhammapada. At the conclusion of the verse, eighty-four thousand beings drank the deathless nectar.

Aparampi vatthu – rāhu kira asurindo cattāri yojanasahassāni aṭṭha ca yojanasatāni ucco, bāhantaramassa dvādasayojanasatāni, hatthatalapādatalānaṃ puthulatā tīṇi yojanasatāni, aṅgulipabbāni paṇṇāsayojanāni[M 3.0288], bhamukantaraṃ paṇṇāsayojanaṃ, nalāṭaṃ tiyojanasataṃ, sīsaṃ navayojanasataṃ. So – “ahaṃ uccosmi, satthāraṃ onamitvā oloketuṃ na sakkhissāmī”ti na gacchati. So ekadivasaṃ bhagavato vaṇṇaṃ sutvā “yathā kathañca olokessāmī”ti āgato. Bhagavā tassa ajjhāsayaṃ viditvā “catūsu iriyāpathesu katarena dassemī”ti cintetvā “ṭhitako nāma nīcopi ucco viya paññāyati, nipannovassa attānaṃ dassessāmī”ti, “ānanda, gandhakuṭipariveṇe mañcakaṃ paññāpehī”ti vatvā tattha sīhaseyyaṃ kappesi. Rāhu āgantvā nipannaṃ bhagavantaṃ gīvaṃ unnāmetvā nabhamajjhe puṇṇacandaṃ viya ulloketi. Kimidaṃ asurindāti ca vutte, bhagavā onamitvā oloketuṃ na sakkhissāmīti [P 3.0422] na gacchinti. Na mayā asurinda adhomukhena pāramiyo pūritā, uddhaggaṃ me katvā dānaṃ dinnanti. Taṃdivasaṃ rāhu saraṇaṃ agamāsi. Evaṃ bhagavā akhuddāvakāso dassanāya.

There is another story. It is said that Rāhu, the lord of the asuras, is four thousand and eight hundred yojanas tall. The space between his arms is twelve hundred yojanas, the breadth of his palms and soles is three hundred yojanas, his finger joints are fifty yojanas, the space between his eyebrows is fifty yojanas, his forehead is three hundred yojanas, and his head is nine hundred yojanas. He, thinking, “I am tall; I will not be able to see the Teacher by bowing down,” did not go. One day, having heard the praise of the Blessed One, he thought, “I will see him somehow or other,” and came. The Blessed One, knowing his intention, thought, “In which of the four postures shall I show myself? One who is standing, though short, appears as if tall. I will show myself to him while lying down.” Thinking thus, he said, “Ānanda, prepare a couch in the enclosure of the Perfumed Chamber,” and there he adopted the lion's posture. Rāhu, having come, raising his neck, looks up at the reclining Blessed One as one looks up at the full moon in the middle of the sky. And when it was said, “What is this, lord of asuras?”, he replied, “Venerable Sir, thinking, ‘I will not be able to see by bowing down,’ I did not come.” The Blessed One said, “Lord of asuras, the perfections were not fulfilled by me with face downturned. Gifts were given by me having made them pre-eminent.” On that day, Rāhu went for refuge. Thus, the Blessed One is not of limited opportunity for seeing.

Catupārisuddhisīlena sīlavā. Taṃ pana sīlaṃ ariyaṃ uttamaṃ parisuddhaṃ, tenāha ariyasīlīti. Tadeva anavajjaṭṭhena kusalaṃ, tenāha kusalasīlīti. Kusalena sīlenāti idamassa vevacanaṃ. Bahūnaṃ ācariyapācariyoti bhagavato ekekāya dhammadesanāya caturāsītipāṇasahassāni aparimāṇāpi devamanussā maggaphalāmataṃ pivanti. Tasmā bahūnaṃ ācariyo, sāvakavineyyānaṃ pācariyoti.

He is virtuous through the fourfold purity of moral conduct. Now, that moral conduct is noble, supreme, and pure; therefore, he is called ‘one of noble moral conduct’. That very same moral conduct, in the sense of being blameless, is wholesome; therefore, he is called ‘one of wholesome moral conduct’. ‘With wholesome moral conduct’ is a synonym for this. As for ‘teacher and teacher of teachers of many’: with each and every Dhamma discourse of the Blessed One, eighty-four thousand beings and also immeasurable devas and humans drink the deathless nectar of the path and fruit. Therefore, he is the teacher of many, and the teacher of teachers of the disciples to be trained.

Khīṇakāmarāgoti ettha kāmaṃ bhagavato sabbepi kilesā khīṇā, brāhmaṇo pana te na jānāti, attano jānanaṭṭhāneyeva guṇaṃ katheti. Vigatacāpalloti “pattamaṇḍanā cīvaramaṇḍanā senāsanamaṇḍanā imassa vā pūtikāyassa…pe… kelanā paṭikelanā”ti evaṃ vuttacāpalyavirahito.

Regarding ‘whose sensual lust is destroyed’: Indeed, all the defilements of the Blessed One are destroyed, but the brahmin does not know them; he speaks of the quality only in the sphere of his own knowing. ‘Devoid of fickleness’ means: he is devoid of the aforementioned fickleness, such as “adorning the bowl, adorning the robe, adorning the lodging, or, with regard to this foul body… playing and repeatedly playing.”

Apāpapurekkhāroti [V 3.0297] apāpe navalokuttaradhamme purato katvā vicarati. Brahmaññāya pajāyāti sāriputtamoggallānamahākassapādibhedāya brāhmaṇapajāya. (Aviruddho hi so) etissāya pajāya purekkhāro. Ayañhi pajā samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ purato katvā [M 3.0289] caratīti [P 3.0423] attho. Apica apāpapurekkhāroti na pāpupurekkhāro, na pāpaṃ purato katvā carati, pāpaṃ na icchatīti attho. Kassa? Brahmaññāya pajāya attanā saddhiṃ paṭiviruddhāyapi brāhmaṇapajāya aviruddho hitasukhatthikoyevāti vuttaṃ hoti.

‘Having the non-evil as a forerunner’ means: he fares along having placed the nine supramundane states, which are not evil, in the forefront. ‘For the brahmin folk’ means: for the brahmin folk distinguished as Sāriputta, Moggallāna, Mahākassapa, and others. He is unopposed to this folk and is their forerunner. For this folk fares along having placed the ascetic Gotama in the forefront; this is the meaning. Furthermore, ‘having the non-evil as a forerunner’ means he is not one who has evil as a forerunner; he does not fare along having placed evil in the forefront; he does not desire evil. This is the meaning. It is said that even towards the brahmin folk who are opposed to him, he is unopposed, desiring only their welfare and happiness.

Tiroraṭṭhāti pararaṭṭhato. Tirojanapadāti parajanapadato. Saṃpucchituṃ āgacchantīti khattiyapaṇḍitādayo ceva brāhmaṇagandhabbādayo ca pañhe abhisaṅkharitvā pucchissāmāti āgacchanti. Tattha keci pucchāya vā dosaṃ vissajjanasampaṭicchane vā asamatthataṃ sallakkhetvā apucchitvāva tuṇhī nisīdanti, keci pucchanti, kesañci bhagavā pucchāya ussāhaṃ janetvā vissajjeti. Evaṃ sabbesampi tesaṃ vimatiyo tīraṃ patvā mahāsamuddassa ūmiyo viya bhagavantaṃ patvāva bhijjanti. Sesamettha tathāgatassa vaṇṇe uttānameva.

‘From across the country’ means from another country. ‘From across the district’ means from another district. ‘They come to question’ means: learned khattiyas and others, and brahmins, gandhabbas, and others, having formulated questions, come thinking, “We will ask.” Among them, some, perceiving a fault in the question or their inability in answering and accepting, sit silently without asking. Some ask. For some, the Blessed One, having generated enthusiasm for the question, answers. Thus, all their doubts are shattered upon reaching the Blessed One, just as the waves of the great ocean are shattered upon reaching the shore. The rest here concerning the Tathāgata's qualities is clear.

Atithī no te hontīti te amhākaṃ āgantukā navakā pāhunakā hontīti attho. Pariyāpuṇāmīti jānāmi. Aparimāṇavaṇṇoti tathārūpeneva sabbaññunāpi appameyyavaṇṇo, pageva mādisenāti dasseti. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

‘They are our guests’ means: they are our visitors, newcomers, guests. This is the meaning. ‘I master’ means: I know. ‘Of immeasurable praise’ shows that his praise is immeasurable even for an Omniscient One of such a nature, what then to speak of one like me? And this was also said:

“Buddhopi buddhassa bhaṇeyya vaṇṇaṃ,

Kappampi ce aññamabhāsamāno;

Khīyetha kappo ciradīghamantare,

Vaṇṇo na khīyetha tathāgatassā”ti.

“If a Buddha, for a whole kappa, speaking nothing else, were to speak the praise of another Buddha; in that long interval the kappa would be exhausted, but the praise of the Tathāgata would not be exhausted.”

Imaṃ pana guṇakathaṃ sutvā te brāhmaṇā cintayiṃsu “yathā, caṅkī, samaṇassa gotamassa vaṇṇaṃ bhāsati, anomaguṇo [P 3.0424] so bhavaṃ gotamo, evaṃ tassa guṇe jānamānena kho pana iminā aticiraṃ adhivāsitaṃ, handa naṃ anuvattāmā”ti anuvattamānā “tena hi, bho”tiādimāhaṃsu.

Now, having heard this talk on his virtues, those brahmins thought: "According to the way that Caṅkī speaks in praise of the ascetic Gotama's virtues, that venerable Gotama must have virtues that are not inferior. Indeed, this Caṅkī, knowing his virtues, has been deeply influenced for a very long time. Come now, let us follow his example." Thus, wishing to follow his example, they said, "Well then, venerable sir," and so on.

426. Opātetīti [V 3.0298] paveseti. Saṃpurekkharontīti puttamattanattamattampi samānaṃ purato katvā vicaranti.

426. ‘Causes to fall in’ means causes to enter. ‘They place at the forefront’ means they go about having placed in front even someone of the measure of a son or a grandson, or an equal.

427. Mantapadanti mantāyeva mantapadaṃ, vedoti attho. Itihitiha paramparāyāti evaṃ kira evaṃ kirāti paramparabhāvena āgatanti dīpeti. Piṭakasampadāyāti [M 3.0290] pāvacanasaṅkhātasampattiyā. Sāvittiādīhi chandabandhehi ca vaggabandhehi ca sampādetvā āgatanti dasseti. Tattha cāti tasmiṃ mantapade. Pavattāroti pavattayitāro. Yesanti yesaṃ santakaṃ. Mantapadanti vedasaṅkhātaṃ mantameva. Gītanti aṭṭhakādīhi dasahi porāṇakabrāhmaṇehi padasampattivasena sajjhāyitaṃ. Pavuttanti aññesaṃ vuttaṃ, vācitanti attho. Samihitanti samupabyūḷhaṃ rāsikataṃ, piṇḍaṃ katvā ṭhapitanti attho. Tadanugāyantīti etarahi brāhmaṇā taṃ tehi pubbe gītaṃ anugāyanti anusajjhāyanti vādenti. Tadanubhāsantīti taṃ anubhāsanti, idaṃ purimasseva vevacanaṃ. Bhāsitamanubhāsantīti tehi bhāsitaṃ sajjhāyitaṃ anusajjhāyanti. Vācitamanuvācentīti [P 3.0425] tehi aññesaṃ vācitaṃ anuvācenti. Seyyathidanti te katameti attho. Aṭṭhakotiādīni tesaṃ nāmāni, te kira dibbena cakkhunā oloketvā parūpaghātaṃ akatvā kassapasammāsambuddhassa bhagavato pāvacanena saha saṃsandetvā mante ganthesuṃ, aparāpare pana brāhmaṇā pāṇātipātādīni pakkhipitvā tayo vede bhinditvā buddhavacanena saddhiṃ viruddhe akaṃsu.

427. "Mantapada" means the hymn itself; the meaning is the Veda. "By tradition from hearsay" shows that it has come down through successive generations as "so it is said, so it is said". "By the tradition of the canon" means by the accomplishment known as the teaching. It shows that it has come down, having been compiled with metrical compositions like the Sāvittī and with chapter compositions. "And therein" means in that mantapada. "Creators" means propagators. "Whose" means of whom it is the possession. "Mantapada" means the hymn itself, known as the Veda. "Chanted" means recited by the ten ancient brahmins, such as Aṭṭhaka, by way of accomplishment in words. "Promulgated" means spoken to others; the meaning is "taught". "Compiled" means collected, made into a heap; the meaning is made into a mass and established. "They chant after them" means that the brahmins of today chant in accordance with that which was chanted by them in the past; they recite after them; they teach. "They speak after that" means they speak after it; this is a synonym for the preceding term. "They speak after what was spoken" means they recite in accordance with what was spoken and recited by them. "They teach what was taught" means they teach in accordance with what was taught by them to others. "Namely" means "who are they?". Aṭṭhaka and so on are their names. It is said that they, looking with the divine eye and not causing harm to others, composed the hymns after comparing them with the teaching of the Blessed One, Kassapa the Perfectly Enlightened One. But later brahmins, inserting things like the killing of living beings, corrupted the three Vedas and made them contradictory to the word of the Buddha.

428. Andhaveṇīti andhapaveṇī. Ekena hi cakkhumatā gahitayaṭṭhiyā koṭiṃ eko andho gaṇhāti, taṃ andhaṃ añño, taṃ aññoti evaṃ paṇṇāsa saṭṭhi andhā paṭipāṭiyā ghaṭitā andhaveṇīti vuccati. Paramparāsaṃsattāti aññamaññaṃ laggā, yaṭṭhiggāhakenapi cakkhumatā virahitāti attho. Eko kira dhutto andhagaṇaṃ disvā “asukasmiṃ nāma gāme khajjabhojjaṃ sulabha”nti ussāhetvā tehi “tattha no sāmi nehi, idaṃ nāma te demā”ti vutte lañjaṃ gahetvā antarāmagge maggā okkamma mahantaṃ gacchaṃ anuparigantvā purimassa hatthena pacchimassa kacchaṃ gaṇhāpetvā “kiñci kammaṃ atthi, gacchatha tāva tumhe”ti vatvā palāyi. Te divasampi gantvā maggaṃ avindamānā “kahaṃ, bho, cakkhumā kahaṃ maggo”ti paridevitvā maggaṃ avindamānā tattheva mariṃsu. Te sandhāya vuttaṃ “paramparāsaṃsattā”ti. Purimopīti purimesu dasasu brāhmaṇesu ekopi. Majjhimopīti [P 3.0426] majjhe ācariyapācariyesu ekopi. Pacchimopīti idāni brāhmaṇesu ekopi.

428. "A line of the blind" means a lineage of the blind. For instance, one blind man grasps the end of a staff held by a sighted person, another blind man grasps that blind man, and another grasps him, and so on. In this way, fifty or sixty blind people connected in a sequence are called "a line of the blind." "Clinging one to another in succession" means they are attached to one another; the meaning is that they are without even a sighted person holding a staff. It is said that a certain rogue, seeing a group of blind men, encouraged them, saying, "In such-and-such a village, food is easy to obtain." When they said, "Master, lead us there, and we will give you such-and-such," he took the bribe. Midway, he turned from the path, and leading them around a large thicket, he had the first one grasp the waist-belt of the last one with his hand. Then, saying, "I have some business to attend to; you all go on ahead," he fled. They, wandering for a whole day but not finding the path, lamented, "Oh, sighted one, where are you? Where is the path?" Not finding the path, they died right there. It was with reference to them that it was said, "clinging one to another in succession." "The first" means not even one among the first ten brahmins. "The middle" means not even one among the teachers and their teachers in the middle. "The last" means not even one among the brahmins of today.

Pañca [V 3.0299][M 3.0291] khoti pāḷiāgatesu dvīsu aññepi evarūpe tayo pakkhipitvā vadati. Dvedhāvipākāti bhūtavipākā vā abhūtavipākā vā. Nālametthāti, bhāradvāja, saccaṃ anurakkhissāmīti paṭipannena viññunā “yaṃ mayā gahitaṃ, idameva saccaṃ moghamañña”nti ettha ekaṃseneva niṭṭhaṃ gantuṃ nālaṃ na yuttanti upari pucchāya maggaṃ vivaritvā ṭhapesi.

"Five": He speaks of five by adding three others of a similar nature to the two that come in the Pāḷi text. "Twofold in result" means either having a true result or an untrue result. "It is not proper here": Bhāradvāja, for a wise person who has undertaken, "I will protect the truth," it is not proper, not suitable, to arrive at a definite conclusion in this matter, thinking, "What I have grasped, this alone is true, the other is false." Thus, he opened up the way for the question that follows and established it.

430. Idha, bhāradvāja, bhikkhūti jīvakasutte (ma. ni. 2.51 ādayo) viya mahāvacchasutte (ma. ni. 2.193 ādayo) viya ca attānaññeva sandhāya vadati. Lobhanīyesu dhammesūti lobhadhammesu. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo.

430. "Here, Bhāradvāja, a bhikkhu": He speaks referring to himself, as in the Jīvaka Sutta and the Mahāvaccha Sutta. "In regard to enticing things" means in regard to things of greed. This same method should be understood for the remaining two phrases as well.

432. Saddhaṃ nivesetīti okappaniyasaddhaṃ niveseti. Upasaṅkamatīti upagacchati. Payirupāsatīti santike nisīdati. Sotanti pasādasotaṃ odahati. Dhammanti desanādhammaṃ suṇāti. Dhāretīti paguṇaṃ katvā dhāreti. Upaparikkhatīti atthato ca kāraṇato ca vīmaṃsati. Nijjhānaṃ khamantīti olokanaṃ khamanti, idha sīlaṃ kathitaṃ, idha samādhīti evaṃ upaṭṭhahantīti attho. Chandoti kattukamyatā chando. Ussahatīti vāyamati. Tuletīti aniccādivasena tīreti. Padahatīti maggapadhānaṃ padahati. Kāyena ceva paramasaccanti sahajātanāmakāyena ca [P 3.0427] nibbānaṃ sacchikaroti, paññāya ca kilese nibbijjhitvā tadeva vibhūtaṃ pākaṭaṃ karonto passati.

432. "He establishes faith" means he establishes a faith of conviction. "He approaches" means he goes near. "He attends upon" means he sits near to serve. "He inclines the ear" means he applies the faculty of hearing. "He hears the Dhamma" means he listens to the teaching-Dhamma. "He bears it in mind" means he bears it in mind after making it familiar. "He examines the meaning" means he investigates it by way of its meaning and its reason. "The teachings endure reflection" means they endure scrutiny; the meaning is that they become apparent thus: 'Here virtue is taught, here concentration is taught.' "Desire" means the wholesome desire which is the wish to act. "He makes an effort" means he strives. "He weighs" means he decides by way of impermanence and so on. "He strives" means he undertakes the great striving of the path.
