"And with the body he realizes the ultimate truth" means he realizes Nibbāna with the co-arisen mental body, and with wisdom, having penetrated the defilements, he sees that very truth, making it manifest and plain.

433. Saccānubodhoti maggānubodho. Saccānuppattīti phalasacchikiriyā. Tesaṃyevāti heṭṭhā vuttānaṃ dvādasannaṃ, evaṃ dīghaṃ maggavādaṃ anulometi, tasmā nāyamattho. Ayaṃ panettha attho – tesaṃyevāti tesaṃ maggasampayuttadhammānaṃ. Padhānanti maggapadhānaṃ. Tañhi phalasacchikiriyasaṅkhātāya saccānuppattiyā bahukāraṃ, magge asati phalābhāvatoti. Iminā nayena sabbapadesu attho veditabbo. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

433. "The understanding of the truths" is the understanding of the path. "The attainment of the truths" is the realization of the fruit. [The interpretation of] "Of these very" as referring to the twelve [factors] mentioned above conforms to the long discourse on the path; therefore, this meaning should not be taken. This, however, is the intended meaning here: "of these very" means of those states associated with the path. "Striving" means the striving associated with the path. Indeed, that is of great assistance for the attainment of the truths, which is described as the realization of the fruit, because when the path is absent, there is an absence of the fruit. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all terms. The remainder is clear everywhere.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

Of the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Caṅkīsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Caṅkī Sutta is finished.

6. Esukārīsuttavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Esukārī Sutta

437. Evaṃ [V 3.0300][M 3.0292] me sutanti esukārīsuttaṃ. Tattha bilaṃ olaggeyyunti koṭṭhāsaṃ laggāpeyyuṃ, iminā satthadhammaṃ nāma dasseti. Satthavāho kira mahākantārapaṭipanno antarāmagge goṇe mate maṃsaṃ gahetvā sabbesaṃ satthikānaṃ “idaṃ khāditvā ettakaṃ mūlaṃ dātabba”nti koṭṭhāsaṃ olaggeti, goṇamaṃsaṃ nāma khādantāpi atthi akhādantāpi, mūlaṃ dātuṃ sakkontāpi asakkontāpi. Satthavāho yena mūlena goṇo gahito, tassa nikkhamanatthaṃ [P 3.0428] sabbesaṃ balakkārena koṭṭhāsaṃ datvā mūlaṃ gaṇhāti, ayaṃ satthadhammo. Evamevaṃ brāhmaṇāpi lokassa paṭiññaṃ aggahetvā attanova dhammatāya catasso pāricariyā paññapentīti dassetuṃ evameva khotiādimāha. Pāpiyo assāti pāpaṃ assa. Seyyo assāti hitaṃ assa. Atha vā pāpiyoti pāpako lāmako attabhāvo assa. Seyyoti seṭṭho uttamo. Seyyaṃsoti seyyo. Uccākulīnatāti uccākulīnattena seyyo. Pāpiyaṃsoti pāpiyo. Uccākulīnatā ca dvīsu kulesu vaḍḍheti khattiyakule brāhmaṇakule ca, uḷāravaṇṇatā tīsu. Vessopi hi uḷāravaṇṇo hoti. Uḷārabhogatā catūsupi. Suddopi hi antamaso caṇḍālopi uḷārabhogo hotiyeva.

437. “Thus have I heard”—this is the Esukārī Sutta. Therein, ‘they would hang up a portion’ means they would have a share hung up; by this, what is called the caravan custom is shown. It is said that a caravan leader, while traveling through a great wilderness, when an ox dies along the way, takes the meat and hangs up a portion for all the caravan members, saying, “After eating this, such and such a price must be given.” There are those who eat the ox meat and those who do not, those who can pay the price and those who cannot. The caravan leader, in order to recover the price for which the ox was bought, forcibly gives a share to everyone and collects the price—this is the caravan custom. To show that, similarly, the brahmins, not accepting the world's consensus but by their own nature, establish the four kinds of service, he said, “Just so,” and so on. “It would be worse” means it would be bad for him. “It would be better” means it would be beneficial for him. Alternatively, “worse” means he would have a bad, inferior existence. “Better” means noble, supreme. “He is better” means he is better. “By high birth” means better by being of high birth. “He is worse” means he is worse. High birth is applicable to two families—the khattiya and brahmin families, while noble appearance is applicable to three. For indeed, a vessa can also have a noble appearance. Great wealth is applicable to all four. For indeed, a sudda, and at the very least even a caṇḍāla, can certainly possess great wealth.

440. Bhikkhācariyanti koṭidhanenapi hi brāhmaṇena bhikkhā caritabbāva, porāṇakabrāhmaṇā asītikoṭidhanāpi ekavelaṃ bhikkhaṃ caranti. Kasmā? Duggatakāle carantānaṃ idāni bhikkhaṃ carituṃ āraddhāti garahā na bhavissatīti. Atimaññamānoti yo bhikkhācariyavaṃsaṃ haritvā sattajīvakasikammavaṇijjādīhi jīvikaṃ kappeti, ayaṃ atimaññati nāma. Gopo vāti yathā gopako attanā rakkhitabbaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ thenento akiccakārī hoti, evanti attho. Iminā nayena sabbavāresu attho veditabbo. Asitabyābhaṅginti [P 3.0429] tiṇalāyanaasitañceva kājañca. Anussaratoti yattha jāto, tasmiṃ porāṇe mātāpettike kulavaṃse anussariyamāneti attho. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

440. “Regarding the life of alms-going”: For even a brahmin with a crore of wealth should indeed go about for alms. The ancient brahmins, even those with eighty crores of wealth, go for alms once a day. Why? So that when they go about in a time of hardship, there will be no criticism, such as, ‘Now they have started to go about for alms.’ “One who despises” means a brahmin who, having abandoned the lineage of the practice of alms-going, makes a living by means such as caravan trading, farming, commerce, and so on—this one is called ‘one who despises’. “Like a cowherd” means: just as a cowherd who steals the goods he should be guarding does what should not be done, so is the meaning. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all instances. “A sickle and carrying-pole” means a grass-cutting sickle and a carrying-pole. “Because of recollecting” means because of constantly recollecting the ancient, ancestral lineage in that family where one was born. The rest is clear everywhere.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya

Esukārīsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Esukārī Sutta is finished.

7. Dhanañjānisuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Dhanañjāni Sutta

445. Evaṃ [V 3.0301][M 3.0293] me sutanti dhanañjānisuttaṃ. Tattha dakkhiṇāgirisminti girīti pabbato, rājagahaṃ parikkhipitvā ṭhitapabbatassa dakkhiṇadisābhāge janapadassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Taṇḍulapālidvārāyāti rājagahassa kira dvattiṃsamahādvārāni catusaṭṭhikhuddakadvārāni, tesu ekaṃ taṇḍulapālidvāraṃ nāma, taṃ sandhāyevamāha. Rājānaṃ nissāyāti “gaccha manusse apīḷetvā sassabhāgaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti raññā pesito gantvā sabbameva sassaṃ gaṇhāti, “mā no, bhante, nāsehī”ti ca vutte – “rājakule vuttaṃ mandaṃ, ahaṃ raññā āgamanakāleyeva evaṃ āṇatto, mā kanditthā”ti evaṃ rājānaṃ nissāya brāhmaṇagahapatike vilumpati. Dhaññaṃ yebhuyyena attano gharaṃ pavesetvā appakaṃ rājakule paveseti. Kiṃ brāhmaṇagahapatikānaṃ na pīḷaṃ akāsīti ca vutto – “āma, mahārāja, imasmiṃ vāre khettāni [P 3.0430] mandasassāni ahesuṃ, tasmā apīḷentassa me gaṇhato na bahuṃ jāta”nti evaṃ brāhmaṇagahapatike nissāya rājānaṃ vilumpati.

445. "Thus have I heard"—this is the Dhanañjāni Sutta. Therein, regarding "in Dakkhiṇāgiri": 'giri' means mountain; this is the name of the region in the southern part of the mountains that stand encircling Rājagaha. Regarding "at the Taṇḍulapāli Gate": it is said that Rājagaha has thirty-two great gates and sixty-four small gates; among them, one is called the Taṇḍulapāli Gate, and it is said thus with reference to that. Regarding "relying on the king": sent by the king with the order, "Go, taking a share of the crop without oppressing the people," he goes and takes all the crop. When told, "Do not ruin us, sir," he says, "The grain in the royal household is scarce; I was ordered thus by the king at the very time of my coming, do not weep"—thus, relying on the king, he plunders the brahmins and householders. He brings most of the grain into his own house and puts little into the king's store. When asked, "Did you not oppress the brahmins and householders?" he replies, "Yes, great king, in this instance the fields yielded poor harvests, so when I collected without oppressing, not much was produced"—thus, relying on the brahmins and householders, he plunders the king.

446. Payo pīyatanti taruṇakhīraṃ pivatu. Tāva bhattassāti yāva khīraṃ pivitvā nisīdissatha, tāvadeva bhattassa kālo bhavissati. Idheva hi no pātarāsabhattaṃ āharissantīti dasseti. Mātāpitarotiādīsu mahallakā mātāpitaro mudukāni attharaṇapāvuraṇāni sukhumāni vatthāni madhurabhojanaṃ sugandhagandhamālādīni ca pariyesitvā posetabbā. Puttadhītānaṃ nāmakaraṇamaṅgalādīni sabbakiccāni karontena puttadāro posetabbo. Evañhi akariyamāne garahā uppajjatīti iminā nayena attho veditabbo.

446. "Payo pīyatanti" means "let him drink fresh milk." "Tāva bhattassā" means "for as long as you drink the milk and sit, just so long will it be time for the meal." This shows that they will bring our morning meal right here. In cases such as "parents," elderly parents should be cared for by seeking out and providing soft bedding and coverings, fine clothes, sweet food, fragrant perfumes and garlands, and so on. One's wife and children should be supported by performing all duties such as naming ceremonies and other auspicious rites. For if this is not done, blame arises. In this way, the meaning should be understood.

447. Adhammacārīti pañca dussīlyakammāni vā dasa dussīlyakammāni vā idha adhammo nāma. Upakaḍḍheyyunti pañcavidhabandhanādikammakaraṇatthaṃ taṃ taṃ nirayaṃ kaḍḍheyyuṃ.

447. "Adhammacārī" (one of unrighteous conduct): Herein, the five or ten kinds of immoral actions are called 'adhamma' (unrighteousness). "Upakaḍḍheyyuṃ" (they would drag down): they would drag him to this or that hell for the purpose of performing actions such as the fivefold bondage.

448. Dhammacārīti [V 3.0302] dhammikasivavijjādikammakārī. Paṭikkamantīti osaranti parihāyanti. Abhikkamantīti abhisaranti vaḍḍhanti. Seyyoti varataraṃ. Hīneti nihīne lāmake. Kālaṅkato ca sāriputtāti idaṃ [M 3.0294] bhagavā “tatrassa gantvā desehī”ti adhippāyena theramāha. Theropi [P 3.0431] taṃkhaṇaṃyeva gantvā mahābrahmuno dhammaṃ desesi, tato paṭṭhāya cātuppadikaṃ gāthaṃ kathentopi catusaccavimuttaṃ nāma na kathesīti.

448. "Dhammacārī" (one of righteous conduct) means one who performs righteous actions such as agriculture and trade. "Paṭikkamanti" (they fall back) means they go down, they decline. "Abhikkamanti" (they go forward) means they advance, they grow. "Seyyo" means more excellent. "Hīne" means in a low, base state. Regarding "Kālaṅkato ca, Sāriputta" (Sāriputta, [Dhanañjāni] has passed away): the Blessed One spoke this to the elder with the intention, "Go there and teach him." The elder too, at that very moment, went and taught the Dhamma to the great brahmā, Dhanañjāni. From then on, even when teaching a four-lined stanza, he did not teach anything that was devoid of the Four Noble Truths.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya

Dhanañjānisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Dhanañjāni Sutta is concluded.

8. Vāseṭṭhasuttavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Vāseṭṭha Sutta.

454. Evaṃ [V 3.0303] me sutanti vāseṭṭhasuttaṃ. Tattha icchānaṅgalavanasaṇḍeti icchānaṅgalagāmassa avidūre vanasaṇḍe. Caṅkīti ādayo pañcapi janā rañño pasenadissa kosalassa purohitā eva. Aññe ca abhiññātāti aññe ca bahū abhiññātā brāhmaṇā. Te kira chaṭṭhe chaṭṭhe māse dvīsu ṭhānesu sannipatanti. Yadā jātiṃ sodhetukāmā honti, tadā pokkharasātissa santike jātisodhanatthaṃ ukkaṭṭhāya sannipatanti. Yadā mante sodhetukāmā honti, tadā icchānaṅgale sannipatanti. Imasmiṃ kāle mantasodhanatthaṃ sannipatiṃsu. Ayamantarā kathāti yaṃ attano sahāyakabhāvānurūpaṃ kathaṃ kathentā anuvicariṃsu, tassā kathāya antarā ayamaññā kathā udapādi. Sīlavāti guṇavā. Vattasampannoti ācārasampanno.

454. The Vāseṭṭha Sutta is that which begins, 'Thus have I heard.' Therein, 'in the Icchānaṅgala forest grove' means in a forest grove not far from the village of Icchānaṅgala. The five persons, Caṅkī and others, were indeed the royal chaplains of King Pasenadi of Kosala. 'And other well-known ones' means many other well-known brahmins. It is said they would gather every six months in two places. When they wished to purify their lineage, they would assemble in the presence of Pokkharasāti in Ukkaṭṭhā for the purpose of purifying their lineage. When they wished to purify the mantras, they would gather in Icchānaṅgala. At this time, they had assembled to purify the mantras. 'This intermediate discussion' means that while they were wandering about, conversing in a manner suitable for their companionship, another discussion arose in the midst of that conversation. 'Virtuous' means endowed with good qualities. 'Accomplished in conduct' means accomplished in behavior.

455. Anuññātapaṭiññātāti [P 3.0432] sikkhitā tumheti evaṃ ācariyehi anuññātā, āma ācariya sikkhitamhāti evaṃ sayañca paṭiññātā. Asmāti bhavāma. Ahaṃ pokkharasātissa, tārukkhassāyaṃ māṇavoti ahaṃ pokkharasātissa jeṭṭhantevāsī aggasisso, ayaṃ tārukkhassāti dīpeti.

455. 'Acknowledged and professed' means they were authorized by their teachers thus, 'You are trained,' and they themselves also professed thus, 'Yes, teacher, we are trained.' 'We are' means we are. 'I am of Pokkharasāti, and this young man is of Tārukkha' indicates: 'I am the senior resident disciple, the chief disciple of Pokkharasāti, and this one is the senior resident disciple, the chief disciple of Tārukkha.'

Tevijjānanti tivedānaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ. Yadakkhātanti yaṃ atthato ca byañjanato ca ekaṃ padampi akkhātaṃ. Tatra kevalinosmaseti taṃ sakalaṃ jānanato tattha niṭṭhāgatamhāti attho. Idāni taṃ kevalibhāvaṃ āvikaronto padakasmātiādimāha. Tattha jappe ācariyasādisāti kathanaṭṭhāne mayaṃ ācariyasadisāyeva.

'Of those with the three knowledges' means of the brahmins who know the three Vedas. 'Whatever has been declared' means whatever single term has been declared, both in meaning and in phrasing. 'Therein we are complete' means: 'Because of knowing it all, we have reached completion therein.' This is the meaning. Now, making that state of completeness clear, he said the words beginning with 'We are grammarians...' Therein, 'in recitation, like the teacher' means 'in the place of speaking, we are just like the teacher.'

Kammunāti [M 3.0295] dasakusalakammapathakammunā. Ayañhi pubbe sattavidhaṃ kāyavacīkammaṃ sandhāya “yato kho, bho, sīlavā hotī”ti āha, tividhaṃ manokammaṃ sandhāya “vattasampanno”ti. Tena samannāgato hi ācārasampanno hoti. Cakkhumāti pañcahi cakkhūhi cakkhumantabhāvena bhagavantaṃ ālapati.

'By action' means by the action of the ten wholesome courses of action. For this one previously, referring to the sevenfold bodily and verbal action, said, 'Because, good sir, one is virtuous'; and referring to the threefold mental action, he said, 'accomplished in conduct.' Indeed, one endowed with that is accomplished in conduct. 'O one with vision' means he addresses the Blessed One as one who possesses vision by means of the five eyes.

Khayātītanti [V 3.0304] ūnabhāvaṃ atītaṃ, paripuṇṇanti attho. Peccāti upagantvā. Namassantīti namo karonti.

'Gone beyond decay' means having transcended a state of deficiency; the meaning is 'complete.' 'Having approached' means having gone near. 'They pay homage' means they make reverence.

Cakkhuṃ loke samuppannanti avijjandhakāre loke taṃ andhakāraṃ vidhamitvā lokassa diṭṭhadhammikādiatthadassanena cakkhu hutvā samuppannaṃ.

'An eye arisen in the world' means that, in a world dark with ignorance, having dispelled that darkness, he has arisen, having become an eye for the world for the seeing of benefits, such as those in this present life.

456. Evaṃ [P 3.0433] vāseṭṭhena thometvā yācito bhagavā dvepi jane saṅgaṇhanto tesaṃ vo ahaṃ byakkhissantiādimāha. Tattha byakkhissanti byākarissāmi. Anupubbanti tiṭṭhatu tāva brāhmaṇacintā, tiṇarukkhakīṭapaṭaṅgato paṭṭhāya anupaṭipāṭiyā ācikkhissāmīti attho. Jātivibhaṅganti jātivitthāraṃ. Aññamaññā hi jātiyoti tesaṃ tesañhi pāṇānaṃ jātiyo aññamaññā nānappakārāti attho.

456. Thus, having been praised and requested by Vāseṭṭha, the Blessed One, wishing to accommodate both persons, said the words beginning with, 'To you... I will explain.' Therein, 'I will explain' means 'I will expound.' 'In due order' means: 'Let the brahmins' concern stand for now; starting from grass, trees, worms, and moths, I will declare in sequence.' 'The analysis of birth' means the detailed account of birth. 'For births are distinct from one another' means that the births of those various beings are distinct from one another and of various kinds.

Tiṇarukkheti anupādinnakajātiṃ katvā pacchā upādinnakajātiṃ kathessāmi, evaṃ tassa jātibhedo pākaṭo bhavissatīti imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi. Mahāsīvatthero pana “kiṃ, bhante, anupādinnakaṃ bījanānatāya nānaṃ, upādinnaṃ kammanānatāyāti? Evaṃ vattuṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti pucchito āma na vaṭṭati. Kammañhi yoniyaṃ khipati. Yonisiddhā ime sattā nānāvaṇṇā hontīti. Tiṇarukkheti ettha antopheggū bahisārā antamaso tālanāḷikerādayopi tiṇāneva, antosārā pana bahipheggū sabbe rukkhā nāma. Na cāpi paṭijānareti mayaṃ tiṇā mayaṃ rukkhāti vā, ahaṃ tiṇaṃ, ahaṃ rukkhoti vā evaṃ na jānanti. Liṅgaṃ jātimayanti ajānantānampi ca tesaṃ jātimayameva saṇṭhānaṃ attano mūlabhūtatiṇādisadisameva hoti. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Aññamaññā hi jātiyo. Yasmā aññā tiṇajāti, aññā rukkhajāti. Tiṇesupi aññā tālajāti, aññā nāḷikerajāti, evaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ. Iminā idaṃ dasseti – yaṃ jātivasena nānā [M 3.0296] hoti, taṃ attano paṭiññaṃ paresaṃ vā upadesaṃ vināpi aññajātito visesena gayhati. Yadi ca jātiyā brāhmaṇo [P 3.0434] bhaveyya, sopi attano paṭiññaṃ paresaṃ vā upadesaṃ vinā khattiyato vessato suddato vā visesena gayheyya, na ca gayhati. Tasmā na jātiyā brāhmaṇoti. Parato pana “yathā etāsu jātīsū”ti gāthāya etamatthaṃ vacībhedeneva āvikarissati.

'Regarding grass and trees,' he began this discourse, thinking: 'First I will speak on unappropriated birth, and afterwards I will speak on appropriated birth; in this way the distinction of birth will become clear to him.' The Venerable Mahāsīva, however, when asked, 'Venerable sir, is the unappropriated diverse due to the diversity of seeds, and the appropriated diverse due to the diversity of kamma? Is it not proper to say so?' replied, 'Indeed, it is not proper. For kamma casts beings into an origin. These beings, established by their origin, become of diverse kinds.' Herein, regarding 'grass and trees': those with soft tissue inside and hard tissue outside—even down to palm and coconut trees—are called 'grasses.' But all those with hard tissue inside and soft tissue outside are called 'trees.' Nor do they profess, 'We are grasses,' or 'We are trees,' nor do they know, 'I am a grass,' or 'I am a tree.' 'Their mark is determined by birth' means that even though they do not know, their form, which is determined by their birth, is just like the grass or tree that is their origin. For what reason? Because births are distinct from one another. For the birth of grass is one thing, and the birth of a tree is another. Even among grasses, the birth of a palm is one thing, and the birth of a coconut is another; thus it should be elaborated. By this, he shows the following: that which is different by way of birth is distinguished from another birth without any profession by itself or instruction from others. And if one were a brahmin by birth, he too would be distinguished from a khattiya, a vessa, or a sudda without any profession by himself or instruction from others; but he is not so distinguished. Therefore, one is not a brahmin by birth. Further on, in the verse beginning 'Just as among these births,' he will make this very meaning clear simply by the phrasing of his words.

Evaṃ [V 3.0305] anupādinnakesu jātiṃ dassetvā upādinnakesu dassento tato kīṭetiādimāha. Yāva kunthakipilliketi kunthakipillikaṃ pariyantaṃ katvāti attho. Ettha ca ye uppatitvā gacchanti, te paṭaṅgā nāma. Aññamaññā hi jātiyoti tesampi nīlarattādivaṇṇavasena jātiyo nānappakārāva honti.

Thus, having shown birth among unappropriated beings, while showing it among appropriated beings, he said the words beginning with, 'Then among worms...' 'Down to insects and ants' means having made insects and ants the limit. And here, those that go by flying up are called moths. 'For births are distinct from one another' means that for them too, by way of their colors such as blue, red, and so on, their births are indeed of various kinds.

Khuddaketi kāḷakādayo. Mahallaketi sasabiḷārādayo.

'The small ones' means creatures such as black squirrels. 'The large ones' means creatures such as rabbits and cats.

Pādūdareti udarapāde, udaraṃyeva nesaṃ pādāti vuttaṃ hoti. Dīghapiṭṭhiketi sappānañhi sīsato yāva naṅguṭṭhā piṭṭhiyeva hoti, tena te “dīghapiṭṭhikā”ti vuccanti.

'Belly-footed' means those whose feet are their belly; for them, their belly itself is their feet—this is what is said. 'The long-backed ones' means that because snakes have only a back from their head to their tail, they are called 'long-backed.'

Udaketi odake, udakamhi jāte.

'In the water' means in an aquatic environment, born in the water.

Pakkhīti sakuṇe. Te hi pattehi yantīti pattayānā, vehāsaṃ gacchantīti vihaṅgamā.

'Birds' refers to winged creatures. For because they go with wings, they are called 'wing-goers'; because they go through the sky, they are called 'sky-goers.'

Evaṃ thalajalākāsagocarānaṃ pāṇānaṃ jātibhedaṃ dassetvā idāni yenādhippāyena taṃ dasseti, taṃ āvikaronto yathā etāsūti gāthamāha. Tassattho saṅkhepena vuttova. Vitthārato panettha yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ [P 3.0435] sayameva dassento na kesehītiādimāha. Tatrāyaṃ yojanā – yaṃ vuttaṃ “natthi manussesu liṅgajātimayaṃ puthū”ti, taṃ evaṃ natthīti veditabbaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ? Na kesehīti. Na hi – “brāhmaṇānaṃ edisā kesā honti, khattiyānaṃ edisā”ti niyamo atthi yathā hatthiassamigādīnanti iminā nayena sabbaṃ yojetabbaṃ.

Having thus shown the distinction of species among beings that move on land, in water, and in the sky, now, wishing to make clear the intention with which He showed it, He spoke the verse beginning with 'yathā etāsu.' Its meaning has already been stated in brief. Now, wishing to show in detail what should be said here, He Himself spoke the words beginning with 'na kesehi.' Therein, this is the connection: what was said—'Among humans, there is no separate distinction consisting of marks of birth'—should be understood as 'it does not exist thus.' How is this? 'Not by hair.' For indeed, there is no fixed rule that 'Brahmins have such hair, Khattiyas have such hair,' as there is for elephants, horses, deer, and so on. In this way, all terms should be connected.

Liṅgaṃ jātimayaṃ neva, yathā aññāsu jātisūti idaṃ pana vuttassevatthassa nigamananti veditabbaṃ. Tassāyaṃ yojanā – evaṃ yasmā imehi [M 3.0297] kesādīhi natthi manussesu liṅgaṃ jātimayaṃ puthu, tasmā veditabbametaṃ “brāhmaṇādibhedesu manussesu liṅgaṃ jātimayaṃ neva, yathā aññāsu jātisū”ti.

Now, this phrase, 'The mark consisting of birth does not exist at all, as it is in other species,' should be understood as the conclusion of the meaning that has already been stated. Of that, this is the connection: Thus, because by these things such as hair, there is no separate mark consisting of birth among humans, therefore this should be understood: 'Among humans with distinctions such as Brahmin and so on, the mark consisting of birth does not exist at all, as it does in other species.'

457. Idāni evaṃ jātibhede asatipi “brāhmaṇo khattiyo”ti idaṃ nānattaṃ yathā jātaṃ[V 3.0306], taṃ dassetuṃ paccattanti gāthamāha. Tattha vokāranti nānattaṃ. Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepattho – yathā hi tiracchānānaṃ yonisiddhameva kesādisaṇṭhānena nānattaṃ, tathā brāhmaṇādīnaṃ attano attano sarīre taṃ natthi. Evaṃ santepi yadetaṃ “brāhmaṇo khattiyo”ti vokāraṃ, taṃ vokārañca manussesu samaññāya pavuccati, vohāramatteneva pavuccatīti.

457. Now, to show how this diversity—'Brahmin,' 'Khattiya'—arose even though such a distinction of birth does not exist, He spoke the verse beginning with 'paccattaṃ.' Therein, 'vokāra' means diversity. This is the concise meaning here: Just as for animal species there is a diversity established by birth through the form of hair and so on, so for Brahmins and others, that diversity does not exist in their own respective bodies. Even so, that diversity which is 'Brahmin,' 'Khattiya'—that diversity is spoken of among humans by designation; it is spoken of merely by convention.

Ettāvatā bhagavā bhāradvājassa vādaṃ niggaṇhitvā idāni yadi jātiyā brāhmaṇo bhaveyya, ājīvasīlācāravipannopi brāhmaṇo bhaveyya. Yasmā pana porāṇā brāhmaṇā tassa brāhmaṇabhāvaṃ na icchanti, loke ca aññepi paṇḍitamanussā, tasmā vāseṭṭhassa vādaṃ paggaṇhanto yo hi koci manussesūti aṭṭha gāthā āha. Tattha gorakkhanti khettarakkhaṃ, kasikammanti vuttaṃ hoti. Goti hi pathaviyā nāmaṃ, tasmā evamāha. Puthusippenāti tantavāyakammādinānāsippena. Vohāranti vaṇijjaṃ. Parapessenāti [P 3.0436] paresaṃ veyyāvaccakammena. Issatthanti āvudhajīvikaṃ, usuñca sattiṃ cāti vuttaṃ hoti. Porohiccenāti purohitakammena.

With this much, the Blessed One, having refuted the view of Bhāradvāja, now considers: If one were a Brahmin by birth, then even one corrupt in livelihood, virtue, and conduct would be a Brahmin. But since the ancient Brahmins do not desire the Brahmin-hood of such a person, and nor do other wise people in the world, therefore, supporting the view of Vāseṭṭha, He spoke the eight verses beginning with 'yo hi koci manussesu.' Therein, 'gorakkhaṃ' means protecting the fields; this is said to be agriculture. For 'go' is a name for the earth; therefore, He said thus. 'Puthusippena' means by various crafts such as weaving. 'Vohāraṃ' means trade. 'Parapesena' means by service to others. 'Issattaṃ' means living by weapons; this is said to mean by arrow and spear. 'Porohiccena' means by the work of a chaplain.

Evaṃ brāhmaṇasamayena ca lokavohārena ca ājīvasīlācāravipannassa abrāhmaṇabhāvaṃ sādhetvā evaṃ sante na jātiyā brāhmaṇo, guṇehi pana brāhmaṇo hoti. Tasmā yattha katthaci kule jāto yo guṇavā, so brāhmaṇo, ayamettha ñāyoti evametaṃ ñāyaṃ atthato āpādetvā idāni naṃ vacībhedena pakāsento na cāhaṃ brāhmaṇantiādimāha. Tassattho – ahañhi yvāyaṃ catunnaṃ yonīnaṃ yattha katthaci jāto, tatrāpi visesena yo brāhmaṇassa saṃvaṇṇitāya mātari sambhūto, taṃ yonijaṃ mattisambhavaṃ, yā cāyaṃ ubhato sujātotiādinā nayena brāhmaṇehi brāhmaṇassa parisuddhauppattimaggasaṅkhātā yoni vuttā, saṃsuddhagahaṇikoti iminā [M 3.0298] ca mātisampatti, tatopi jātasambhūtattā yonijo mattisambhavoti vuccati, taṃ yonijaṃ mattisambhavaṃ iminā ca yonijamattisambhavamattena na brāhmaṇaṃ brūmi. Kasmā? Yasmā, bho bhoti, vacanamattena aññehi sakiñcanehi visiṭṭhattā bhovādi nāma so hoti, sace hoti sakiñcano sapalibodho. Yo panāyaṃ yattha katthaci jātopi rāgādikiñcanābhāvena akiñcano, sabbagahaṇapaṭinissaggena anādāno, akiñcanaṃ anādānaṃ, tamahaṃ brūmi [P 3.0437] brāhmaṇaṃ. Kasmā? Yasmā bāhitapāpoti.

Thus, having established by both Brahmin tradition and worldly convention the non-Brahmin status of one corrupt in livelihood, virtue, and conduct, it follows that one is not a Brahmin by birth, but rather by qualities. Therefore, whoever is born in any family whatsoever, if he is virtuous, he is a Brahmin. This is the right principle here. Having thus established this principle in terms of meaning, now, clarifying it with a verbal distinction, He spoke the words beginning with 'na cāhaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ.' Its meaning is this: I do not call someone a Brahmin merely for being born of a particular lineage and from a particular mother. Why? Because if he has attachments and impediments, he is called a 'bhovādi' (one who says 'bho'), being distinguished from other attached people merely by the word 'bho.' But whoever, though born anywhere, is without attachments due to the absence of defilements like lust, and is without grasping due to the relinquishing of all appropriation—that person, without attachments, without grasping, I call a Brahmin. Why? Because he has banished evil.

458. Kiñcabhiyyo [V 3.0307] sabbasaṃyojanaṃ chetvātiādi sattavīsati gāthā. Tattha sabbasaṃyojananti dasavidhasaṃyojanaṃ. Na paritassatīti taṇhāparitassanāya na paritassati. Saṅgātiganti rāgasaṅgādayo atikkantaṃ. Visaṃyuttanti catūhi yonīhi sabbakilesehi vā visaṃyuttaṃ.

458. Furthermore, there are twenty-seven verses beginning with 'Having cut off all fetters...' Therein, 'all fetters' means the ten kinds of fetters. 'He does not tremble' means he does not tremble with the trembling of craving. 'Gone beyond attachment' means one who has overcome attachments such as lust. 'Disjoined' means one who is disjoined from the four kinds of birth or from all defilements.

Naddhinti upanāhaṃ. Varattanti taṇhaṃ. Sandānanti yuttapāsaṃ, diṭṭhipariyuṭṭhānassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sahanukkamanti anukkamo vuccati pāse pavesanagaṇṭhi, diṭṭhānusayassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Ukkhittapalighanti ettha palighoti avijjā. Buddhanti catusaccabuddhaṃ. Titikkhatīti khamati.

'The thong' means resentment. 'The strap' means craving. 'The tether' means the associated fetter; this is a designation for the obsession of wrong views. 'With its appendage': the appendage is said to be the knot for entering the snare; this is a name for the underlying tendency of wrong views. 'With bolt uplifted': herein, 'the bolt' is ignorance. 'Awakened' means one who has understood the Four Truths. 'He endures' means he is patient.

Khantibalanti adhivāsanakhantibalaṃ. Sā pana sakiṃ uppannā balānīkaṃ nāma na hoti, punappunaṃ uppannā pana hoti. Tassā atthitāya balānīkaṃ.

'The strength of endurance' means the power of patient endurance. But that endurance, when it has arisen once, is not called an 'army of strength' (balānīkaṃ); however, when it has arisen again and again, it is. Because of its existence as such, it is called an 'army of strength'.

Vatavantanti dhutaṅgavantaṃ. Sīlavantanti guṇavantaṃ. Anussadanti rāgādiussadavirahitaṃ. “Anussuta”ntipi pāṭho, anavassutanti attho. Dantanti nibbisevanaṃ.

'Observant of vows' (vatavantaṃ) means one who possesses the ascetic practices. 'Virtuous' (sīlavantaṃ) means one who possesses good qualities. 'Without prominence' (anussadaṃ) means one who is free from the prominence of lust and so on. There is also the reading 'anussutaṃ,' meaning 'not oozing' with defilements. 'Tamed' (dantaṃ) means one who is not coarse.

Na limpatīti na allīyati. Kāmesūti kilesakāmavatthukāmesu.

'He is not smeared' means he does not cling. 'In sensual pleasures' means in sensual pleasures as defilements and sensual pleasures as objects.

Dukkhassa [P 3.0438] pajānāti, idheva khayanti ettha arahattaphalaṃ dukkhakkhayoti adhippetaṃ. Pajānātīti adhigamavasena jānāti. Pannabhāranti ohitabhāraṃ, khandhakilesaabhisaṅkhārakāmaguṇabhāre otāretvā ṭhitaṃ. Visaṃyuttapadaṃ vuttatthameva.

In the phrase 'He understands the destruction of suffering right here,' the destruction of suffering is intended to mean the fruit of Arahantship. 'He understands' means he knows by way of realization. 'With burden laid down' means one who has laid down the burden; one who stands having put down the burdens of the aggregates, defilements, formations, and sensual pleasures. The term 'disjoined' has the meaning already stated.

Gambhīrapaññanti gambhīresu ārammaṇesu pavattapaññaṃ. Medhāvinti pakatipaññāya paññavantaṃ.

"One with profound wisdom" (gambhīrapaññaṃ) refers to a person whose wisdom arises in profound objects. "Intelligent" (medhāvī) refers to a person who is wise by means of natural wisdom.

Anāgārehi [M 3.0299] cūbhayanti anāgārehi ca visaṃsaṭṭhaṃ ubhayañca, dvīhipi cetehi visaṃsaṭṭhamevāti attho. Anokasārinti okaṃ vuccati pañcakāmaguṇālayo, taṃ anallīyamānanti attho. Appicchanti anicchaṃ.

"Unassociated with both" (anāgārehi cūbhayaṃ) means unassociated with both monks (anāgārehi) [and householders]. Indeed, one is unassociated with both of these two; this is the meaning. "Not resorting to a home" (anokasāriṃ): 'home' (okaṃ) refers to the abode of the five strands of sensual pleasure; [the phrase] refers to one who does not cling to it; this is the meaning. "Of few wishes" (appicchaṃ) refers to one who is without desire.

Tasesūti [V 3.0308] sataṇhesu. Thāvaresūti nittaṇhesu.

"Among the trembling" (tasesu) means among those with craving. "Among the stable" (thāvaresu) means among those without craving.

Attadaṇḍesūti gahitadaṇḍesu. Nibbutanti kilesanibbānena nibbutaṃ. Sādānesūti saupādānesu.

"Among those who have taken up the rod" (attadaṇḍesu) means among those who have grasped a rod. "Extinguished" (nibbutaṃ) refers to a person who is at peace through the extinguishing of defilements. "Among those with grasping" (sādānesu) means among those with clinging.

Ohitoti patito.

"Cast down" (ohito) means fallen.

459. Akakkasanti niddosaṃ. Sadoso hi rukkhopi sakakkasoti vuccati. Viññāpaninti atthaviññāpanikaṃ. Saccanti avisaṃvādikaṃ. Udīrayeti bhaṇati. Yāya [P 3.0439] nābhisajjeti yāya girāya parassa sajjanaṃ vā lagganaṃ vā na karoti, tādisaṃ apharusaṃ giraṃ bhāsatīti attho.

459. "Not harsh" (akakkasaṃ) means faultless. Indeed, even a faulty tree is called "harsh" (sakakkaso). "That which makes known" (viññāpaniṃ) means that which makes the meaning known. "True speech" (giraṃ saccaṃ) means speech that is not deceptive. "One should utter" (udīraye) means one speaks. "By which one does not cause clinging" (yāya nābhisajje) means: by which speech one does not cause attachment or clinging in another, one speaks such speech that is not rough; this is the meaning.

Dīghanti suttāruḷhabhaṇḍaṃ. Rassanti vippakiṇṇabhaṇḍaṃ. Aṇunti khuddakaṃ. Thūlanti mahantaṃ. Subhāsubhanti sundarāsundaraṃ. Dīghabhaṇḍañhi appagghampi hoti mahagghampi. Rassādīsupi eseva nayo. Iti ettāvatā na sabbaṃ pariyādiṇṇaṃ, “subhāsubha”nti iminā pana pariyādiṇṇaṃ hoti.

"Long" (dīghaṃ) refers to goods strung on a thread. "Short" (rassaṃ) refers to scattered goods. "Small" (aṇuṃ) refers to small goods. "Large" (thūlaṃ) refers to large goods. "Good and bad" (subhāsubhaṃ) refers to beautiful and unbeautiful goods. Indeed, "long" goods can be of little value or of great value. This same principle should be understood for "short" and the others. By this much, not everything is encompassed; but by "good and bad," everything is encompassed.

Nirāsayanti nittaṇhaṃ.

"Without longing" (nirāsayaṃ) refers to a person who is without craving.

Ālayāti taṇhālayā. Aññāyāti jānitvā. Amatogadhanti amatabbhantaraṃ. Anuppattanti anupaviṭṭhaṃ.

"Attachments" (ālayā) refers to the attachments of craving. "Having understood" (aññāya) means having known. "Gone to the Deathless" (amatogadhaṃ) means into the interior of the Deathless. "Attained" (anuppattaṃ) means entered.

Ubho saṅganti ubhayampetaṃ saṅgaṃ. Puññañhi sagge laggāpeti, apuññaṃ apāye, tasmā ubhayampetaṃ saṅganti āha. Upaccagāti atīto.

"Both attachments" (ubho saṅgaṃ) means both of these are an attachment. Indeed, merit causes attachment in the heavenly realm, and demerit causes attachment in the woeful states. Therefore, it is said, "both of these are an attachment." "Has passed beyond" (upaccagā) means has transcended.

Anāvilanti āvilakaraṇakilesavirahitaṃ. Nandībhavaparikkhīṇanti parikkhīṇanandiṃ parikkhīṇabhavaṃ.

"Undisturbed" (anāvilaṃ) refers to a person free from the defilements that cause turbidity. "One for whom delight and existence are exhausted" (nandībhavaparikkhīṇaṃ) refers to a person whose delight is exhausted and whose existence is exhausted.

“Yo [V 3.0309] ima”nti gāthāya avijjāyeva visaṃvādakaṭṭhena palipatho, mahāviduggatāya duggaṃ, saṃsaraṇaṭṭhena saṃsāro, mohanaṭṭhena mohoti vutto. Tiṇṇoti [P 3.0440] caturoghatiṇṇo. Pāraṅgatoti nibbānaṃ gato. Jhāyīti ārammaṇalakkhaṇūpanijjhānavasena jhāyī. Anejoti nittaṇho. Anupādāya [M 3.0300] nibbutoti kiñci gahaṇaṃ aggahetvā sabbakilesanibbānena nibbuto.

In the verse beginning "He who this..." (yo imaṃ), ignorance itself is called a "bog" (palipatha) because of its deceptive nature; a "difficult passage" (duggaṃ) because it is extremely hard to get through; "saṃsāra" because of its nature of wandering on; and "delusion" (moha) because of its bewildering nature. "Crossed over" (tiṇṇo) means one who has crossed the four floods. "Gone to the far shore" (pāraṅgato) means gone to Nibbāna. "Meditative" (jhāyī) means one is meditative by means of absorption upon an object and absorption upon characteristics. "Unshaken" (anejo) means without craving. "Extinguished without grasping" (anupādāya nibbuto) means one is extinguished by the extinguishing of all defilements, without grasping anything at all.

Kāmeti duvidhepi kāme. Anāgāroti anāgāro hutvā. Paribbajeti paribbajati. Kāmabhavaparikkhīṇanti khīṇakāmaṃ khīṇabhavaṃ.

"Sensual pleasures" (kāme) refers to both kinds of sensual pleasures [i.e., objects of sensual pleasure and the defilement of sensual pleasure]. "Homeless" (anāgāro) means having become homeless. "Wanders" (paribbaje) means one wanders forth. "One for whom sensual pleasure and existence are exhausted" (kāmabhavaparikkhīṇaṃ) refers to a person whose sensual pleasure is exhausted and whose existence is exhausted.

Mānusakaṃ yoganti mānusakaṃ pañcakāmaguṇayogaṃ. Dibbaṃ yoganti dibbaṃ pañcakāmaguṇayogaṃ. Sabbayogavisaṃyuttanti sabbakilesayogavisaṃyuttaṃ.

"The human yoke" (mānusakaṃ yogaṃ) means the yoke of the five strands of human sensual pleasure. "The divine yoke" (dibbaṃ yogaṃ) means the yoke of the five strands of divine sensual pleasure. "Disjoined from all yokes" (sabbayogavisaṃyuttaṃ) refers to a person who is disjoined from the yoke of all defilements.

Ratinti pañcakāmaguṇaratiṃ. Aratinti kusalabhāvanāya ukkaṇṭhitaṃ. Vīranti vīriyavantaṃ.

"Delight" (ratiṃ) refers to delight in the five strands of sensual pleasure. "Discontent" (aratiṃ) refers to discontent with the cultivation of the wholesome. "Heroic" (vīraṃ) refers to a person who possesses energy.

Sugatanti sundaraṃ ṭhānaṃ gataṃ, sundarāya vā paṭipattiyā gataṃ.

"Well-gone" (sugataṃ) refers to one who has gone to a good place, or alternatively, one who has gone by means of a good practice.

Gatinti nibbattiṃ. Pureti atīte. Pacchāti anāgate. Majjheti paccuppanne. Kiñcananti [P 3.0441] kiñcanakārako kileso.

"Destination" (gatiṃ) means rebirth. "Before" (pure) means in the past. "After" (pacchā) means in the future. "In between" (majjhe) means in the present. "Impediment" (kiñcanaṃ) is the defilement that causes impediments.

Mahesinti mahante guṇe pariyesanaṭṭhena mahesiṃ. Vijitāvinanti vijitavijayaṃ.

"Great seer" (mahesiṃ) refers to one who is a 'great seeker' in the sense of seeking great qualities. "Victorious" (vijitāvinaṃ) refers to one who has won the victory.

460. Evaṃ bhagavā guṇato khīṇāsavaṃyeva brāhmaṇaṃ dassetvā ye jātito brāhmaṇoti abhinivesaṃ karonti, te idaṃ ajānantā, sāva nesaṃ diṭṭhi duddiṭṭhīti dassento samaññā hesāti gāthādvayamāha. Tassattho – yadidaṃ brāhmaṇo khattiyo bhāradvājo vāseṭṭhoti nāmagottaṃ pakappitaṃ kataṃ abhisaṅkhataṃ, samaññā hesā lokasmiṃ, vohāramattanti attho. Kasmā? Yasmā samuccā samudāgataṃ samaññāya āgataṃ. Etañhi tattha tattha jātakāleyevassa ñātisālohitehi pakappitaṃ kataṃ. No ce naṃ evaṃ pakappeyyuṃ, na koci kiñci disvā ayaṃ brāhmaṇoti vā bhāradvājoti [V 3.0310] vā jāneyya. Evaṃ pakappitaṃ petaṃ dīgharattānusayitaṃ, diṭṭhigatamajānataṃ, taṃ pakappitaṃ nāmagottaṃ “nāmagottamattametaṃ, vohāratthaṃ pakappita”nti, ajānantānaṃ sattānaṃ hadaye dīgharattaṃ diṭṭhigatamanusayitaṃ. Tassa anusayitattā taṃ nāmagottaṃ ajānantā no pabrunti, “jātiyā hoti brāhmaṇo”ti ajānantāva evaṃ vadantīti vuttaṃ hoti.

460. In this way, the Blessed One showed that, in terms of qualities, only one whose cankers are destroyed is a Brahmin. Then, to show that those who adhere to the view "one is a Brahmin by birth" do not understand this, and that this view of theirs is a wrong view, he spoke the two verses beginning, "This is a convention." The meaning is this: that which is conceived, made, and constructed as a name and clan—such as 'Brahmin,' 'Khattiya,' 'Bhāradvāja,' 'Vāseṭṭha'—this is just a convention in the world, a mere designation. Why? Because it has arisen by convention. For this name and clan is conceived and made for one by one's relatives at the very time of birth in this or that place. If they did not so conceive it, no one, upon seeing someone, would know, "This is a Brahmin," or "This is a Bhāradvāja." This, though conceived, has for a long time lain latent as a wrong view for those who do not know. For beings who do not know that this conceived name and clan is "merely a name and clan, conceived for the sake of designation," this wrong view has for a long time lain latent in their hearts. Because that wrong view lies latent, those who do not know say, "One is a Brahmin by birth." It means that only those who do not know speak in this way.

Evaṃ [M 3.0301] “ye ‘jātito brāhmaṇo’ti abhinivesaṃ karonti, te idaṃ vohāramattaṃ ajānantā, sāva nesaṃ diṭṭhi duddiṭṭhī”ti dassetvā idāni nippariyāyameva jātivādaṃ paṭikkhipanto kammavādañca patiṭṭhapento na jaccātiādimāha. Tattha “kammunā”ti upaḍḍhagāthāya vitthāraṇatthaṃ kassako kammunātiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha kammunāti paccuppannena kasikammādinibbattakacetanākammunā.

Thus, having shown that "those who adhere to the view 'one is a Brahmin by birth' do not understand that this is a mere designation, and this view of theirs is a wrong view," now, directly rejecting the doctrine of birth and establishing the doctrine of kamma, he spoke the words beginning, "Not by birth..." To explain in detail the half-verse "by kamma," the words beginning "a farmer by kamma" were spoken. Therein, "by kamma" means by present volitional kamma that brings about the work of farming and so on.

Paṭiccasamuppādadassāti [P 3.0442] iminā paccayena evaṃ hotīti evaṃ paṭiccasamuppādadassāvino. Kammavipākakovidāti sammānāvamānārahakule kammavasena uppatti hoti, aññāpi hīnapaṇītatā hīnapaṇīte kamme vipaccamāne hotīti. Evaṃ kammavipākakusalā.

"Seers of dependent origination" (paṭiccasamuppādadassāvino) are those who see, "With this as condition, this comes to be." "Those skilled in kamma and its result" (kammavipākakovidā) means [they understand that] birth occurs in families worthy of respect or disrespect due to kamma, and that other inferior and superior states come to be when inferior and superior kamma ripens. Thus, they are skilled in kamma and its result.

Kammunā vattatīti gāthāya pana lokoti vā pajāti vā sattoti vā ekoyevattho, vacanamattabhedo. Purimapadena cettha “atthi brahmā mahābrahmā seṭṭho sajitā”ti diṭṭhiyā paṭisedho veditabbo. Kammunā hi tāsu tāsu gatīsu vattati loko, tassa ko sajitāti. Dutiyapadena “evaṃ kammunā nibbattopi ca pavattepi atītapaccuppannabhedena kammunā vattati, sukhadukkhāni paccanubhonto hīnapaṇītādibhedañca āpajjanto pavattatī”ti dasseti. Tatiyena tamevatthaṃ nigameti “evaṃ sabbathāpi kammanibandhanā sattā kammeneva baddhā hutvā pavattanti, na aññathā”ti. Catutthena tametthaṃ upamāya vibhāveti. Yathā hi rathassa yāyato āṇi nibandhanaṃ hoti, na tāya anibaddho yāti, evaṃ lokassa nibbattato ca pavattato ca kammaṃ nibandhanaṃ, na tena anibaddho nibbattati na pavattati.

In the verse 'By kamma the world turns,' the terms 'world,' 'progeny,' or 'beings' all have one and the same meaning; the difference is only in the word. By the first phrase, the refutation of the view, 'There is Brahmā, Mahābrahmā, the supreme, the creator,' should be understood. For it is by kamma that the world turns in those various destinations; who then is its creator? By the second phrase, it shows: 'Thus, having arisen by kamma, one also continues in the course of existence by kamma—distinguished as past and present—experiencing pleasure and pain and encountering distinctions such as inferior and superior.' By the third, it concludes that very meaning: 'Thus, in every way, beings are bound by kamma; being bound by kamma alone, they continue, not otherwise.' By the fourth, it clarifies this meaning with a simile: Just as for a moving chariot the linchpin is the binding, and it does not go unbound by it, so too for the world that is arising and continuing, kamma is the binding; unbound by it, one neither arises nor continues.

Idāni yasmā [P 3.0443] evaṃ kammanibandhano loko, tasmā seṭṭhena kammunā seṭṭhabhāvaṃ dassento tapenāti gāthādvayamāha. Tattha tapenāti dhutaṅgatapena. Brahmacariyenāti methunaviratiyā. Saṃyamenāti sīlena[V 3.0311]. Damenāti indriyadamena. Etenāti etena seṭṭhena parisuddhena brahmabhūtena kammunā brāhmaṇo hoti. Kasmā? Yasmā etaṃ brāhmaṇamuttamaṃ, yasmā etaṃ kammaṃ uttamo brāhmaṇaguṇoti vuttaṃ hoti. “Brahmāna”ntipi pāṭho. Ayaṃ panettha vacanattho – brahmaṃ ānetīti brahmānaṃ, brāhmaṇabhāvaṃ āvahatīti vuttaṃ hoti.

Now, since the world is thus bound by kamma, the Blessed One, wishing to show that the state of excellence is attained through excellent kamma, spoke the two verses beginning with 'By austerity.' Therein, 'by austerity' means by the austerity of the ascetic practices. 'By the holy life' means by abstention from sexual intercourse. 'By restraint' means by virtue. 'By taming' means by the taming of the senses. 'By this' means by this excellent, pure, sublime kamma one becomes a brahmin. Why? Because this is supreme for a brahmin, and because this kamma is the supreme quality of a brahmin; this is the intended meaning. There is also the reading 'brahmānaṃ.' Herein, this is the etymological explanation: 'It brings excellence' (brahmaṃ āneti), thus it is 'brahmānaṃ'; it brings about the state of a brahmin, this is the intended meaning.

Dutiyagāthāya [M 3.0302] santoti santakileso. Brahmā sakkoti brahmā ca sakko ca, yo evarūpo, so na kevalaṃ brāhmaṇo, atha kho brahmā ca sakko ca so vijānataṃ paṇḍitānaṃ, evaṃ vāseṭṭha, jānāhīti vuttaṃ hoti. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

In the second verse, 'santo' means one whose defilements are stilled. 'Brahmāsakko' means he is a Brahmā and a Sakka. A person of such a nature is not merely a brahmin, but indeed, for the wise who truly understand, he is a Brahmā and a Sakka. 'Vāseṭṭha, know this thus'; this is the intended meaning. The rest is clear everywhere.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Middle Length Discourses.

Vāseṭṭhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Vāseṭṭha Sutta is concluded.

9. Subhasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Subha Sutta

462. Evaṃ [V 3.0312] me sutanti subhasuttaṃ. Tattha todeyyaputtoti tudigāmavāsino todeyyabrāhmaṇassa putto. Ārādhako hotīti sampādako hoti paripūrako. Ñāyaṃ dhammanti kāraṇadhammaṃ. Kusalanti anavajjaṃ.

462. Thus have I heard—this is the Subha Sutta. Therein, 'the son of Todeyya' means the son of the brahmin Todeyya, a resident of Tudi village. 'He is an accomplisher' (ārādhako hoti) means he is one who brings to completion, one who fulfills. 'The right principle' (ñāyaṃ dhammaṃ) means the appropriate principle. 'Wholesome' (kusalaṃ) means faultless.

463. Micchāpaṭipattinti [P 3.0444] aniyyānikaṃ akusalapaṭipadaṃ. Sammāpaṭipattinti niyyānikaṃ kusalapaṭipadaṃ.

463. 'Wrong practice' (micchāpaṭipatti) means the unwholesome practice that does not lead to liberation. 'Right practice' (sammāpaṭipatti) means the wholesome practice that leads to liberation.

Mahaṭṭhantiādīsu mahantehi veyyāvaccakarehi vā upakaraṇehi vā bahūhi attho etthāti mahaṭṭhaṃ. Mahantāni nāmaggahaṇamaṅgalādīni kiccāni etthāti mahākiccaṃ. Idaṃ ajja kattabbaṃ, idaṃ sveti evaṃ mahantāni adhikārasaṅkhātāni adhikaraṇāni etthāti mahādhikaraṇaṃ. Bahūnaṃ kamme yuttappayuttatāvasena pīḷāsaṅkhāto mahāsamārambho etthāti mahāsamārambhaṃ. Gharāvāsakammaṭṭhānanti gharāvāsakammaṃ. Evaṃ sabbavāresu attho veditabbo. Kasikamme cettha naṅgalakoṭiṃ ādiṃ katvā upakaraṇānaṃ pariyesanavasena mahaṭṭhatā, vaṇijjāya yathāṭhitaṃyeva bhaṇḍaṃ gahetvā parivattanavasena appaṭṭhatā veditabbā. Vipajjamānanti avuṭṭhiativuṭṭhiādīhi kasikammaṃ, maṇisuvaṇṇādīsu acchekatādīhi ca vaṇijjakammaṃ appaphalaṃ hoti, mūlacchedampi pāpuṇāti. Vipariyāyena sampajjamānaṃ mahapphalaṃ cūḷantevāsikassa viya.

In terms such as 'of great affair' (mahaṭṭhaṃ): because there is great need for many services or many implements, it is called 'of great affair'. Because there are many duties such as naming ceremonies, it is called 'of great duty' (mahākiccaṃ). Because there are many great administrative tasks, known as 'adhikāra', such as 'this must be done today, this must be done tomorrow', it is called 'of great administration' (mahādhikaraṇaṃ). Because there is a great exertion, known as affliction, by way of being much engaged in the work of many, it is called 'of great undertaking' (mahāsamārambhaṃ). 'The householder's sphere of work' (gharāvāsakammaṭṭhānaṃ) means the work of a householder. The meaning should be understood thus in all these phrases. Herein, in the case of farming, the state of being 'of great affair' is to be understood by way of seeking out equipment, beginning with the plowshare and so on. In the case of trade, the state of being 'of little affair' is to be understood by way of taking goods as they are and exchanging them. When failing (vipajjamānaṃ), farming yields little fruit due to drought, excessive rain, and so on; and the work of trade yields little fruit due to lack of skill regarding gems, gold, and so on, and one can even lose one's capital. Conversely, when succeeding, it is of great fruit, like for a junior disciple.

464. Evameva khoti yathā kasikammaṭṭhānaṃ vipajjamānaṃ appaphalaṃ hoti, evaṃ gharāvāsakammaṭṭhānampi. Akatakalyāṇo hi kālaṃ katvā niraye [M 3.0303] nibbattati. Mahādattasenāpati nāma kireko brāhmaṇabhatto ahosi, tassa maraṇasamaye nirayo upaṭṭhāsi. So brāhmaṇehi “kiṃ passasī”ti vutto? Lohitagharanti āha. Brahmaloko bho esoti. Brahmaloko nāma bho kahanti? Uparīti. Mayhaṃ heṭṭhā upaṭṭhātīti. Kiñcāpi heṭṭhā upaṭṭhāti[P 3.0445], tathāpi uparīti kālaṃ katvā niraye nibbatto. “Iminā amhākaṃ yaññe doso dinno”ti sahassaṃ gahetvā [V 3.0313] nīharituṃ adaṃsu. Sampajjamānaṃ pana mahapphalaṃ hoti. Katakalyāṇo hi kālaṃ katvā sagge nibbattati. Sakalāya guttilavimānakathāya dīpetabbaṃ. Yathā pana taṃ vaṇijjakammaṭṭhānaṃ vipajjamānaṃ appaphalaṃ hoti, evaṃ sīlesu aparipūrakārino anesanāya yuttassa pabbajjākammaṭṭhānampi. Evarūpā hi neva jhānādisukhaṃ na saggamokkhaṃ labhati. Sampajjamānaṃ pana mahapphalaṃ hoti. Sīlāni hi pūretvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhento arahattampi pāpuṇāti.

464. Indeed, it is just so: just as the occupation of farming yields little fruit when it fails, so too does the householder's sphere of work. For one who has done no good deeds, upon dying, is reborn in hell. It is said there was a certain general, Mahādatta, who was a patron of brahmins. At the time of his death, hell appeared to him. When asked by the brahmins, 'What do you see?' he said, 'A house of blood.' They said, 'Sir, that is the Brahma-world.' 'Sirs, where is this Brahma-world?' he asked. 'It is above,' they replied. 'But to me, it appears below,' he said. The brahmins insisted, 'Even though it appears below, it is nevertheless above.' Then he died and was reborn in hell. Saying, 'This man has brought blame upon our sacrifice,' the brahmins gave a thousand to have his body removed from the house. But when it succeeds, it is of great fruit. For one who has done good deeds, upon dying, is reborn in heaven. This should be illustrated with the entire story of the Guttila celestial mansion. Furthermore, just as the occupation of trade yields little fruit when it fails, so too does the sphere of work of the renunciant who does not fulfill the moral precepts and is engaged in wrong livelihood. For such a person attains neither the bliss of jhāna and so on, nor heaven and liberation. But when it succeeds, it is of great fruit. For by fulfilling the moral precepts and developing insight, one can even attain Arahantship.

Brāhmaṇā, bho gotamoti idha kiṃ pucchāmīti pucchati? Brāhmaṇā vadanti – “pabbajito ime pañca dhamme pūretuṃ samattho nāma natthi, gahaṭṭhova pūretī”ti. Samaṇo pana gotamo – “gihissa vā ahaṃ māṇava pabbajitassa vā”ti punappunaṃ vadati, neva pabbajitaṃ muñcati, mayhameva pucchaṃ maññe na sallakkhetīti cāgasīsena pañca dhamme pucchāmīti pucchati. Sace te agarūti sace tuyhaṃ yathā brāhmaṇā paññapenti, tathā idha bhāsituṃ bhāriyaṃ na hoti, yadi na koci aphāsukabhāvo hoti, bhāsassūti attho. Na kho me, bhoti kiṃ sandhāyāha? Paṇḍitapaṭirūpakānañhi santike kathetuṃ dukkhaṃ hoti, te pade pade akkhare akkhare dosameva vadanti. Ekantapaṇḍitā pana kathaṃ sutvā sukathitaṃ pasaṃsanti, dukkathite pāḷipadaatthabyañjanesu [P 3.0446] yaṃ yaṃ virujjhati, taṃ taṃ ujuṃ katvā denti. Bhagavatā ca sadiso ekantapaṇḍito nāma natthi, tenāha “na kho me, bho gotama, garu, yatthassu bhavanto vā nisinno bhavantarūpo vā”ti. Saccanti vacīsaccaṃ. Tapanti tapacariyaṃ. Brahmacariyanti methunaviratiṃ. Ajjhenanti mantagahaṇaṃ. Cāganti āmisapariccāgaṃ.

He asks, thinking, 'What should I ask here?' The brahmins say: 'There is no one gone forth who is capable of fulfilling these five things; only a householder fulfills them.' But the ascetic Gotama repeatedly says, 'Whether for a householder, young man, or for one gone forth,' not exempting the one gone forth. Thinking, 'It seems he was addressing me, but I did not take note,' he then thinks, 'I will ask about the five things, beginning with generosity,' and so he asks. 'If it is not burdensome for you' (sace te agarū) means: 'If it is not too heavy a task for you to speak here in the way that the brahmins declare, if there is no discomfort, then please speak.' This is the meaning. In reference to what did he say, 'It is no burden for me, sir'? Because it is difficult to speak in the presence of those who only seem wise; at every word, at every syllable, they speak only of faults. But those who are truly wise, having heard a statement, praise what is well-spoken. In what is poorly spoken, whatever is contradictory in the Pali text, the words, the meaning, or the phrasing, they correct it and present it straightened out. And there is no one who is truly wise equal to the Blessed One. Therefore, he said: 'It is no burden for me, venerable Gotama, where the venerable one is seated, or one like the venerable one.' 'Truth' (saccaṃ) means verbal truth. 'Austerity' (tapaṃ) means the austere practice of fire-worship. 'The holy life' (brahmacariyaṃ) means abstinence from sexual intercourse. 'Study' (ajjhenaṃ) means learning the sacred texts. 'Generosity' (cāgaṃ) means the relinquishing of material things.

466. Pāpito bhavissatīti. Ajānanabhāvaṃ pāpito bhavissati. Etadavocāti bhagavatā andhaveṇūpamāya niggahito taṃ paccāharituṃ asakkonto yathā nāma dubbalasunakho migaṃ uṭṭhapetvā sāmikassa abhimukhaṃ [M 3.0304] katvā sayaṃ apasakkati, evamevaṃ ācariyaṃ apadisanto evaṃ “brāhmaṇo”tiādivacanaṃ avoca. Tattha pokkharasātīti idaṃ tassa nāmaṃ, “pokkharasāyī”tipi vuccati. Tassa kira kāyo setapokkharasadiso devanagare ussāpitarajatatoraṇaṃ viya sobhati, sīsaṃ panassa kāḷavaṇṇaindanīlamayaṃ viya, massupi candamaṇḍale kāḷamegharāji viya khāyati, akkhīni nīluppalasadisāni, nāsā rajatapanāḷikā viya suvaṭṭitā suparisuddhā, hatthapādatalāni ceva mukhañca katalākhārasaparikammaṃ [V 3.0314] viya sobhati. Ativiya sobhaggappatto brāhmaṇassa attabhāvo. Arājake ṭhāne rājānaṃ kātuṃ yuttamimaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ, evamesa sassiriko, iti naṃ pokkharasadisattā “pokkharasātī”ti [P 3.0447] sañjānanti, pokkhare pana so nibbatto, na mātukucchiyanti iti naṃ pokkhare sayitattā “pokkharasāyī”tipi sañjānanti. Opamaññoti upamaññagotto. Subhagavanikoti ukkaṭṭhāya subhagavanassa issaro. Hassakaṃyevāti hasitabbakaññeva. Nāmakaṃyevāti lāmakaṃyeva. Tadeva taṃ atthābhāvena rittakaṃ. Rittakattā ca tucchakaṃ. Idāni naṃ bhagavā sācariyakaṃ niggaṇhituṃ kiṃ pana māṇavātiādimāha.

466. “He will be caused to reach” means: he will be caused to reach a state of not knowing. Regarding “Thus he spoke”: Being rebuked by the Blessed One with the simile of the line of blind men and being unable to refute it, just as a weak dog, having roused a deer, makes it face its master and then retreats itself, even so, he, referring to his teacher, spoke the words beginning with “This brahmin...”. Therein, Pokkharasāti is his name; he is also called Pokkharasāyī. His body, it is said, was like a white lotus, shining like a raised silver archway in a celestial city. His head, moreover, was like a dark-colored sapphire; his mustache, too, appeared like a streak of black clouds against the moon; his eyes were like blue water lilies; his nose was well-rounded and perfectly pure, like a silver tube; and the palms of his hands, the soles of his feet, and his face shone as if treated with lac-dye. The brahmin's person was exceedingly splendid. This brahmin was fit to be made a king in a place without a king; so glorious was he. Therefore, because of his resemblance to a lotus, they know him as “Pokkharasāti.” Moreover, he was born on a lotus, not in a mother's womb; therefore, because he lay on a lotus, they also know him as “Pokkharasāyī.” “Opamañño” means he was of the Upamañña clan. “Subhagavaniko” means he was the lord of the Subhagavana in Ukkaṭṭhā. “Hassakaṃyeva” means just fit to be laughed at. “Lāmakaṃyeva” means just something base. That very thing is empty, being devoid of meaning. And because it is empty, it becomes worthless. Now, in order to rebuke him together with his teacher, the Blessed One said the words beginning with, “What then, young man?”

467. Tattha katamā nesaṃ seyyoti katamā vācā tesaṃ seyyo, pāsaṃsataroti attho. Sammuccāti sammutiyā lokavohārena. Mantāti tulayitvā pariggaṇhitvā. Paṭisaṅkhāyāti jānitvā. Atthasaṃhitanti kāraṇanissitaṃ. Evaṃ santeti lokavohāraṃ amuñcitvā tulayitvā jānitvā kāraṇanissitaṃ katvā kathitāya seyyabhāve sati. Āvutoti āvarito. Nivutoti nivārito. Ophuṭoti onaddho. Pariyonaddhoti paliveṭhito.

467. Therein, “which of these is better?” means: which speech of theirs is better, more praiseworthy? This is the meaning. “Sammuccā” means by convention, by worldly usage. “Mantā” means having weighed, having comprehended. “Paṭisaṅkhāya” means having known. “Atthasaṃhitaṃ” means based on reason. “Evaṃ sante” means: this being so, when there is a better state for speech that is spoken without abandoning worldly usage, after having weighed, known, and made it based on reason. “Āvuto” means obstructed. “Nivuto” means prevented. “Ophuṭo” means bound up. “Pariyonaddho” means enveloped.

468. Gadhitotiādīni vuttatthāneva. Sace taṃ, bho gotama, ṭhānanti sace etaṃ kāraṇamatthi. Svāssāti [P 3.0448] dhūmachārikādīnaṃ abhāvena so assa aggi accimā ca vaṇṇimā ca pabhassaro cāti. Tathūpamāhaṃ māṇavāti tappaṭibhāgaṃ ahaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yatheva hi tiṇakaṭṭhupādānaṃ paṭicca jalamāno aggi dhūmachārikaṅgārānaṃ atthitāya sadoso hoti[M 3.0305], evamevaṃ pañca kāmaguṇe paṭicca uppannā pīti jātijarābyādhimaraṇasokādīnaṃ atthitāya sadosā. Yathā pana pariccattatiṇakaṭṭhupādāno dhūmādīnaṃ abhāvena parisuddho, evamevaṃ lokuttarajjhānadvayasampayuttā pīti jātiādīnaṃ abhāvena parisuddhāti attho.

468. The words beginning with “Gadhito” have the meaning already stated. “Sace taṃ, bho gotama, ṭhānaṃ” means: if this cause exists. “Svāssa” means: in the absence of smoke, ash, and so on, that fire would be flaming, colorful, and radiant. “Tathūpamāhaṃ, māṇava” means: I am comparable to that. This is what is meant: Just as a fire burning in dependence on the fuel of grass and sticks is defiled by the presence of smoke, ash, and embers, even so, the joy that arises in dependence on the five strands of sensual pleasure is defiled by the presence of birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, and so on. And just as a fire for which the fuel of grass and sticks has been abandoned is pure in the absence of smoke and so on, even so, the joy associated with the two supramundane jhānas is pure in the absence of birth and so on. This is the meaning.

469. Idāni ye te brāhmaṇehi cāgasīsena pañca dhammā paññattā, tepi yasmā pañceva hutvā na niccalā tiṭṭhanti, anukampājātikena saddhiṃ cha āpajjanti. Tasmā taṃ dosaṃ dassetuṃ ye te māṇavātiādimāha. Tattha anukampājātikanti anukampāsabhāvaṃ.

469. Now, regarding the five qualities declared by the brahmins with generosity as the foremost: since they do not remain fixed as only five, but become six together with that which is of the nature of compassion, therefore, to point out that fault, He said the words beginning with, “Those qualities, young man...”. Therein, “anukampājātikaṃ” means having the nature of compassion.

Kattha bahulaṃ samanupassasīti idaṃ bhagavā yasmā – “esa ime pañca dhamme pabbajito paripūretuṃ [V 3.0315] samattho nāma natthi, gahaṭṭho paripūretī”ti āha, tasmā – “pabbajitova ime pūreti, gahaṭṭho pūretuṃ samattho nāma natthī”ti teneva mukhena bhaṇāpetuṃ pucchati.

The Blessed One asked this question, “Where do you mostly observe this?”, because he had said, “There is no one gone forth who is capable of perfecting these five qualities; a householder perfects them.” Therefore, He asks in order to make him state from his very own mouth that “It is only the one gone forth who perfects these qualities; a householder is not capable of perfecting them.”

Na satataṃ samitaṃ saccavādītiādīsu gahaṭṭho aññasmiṃ asati vaḷañjanakamusāvādampi karotiyeva, pabbajitā asinā sīse chijjantepi dve kathā na kathenti. Gahaṭṭho ca antotemāsamattampi sikkhāpadaṃ rakkhituṃ na sakkoti, pabbajito niccameva tapassī sīlavā tapanissitako hoti. Gahaṭṭho māsassa aṭṭhadivasamattampi uposathakammaṃ [P 3.0449] kātuṃ na sakkoti, pabbajitā yāvajīvaṃ brahmacārino honti. Gahaṭṭho ratanasuttamaṅgalasuttamattampi potthake likhitvā ṭhapeti, pabbajitā niccaṃ sajjhāyanti. Gahaṭṭho salākabhattampi akhaṇḍaṃ katvā dātuṃ na sakkoti, pabbajitā aññasmiṃ asati kākasunakhādīnampi piṇḍaṃ denti, bhaṇḍaggāhakadaharassapi patte pakkhipantevāti evamattho daṭṭhabbo. Cittassāhametenti ahaṃ ete pañca dhamme mettacittassa parivāre vadāmīti attho.

Regarding the words beginning with “Not constantly, not perpetually a truth-speaker”: A householder, even when no serious falsehood is involved, will still engage in conventional lying; but those who have gone forth, even if their heads were being cut off with a sword, would not speak duplicitously. A householder is unable to keep the training rules even for the three months of the rains-retreat; but one who has gone forth is always an ascetic, virtuous, and reliant on austerity. A householder is unable to perform the Uposatha observance even for eight days a month; but those who have gone forth are celibate for life. A householder merely writes down texts like the Ratana Sutta and the Maṅgala Sutta in a book and sets it aside; but those who have gone forth constantly recite them. A householder is unable to give even a ticket-meal without interruption; but those who have gone forth, when there is no other recipient, give almsfood even to crows and dogs, and will even place it in the bowl of a young novice who carries the requisites. In this way the meaning should be understood. “Cittassāhamete” means: I declare these five qualities to be the retinue of a mind of loving-kindness. This is the meaning.

470. Jātavaddhoti jāto ca vaḍḍhito ca. Yo hi kevalaṃ tattha jātova hoti, aññattha vaḍḍhito, tassa samantā gāmamaggā na sabbaso paccakkhā honti, tasmā jātavaddhoti āha. Jātavaddhopi hi yo ciraṃ nikkhanto, tassa na sabbaso paccakkhā honti, tasmā tāvadeva avasaṭanti āha, taṃkhaṇameva nikkhantanti attho. Dandhāyitattanti “ayaṃ [M 3.0306] nu kho maggo ayaṃ na nu kho”ti kaṅkhāvasena cirāyitattaṃ. Vitthāyitattanti yathā sukhumaṃ atthajātaṃ sahasā pucchitassa kassaci sarīraṃ thaddhabhāvaṃ gaṇhāti, evaṃ thaddhabhāvagahaṇaṃ. Natvevāti iminā sabbaññutaññāṇassa appaṭihatabhāvaṃ dasseti. Tassa hi purisassa mārāvaṭṭanādīnaṃ vasena siyā ñāṇassa paṭighāto, tena so dandhāyeyya vā vitthāyeyya vā, sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ pana appaṭihataṃ, na sakkā tassa kenaci antarāyo kātunti dīpeti.

470. “Jātavaddho” means both born and grown up. For one who is merely born there but has grown up elsewhere, the village paths all around are not entirely apparent to him. Therefore, He said, “jātavaddho.” Indeed, even for one who was born and grew up there but has been gone for a long time, the paths are not entirely apparent to him; hence it is said, “tāvadeva avasaṭanti”—the meaning is, he has left at that very moment. “Dandhāyitattaṃ” refers to the state of being slow on account of doubt, thinking, “Is this the path, or is this not the path?” “Vitthāyitattaṃ” means the state of stiffness, just as when someone is suddenly asked about a subtle matter, their body assumes a state of stiffness. “Natveva” demonstrates the unobstructed nature of the omniscient knowledge. For that person, there might be an obstruction to his knowledge on account of things such as Māra’s wiles; because of that, he might be slow or become stiff. But the omniscient knowledge is unobstructed—it clarifies that no one can create any obstacle to it.

Seyyathāpi māṇava balavā saṅkhadhamoti ettha [P 3.0450] balavāti balasampanno. Saṅkhadhamoti saṅkhadhamako. Appakasirenāti akicchena adukkhena. Dubbalo hi saṅkhadhamako saṅkhaṃ dhamantopi na sakkoti catasso disā sarena viññāpetuṃ, nāssa saṅkhasaddo sabbaso phari. Balavato pana vipphāriko hoti, tasmā balavāti āha. Mettāya cetovimuttiyāti ettha mettāyāti vutte upacāropi [V 3.0316] appanāpi vaṭṭati, cetovimuttiyāti vutte pana appanāva vaṭṭati. Yaṃ pamāṇakataṃ kammanti pamāṇakataṃ kammaṃ nāma kāmāvacaraṃ vuccati, appamāṇakataṃ kammaṃ nāma rūpārūpāvacaraṃ. Tesupi idha brahmavihārakammaññeva adhippetaṃ. Tañhi pamāṇaṃ atikkamitvā odhisakaanodhisaka disāpharaṇavasena vaḍḍhetvā katattā appamāṇakatanti vuccati. Na taṃ tatrāvasissati, na taṃ tatrāvatiṭṭhatīti taṃ kāmāvacarakammaṃ tasmiṃ rūpārūpāvacarakamme na ohīyati na tiṭṭhati. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Kāmāvacarakammaṃ tassa rūpārūpāvacarakammassa antarā laggituṃ vā ṭhātuṃ vā rūpārūpāvacarakammaṃ pharitvā pariyādiyitvā attano okāsaṃ gahetvā patiṭṭhātuṃ vā na sakkoti, atha kho rūpārūpāvacarakammameva kāmāvacaraṃ mahogho viya parittaudakaṃ pharitvā pariyādiyitvā attano okāsaṃ gahetvā tiṭṭhati, tassa vipākaṃ paṭibāhitvā sayameva brahmasahabyataṃ upanetīti. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

“Just as, young man, a strong conch blower”—here, ‘strong’ means endowed with physical strength. ‘Conch blower’ means one who blows the conch. ‘With little effort’ means without difficulty, without hardship. Indeed, a weak conch blower, even when blowing the conch, cannot make the sound known in the four directions; the sound of his conch does not spread everywhere. But for a strong one, it is far-reaching—therefore, He said, ‘strong.’ In “liberation of mind through loving-kindness”—here, when ‘loving-kindness’ is said, both access concentration and absorption concentration are suitable. But when ‘liberation of mind’ is said, only absorption concentration is suitable. “That kamma which is limited”—what is called limited kamma is said to be kamma of the sense-sphere. What is called immeasurable kamma is said to be kamma of the form and formless spheres. Among those, here only the kamma of the divine abidings is intended. Indeed, because it is done by developing it, having transcended the limited kamma, by way of pervading the directions with and without limitation, it is called ‘immeasurable.’ “It does not remain there, it does not stay there” means: that sense-sphere kamma does not remain behind in, does not stay in that form and formless-sphere kamma. What is meant? The sense-sphere kamma is not able to cling to or stay within that form and formless-sphere kamma, nor is it able to pervade and overcome the form and formless-sphere kamma, and having taken its own opportunity, establish itself. Rather, it is the form and formless-sphere kamma itself that, like a great flood pervading and overwhelming a small amount of water, pervades and overwhelms the sense-sphere kamma, and having taken its own opportunity, it stands. Having obstructed the result of that sense-sphere kamma, it is itself that leads to companionship with Brahmā. This is what is meant. The rest is clear everywhere.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

The Commentary on the Middle Length Discourses, Papañcasūdanī.

Subhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Subha Sutta is completed.

10. Saṅgāravasuttavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Saṅgārava Sutta

473. Evaṃ [V 3.0317][P 3.0451][M 3.0307] me sutanti saṅgāravasuttaṃ. Tattha cañcalikappeti evaṃnāmake gāme. Abhippasannāti aveccappasādavasena pasannā. Sā kira sotāpannā ariyasāvikā bhāradvājagottassa brāhmaṇassa bhariyā. So brāhmaṇo pubbe kālena kālaṃ brāhmaṇe nimantetvā tesaṃ sakkāraṃ karoti. Imaṃ pana brāhmaṇiṃ gharaṃ ānetvā abhirūpāya mahākulāya brāhmaṇiyā cittaṃ kopetuṃ asakkonto brāhmaṇānaṃ sakkāraṃ kātuṃ nāsakkhi. Atha naṃ brāhmaṇā diṭṭhadiṭṭhaṭṭhāne – “nayidāni tvaṃ brāhmaṇaladdhiko, ekāhampi brāhmaṇānaṃ sakkāraṃ na karosī”ti nippīḷenti. So gharaṃ āgantvā brāhmaṇiyā tamatthaṃ ārocetvā – “sace, bhoti ekadivasaṃ mukhaṃ rakkhituṃ sakkuṇeyyāsi, brāhmaṇānaṃ ekadivasaṃ bhikkhaṃ dadeyya”nti āha. Tuyhaṃ deyyadhammaṃ ruccanakaṭṭhāne dehi, kiṃ mayhaṃ etthāti. So brāhmaṇe nimantetvā appodakaṃ pāyāsaṃ pacāpetvā gharañca sujjhāpetvā āsanāni paññāpetvā brāhmaṇe nisīdāpesi. Brāhmaṇī mahāsāṭakaṃ nivāsetvā kaṭacchuṃ gahetvā parivisantī dussakaṇṇake pakkhalitvā “brāhmaṇe parivisāmī”ti saññampi akatvā āsevanavasena sahasā satthārameva anussaritvā udānaṃ udānesi.

473. The Saṅgārava Sutta begins with 'Thus have I heard.' Therein, 'at Cañcalikappa' means in a village so named. 'Deeply devoted' means devoted by way of unwavering confidence. She, it is said, was a noble female disciple, a stream-enterer, the wife of a brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan. That brahmin would previously, from time to time, invite brahmins and make offerings to them. But after bringing this brahmin woman home, being unable to disturb the mind of this exceedingly beautiful brahmin woman of high birth, he was unable to make offerings to the brahmins. Then, other brahmins, in whatever place they saw him, would oppress him, saying, 'Now you are not one who holds the views of brahmins; you do not make offerings to the brahmins even for a single day!' Having come home, he related that matter to the brahmin woman and said, 'Madam, if you could guard your mouth for one day, I would give a meal to the brahmins for one day.' She said, 'Give your gift-offering in a place that pleases you. In this, what is it to me?' He invited the brahmins, had a thick milk-porridge prepared, had the house cleaned, had seats prepared, and had the brahmins seated. The brahmin woman, having put on a fine cloth and taking a ladle, while serving, stumbled on the corner of her garment, and without even the perception 'I am serving the brahmins,' through the force of habit, she suddenly recollected the Teacher and uttered an inspired exclamation.

Brāhmaṇā udānaṃ sutvā “ubhatopakkhiko [P 3.0452] esa samaṇassa gotamassa sahāyo, nāssa deyyadhammaṃ gaṇhissāmā”ti kupitā bhojanāni chaḍḍetvā nikkhamiṃsu. Brāhmaṇo – “nanu paṭhamaṃyeva taṃ avacaṃ ‘ajjekadivasaṃ mukhaṃ rakkheyyāsī’ti, ettakaṃ te khīrañca taṇḍulādīni ca nāsitānī”ti ativiya kopavasaṃ upagato – “evameva panāyaṃ vasalī yasmiṃ vā tasmiṃ vā tassa muṇḍakassa samaṇassa vaṇṇaṃ bhāsati, idāni tyāhaṃ vasali tassa satthuno vādaṃ āropessāmī”ti āha. Atha naṃ brāhmaṇī “gaccha tvaṃ, brāhmaṇa, gantvā vijānissasī”ti vatvā “na khvāhaṃ taṃ, brāhmaṇa, passāmi sadevake loke…pe… vādaṃ āropeyyā”tiādimāha. So satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā –

Hearing the inspired exclamation, the brahmins became angry, saying, 'This one is partisan to both sides, a companion of the ascetic Gotama. We will not accept his gift-offering.' They threw down their food and departed. The brahmin, having become exceedingly overcome by anger, said, 'Did I not tell you beforehand, “Guard your mouth for today”? You have wasted so much milk and rice and other things!' He then said, 'Furthermore, this outcaste woman just praises that shaven-headed ascetic in any place whatsoever. Now, you outcaste, I will bring a charge against that teacher of yours!' Then the brahmin woman said to him, 'Go, brahmin. Having gone, you will find out.' And she said, 'Brahmin, I do not see anyone in this world with its devas… who could bring a charge against him,' and so on. He approached the Teacher and—

“Kiṃsu [V 3.0318][M 3.0308] chetvā sukhaṃ seti, kiṃsu chetvā na socati;

Kissassu ekadhammassa, vadhaṃ rocesi gotamā”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.187) –

“Having cut off what does one sleep soundly? Having cut off what does one not grieve? The slaying of what one thing do you approve of, Gotama?”

Pañhaṃ pucchi. Satthā āha –

He asked the question. The Teacher said:

“Kodhaṃ chetvā sukhaṃ seti, kodhaṃ chetvā na socati;

Kodhassa visamūlassa, madhuraggassa brāhmaṇa;

Vadhaṃ ariyā pasaṃsanti, tañhi chetvā na socatī”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.187) –

“Having cut off anger, one sleeps soundly; having cut off anger, one does not grieve. O brahmin, the slaying of anger, with its poisoned root and honeyed tip—this the noble ones praise. For having cut that off, one does not grieve.”

Pañhaṃ kathesi. So pabbajitvā arahattaṃ patto. Tasseva kaniṭṭhabhātā akkosakabhāradvājo nāma “bhātā me pabbajito”ti sutvā bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā akkositvā bhagavatā vinīto pabbajitvā arahattaṃ patto. Aparo tassa kaniṭṭho sundarikabhāradvājo nāma. Sopi bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā pañhaṃ pucchitvā vissajjanaṃ sutvā pabbajitvā arahattaṃ patto. Aparo tassa kaniṭṭho piṅgalabhāradvājo nāma. So pañhaṃ pucchitvā pañhabyākaraṇapariyosāne pabbajitvā arahattaṃ patto. Saṅgāravo [P 3.0453] māṇavoti ayaṃ tesaṃ sabbakaniṭṭho tasmiṃ divase brāhmaṇehi saddhiṃ ekabhattagge nisinno. Avabhūtāvāti avaḍḍhibhūtā avamaṅgalabhūtāyeva. Parabhūtāvāti vināsaṃ pattāyeva. Vijjamānānanti vijjamānesu. Sīlapaññāṇanti sīlañca ñāṇañca na jānāsi.

He answered the question. Having gone forth, he attained arahantship. His younger brother, named Akkosaka Bhāradvāja, heard, 'My brother has gone forth,' approached the Blessed One, reviled him, was tamed by the Blessed One, went forth, and attained arahantship. Another younger brother of his was named Sundarika Bhāradvāja. He too approached the Blessed One, asked a question, heard the answer, went forth, and attained arahantship. Another younger brother of his was named Piṅgala Bhāradvāja. He asked a question, and at the conclusion of the explanation of the question, went forth and attained arahantship. 'Saṅgārava the young man'—this one was the youngest of them all; on that day he was seated at a single meal-hall with the brahmins. 'Avabhūtā' means having become unprosperous, having become inauspicious. 'Parabhūtā' means having met with destruction. 'Vijjamānānaṃ' means among those who exist. 'Sīlapaññāṇaṃ' means you do not know virtue and wisdom.

474. Diṭṭhadhammābhiññāvosānapāramippattāti diṭṭhadhamme abhiññāte imasmiññeva attabhāve abhijānitvā vositavosānā hutvā pāramīsaṅkhātaṃ sabbadhammānaṃ pārabhūtaṃ nibbānaṃ pattā mayanti vatvā ādibrahmacariyaṃ paṭijānantīti attho. Ādibrahmacariyanti brahmacariyassa ādibhūtā uppādakā janakāti evaṃ paṭijānantīti vuttaṃ hoti. Takkīti takkagāhī. Vīmaṃsīti vīmaṃsako, paññācāraṃ carāpetvā evaṃvādī. Tesāhamasmīti tesaṃ sammāsambuddhānaṃ ahamasmi aññataro.

474. 'Having attained the perfection of the conclusion of direct knowledge in the visible dhamma' means this: having specially known in this very existence the directly known dhammas, having become one for whom the conclusion is concluded, they declare, 'We have attained Nibbāna, which is called 'perfection' and is the further shore of all dhammas,' and thus they profess the beginning of the holy life. 'The beginning of the holy life' means it is said that they profess thus: 'We are the beginning, the producers, the generators of the holy life.' 'Takkī' means one who holds to reasoning. 'Vīmaṃsī' means an investigator; having engaged in the practice of wisdom, one speaks thus. 'Tesāhamasmi' means: I am one among those Perfectly Enlightened Ones.

485. Aṭṭhitavatanti [V 3.0319] aṭṭhitatapaṃ, assa padhānapadena saddhiṃ sambandho, tathā sappurisapadassa. Idañhi vuttaṃ hoti – bhoto gotamassa aṭṭhitapadhānavataṃ ahosi, sappurisapadhānavataṃ ahosīti. Atthi [P 3.0454] devāti [M 3.0309] puṭṭho samānoti idaṃ māṇavo “sammāsambuddho ajānantova pakāsesī”ti saññāya āha. Evaṃ santeti tumhākaṃ ajānanabhāve sante. Tucchaṃ musā hotīti tumhākaṃ kathā aphalā nipphalā hoti. Evaṃ māṇavo bhagavantaṃ musāvādena niggaṇhāti nāma. Viññunā purisenāti paṇḍitena manussena. Tvaṃ pana aviññutāya mayā byākatampi na jānāsīti dīpeti. Uccena sammatanti uccena saddena sammataṃ pākaṭaṃ lokasmiṃ. Adhidevāti susudārakāpi hi devā nāma honti, deviyo nāma honti devā pana adhidevā nāma, loke devo devīti laddhanāmehi manussehi adhikāti attho. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

485. 'Aṭṭhitavataṃ' means steadfast ascetic practice; its connection is with the word 'padhāna' (striving), and likewise with the word 'sappurisa' (virtuous person). For this is what is meant: 'The venerable Gotama had the practice of steadfast striving; he had the practice of striving of a virtuous person.' Regarding 'When asked, “Are there devas?”': the young man said this with the perception, 'The Perfectly Enlightened One declares this without knowing.' 'Evaṃ sante' means: while you are in a state of not knowing. 'It is empty and false' means: your speech is fruitless, without result. Thus the young man rebukes the Blessed One with a false accusation. 'By a wise person' means by an intelligent person. He indicates: 'But you, due to your lack of wisdom, do not understand even what has been explained by me.' 'Uccena sammataṃ' means agreed upon with a loud voice, manifest in the world. 'Adhideva' means: for even very young boys are called 'devas' and girls are called 'devīs', but celestial beings are called 'adhidevas'. The meaning is that they are superior to humans in the world who have obtained the names 'deva' or 'devī'. The rest is clear everywhere.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya

Saṅgāravasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Saṅgārava Sutta is concluded.

Pañcamavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Fifth Chapter is concluded.

Majjhimapaṇṇāsa-aṭṭhakathā niṭṭhitā.
